text:
The story has an excellent premise, as evinced by the extensive efforts of Square Enix to milk the universe of all its worth (spin-offs include
and even a movie,
among others). You start with Cloud Strife (employed as a mercenary) and long-time friend Tifa Lockheart as members of eco-terrorist group AVALANCHE, under the command of Barrett Wallace. The underlying belief of the group is that the planet's life energy is being consumed by Shinra Corporation's reactors, slowly but surely destroying the planet. The group organise attacks against the reactors in the belief they are saving the planet. These events are eventually dwarfed by a new threat to the planet: Sephiroth.
The game has done well over the years thanks to a whole plethora of reasons that help make it come alive, and it often stays alive in the minds of gamers long after players have experienced it. The engaging story, of which I have only touched upon here, is littered with so many twists and turns and shocking discoveries that you'll likely be dizzy with awesomeness by the end of it.
Gameplay is much the same as previous titles, using the standard random encounter mechanic we all know and love to initiate fights with monsters or people. Equipment is limited to one weapon and one armor at a time, but these can have various materia slots. Materia is crystallised Mako, or lifestream energy, and is the source of many abilities and enhancements characters can make use of in the game, not the least of which is magic spells, summons, auto-abilities and stat boosts. Materia can be levelled, and once mastered can spawn a duplicate materia, allowing much customisation and experimentation.
The game really is an emotional rollercoaster. The characters are a lot more fully realised than many of those in previous titles in the series - Barrett's concern for Marlene, Tifa's concern for Cloud ... even some of the Turks inspire our empathy at times (eg, Reno and Rude deciding they are 'off-duty' in regard to orders to search for Cloud, after working together briefly). Cloud's cross-dressing scene is good for a laugh. People are killed. Truths are learnt. A good game is a game that holds our attention, and that is what FFVII and its characters do as we strive to know more about what is happening and why. Indeed, the shock death of one of our own team members definitely added to the game's infamy. Most of you already know who I'm talking about. And perhaps because of this, Sephiroth is often lauded as one of, if not
, greatest game villain of all time. I know my own feelings are a mix of admiration and hate when I think of him.
The art style was a leap ahead in its time, but in today's world of newest releases it does have a dated feel to it, with chunky 3D graphics on par with much of the earliest games to implement 3D graphics. On the PC version little has changed, although it has been criticised for its lower quality graphics, installation and framerate problems. I did not experience any problems personally, and have come to not expect vast improvements in framerate from FF re-releases.
Some would say the PS version is more impressive - I myself cannot say as I never got around to playing that version. It does seem as though Square Enix has only done the bare minimum to get the game to work on PC - a trait shared by many FF PC ports, much to the disgust of expectant PC FF fans.
The music is excellent, but many of its most loved tracks have been reworked for
and it is these versions I enjoy the most, especially
As it happens, the FFVII version is also composer Nobuo Uematsu's favourite from the soundtrack, and his favourite battle theme from any Final Fantasy game.
Some cons I believe are worth noting:
- Cheap final boss fight, impossible to lose
- A minority might find the plot very confusing to grasp as more facts are brought to light
I would have listed the game's linear nature, but this isn't so bad when you consider it as a trade-off for good story. Also to make up for this are the game's various mini games, helping to beef up an already impressive game. There is a barrel pushing game in the Sector 5 Church, a 'squats' mini game at the Wall Market, a sneaking game in the Shinra Building, in addition to various mini games that can be played at the Gold Saucer, including G Bike, the Fort Condor strategy minigame, and of course the chocobo racing game, among others. Some of these are easy while others can be hard.
With the inclusion of Steam achievements, there is plenty for the aspiring completionist to aim for. Be sure to add this piece of gaming history to your library, you won't regret it.

I haven't played a GC game before, so I was not coming in expecting any nostalgia factor, nor did I have any previous installments to compare it to.  That being said, I enjoy GC3.  I find it to have great depth, content, mechanics and graphics.  I like it more so than any other Space 4x I have played or own, in fact.

So why is that?
So hear me out, don't just leave a thumb down, I hope you'll be willing to listen even if you like the game.
Well, here's some points:
I love good Pixelart...I really do, but this mostly isn't good one.
The artists are using the same colour for too many pixels on many images, making it look very very old fashioned. Some look good but too many don't
If you wanna see really good Pixelart go check out Stardew Valley, Nuclear Throne, or Starbound, they all have their own take on Pixelart and they all look gorgeous. Sadly, CotND doesn't.
The game forces you to make quick decisions.
There is not a single time you can have a break, except for maybe switching between two tiles in an empty room.
For a game that mostly has a puzzle take on Roguelikes this isn't good, since you barely can concentrate and are gonna panic move a lot which just leads to unnecessary frustration.
If you wanna see difficult, but non-frustrating games check out the Dark Souls series, Nuclear Throne, Super Meat Boy, Geometry Dash, The Witness...and many many more, there seriously is a lot of them!
The tutorial doesn't show you how to use items and how the gold multiplier works, enemy health and strength aren't shown, so you either have to remember or guess. Items in the shop aren't explained, so you never know what you're buying, neither are alternative gamemodes.
The game really needs to get a little more polished.
Let's compare to other Roguelikes.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth has a huge amount of different and unique items, enemies, playable characters and gamemodes, also a lot of them you have to unlock through certain actions.
Rogue Legacy has a big Skilltree, many character traits and a fluent progress system.
Faster than Light has a huge learning curve, and also a big amount of upgrades and unlockables.
Nuclear Throne got at least a decent amount of weapons, playable characters, character perks and secrets, but therefore it still beats CotND in almost every other cathegory and takes long enough to play through anyways, due to its difficulty.
So where's any of that in CotND? At least one thing should be worked out deeply.
other Roguelikes got great OST too.
Okhlos: Omega for example got way better one in my opinion and even other Roguelikes like The binding of Isaac, Dead Cells or Nuclear Throne can keep up with CotND
To Masterpiece Soundtracks like the ones of Dear Esther, Clannad, Rabi-Ribi or the Final Fantasy games it's not comparable at all and unlike them this is a music game!
There's simply better ones. Point. Ones where you don't have to solve a puzzle while keeping the Rhythm, ones where you're not feeling like a metronome after 5 minutes.
Check out Geometry Dash, Osu, DDR or Final Fantasy Theatrhythm...and guess what: Osu and DDR and Geometry Dash let you add your own music too.
In addition it's one of those games with a horrible DLC policy, I mean, the soundtrack (split among multiple DLC's) costs more than the actual game, who did get that idea?

But the combat,the voice acting,the characters,the graphics,the world,the enemies,the music,the leveling system,and anything else i forgot to mention,they were all amazing,and easily made up for my lack of interest in the story.
8/10

Stellaris is dry, slow, and addictively boring in the same way that Civilization is, yet for anyone who cherishes Star Trek (or any fan of sci-fi) and the occasional challenges and thrills of real-time strategy, Stellaris can be much more enjoyable. It's true that much of the game consists of driving a science ship around and text bubbles that are vaguely rewarding, but the real fun comes in the late game; your battered and veteran fleet pulls out a surprise win against a bitter enemy, securing your conquest; your attempts at forming a federation are stymied by a sudden mass invasion from a militaristic founder race; you unlock a technology that complety changes your strategy; etc. The more you can bury yourself in the lore that evolves in each game, the better the experience.

Though I've logged only 4 hours on this game, I am quite familiar with Red Alert 2 and other RTS games. Simply, EA has destroyed what was once a great franchise. The units themselves are woefully balanced with some units being destroyed instantly. The difficulty of the game is quite frustrating considering that the game itself is poorly scripted, as there are multiple bugs. I've had problems with units failing to complete their movement due to poor pathing. Some units will just stop if their path is momentarily blocked. Siege units are insanely powerful while infantry and many other units are simply irrelevant. It seems that the Soviets in particular lack any sort of meaningful anti air units as the Bullfrogs and MiGs have light armor values and can be decimated by units of other regions. Flak troopers may be cheap but without any ability to traverse water, there is essentially no sufficient anti air. The Scorpion unit of RA2 was completely removed, which were some of the best anti air units that the Soviets had at their disposal.
In addition, the campaign missions seem to be poorly designed. Just recently I played a mission in which the Soviet player had to assassinate the Emperor of the Rising Sun with a single Conscript. It seemed as illogical that there were areial units flying that failed to notice the enemy Conscript. As the mission continued, my base was assaulted by a wave of enemy tanks before any sort of player could mount a resistance force. The missions are boring and uninteresting. The acting and writing is subpar. The unit AI seems almost idiotic and inconsistent with some units agressively pursuing enemy units while other times standing their ground and just letting themselves be defeated.
In sum, I was wholeheartedly dissapoointed at this game. EA has (unsurprisingly) ruined another franchise. Just play RE2, which I still do. It may be older but at least it was well made in comparision to RE3, a♥♥♥♥♥♥game.

I'm gonna keep this pretty short.
If you like space 4X games, this game is for you. Just don't fall for the same trap that most of these negative reviews have in comparing a brand new title with games that have years of content update, expansions, and/or dlc behind them. I've been in on the ground floor for an awful lot of 4X game releases, and Stellaris has outperformed them on nearly every point, and in the ones it hasn't, I can point to a half dozen titles that its got the same features.
I'm fairly sure most of the negative reviews are from people coming from either other paradox games expecting this to be grand strategy and not 4X, or people who hear the hype but don't play 4X, or people that have been playing games that have been around for ages with lots of expansions, like Sins or GalCiv. (Yes, I count Galciv as being around for years, its been in EA for ages, and it was terrible at first imo, just like Civ5 was).
--------------
Does it have bugs? Yes of course. Its brand new, and it didnt have an Early Access period. Personally I count that as a good thing.
Are the bugs annoying? I don't really think so. Much like with Bethesda games, I find most of them to be amusing more than anything else when taken with a grain of salt.
Are there showstopper bugs? I've only found one, and that one hasnt repeated itself since the first hotfix, and I've never met anyone else who had it, so I'd honestly have to say 'no'.
And here I am with almost 100 hours played now. Its a fantastic new entry into the scifi 4X genre. (And don't let anyone try and tell you its Grand Strategy. This is Master of Orion / Endless Space on steroids, pure and simple.)
I enjoyed this game and would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a fun platformer with great atmosphere and a decent story.

So overall I would recommend this game. I just hope they don't do what they did to EU4 with dlc.

Farming Simulator isn't just a simulator for farming. It's THE simulator for farming. I've spent nearly 30 hours, on a farming game. It's that addicting. My mind is simply numb from the hours spent behind the wheel of the many tractors i've bought, the golf course lawns i've mowed, and the pallet crates i've dropped off.
This game isn't for anyone by any means. In fact, if you like fast-paced action, storylines, or engaging puzzles this game would definately not be for you. The game is better played with friends who would likely enjoy slow, time-consuming projects, and it just so happens there are few of us out there who are willing to enjoy that.
Not recommended for everyone, but simulator fans are going to enjoy it.

This review will only touch on the game breaking performance issues and the bugs.  Everything runs smooth on an Intel i7, GT 750, 16GB, and an SSD, UNTIL mid to late game.  Then there is just stuttering everywhere, its impossible to really do anything.  Add that on top of the fact that the AI for your own navy is just terrible.  Don't let your ships get "stuck" between two enemies.  It doesn't know what to do, gets confused, and just sits there.  You can't do anything but retreat which takes a bunch of hitpoints away from your overall health (hull).  Its terrible in the current state.
Hoping that they fix the issues, because the early game is extremely fun.  However the game was rushed without testing to make a buck, very disappointing.
Overall a very beautiful game, although a bit short. ABZU's stunning visuals make up for any flaws it contains. I would recommend for anyone that wants to see an underwater wonderland.

I admit I got this game while it was on sale but wish I bought it for full price. Don't judge it as a "furry" fandom type game all because the world has anthro animals in it. The game is just the same and care taken into it as any game with human characters.
- Beautiful world
The environments and backgrounds are stunning and lovely, giving each area a breath of fresh air. I had fun going back to other maps just to learn of secret rooms.
- Great Combo System
The combo system is spot on in my opinion, specially for keyboard users with minimun controls so anyone can pick it up and try all of the combos without having to master the game. Not many games like this are spot on for keyboard users but this one is for sure.
I had so much fun comboing the enemies and it never felt like a chore, you really feel the damage you are doing in every swing of your sword.
- No Material Grinding
The shop system is a  lovely touch, trade in a material you found and the shop will restock it over time, helping to lower the need to grind for materials so you can focus on the story.
- Beautiful Story
I was shocked and crying when I found out who Dust was, for ages I was curious from others reviews thinking it couldn't be any different then most cliche games have but I am so happy I was wrong. You really feel sorry for the characters including a few NPC's who you do quests for.
One of the more original plot-twists to a story I have seen in a while, specially for a video game.
- Funny Characters
This game is full of sad and funny characters all standing out from one another. I don't think I need to mention how Sassy Fidget can be while also being adorable. Some NPC's also have some lively comments to add into the humor of the game and make them appear more lively and not just there to be mere NPC's.
I really would recommend this to anyone, not just those who are into the Hack & Slash genre of games. It is really fun and well worth buying.

This game allowed me to create the Democratic Lizard People's Republic of Space Korea. After discovering modern Earth, my lizard people began covertly replacing world leaders and celebrities with lizard people lookalikes. It was going well until one of my agents fell in love with a human woman and ran off. The rogue agent then sent me an ultimatum. Leave Earth alone or else.
Well, the DLPRSK does not give in to threats so we narrowed his transmission down to a city block and utterly destroyed it with an orbital bombardment. We disseminated a cover story through the media that the city block was destroyed by an astroid impact. It seemed like the problem was solved. That is, until my agents started disappearing rapidly. It seems we did not kill rogue agent and he was going all Jason Bourne all over my infiltrators. I speculate that we might have inadvertantly killed his human mate instead of him.

Fear is one of those games that has a lasting memory. No, it didn't revolutionize the horror genre or provide an experience such that the FPS genre is better off as a whole, but it did enough things right with such a unique setting that I still remember nearly every level of this game almost 10 years later.
The combat in Fear, all things considered is actually pretty fantastic. The gunplay feels good and the enemy uses intelligent tactics most of the time to try and snuff you out.
The horror aspect of the game comes in bursts and segments the different action components of the game. While some of the horror comes from the sudden jump scares, there's really a lot to be said about how well the developers were able to build an atmosphere of terror and loneliness. The lighting and music are enough to keep you moving forward even though the hair on the back of your neck is sticking straight up.
The last part of this game that surprised me was how solid the story was. I was thoroughly enthralled with how focused this game directed you forward and how the set pieces were so interesting;I wasn't bored by the game's linearity or it's lack of choices.
While not on my top 10 list, F.E.A.R. is a game that every shooter fan should play through at least once

An interesting blend of the action, flight and strategy game genres where you try to fight off a virus infecting your computer from the inside. The game has a very retro/Tron feel to it.
You play as Flash Bios, a scandisk pilot who must transport Bits (small virus fighing programs) around the computers circuits to fight the virus infection while at the same time protecting the bits for enemy programs and preventing the main data stream from becoming infected.
There can also remove system bugs which work as both currency and a level up mechanic allowing you to upgrade your ship and also repurpose some parts of the system to create new bonuses such as bombs and health packs.
Overall a very fun game and well polished considering it is in early access,  The only downfall I can see at the present is while in early access you only have access to one zone (21 levels) with the remainiung 2 zones (40+ more levels) coming later in early access.
+ Very well polished for an Early Access game
+ Circuit board level layouts allow you to see how the virus will spread
+ Simple intuitive controls (Apart from raise and lower height)
- Only 1 Zone currently available

Bit Shifter is a fun and challenging action/strategy game within the genre of "hey, I'm part of a computer system,  fighting the virus" category.  You are "Flash Bios", a pilot that must fight the virus in a series of increasingly harder missions while flying a "scandisc" (ship), with the primary goal of preventing the virus from reaching the main data stream.  One of your primary resources are your deployable "bits" that fight the virus on the battleground of the circuit board while you fight using a growing arsenal of other tools aboard your ship while supporting and defending your bits.
Many games that came through greenlight have a good concept, but even after evolving never reach beyond "amateur" quality.  Bit Shifter easily exceeds that status, having solid core gameplay elements and the relatively well polished feel that is causing some players to mention their favorite N64 or Playstation games.  Plastic Games started with a goal closer to the retro look and feel of 16 bit gaming.  The current state has gone beyond that look, but still maintains a somewhat retro look and feel.
I have not completed the game, and may eventually update my review with a simple list of pros and cons, but so far it's just been a fun pastime.  As the game is still in early access I will post a couple of other constructive observations.  For one, the music is alright, but I would enjoy some options.  The controls work well for me, but as a mouse and keyboard player I am not entirely comfortable with flying my ship in the default settings.  Most notably I would  recommend players resetting the up (space bar) and down (Q) keybinds.
I sometimes experience a slight but noticeable "hang" in the loading screens before a mission, and the developer quickly responded to my bug report to indicate that they are aware of this.  It has not been a game killer at all.  I have completed 17 missions thus far during several game sessions, and on one occasion the screen did hang and crashed me to desktop, but this has never occurred within an actual mission, where I've yet to have any issues.
I have so far found the game play to be relatively simple in depth, but as I said, good action/strat fun of an old school type, and I've already played this game longer than most any green light graduate.  Well done Plastic Games, keep up the good work!

Bit Shifter captures all the rights feels when it comes to gaming. From the moment I started playing Bit Shifter, my mind felt like it was playing a classic N64 game but on my PC. It should be noted I mean that in the most praising of terms. The graphics, the gameplay, the controls, all feel wonderful and fun in this hybrid of Action/Strategy game. The mission is simple, clean out the virus by battling your way across the battlefield using soldiers, turrets, and other power ups such as bombs. Your soldiers clean the virus but cannot defend themselves, which leaves only you and towers to defend them. Needless to say Bit Shifter is a game that constantly keeps you busy. You're always fighting a battle on multiple encroaching fronts, this is what makes the game exciting and difficult. Throw in some bonus levels such as a collectathon and occasional boss fights and this game captures everything I would want in a game. It should be noted that for an Early Access game, Bit Shifter is very well put together and hardly has any bugs to speak of. This means the game has more room to grow in the features department, adding hopefully a little bit more complexity. Maybe different ship types, deeper customization, multiplayer, soldier types, more enemies, more powers. These idea would take already a great game and bring it up even higher. That being said, if you bought the game now and it never changed, that would be perfectly okay. The game is simple to grasp and becomes exciting and hectic fairly quickly. So if you are in the market for some fun, quick action that has a good mix of retro and modern designs. Check out Bit Shifter.

So Bit Shifter, Plastic Games first game they have ever made. How well does it hold up?
Surprisingly well actually, for an early access game anyhow.
So what is bit shifter. Well, imagine a world where everything is a pc part, program or tech pun(Reboot if you will). Now imaging you are a firefighting drop ship constantly flying around dealing with varius "fires" in the form of a Virus. On a base level, this seems very very simple, but it's really not. See your ship itself is  faily poor at dealing with these fires, but some of the equipment you carry with you are exceptional at dealing with this fire. One of those are little robots called bits that are exceptional at cleaning up the fire.
Bit Shifter is a game of pacing and resource management more so than anything. Anticipating where virus will spread to and stopping it before it makes you lose the level(by reaching  a massive river of data). Having your bitsa at the right place at the right time as well as having the right gear is very important.
So, what's wrong or needs fixed?
Well, the options menu is a  bit on the lacking side. The game supports a wide array of resulotion options  as well as draw distance, but nothing else. However it does have a colorblind mode, which I'm sure folks will appreciate. Maybe add more video options down the line would be nice. There is also some kind of  window minimizing UI bug in the game currently, but it only really occurs at the end of stages or when messing with options. The team is  currently trying to fix it.
The sound track is hit or miss, it doesn't personally bother me but techno/dubstep like beats is not everyones flavor of tea. Personal mileage may vary.
The game has entirely rebind-able keyboard controls and to its credit they work exceptionally well. However the only game pad it seems to support right now is the 360 pad, which is not rebind-able. The game also does not seem to support Logitech game pads at the moment as both of  mine had an absolute fit when using them IE buttons not working and the analog stick suddenly becoming the fire control. I would like to see more gamepad controls in the future, possibly more supported gamepads since I have dainty little girl hands and hate the over-sized behemoth that is the 360 pad with every fiber of my being.
So other nitpicks; the game looks fairly dated, but that is to be expected since well, indie game. The game looks like it would easily run on someones phone or a late ps1/early ps2 game. It doesn't really bother me  since I review far uglier games on a daily basis and the graphics are at least very clean. They don't get in the way of you doing your job and glitches are infrequent(such as bits walking through buildings for example).
My biggest problem with the game is  the lack of variety in enemies. The enemy that you will encounter the most are these little robot octorocks (at least that's what I call them) That spawn along the the path the virus takes/will take and attempt to shoot you down. On some stages these alone will be the bane of your existence, especially when in clusters of 4 or more. Other times not so much. They don't shoot all that fast, you can strafe slower than molasses on a  cold day and still dodge most of their fire and the damage they do when harassing your bits is pitiful; almost to the point where you can cheese them entirely by just fire and forgetting your bits, then swooping in and refiring them when they are damaged.
The game could definitely use some air to air harassment, say a corrupted scandisk(your ships name, told you it was punny) that attacks you on sight and harasses your bits. Making bis a little less godly might help as well since they can take an absolute mauling and still do their job incredibly well, often cleaning up large chunks of virus before the Stormtrooper aimlike octorocks eventually knock them over.
My other minor problem is the game is  on the short side, 20 stages and 1 boss stage which clocks in at around 3 hours on normal and maybe 5 to 8 hours on the hardest difficulty depending on personal operator headspace.
So is it worth your time and money is the real question. Well, yes. Personally the novel idea alone nearly carries the whole game in itself. The game is  not  perfect by any means, but it doesn't have to be. Fast paced gameplay, varied levels, personal gear loadouts and  collectible stuff for the super completionist out there all make for an enjoyable is a bit short experience.
I will say this though, it's a damn solid first try by this development team and easily light years ahead of all the zombie apocalypse crafting survival "we buy/steal our assets!" crap that SOMEHOW keeps getting through greenlight ahead of far more novel and original games.
The developer has also stated they are planning on adding more content to the game and I'm intrigued as to where the game will go from here, but even now, it's a very solid  first try.

Avoid like the plague, I don't know why I haven't posted a review before this but it's high time to do so, it is dull bordering on torture at times, repetitive, click heavy, uninvolving and heavily P2W.
The only actual thing to do in the game is to build/generate/produce ever more stuff for no real reason but to have more stuff to generate yet more stuff, nothing else really matters.
PvE Combat is very simplistic, it relies on proto-bugs and workarounds to play optimally requiring uncomfortable unintuitive puzzle level attack timing rather than any tactical thinking.
PvP combat is likewise simplistic and seemingly only intended as a resource dum, wholly based on rock paper scissors where you pick which of the three or so types of units to attack with against another of the three in a queue style system one after another.
It is a minimal effort cash cow intended to just rake in easy revenue, an interactive platform where people can spend money and watch counters and timers to dull their senses.
Don't misinterpret my rather vast playtime as a positive sign of a playable game, I idle a lot and notably nostalgia from the older titles is much of the reason I remained this long, in a futile sense hoping it would become something else more playable. Rather than a game it is more of a social experiment on how sad some OCD completionist players can be and how to take advantage of them.
I don't recommend this game to anyone, it's the shameful pinnacle of greedy hamster-wheel game design and should not be on Steam in my opinion.

As a fan of Red Alert 2, I was pretty hyped for this game. When the reviews came out, it was clear it wasn't the same experience as before, so I held off purchase. But when it came to sale for the low, low price of €3, I couldn't resist picking it up. It can't be a bad deal for that price, right?
Wrong. The inclusion of an Allied AI commander clearly supposed to carry the single player campaign in absence of a multiplayer buddy just doesn't work. It's frustrating to have a lot of your fun depend on a dead weight ally. Single player campaign play is frustrating, and only really worth it for the FMV cutscenes. The casting choices are great, including the awesome George Takei as the Japanese Emperor. But, on that subject, the faction of Japan just doesn't feel right in Red Alert, and tries to steal the spotlight from the established factions in a way that just doesn't work. Red Alert's campy plots and cutscenes thrived on its mock Cold War feeling.
From a technical standpoint, it's a fine game. Units are diverse, mechanics are solid enough. Undoubtedly the strength of the game is in multiplayer, which I haven't tried. But it just doesn't feel like it's a proper Red Alert game. Plainly put, I wasn't having fun with this, and rarely have I been so disappointed in a purchase.

I put a couple of hundred hours into this game right after it came out. It was way too easy then, and I lost interest after a few games.
I tried it again after the 1.9 update. The good news? The AI is vastly improved and occasionally competitive even on normal difficulty.
The bad news? Bugs, bugs, and more bugs. The game hangs constantly. You can't always click on certain things without following elaborate work-arounds. Dialog boxes get hidden behind other boxes. Some dialog boxes open and close so fast they're unreadable. Settings for starbases and shipyards change for no discernable reason.
My rule is this: I'll forgive a few bugs unless you're putting out paid DLC. If you've got time to work on paid DLC but aren't making sure the basic product is high quality, then you've got ethical issues as a game company. Developers seem to think that killing bugs isn't as profitable as DLC. I bet they're wrong. I can afford to buy all the DLC for GC3, and I would if it were working properly. Stardock is also quickly becoming one of my 'never buy' companies along with the likes of Paradox. If you put out enough bad product, eventually your reputation will catch up with you. Not recommended.
p.s. I'm playing on a 2-week-old Windows 10 gaming desktop. If it won't run well on this, it won't run well on anything.
Edit 2/20: I'm trying it again on v2.0. They still haven't fixed the bug that causes dialog boxes to occasionally open behind other screens. Or the bug that makes dialog boxes flash past too fast to read. Or the bug that makes some items in various lists unclickable. But I hear they're working on some kind of new #%@# DLC!
Edit 2/23: I just got the bug where the game hangs. So they went from 1.9 to 2.0 without fixing a SINGLE BUG. Pitiful.

There's quite a few things that can be said about Farming Simulator 2013. I'd say it is aimed at a specific audience for a start. Some may find the gameplay potentially mind-numbing due to the whole repetitiveness with no action, but personally I find it's not too bad to play, because in some points you can also hire workers if you find it too stretching. It is better with friends (as are most games) as it creates more of a mood as well as splitting up the work between you.
Essentially: Start with a little bit of money and some vehicles. Plant stuff, harvest, sell, repeat and get more income so that you're able to upgrade your vehicles, equipment and buy more land to maximise your profit. Pretty much an endless cycle until you have the best equipment and vehicles.
The graphics aren't particularly good, but if you're someone that isn't bothered by that - You'll be right.
The physics are pretty weird, but that's fine because they're pretty funny to play with. The game can also be customised to a certain degree with a large variety of community maps and vehicles that can be downloaded in.
Once again, I say that this game is surely not for everyone, but it's not bad if you don't mind the straight forward farming concept with partial monetary and banking section involved.
In final, I'd say pick this up on a sale if you like the look of it. What you see from gameplay and trailers are essentially what you get. You're in charge of your own wallet here.

This is my first and hopefully last review, that I 'll ever write for steam. The general ratings you find on steam are typically trustworthy, unfortunately Stellaris does not follow suit. Before I go any further, may I say for the record, that I have shown ferverous support for Paradox. I have well over 1200 hours played on Ck2 and over 500 on EU4. Within 40 hours of playing Stellaris, I was dumbfounded by how unfinished of a product this truly is. The tiny intricate marvels the player experiences within the first half of the game become irrelevant by the time Big powers have become established. Races, Politics, decision making, even research, becomes almost arbitrary. The game boils down to how many ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ships do you have in your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ death congolomerate and how many ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ships do the other powers have in theirs. Paradox has never been known for detailed combat sequences, which I have always been okay with. Combat was never a major focus, for the majority of the titles they put out. Stellaris was not meant to be one of paradox's few excepetions. Unforatuntely the game becomes too restricted, in all facets of the word space, that the last half of the game ends up you declaring mind numbing wars for the however many hours it takes you to win.
In addition, There are tons of bugs. Just to name a few,
Missing armies - If a war ends and you have armies stuck on a planet that you do not own, they end up "dissappearing". They will still show up on the side panel, and you will still have to pay upkeep for them, but you are unable to locate them and or disband them.
Never Growing Pops-. There is a feature in the game in which you may allow your pops to freely migrate from planet to planet, not only within the confines of your empire, but other space empires if you so make an agreement with said parties. What ends up happening is, a pop of a particular race will move to your planet and then say "eh, this place ♥♥♥♥ing sucks" and leaves a solid 3 minutes later. once the pop gets there it starts to "Reproduce". a sillouhette will appear in a production slot of said species, but won't produce anything till it's fully grown. when the original pop migrates away. the shadow pop will stop growing because there are no more members of the same species on that planet. Instead of the shadow pop dissapearing it stays there stuck on 0.0 growth.
Gene mutation - ♥♥♥♥ed, ♥♥♥♥ed, ♥♥♥♥ed. ♥♥♥♥ed.
The interface, is also really ♥♥♥♥ing clunky. It's extremely unfriendly and I constantly find myself saying "why wouldn't they do this a different way" It seems as though it was an afterthought. Unfinished, much like the rest of the game.
That being said, there are some wonderful features. tons of intricacies that will literally help you forget all the other♥♥♥♥♥♥the game has been throwing in your face. The initial option of race/ empire creation is extremely detailed. It allows the player to really immerse him/herself into the game before it's even begun. It allows for a full range of motion in choosing a player's species' ideologies, short comings and strengths.
Early game alien interactions, research and discovery are also incredibly detailed and really help guide the game without it feeling too restricted.
I just feel that, after spending 40 hours playing Stellaris and witnessing such an unfinished game, that I cant help but think that Paradox is taking full advantage of a loyal fanbase. This game was pegged as being one of the most colossal games they have ever released, and so far it seems as though they put such little time into it. I'm sure Paradox will fix it, but how many DLC's and expansions will I need to buy? How many mods will I need to download? I'm sorry, but for anyone who is thinking of buying this game, realize that despite paying 40 dollars for this game, you will not recieve a product worth the money in return.

I remember back in 2005 getting my brand new PC with an AMD FX-57 CPU(Which I won in a competition), Dual Nvidia 7600GTs and 2GB of RAM. You don't get shooters like this any more and if you love shooters and horror then get this game.

So here is my story. I was really young and didn't have a gaming computer. I first tried playing this game when i was about 11 or 12. All my friends had heard about it and played it. One of them bought it for me to try to play in the dark at midnight in my basement with cobwebs and♥♥♥♥♥♥
I still remember that night because I was absolutely terrified because of what I had heard of this game. Needless to say it did not disappoint my 11 year old imagination. Although this game doesn't terrify my anymore I decided to purchase it again just to make a clean run through it with my gaming PC. :) Now onto the review.
First off I'll get the rating out of the way for you ADHD people. 9/10 Why? Read on.
A.I. (Now we are talking for a game released in 2005 keep in mind) The A.I. in F.E.A.R. is top notch on a scale that matches that of Halo, which is very good contrary to popular belief. Never did I encounter a bug with the A.I. where they didn't search for me and pursue me or sneak up behind me and scare me ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I like that in a game haha. I give the A.I. a 9/10 too.

The artwork is never foreign to environment and atmosphere that this game is trying to set which is Dark and Scary. With shading to make you think twice about going around a corner to the shading of the fire on Alma's back, (or however you spell her name that little ♥♥♥♥♥) this game knows what it's doing when it comes to matching it's art with it's environment. I give the Artwork/Textures/Graphics a solid 10/10
Gameplay (from beginning to end): From the slow beginning of the ride in the car to the fights with the soldiers to the encounters with Alma, F.E.A.R.'s gameplay keeps you on edge and makes you thinkt hat you'll die at any moment. Oh, and the ending is to DIE for. ;) I won't get too in depth because I don't want to spoil anything, but just know that this game is worth every penny. F.E.A.R. First Encounter Assault Recon. This game was ahead of its time both graphically and gameplay. The story goes you play as Pointman (or as I tend to call him John since he doesn't have a real name) who is a rookie on special military team known as F.E.A.R. They are the people you bring in when things go "bump in the night" You are soon thrown into a nightmare and a conspiricy that includes you, Paxton, and a little girl named Alma. All three of you share a story that is told through the game and laptops that are really meant to be found to understand the background and what really went on.
The gameplay is really well off. The A.I. is smart even smarter then A.I. in mutimillion dollar budget FPS's. They will run to cover and stay in cover till you stop firing. They will try to get around and flank you and much more. The combat can get challanging in some places, especially with the honking robots that pratically needs explosives to take down and can kill you very quickly if you're not careful enough.
This game, if you haven't played it will give you goosebumps. Alma is already already a terrifying entitiy but given she can take you to a alternative world where fire and (I think ghosts) can kill you, forget it. Paxton can be just as terrifying in some brilliantly lighten rooms and with no music playing you're left to wonder if you're truly alone.
The two expansions while they are fun aren't as good as the original and given they aren't cannon makes it even less enganging knowing John and his team never went through the stuff they did after the original F.E.A.R. game. But that doesn't mean they aren't fun, no, I've enjoyed them very much and they even turned up the "scare factor" in the expansions then in the original.
In all I say F.E.A.R. is one of those games that you will probably never find again in today's world and its hard to create a horror game that is actually horror. When I played this back when I was younger, man was I freaked out. This was one of the first horror games I played and I'm glad i did. Got me into the genere in the first place. I would recommend this and the not so scary sequels to really anyone. This game series you play for the story and the horror. The next games... while their not AS scary as this one, they're still worth a playthrough or two.

YES! This is what I was looking for! Open sandbox space sim where you choose your own path! Oh man I don't even know where to start, so I'll give a summary of my playthrough so far:
I fired it up, set it to normal and rand-gen'd some bloke to play as (ended up with a guy with a pink mohawk and a hawaiian shirt. The absurdity has grown on me a bit). And I hit it right off. The interface and controls weren't too intuitive, but not too cryptic either. I had it pretty well figured out in under 5 minutes, and started working for the tutorial guy. And he taught me asteriod mining and mission running and trading and some basic combat and and then gave me a run down of what's going on in the sector then it was a pat on the butt and off you go. That's it. You get to kick it into high drive within.. 30 minutes? Of the game start.
And the depth of the game is great. There's 5 factions, only one of which I know well, one I have a good idea of, and one that's a mystery to me, one's pirates and the last one is the EVIL ALIENS (TM). You level up and allocate your XP points to your skills, which go all the way from asteriod mining up to PEW PEW BANG and everything inbetween. And I mean everything. There's some really weird skills in there.
Combat can leap between fairly routine to very surprising, depending on how high you keep your guard up. I was doing pretty damn well off the start beating up pirates and mining rocks, so I got pretty full of myself and headed into a fairly dangerous system to rack up some XP.
Ha ha they beat my♥♥♥♥♥like a drum. I needed a bigger ship.
Now, ship size isn't terribly noticable. I suppose because they'd have to zoom the screen out a lot to make a difference. It's basically just better hull, and better weapon placement. Which is a huge thing in combat. It's not so much the size of your gun, but whether or not you can bring it to bear! Some turrets point forwards, to the sides, out the back, etc! And also you have to match them up to their type of weapon. Energy/Kinetic/Missile/Mine. So, each ship has its own style of combat.
Ship equipment is fairly straightforward. You want bigger and better, but you need to carefully manage how much fuel and power your fuel tank and reactor can provide. The thing I like is the fact you don't need to strip old ships for parts. No, your hull is literally just another equipment slot. You just swap it out and bang, new hull same equipment.
Very enjoyable and challanging at times. It's going to see hundreds of hours from me.

Doom 2 is the second game of the franchise coming out only a year after the original was released. It is set right after the events that took place in Episode 3 of the first game where you have managed to return to Earth only to discover that it has come under attack by the forces of hell. It doesn't take long to find out why humanity is on the verge of extinction as the amount of monsters you see on Earth is more than you even see exploring hell in the first game. To make matters worse they have sent brand new demons such as the Archvile, chain-gun wielding zombies and other demons far more powerful than those you spent the majority of the time fighting in Doom 1. This is definitely a sequel made for those with lots of experience playing the original and will hold no punches back. It is a far more difficult game than the original, as such I would suggest starting with that one if you are looking to get in to the series. If you simply want to play some of the insane number of mods available then this is the one to get since must mods are for Doom 2.
The only new gun in your arsenal will be a double barreled shotgun and packs a heck of a punch to anyone in its path but lacks the great range of the single barreled shotgun making both viable options instead of a straight upgrade. One of the first things you may notice is that there are no longer any Episodes to choose from. Instead you start from level 1 and make your way to the end of the game from there. It sucks not being able to start at the middle or the end of the game anymore though I did find this change to be for the better overall as you no longer end an episode and have to collect all your weapons over again when you start the next one. You may be thinking that has the potential to make the game too easy as you can now stock up on tons of ammo but that is not the case. Due to the powerful new enemies and the sheer amount of numbers they throw at you, ammo feels more valuable than ever. In the original game you would tend to stick to the shotgun the majority of the time to save ammo for Cyberdemons but in Doom 2 that will more likely than not get you killed as it is very difficult to handle the new monsters with a shotgun alone.
While the Cyberdemon is still the most powerful enemy you will face I somehow fear the Archvile just as much or even more. It is quite a nasty monster that will set you on fire if it can see you requiring you to hide behind any objects or walls to break its line of sight. All the while it resurrects previously defeated enemies making your situation far more dire every moment that it remains alive. Those are the kind of moments you will more likely than not swap out your trusty shotgun and use up much rarer ammo types in the hopes that you won't need it later. The level design in this is downright sadistic and will lock you into small rooms full of enemies, descend the floor beneath you to fall face to face with an enemy or place enemies in hard to reach vantage points as they suddenly pelt you from above. Levels are much larger this time around and there is a big focus on verticality. The verticality can be very annoying as you cannot look up to shoot at them unless you are playing Doom 2 via a source port that gives you mouse aiming. Even then it is quite a rush as you are surrounded on from all sides and are even being shot at from above lending the game the feel that you are really fighting for your survival.
In Doom 1 more often than not you felt like you were a badass but in Doom 2 you really get the feeling that you are just surviving as the slightest mistake can be the end of you. Many of the times you will not see the fight coming as the walls drop around you to reveal that you are indeed surrounded in a room that appeared safe. It is a lot more action oriented than the original that had the sounds and groans of the enemy far before you see it to give it a bit of a horror feel. In this it is a lot more in your face merely dropping enemies without much indication. Whichever you enjoy more is up to preference though in some occasions Doom 2 does end up feeling down right cheap. One other thing I am not too crazy about is the obscurely hidden keycards for a few levels. I usually ended up finding them while searching for secrets only to discover that is actually the right way to go. I can see many players being completely stuck in some levels and ending up searching for a walkthrough. Thankfully most of the levels do not have obscure level design and flow rather well with you knowing where to go at all times.
All of the items make a return like the hazmat suit, night vision and soul spheres with no new additions. Secrets are still plentiful and more important than ever as finding a crate of rare ammo can be the difference between life or death down the road. If you die you start at the beginning of the level with only a pistol like in the original Doom. Environments were very impressive for their time featuring giant cities with skyscrapers and tons of things on screen. I still find it rather cool even today as everything you see will eventually be explored and is not just set dressing. Being able to fight in a large nonlinear city, shooting rockets while running faster than Sonic the Hedgehog is a lost art in modern FPS games sadly. Music is strangely enough no longer guitar shredding Metal and is instead a more laid back Industrial Techno sounding type of genre. It is strange as Doom 2 is a lot more action packed than the original and yet is the one with music that doesn't get you pumped. It has some really good tracks nonetheless and is really just up to personal preference. Controls have been modernized and has movement set to “WASD” with the mouse controls allowing you to look left and right. Pushing the mouse forward causes your character to walk forward which is annoying and cannot be disabled without the use of a mod.
Your main mission is to help the remnants of humanity off the planet before being completely wiped out. Eventually you succeed in your mission and lay down your gun, sit back and wait for death while proud of the fact that you saved humanity. You get a call telling you that they found where the demons are pouring in from and you wearily stand back up to continue the fight. It sounds a lot better than it is to be honest. Story is minimal and you only get a bit of text from time to time. Like pretty much any other shooter at the time it is all about gameplay and it is still as fun now as it was back then. It is the same timeless gameplay from Doom 1 but with the addition of plenty of new powerful demons and much harder levels. If you liked Doom this is really more of the same only bigger, badder and more likely to make you John Romero's b****. At the low price it is now being sold at it is more than worth it to take a trip back to memory lane or to any fan of fast and frantic FPS action that's willing to look past the dated graphics. So rev up your chainguns and mow down demons until you are knee deep in the dead.

Paladins is not an Overwatch clone. They have their similarities but are two quite distinct games.
- Lots of different champions to choose from.
- Champions loadouts are customizable, essentially changing how you play the same champion.
- I like the inclusion of items. Allows you to react to your enemies better.
- I enjoy the addition of mounts -> it changes game dynamics and you can force people off their mounts.
- Games are fairly short (5-20 minutes).
- Team interactions and combinations is exciting and fulfilling when properly executed.
- Frequent updates and new content (maps, champions, skins).
- I like that games cannot be won by simply defending the payload. You must capture the objective to win (allows for comebacks).
- Different game modes and you can play on test maps.
- No 'undo' button when buying items. Made a mistake? Too bad.
- Occassional hacker (haven't spotted one in a while)
- Like any online game, uncooperative teammates can be frustrating to deal with.
- Matchmaking is not always fair.
- Occassional bugs, lag-spikes, and downed servers.
- Requires some grinding (like any other MOBA)
Remember, Paladins is still in open-beta. It still has a lot of flaws, but I believe the developers are working hard to improve this game. In the end it comes down to this: do I enjoy playing Paladins? Yes. It's free, so why not give it a try?

Now. As a player of the original Dungeon Defenders, I looked forward to this. Now, unlike everyone else.. ranting and raving about how Crap this is. Let me start off with the good stuff.
1: You don't have to pay to unlock all the characters. They are all there ready for you.
2: The UI for your Character Sheet is much better. It allows you to easily swap over gear
3: The bonus of your armour ACTUALLY changes when you put it on. For EG: I picked up a crown and I saw the crown on my charaters head.
4: The abillity to create a character and name it without having to go out of the game and back to the menu to name it, colour it, and all that.
5: The open tavern. Alot don't like the idea as Whining, Rude people, Noobs and such. The open tavern is a place where people can meet up, stuff like that instead of having a game on a menu to pick from. and not knowing who you might be playing with. At least with the open tavern, you can get a rough idea.
6: The abillities. Nothing makes Dungeon Defenders like the placement of towers and useage of abillities. That is still all there, but with a little more. There are now ingame items which can be used to assist gameplay. Of course these can be bought from the tavernkeeper, or you can find them randomly drop from Goblins, Orcs, Dark Elves and the such or from chests.
7: The Character Model. The Character sheet now has a model of your character. It allows for 360* rotation to view all angles of your character.
8: Cross-Platform. Got a friend who is waiting for a new PC? Well why not buy them a copy of Dungeon Defenders Eternity on a different platform and let them play with you.
9: Same classic music... it even sounds clearer
10: The map selection is easier to traverse
11: The portraits of the parents look better
12: When dying, you have 6 colour slots instead of 3 making for more customization
13: (Just Played Multiplayer) The drops are individual and so are the chests. no longer shared mana
Now that I belive I have done all the Pros, its time for the cons.
1: Lack of instant customization. Sure you can pick a skin to use on a hero, but to customize it more, you need to buy Dye from the tavern keep. Oh If you make a mistake, buy a bucket of white wash and start again with buying more dye.
2: Limited Skins. Heroes have custom skins, but they are limited.
3: One Server. From what I can tell, there is one server.
4: The Cash Shop. Yep, the annoying Cash shop to get more stuff. Usually associated with Pay 2 Win games. Though in Dungeon Defenders Eternity, it is thankfully only for cosmetics.
5: While an open tavern is good, It also does have its cons. With an open tavern, The abillity to move around is hard. The lack of space to find friends, or even preview your character are hindered.
6: Online. Now, I know you might rage at this, saying online is a con? well, It is and it isnt. The con of the online is that if your not connected to the internet, you can't play.
7: Currency. You no longer use Mana crystals. You use gold coins to buy stuff which you find randomly in chests and from enemy drops and buy sellling old gear. (Not to sure about after completing a wave or a map as my game wasn't completely downloaded when I stated to play)
8: Wait time. You join a game wether its private or public and you have to wait.
9: It doesn't use Steam UI for invites
10: You can't customise your Crystal
11: The Defence Units are shared among all players, including those playing summoner
There are more pros and cons, but as of this time of what I have played, This is all I can give. I am bound to do another Review after more playtime.
Now, Some people might like the original Dungeon Defenders and hate this, or vice versa or like both. It doesn't matter as everyone is different. So I am not going to say YES buy this or NO don't buy this. I will let you decide if you want to buy it or not. I wouldn't based your decision on the reviews, but on videos on gameplay, demos or trying it at a friends place. But as a gamer and lover of Dungeon Defenders (note Dungeon Defenders was one of the first games I bought on steam when it first came out many years ago near christmas) I would recommend this if you want to just have fun without the worry of paying for more characters, maps, skins etc.

is long on art assets but short on design.  It looks good and sounds good, briefly, but it won't hold your attention long at all.
The first thing you'll probably notice is that the menu is poorly designed.  It accepts mouse-clicks as input, but doesn't acknowledge the pointer, so you'll likely confuse yourself greatly until you realize that the menu must be navigated with keyboard commands.  Don't take your hand off the mouse, though, because you'll need it in play.  And try not to lose track of where the pointer is, which will be tricky, because the pointer is rather small and bland against a very vibrant and cartoony playfield.
You will have a choice from a rogues' gallery of a dozen goofy characters.  It doesn't matter which one you pick, for gameplay purposes -- they perform identically.  Assuming that you actually play more than once, you might want to find one whose attack phrase you find the least annoying.
Gameplay is very simple, and more strategic than it appears at first glance.  Four characters with identical abilities run around in an arena full of hazards.  You want to kill each other in a manner consistent with the match goal (most kills, highest kill streak, whatever) and have only one attack with which to do it.  Your attack is a slow-firing "special attack" that kills everyone in a small radius around you, but is interruptable.  You also have a hook-shot weapon,
Scorpion from
which targets with the mouse (that's why you're trying not to lose the pointer) and can be used to pull an enemy to you, or to pull yourself to an enemy.  Either way, the hookshot stuns enemies, giving you an opportunity to get your attack off.  The hook can also pull your enemies into hazards.  You also have a dash move that's good for avoiding hooks -- CPU-controlled characters don't use it much.
Because your attack is so slow, strategic play tends to involve prowling around looking for opportunities.  Running up to an enemy and attacking will probably result in a stunning hook to your face, breaking your attack and making you vulnerable to a counter-attack.  Hooking an enemy while he's in the process of attacking someone else, however, will give you easy prey.
When you die, and you will die often, since this is a one-hit kill system, you respawn somewhere on the playfield.  Find yourself quickly, because spawn protection is fleeting, and it's possible for someone to have killed you again before you even see where you are.
Powerups appear on the screen from time to time.  Some change the game briefly but significantly, like the item that puts a temporary moratorium on hooks.  A sword that fills your screen with text is a trap-item.  Other powerups have an imperceptible effect.  I collect them anyway, because grabbing a powerup is a long-conditioned reflex, but I still don't know what half of them do.
The simplicity of the gameplay suggests that
is trying to be like
, a game that is deliberately simple and short on tactical options, to invite the player to really master range and timing.  Unfortunately, I can't see much reason to do so.  NPC opponents are pushovers, and on the rare occasions I can manage to schedule friends to multiplay something, I'd prefer to spend the time something with more depth.

At the time of writing I am in at 1200+ hrs. The extraordinary thing is the title is a bland, no bells and whistles sim.
So what's the attraction?
Initially, starting with 1 paddock on the stock map and a small amount of equipment provides an impetus to do what farmers do. Plant, reap, sell, expand. But it doesn't take long to learn the quirks and the cash points so "expansion" and accummulation of wealth becomes kinda pointless soon enough.
The scenery can be special, the fields and textures quite mundane. Equipment modelling is very nice. The AI can be quite stupid at times (but I couldn't imagine playing this without them) and it's got a definite farm feel. On it's own, it might get 300-400 hours to dedicated tycoon-sim fan.
So what is it? What made me do (and will probably continue) over 1200+ hrs of playtime?
FS2013, to me, is all about the mods. New maps, new equipment, new fruits, new animals and new ways to do things are offered by a very dedicated modding community and have been since the game first released.
The ability to connect the dots to create any specific industry on the farm has increased exponentially. New animal mods, such as the piggery, provide for a very diverse form of infrastructure modelling to run successfully. From grain to root vegetables to water to straw to mixed rations and onwards.
Giants themselves have done very little to gameplay and it took them 12 months to release a new map and some new equipment, along with an engine update. They have not added new animals or fruits and even the new farm and new equipment was a DLC purchase. Pretty poor tbh, given the money made (and continues) from this, one of the most popular farming sims out there.
Mod it up and it's worth every single cent and will remain a stalwart amongst the box of games we call sims.

If you read many of the other reviews, let me set the recond straight on a few things:
Settlers online is not a p2w game!  pvp is purly optional and I have never played it.

There are 4 events a year: Easter, Summer, Halloween, and Christmas for 3 weeks each.  For event resources (presents, pumpkins,  eggs, soccer balls, etc) you can buy a lot of premium items.
Also, by joining a guild and doing your guild quest each day, you can earn guild coins and buy additional premium items.
Also, you earn 100 gems (the premium currancy) every 7 login days (400 to 500 a month), as well as when you level up and meeting other goals.   You can use gems to also buy premium items.
The devs are very reponsive if you post on the official Settlers Online forums.  Not the ones on Stream. Also you can Contact Customer Support via the login screen.
This IS a city builder for sure.  And like all city builders, yes, it can take up to 1 week to update a building.
Let me make this clear:  Settlers Online is a game you can play for an hour or so each day.  It is not a game you can play for hours at a time.  If you want to play an online game for hours at a time, try Gems of War, Terra, Atlantica Online, or Path of Exile all available on Steam.
A major update to this game is on the way for September with the Halloween Event to follow in October and Christmas Event to follow 1 month after the Halloween Event ends.   This is the perfect time to start playing this game.
This game is about building up a city to raise armies.  The armies are use to do Adventures, Ventures, or Expeditions.
.
There are two Settlers Online wikis that give guides for doing any of these which you can use or you can figure out on your own how to do battles.  The choice is really yours.
Yes, it is true you have to send explorers out to find adventure or you can buy them in the market or trade for them. I must have close to 100 adventures now.  So, you will get a lot of them fast.
Yes, it does take resources to make weapons.
Note:  DO NOT use gems to speed up builds or upgrading a building.  If you do, don't complain about it.  Remember, that was your decision.
As far as I know, there are no bugs in the quest chain either.  I'm lvl 44 right now and had no problems at all.  So, I don't know what is the suppose bug you might encounter at lvl 7.  Granted, it is about 11 months since I was lvl 7.
All in all, this is a fun game to play for a hour or so each day.

Started to play this game when I first got it in 2011. The killer for me was twofold:
- The graphics sucked. I mean, really sucked. I was unable to fix it. I've since changed my graphics card, maybe it'll be better. (still re-installing)
- The complete inability to reprogram the keys from within the game, AND the complete inability to remind myself what the key bindings are from within the game. Sorry, but we're in the 2010's now, not the 1980s! The people who thought that was a good idea should be taken out behind the shed and slapped. Hopefully they've put an update since to change that idiotic, poorly considered decision. The idea that I can't easily experiment with better control schemes is either extraordinarily arrogant or insanely stupid. Quite possibly both.
So now I'm re-installing to see if it's worth playing. I have many, many enjoyable hours on Witcher 1. I hope I didn't waste my money on Witcher 2, even if I had to wait 5 years to play it. More later.
ps: since I'm unable to post without a thumbs up or down, doing with my original opinion until proven otherwise. Steam really needs to introduce a more nuanced scale, or at least introduce a "meh".
OK, finally got the game to re-install after a lot of faffing about. Verdict? No. Don't go there. Another game whose mechanics and controls are so BAD that I'm completely unwilling to subject myself to that kind of torture in order to attempt to finish the game. It's just bad. Pure, unadulterated bad. Distilled bad.
- tutorial graphics suck. Period. I don't know if it's some setting somewhere, but on my relatively high-end system, they suck. Dark, lack of contrast, weird colours, the works.
- the combat system sucks farts from dead goats. They took what was once an elegant system and turned it into something only a Street Fighter multi-combo twitch gamer could love. Button mashing works too though, so much for anything resembing "elegance".
- the inventory system? wow, original Skyrim was better, and it was bad. Lots of junk, almost no way to sort through the stacks of loot.
- alchemy? No more experimentation. You'll get the recipe when the game gives you the recipe, that is all.
- Character upgrading. 120 possible selections. But you only get 1 selection per level, and it's capped at 34 levels. Geralt was a master witcher when you finished Witcher 1. By the end of this game, you're going to barely be an apprentice.
- Quicktime events (and there are many of those) are so badly done even the developers provided a "disable events" button. At least they were self-aware enough to do that. Prime example is the (spoiler!) dragon scene in the prologue. Supposed to "dodge attacks" when you see the button, except the colours and contrast are so bad you can never see the button. So you die. And you die again. Until you turn off the quicktime event and turn the thing into a boring "press the down button to run away until it ends".
- Potions are next to useless. They've cut the duration down to 5 minutes real time. Using cat potion to explore a dungeon? Better have a dozen, they only give you enough time with one to race through it. Once.
- Doorways. Really, doorways. It's an "event" to get through them. You can't trigger events when in combat. So you can't go through an open door at all when in combat. Even if your opponent is on the other side of the door, you can see them, and they can see you. You can move right up to the doorway sill and hit your opponent on the other side of the door, but you can't go through the doorway to actually get to him if he moves away from you just a little. It's just stupid.
- Finally, I despise games that feel they have to cheat by suddenly changing the game physics in order to make something "challenging". Probably because the designers couldn't actually come up with something validly challenging. Take the dagger contest with Ves. Now, I've gotten fairly good at daggers, but in THIS contest the target acts like it's a magnet with the opposite charge of what you're aiming at. So you'll aim at the specfied target and the aim point will go anywhere BUT where you're actually aiming at. It actually jumps OVER the target to the other side, and it's basically a game of complete chance to hit the target. Even though I can hit a running nekker at dozens of paces. They do the same with the arm-wrestling contest, where they take the already assinine mouse lag and make it far, far worse. Randomly. These aren't "games". They're just exercises in frustration created by game developers who hate and despise gamers.
The entire interface feels like a bad port from a game solely intended to be played by console gamers who play a lot of "fighting" games. Overcomplicated combos for combat, easily replaced by just button mashing. Automatic sneak mode when they want you to, not when you choose to do (there's no "sneak" button, yet they still implemented "sneak"?). So I'm an avid Sins of a Solar Empire/Dawn of War/Sid Meier's Civilization player. There was barely a week where I didn't play one of those titles...until Stellaris. I can agree, the execution of the game is amazing if a little weak towards the end. If anything, there are mods in the workshop that more than make up for the fantastic if just a little spotty execution. I feel like as Paradox releases DLCs and expansions for Stellaris, it will make up for the spots in the game that were just a little lackluster.
Pros:
- Paradox perfected the blend of Sins of a Solar Empire with Sid Meier's Civilization
- Customize practically everything. And if you can't, then you're just not using the right mods.
- Sci-fi Conquesting doesn't get boring. I can't tell you just how unique every playthrough I've done has been. I haven't logged 100+ hours on Stellaris just for anything.
Cons:
- Sector AI could be better. There's a mod for it in the workshop but I haven't used it yet.
- Fleet battles look a little messy without the Beautiful Battles mod.
- Ground invasions are literally a 3-step process; 2-step if you're invading primitives (not recommended since most governments get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you for doing so). There's a mod in development that's attempting to make it more dynamic. I seriously just want an animated screen of troops going at it or something a little more interactive maybe.
- No actual population statistics yet (game refers to them simply as Pops. Think Civilization). I'm hoping a mod will come along to determine that stuff as well. Doesn't even need to be accurate, just look accurate.
Overall:
Yes, I agree with earlier reviewers who say that this is the rightful successor to Sins of a Solar Empire/Civilization if there was any need for a successor to begin with. Yes, the gameplay is great, but there are parts about the game that are lackluster if playing vanilla and vanilla only.
I'd give it a good 8.5/10

This game has everything I like in it. Spaceships, free exploration, trading, mining, missions, and an optional story. If you liked Privateer and always wanted a 2d version of Privateer, that's almost exactly what this game is. And that might be enough for some people.
Unfortunately, the game is lacking polish in many respects. There are plenty of weapons, but aren't enough ships, engines, and shields to really create the kind of ship that will work well in the game. I think that the devs figured players would create these assets using mods, but the only mods out so far are cheaty ones. The economy is a bit off -- ships are a bit too cheap for what they are. There's no ties between resources being available and stations having more products or anything like that.
Piloting needs some work. Colliding with NPCs is far too easy (in fact, it's the only maneuver some NPCs know). Most player ships can't turn fast enough or move their weapons fast enough to target NPCs without themselves striking NPCs.
XP and leveling needs some work. Right now, the only way to level up quickly and easily is to shoot things. You can't level up easily by trading, hacking, or mining, except at the most basic levels. That might be because there are ways to break the system at later points in the game, but that just means that the system is weak and needs polish.
There are distinct periods of boredom in between being able to do things in game. You finish the first couple of missions at level 3 or 4. You can't take on the next storyline mission until Level 10, and can't upgrade ships until Level 15. To get to level 15, you need to clear approximately two low-level systems of pirates. That's a lot of pew pew pew. And it's only reasonable to gain that XP by going pew pew pew, even if you classed as a miner or trader.
I don't know right now if the game will age well and develop a following and some decent mods that will fix these problems. I haven't looked too closely at modding yet. There's a ton of promise here, but unless you're really grabbed by the story, there's very little good reason to play the game past the initial few hours.

I am going to get so ridiculed for this because of the huge cult following for this game, but I must be absolutely honest here as I am not bound by the nostalgia of rose-coloredglasses. Yes, I only played 4.9 hours on steam. I played more of the PSN version on PS3/PS4 because my computer was in a "mood". My PC however will have no major bearing on this review other than to say that I did try this game heavily modded on Steam before my computer decided to hate life.
So here is my honest assessment. I would give the game a 6/10 and I only rate it that high because I liked the combat and music. If the combat and music werent so good, I would have given it alot less. I also got the game through a steam sale, (paid $3) though it is normally priced decently for what you get, either way. So that's another reason I rated it a little better than I would have.
Here's a breakdown of how I felt about the game.
DATED - This is a slightly more beefed up version of the original PS1 game and as such, its dated for this generation of computers and consoles. This isnt a deal breaker, just an observation. You can however heavily mod the beejeebus out of the game on PC, though to me it was more effort than it was worth and my computer decided shortly after starting that it wasnt having any of it. At that point I switched to PS4 to continue playing.
STORY - The story would be great if it were fleshed out more to make more sense. As this was my first real play through, I actually had to look up summaries, synopsis and other videos to get the whole picture after I played. IGN's 7 min recap video of the FF7 world was very useful after I'd played through the game and included some information that was added in from Crisis Core, etc.
The dialogue and story itself in FF7 felt incredibly rushed and left me slightly confused at times as to what was going on... Though I will admit a good chunk of the confusion here likely stemmed from poor or mistranslations, as I am assuming Square didnt change/fix the dialogue from the PS1 version.
I am a huge fan of story-driven games, but this just felt muddled to me.
COMBAT - Okay this is where the game shined for me. The turn-based ATB style combat is exactly what I love about old Final Fantasy titles and its just as good here as when I played FF6, FF8, and FF9. So I give a big plus to it for the combat. That was fun.
VISUALS - Okay, this is where I have to give a huge MINUS to this game. The background graphics made it severely difficult for me to play this for lengthy periods of time. The game (especially unmodded) would literally give me headaches andI'dhave to stop playing. I had this problem back when I tried to play the original on PS1. I ended up giving my original PS1 game to a friend back in the day because I just couldnt deal with the eye strain and headaches from the visuals at the time. I was hoping that had changed, but not as much as I would have liked. I stillhad to take frequent "recovery" breaks. This is something to think about if your like me and had eye strain from the original.
Also, Trying to find my way around a given section of map was often unclear because the flat 2D graphics made it hard to determine what was actually traversible area or what was just background. I literally got stuck so many times where I had to load up a video walkthrough to figure out where I was supposed to go, and then I'd facepalm because I had missed a path that was right in front of me because it didnt seem like it was traversable because of the way the backgrounds are designed/rendered.
SOUNDTRACK - Okay another huge plus! The music in this game is epic. But then of course it is. It's Final Fantasy! :)
I loved FF7's music for years, even though I had never managed to get through the game before. You don't really need to play the game to enjoy its music though. I mean, who hasnt heard One Winged Angel and loved it :)
----
So that's my honest assessment. Headaches and Eyestrain aside, Immersive Story is a HUGE deal for me, and its what I come to expect from Final Fantasy titles but it just didnt do it for me, so I sadly am rating this a no-go.
That being said, I am probably the only person who never got to play this as a kid, and so my lack of nostalgia for this game has no factor in my review.
Take my words with a grain of salt. If you loved this game as a kid, you'll probably love it now. But if you've never played FF7 at all, ever in your life, I'll give you a simple and fair advice:  Be wary that it may disappoint due to its age and the translation of the story, but If you can pick it up on steam sale like I did, it's worth deciding for yourself if you love it or hate it :)
PS. FF7 lovers. Please don't hate me for the negative review. I reserve judgement on the FF7 world as a whole until after I play the new remake. I just cant like this version ^^;
