A lot of people say FF7 is the most overrated FF game/RPG game and guess what? I disagree with that.
If you wanted to play a game that best defines the RPG genre, there's so many titles like SMT Nocturne, Persona 3 FES/4, Dark Soul, Deus Ex etc. to choose from but I think FF7 is the best starter if you're looking to try to get into RPG games.
From what I've played, this is the only good FF game with an interesting cast of characters, story and setting. There's something special about this game that puts it above the others really. It feels like the rest just haven't quite captured that same magic FF7 did.  It's no wonder that this has been the most popular FF game to begin with and the most demanded for a remake (and we finally got it thankfully).
The gameplay itself is turn based combat which requires good strategy and decision making, with battles happening randomly on the field or getting triggered by specific points along the story.
Although the characters look like miniature polygon block versions of themselves when not fighting, the character models are more realistic and proportioned correctly in combat. For its time it was a big step forward because FF7 was the first game in the series to have character models with fully rendered polygons, rather than 2D sprites. Therefore battles take place using a 3D representation of the characters, enemies and the area itself.
Moreover, there are 9 playable characters:
You have Cloud- an blue eyed blonde haired big lad wielding a bigass greatsword.
Tifa- a kind and strong willed tiddy fighter who applies her martial arts skills in combat.
Barret- a very burly, built and all around cool Mr.T who uses guns ( think).
Yuffie, who acts as a nimble ninja and many more.
With a diverse set of characters like I've just described, it's easy to see why something like Final Fantasy 7 was such a huge hit amongst many. It's just a shame that not everyone gets as much development you'd like them to have, which is something I hope the remake really fleshes out considering it's going to be episodic.
Fingers crossed that the remake surpasses the huge waves FF7 made in its time and that the devs won't reduce Tifa's bust size to please non-players who complain about petty things.

F.E.A.R. is a game that is like a mix of Counter-Strick, Japanese style horror and the Matrix lobby fight scene. And that's a good thing.
The main draw of the game is the very intensive gun fights. They are very enjoyable and visually appealing thanks to the "bullet time" feature and the very destructable environment (so expect to see lots of debris and dust clouding your view). Thankfully this game has very good A.I. enemies so some planning is needed when attacking. So this is what the game is basically about: epic gun fights. The storyline is pretty weak and boring honestly... some psychic was used in science experiments which resulted in clones, mind control, creepy ghosts. The story is given gradually through PC data and phone messages you collect but that's so tedious I just made up the story as I went.
The soundtrack is pretty damn cool. It seems very fitting, like it could easily be in a Die Hard or John Woo film. The controls are perfect, easy to master. Visually it's great, still holds up today.
With F.E.A.R. you get two expansion packs (Perseus Mandate and Extraction Point). P.M. is the more fun of those two while E.M. seems to focus more on the horror/psychic theme.
So yeah, this game is a must if you love FPS games. The storyline is generic but the gameplay is very addictive.

To be perfectly honest, this game was above-average. It wasn't amazing, it wasn't bad. Just about above average. This does not mean it isn't worth playing though.
I originally thought this game was supposed to be way scarier than it was. It was creepy at parts, but never really scary. This did not affect my overall experience of it though, since the gameplay (mainly the awesome slo-mo feature) was very good. The beginning of the game had me right off the bat. I wanted to answer all the questions the game slowly opened up, and find Paxton Fettel and stop his evil plan. Then, the game kind of trailed off though. I was just going through somewhat generic FPS missions, with barely any leadway in the story other than some laptops. To be honest, I was kind of lost, and maybe that was because I was focusing on doing a let's play at the same time, but I just felt bored like I was not accomplishing anything other than chasing the main antagonist and ultimately failing every single interval. Then though, the last couple missions kicked it into high gear. It started answering everything I wanted to know, and led to an "explosive" conclusion along with a cliffhanger that really makes me want to continue the series.
So that's basically it. It was a great concept executed very well, the influence of Japanese horror films really helped this game stay unique, the slow-motion mechanic was awesome, the ending was great. This game would have gotten an even better score if the middle of it wasn't so boring for me, but since that was the case, it's a 7/10 for me. Now it's YOUR turn to see what YOU think and play this game, because it's worth it.

Sandbox-esque space combat
Top down space combat has been done before, lets get that out of the way.  From some of my earliest video game memories playing Star Control till recently with S.P.A.Z. this game follows a familiar combat formula.  But that's not a bad thing in any way.  Strafe, steer, and blast your way through your enemies with a bunch of changeable loadouts, ships, and different classes of 'hulls'  (the skeleton for the ship you'll use).  What makes this game great is the sandbox element.  It doesn't tell you what to do, but it does have branching quests.  Of course you're free to completely ignore them and just while away the hours mining asteroids if you so chooose.  Go to war with one of the factions in the game, or try to eliminate the alien menace that dominates a large chunk of the galaxy.  Ultimately it's up to you.
If there's one big complaint about the game it's that it feels a little empty.  You hit a wall around your late 30s where the experience points seem to take a lot longer and the upgrades are much further apart then you'd like.  With some of them being only say, a 3% to your cruising speed, leveling feels pretty underwhelming after a while.  Thankfully you get experience for doing pretty much anything in this game.  Also combatting the emptiness is the modding community which already has full game overhauls, rebalanced skill trees, new hulls, new weapons, new quests, and more.  I'd like to see even more modding for this game personally, as more content can only improve an already great game.
If you like this style of game, it's well worth the purchase price.

Summary:
9/10
Pretty visuals, good fighting mechanics, some interesting shop interactions, and gameplay mechanics.
Downside: short, and a bit repeative.
Story:
Fairly interesting with an unique idea. Realism is used over and over again. So as not to spoil anything and be even more vague, if you like sadish stories, then you will like this one. If I go anymore into depth, I feel like I will blow the whole shebang.
Gameplay:
Fighting game mechanics with RPG elements. So you have three standard combo's on the ground, and two standard combo's in the air. The wild card is the dust storm plus fidget projectiles. So fairly early on you will explore every combo, plus dodge and parry mechanics. Towards the end, things can be difficult, but that is only if you did no extra exploring or looting. So, you can get incredibly overpowered equipment and max out your level quickly. To give an example: With the best rings, best armor, best sword and the most offensive style amulet, you get 100% crit, over 4000 attack damage without crit and fidget's unblockable attacks deal nearly 1000 damage per tick in a dust storm combo. Yeah, enemies melt as you give them a love tap, and the final boss dies quickly, but not too quickly because the transition scenes take time.
There is one or two things that should be mention as well for players that don't know.
1. Your air dust storm actually can get unlimited height. You can use it to get into areas that actually require this ability or get into areas where other movement abilities are supposed to be used. To execute, you have to have enemies on screen and then initiate the air dust storm. Once in the air, rapidally press left and right and you will shoot into the air.
2. Air travel is so much faster then ground travel and you can nearly remain in air for an entire screen. Basically, jump then attack twice, then dust storm for a second. Continue to do this and you will move really fast and maintain your height.
Visuals:
Beautiful, hand drawn art. Plus, it is the main draw for bring you into the game. The story will take you the rest of the way.

Alright I have seen both positive and negative reviews on the version released on Steam.
Here is my take

Limitied Spoilers
Yes they messed up the bio about the game.  Final Fantasy 8 follows the lone wolf Squall on his journey to become a SeeD member. SeeD is the elite mercenary force of Balamb Garden. Seifer is pretty much Squalls rival in all regards. The game begins with Squall having to pass a GF exam to participate in the offical SeeD mission for cadets. After he passes that he along with 12 Seed and 12 Cadets must save Dollet from a Galbadian takeover.
That is all I want to reveal as the story
Now most reviews talk about how the MIDI music adversly affects the gameplay. Now while I agree the music isnt that extremely different from the PS1 Version.  SE could have taken the time to add the original ST in but it wasnt needed. I am sure there will be a mod for the game that fixes it, however I personally like the music. It is uniue to the PC version.
Now another aspect that reviews hate on: MAGIC BOOSTER
This is a neat little feature to the game but it isnt needed at all. Just click PLAY and never touch the BOOSTER icon if you want the original play style, having to draw and junction magic, as well as refining it from items. I started playing and my old PS1 instincts kicked in, never having to think about MB. I had Card, Card Mod, HP-J and 1000 affection with Quezacotl before even leaving for the Dollet Mission. You dont have to use MB but its there if you want it.
Finally the GF summoning sequences and sounds
THe only GF that is horrible is Quezacotl but it is endurable because his sequence isnt long, every other GF has been accurate to the PS1 Version.  If you dont like Quezacotl then dont use him but that again doesnt diminish the gameplay experience. Everything you had to do on the PS1 version you need to do here
Anyway I recommend people who have never played FF8 to play it on Steam. It is worth it considering everything from the storyline to mechanics are the same.

I love James Rolfe, this movie is great, but isnt exactly the best work of art he's made. But I support him and the movie. Hell I've bought it once on vimeo when it first got released, just bought it again on steam, and plan to buy it a third time when he releases the DVD of it. I do really enjoy this movie, it just feels like he sacrificed a lot more entertaining videos he coulda made to make this movie. With that being said, onto the review of his... review.
Point 1: Plot
So here we meet James Rolfe, or Angry Video Game Nerd as he is known in the movie, which is his internet alias. He is being passed through virally for his crude humor and hilarious jokes and ways of destroying/mocking games. He is working at a games store when a fan of his, played by the host of the youtube channel Black Nerd Comedy (The creator's name eludes me, I don't watch his videos) tells him he should do a review of the worst game ever made for the Atari 2600, and was also speculated to cause the video game crash, E.T.
The Nerd declines the offer, saying it's just "too ♥♥♥♥♥♥" and a few minut's later, finds out a sequal to this abomination is being made. He confronts his boss when he calls the Nerd in to tell him to "sell more ♥♥♥♥ing pre orders" and all that Jazz. The Nerd and his friend decide to visit the Atari landfill with all the cartridges of the game, accompanied by one of the representatives of the company making "E.T. 2" (which funny enough has the selling point that it's gonna be worse than the Atari version)
The millitary gets involved, his fans then get involved, mad scientists, giant robots, cheesy effects, and cameos ensue, it is all a good time. I can't really go into too much else without either spoiling it, or making this a book and taking out all the fun of watching the movie, so let's move on.
Point 2: The humor, setup, and effects
You expect the nerd to be raunchy right? You expect the♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, the cursing, the cheesy effects, all that good stuff eh? Well it all delivers. All the humor is what you would see in a Nerd video but with much, much higher quality. Hollywood Quality I would say, it is filmed so expertly, that if I had no idea who the nerd was, no idea this was an indie movie, no context on this movie whatsoever, I'd think it came straight from a big budget director. Funny enough, this movie was made on a few hundred thousand dollars, yet it is much more well made than a lot of movies with millions put into it by hollywood "professionals."
James used maybe a couple CG effects in this movie, but he used them on stuff you can't really create without a computer, like a laser beam blast for example. Stuff like a monster crushing the Nerd Mobile (You'll know what I mean if you watch the movie) are done with a guy in a suit and a replica model of the set. It is a real treat being able to see these older effects being put to use instead of "Well we COULD make it look good, but let's half♥♥♥♥♥it in Photoshop so we save a few thousand dollars."

Point 3: conclusion and final thoughts
All in all I would say if you are a huge fan of James Rolfe's work, pick this movie up, you will not be disapointed. For others who are kindas into the videos but not a huge fan, it's still a good watch with plenty of laughs (Around 59 minutes or so, him and the girl who's name eludes me right now are playing track and field, that got some of my friends who dont even like AVGN to laugh, it shows the power of this movie) If you absolutely hate AVGN, well then why the hell are you reading this review? But this movie is a great time, and I don't normally watch movies, but this one is very well made and worth the time and money I have spent watching and purchasing it. I expect great things from James and everyone who works with him on his videos (Yes I haven't forgot about them even though I don't mention them a lot) and this movie shows that they can achieve great things with their skills in comedy and film making.

Great concept but terrible execution. Game is unbalanced as hell, and bug ridden. Every update introduce new unbalanced items and new bugs. Old bugs drag on for years and the devs pay little attention to the quality. The game started on a good concept but was ruined by the developers due to ignorance and incompetence.
There were 3 maps in the game, 2 of which were rubbish and nobody used to play maps other than the chaos/moba map. Instead of improving the other maps, they would force players to play random maps so the un-performing maps would be played. In addition, the 3 maps play differently, and the dragon/weapon selection would perform very differently depending on the map. This means no matter how much effort you put into this game, the outcome of a match is randomized, depending on which map it puts you into. This gives you an idea of the kind of people they are.
The dragon and weapon selection is made before entering a game, and before you see any of your teammates or their selections. This means the player cannot choose combos that compliment the teammates. For a moba game this is horrible as players can never find a balanced team. Getting into a game with all support units against all attackers means a waste of 5-20 minutes of time.
The game had a skill shot pvp system where players had to aim their shots. To dumb it down in a failed attempt to attract players, it was chcanged to auto-aim. So instead of maneuvering and finding an opening to shoot the opponent, players now hold down the mouse button and sit idle until someone dies or escapes. The weapons/dragons that are harder to hit but hits harder, are now auto-aimed just like the easier to hit pee shooters. They were left un-balanced after auto aim was implemented 1-2 years ago. Very little attention was paid to balance the gameplay, as a matter of fact, that there are only about a quarter of the dragons/weapons that provide competitive performance. The rest create useless combos that cause teammates to hate you.
The game is plagued with hackers and lag bugs. Hackers would speed hack to win. They are reported by various over a year and no action would be taken. As a matter of fact, we would write support/report emails and would not hear answers for months, or ever in most cases. The lag bugs cause problem in gameplay where players take damage from the position they were in 1-2 seconds ago. Thus from your own computer, you'd think you are out of fire range but would still be taking damage. Furthermore, players are harmed by all kinds of invisble fireball, dragon breath that the server decided not to display.
It is not bad to try out the game to taste the concept of a lighter version of moba. But the game is far from good and the devs are less than competent to bring it up to standard.

There is a warning when you access the online mode telling you that it's experimental, but you'll only realize this after playing the game. They don't mention it on the store page or anywhere else as far as I know.
AVOID the game at all costs if online MP is all you're looking for. Now, onto reviewing the other parts of the game.
Pros:
+ Cool original character designs, nice animations and sprites. Good overall graphics.
+ Some of the levels were more challenging than I was expecting and work well with the scorpion "get over here" move.
+ The AI for the bots is pretty good if you plan on playing the game alone, and in certain game modes provide a good challenge.
Cons:
- Scorpion gimmick gets old fast, providing maybe an hour or so of gameplay before the fun runs out.
- Bots sometimes don't attack you after they've stunned you, which makes overcoming them a little too easy occasionally.
- No real incentive to keep you playing, there's no campaign or rewards for winning. Would be nice if they added unlockable characters, costumes, or literally any kind of reward for progressing. It doesn't even have achievements.
- As stated before, the online multiplayer is completely broken. I'm willing to try almost any game, no matter how bad it is in online MP so the lack of it is very disappointing.
For a local multiplayer game, it's probably not too bad but there are much better multiplayer arena games you can play and the scorpion gimmick isn't really adding anything you can't live without. Not worth the $9.99. If you're intent on buying it, only get this if you can get it for $0.50 or in a bundle.

Paladins is not an Overwatch clone. They have their similarities but are two quite distinct games.
- Lots of different champions to choose from.
- Champions loadouts are customizable, essentially changing how you play the same champion.
- I like the inclusion of items. Allows you to react to your enemies better.
- I enjoy the addition of mounts -> it changes game dynamics and you can force people off their mounts.
- Games are fairly short (5-20 minutes).
- Team interactions and combinations is exciting and fulfilling when properly executed.
- Frequent updates and new content (maps, champions, skins).
- I like that games cannot be won by simply defending the payload. You must capture the objective to win (allows for comebacks).
- Different game modes and you can play on test maps.
- No 'undo' button when buying items. Made a mistake? Too bad.
- Occassional hacker (haven't spotted one in a while)
- Like any online game, uncooperative teammates can be frustrating to deal with.
- Matchmaking is not always fair.
- Occassional bugs, lag-spikes, and downed servers.
- Requires some grinding (like any other MOBA)
Remember, Paladins is still in open-beta. It still has a lot of flaws, but I believe the developers are working hard to improve this game. In the end it comes down to this: do I enjoy playing Paladins? Yes. It's free, so why not give it a try?

Game manages to improve on Galactic civs 2 while still maintaining its challenge.  in particular the game is gorgeous, even the art which displays during events. I'm curious if its possible to set certain ships as default for custom races so I don't need to constantly fiddle around in the designer for every game with them but thats something else entirely. Being a long-time fan of the Red Alert series, I was excited to try the latest instalment. I was a little bit sceptical of the new features like transforming units and the ability to build a base on water, because I wondered if some of the magic of the first two games had been lost.
I was wrong. This game has kept my attention enough to beat each faction's campaign at least once, if not twice, and these missions present a challenge even if you have been playing RA2 for a while. The skirmishes, however, kept me coming back and they are what I play these days. There are so many different configurations, playstyles and challenges that you can try and overcome, like winning a match with only infantry units.
I highly recommend this game to fans of the series and newcomers to the RTS genre.

I am going to get so ridiculed for this because of the huge cult following for this game, but I must be absolutely honest here as I am not bound by the nostalgia of rose-coloredglasses. Yes, I only played 4.9 hours on steam. I played more of the PSN version on PS3/PS4 because my computer was in a "mood". My PC however will have no major bearing on this review other than to say that I did try this game heavily modded on Steam before my computer decided to hate life.
So here is my honest assessment. I would give the game a 6/10 and I only rate it that high because I liked the combat and music. If the combat and music werent so good, I would have given it alot less. I also got the game through a steam sale, (paid $3) though it is normally priced decently for what you get, either way. So that's another reason I rated it a little better than I would have.
Here's a breakdown of how I felt about the game.
DATED - This is a slightly more beefed up version of the original PS1 game and as such, its dated for this generation of computers and consoles. This isnt a deal breaker, just an observation. You can however heavily mod the beejeebus out of the game on PC, though to me it was more effort than it was worth and my computer decided shortly after starting that it wasnt having any of it. At that point I switched to PS4 to continue playing.
STORY - The story would be great if it were fleshed out more to make more sense. As this was my first real play through, I actually had to look up summaries, synopsis and other videos to get the whole picture after I played. IGN's 7 min recap video of the FF7 world was very useful after I'd played through the game and included some information that was added in from Crisis Core, etc.
The dialogue and story itself in FF7 felt incredibly rushed and left me slightly confused at times as to what was going on... Though I will admit a good chunk of the confusion here likely stemmed from poor or mistranslations, as I am assuming Square didnt change/fix the dialogue from the PS1 version.
I am a huge fan of story-driven games, but this just felt muddled to me.
COMBAT - Okay this is where the game shined for me. The turn-based ATB style combat is exactly what I love about old Final Fantasy titles and its just as good here as when I played FF6, FF8, and FF9. So I give a big plus to it for the combat. That was fun.
VISUALS - Okay, this is where I have to give a huge MINUS to this game. The background graphics made it severely difficult for me to play this for lengthy periods of time. The game (especially unmodded) would literally give me headaches andI'dhave to stop playing. I had this problem back when I tried to play the original on PS1. I ended up giving my original PS1 game to a friend back in the day because I just couldnt deal with the eye strain and headaches from the visuals at the time. I was hoping that had changed, but not as much as I would have liked. I stillhad to take frequent "recovery" breaks. This is something to think about if your like me and had eye strain from the original.
Also, Trying to find my way around a given section of map was often unclear because the flat 2D graphics made it hard to determine what was actually traversible area or what was just background. I literally got stuck so many times where I had to load up a video walkthrough to figure out where I was supposed to go, and then I'd facepalm because I had missed a path that was right in front of me because it didnt seem like it was traversable because of the way the backgrounds are designed/rendered.
SOUNDTRACK - Okay another huge plus! The music in this game is epic. But then of course it is. It's Final Fantasy! :)
I loved FF7's music for years, even though I had never managed to get through the game before. You don't really need to play the game to enjoy its music though. I mean, who hasnt heard One Winged Angel and loved it :)
----
So that's my honest assessment. Headaches and Eyestrain aside, Immersive Story is a HUGE deal for me, and its what I come to expect from Final Fantasy titles but it just didnt do it for me, so I sadly am rating this a no-go.
That being said, I am probably the only person who never got to play this as a kid, and so my lack of nostalgia for this game has no factor in my review.
Take my words with a grain of salt. If you loved this game as a kid, you'll probably love it now. But if you've never played FF7 at all, ever in your life, I'll give you a simple and fair advice:  Be wary that it may disappoint due to its age and the translation of the story, but If you can pick it up on steam sale like I did, it's worth deciding for yourself if you love it or hate it :)
PS. FF7 lovers. Please don't hate me for the negative review. I reserve judgement on the FF7 world as a whole until after I play the new remake. I just cant like this version ^^;

A lot of people say FF7 is the most overrated FF game/RPG game and guess what? I disagree with that.
If you wanted to play a game that best defines the RPG genre, there's so many titles like SMT Nocturne, Persona 3 FES/4, Dark Soul, Deus Ex etc. to choose from but I think FF7 is the best starter if you're looking to try to get into RPG games.
From what I've played, this is the only good FF game with an interesting cast of characters, story and setting. There's something special about this game that puts it above the others really. It feels like the rest just haven't quite captured that same magic FF7 did.  It's no wonder that this has been the most popular FF game to begin with and the most demanded for a remake (and we finally got it thankfully).
The gameplay itself is turn based combat which requires good strategy and decision making, with battles happening randomly on the field or getting triggered by specific points along the story.
Although the characters look like miniature polygon block versions of themselves when not fighting, the character models are more realistic and proportioned correctly in combat. For its time it was a big step forward because FF7 was the first game in the series to have character models with fully rendered polygons, rather than 2D sprites. Therefore battles take place using a 3D representation of the characters, enemies and the area itself.
Moreover, there are 9 playable characters:
You have Cloud- an blue eyed blonde haired big lad wielding a bigass greatsword.
Tifa- a kind and strong willed tiddy fighter who applies her martial arts skills in combat.
Barret- a very burly, built and all around cool Mr.T who uses guns ( think).
Yuffie, who acts as a nimble ninja and many more.
With a diverse set of characters like I've just described, it's easy to see why something like Final Fantasy 7 was such a huge hit amongst many. It's just a shame that not everyone gets as much development you'd like them to have, which is something I hope the remake really fleshes out considering it's going to be episodic.
Fingers crossed that the remake surpasses the huge waves FF7 made in its time and that the devs won't reduce Tifa's bust size to please non-players who complain about petty things.

Created behind the same mind that brought you Super Meat Boy, The Binding of Isaac is a randomly-generated dungeon crawler with light rpg elements present and constant action. Set in a twisted atmosphere with dark themes ranging from child abuse, gender identity, suicide, abortion and how religion might negatively affect a child, you play as Isaac; a child who is relentlessly being hunted by his mother, who believes her son is corrupted by sin and must sacrifice him to prove her love to her god after hearing his voice. The game can be brutal at moments, due to not knowing how the game is played and randomly generated levels. However, the longer you play the game, the better you will understand how the game is played and where secrets are placed, what the items do and attack patterns your enemies display. It instructs you with trial and error gameplay and it's random but understandable level design. This is easily one of the best designed games I've ever played, and look forward to the remake of this game.
Since this is a flash game,however, expect to have random framerate crashes, as the game is packed with so much content there will be moments where the game will slow down and may even stop responding.
If you are a fan of the NES Legend of Zelda dungeioneering and/or a challenging game with a test of wits and reflexes, this is for you.

I don't understand all the hate this is getting. This game's base mechanics are so similar to the origional that it's extremely difficult for me to even think this was ported TO mobile. Besides, it seems you need gamepad attachments for your phone or something, so why even play it on a phone or anything if you're just gonna slap on some gamepad bits... This is a game that's available on mobile, but doesn't CATER to mobile. Stop calling it a "cheap port from mobile", because that's totally not what it is.
Anyway, my friends and I were a bit skeptical at first because of all the horrible reviews here, but after we bought the game, well, you can see how we liked it from the eighty hours I've clocked in. It's a good game with a few balancing issues still, but they've shown alot of real effort towards balancing progression, stats, gear, and all that fun stuff. It's alot better than it was in DD1.
Why's everyone complaining about summoner? Him having his own personal DU pool was just absurd from a game design perspective. He's no longer OP and uses regular DU like everybody else. I mean sure, he can't attack, but that's kinda the reason his soldiers can move. RTS-em-up, yaknow?
They added amulets (which act as standalone spells) which are pretty nice. They even made new assets and everything for them, it's great. They also help give the player more power to do stuff and aid in balancing out the game. Sure, some have trolling potential, but just get together some friends and play yourselves then.
Public tavern/hub world. I was cool with it, it's not gonna kill me to holler at a few people for friks and giggles, and helps the tavern not be creepily empty like it was all the time in DD1.
If you liked DD1, you'll like this. Also, the "cash shop"? Just a bunch of emoticons as of the time of this review, they're not even worth buying and don't affect the game at all. Dunno if it'll be expanded upon, but right now nothin really freemium or microtransaction-y has happened.
It has always-online servers, and you can only play online. Don't get the complaints about this; this is how MMOs work. Yeah, this isn't an open-world MMO persay, but you could call it an MMO. Plus, when Trendy's servers DO bite the big one, they'll hopefully pass the torch to dedicated servers or something. If they don't, well, SOMEONE's gonna do something about it since this game is online-drivin (at the moment of this review). I don't think they'd just shut the game down and lose all the potential customers. Matchmaking for the game derps now and then, but even big companies have server problems, so should we REALLY bash an INDIE company over such a trivial issue?
No splitscreen yet, the game's being "developed" in a way, as in it's still receiving updates (which is something you should expect from an online MMO-esque game). Splitscreen was initially removed due to exploits involving it from what I've gathered.
I keep calling it "MMO-esque" and the like because, while the public taverns are where you see the bulk of players, each actual game map supports 1-4 players, barring some huge maps which allow 1-6 players if I recall correctly. If you can't deal with trolls or the incompetence of the players in public servers, just get some friends and host private matches.
Content is streamed in, instead of downloaded all at once. Honestly, I prefer it this way. It means I don't have to wait an hour for the game to download if I want to play right away. On the other side the content has to download when you get to it, but I'm cool with that. Core game mechanics are loaded right away, so you won't be bumbling around in a disjointed mess or anything.
Again, this game has a few balancing issues still, but givin the nature of everything I feel that most of them will be ironed out at some point. The game's still a hell of a lot of fun, and it'd be a shame not to give it a try. Don't listen to those clowns who only clocked in under an hour, or barely over an hour, of playtime. Listen to a real Dungeon Defender.
...Besides, if you've owned DD1, discounts stack. I got this for six bucks. That's like, a happy meal at mcdonalds or something. It won't bite back, trust me.
(Oh yeah, by the way, this game has all the relevant DLC of DD1 pre-installed. Knock yourself out, buddy.)

If you're looking for a game with an well excecuted control gimmick, high skill ceilings, appealing simple aesthetic and a groove to go with it, Crypt of the NecroDancer may just be for you.
Not only that, you've got covers of Danny B's amazing original soundtrack for the game by various artists, such as the Aria's Awakening by FamilyJulez, a metal remix of the entire OST or the synthwave covers by Sister Records.
It also comes with a level editor, letting you experiment and get creative with the mechanics of the game and to top it all off, it's easily moddable, with a fully functioning Steam Workshop page that supports both custom levels and mods made by the community.
The only true downsides to this game are it's lackluster story that, while it gives context to the gameplay, doesn't give a depth of lore that, let's be honest, a game like this doesn't need. The second true downside is it's, of course, the signature difficulty curves that comes with many Rouge-lites, though it's multiplied here as one has to memorize enemy patterns, terrain effects, weapon patterns and so much more.
So, if you're ready to dedicate time to learn the ins and outs of this game, give it a go. It's ight.

Final Fantasy 7 has tons of content and lots of replay value, with many quest and party members being easily missable on your first playthrough. On top of this, lots of different materia can be swapped out to change the game completely, and depending on how you level up your party, there can be drastic changes in play style. While the story is engaging and exciting, it does get confusing, and it is ended quite poorly, with little being explained. The game is of a fair length, averaging 50-60 hours, packed with lots to keep your attention. The music and visuals help set the atmosphere in an amazing way, and pull the whole game together, looking somewhat impressive even today in 2016, almost 20 years after the game was originally released. It is clear much heart and soul was put into the game, as there is lots of polish, and many fun little extras. Final Fantasy 7 is a great game for anyone to enjoy, die-hard fan, or complete newbie.

Absolutely gutted to be giving this a thumbs down. Came back to pc gaming after a bit of a hiatus and seen a trailer for a game called Witcher 3, thought it looked awesome so thought i would work my way through this second instalment ready to pick up the third one. Poor control mechanics, you need to be standing in an exact location in order to interact with objects, be it picking herbs or looting a corpse of someone/thing you just wasted. I mean it cannot be that difficult to be able to set a trigger that when within a certain radius of something you are given an option to loot it, not to waste time having to manouver your character into a specific spot in order for the loot option to pop up, same thing with climbing ladders etc. Thats just one of the stupid little niggles that stop this from being a good game, the story looks interesting enough and the fact there is little to no 'hand-holding' as well as a number of paths to take which would alter the gameplay experience (never got that far, got as far as the first village and couldn't find some npc i needed to talk to, yep 6 hours to get through the prologue and the first village - i know i suck at games, lol). This game tries to make you feel like its free-roaming when it is actually on rails, you need to go to certain areas in a specific order in order to activate invisible trigger points that will allow you to progress. One example is i needed to get through some gates to find something, i took a shortcut to the gates and they were locked, went back to where i started, took an alternative way which trigger a pointless cut scene and then when i next approached the gates they were magically unlocked (no npc interaction, didn't pick up a key or anything, it just happened). I know these are only little annoyances but in this day and age they are things that simply should not be happening in games. I mean WoW is what, well over 10 years old now ? Kill something in that and as long as you are in close proximity you can loot it, no need to be having to move your character by a hairs width in order to trigger the loot option. Maybe there are mods that fix this, i dunno but when you buy a game you should not have to rely on mods in order to get the thing to run as it should.

ps: since I'm unable to post without a thumbs up or down, doing with my original opinion until proven otherwise. Steam really needs to introduce a more nuanced scale, or at least introduce a "meh".
OK, finally got the game to re-install after a lot of faffing about. Verdict? No. Don't go there. Another game whose mechanics and controls are so BAD that I'm completely unwilling to subject myself to that kind of torture in order to attempt to finish the game. It's just bad. Pure, unadulterated bad. Distilled bad.
- tutorial graphics suck. Period. I don't know if it's some setting somewhere, but on my relatively high-end system, they suck. Dark, lack of contrast, weird colours, the works.
- the combat system sucks farts from dead goats. They took what was once an elegant system and turned it into something only a Street Fighter multi-combo twitch gamer could love. Button mashing works too though, so much for anything resembing "elegance".
- the inventory system? wow, original Skyrim was better, and it was bad. Lots of junk, almost no way to sort through the stacks of loot.
- alchemy? No more experimentation. You'll get the recipe when the game gives you the recipe, that is all.
- Character upgrading. 120 possible selections. But you only get 1 selection per level, and it's capped at 34 levels. Geralt was a master witcher when you finished Witcher 1. By the end of this game, you're going to barely be an apprentice.
- Quicktime events (and there are many of those) are so badly done even the developers provided a "disable events" button. At least they were self-aware enough to do that. Prime example is the (spoiler!) dragon scene in the prologue. Supposed to "dodge attacks" when you see the button, except the colours and contrast are so bad you can never see the button. So you die. And you die again. Until you turn off the quicktime event and turn the thing into a boring "press the down button to run away until it ends".
- Potions are next to useless. They've cut the duration down to 5 minutes real time. Using cat potion to explore a dungeon? Better have a dozen, they only give you enough time with one to race through it. Once.
- Doorways. Really, doorways. It's an "event" to get through them. You can't trigger events when in combat. So you can't go through an open door at all when in combat. Even if your opponent is on the other side of the door, you can see them, and they can see you. You can move right up to the doorway sill and hit your opponent on the other side of the door, but you can't go through the doorway to actually get to him if he moves away from you just a little. It's just stupid.
- Finally, I despise games that feel they have to cheat by suddenly changing the game physics in order to make something "challenging". Probably because the designers couldn't actually come up with something validly challenging. Take the dagger contest with Ves. Now, I've gotten fairly good at daggers, but in THIS contest the target acts like it's a magnet with the opposite charge of what you're aiming at. So you'll aim at the specfied target and the aim point will go anywhere BUT where you're actually aiming at. It actually jumps OVER the target to the other side, and it's basically a game of complete chance to hit the target. Even though I can hit a running nekker at dozens of paces. They do the same with the arm-wrestling contest, where they take the already assinine mouse lag and make it far, far worse. Randomly. These aren't "games". They're just exercises in frustration created by game developers who hate and despise gamers.
The entire interface feels like a bad port from a game solely intended to be played by console gamers who play a lot of "fighting" games. Overcomplicated combos for combat, easily replaced by just button mashing. Automatic sneak mode when they want you to, not when you choose to do (there's no "sneak" button, yet they still implemented "sneak"?). Automatic targeting that you cannot override because the "target areas" are so freaking huge for some items, which means some targets can "hide" inside other target areas and be inaccessible. (ref: anything near a torch). It's as if they don't expect anyone to be able to point to specific spot or something. Automatic cover in some situations, even when you want to fight - nope, game says "duck and cover". Screw what you want to do. The list goes on, and on, and on.
Example: in the prologue you're supposed to "sneak up on a guard". Well, if the guard happens to be anywhere near a torch, which you're supposed to extinguish, there is no way to force the game to distinguish between the two targets. So you cannot attack the guard if they're anywhere near a torch, simply because the game mechanics never seem to have heard of "letting the user select the target".
I wouldn't know much about the story so far. I've been too busy fighting the interface to be able to get into that. So far though? MASSIVE fail compared to a game I loved, which was Witcher 1. I understand they've provided multiple paths and endings. That's nice. If I finish it once it'll be too often. Unless I can find mods that make the game playable. And viewable.
A definite "do not get this if you can avoid it" thumbs down.

First Encounter Assault Recon is one of the finest first-person shooters I've ever played, as well as one of my favorite games of all time. The level of distinction in F.E.A.R. cannot be overstated enough, so I'll have no-holds-barred in this review when it comes to praise.
F.E.A.R. was originally released on PC in 2005, and was later re-released on Steam in 2010 alongside its expansion packs and some other bonus content not present in the original release. The success of the game's original release eventually lead to it being ported to the Xbox 360 in 2006, and to the Playstation 3 in 2007. The game also received two expansion packs after its release, and spawned an entire first-person shooter series, with the latest release being the inauspicious F.E.A.R. 3 in 2011.
F.E.A.R., named after the similarly-titled emotion
is a primarily single-player FPS. However, it had a multiplayer component which unfortunately is now defunct, as Gamespy (the basis of the game's multiplayer service) was shut down in 2013, with the system's game servers going down for good on May 31, 2014. Still though, multiplayer for F.E.A.R. continues through a fan-made network of servers, based here
As you may have deduced from the game's title and the review before this point, FEAR is a first-person shooter with psychological horror elements. While the game is not very strong strictly from a horror point of view, FEAR still has a very unique and well-implemented atmosphere, and the horror aspects play a big role in what constitutes FEAR as a whole package, and are part of what makes the game such a distinctive experience.
Nevertheless, FEAR's gameplay is that of a first-person shooter, and plays entirely through a first-person perspective. There are very little if any survival horror or similar non-FPS mechanics in this game, and the use horror does not rely on making the player helpless or vulnerable as in traditional horror games. The primary purpose of FEAR's strong atmosphere is to make the player feel paranoid, as if the threat is something internalized, rather than simply an external force threatening them. To that end, the player has full control of their character throughout the entire game, and is never restricted from fighting normally. FEAR does a good job of getting under the player's skin at many points, and scenarios where the player shoots at perceived noises or things that aren't there ("jumping at shadows", for lack of a better term) are common throughout FEAR. Even if this game doesn't scare you entirely, you'll still be treated quite a number of very neat-looking, well-designed set pieces that serve as bridges between the game's more intense shooting sections. My personal favorite is this one hallway where the ceiling starts bleeding, and the player is killed if the downwardly-expanding river of blood touches them before they reach the exit.
Perhaps the most impressive part of FEAR (besides the gameplay itself) is the very detailed use of physics and special effects in the game. FEAR is a very high-technology game, even more so given that it was released in 2005. The grand majority of games released today aren't nearly this well-detailed. Objects will react when shot or when in the midst of explosions; lighting will change when light sources are broken; and pieces of walls and cover can be damaged from gunfire, to say the least. The player's body is also present 100% of the time, in all animations, whether they're climbing a ladder, slide-kicking into an enemy, or simply looking downwards. Such a simple feature as being able to see your own body shouldn't be such an impressive feature by today's standards, but unfortunately, very many modern games have a definite lack of detail and effort put into them. FEAR is not one such title.
Now, as for the gameplay itself: FEAR is a relatively fast-paced first-person shooter, somewhere in-between an arena shooter and something like Half-Life in terms of speed. The player can hold up to three weapons, which they can switch between/swap for other weapons at any point, and they can hold a number of health packs which they can use at any point to heal, as well as a collection of throw-able explosives, including grenades and landmines. The player also has access to a neat albeit somewhat tricky to use melee system, where the player character will do a variety of martial arts moves that can very rapidly disable standard enemies. The most important mechanic in FEAR, as well as one of its main selling points is the ability of the player to slow time at will. This mechanic, aptly called "reflex time", is instrumental to getting through firefights successfully, and provides an excellent context for the player to notice the game's considerable amount of detail in its ballistics and decals even while fighting. Reflex time is also a great help when it comes to getting the upper hand on enemies, as the artificial intelligence in FEAR is extremely advanced. FEAR has been touted as having some of the most advanced AI in video gaming, and this is difficult to question after observing them in actual gameplay.
"Whoa." - Keanu Reeves on FEAR
The way that FEAR relays information and backstory to the player is impressive, as well as a refreshing break from the way most modern games handle storytelling, with large exposition dumps involving poorly-developed, confusingly-motivated characters. To that end, nothing in FEAR is spoon-fed to the player, in neither gameplay nor story. If the player is interested in understanding the story, they need to listen and pay attention to various messages left behind by characters throughout the game, sort of how journal entries work in other games. Everything in this game is given an explanation or history of some sort, and there are few plot holes to be found. Aspects of the story even complement the game at large and make sense when put together with the gameplay or atmosphere, rather than serving as something useless or inconsequential. For example, the main enemies the player fights in the game are made more intelligent and more aware of what they do as on top of being clones of each other, they are also psychically linked to each other.
Psychic powers are a major theme through FEAR. The majority of the horror set pieces are caused by them, and they're the cause of the game's plot at large. The player has frequent encounters with Alma, the psychic antagonist of the game. Unfortunately though, the player is never given any psychic abilities of their own. They do, however, become a mechanic in later FEAR games, but that's another story.
Anyway, FEAR is an amazing game from all angles, and I recommend it to everyone, especially people who are looking for a challenging, intense, and unique experience compared to what most games offer. I have played two games of Stellaris at the time of this writing in a little over 60 hours.
This is the most approachable Grand Strategy game Paradox has ever released.
It makes a good bridge for general strategy players and a great bridge for 4X players into Grand Strategy.
The game pushes the boundary on random vs scripted in it's procedural generation, but I feel that leaves it feeling fresh each time I play. I never know exactly what I'm going to get. Plenty of other items continue to appear regularly from game to game, but racial trait choices change up the decision points. Don't expect a clear overaching narrative, and bring plenty of imagination, and you'll be much happier.
For example in my second game, I choose to mentally skin my cat race as the Wing Commander Kilrathi, making choices not based merely on statistical advantage, but my internal narrative. I was throughly enthralled, and quite tempted by the available modding tools to take it further with custom portraits and name lists, but have not yet dove in.
The UI requires some learning curve, so make sure to take advantage of the many YouTube Let's Plays, the tutorial tips, forums, and in-game browsable wiki. But compared to Crusader Kings 2 I found the systems a breeze to navigate.
The game has been well supported, with three hotfixes in the two weeks since release. A developer post has made clear where the game will be improved and timetables for both free and paid expansions.
Don't expect strong narrative, easy UI, or tactical combat and you'll be happy. Bring imagination, curiousity, and a love for Grand Strategy and you'll have a great time.

Stellaris is an amazing game if you like grand strategies and space. Compared to Paradoxes other grand strategies this one is fairly easy to learn and just generally get into, the resource management isn't very hard and could almost be compared to the Civilization series with the "unique" resources for specific buildings, just as Civ as resources for units. Simple currency management is another thing Stellaris has, it's simple really just make sure your economy can sustain your navies, mining/research stations and buildings on your planet and everything will be alright just to note there is two different type of currencies, Minerals and Energy Credits there isn't a major difference other than the fact they both are used as upkeep for your navies, credits are used for Buildings, stations and armies, as you can tell it's fairly simple just make sure it's not in the minus and you'll be fine.There is also 3 different type of research points you can use to increase research but that's pretty self explanatory if you get the game.
Now, when (and if) you get the game you won't actually have a tutorial unlike most other Paradox titles which normally have a tutorial of sorts, Stellaris offers you a robot called VIR that will help you by giving you tips and giving you a brief explanation of almost everything. A few examples of this is if you were to click on your navy, VIR will give you a brief idea of what a navy does and how you can expand it and upgrade it. The mechanics of Stellaris is fairly simple, in about 20 hours of a singeplayer game I got the general idea of the basics, at 40 hours I now have a general understanding of most techs and how the game plays such as how to expand and what not.  The game isn't hard to get into but if you've played previous titles by Paradox you will almost feel at home with their simple and easy to navigate UI system. Though the game may seem like you'll get bored there is a lot to do and the empire creator aspect of this game is easily one of the best things currently in it.
The game at the moment is well worth it's price but some people don't think it has much to offer even though it is a pretty huge game. at the moment I'd recommed it for it's current price range. And if you're worried about something you read on a website or another review about lack of content or bugs, paradox is currently working on patches and will almost always work on patches to keep the game bug free and add fresh content that people have requested. (They're currently working on a patch right now that'll add more feautures to the empire creator. 19th/May/2016)

Overall if you want a fairly simple and fun Grand Strategy made by one of the best Game Development companies out there, I wholeheartedly recommend you to purchase this, if you don't think it's worth it's price I recommend you  at the least wishlist it and wait for a sale to pop up and then get it.

Take the linearity of Half-Life, but create a game that's actually fun and you have FEAR. Actually, this game is more linear than Half-Life, if that's even possible. It's entirely understandable if you grow tired of corridors and start to feel like you're just going down a conveyor belt with enemies ocassionaly popping out of the darkness in front of you. It's telling when even in a vehicle during the game's intro you're going down an incredibly narrow path whereby there's barely any space between the car and the walls. It's as if the developers refused to have any sort of open areas present in even the most sensible of places.
But linearity isn't bad. In fact, this game is a strong showcase of how linearity can be used to craft a strong single-player experience. While the corridors may make you feel constricted, at the same time they are conducive to brilliant enemy ai that knows its surroundings and moves accordingly. Linearity also allows a developer to craft an experience that ensures certain events are experienced a particular way and come about in proper order. Linear progression in level design means that you are strapped to a roller coaster and ride through all events in a manner that leaves no doubt in the creator's mind that you got the specific emotional ride he/she was looking to put you through.
The game is littered with many events where something 2spooky happens which is only possible through a constricted experience whereby the developer knows you are looking a particular way or going down a particular path. While getting the exact reaction out of you is only possible through linearity, it's a positive that quickly falls back down to neutral due to the negatives that weigh it down. You see, because all the 'scares' are crafted in a linear experience, you can often see them coming. It doesn't help that you get a little 'UNKNOWN SIGNAL' prompt at the top left of the screen whenever the little girl appears somewhere in the map trying to scare you. It aids in letting you know that an event is occuring and you might miss it, but that defeats the purpose of surprising/scaring you.
Not that the 'fear factor' in the game is that great anyway. Personally I wasn't frightened by the title, but it does do a fantastic job at crafting some good atmosphere. Remember: you don't actually have to succeed at scaring people to create an atmosphere that is eerie. Theres excellent use of lighting throughout and great pacing between the game's more hectic moments that leaves you wondering if a firefight is afoot or a 'jump scare'. Trying to create an FPS that is also horror-based is a tough balancing act, and this game pulled off that tight rope walk admirably.
It's a shame that the plot itself couldn't have more meat to it. It feels a little bare-bones, with the story feeling more like justification for the little girl character and all the creepy shenanigans. It's as if they created the game and characters first, and then realized they needed a plot to tie it together; story came towards the end of development, essentially. But something tells me they had the plot down, and then got down to level creation and just kept on creating more and more until they had to stretch the already thin plot even thinner to last through the constant stream of levels. So I guess it's excusable, if not a shame. After all, gameplay comes first, even if plot is the motivator for me to keep progressing.
All said, if you don't mind linearity and a rather simple plot it's a great experience that is held up by its atmosphere and enemy ai that is carefully balanced between eerieness and enjoyable firefights.

Why I like Final Fantasy VIII more than most: (Warning contains major spoilers to the plot)
1 - The music. Sure every Final Fantasy has a few good songs out of their soundtrack, but Final Fantasy VIII, almost every other song is excellent!
2 - The Characters. Yes, sure most say that Final Fantasy VIII has the weakest character selection and is a cliche. And the student/teacher relation plot is overused. But it's not the relationship, it how you relate to them. Everyone can be like Squall; quiet, sticks to themselves, and puts themselves first. Say you don't have any of those qualities, I dare you! If Squall isn't you then you must be Zell (Jock) or Irvine (Playboy)?
3 - The Secondary Plot Line. Sure, I'm not big on the whole war thing... But hear me out. It's not really about fighting the sorceress from the future who corrupted the sorceresses of the past and today. Well, it kinda is. But the back plot is: As much as Squall looks quite on the inside, he really want's acceptance. Most orphans are like that; stick to themselves because they don't want to get hurt again.
4 - The Story. Now I'm going to the primary plot line. Squall is a SeeD (a mercenary) who's sole job is to defeat the Sorceress Edea along with the other SeeD cadets to ultimately gain peace. Though the story to Final Fantasy VII was a bit better... But this is about VIII! But then... Squall finds out that Edea is/was the lady in charge in the orphanage (What a twist!) along with the other party members, they all were orphans together (except Rinoa) And now Squall want's the Sorceress to live. Fights her hoping for the best, then Rinoa gets possessed. Later in the game, he will forgo all he knew and lived by if Rinoa wasn't cured and become a Sorceress' Knight. That's what makes this story so compelling and an emotional journey. The emotion put in this game is stronger than VII.
5 - The Side Quests. Triple Triad was the best side quest out of every Final Fantasy. Sure Final Fantasy IX had a card game... But there were no REAL rules or at least none that were explained in depth. In VII you could raise Chocobos which was fun to a point, but very repetitive! The card game in VIII if you got one of Quetzalcoatl's abilities you could mod the cards into items. That made getting a perfect 100% hard!
6 - Sis, come back to me... I'm all alone (Ellone). She is the key to the whole game. She doesn't get much screen time. But is a very key character! She takes Squall and gang to 'The Dream World' where they see through Laguna, Kiros and Ward's eyes. To understand the sorceress and what went on before the war. But that wasn't really her motive. Her motive was to make Uncle Laguna stay with her. This is where Rinoa comes into play. Laguna was madly in-love with a singer at a bar named Julia. And Julia's song 'Eyes on Me' (voiced by Faye Wong. That song makes me want to cry...) was all about Laguna. But since Laguna kept getting called all over the world (since he was a soldier and all) she married another, General Caraway. Even though her last name is Heartilly (Presumed to be Julia's last name). So that would make Laguna a very key part in the story... Well he is! He put a stop to Sorceress Adel (Though... Adel looks like a man...). But I guess where I'm going with this point is: Knowing the past, is the key to the future. He then became the President of Esthar (who was the very enemy when he was a Galbadian Soldier). All in search of his little Elle. Ellone was searching for Laguna, whilst he did the same.
Well, I can go on-and-on on how perfect Final Fantasy VIII is, but I won't. I'm probably boring you all to tears. Well I guess "It's like killing two pigs with one stone. I'm just so awesome... Genius, I tell you..." "Pigs? I think you mean birds."
Well no... I was just trying to get a point across! Final Fantasy VIII is one of the most unappreciated Final Fantasies of all time!

So far, so good. And I mean
good. The story, admittedly, has been done before (Ex-superevilarmy soldier suddenly can't remember things because reasons and is now good guy but slowly uncovers his dark past and has to reconcile with his sins etc etc), but it isn't presented or executed (at least so far) in an incredible cliched or dull manner. It's clear that Dust, the main protagonist and player character, actually did some pretty evil stuff and assisted in the annihilation of a race (or maybe only partially). When you figure out more about Dust, you start to become wary of learning about his past, afraid of what you might uncover and realize who you are playing as.
Gameplay is solid, hack-and-slash type deal with mobs of enemies coming at you once. I immediately went to hardcore mode starting out, and personally I feel like a lot of the difficulty does come simply from damage outputs from enemies being increased. I can be dancing around everyone, sawing through flocks of those flying toad dudes with dust storm, and suddenly git rekt if I get hit like once or twice (ie the insta-kill giants, but considering they're giants that makes sense). This isn't to say the enemy AI aren't smart in their own right, definitely not a bunch of bumbling idiots with aim-bot and ridiculous stats (*cough*modernfps*cough*), but it does effect my experience enough to be noted. The combos, tho,
. I swear I feel like a Touhou character whizzing around and throwing everyone and everything into the air and then showering the battlefield with bullets from Fidget and making Storm from the X-Men look like a South Dakota summer breaze on a Sunday in July. I am rewarded executing a long chain of combos and moves and what nots with extra experience rather than just spamming a basic or other attack. In fact, you can't even spam a single attack or any single set of attacks, because you'll git rekt. The mechanics of each move or dust storm or Fidget's bullets force you to change things up as you go along because even these super-amazing-I'm-a-♥♥♥♥ing-god move sets have their limits, even hurting yourself in some casese if not executed properly. Skill is needed to cut through literal armies of monster mooks.
Speaking of the enemies, the design is repititive but at the same time varied. In the first chapter, you'll see the same monsters from the beginning continuously re-appear throughout to the end, while others are still added as you go along. However, very rarely did I see more than two of the same looking hairless-club-wielding-dog-thing, each enemy type has several skins to change around and add some color to what would otherwise be a boring homogeneous legion. Even futher, the basic design and look of each enemy is pleasant to look at in itself. They're colorful and full of little details that give the mooks some character of their own. I even found myself feeling a little sorry for them, wondering if they had hopes and dreams of their own, but I guess that's just my traumatization from Undertale talking.
The final boss of chapter one definitely threw the plot for a loop. At first I thought "oh no super cliche warlord guy rallying usually non-threatening army of mountain monsters into a full-fledged and organized assault where HAVEN'T I seen this before", which is still technically true even after defeating him and listening to his dialogue. This game feels like a pale shadow of GC2. I loved that game. My parents bought a battered copy of the collectors edition for me as a Christmas present many years ago. I remember obsessively reading about the development of the expansions in PC Gamer and I bought all of them on Stardocks unique service (which I haven't used in years). When I saw GC2 on steam, I bought it in a heartbeat and got a good 50hrs of play out of a game I had already played thousands of hours over the course of my childhood. I honestly consider GC2 to be one of the best, if not best, 4x games I have ever played. So it  pains me to say GC3 feels like, in many ways, a step back. It lacks much of the complexity GC2 had at its end of development state. Gone are the unique tech trees and planetary super weapons. I hear asteroid mining has finally been added and the AI has been brought up to a respectable level of quality so thank god for that.
Perhaps what irks me the most is the loss of detail and ease of use when it comes to managing your very large empire. GC2 had sliders for everything and a big, in game spreadsheet where you could interact with all your planets without having to view each one. This made playing super large maps very easy and while the new circle slider may look pretty on small maps, it is painful to use when you have 100+ planets under your sway. Then there's the starbase management. This was a problem even in GC2 and you think they'd come up with a solution in all these years.
My final gripe is the DLC. Really Stardock? I used to admire you for releasing respectable expansions but this is just pathetic. Lump all those DLCs into one or two expansions packs because the one you have (mercenaries) is paper thin by your own previous standards. I don't understand. Do you guys feel you need more money so you're releasing tidbits of content? If  that's so, why did you almost immediately sell this game at $25? I would have gladly paid $60 if it meant you guys would actually put out meaty expansion packs.
So yeah, I don't recommend this game. It looks a little bit prettier than GC2 but is inferior in just about every way to a varying degree. I feel like crying after writing this.
Feels very lackluster with tons of content to make you pay. I guess to each his own but personally I'd recommend giving it some time before making a hasty purchase.

Dungeon Defenders: Eternity, a sort of hold over title released by TrendyENT to test out their playverse system and to tide Dungeon Defender fans over until the awaited sequal releases, is quite the game.
Eternity holds true to the core game in that you grind through numerous dungeons... Kill tons of enemies and bosses... and farm for even better loot to upgrade and destroy "The Old Ones" with. That said, the game has been changed around plenty enough to give a new feel to even the most veteran of defenders.
Added to Eternity are a plethora of new systems and tweaks that really give the game that fresh coat of paint it deserves. Eternity starts you off with all 12 of the games classes right off of the bat, as well as all of the maps from the core game, and the download packs(holiday maps aside) rolled into one. On top of that it starts you off with several costumes unlocked, with some being put behind achievement walls giving you something extra to work towards just as you had to with the first game. Aside from the characters and maps, TrendyENT added in a much welcomed dodge mechanic that allows you to jump out of harms way in an instant, so long as you have the energy for it. Both hero and monster damage has been reworked, the overall games balancing has been given some loving, and the overall display has been given a fresh look. The game also features new maps not seen in the core game or in any of it's downloadable packs, as well as a new looting and crafting system. Gone is the mana bank and coins have taken their place. Coins can be used to upgrade weapons, buy items/consumables that you can use in battle, and even to purchase colored dyes which can be used to recolor practically every inch of your character in numerous ways. The pet system was also given an overhaul, as you now collect pets by gathering eggs mid-battle and hatching them. You'll never know what pet species you'll get until it hatches!
My only real gripe with the game so far is it's launcher. The launcher itself is horrible... It can take quite a while to download a patch, or the core game resources, which most will find to be annoying. Aside from that the game feels, looks, and plays like Dungeon Defenders, but better. I've spent roughly 15 hours at this point actually playing the game, and it's a purchase I most certainly do not regret!!
I highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys Action RPGs, Loot grinding games(similar to diablo and borderlands), Tower Defense games, Co-op titles, and fantasy styled games. It's a lot of fun, and even more so when you play with friends. With plenty of maps, challenges, and classes (With more maps coming soon for free), there is always a ton to do in Etheria.
Happy Defending, and see you in the Playverse!

Want to play a MOBA without microtransactions?
Titans pass gives you x4 gems which is the currency used to buy dragon eggs and weapon packs.
Dragon egg packs cost 5000 gems  and weapon packs cost 2500 gems.
Gems are earned by playing matches and is the only currency in game.
Titans pass gives you all the dragons and weapons available. So you don't need to buy weapon. But that dosn't mean you need to stop buying  dragon packs. Because in this game. There are ways of making your favored combo stronger.
BUT this involved getting to know every dragon. So dragon packs are the only way to do this. You combine 3 of the same dragons to increase its teir. A higher teired dragon has more health and reduced cooldown for abilities. There is also more health regen. Likewise. Weapons themselves can be paired with any dragon. Allowing versitility of the play style of over 27 dragons and weapons to make combinations with, and a growing list of weapons and dragons monthly.
Titans pass gives you all the content you would get from microtransactions for a solid year.
So any dragon or weapon to be released is yours. But as mentioned. Your farming quest is not over when you buy Titans pass.
Because you still need to farm Mastery, another way to maximize your dragon. By playing your dragon more, the dragon itself gains xp going up in mastery rank with 5 teirs. First teir is basic, Second teir is bronze theird is silver fourth is gold and 5th is platnium.
With each mastery upgrade to your favored dragon it gains more health and becomes faster and stronger.
But don't let that fool you into thinking its an automatic win. Because combos and team mate support is the basic structure of this game.
With good combos, and good team support. You have a better chance of winning. And with titan pass. You get to start with your favored combos early. And believe me there are over 70 combos currently to chose from. How?
Because of runes and weapons forge. That is why.
Not only do weapons have their own play style coupled with dragons. But there are 30 ranks which you the player earn.
You buy runes packs of 3 to give your dragon those extra stats you need to make your combo you want TO WORK. THAT'S RIGHT. 2 runes activate every time you level. So you need to pick wisely what your combo will be. Survivability? Damage? Support? Tank? What will you play?
There is so much to chose from. In any other MOBA you would have to shell out hundreds of dollars to get the oppertunity you get here for 20$. And even if you don't pay. You could easily achieve such status in a month of playtime.

Stellaris is an amazing game if you like grand strategies and space. Compared to Paradoxes other grand strategies this one is fairly easy to learn and just generally get into, the resource management isn't very hard and could almost be compared to the Civilization series with the "unique" resources for specific buildings, just as Civ as resources for units. Simple currency management is another thing Stellaris has, it's simple really just make sure your economy can sustain your navies, mining/research stations and buildings on your planet and everything will be alright just to note there is two different type of currencies, Minerals and Energy Credits there isn't a major difference other than the fact they both are used as upkeep for your navies, credits are used for Buildings, stations and armies, as you can tell it's fairly simple just make sure it's not in the minus and you'll be fine.There is also 3 different type of research points you can use to increase research but that's pretty self explanatory if you get the game.
Now, when (and if) you get the game you won't actually have a tutorial unlike most other Paradox titles which normally have a tutorial of sorts, Stellaris offers you a robot called VIR that will help you by giving you tips and giving you a brief explanation of almost everything. A few examples of this is if you were to click on your navy, VIR will give you a brief idea of what a navy does and how you can expand it and upgrade it. The mechanics of Stellaris is fairly simple, in about 20 hours of a singeplayer game I got the general idea of the basics, at 40 hours I now have a general understanding of most techs and how the game plays such as how to expand and what not.  The game isn't hard to get into but if you've played previous titles by Paradox you will almost feel at home with their simple and easy to navigate UI system. Though the game may seem like you'll get bored there is a lot to do and the empire creator aspect of this game is easily one of the best things currently in it.
The game at the moment is well worth it's price but some people don't think it has much to offer even though it is a pretty huge game. at the moment I'd recommed it for it's current price range. And if you're worried about something you read on a website or another review about lack of content or bugs, paradox is currently working on patches and will almost always work on patches to keep the game bug free and add fresh content that people have requested. (They're currently working on a patch right now that'll add more feautures to the empire creator. 19th/May/2016)
It's a solid 6/10. The game, as it stands doesn't have the best diplomacy with A.l. It can be quite boring as it's easy to beat the AI unless you're at a major disadvantage. Though to shine some light on Singeplayer, they have more missions that you'll receive as you go on playing the game. Also playing ironman to get achievements is nice if you want to try and get a few.
It's around about 8-9/10. Multiplayer is very fun at the moment, it's probably going to be one of the only times you'll experience a real space battle with tactics and mixed weaponary as the AI just doesn't seem to do that. Diplomacy can work slighty better than how it would with the AI and alliances/federations will become something people might need to survive or just to prevent a intergalactic war from happening. (Also conflict is amazing when you steal someones planet they wanted to colonize.)
Overall if you want a fairly simple and fun Grand Strategy made by one of the best Game Development companies out there, I wholeheartedly recommend you to purchase this, if you don't think it's worth it's price I recommend you  at the least wishlist it and wait for a sale to pop up and then get it.
