Stellaris is atmospheric and engrossing. It certainly comes with its share of frustrations and strange design choices, but it nevertheless works on many levels: as a compulsive 'just five more minutes' strategy game, an intriguing political, diplomatic, economic and military simulator, a generator of stories both emergent and writerly, and a love-letter to classic literary science fiction. That's the game now - I imagine it will be quite extraordinary in a couple of updates' time.
Much has been said and written about the unfriendly user interface in this game, but frankly I thought the whole thing was quite streamlined and accessible, particularly compared to other entries in the sub-genre (Gal Civ 3, I'm looking at you!). Once you've mastered the basics - and the tutorial system actually works quite well for this, for a change - the game will open up to you.
Now, about those frustrations: some are simply glitches, like a bit of questionable AI here and there. Others feel like big blank gaps, awaiting the announcement of some future update or DLC (like the relatively saggy mid-game, the strange uniformity of end-game crises, the weird lack of options for sophisticated features like alliances, the half-baked political systems, the noticeable lack of stats and graphs to help track your empire's performance). Some frustrations seem to be firm design choices, though, which means you'll have to get on board or give up: technological research isn't targeted with use of a tech tree, as in most games, but is random - a constant feeling-your-way exercise that might, with a bit of bad luck, leave you unable to colonise whole types of worlds until near the endgame (for example) or keep throwing you options to upgrade weapons systems that you don't need.
But none of this matters in the context of the game's bigger achievements: big, broad-brushstrokes imperial competition; exciting, well-written adventures and sci-fi scenarios; tons of atmosphere. The latter achievement is hugely aided by this game's soundtrack, which is about as close to perfect as game soundtracks get.
So: it's definitely a 'buy' now, and it'll be an even more firm 'buy' later, after a bit of polish and new content. That's it.

I would really, really like to write a great, well-formulated and sophisticated review for Stellaris... but for that I would have to stop playing it. And that's not going to happen anytime soon. 10/10
UPDATE:
1 1/2 years later. I have now spent 2000 hours in this game, bought every DLC and Expanison, achieved every Achievement, won on hardest difficulty and I guess it is time to write a proper review.
This game has replaced CIV as my all-time favorite game. When Stellaris came out, it was fun, but pretty barebones. Yet it showed enormous potential and the developers have delivered on this promise. Stellaris offers a solid 4X-experience with a twist, is viually stunning, and due to its focus on storytelling is one of the most immersive strategy games I know. Despite some issues, the gameplay is great and if the looks and feel were not enough, Stellaris features an amazing soundtrack as well.
But one of the best things about Stellaris is the community. The devs - foremost Martin "Wiz" Anward, are in constant communication with the player base, keeping us updated about what is going on, demonstrating new features and taking in feedback. They do not shy away from rethinking the game if the players clearly demonstrate some imbalance or other issues, and incorporate ideas from the online discussions.
Currently, we are at version 1.9, with most of the updates bringing in improved and expanded game mechanics or new content. While the improvements to the game are free, I have bought all DLCs as well, because they usually add some worthwhile content. But not only that, but I want to support the continued developement of this game with every Euro I can spare. If it had a Patreon, I would voluntarily pay extra money for this great game.
Wiz is now telling us about Stellaris 2.0 and this will be a major overhaul of the game. Everything we have been shown so far clearly says, that Paradox is determined to make this the best game possible, because they love this game as much as I and so many others do.

Witcher 2 is a major improvement of the previous game: it has a more intricate story, the combat is not dull anymore and it's even more atmospheric. and graphics are spectacular even by today's standards.
However, there are some old issues that haven't been addressed since the first game. I've recently started playing Witcher 3, and it seems that those flaws are consistent throughout the trilogy, namely:
1. The game offers choices. But the consequences aren't very different. Your choices mostly determine, who will be your ally, who dies and who lives. OK, it's kind of relevant, but it's nothing radical, because the global events stay the same, no matter what you do. The protagonist is a mere pawn in the hands of the destiny as any other character.
What I'm trying to say, is that THE GAME DOESN'T PUNISH OR REWARD YOU FOR YOUR CHOICES IN ONE WAY OR THE OTHER. And in that aspect, your choices don't really matter.
(Note: Ok, in Witcher 3 choices matter, but no matter what you do - someone dies :D)
Although, I must admit that Witcher 2 is a minor step forward in this aspect, because what you did in Witcher 2 partially determines who is your ally in Witcher 3 and how strong/independent are some of the fractions in the game universe. Whereas nothing but tiny details were transfered from Witcher 1 to Witcher 2. It was like starting from a blank page.
2. Level scaling problems. Gameplay is challenging in the beginning, but a cakewalk towards the end.
3. Constant shortage of money (orens). I used two mods to address this problem: Zero Weight mod that allows to infinitely store items in your inventory and a Price Changer mod that makes everything cheap, except the armor.
Witcher 2 is very atmospheric, as are the other games in the trilogy. It offers a very tangible experience of a medieval world. And the NPCs are very complicated and interesting. However, it's much shorter and the story felt rushed towards the end. There was less and less to do with each following chapter. It takes ~70 h to complete every quest in Witcher 1 and only ~30-35 h to complete every quest in Witcher 2.
Also, there are only a few sexual encounters, contrary to Witcher 1, where there were many and you could collect romance cards. Not that it really matters, but I liked that card feature quite a bit.
On a side note, I would like to say that some of the bombs and all the throwing daggers are too weak. Only Stinger is quite strong, but, anyway, the daggers have limited number of situations were they are useful, as is the case with traps. The opportunity windows are just too narrow. They are cool weapons and bombs like Grapeshot, Dragon's Dream and Dancing Star, do come in handy, but, in overall, swords and magic are superior to alchemy, meaning that the Alchemy path is not equal to Magic and Swordsmanship path. One would expect that all the paths are balanced.
On the bright side, there are barely no fetch quests in Witcher 2. You do a lot of interesting investigation and every quest falls in the overall picture nicely. As you are working on one quest, you are simultaneously solving the others. I very much liked that. Everything was well thought through. And the amount of detail – it's just lovely.
I am writing this review after my second playthrough, and I must say that I still enjoyed the game very much. Witcher 2 is one of my all time favourite games. I have started Witcher 3 now and it seems that it's going to be my number 1 game of all time.
CD Projekt Red, keep it up!

F.E.A.R is really fantastic.
The textures/graphics are pretty dated, but Lighting and Smoke effects actually hold up really well and cover up the blemishes.
The Enemy AI, weapon balance, weapon handling and "horror" elements are all equal to the best examples in modern gaming, which is both a tribute to the great people who built this game, and also exposes most modern game designers who haven't learned from it.
There is lots of "gameyness" in this, but it's only done for the benefit of gameplay. You can always hear enemies chatting before you see them, and when they're all dead, the music gets quiet and stops, so you always know when you should have your finger on the trigger.
Horror and action elements are kept pretty separate. Horror elements NEVER involve monster closets opening behind you (only the occation vision when you turn around), and at all points, the games plays very fair with allowing you to see enemies before they see you.
The game is very linear, but there are enough secrets that lead to either slight powerups or creepy horror visuals that there's just enough exploration to scratch that itch.
Physics are pretty basic and exaggerated, but only in a way that increases the fun. Enemies' heads and limbs really fly, but not too far.
Weapons are all useful and balanced (except maybe the crappy submachine gun) in terms of ammo capacity, accuracy, damage and availability, and chopping off heads with the laser cutter and pinning enemies to walls with the nailgun are both among the best shooting experiences across the entire genre.
The only real faults I have with F.E.A.R and and its expansions are that there's not enough environmental and enemy variety, and that the story is crappy and not very well presented. But the gameplay more than makes up for that.
Each expansion adds a couple new enemy types and a couple new guns. That means Perseus Mandate is by far the most varied gameplay-wise, but by that point, you might be a bit burned out. Main game takes around 10-14 hours to play through while each expansion is around 4-6 hours. Perseus mandate involves a different character than base game and extraction point, so after the first game, if you're feeling a bit burnt out, I'd actually recommend playing perseus first since it's better than Extraction point.
NOTE: Neither expansion is "canon" to the series, so if you plan on playing FEAR2, you won't miss anything by skipping them.

It gives all sorts of great combat stats, but wrecks your cruising speed, which is the speed the autopilot mostly uses... and boy, do you spend a lot of time using autopilot in this game (backtracking to turn in quests, etc.). So when trying to decide whether to use this item, you're really trying to decide whether you're willing to endure more tedium than you already are.
How many decisions like that is a player going to make before quitting?

As a player who has put in over 450 hours of game play for DD1, I was excited to hear about this "definitive" version. I knew from the start that yes it was the same game just with new features, no I won't have any of my old DLC since this is a new/separate game, and was excited about the visual gear (because I'm a firm believer in personal customization).
So lets jump into the game.
We start by making a profile which is fine. We did this in the old game, then we hit the “Play” button. I'm expecting to see a choose or create a character screen, but instead I'm in the tavern as a random cavern with a few dozen other people. In my confusion I just have to ask how do I make a character because nothing explains how. No brief tutorial, no inn keeper popping up on the side of my screen saying “hey, welcome, lets start by showing you around”. I actually restart the game a few times thinking this was a bug.
Once I find out how to change my character, I decide to start how I started in the old game. Playing solo and leveling three different characters: Mage, Series EV, and the Summoner.
Hours into the game, I find a few things very pleasing:
Coin System: New currency system.
Eggs: Pets in the old game were super rare.
Pet abilities: Being able to have certain pets that do certain things helps with customization.
4 new player abilities: These can be either eggs, consumables, or new skills.
Trading through Play-verse: I can trade gear with friends even when they are offline.
Visual gear & Dye: Again, I'm am all for customization.
New Survival system: Rather then just more waves, you start and are pressured to build as the waves progress. More skill intensive.
However I also find other things displeasing:
Having to use play-verse to create groups with friends. Now I have no problem with games using their own system. Especially when multi-platform games. But the system its self is just super slow. Nothing shows you how to use it. Like having to create a party first, THEN add your friends rather then adding a friend and a party automatically being created.
The Tavern: I know this is supposed to act like a main player hub. I nick-named it “Stormwind” from World of War craft. A place where all players go to when not doing quest's or missions. However the Tavern was originally built for a single player. Being able to show case mission rewards and host there own shops to earn mana. A system no longer in the game.
The timer before a match starts: Maybe its just be being used to the old game where the match would immediately begin. I'm guessing it's like your League of Legends before play screen where it waits for everyone to load the data so the game play it's self can be smoother. But this is still the case for solo play.
Make one character: Unlike the old game, you do no have split-screen capabilities that allow you to level up multiple characters, or invite friends to play on your account. This is more of a “if you want to play it, you must buy it on your own system.” which is in a total different direction then the first. But $$$ is $$$.
Character swapping not as relevent. In the old game, to be a good solo player, you had to swap between characters during build phases. Build your towers, build your a.o.e bubbles, build your summoner minions, kill with your warrior. Now it's still possible to do this, but it's so hard to level a new character since you cannot run it yourself. Maybe running your own alts wasn't a normal intention even in the first game.
What it needs:
Some way to help players better understand what it is they are doing. What to do, and what everything means.
If it is so hard to level up multiple classes, show a preview or have a detailed list on what a character does. Like e.g. Barbarian. “Since he cannot build defense, he uses two weapons and stances to destroy waves of enemies” before players embark on the journey and waste their time.
Overall:
If you own the first DD, if your looking for new new, this isn’t it. However this is a good refresher.
I will stick in a few more hours because I just like the overall feel that DD gives and I know that this is still early and it's a preview for whats to come in DD2. Using DD as a trial and error system.

Game Review:


New system allows for a more rebalanced look at the classic dungeon defenders and grants old players that new player experience. While some feel that this is not true, I feel after playing DD1 for hours on end that this is in fact true. Keep in mind that the game does not allow you to transfer over a character from DD1, so you will have to start over at level 0. Each game you play presents the same thing you saw in DD1, chests, monsters, etc. However the chests are now for you only. What does this mean? Every player sees a chest and, lets just say that if another player tries to take it then they would just opened a chest that was for them specifically, you still have yours! Pretty cool... this means more mana than normal to start with, if you have enough players.
The game drops coins and mana now. Mana is used for upgrading towers and using special abilities like amulets, pets, and hero skills. Coins are used for upgrading armor and weapon pieces. This does provide a nice divide between the fighting environment and the tavern environment.
Wait what? Why did I list this as a pro? Okay, so here's the deal. Trendy decided to setup any real money transactions that will allow people to buy emotes... and that's it. Good job on that one, I'm cool with this. If you need a little extra cash for emotes, I'll do that.
New items have been added to help boost the gameplay. The amulets can do multiple types of abilities depending on which one of 4 you can bring into battle. Some of the abilities that you can choose are repair towers, weaken enemies, heal players, boost weapon damage, and so on.
Blueprints drop randomly throughout maps you play. You can use ingredients found in chests to then craft the item on the blueprint at the craftmaster found in the tavern. Some people say that this provides an overall better stats item, however, I did not notice this. But I will say you can save the blueprint and make multiple weapons or armor if you wish, which is cool if you want to have multiple pieces of the same armor because it has awesome tower stats!
The new inventory system is much easier to use
you get through the challenges of learning how to manipulate the commands. For example "M" unlocks all items that are displayed, "A" sells all items that are displayed. I'm being specific in saying "that are displayed" because if they aren't displayed with your filter settings on, then you won't sell them on accident... huge bonus :) They also added folders just like the old game, however you have a bit more freedom with how many you can add. Oh yeah... did I mention 0/1000 slots? That's much better.
Dyes are cool if you are into asthetics, however, I am not. But none-the-less this is an awesome feature for people who like to get off on detailed coloring of their armor pieces. The amount of detail that was added so you can completely customize the color scheme is, to me, a bit more than I care to do, especially since I'm swapping gear so often. Until the recent patch v3.2 you were unable to sell dye and it would stack in your inventory. Now it's been fixed.
Pets are different in this game than the original DD1. In this game you find eggs and you hatch them by putting them in your amulet slots and let them get exp while you fight. Once it notifies you that the egg is ready to hatch then you go into a forge and inspect the egg. There will be an option to hatch the egg and it will produce for you a random pet. Each pet has it's own passive ability as well as an activated ability, which is hotkeyed to "X". This system allows you to experiment and determine which pet you want for yourself rather than run a map over and over for, I dunno, something like a kobold?
While a lot of people complain about the color of the texture and say "it's blurry" etc, I want to let everyone know that the game does say "Please allow for images to stream because they may be blurry in the beginning", which was true. Once I allowed for the game to play for a while, the color system worked pretty well. There is a difference and after going back to DD1 to help a friend, I prefer the new DDE colors.
The game no longer seems to be running through steam systems. When I attempt to go visit "who I've partied with recently" it no longer records them. In addition, the overlay menu that trendy uses is extremely difficult and in what appears to be a beta type version. Nothing is easy or smooth. To access the menu first press F11, completely out of the way and not as easy as Shift-Tab for Steam Overlay menu.
If you want to party with your friends get ready for a challenge. If they are in the same tavern as you, awesome you are in luck! Press Esc and look for their name and "add to party", cool right? Okay what if they aren't one of the 16 players in the tavern? Sh!t.... ok go to Overlay menu F11, go to the second tab from the top, click right twice until you get to friends, click the dropdown on your friends name, click add to party and wait... did he add? Oh he's gotta accept.... ok he finally accepted. F11 to get back outta overlay menu. They could make it much more user friendly if they tried.
Survival maps used to be in waves, 1 to 35 for tavern defense in DD1. NO LONGER IS THIS TRUE, this is pretty cool in my book. This does present a problem because now you are confined to 1 character through the entire survival, not cool;  sometimes we want to level our alts. In addition to this issue there is also an issue with mana in the beginning. Each player has their own chest as mentioned before, which would limit you as a single player trying to build for an entire survival because you cannot switch and build the build completely as you would in DD1. For example Endless Spires Survival, if I run it as a single player I get 375 total from all the chests, if I have 3 other players I would get 1500 mana for my build because players can pool mana like in DD1. So at the moment survival sucks because we HAVE to bring in other players in order to build the build we want.
None. They don't have it in the game. If you wanna go in and afk 24/7 to get up to level 60, go for it. The only thing they have to prevent afking is a very long timer that attempts to sense if you are afk after something like 25 minutes of "not moving" which doesn't include being dead. So if someone is afk and keeps dying, well they get to be in the game the entire time.
The stage selection screen is quite nice, however it's just my personal opinion that the screen is larger than need be and not as concise in the information presented. The biggest drawback looking for a game to play with random people is that you cannot see all of the maps that are in play. If you haven't completed the stage, it won't show for you if others have space. This really limits the number of people who join your game, especially if you are doing end game content and need the help of others.
There is an issue that causes the game to not hold the comparison window up of an equipped item and an item you are mousing over. This blip of disappearance is on-set by people joining the tavern, and taverns are public so this happens very often.
The game has it's pro's and con's as you can see above. After being a fan of DD1 and coming to DDE I was originally seething with anger because of what I saw, however, now I can say that I really enjoy DDE more than DD1. You just gotta get in the game and play it a bit. It's worth it in the end and I support it, even with all it's terrors.

It's Minecraft without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It's Farmville without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
It's a deconstruction of the whole RPG genre. The only castle you have is your home, the only quests are the future.
Yes, it's aggravating at first. You search desperately for the bandits and the dragons and pretty princesses. You watch videos and expect extreme dubstep drops from space.
But, spoiler alert, you won't miss such trivialities. The game wakes you up from such petty tropes. What good is a princess with 2 lines of text? Or a recurring enemy who appears hundreds of times in the course of walking from 1 town to another?
Farming Simulator 2013 doesn't try lying to you, not once. The game offers you quests every so often, to mow a lawn or haul a crate across the lush, bountiful countryside. A simple diversion to earn a simple amount of cash while your farm hands do the repetitive tasks.
And then oh god yes, the multiplayer. Sublime bliss, shared amongst your friends.

I'm a long time fan of Paradox games, having played Mount and Blade: Warband, Europa Universalis IV (all expansions), Crusader Kings II (all expansions, again), and Cities: Skylines. Stellaris is just  like any other Paradox game: detailed and made as a labor of love.
Pros:
- Very immersive experience, letting you fine tune most, if not all aspects of your chosen spacefaring empire, from their biology and architecture to their base habits and societal views. Will they be peace loving space hippies, totalitarian slavers, budding economists, or something inbetween- possibly sillier.
- Excellent micromanagement in the form of colonies. As of now, there aren't *very* fleshed out, but you still have plenty of options available to  you, such as what buildings to place and what the spaceport should produce.
- The thrill of exploration in the early game is matched by none. Period. Sending out your ships to scan the planets around you for the first time, with no idea what- or who- you may find. Every start up gives a sense of true wonder.
- Tactical space combat. You have three weapon divisions, and three defense types. Nuclear, projectile, and laser, and corresponding defenses (i.e. deflector shields for lasers). Your possible enemies have access to the same technology, thus it is necessary to pay attention to who you're fighting! I was involved in a losing war against a *massive* empire, until I realized they had no armor. I immediately updated my ship designs (possible in a very intuitive and fun to use designer) to include nuclear missilse and projectile launchers with heavy deflectors, and the scales soon tipped in my favor.
Cons
- It's been said before, and while I haven't had a problem with it, it does need to be addressed. The mid game has almost nothing really in it. Once you finish exploration, unless you truly love the roleplaying possibilities, you may find that you've little else to do but sit and research, hoping for something to happen.
- The AI is a bit wonky at the moment. This will be fixed, I'm sure, but right now they range from incredibly ruthless and strategic, to completely passive. An example being that in one game, I didn't see a single war (I didn't reach  late game, mind you, but I play at very fast at all times), despite several hostile empires. In another, my pacifist neighbors declared war  on a third neighbor of ours for.. reasons I still haven't figured out.
- Diplomacy could also stand to be fleshed out, as right now it consists of trade deals that are hit-or-miss when it comes to the AI agreeing to things, the alliance system is a bit rough around the edges ( a nice feature would be the ability for alliances to merge if all members of both agree), and rivalries don't seem to promote warfare anymore than holding a resource filled system.
All in all, Stellaris is a fantastic space grand strategy with limitless potential, and I believe in Paradox when it comes to this potential.

Short, elegant, and soothing. Abzu can be played in an afternoon, but is still a satisfying experience that provides easy access to return to points of interest for wildlife watching (and to the game's different chapters so you can find things you missed) after you've completed it. The only "strenuous" (and it must be said lightly) aspect of gameplay is the swimming controls can take a little getting used to, and there are several sections of the game where you will benefit from having practiced. It is, however, not necessary to be graceful to advance or to complete the game.
The game does have a plot, which is conveyed entirely without words. (The only text encountered is in controls prompts and the species names given when interacting with animals.)
The soundtrack is unobtrusive choral music throughout, and it works very well with Abzu's visuals, which are somewhat stylized but gorgeous. The environments convey a sense of joy, wonder, or dread (in a handful) as you explore them, and are well-laid-out with clear visual cues to help you find what you need to move forward. While many of the collectibles are in the open, you will have to search a bit to get all of them if you are so inclined.
My only complaint is that it can be difficult to select the creature you want to observe or ride when there are many of them close together (I spent a solid five minutes trying to grab a marlin and getting sharks instead), but I wouldn't say it ruined my experience.
If you need difficulty or real tension/punishment to enjoy a game, Abzu is not for you.
If any of this sounds good to you, it is a steal for the summer sale price.

Saying I went into this game with high expectations is the understatement of the year. I came into this game with no nostalgia, but I came into this game absolutely sure it would be some sort of narrative masterpiece I could recommend to everyone else on earth and play for four hundred hours and at the end still love it as much. Can you really blame me? I mean, LOOK at the reviews! Everyone on steam and amazon and all over the internet seemed to collectively agree it was the most amazing game ever to grace our mortal minds. But when I actually played the game? Well...
GAMEPLAY: I do actually really like the gameplay in this game. I will admit, the mixture of turn based and time based RPG combat is interesting, but it really takes some getting used to. I had never played a Final Fantasy game previously I came from playing Pokemon competetively, so I was expecting something more like that, but after you get used to it (and the inability to pause during battles) it's kind of fun. Also, if you really don't like it, there is a menu option to change it to completely static. I really like the Materia. Like I said, This was my first Final Fantasy, so I can't really say how it compares with other games in the franchise, but I thought it was a really neat addition to the game. It's pretty much necessary to have magic in a JRPG, but they could've just left it at magic materia and have been on their way but they decided to add independent, support, command, and summon materia, all with different uses and able to pair with other materia for some deadly combonations (my favorite is Final Attack+Phoenix. It's brutal and as long as you have the magic, you're unkillable). It's a little difficult to master, but the core gameplay is one of my favorite takes on this type of RPG. There really isn't that much else to say.
I don't know if this counts under gameplay, but I think it does, so I'm putting it there. All this game's versions of quick time events are just insufferable in my opinion. It tells you the controls and I spend two minutes mashing the keys I'm supposed to how it says I'm supposed to while nothing happens on the screen. It's totally responsive every other time, why not now?! I've never really failed any of them, even the one with the train in North Correl, but a lot of them I just found completely pointless and taking away from my enjoyment of the game. The only one I really liked was Tifa's slapping contest and the Piano in Nibelheim, if you can call that a quick time event.
As far as minigames, Chocobo racing is amazing. I know I spent at least four hours riding around the Overworld on my Gold Chocobo Ra, so do consider breeding one of those. All other minigames are just sort of meh in my opinion.
VISUALS: Yeah, ok, I get this is an old game and I know the graphics were revolutionary for it's time, I'm not going to get on it about that, but I had an issue (and still sort of have, although not as strong) with knowing where I can go. Everything always has a habit of blending into the background and I still have to use the assist thing that shows you what you can climb and what is a door you can go through. It makes everything about 20 times easier. Also, this is expected, but although the background visuals are beautiful, sometimes they don't mesh at all with the character models or Materia laying on the ground. This, like the inability to tell where to walk, is somehow more prevalent at the beginning of the game than any other time.
STORYLINE: I tried my hardest.
The first three and a half hours I hated everyone. You had nearly every cliche in the book- Token Main Character who has a big sword, sort of angsty and doesn't particularly care about anyone else or feel emotion for some reason, Token Childhood Friend who probably secretly likes you because of course (Cloti over Clerith regardless), Token Love Interest, Token Angry Guy who curses every other sentence and is also black because of course he is all on a token mission to destroy the token evil corporation who has taken over the government. I realize this was probably intentional so there could be a subversion of expectations later on when this has a better narrative, but this is a FINAL FANTASY GAME. I'm expecting hundreds of hours of amazing plot more akin to a rollercoaster than a story, not a token game with good gameplay being it's redeeming factor like Call of Duty or something. JRPGs don't roll like that.
*SPOILERS*
I'll admit, maybe knowing Aeris was going to die from the second I heard about this game (That's HOW I heard about this game, actually) turned me off from getting to know her. But do you want to hear a way better version of this? Fire Emblem Awakening. You're told that Chrom is going to die from the prologue and even the name of the chapter he's going to die in. And you're told that you're going to be the one killing him. All of the dialogue and everything that happens is subtly accenting Chrom's character and you're always thinking how tragic it will be when he dies through small bits of character development and interactions make you feel more guilty by the second, eventually culminating into me nearly breaking down as the cutscene rolled. And this was knowing what was going to happen. I couldn't even force myself to care about Aeris. I wanted to make her death more meaningful or as emotionally destructive as everyone says it was but I just... didn't care. Sorry.
*END SPOILERS*
Most of the plot centers around giving the main characters backstories and developing them like that, but it still couldn't force me to care about Barret and I still hated Yuffie just as much, so I felt like I just had a character with a backstory rather than giving these characters more of a drive or reason as to how they act. Tifa, Cloud, and Vincent's stories were pretty great, the rest were all decent, I just didn't really get why we had to spend so much time on them. I like these characters, I just didn't particularly care for their stories.
The rest of the story, There really isn't that much to say. Really I found the rest of the story completely unworthy of note. Not that nothing happened, because believe me it did, but I was extremely unimpressed. Everything that happened I was either too confused by or didn't care enough about the characters to be surprised at or react much more than "Oh. That happened. But what happened?"
Another thing this narrative has it it has the same problems that I had when I played Okami. It just doesn't get when it makes no sense where I'm supposed to be going and what I'm supposed to be doing when I get there (although Okami was a little tamer with this). I've had to look up things that they should've made absolutely crystal clear, the most insufferable of which I remember being where to go to fight Sephiroth when they first tell you to do that in Disc 2, so circuitous and confusing not even a guide could really help me. "Soooo... are we going to the Shinra HQ? I thought I saw that was on disc 2... Nope, doesn't even mention it... how about just going back up north? Well, I can't get to the crater by Chocobo and he won't let me climb the cliff because It's too windy or something... nothing here... THIS IS PROBABLY A CLIMACTIC FIGHT, WHY IS THIS SO HARD TO FIND?!" Even if it's not, GIVE ME SOME INDICATION OF THAT! I don't know where I should be going. I don't want these games to hold my hand, but come on! Give me SOME indication of where I should be going to progress the story. I eventually stopped trying here. I'm planning to finish it but mostly out of personal obligation.
The narrative was ok to good at best and I didn't particularly care about more than three of the characters. This is a fantastic game. Due to always being very far behind with computer hardware, I missed F.E.A.R. when it was first released in 2005 and only played it through recently. I went in worried that F.E.A.R. would just be a generic FPS with some jump scares thrown in, but came out very pleasantly surprised. Admittedly, I thought that the game started off a bit slow, with the first level (probably deliberately) presenting itself pretty much as I described in the previous sentence, but I persevered through the first mission and it's rare that I'm this glad that I did.
In terms of gameplay, the game has very solid shooter mechanics which are extremely enjoyable. You never feel severely overpowered (maybe a little if you rely on the slow-mo reflexes ability), but you also never feel like fights are unfair. Enemies are neither damp paper nor bullet sponges so fights never drag on for too long. The main challenge in firefights is just how impressive the AI is; enemies will usually be smart enough to know when and where to take cover, even being able to move some objects to create their own cover, work together effectively by using techniques such as suppressive fire and flanking whenever possible and communicate with each other so effectively (both verbally and through their actions) that they seem like real people - so much so that there were a few points where I nearly felt bad for killing the last one in a group. One particular instance that stuck with me as the moment that sold the AI for me was when I was walking through a series of corridors with my flashlight switched on, heard a squad of replicants nearby and tried to sneak a bit loser to them while forgetting to turn my flashlight off - one of them saw the light from around the corner, yelled "flashlight!" and ordered another squad member to check it out, surprising me so much that I fumbled and was forced to drop my plan of getting the drop on them. Some time after that, I ended up developing a tactic of luring an enemy around a corner by flashing my flashlight at the wall and then ambushing them with my shotgun when he came to check it out, thinning out the squad just a little.
To combat this, you're given a solid array of weapons - you can hold up to three at once, which is generally a love-it-or-hate-it trope in shooters but used very effectively here. What impressed me most about the weapons is that no single weapon in the game is clearly more powerful than any other; instead, they're balanced extremely well and all very useful for different situations and playstyles (I ended up settling on a favourite set about halfway through the game - shotgun for close range, assault rifle for medium range and particle weapon for sniping - and never changing them because they fit the way I played so well). Each weapon also takes into account the weight, with heavier weapons making you move noticably slower and lighter weapons increasing your speed and making melee combat a very viable tactic - if you can get close enough, it's usually an instant kill. There are also three grenade types (standard frag, proximity mine and remote sticky mine) that are great for flushing out enemies and laying traps; I generally hate using grenades and explosive weapons in shooters because I'm terrible with them, but, in F.E.A.R., I found myself accurately lobbing grenades to flush out entrenched enemies, laying mines to catch out anyone who tried to flank me and sending enemies screaming into their squad with a sticky mine lodged on their back. Generally, F.E.A.R. favours a nearly-cover-shooter tactic - full-on assault against a squad of replicants will usually get you ripped to shreds so you need to plan carefully, look for good cover, watch your back and make good use of the lean keys to drop in and out of cover. Health is not infinite; it doesn't regenerate and the only form of healing is from medkits which you can take with you and use at will and rare health upgrades which permanently increase your health by five points. F.E.A.R. also features a "reflex" mechanic, which is basically an ability to temporarily slow down time (I was sceptical of this at first, but it makes sense in the context of the game's story), in which everything - enemies and your own movement speed and fire rate - slow down apart from your own turning speed, allowing you to get an aim on enemies very quickly. There were times when I felt like this made the game a bit too easy, but, because it still slows you down as much as the enemies, activating it while out of cover can still be a very foolish move, and it's always great fun to see your enemies terrified and bewildered at how fast you've suddenly started reacting to them.
As for atmosphere, as I said before, I was initially worried that the game would just be loaded with jump scares. I was very wrong; there is a bog-standard jump scare close to the beginning of the first mission, but, right after that, the game gives up pretending that it's your run-of-the-mill, "edgy" shooter and unrelentingly toys with you up to the very end of the game. F.E.A.R.'s scare factor relies very heavily on atmosphere - light and dark, loud and quiet. Small, unnerving noises somewhere nearby that make you edgy about turning the next corner, dimly-lit rooms that you know you have to stay in for a minute to catch part of the story but make you constantly nervous enough to be checking the doors, a ghostly figure just catching your eye as it passes by the next room. The game is
aware of when you're expecting something to happen and loves nothing more than to suddenly take that tension away, then throw it right back at you when you've let your guard down. I admittedly haven't played many horror games, but I can happily say that there has been no other game so far that has made me as nervous about my surroundings as F.E.A.R. has. Monolith took heavy cues from classic Japanese horror films, the likes of The Ring and Dark Water, so anyone who has seen films like this knows a bit of what to expect in the story and presentation. The only thing I didn't like about the horror aspects were that any "hallucinated" characters invariably withered away into dust after they'd performed their bit, leaving you with absolutely no sense of ambiguity on whether they were really there or not. Nevertheless, even though I'm no horror junkie, the spook sections were such an enjoyable thrill that I often found myself hoping that there would be another soon.
One of the most enjoyable aspects of the game for me was that, if you want to get the whole story, you have to work for it. Almost the entire story plays out through listening to voice messages on phones and taking information from laptops that a surprising number of people left lying around and, while none are particularly hard to find, it adds a small layer of exploration into the unnerving surroundings, often requiring you to go just a little bit out of your way in an area where you really don't want to do that because you're worried that something is lurking just around that corner, or because the flashing voice message light on that phone is the only source of light in the room. It's always a rewarding experience, both for the little thrill of defying your own logic telling you not to hang around there and for adding another piece to the fascinating puzzle that is the story. I may not be the best person to comment on it - and am rather annoyed at myself - because, some time ago, I decided that I'd probably never end up playing this game and read the story to see what the game was like, and so spoiled some rather big details that I wish I hadn't, but I was still pulled enough into the story and immersed so heavily into the game that I wanted to find out every minute detail I could about what was happening.
If you love FPS and/or horror games, not giving yourself the opportunity play this would be an injustice. I could not possibly recommend this enough.

Ah, Space... it seems like space games are having a whole new renaissance these days. VoidExpanse is one of those games that sounds very simple, and even looks very simple. So, you start up a new game, and start mucking about, and then realize what feels like half an hour later that you've somehow lost several hours. The skill trees, the different ship hulls that actually FEEL like different ships, instead of just looking like them, and the fun of the combat... I'll be blunt: This game isn't a shiny polished AAA title. It has some quirks, particularly in the dialogue. However, VoidExpanse gets it right where it actually counts: It's fun to play, and the developers have a love for the game and community that shows in their continuing efforts to constantly improve and even expand the game. Lurler and co at Atomic Torch have built not just an excellent 2D space sandbox, they've built a devoted community, and the beginning of a reputation as a stand-up group of talented developers that actually care about their fans.
Putting the developer and community aside, though, let me explain the game, since that's what's actually being reviewed. Firstly, you won't play the same exact game twice, even if the main story(ies) don't radically change. VoidExpanse is a 2D space sandbox kind of game in the vein of Space Rangers, Solar Winds, or (to a lesser degree) S.P.A.Z. You start off customizing you character portrait with a number of options (which can be expanded via workshop), pick a trade/class which will allot your starting skills, and then start off in a low-tech backwater space base. The game has a pretty low learning curve, and piloting your ship will become natural very quickly.
There are two primary things that will determine your playstyle:
1) your skills, which will establish everything from what kinds of ship hulls you can pilot, how well you can pilot them, what kinds of weapons you can use, how well you can use those weapons, the types of trade and dialogue options available, what types of equipment you can use, and how efficient everything from mining lasers to fuel are.
2) your ship hull, which will determine cargo capacity, speed, maneuvering, and types of weapon mounts.
You can spend your time just following the main story, and only doing odd jobs, trading, or mining as needed to upgrade your equipment as needed, or you can bum about as a space miner and make your fortune hunting rare ores to sell to the highest bidder. You can establish trade routes, become a bounty hunter... it's up to you. Granted, the actual variety of missions can be limited, but there are a few standout side missions that are truly unique.
If you like the idea of a 2D space sandbox, they don't get much better than this. It has some flaws, but it delivers a solid and engaging experience, and is just loads of fun to play.
Oh yeah... and you can play online. Just saying.

A little sceptic at first, having loved this on the playstation one, I hesitantly bought this game.

I'm gonna be honest here, this game is great. At first glance I thought I wouldn't like it, but looked more into, (looking at let's plays and what not) and actually seemed to be my type of game. (Despite the anthropamorphic animal characters, but it's quite easy to look past one of my few pet-peeves in life with this masterpiece). I played it, and I gotta say, I wasn't dissapointed. The first thing that reeled me into this gorgeous game was the ambience. The art was beautiful, and I probably spent way more time on this than the average player simply because I took a few pauses just to enjoy the artisitic masterpiece that is Dust: An Elysian Tail.
Gameplay wise, this game doesn't let you down. It's more of a brawler than any other Genre, in my opinion. It has smooth combos and actually prooves to be challenging in many stages. I would say that the leveling system needs a bit more depth, but really with all that the game offers that's a pretty minor complaint. However the aerial dust storm seems to a bit imbalanced, as I can just constantly use that attack to defeat really any boss that gets in my way rather easily.
The soundtrack is AMAZING. I'm a sucker when it comes to good music in games, and this did not let me down. At all. Even when I got stuck in a death loop at the challenging parts, the soundtrack is what prevented me from raging, just because each time I respawn the ear candy will feed me once more.
Lastly, I gotta say I was a tad dissapointed with the story. It's still really well done, don't get me wrong. However, and I know it's hard avoid this in games, it's kind of cheesy in a lot of places. Fidget's bickering almost made me cry sometimes, because she's just SO DAMN ANNOYING. That high pitched voice irked me everytime she was trying to be sassy with me, or just freaking out over monsters everytime we encountered them. Also, Arah the talking sword is a pretty cool guy, I guess. He's the only non-furry character in the game so there's a bonus for me, but really? A talking sword? Cryptic tutor? I've heard WAY too many times in fantasy books/movies and the like, and both elements are usually in the same place. It was kind of sad to hear the words "You shall know in time, Dust." Or "Now is not the place nor the time" and other famous words of the ol' cryptic teacher guy. I feel like the dialogue in this could've been more excuted, and the when the real plot is revealed the way I found out didn't seem natural.
All in all, though, this game is still held up there in my "Was gud game wud pley agan" category, and quite frankly it deserves that place. The fact that this was mostly created by one person only further impresses me. Nice game.
8.5/10.

So, Stellaris.
We'll start with the positives, The game is definitely remarkable in the aspesct that it brings us some genuinely enjoyable gameplay in the form of 4X real time elements. There are no turns to take, everything happens in front of you.
Early on in the game there is much to do, technologies to research, planets to colonize, learning who your galactic neighbors are, what they are.
In my case, in a game with a friend, I spawned in dangerously close to a fallen empire.
That was a good and bad thing, being xenophiles they had no intention of killing me out as long as I do not enslave/purge my citizens. This essentially meant that my border was secure, so long as I didn't atttract their Ire. The bad thing was that I could no longer expand to the south of the galaxy.
I soon learned that I was surrounded by many different empires, that the west side of the galaxy was densely populated by different alien races whose goals and ideals differed exponentially.
My friend in game, spawning on the far eastern side of the galaxy, was having a completely different experience. His empire expanded quickly and was given an opportunity to really grow his borders, While his empire was bigger, this also meant that all the other empires in the east were also a healthy size due to the sparcity of galactic neighbors.
Soon, both east and west started to effectively garner their own cultures, if you will.
The west was densely populated with many small nations in alliances, and also highly technologically advanced due to their being very few wars.
The east was the exact opposite, no alliances, many large nations, many large fleets. Huge wars raged all over the East, and due to their increased military spending, those nations could not afford to invest in technological advancement.
I thought this to be a truly interesting parallel, one the game definitely delivers well.
The late-mid game is dull however, I eventually declared war on my neighbor when the West fell to pieces and started tearing itself apart with massive battles with highly technologically advanced fleets, completely reshaping the western borders.
I vassalized a smaller nation, while simultaneously taking some planets from another nation by force. The vassal was fiercely loyal before being integrated. While the other nations' planets I had annexed inhabitants started a faction in order to defy my rule.
After dealing with the insurrectionists and succesfully integrating the other nation, the prethoryn appeared in our galaxy to the east.
Spawning in my friends' empire, decimating it in mere minutes.
He now has his last fleet holding at his nations' capital. With massive defensive starbases and stationary weapons waiting for an overwhelming extragalactic force to consume his people.
While I sit comfortably in the West, building up my fleet for an opponent I may never actually fight.
Better him than me, I suppose.

the good:
- early game feels well balanced has fun events tailored to your civ ideology

the bad:
ai is among the dumbest of all strategy games I've played
-at war they always try creating a doom stack following you like little puppies
-in alliance they always refuse your war declarations if you dont give them a treat but will blindly accept totally one sided declarations of other ai
- during catastrophe they will watch as they get slaughtered and are more focused on their rivaling neighbours
- by the time a catastrophe happens usually nearly all systems are claimed and you have no other way of preventing it without declaring war to any ai in the way to pass through, very few will allow you military border access for outrageous prices
diplomacy itself is severly lacking:
- alliances/federations are ironclad bounds, ai's will never leave or backstab

It is hard to not expect too much from a game by a studio that has created such wonderful time-consumers as Hoi3, EU4 and Crusader Kings 2, and it is hard to not be too unfair in the face of such disappointment. But this game just isn’t ready yet.
There are several new and original ideas, like edics (political decision) and factions (political organizations of discontent citizens), individual ethics (political preferences of each single population) and fun government types, like you would expect from paradox’ rich and fruitful strategy experience. But the fact that any cool empire management feature (edicts, allicances, planetary programs, border expansion, faction management, government decisions, leaders and governors, even certain buildings and moving population around) requires “influence”, by far the most valuable resource, effectively takes all of this out of the game, since you are always trying to save your points and do without.
Sound and graphics are from 10-15 years ago, surely not as important in a strategy game, but in this case made so lackluster and dull, it hurts the gaming experience. At least an animated landing of a colony ship should have made it into the budget. What you get is a stamp-size picture with the graphics quality of a steam achievement.
The menu is intricate and counterintuitive. You have a colony ship and want to see a list of possible planets? Not possible. You are on the star chart and want to click on your colony directly? Not possible. You are on a planet and want to switch though to the next? Not possible. You always have to click all the way up, all the way down. To put something on a building list requires all the resources immediately, which you can never afford. So no building lists either. Click, click, click. The game should come with an extra mouse, for wear and tear reasons.
The entire gaming experience feels like an Early Access. There are just so many things that remain unfinished and incomplete, it seems that the developers have first and foremost spent their creativity on one question: what else of the things you would normally expect from a 4x space game (and that was already there as early as Master of Orion 2) can we take out of the game to later sell it to the players as DLC?
It’s almost funny the race designer made it in, you would think they’d have made that a DLC too.
Apparently the developers don’t care for the game or the players, only of your money. Do so too. And save it.

Saying I went into this game with high expectations is the understatement of the year. I came into this game with no nostalgia, but I came into this game absolutely sure it would be some sort of narrative masterpiece I could recommend to everyone else on earth and play for four hundred hours and at the end still love it as much. Can you really blame me? I mean, LOOK at the reviews! Everyone on steam and amazon and all over the internet seemed to collectively agree it was the most amazing game ever to grace our mortal minds. But when I actually played the game? Well...
GAMEPLAY: I do actually really like the gameplay in this game. I will admit, the mixture of turn based and time based RPG combat is interesting, but it really takes some getting used to. I had never played a Final Fantasy game previously I came from playing Pokemon competetively, so I was expecting something more like that, but after you get used to it (and the inability to pause during battles) it's kind of fun. Also, if you really don't like it, there is a menu option to change it to completely static. I really like the Materia. Like I said, This was my first Final Fantasy, so I can't really say how it compares with other games in the franchise, but I thought it was a really neat addition to the game. It's pretty much necessary to have magic in a JRPG, but they could've just left it at magic materia and have been on their way but they decided to add independent, support, command, and summon materia, all with different uses and able to pair with other materia for some deadly combonations (my favorite is Final Attack+Phoenix. It's brutal and as long as you have the magic, you're unkillable). It's a little difficult to master, but the core gameplay is one of my favorite takes on this type of RPG. There really isn't that much else to say.
I don't know if this counts under gameplay, but I think it does, so I'm putting it there. All this game's versions of quick time events are just insufferable in my opinion. It tells you the controls and I spend two minutes mashing the keys I'm supposed to how it says I'm supposed to while nothing happens on the screen. It's totally responsive every other time, why not now?! I've never really failed any of them, even the one with the train in North Correl, but a lot of them I just found completely pointless and taking away from my enjoyment of the game. The only one I really liked was Tifa's slapping contest and the Piano in Nibelheim, if you can call that a quick time event.
As far as minigames, Chocobo racing is amazing. I know I spent at least four hours riding around the Overworld on my Gold Chocobo Ra, so do consider breeding one of those. All other minigames are just sort of meh in my opinion.
VISUALS: Yeah, ok, I get this is an old game and I know the graphics were revolutionary for it's time, I'm not going to get on it about that, but I had an issue (and still sort of have, although not as strong) with knowing where I can go. Everything always has a habit of blending into the background and I still have to use the assist thing that shows you what you can climb and what is a door you can go through. It makes everything about 20 times easier. Also, this is expected, but although the background visuals are beautiful, sometimes they don't mesh at all with the character models or Materia laying on the ground. This, like the inability to tell where to walk, is somehow more prevalent at the beginning of the game than any other time.
STORYLINE: I tried my hardest.
The first three and a half hours I hated everyone. You had nearly every cliche in the book- Token Main Character who has a big sword, sort of angsty and doesn't particularly care about anyone else or feel emotion for some reason, Token Childhood Friend who probably secretly likes you because of course (Cloti over Clerith regardless), Token Love Interest, Token Angry Guy who curses every other sentence and is also black because of course he is all on a token mission to destroy the token evil corporation who has taken over the government. I realize this was probably intentional so there could be a subversion of expectations later on when this has a better narrative, but this is a FINAL FANTASY GAME. I'm expecting hundreds of hours of amazing plot more akin to a rollercoaster than a story, not a token game with good gameplay being it's redeeming factor like Call of Duty or something. JRPGs don't roll like that.
*SPOILERS*
I'll admit, maybe knowing Aeris was going to die from the second I heard about this game (That's HOW I heard about this game, actually) turned me off from getting to know her. But do you want to hear a way better version of this? Fire Emblem Awakening. You're told that Chrom is going to die from the prologue and even the name of the chapter he's going to die in. And you're told that you're going to be the one killing him. All of the dialogue and everything that happens is subtly accenting Chrom's character and you're always thinking how tragic it will be when he dies through small bits of character development and interactions make you feel more guilty by the second, eventually culminating into me nearly breaking down as the cutscene rolled. And this was knowing what was going to happen. I couldn't even force myself to care about Aeris. I wanted to make her death more meaningful or as emotionally destructive as everyone says it was but I just... didn't care. Sorry.
*END SPOILERS*
Most of the plot centers around giving the main characters backstories and developing them like that, but it still couldn't force me to care about Barret and I still hated Yuffie just as much, so I felt like I just had a character with a backstory rather than giving these characters more of a drive or reason as to how they act. Tifa, Cloud, and Vincent's stories were pretty great, the rest were all decent, I just didn't really get why we had to spend so much time on them. I like these characters, I just didn't particularly care for their stories.
The rest of the story, There really isn't that much to say. Really I found the rest of the story completely unworthy of note. Not that nothing happened, because believe me it did, but I was extremely unimpressed. Everything that happened I was either too confused by or didn't care enough about the characters to be surprised at or react much more than "Oh. That happened. But what happened?"
Another thing this narrative has it it has the same problems that I had when I played Okami. It just doesn't get when it makes no sense where I'm supposed to be going and what I'm supposed to be doing when I get there (although Okami was a little tamer with this). I've had to look up things that they should've made absolutely crystal clear, the most insufferable of which I remember being where to go to fight Sephiroth when they first tell you to do that in Disc 2, so circuitous and confusing not even a guide could really help me. "Soooo... are we going to the Shinra HQ? I thought I saw that was on disc 2... Nope, doesn't even mention it... how about just going back up north? Well, I can't get to the crater by Chocobo and he won't let me climb the cliff because It's too windy or something... nothing here... THIS IS PROBABLY A CLIMACTIC FIGHT, WHY IS THIS SO HARD TO FIND?!" Even if it's not, GIVE ME SOME INDICATION OF THAT! I don't know where I should be going. I don't want these games to hold my hand, but come on! Give me SOME indication of where I should be going to progress the story. I eventually stopped trying here. I'm planning to finish it but mostly out of personal obligation.
The narrative was ok to good at best and I didn't particularly care about more than three of the characters. I give it 6/10 but don't recommend it only because I enjoy the gameplay and narrative isn't too insufferable, it's just not as great of a game as everyone makes it out to be. In my opinion, at least.

Little Inferno is a little game that's easy to pick up and play.
So, our world is getting colder and colder, so, Tomorrow Corporations created the Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace to keep the player and everyone else warm. You play as a kid that has a friend named Sugar Plumps, she also has a Little Inferno Fireplace. One flaw with the gameplay is that you have to wait to get the items, sometimes it will take like 12 seconds, but some items can take over 2 mins long.
The soundtrack consists of a few songs, each one of them is fantastic.

While Half-Life back in 1998 hypnotized the stagnated first-person-shooter genre with groundbreaking narrative, enhanced puzzle elements, immersed atmosphere within cinematic settings and intelligent artificial intelligence, F.E.A.R. expertly continued to elevate the modern shooter in 2005, primary from an outstanding cinematic standpoint. Although essentially recapturing the spirit of creative Hong Kong filmmaker John Woo, the sci-fi classic The Matrix and terrifying The Ring remake, developer Monolith ambitiously established an intriguing original concept as well as an iconic figure no matter the various influences.
The first-rate atmosphere became apparent immediately as the newest member (that would be you) of the First Encounter Assault Recon is set to carry out a classified objective within a military task force that deals with paranormal circumstances. Apparently, a mad military commander has become a liability after taking command of a secret army of cloned soldiers that are telepathically linked to him, causing mayhem within a restricted area in an unspoken American city in order to acquire something unknown. The F.E.A.R. team along with a Delta Force unit obviously issue a respond to this threat. Strengthened by frequent voice mails and radio news reports, the twisted story of the commander and the mysterious appearance of Alma unfold engaging and dramatic.
A hectic blend of dynamic action and suspenseful horror was presented. Distinguished gun battles were downright spectacular to witness, creating stunning particle effects that in combination with the finest bursts of exciting slow-motion provided dramatically beautiful and wickedly entertaining action sequences in remarkably bloody repercussions. The lighting and shadowing model kept high class in bringing the mood, and so did the excellent music and solid voice-over. The movement patterns and animations of the enemies were well-made, but were obviously not as talked-about as their strikingly sharp artificial intelligence. Encountering these aggressive and tactically oriented opponents was challenging and incredibly unpredictable; they took advantage of the game’s physics system by knocking over objects to create cover, they fiercely reacted to your presence and actively communicated with one another. The weapons at your disposal, though only capable of carrying three at a time, were versatile, relatively equally efficient (if approached correctly) and actually dangerous, providing powerful punches to both enemies and surroundings, meaning they were implemented for a reason since you were as vulnerable as the enemy.
Although the spiritual follow-up of Half-Life came out strong on so many levels, F.E.A.R. clearly fell short on some of them. The mention of repetitive environments that basically consisted of an industrial area and an office complex could not be ignored; at times the second-rate variety made progression jaded which fuelled a negative impression that the levels lasted too long. While the atmosphere was strong and coherent, the actual horror aspect came out less effective. The imagery was certainly on several occasions unsettling, showing off a few successful jump scares, but the scare tactics became slightly familiar over time and the pattern of predictability indisputable. However, just like Doom 3 at that time, certain tension brought out from the atmosphere was consistent enough to keep you alert and that quality somewhat redeemed the mentioned predictability. While particle effects, lighting and sound were astounding, the level design and textures were less complex and kind of mediocre looking. In addition, some of the character models felt wooden and appeared like plastic dolls.
Essentially innovative and distinctly competent, F.E.A.R. elevated the modern shooter in spectacular proportions, which reasonably ended with an explosive cliff hanger. While combining action and horror, the incredibly beautiful and dynamic action portion - intensified by outstanding bullet time and amazingly clever opponents - clearly surpassed (and even to some extent neutralized) the fairly weakened horror note. Still, the unshakable lack of variety associated with the environments and level design had a significant impact on the general impression. All things considered, F.E.A.R. was and still is a skilful and relevant yet slightly jaded and overrated contribution of first-person-shooter history.

Great game from the 90's with a decent touch up. The only problems i've seen so far are the environments are sort of pixelated on higher resolutions and the music is just hollow MIDI instead of the higher quality PS1 music. Other than those two gripes the game is still as great as i remember. I wont spoil anything here but the game is worth its pricetag as it was one of the greatest Final Fantasys in my opinion.
As with its newer aged brethren FF8 uses the ATB system meaning the enemy can attack before your party and vice versa. Faster characters or ones with a higher SPD stat will see their bar fill up faster and thus get to attack more often. This iteration also introduced the Junction system which honestly is a love or hate change. With the junction system you link or "junction" magic to your stats to increase them further. The more magic you have linked to a stat the better the boost. However, some magic boosts other stats better than others and what stats are junctionable is solely determined by what GF's are equipped.
Thats the next topic though. Your summons in this game are called GF's or Guardian Force. Most of the FF staples are here including Ifrit, Shiva, Alexander, Odin and so on. They level up seperately from the characters as well as seperate health bars and also gain AP or Ability Points. AP is used to learn new moves for them like SumMag+10% which increases their damage by 10%. Through this system they can also learn other abilities aside from health and damage boosting abilities for instance Quazecolt (unsure of spelling at this time) can learn the ability Card which will in battle turn a monster into a Triple Triad card. The separate health bar comes into play during summoning. For a set amount of time based off affinity with a GF (increased by use of said GF) your health is taken over by their health bars as an ATB bar ticks down. Once it emptys the GF is summoned to do its attack or whatever ability it may have (Support GFs are here) and then the players health bar is restored to its place. Any attacks suffered before the GF attacks during that time period though causes damage to the GF until it is KO'd and needs to be revived before summoning again. Its something i enjoy but newer audiences may not is that GF's can have summon animations lasting only a couple seconds to minutes (i believe the final summon has a length 4 minute animation but does insane damage).
There's a lot more to this game as well but the last topic i'll touch up on here is the Triple Triad mini-game. Triple Triad is a card game played in-game completely optionally (it has its own line of sidequests as well) but is very well put together and is probably the funnest mini-game in any FF. The game updates itself as you explore new areas of the world by adding new rules and winning options (like getting to choose one card they used for yourself or taking their entire hand of cards) all of which can be changed by visiting the Queen of Cards who will with a small fee strike down rules you picked up and/or win rewards. The game is a load of fun and can make the main game even easier for you when mixed with Quezacolts "Card Mod" ability. Which is were his Card ability comes into play. You can earn all the cards by winning Triple Triad or you can turn real monsters into a card for use or even refine the card with Card Mod to turn the monster into a set item(s). Through this it's actually possible to get the Main Character Squall's ultimate weapon on the very first disc provided you have the patience or card battlling prowress.
Well this reviews gone on long enough. I sincerely hope you consider picking this game up if you haven't played it before or if you're a returning veteran to FF8. Happy gaming everyone!

I can't really speak to multiplayer as I haven't gotten into it yet but my solo experience thus far has been a lot of fun.
I started out as a fighter, I knew that combat was going to be prevalent no matter where I went so I wanted a little head start in that department. After taking a good look at the skill trees I decided that I actually wanted most if not all of them so throughout my playtime I have been carefully managing what I invest in next. The game can be a little grindy, especially if you've *chosen* to grind as I have, but it's always felt rewarding. Getting that next skill, being able to buy and then use that shiny new hull or weapon or ship upgrade is satisfying.
A lot of zones unfortunately feel a little empty. Filled to the brim with pirates and aliens and in some cases more asteroids than you can mine in half a day, yes, but still empty as from a certain standpoint they're essentially just waypoints to your next stop. Hopefully in the (near) future we'll have more interactivity with these places if the game evolves to a point where we can actually claim and populate them. Extended main storylines to send you to more places would be great, too. All the same, if you're in need of exp or loot to sell it's easy to just pick a zone whose agression level is close to yours and have at it.
Storywise it's pretty solid. You'll have access to a few missions to raise your rep with three of the factions before you actually join any of them. The main quest for the two I've seen are pretty short but well written and the difficulty in terms of how aggressive the zones you'll be visiting is pretty steep so your first playthrough with a new character will feel a lot longer as you level and gear up. There are also missions you can do for the commander at any station you visit. They're selected randomly from a preset list and it's totally up to you if you want to accept them or not. I found that fact to be irritating as I was only really interested in bounty and mining missions, thankfully loudent2 published a mod that allows you access to the whole list so you can just pick the one you want. Much more convenient and a must if you ever get frustrated at the random factor.
There are a lot of items and upgrades to choose from at the beginning, which is awesome, but as you get into the higher levels (I was 146 at the time of writing this... yes I was lazy and copy/pasted my three day old forum post. Deal with it :P) you'll find yourself invariably with the same set of gear as most people; primarily speaking a dark matter generator, a dimensional fuel tank, and either a Hammer or a Death Bringer hull. And lasers. Lots of love for the lasers :).
This is where modding really adds more life to it all. Last week I wanted a (much) shorter range laser that did more damage, I made one. It uses way too much energy imo but I made it, I use it, and so do a few other people now that it's on the Workshop. Then I wanted a rapid fire ballistic weapon that shoots fireballs, made that too. It's a little OP for anything under aggression level 70 or so but it's fun all the same. Got tired of shields, made new armor plating. So my modding skills are amateurish at best but more importantly I'm having a good time doing it, even learned a thing or two about XML along the way. Taking that into consideration, there are a lot of other people writing fantastic mods for the game and publishing them fairly regularly, it's been just over two weeks and there are 50 items in the Workshop already (albeit some of them are translations and don't really affect the core gameplay but I imagine they took a LOT of work and it's quite appreciated to a lot of players). It feels like there's always some cool new user made content to check out and maybe take for a spin. Maybe even share a few of your own ;).
All in all it's a great game. Simple yet very well written, looks fantastic, controls are solid, great support and frequent updates. It has a lot to offer both in terms of content and expandability and it's a lot of fun, right to the point where I started playing one morning and actually forgot to eat anything until mid afternoon. Definitely worth the pricepoint.

You play as Dust, a warrior who got woken up in a forest by a magical blade named Ahrah and its guardian Fidget who from there on are your companions throughout the rest of the story. In short; Dust must work towards retrieving his/its memory in order to bring Justice to a land terrorised by monsters, war and other events you'll encounter. In the beginning and mid game the story was not really something to write home about BUT it was interesting enough for me to keep playing the main plot line and it got more interesting as I progressed towards the end. I can't comment on side missions, didn't play them.
Each area has it's own unique environment and beautiful art style with accompanying enemy mobs. None of them are in my opinion dull or generic. Aside from the beautiful 2d graphics the combat graphical effects are pleasant to watch at and fit right in.
Combat itself was interesting for me due to the variety of enemies encountered. There are enough guides to explain the easy to remember combos for you to use. There could have been a bit more complexity on that part but that gets balanced by the enemy's difficulty as you progress through the game. In the beginning and mid game most of them are easy to beat (depending on difficulty mode) but towartds late game I died a lot =).
Aside from enemies there are some environmental dangers to be dealt with in certain areas, each specific to the level you're playing in. They're not super unique but it does give more depth to the gameplay.

It's a work in progress. It has a lot of potential, but it should really be an early access title.
It's definitely playable now, but pretty much everything needs either more work or more content. Load times for save games and new systems are pretty long. Combat is really repetitive (and you'll get used to it because it's the only sane way to level up). There are few options for ship and weapon, there are quite a few but generally only one at any given tier so it's "oh I can afford the next ship/gun up I better swap them out." Modders are adding content faster than the devs, but the devs set up modding so that once you use a save file with any mod it permenantly needs that mod to load, there is no removing it if say you don't like it or it completely breaks the game. Back up your save files.
I was a die hard fan of the Escape Velocity games when I was younger and I really wanted a worthy successor to them in this game, but although many of the same elements are there pretty much all the things the EV series did right this title fails at. There's no real feeling of exploration because the procedurally generated systems are all identical other than color scheme and number/strength of bad guys. The storyline missions are uninspired and linear. And there aren't enough options in ships and outfits to make it feel like an inhabited capitalistic universe.
I have hopes that enough of the rough patches will get ironed out as further patches come out that I feel like my money was well spent, but I'm not going to keep playing it while they fix it, and I can't recommend that you do either.
