Cheesy cutscenes are part of this game's charm.  Reawakening a nostalgia in me from the original Red Alert games - I throughly enjoyed my time with this game which actually looks very good.  The macromangement is there with each of the unique factions having their own flavours and feels - each seemingly in a state of adequate "balanced-imbalance" that kept it interesting.  As easy as playing through most of the campaign - the fact that they included an option for Coop the campaign mode with your friends was a very nice touch.
For competitive RTS enthusiasts the deeper level of micro and meta gaming is there for those wanting to polish up their APM and skills and sink their teeth into the multiplayer.  Starting from the collision of units as you nimble side step a falling enemy zepplin with your infantry or position your formation in such a way for their special abilities to get the maximum effectiveness.  The difference between being able to play this game and being a master-class player would be at least a few hundred hours.
Not to say the game doesn't have it's few drawbacks - more times than pure chance units would bug out on the map - whether they got stuck inside of terrain or refuse to function like you are instructing them to - due to pathing errors etc.  The cutscenes themselves have their cheesy charm and the actresses are beautiful but some of the over-the-top acting on cheap sets might turn some people off from it inbetween missions.
I would recommend this title inspite of those issues.

I've been enjoying Stellaris a lot so far, but I have a few issues with it:
+Epic Scale, the largest galaxies can have 1000 Star Systems, each with multiple planets
+Beautiful Graphics, the battles look great, weapon effects and sounds are good for the most part
+Customization of Species traits, Government, Appearance, Names etc.
+Ship design, a very user friendly ship design
+Multiple interesting events and locations to explore
+Different FTL systems that really change how you play and explore the Galaxy
+Long term epic strategy, you can take a species that you discover on a planet from Iron Age tech up to eventually be assimilated into your Empire as an equal member-species (It takes a long time, but I've done it!)
-Limit of 5 planets (Initially, can be increased through tech) that you directly manage. You have to create 'sectors' to control more. The AI that manages you sectors really sucks, I had to take a system out of a sector and manage it myself for a while then put it back it as the AI wasn't doing anything I asked it to do. I supplied the sector with plenty of resources to build up those planets within its control.
-No tech tree, you get a draw of 3 techs to research (initially, you receive more through exploring and tech upgrades) It makes it hard to plan out what tech you want to research initially, but with further play this might be less of an issue
-limited trade with other species, I had a surplus of energy and shortage of minerals, but I couldn't trade away my surplus fast enough to supplement my mineral requirements. The AI usually wants to have a better deal than you are getting otherwise it will reject it. Also, sometimes they won't even trade with you despite you giving them a huge advantage, they still feel insulted that you offered them that deal??
-AI for enemies sucks because they all hate you for going for the win conditions. Its really annoying actually.

The planet/sector management interface is sorely lacking in sorting options.  There is no interface to view potentially colonizable planets, and the only way to do so is by hovering over the galaxy map looing for green planet icons that disappear if you zoom too far out.
That said, the events and race designs are really well done, though the AI seems to balk at the eXpand portion of the 4x genre.  Almost 200 years into a playthrough there were still a LOT of habitable planets on the edge of the galaxy that were sitting uncolonized.  The endgame threats are cool though, and I'm looking forward to what the game will look like in 3-6 months with some TLC centered on the mid game lull and UI shortcomings.

What is there to say? It's quite possibly the most legendary Final Fantasy game of all time, and possibly the most legendary JRPG of all time. No, it isn't in 1080p. No, it doesn't run at 60fps. No, there aren't full voiceovers in 17 different languages. But, it doesn't need any of that. Nearly 20 years after it originally released, it's still an incredible game to play.
The story is fantastic. The battle system is simple and smooth. The materia system allows you to play the character you want, how you want. The music? It's outstanding. Seriously, amazing. Did I mention how great the story is? Well, I'm saying it again. Just the right mix of fantasy, reality, and sci-fi. It's also home to one of the best video game villains of all time; Sephiroth.
All of that aside, there are also plenty of minigames and side quests you can do. Some are largely pointless, others help you access unique items or high-end magic. The minigames unfortunately are a little clunky, and the menus can be a bit awkward at times, but that's about it. There's nothing else you can hold against this game.
If you want a good RPG, or something with a great story... What are you waiting for? Buy it, you won't regret it.
Edit: It requires you to make an account with Square Enix in order to play, which can be a royal pain since their server simply doesn't send emails sometimes. Try a different email address if need be, and just be a little patient if it doesn't work right away. It'll work eventually, and it's totally worth it.

ABZU is a beautiful, relaxing, and truly unique gaming experience.
- Just beautiful. The lighting, colour schemes, the game as a whole is pleasant to look at.
- Atmospheric. Although I knew there is no risk of death or jump scares in this game, the thought of deep diving terrifies me. Amazingly, ABZU manages to capture this primal fear and implements it perfectly.
- The fish AI is noteworthy. I'm not a fish expert, but their reactions and movements seemed realistic.
- Love the inclusion of meditation statues. The focus of ABZU is to explore and observe the underwater world. The meditation statues really enhance the observation element of this game.
- Game length is good. I like that the developers did not try to extend this game unnecessarily. There is enough content for people who want to explore and for people who just want to get through the story.
- Somewhat expensive for a short game.
I recognize that this game isn't for everyone. It is not action packed. It will not test your skills as a gamer. This game is slow, relaxing, and beautiful. If that is not what you're looking for, then don't get ABZU. When I first rented Monolith Productions’ F.E.A.R. on Xbox 360 back in 2007, I was very impressed with the singleplayer campaign. Despite not being able to complete F.E.A.R. before I had to return it to the video store, it left a lasting impression on me and I considered it a modern classic. The recent inclusion of the game as part of the Humble WB Bundle provided the perfect opportunity to re-experience the game and see if my initial impression of it holds to my more refined standards of today.
One element of F.E.A.R. that impresses more than even most newly released games is its beautiful visual effects and physics. Just about everything smaller than entire desks and tables, from office telephones and spinning desk chairs, to paintings on the walls, are physics based. Occasionally, this causes some issues (most of which exist in all games with lots of physics-based objects) such as corpses becoming embedded in walls and floors or clutter bouncing around when they should not, but for the most part lends itself greatly to the experience. It can be terrifying when you are walking down a dark hallway, trying to sneak up on an enemy, when you accidentally walk over a soda can, kicking it down the hall with a silence-breaking twang. The first time you enter a large firefight, enable SloMo, and begin exchanging fire with the Replica soldiers is breathtaking: dust fills the air as bullets impact nearby walls, creating actual holes in the walls rather than just placing a decal; stray bullets knock boxes of papers and electronics off shelves, breaking them; a grenade goes off nearby, knocking the hanging lights around, the game’s marvelous dynamic lighting and shadows changing the entire look of the battlefield; and the opposing forces’ soldiers react realistically, with custom animations dependent on where they are hit that are integrated well with ragdoll physics. Another soldier, panicking, runs away but stumbles and falls over while he attempts to call squad for backup. While these sorts of features are not a new creation for F.E.A.R., they are all used extremely effectively together to create impressive and satisfying scenes that leave a lasting impression, defining F.E.A.R. and setting it apart from other games in people’s minds.
While F.E.A.R. manages to wow with its impressive physics, lighting, and effects; intense soundtrack and Japanese-horror inspired ambience; and solid gunplay and fair difficulty, F.E.A.R. is not a perfect game and many of its elements and tropes undermine the level of immersion needed to truly be disturbed by a horror game. There are a significant amount of attempted jump scares that are ineffective and cheap feeling. The enemies, unless you're playing on the hardest difficulty, lack the power to instill a fear of death in you. Because of this playing on the hardest difficulty is an absolute must, even on a first playthrough. The highest difficulty is the only one that has fair and interesting feelings gunplay, since on lower difficulties enemies are just too weak and easy to kill. The improved gunplay and stronger enemies add both enjoyable skill-based gameplay and intense ambience that greatly improves the overall feel of the game.
Overall, F.E.A.R. is an overall great game that I would reccomend to anyone who enjoys first person games. Despite its age, it is of much higher quality than much newer first person and horror games. F.E.A.R. is a classic that everyone should experience as an important part of the history of modern gaming, regardless of your interest in the genres.

FINAL FANTASY VII is a turn-based RPG that follows the story of AVALANCHE, a group of eco-terrorist trying to prevent Shinra Inc. from draining the life energy right out of the planet.
And then the story derails into something much more complex and dramatic. It's a JRPG at its finest.
The game doesn't add much to the previous installments. It's main new feature is the materia equipment system which is absolutely brillant. You basically equip the materia into individual slots inside your weapon to learn the materia effects. You can learn Fire, Steal, Counter, you name it. You can also link them together like Fire-MP Absorb or Cover-Counterattack. Materia make this game so much more fun and flexible. You can make anybody into any party role. You can get overpowered really fast if you know what you're doing and the strongest materia requires you to work hard for it (sidequest time!)
Another strong feature is the Limit Breaks. In combat, a gauge will fill up when you take damage and you can unleash a powerful attack once the gauge is full. They look amazing and are quite powerful.
The game is simple and pretty linear. It's definitely more easy than hard. Roadblocks are nonexistent. Everybody can only equip one specific type of weapon and anybody can equip the bangles (with very few exceptions) and materias. There is only 3 party members that can enter a battle. The environment is really interactive, you will go up and down ladders and jump small gaps more than any other Final Fantasy game.
The game offers between 35-40 hours of quality storytelling. Those looking to collect and level everything may reach the 70-90 hours count. The party members are a bit odd and doesn't seem to all fit together. It's a varied cast but the story is really centered around Cloud, the protagonist. Cloud is your typical mercenary with a act now, talk later mentality. He's facing issues of his own and the story quickly becomes Cloud's story instead of AVALANCHES's.
Graphics haven't aged well. The models and UI have been improved from it's original state but the pre-rendered background looks old and out of place. The music is as always a masterpiece.
+Strong combat-oriented features (materia system and limit breaks).
+A couple sidequests that gives out great rewards.
+A couple challeging superbosses to really test out your skills.
+Great story.
+Memorable music.
+Good price.
~Party members don't quite fit all well together. It's an odd but effective cast.
~Tedious 100% achievements (leveling up materia, getting max gil, leveling to 99)
~Story can get confusing (its sequels and prequels will fill some gaps making the story so much better).
-Graphics haven't aged well (you really should'nt be playing this for graphics though...)
FINAL FANTASY VII grabs our attention with its great combat and keeps us around with a superb story and masterful music. I do recommend at full price.

You play as Dust, a warrior who got woken up in a forest by a magical blade named Ahrah and its guardian Fidget who from there on are your companions throughout the rest of the story. In short; Dust must work towards retrieving his/its memory in order to bring Justice to a land terrorised by monsters, war and other events you'll encounter. In the beginning and mid game the story was not really something to write home about BUT it was interesting enough for me to keep playing the main plot line and it got more interesting as I progressed towards the end. I can't comment on side missions, didn't play them.
Each area has it's own unique environment and beautiful art style with accompanying enemy mobs. None of them are in my opinion dull or generic. Aside from the beautiful 2d graphics the combat graphical effects are pleasant to watch at and fit right in.
Combat itself was interesting for me due to the variety of enemies encountered. There are enough guides to explain the easy to remember combos for you to use. There could have been a bit more complexity on that part but that gets balanced by the enemy's difficulty as you progress through the game. In the beginning and mid game most of them are easy to beat (depending on difficulty mode) but towartds late game I died a lot =).
Aside from enemies there are some environmental dangers to be dealt with in certain areas, each specific to the level you're playing in. They're not super unique but it does give more depth to the gameplay.

Some people should keep in mind that this is not a remake of any sorts, but the same game that was already released alongside the Playstation version, where MIDIs were the standard for PCs. I know, this is no excuse by today's standards, but I won't let a review become biased because of Square Enix's laziness, I want to rate the game. On top of that, the "Roses and Wine" Mod fixes those issues perfectly.
So, what is there to say about this game that hasn't been said before? I doubt there is much. The story, albeit slow at the beginning, picks up pace really fast and doesn't let you go once you get into it, character development and pacing is really well done. The junction system, while unconventional, gives opportunities for a lot of combinations and is hilariously abusive. The graphics are sub-par, unfortunately. That is because they haven't gotten a makeover with their release, just like it happened to FFVII earlier, but don't let this divert you from this interesting story that you should have experienced at least once.

Probably the best adventure game I ever played in my entire life, the first thing you're likely to notice when you start the game is how it looks. Your journey begins in a magical glade, and takes you through poorly lit ice caves, the dead forests long, snowy mountain ranges, and more. Dust, the main character, and Fidget, your trusty companion that will help you during your journey, you'll travel through a variety of interconnected stages, fighting the enemies, seeking treasures, and unlock new abilities that allow to obtain previously unreachable places. You'll meet a group of animated characters that will give you quests or continue the story in one way or another, and all of them have voice talking. While the gameplay is primarily based around navigating the levels and engaging in melee combat, there are plenty of RPG mechanics in Dust as well. Defeating enemies and solving quests will earn you experience points, and each time you level up, you can pick one of four parameters to improve. You can also craft items to help you along the journey, crafting requires both materials and a blueprint, both of which can be dropped by defeated enemies or found in chests. Opening those chests requires keys, which can be bought at a shop or found hidden in the stages. Keys can be found in secret map spots, and sometime you have to resolve riddles to get a couple of them. I'm not saying that this is the best game ever made, but its not bad either so why not give it a try? Am i right?

Received for free from an IndieGala giveaway.
A first person shooter that is very unpolished but with a price point to match the quality. Animations are mediocre. Level design isn't amazing, there are a few random dead ends with seemingly no point to them. Controls are decent but jumps are unforgiving. Once you jump you're committed to that direction and distance (it doesn't let you adjust your path mid-air).
There are scores but it seems like you only get points for enemy kills (no timer, no health bonuses, etc.)
There are a few weapons but levels generally force you into a specific weapon or give you a small selection. Weapons are pretty standard, not very different except in rate of fire and damage. There is no ammo/heat management; you can shoot forever. The shotgun seems to have a little spread, I couldn't tell if any other weapon had any special properties.
There are no checkpoints but while levels can be long, they didn't feel excessively long. It was still annoying to repeat the whole level if you died at the end but some people like to be forced to do it right in one go.
When you die it takes a little while to try again because it shows a death screen, brings you to the main menu, then you have to load up and start the level and finally wait a few more seconds hovering midair until the game lets you move. I would've liked to be able to skip through some of that (especially the hover) and get back into the action quicker. Hovering is nice to see the map from above the first time you go through but is just a waste of time afterwards.
As a side note, I died a lot more by falling off the world than by actual enemy damage. You need to get a good idea of the terrain because you'll want to strafe or kite while shooting and it's incredibly easy to fall off a level.
Pausing doesn't actually pause the game (you can still move, jump and take damage). Enemies and the world keep going as usual so you can die while 'paused'.
Would've been nice for better volume controls (there is one unlabelled master volume slider in the pause screen but not the main menu). Volume resets to max every time you load a level. It also would be nice to have control mapping (to change key bindings) and have keys for cycling through weapons.
Some other notes:
Worth a look if you like unpolished/bad games. You have to know something's a bit off when one of the store screenshots is of the trading cards.

Stellaris is a grand strategy game mixed with 4x elements. Like Paradox' other titles, this game is made with a lot of love and attention to detail, while still providing a fun gameplay experience with almost infinite replayablity. The personal empire creation and expansion gives the player the perfect pioneer feeling, while the mid-game politics aspects turn the game into a whole new experience.
Mentionable features are the alien race creation with its ethics and the indept ship customization.
Yet, there are stilll some flaws with it. while other paradox titles give you great and well positioned information, once the player got to know the interface, stellaris lacks this comfort. Here you have to do perform 2-5 clicks more to find the info you need. in the mid to late game, the game tends to lag in big universes, even with a decent pc (gtx 980, i5 4690k, 16GB RAM), which makes it less enjoyable.
All in all, this game is totally worth your money, if you like strategy games. it is, in contrast to other paradox titles, very easy to get into, yet lets you improve your skills each time you try a new start. If you are looking for a space exploration and politics game, there are no better alternatives than this!

I've logged quite a few hours on this title already, and I'm already anticipating many many more to come.
Personally, I love the game.  It has (almost) everything I want in a 4x space game; heavy emphasis on early game exploration, event chains emulating my favorite sci-fi tropes, and big gnarly space ships blasting the crap out of each other. The domestic and foreign politics systems are a bit thin for what I was expecting from paradox, but I imagine that will flesh out in time.  Even stripped down, the government and diplomatic options are still far and away more sophisticated then the usual 4X space fare I've seen in the last 10 years (with the exception of Distant Worlds).  In fact, Stellaris reminds me of one of my favorite games from the 4x genre: the Space Empires series.  Just with updated graphics, real time / pause, and a dash of the usual paradox stuff.
Stellaris does what it does very well, and it's firmly rooted in the 4X genre.  If you are expecting it to be more complex and fiddly like other paradox titles, or a soap opera simulator like CK2....well it definitely isn't either of those things.  It has less in common w/ other paradox titles than it does with 4x games like Civ, Galactic Empires, or Endless Space.  The fussy micromanagement stuff isn't there yet, but it seems like more of the more complicated systems will be added over time with patches and expansions.
The AI, whether working for you or against you, needs some work.  The sector system feels artificial and isn't especially well explained.  It doesn't feel organic.  The faction system feels bare bones.  Diplomacy does what you would expect from a 4x, but there could be more done with it.  From what I've seen combat systems could be expanded on, especially fighters/bombers and capital ship effectiveness.

FINAL FANTASY VII is a turn-based RPG that follows the story of AVALANCHE, a group of eco-terrorist trying to prevent Shinra Inc. from draining the life energy right out of the planet.
And then the story derails into something much more complex and dramatic. It's a JRPG at its finest.
The game doesn't add much to the previous installments. It's main new feature is the materia equipment system which is absolutely brillant. You basically equip the materia into individual slots inside your weapon to learn the materia effects. You can learn Fire, Steal, Counter, you name it. You can also link them together like Fire-MP Absorb or Cover-Counterattack. Materia make this game so much more fun and flexible. You can make anybody into any party role. You can get overpowered really fast if you know what you're doing and the strongest materia requires you to work hard for it (sidequest time!)
Another strong feature is the Limit Breaks. In combat, a gauge will fill up when you take damage and you can unleash a powerful attack once the gauge is full. They look amazing and are quite powerful.
The game is simple and pretty linear. It's definitely more easy than hard. Roadblocks are nonexistent. Everybody can only equip one specific type of weapon and anybody can equip the bangles (with very few exceptions) and materias. There is only 3 party members that can enter a battle. The environment is really interactive, you will go up and down ladders and jump small gaps more than any other Final Fantasy game.
The game offers between 35-40 hours of quality storytelling. Those looking to collect and level everything may reach the 70-90 hours count. The party members are a bit odd and doesn't seem to all fit together. It's a varied cast but the story is really centered around Cloud, the protagonist. Cloud is your typical mercenary with a act now, talk later mentality. He's facing issues of his own and the story quickly becomes Cloud's story instead of AVALANCHES's.
Graphics haven't aged well. The models and UI have been improved from it's original state but the pre-rendered background looks old and out of place. The music is as always a masterpiece.
+Strong combat-oriented features (materia system and limit breaks).
+A couple sidequests that gives out great rewards.
+A couple challeging superbosses to really test out your skills.
+Great story.
+Memorable music.
+Good price.
~Party members don't quite fit all well together. It's an odd but effective cast.
~Tedious 100% achievements (leveling up materia, getting max gil, leveling to 99)
~Story can get confusing (its sequels and prequels will fill some gaps making the story so much better).
-Graphics haven't aged well (you really should'nt be playing this for graphics though...)
FINAL FANTASY VII grabs our attention with its great combat and keeps us around with a superb story and masterful music. I do recommend at full price.

I have a 3 year old daughter, and I want to get her into video games. Unfortunately, most games are built around combat, precision platforming, or complicated puzzles. This means that even games that might be combat appropriate (e.g., Fez) are impossible for her to play, so she just watches me play.
ABZU is the perfect game for young children. There's no combat. The gameplay has no fail state, so they're free to spin and dive and explore without consequences. My daughter needed help progressing, so I would steer her through the goals to the next open area, at which point she would take over again. There were a couple of scary moments that we weren't quite prepared for, but still appropriate for a 3 year old.
ABZU is also incredibly pretty, so much so that my daughter asked me this morning if she can be diver when she grows up so she can see all the pretty fish for real.
The cherry on top is that ABZU is thematically very positive, and explores forgiveness, helping those in need, and environmental rejuvination. The ending is one of the most beautiful and hopeful things I've ever seen. Even more impressive, it does all this without a single line of dialog.
If you have young children and you're lost trying to find them games that aren't the same old "learn to count" or "ABCs", get this game. We just finished it for the first time, and will probably start it back up again for playthrough two soon.

Dust is not a masterpiece. I'd say it's nowhere close to a masterpiece. The story is nothing special, the character art and designs are honestly fairly poor, and there were more than a few sequences I felt were just badly-designed. It's got its share of flaws, and its strengths don't completely make up for them. But for a game produced independently by a single man, it's still very impressive.
The scenery is beautiful, the combat is fun (albeit not nearly as great as it sounds; the combat is, in fact, not difficult to master and does not increase in complexity from the beginning of the game), and it's an enjoyable experience. As a whole, the story failed to enrapture me, the characters didn't appeal to me (with the sole exception of Fidget, and even then, it's nothing overly memorable), but I still think I had fun playing it.
This isn't a game I'd go out of my way to recommend. But if you're interested, you might as well give it a go.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a Metroidvania Jump'n'Run/Brawler with an awesome art style, an interesting story and quite a lot of content. It took me ~11 hours to beat the game once (on the second hardest difficulty with 100 % in all areas).
The story and characters (and especially your sidekick) are very anime or cartoon like, so if you are not into this, this game may not be for you. But it genuinely made me smile and laugh several times.
The controls and the combat are very responsive, though the combat does get stale with the time as you basically use the same 3 or 4 attacks over and over again. Although on the higher difficulty setting, enemies hit really hard so you really want to dodge or counter the enemy attacks.
My main complain is maybe, that you have always A LOT of money to just buy health restoring items all day long so even challenging enemies are nothing to really wory about but at the end of the day, I really enjoyed the time I had with this game.

DOOM II was the first DOOM game I played back when I was a teenager.  Back in those days, I spent hours trying to free enough base memory (DOS only gave you 640K) to play games like this.  After getting it running, the frame rate was really choppy and only playable in a reduced size window.  I remember seeing it on a 486 and being wow-ed seeing it run at full screen.  I also remember the first time seeing a chainsaw used as a weapon, which was really unheard of back in those days (Mortal Kombat had not hit the arcades yet).
So how does DOOM II hold up after all these years?  I will admit, when I started it up, it looked down right ugly running at full screen.  No joystick compatibility was a bummer as well.  I seem to remember my Gravis gamepad working on the original DOOM II back in the day, which I bought a Creative Labs Sound Blaster card specifically for the joystick port.  The level design seems to hold up well, and I still remembered many of the secret rooms.  I actually jumped a little when an imp popped out behind a hidden door, which I had forgotten about after all of these years.
To be honest, I had more fun playing this classic than playing any of the current FPS games.  You press enter, pick a difficulty, and you are playing.  In games these days, you have to sit through minutes and minutes of boring dialogue and cutscenes before you can do anything.  That why I always try to put players in the action as soon as possible in the games that I develop.

Man oh man where to begin. This game is a mishmash of so many great sci-fi titles I'm just going to hilight a few of the ones they took the best qualities from. First there's the combat which for oldschool guys will remind you of a modernized Starcontrol 2 melee battle right away with its newtonian physics and fast paced action. Then in 2002 there was this great little SHUMP called Starscape which I beleive to be the true spiritual successor to this title. Look it up on Steam and watch the trailer to know what I mean. It was a blend of the classic arcade game Sinistar that threw a touch of Wing Commander Privateer's exploration, commerce and ship upgrades into the mix. Now add in expansive multiplayer that can support up to 10,000 people per server, RPG dialogue, factions, character creation, player classes, and FTL's hypnotic space opera music score on top of all of that and you've got Void Expanse. You can focus on combat, mining, salvage, exploration, you name it. The learning curve is easy to pick up, controls extremely crisp and the multiplayer features allow for PvE and FFA PvP servers. There's even full steamworks and modding support.
All in all despite the occasional crash/bug, this game is a total package and steal for the modest price tag.

Ahhh finally a good PC version of this game. I am glad I added this to my collection.
After reading some reviews, I was concerned that this version was bad, but it seems that some of the complaints were a little misplaced in my opinion.
Sound
So here is the weird thing, everything sounds like the familiar way it is supposed be. Wav, midi, and old PS1 style. No HD Remastered sound effects or music, this is a good thing to me in this case. If you have problems, you may need to update drivers or your midi set. The orginal PC game had to install Yamaha Extensive MIDI sound library just to get the sounds to work (needless to say, you do not have to go through that trouble anymore).
Graphics
I have not tried the orginal mode, but I can clearly see what is going on. Some people might not know how bad a game designed for 4:3 CRT TVs look like on a 1080p screen, but overall this is a lot better than when it was orginally released. However there are some spots that look silly. You will know them when you see them. Take a deep breath and just keep playing
But the biggest suprise for me, is the overall FMV quality. I am very pleased with this because the FMV in the orginal PC release is more choppy on the recommend 800x600 (for the time).
Controls
I would recommend using a controller, but it is optional. The direction movement is only 8 ways, true to its orginal version. If this puts you off, then this is not the game for you.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who would enjoy an old jrpg from the 1990s. If you are worried about HD grapics and remaster music, then this game is not for you.
Also you will need a facebook account or a square/enix to sign in once before playing this. So make sure you have internet access the first time you start this. After that, you should be good.

After playing many hours of this game, I think its safe to say its Dungeon Defenders 1.5. It isn't a bad thing at all, its a remake with good changes (Even though there's a couple of bad changes, the good outweighs)
Good
-Rebalanced the enemies and classes. It does not feel like there is an exact meta unlike the first game (Harpoons, Minions, EV Buffs, etc etc). You're more free to mix and match with the defenses among several classes.
-Better chance of no hackers. It was a major problem in the first game, but with the playverse feature, it defintely has a much better defense against hackers.
-Game feeling more like a co-op game. Some things made it to where its harder to solo, but thats not bad due to this being a co-op game. Example, survival is one big wave instead of multiple, it requires a builder to stay as that character while others need to DPS to help or even a 2nd builder!
-New gameplay additions. The amulets give useful spells to help with the defense further, even builders can do more than just repair if they didn't spec any hero damage! The dashing mechanic helps slow characters like Squire move across the map with greater ease while it can help some DPS characters dodge attacks that would hurt a lot.
-Not P2W! The only thing that is paid for is the game itself and just some cosmetic taunts. Trendy declared that they would not charge money for new maps! Heck, even the loot and XP boosters are DROPS instead of paid for!
Bad
-Summoner. They tried to make it less relied on compared to the first game, but they went too far to making him near complete useless. Sure you can still try using him like RTS with some improved minions, but lack of MU makes it hard when you have to share DU.
-DPS Balance. UPDATED! They listened to the problem with elemental weapons! Although they're still a bit powerful, they did give a serious nerf to the elemental amulet. (Still listed as a negative due to elemental weapons still being clearly much better than regular damage)
-No local co-op or private taverns. Another issue that is very known, but it would be nice to be given these options!
-No tutorial. Getting friends into this game who haven't played the first is a bit tricky at first, it would be nice to have an actual tutorial.
Overall
I recommend this game to those who liked the first game as well as people who just love tower defense games! It is a remake, and there are somethings not added in yet, but its defintely worth checking out!

Stellaris is my first experience with grand strategy games, and I have to say so far I love it. The game features many elements to it that continually build upon each other throughout the game; resource collection, exploring, research, fleet building, diplomacy (trade/alliances/pacts/war/etc), and even random events. The game runs smoothly, looks great, and it won't play the same way twice with the way each galaxy is crafted. The game is quite easy to dig into due to the tutorial being not too shabby, and it seem liks one playthrough will take quite a long time (my first one is 20+ hours so far and not even close to being done). Paradox has definitely done a great job with this game and it has potential to be even greater.
I highly recommend this game if you like strategy games on a larger scale. You'll be part of an empire that may grow to hundreds of solar systems. The game handles this pretty well with assigning self-governing sections, but in reality you're still the one setting infrastructure and huge decisions. The ethics and actions you perform affect how your empire is perceived and how your populations agree with you! Battles are pretty fun to watch as you make dozens and dozens of variously sized ships fight with weapons (you can design your own ships). Watch a video or of this game being played and you'll know immediately if you want it.
Lastly, I'd like to mention because you can choose and build your own civilization to start the game... it has pretty good role playing capability to the game. Want to be humans that finally reach faster than light travel? War hungry birds? Friendly space fungus? Collectivist bugs? You can do so! The ethics of the civilization you choose directly impact how you can make decisions in the game.
My only qualms with the game is that the user interface can be overwhelming at times (especially mid to late game when you're in control of a lot of things at once). However, Paradox seems and has already been working on improvements thanks to feedback from the community. The future of this game is looking stellar!

Call of Duty: Black Ops is one of the best Call of Duty games to date, offering a brilliant single player, addicting multiplayer and an excellent redux of the Nazi Zombies gamemode originally introduced in Call of Duty: World at War.
The singleplayer campaign is set in the Cold War/Vietnam War era, and follows S.O.G. operative Alex Mason, a soldier under interogation about his previous missions. The gameplay consists of the player visiting flashbacks as missions during the interogation. The storyline is well put together with great character developement, with characters such as Frank Woods and Viktor Reznov quickly becoming fan favourites. The plot is easy enough to follow for anyone playing the game, yet in-depth enough to make the story brilliant.
The multiplayer is very addicting and allows for alot more customisation compared to previous titles in the series. Whilst the player count on PC at the time of writing this review is very low, it is still a blast to play. All the weapons, perks and killstreaks are balanced well, and Treyarch did an excellent job of supporting the game during it's prime, with patches being frequently released.
The Nazi Zombies mode is what makes this title in the series stand out. As a continuation from Call of Duty: World at War's Nazi Zombie mode, Black Ops adds alot more to the mode than before. New weapons, new perks, new maps, new boss fights, and new easter eggs add alot more content than the World at War version. Although the gamemode can get stale and boring after time, playing it with friends will greatly increase the enjoyment and playtime.
Overall, I recommened this game to anyone who loves FPS games. I suggest getting this game on sale, as the playerbase for multiplayer is very low and can be difficult finding a game, but does not take away from the overall experience.

TL;DR: Game is worth buying if you're a fan of 4X or other Paradox games. If you aren't, it's probably easy enough to get into but may not have lasting appeal. Perhaps wait for a sale or a few patches to add more content.
PRO:
- Compelling early game exploration and expansion gameplay.
- Interesting and viable systems for managing multi-species empires through several different approaches.
- Tech system is, at least to me, a welcome change from traditional tech trees.
- Combat and ship design add a lot of potential depth to the normal grand strategy combat (but see CON section).
- Lots of opportunity for creativity and emergent narrative.
CON:
- Midgame feels somewhat sparse. There aren't many events and the AI is a bit on the passive side, so you mostly tech up, fight wars on your terms, and backfill planets you haven't already settled.
- Faction system feels very barebones. It has great potential but doesn't represent any serious threat to your empire in its current state.
- Combat is not exceptionally well balanced. While ship designs have a lot of potential, there are clearly optimal builds that can let you dominate even the strongest empires.

Stellaris is a game where you go in thinking,
And simply speaking, it's not. In fact, I think it's far better than any other futuristic grand strategy I've ever played.
In the vein of Paradox Interactive strategy, Stellaris has an overwhelming amount of information the second you get into it but thankfully they've included an actually-helpful tutorial. This game is also crazy dynamic, and your games will be long and interesting. Sometimes you find Earth controlled by the United Nations, sometimes you find it a barren wasteland undergoing nuclear winter. The galaxy actively develops around you and you never feel cheated by the AI either. Some nations will get bigger, some will get stronger, and some will be smarter, but that doesn't mean you can't catch up nor does it mean you won't ever surpass them.
The sheer scale of this game is hard to explain. Just getting into it, you'll see a lot and think it's as far as you're gonna go, but if you play around and experiment and push boundaries, you're going to find out there's a lot hidden under the hood. None of it is expressly laid out for you to see, but all of it is accessible if you're curious enough.
Surprisingly, the learning curve isn't a steep slope of death and the game is (relatively) forgiving for Paradox. Keep trying and you'll figure things out in no time.
I still haven't beaten the game, not that I don't want to, it's instead that there's so much to do and the challenges are actively evolving around me in a tangible, clear way.
The graphics are simple but they're satisfying. The art style is motion-tweened painted characters but wow it manages to work very well. Cities are static planet art and gloriously glowing beacons on the planets.
The sound is very familiar. That doesn't mean it's stolen or copied or anything, but Stellaris has a very clear sound direction akin to modern sci-fi like Mass Effect.
The similarities do not stop there, though. This game clearly takes many pages from modern sci-fi and fantasy and it works in its favor. It's not contrived, and its references are subtle.
I truly recommend it. Even if I find myself frustrated and upset with how my game is going, I come back hours later with a different strategy and try to overcome anything in my way. I end up satisfied no matter what.

What a hoot of a game, this long arduous descent into a ring of contemptuous shenannigans was a great example, even a good bench-mark, of game design of it's time. Nuanced observation, a fine understanding of simple gamer joys, well thought-out map sections, and a... XD ..deplorable sense of humour lead to a great first-person shooter experience. Claustrophobic and unpredictable, the game had a strange sense of 'coming up for air' all the way through it. The horror aspect was handled well and lead to some stunning situations and visuals that made for creepy times, unfortunately perhaps not really creepy enough. The game, if played right, felt like a personal conquest with one being cast as a purifying agent, an avenging angel on loan to the state, a skilled assassin with almost god-like powers and nasty guns. The labyrinthian nature of the sections have nice bottlenecks and tight gunplay is recommended. Innovations like the NPC bots making snickering jokes about seeing your torchlight in dark areas and blind firing panicking retreating enemies have enhanced the whole FPS game play mode. The background soundscapes scare my roomie =)
Tips of the hat to Doom 3, Max Payne and the movie 'the ring' I recommend this romp for anyone interested in revisiting a grand parent of the modern video-game paradigm and taking it out for a drive.

I have a 3 year old daughter, and I want to get her into video games. Unfortunately, most games are built around combat, precision platforming, or complicated puzzles. This means that even games that might be combat appropriate (e.g., Fez) are impossible for her to play, so she just watches me play.
ABZU is the perfect game for young children. There's no combat. The gameplay has no fail state, so they're free to spin and dive and explore without consequences. My daughter needed help progressing, so I would steer her through the goals to the next open area, at which point she would take over again. There were a couple of scary moments that we weren't quite prepared for, but still appropriate for a 3 year old.
ABZU is also incredibly pretty, so much so that my daughter asked me this morning if she can be diver when she grows up so she can see all the pretty fish for real.
The cherry on top is that ABZU is thematically very positive, and explores forgiveness, helping those in need, and environmental rejuvination. The ending is one of the most beautiful and hopeful things I've ever seen. Even more impressive, it does all this without a single line of dialog.
If you have young children and you're lost trying to find them games that aren't the same old "learn to count" or "ABCs", get this game. We just finished it for the first time, and will probably start it back up again for playthrough two soon.

DOOM II was the first DOOM game I played back when I was a teenager.  Back in those days, I spent hours trying to free enough base memory (DOS only gave you 640K) to play games like this.  After getting it running, the frame rate was really choppy and only playable in a reduced size window.  I remember seeing it on a 486 and being wow-ed seeing it run at full screen.  I also remember the first time seeing a chainsaw used as a weapon, which was really unheard of back in those days (Mortal Kombat had not hit the arcades yet).
So how does DOOM II hold up after all these years?  I will admit, when I started it up, it looked down right ugly running at full screen.  No joystick compatibility was a bummer as well.  I seem to remember my Gravis gamepad working on the original DOOM II back in the day, which I bought a Creative Labs Sound Blaster card specifically for the joystick port.  The level design seems to hold up well, and I still remembered many of the secret rooms.  I actually jumped a little when an imp popped out behind a hidden door, which I had forgotten about after all of these years.
To be honest, I had more fun playing this classic than playing any of the current FPS games.  You press enter, pick a difficulty, and you are playing.  In games these days, you have to sit through minutes and minutes of boring dialogue and cutscenes before you can do anything.  That why I always try to put players in the action as soon as possible in the games that I develop.

Overly I enjoyed the pc version of Final Fantasy 8. There are buggy issues at times which others have mentioned in some of the negative reviews, but I didn't encounter them (or notice them at least) until the very end of the game. The problems at the end being the death animations of the final boss.
The magic booster, which was added to the game, I like. Others call it cheating because it gives you a number of basic magic spells (including such late level magic like curaga) for free, but I personally don't feel like it gives you any magic which wasn't easy to obtain anyway. In my opinion, one of the drawbacks of ff8 was the grind in drawing 100 of each spell (especially if you try to have 100 of each spell on all your characters for various reasons such as refining it later) and I think that adding the magic booster was a good thing.
The FMV's of the game held up well enough to me against the test of time, and hardly seemed that outdated (especially considering the game was released in 1999). Others have reported problems with the music, but I never had a problem with it, though maybe I am old school enough not to care. Pretty much, the music stood up to how I remembered it when I played it when it was first released.
As far as the controls for the game go, they were on ocassion problematic. An example being Zell's limit break which requires you to type in keyboard combinations or the Timber Train Hijacking which required you to do the same thing. Overly, it seemed to me that the keys chosen for these types of tasks were poorly chosen by Square Enix, but I am playing on a laptop and consequently my keyboard may be different than others. Still, in the end, it really wasn't that hard to adjust.
As far as the story and writing go, that didn't hold up to how wonderful I thought they were when I first played it (C'est La Vie), but it was still good enough to finish and having now replayed it as an adult, I can safely say I caught things which I had missed or forgotten.
I do recommend the game as a solid RPG and as a classic for any fans of RPG's. The issues I've talked about in this review really were pretty minor to me and overly I enjoyed replaying the game.

From the team that brought us World of Goo (One of my all time favourite indie games) comes Little Inferno.
A simple drag and drop system where you buy new items from a catalog to successful complete combos and earn more money. It’s a nice little loop. It has a similar art style to that of World of Goo and features some really fun little animations that are tailors to the different items you can use.
Make sure to burn at least one of each item in the catalog. We’ve been doing this as we unlock another one because it makes it easier in the long run plus you get to see all the little fun animations as different things burn up. The second reason for doing this is you’ll find out which items like to explode on their own and which need a little extra to get them started.
There are various ways in this game to progress and upgrade. One of the many ways is using the money you’ve earned in the form of buying new catalogs and extra spaces in your mailbox. The game keeps you aiming for it’s tasks so you’ll have to keep on top of all them combos too if you wanna keep unlocking new stuff.
Running low on money after making some bad combos? Track down them pesky spiders as they give you 3 corns and after collecting a couple of them you’ll be back to no good burning things again.
Using the ‘Tomorrow Stamps’ you can speed up your purchases but we wouldn’t advise this certainly in the early stages of the game because it’s got a good progression speed that keeps in fun and entertaining even whilst you wait for your extra items. We were able to complete the game without using any of these at all so if you are willing to put in the time then try and match us on that.
The max money you can hold is 999 and the max ‘Tomorrow Stamps’ you can hold is 99, any more you collect after that won’t count so if your coming close why not take a minute from completing objectives and just burn some of your favourite in-game items.
As well as completing combos you also have to buy items for the odd little people that like to send you letters.
We didn’t want to spoil the game too much so we’ve picked our favourites from the early sets of items you get, but later on there are some really entertaining ones
– This sure packs a punch with a huge explosion.
– This item has its own gravity similar to the moon and allows you to float all your items in mid air

Word to the wise  - Autopilot is a little drunk at times.
I'll admit the game feels very early access at times, with the amount of crashes and updates that have happened in the last few days, not just patching bugs, but dealing with content and balance issues.  Basically you are put in charge of a single ship of which can be minorly upgraded through various slots of boosters/weapons/otherwise.  There are a good deal of ships, all specializing in some area so it becomes a game of deciding what your play style is and attempting to find the right weapons/ships/addons to facilitate that.
I'd started off a few times as an Adventurer, and found my focus exceedingly split between all the different avenues one can pursue.  Eventually I settled upon Prospector and that I feel gave me a solid base to build from (As it nearly maxes out the Mining Tree).  It doesn't though, seem to matter what class you pick as it throws you down the same funnel as everyone else - and nobody seems to comment or the game adjust itself for your choice outside of the points spent on builds.
Factions are seemingly a big deal,  but having given a cursery look at what was to offer nothing really struck me as a place that is beneficial for someone who just wants to shoot lasers at rocks and collect things.  (There is no, straight up miners guild or anything - and of course you start out with almost maxed stats in that so in there isn't much further progression outside of spending into survivability)
There are quiet a few space stations somewhat randomly laid out dependent upon your specific world seed.  Within these places you can gather quests which fall under the basic structures "Go get this" "Go kill this" "Make sure this doesn't get killed" "Talk to this person" "Deliver this" They don't seem to particularly care who you are as it just appears randomly when you ask the station commander (Sorta wish there was a job board instead)
Outside of that, there is a story that you are trying to progress, and the day to day dealings of being within a space sand box . Of which, there are limited resources and enemies in certain areas, so in, you could go on a mission in faction controlled sections and wipe out every last dirty space pirate you come across.
I do find myself wishing there was the ability to do more with friendly NPC's (As basically you can only ask them the usual questions or attempt to buy fuel off them if you happen to be low).
My limited experience with multiplayer has left me a little skepitcal on that front.  As you start out as a new player in every game you enter (No carrying a ship and progress over from place to place) You are basically at the mercy of a star system that very well might be almost completely devoid of enemies or I imagine ore to mine (As stated before, things can be limited).  The place I was in, I was hard pressed to find anyone in any of the faction sections, and the non-faction sections of space were basically slim pickings.
Also, it should be known that if someone takes their game offline you lose that character and whatever progress/stuff you've accumilated. So in, seemingly less reason to tread in those waters but to hang out with friends and futz around.
I've still been enjoying my time with the game so far - and while I'm not sure if they have loftier plans for the games future, though from what I've been able to gleam, they seem intent upon adding more (How much, only they, and I imagine the funds gotten from selling the game will decide).

Wonderful topdown Elite clone with RPG elements of a skill tree for your character and the customization of your space ship.
The combat is similar to Subspace, not sure if anyone remembers that old space combat multiplayer game from the 90's.
Your ships have hardpoints which can be fixed (you have to turn your ship to aim) or are turrets that turn a certain amount of degrees and you can aim that way.  Either way,  turning the ship around quickly is important and when things get more difficult your skill (not the skill of your character) of piloting your craft will make a big difference.
The fact that the combat is realtime and dependent upon your piloting skill can make the game more frustrating than for example Drox operative which is turn based and the combat is similar to SPAZ.
I am 7.5 hours into my second campaign, my character is level 32 and I am enjoying the game immensely by just farming pirates. I have read some of the negative reviews and I agree that the game probably needs more content but otherwise it is perfect for me. I did encounter two crashes so far which is very annoying.
Pros:
- Open world "feels" open
-RPG skills work for unlocking weapons/ships and make your character more effective. I would have been happy with just
the "RPG" system of upgrading my ship so the added bonus of having a skill tree is awesome
- Combat is fun, I enjoy ploughing through  hordes of pirates/aliens
- The different weapon systems and energy/kinetic weapons work well... seems balanced/make sense
- Ship customization is fun, there are a lot of combination to try. The hull is just another equipment slot so you can
easily swap ships if you want to change from your combat vessel to your mining vessel with more cargo space.
- Hunting pirates, mining, trading is easy to do.. all you need to do is find pirates, asteroids and space stations and you are off.
- Mods, I can't wait for the game to be out longer and having more mods to install :)
- Price, great value for $15
Cons:
- Needs more content, under extras on the main menu there is an "upcoming" button which lists all the things the dev is planning so I think we are good... also the mods will help
- Difficulty can  be frustrating sometimes

One of my favorite shooters of all time, and the game that desensitized me to most horror when I was a lad, FEAR is a wonderful, if not exactly groundbreaking, thriller-esque romp.  The normal points of critique are not really where FEAR excels. The graphics aren't spectacular, even for their age (though there are about a billion particle effects), character facial models look like they're made of clay.  The level design isn't particularly inspired, mostly taking place in industrial complexes or office environments.  There are generally side-paths you can take to locate goodies or flank enemies, but it isn't as open as, say, Crysis.  Bullet time is well-implemented and something of a necessity to deal with the rather intelligent enemy AI, but it's nothing new.  The horror mostly amounts to jump scares, though there are some tense moments (and disturbing ones, for the faint of heart).  The story is pretty cheesey, and is really nothing more than an excuse for the rather bizarre collection of sci-fi elements: clone supersoldiers, psychics, reflex-induced bullet time, guns that nail people to walls or roast them into charred skeletons or explode them into a fine red mist.
Oh yeah, there's those.  While the gunplay isn't stellar, the weapon selection is actually pretty enjoyable. You start off with a semi-auto pistol (which you can dual-wield), a decent SMG that you're nonetheleses going to want to ditch, and an assault rifle with a double-drum magazine. These are the boring guns. As you progress, you find a seemingly-ordinary SPAS-12 knockoff that is capable of reducing mooks to a fine red mist at point-blank range in one or two shots and is so ridiculously common and has such a massive reserve ammo capacity you'll never need to discard it, a pneumatic rifle that fires 10mm spikes, capable of ragdolling mooks on death and nailing them to any nearby surface (think the crossbow from Half-Life 2, but with a magazine and an automatic firing mode), a particle beam that reduces enemies to skeletons when they die, a tri-barrel rocket launcher like something out of Quake or Unreal Tournament, and at least half a dozen more. Each has its uses and plays really well with the bullet-time mechanic, allowing you to pretty much wreck anything you come across, provided you have the right selection, and a sharp mind.  Combine that with some kung-fu moves, and you're like an action hero.
Which is really what the game is, and why I love it. It's not some complex and deep BioWare-esque world or storyline.  It's a silly 90s action movie that, while it isn't really self-aware, nonetheless doesn't try to take itself too seriously.  You show up, blow off the heads of masked clones with your superhuman reflexes and martial prowess, and save the day from the psycho-terrorist.  Not a smart game, but nonetheless made of awesome.  If nothing else, it's a good way to kill a weekend.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is absolutely fantastic, and a no-brainer to pick up when it's on sale (Steam Summer Sale, 80% off at $2.99).  Even still, at the regular price this game is definitely worth picking up.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is an old-school Zelda style dungeon crawler (think, A Link to the Past) that requires the player to take on challenging dungeons and bosses to progress through the game.  What sets it apart from any other games is its use of a music/rhythm mechanic for movement; you can only move one "block" of space at a time along with the beat of the games soundtrack (or your own music, if you want to use a custom soundtrack!).  Moving constantly with the beat and not taking damage from enemies builds your gold multiplier, allowing you to get more gold for character upgrades, items, and weapons to use through your run.  Stop moving to the beat, make a wrong move (i.e. jumping into a wall/trap) or take a hit, and your multiplier resets.  Does the rhythm movement mechanic seem gimmicky?  Not to worry, it's incredibly fun and the phenominal soundtrack makes for a great experience.  Custom soundtrack options are also great; the auto-beat-importer works very well, and if necessary you can create custom beats for any songs you import.
Combat in Necrodancer is fast and incredibly fun.  There's no "attack wildly and pray for success" here; successful combat requires deliberate and calculated attacks/movement.  In addition to the fun beat mechanic, weapon variability is what makes Necrodancer so fun and engaging.  Weapons vary greatly in attack types, range, buffs (i.e. knockback, freezing, etc.), and strength.  Certain weapons will definitely be more successful against some enemies than others, and your preference will largely depend on the play style you prefer.
In addition to combat, the other two mechanics you'll consider are digging (via your shovel) and vision.  A large part of dungeons is finding your way around, digging up "diamonds" to use for permanent upgrades and other unlockables, and finding hidden rooms for temporary items or character buffs.  Both your shovel and vision (view distance) can be upgraded to allow more efficient exploration and finding better items for your runs.
Runs last until you complete the dungeon and move on to the next, die, or the level's song ends (~5 minutes) and kicks you to the next level of the dungeon automatically (but, if you dont find the exit and the level auto-ends, you lose your score multiplier).
Progression in Necrodancer is very difficult, but fair and rewards mastering the movement/beat mechanic.  Learning enemy and boss attack patters is paramount to success, and enemies very greatly from level to level and present a great challenge as you progress.
Each time you die you are returned to a lobby where you can buy upgrades for your character to improve for your next run.  You can only spend "diamonds" in the lobby earned from your immediate previous run, and starting a new one resets all of your "diamonds" that can be spent in the lobby.  With a variety of dungeons, bosses and increasing difficulty as you progress you'll definitely get some good (and fun) play time out of this game.  There are also a large variety of different playable characters that change game mechanics and add tons of play time and very high replay value.  For example, the "Bard" can move freely (is unlocked from the beat mechanic), but every time you move functions as a "beat" in the game - so as you move, enemies move, and the faster you move, the faster they move, and the faster you move, the faster the timer for the level expires still requiring you to be deliberate in movement.
, one of the best casual, low-commitment games I've played in a very, very long time.

I've had this game in my library for a while now, and it's long overdue for a review. Crypt of the Necrodancer is a rogue-like rhythm game with a bumpin' soundtrack, great visuals, and a unique style of gameplay to keep you occupied for hours. Keeping time with the music while dancing around enemies is rewarded with multipliers that enhance the player character's capabilities and set you into a groove that really lets the mechanics shine and put you in a game feel induced trance.
There's not much to say about the game in terms of cons, because you'll find that the good outweighs the bad fairly well, however, this game is not without its flaws.
Sometimes the screen will be clogged with enemies, leaving you no room for options if you're not prepared. While this may be simply be attributed to the game being a roguelike and you, as the player, not being as ready as you should be, it's also worth noting that this becomes increasingly clearer as enemies that can attack diagonally start showing up in the lategame, which never feels fair when you're slain by one.
Overall though, this game is a worthwhile experience that I would happily pay $15 for, and if you can get it for cheaper than $10, then I can't see a reason that you wouldn't have this little gem in your library, even if just to save it for a rainy day.

The visuals are outstanding. Each location is gorgeous. The crafting system, while limited, is simple and wields worthwhile results.
The story is entertaining with moments are sadness. The revelation of who Dust is was unexpected and creative, an outcome that worked extremely well with the story being told.
The combat is simple and enjoyable, though it does grow repetitive and tiresome after a while. It's basically hack and slash your way through everything with a few special moves thrown in.
The voice acting is solid, though a little over-acted at times. Fidget added a lot of humor to the story, though some people might find her high-pitched voice annoying.
It's a very linear game but as you progress and gain new abilities, you are able to go back through levels and acquire treasures. The treasures aren't particularly mind-blowing, though I did get an excellent ring at the end. Most of my best items were acquired through crafting. I finished the game without 100% completing all the treasures, but never felt a need to go after them.
By 7-8 hours into the game, I just wanted to finish, due to the repetitive combat. The last area or two did mix things up a bit with increasingly difficult platformer aspects.
My game froze repeatedly with one glitch in the Abadis Forest. It wasn't game-breaking though would have prevented 100% completion. Other than that, the game ran excellently on my PC. XBOX wired controller for Windows worked great. Seemless switching between controller and keyboard/mouse, but I did play exclusively on controller.

At the risk of sounding a litle too "me too!" I feel obligated to weigh in on this game. It has the potential to be great, and I love the art style and mimalistic UI, but it doesn't have enough rich content yet. If you read no further, wishlist this title and check on it from time to time. I don't think my "no" will stick forever.
For those of you with longer attention spans, I'll expound a bit. VoidExpanse is the type of game I'm really wanting to sink my teeth into, but can't. Similiar titles in the genre include things like Spaz and Drox Operative (definitely check both of those out for similiar (but different) experiences. VoidExpanse gives you a nice-looking sandbox to play in, but doesn't give you all the toys necessary to have a good time. The skeleton is all here, but the experience feels empty a few hours in.
There simply isn't enough breadth/depth to what you can do to (or with) your character. The classes and ship options are fairly one-dimensional, and the quests are still pretty rinse and repeat. I'd love to see more dynamic quests involving attacks on space stations, some kind of hacking interface/skill tree, true smuggling runs, more interaction (even the ability to join) with the pirate faction, etc. The game just doesn't do interesting things with it's own universe yet.
I love this game for what it is, and for the price point I'm still happy with my purchase, I'm just hoping that they take this brilliant foundation and build something atop it. I know there are countless ideas floating around the community - let's hope some of them see the light of day.

I have played this game extensively, but not on Steam.
Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 is a Real Time Strategy (RTS) game serving as the third installment of the popular Command & Conquer series.  It features a rebooted story and a brand new faction called 'The Empire of the Rising Sun'.  However, unlike its predecessors,  Electronic Arts who acquired Westwood Studios, the original developers of the game, produced Red Alert 3.  It is one of the last few remaining franchises who use live action cutscenes which the series is known for.
Players once again take the role of the unknown commander who leads either the Allied Forces, the Soviet Army, or the newly resurrected Imperial Armed Forces to ultimate victory.
Red Alert 3's story starts with the Soviet Union in complete collapse after the events of Red Alert 2.  In an effort to stop the USSR's defeat, surviving Soviet leaders use a time machine to go back in history and erase Albert Einstein in order to prevent him from developing Allied technology.  Upon returning to the Present day however, they discover that without Einstein, nuclear technology was  never developed.  With this turn of events, this meant that the US never bombed Japan and the Empire never surrendered during World War 2.  Now the Empire has risen once more and poses a new threat to both the Soviets and the Allies prompting the hilarious line by actor Peter Stormare as Dr. Gregor Zelinsky: “We now have...two mortal enemies?”
+ Colorful visuals and very nice graphics with good use of Physx technology
+ New 'Empire of the Rising Sun' faction is fun to play featuring highly advanced, extremely versatile, very expensive, and unhealthily suicidal units (ex. Tsunami Tank:
Imperial Warrior:
Shogun Battleship:
Yari Sub:
+ Fun campaign for all 3 factions
+ Hilarious, Hammy, Cheesy but overall good voice acting
+ Humorous and entertaining Tutorial
+ All units for all factions now have secondary abilities
+ Co-op campaign
+ Very nice Music and Sounds
- The very colorful art-style that could cause headaches for some people
- Some low polygon models, low resolution shadows, and poor textures can be seen here and there
- Short campaign for each faction
- Story is shallow and uses way to many cliche elements from the previous Red Alert 2
- Occasional pathfinding problems
- Balance issues with some of the units
- Some outstanding bugs that was never fixed (for some reason, changing the graphics quality and  resolution at the same time MAY cause a crash)
- Despite EA's vast resources and use of big name actors like Peter Stormare and George Takei, I can't help but feel that they were not able to live up to the standard of Westwood.
- Broken multiplayer on Steam (No idea if it works in Origin)
GREAT RTS GAME.  Although it does not fully capture the magic of Red Alert 2, Red Alert 3 still delivers a great fast paced experience for RTS fans looking for a quick fix.  The campaign is fun with a story that is easy to follow but uses a lot of cliche plot elements.  The Soundtrack is excellent and the over-the-top, hammy, and cheesy voice acting are very entertaining.  Multiplayer is also fun if you're looking for a casual RTS experience since the AI does pose a challenge on higher difficulties.  In addition, new game mechanics such as the secondary abilities and the new faction spices up the action.
Now we come on whether or not I recommend this game.  If you're in this for the single player experience, sure I can RECOMMEND this game easily.  If you're in this for the multiplayer experience, I DO NOT RECOMMEND this game here on Steam because for some reason the Servers are broken so you're better off purchasing this in EA's Origin Platform.

I've logged quite a few hours on this title already, and I'm already anticipating many many more to come.
Personally, I love the game.  It has (almost) everything I want in a 4x space game; heavy emphasis on early game exploration, event chains emulating my favorite sci-fi tropes, and big gnarly space ships blasting the crap out of each other. The domestic and foreign politics systems are a bit thin for what I was expecting from paradox, but I imagine that will flesh out in time.  Even stripped down, the government and diplomatic options are still far and away more sophisticated then the usual 4X space fare I've seen in the last 10 years (with the exception of Distant Worlds).  In fact, Stellaris reminds me of one of my favorite games from the 4x genre: the Space Empires series.  Just with updated graphics, real time / pause, and a dash of the usual paradox stuff.
Stellaris does what it does very well, and it's firmly rooted in the 4X genre.  If you are expecting it to be more complex and fiddly like other paradox titles, or a soap opera simulator like CK2....well it definitely isn't either of those things.  It has less in common w/ other paradox titles than it does with 4x games like Civ, Galactic Empires, or Endless Space.  The fussy micromanagement stuff isn't there yet, but it seems like more of the more complicated systems will be added over time with patches and expansions.
The AI, whether working for you or against you, needs some work.  The sector system feels artificial and isn't especially well explained.  It doesn't feel organic.  The faction system feels bare bones.  Diplomacy does what you would expect from a 4x, but there could be more done with it.  From what I've seen combat systems could be expanded on, especially fighters/bombers and capital ship effectiveness.
Even with that, I absolutely recommend the game for space fans, 4x fans, and strategy fans in general.  It hits just enough of the right notes to make me feel like I'm participating in a sci fi story of my own.  For me everything else is just details.

I want to make a note, that I've only played RA3 for about 6 - 7 h when writing this "review".
I can see a fun game in there somewhere, but one major thing really kills the gameplay for me; at least during th solo campaing, and that is the shared economy. I really hate that. Since the AI is always building stuff you can't save up money for things to build, and you are ALWAYS short of resources because of this. It is really frustrating! I was looking forward to having a full co-op campaign when I bought this game, but I was not ready for that design decision.
Otherwise I've been surprised about how well this holds up as a sequel to RA2 and YR. And it is fun that we finally get a main campaign that focuses on the Sovjet side. Sure, previous games have always had the sovjet campaign aswell, but that was not the main story. And having such a great actor-rooster adds to the experience.
The amoun of bewbs (or cleavage) this game shows can be discussed. The twelve-year old inside my 25 year old body is happy, but the game would have been just as good (perhaps better) without it.
So how does the game feel then?
Basically this game is a mixture of the previous C&C titles. You've got the familiar units, all though redesigned, from the RA-series with addition of new units. You've also got the micromanagment system from RA2, which was lacking in the Generals-series; waypoints and hold-fire and stuff like that. Then again, some controls and features from the Generals series have found its way in here. It is really odd to see units and gameplay first feeling like generals, but then also feeling like RA2. I've had this game in my library for a while now, and it's long overdue for a review. Crypt of the Necrodancer is a rogue-like rhythm game with a bumpin' soundtrack, great visuals, and a unique style of gameplay to keep you occupied for hours. Keeping time with the music while dancing around enemies is rewarded with multipliers that enhance the player character's capabilities and set you into a groove that really lets the mechanics shine and put you in a game feel induced trance.
There's not much to say about the game in terms of cons, because you'll find that the good outweighs the bad fairly well, however, this game is not without its flaws.
Sometimes the screen will be clogged with enemies, leaving you no room for options if you're not prepared. While this may be simply be attributed to the game being a roguelike and you, as the player, not being as ready as you should be, it's also worth noting that this becomes increasingly clearer as enemies that can attack diagonally start showing up in the lategame, which never feels fair when you're slain by one.
Overall though, this game is a worthwhile experience that I would happily pay $15 for, and if you can get it for cheaper than $10, then I can't see a reason that you wouldn't have this little gem in your library, even if just to save it for a rainy day.
