Extremely fun shooter with a unique style and some good scares!  The guns all feel as though they belong in the game, and the atmosphere, when not in a firefight, is intense.  For being made in 2005, the graphics are outstanding!  Some bland textures will be noticed, but the particle affects and fire animations are a splendid sight.
The combat is rough at first.  The player is given a slow-mo ability, "bullet time," that takes a little getting used to.  Once the player has a better understanding of the AI and the use of the bullet time, things will start to get interesting, and by "interesting" I mean out of control!  Watching the chaos unfold in slow-motion is a lot of fun, and the ability will be VERY important in the late game fights.
The characters are all well made and the voice actors are good as well.  The game does a great job making the player feel isolated from the rest of the friendly NPCs.  It wouldn't be very scary if a team of bots came along for the ride.  Just like Gordon Freeman, the main character has no input to the events around him, which seems a bit odd considering some of the♥♥♥♥♥♥that unfolds.
The weapons themselves work well for the game, but they were far from my favorite part.  Apart from the pistols and a small number of other guns, almost every weapon in the game is burst fire, even the sniper rifle and rocket launcher, and that was a bit frustrating.  As the game progresses, some additional weapons, that are not burst fire, will be found: the shotgun and a type of bolt thrower are awesome.
The scary portions of the game seemed a little skewed at times, and at others, some of the best in an FPS.  Even though the use of a loud screeching sound was over-used, a lot of the spooks came from deep within -- that voice and feeling in the back of the player's mind that does not agree with what's on screen; unfortunately, the placement of these scares were a little off some times.  There were a number of scares that I missed and had to reload a section to see what happened due to a misjudgment of the player's actions.
The balance of action with tension was great.  Even if it was a mite predictable at times, there were plenty of moments that had me jumping out of my seat!  Worth every penny.
F.E.A.R.: Extraction point review below:
The follow-up dlc for F.E.A.R, aka Extraction point, picks up right where F.E.A.R. leaves off.  F1 leaves the player with an amazing ending to the game and choosing for the dlc to work as a conclusion is a grand idea!
The dlc starts out fast and wastes no time throwing the player right back into the mix; unfortunately, if the two games are played back to back, the combat can and will become extremely repetitive!  The  first two thirds of the game are top notch.  The combat is more furious than the first game, and there is no need to slowly work the player into the tension.  The cards are on the table and Alma is out of the bag --  so to speak.
Personally, the horror moments of Extraction point are better than it's predecessor's; however, like it was mentioned already, after the first half of the game or so, the horror segments and hallucinations become the only thing worth working towards.
The combat fails towards the end due to the fact that the same tactic works for the whole game!  On top of that, the longer the point man (your character) makes his way through the city, the less and less it makes sense that there has been ZERO military or police response to the numerous explosions happening though-out the subway and surround buildings.  A one man army scenario can work, Gordon Freeman, but the setting has to make sense.  Gordon was stuck in a city that was controlled by the same people attempting to kill him.  In extraction point, it just feels like the world has forgotten about you.
Lastly, there's the silent hero gig...  It worked for Gordon because he was never actually put into a situation where his lack of response didn't some how "work" with the dialog.  In Extraction point, the point man simply ignores the people talking to him even when it's a desperate plea for help or acknowledgment.  Friendly NPCs die because it.
If you plan on playing Extraction point, do not play it right after F1, do yourself that favor.  It's a fun and tense game, but it can be really frustrating.

What can I say about this game that hasn't already been said before? Despite the obvious flaws, it's one of the few first person shooters.. well games in general, that I keep coming back even now, many years after my first playthrough.
I'll get the negative points out of the way first. Yes, the majority of the game takes place in the same bland office building. And yes, a large portion of the story is presented through boring audio files scattered throughout each area. But what makes F.E.A.R. such a special game is the combat. It is absolutely phenomenal. I still cannot believe this game arrived in late 2005. The majority of shooters these days don't even come close to the level of quality presented in F.E.A.R.'s engaging combat scenarios. The enemy AI is among the most intelligent i've ever faced off against in a shooter. They actively work to outsmart the player, going as far as to take alternate routes completely out of their way in an effort to sneak up on the player's flank for an easy kill. They're fast, and deadly accurate. On the harder difficulties, every mistake is quickly punished leading to a near instant death. This is all partly to balance the slow-motion reflex system, which does more to add real tactical depth to the combat rather than a crutch. Enemies can and will still hit you even with reflexes engaged and with its relatively short duration, every use must be carefully planned out to ensure success.
The difficulty of the combat is what makes this game so rewarding, and why I continue to come back to it after all these years. I've played this game to completion at least a half dozen times on several difficulty settings and it still feels fresh. The graphics are extremely dated. It looks downright ugly most of the time.. but the gameplay more than makes up for it. I always found the story interesting, even if it wasn't presented in a very consistant and informative manner. F.E.A.R. does offer some legitimate scares as well, but at times they feel like more of a distraction. These moments do add mystery and a sense of forboding to the game though, and helps to set the atmosphere more than any combat scenario does.
I'm currently playing through this game again on the Extreme difficulty, and I'm loving almost every moment. The brutal efficiency of the enemy AI makes every combat scenario a tactical engagement, with the threat of a quick death ever present. Easily one of my favorite first-person shooters of all time. And in my opinion much better than the sequels.

Little Inferno is a game about exactly that, a little inferno. Inside that inferno you burn things. Those things you must buy, but no worries, you get more money out of them than you pay for 'em. Rather odd, I know. So anyways, you buy those things from a catalog and burn them brutally (not really) and then repeat the same steps. But there are also combos that you must find in order to unlock the next catalog. They make the game a lot more interesting as you only have the name of the combo which is basically the only hint you get. The combos reward you with stamps that you use to get the stuff delivered to you faster if you are impatient.
The gameplay itself is rather fun due to the a bit humorous descriptions of the items on the catalogs and due to the items themselves (and of course due to fire). Sometimes they're something simple, like a spoon or a brick, but sometimes they're something very very special, like a credit card or a TV! Awesome, I know. And they actually are a lot more interesting. They aren't the only not-that-ordinary items, there are plenty of them to keep the game interesting, and it does it successfully.

Great game for the 1st 20 hours or so. After that it becomes brutally hard (in an unbalanced manner, not in a hard-but-fun Dark Souls manner), and as some have noted the mid/end-game is lacking in content. In mid to end-game your RPG skills/ship progression comes to a crawl as difficulty ramps up very suddenly (too suddenly IMHO) while remaining repetitive (combat becomes harder but there's not anything really 'new' to it - compare this to S.P.A.Z. which introduces a whole new combat dynamic (the zombies) mid-game, which keeps things fresh.) Combat at level 5 feels much like combat when you're level 40, it's just much harder. So after a while the game starts to feel like a real grind.
This game is like a cross between a prettier S.P.A.Z. and a more action-oriented Space Rangers 2, albeit in a 'light' form. It feels superior to S.P.A.Z.  for the first 10-20 hours because the basic combat mechanics work very well - I love using mines, and it's fun to find just the right weapon combo amongst a pretty good selection of weapons. However VoidExpanse runs out of steam at about level 35-40. Some of the quests are interesting but a most of them get very grindy/cliche/repetitive fast. Still, production values are higher than with SPAZ or Space Rangers 2, and combat is a lot of fun, at least for a while. If the developers put in more mid to end-game content, more high-end ship components, and did more balancing in mid/late game, and added more features like the ability to hire henchman (sometimes you're given a henchman, but it'd be great to hire and manage them at will) then this game would be AWESOME! As it is, like I said it's fun for the first 20 hours, so for $15 I got my money's worth and I give it a thumbs up.

Dead Bits is a FPS game with voxel graphics on most of it. There are 9 levels in total, each can be completed in less than 10 minutes. The game is quite difficult and you'll need several tries to beat it.
The graphics are decent for a game with this price, although the UI can be improved. You can't pause in game although there is an option to do it (there won't be any difference except that you can't attack if you "pause" it).
Although the music is quite cool, it's not pleasant to be heard long term, as it gives me headache just listening to it a few times (especially when you need to redo the levels). There is also no mute button.
After you select a level, you'll be brought to a world with no weapon most of the time. You'll need to pick up a weapon, which can be a gun or simply a bat to swing around. There will be "health box" in some level to restore your HP. Most of the level has no platform and you can die if you fall in it. There are several objective in each level, although most of them require you to kill the enemies. In level 6 onwards, there are some variation in the game, such as dodge the attacks (level 6), time-attack level (level 7), and defeat all monsters in a wave (level 8).
Although the game is quite enjoyable, it can be tiresome when you have to redo the levels because you can't skip the dying animation and there is no replay button. There is also a lag if there are a lot of enemies in one screen, making me to stop playing at level 8.
Pros:
- Great game mechanics
Cons:
- Lag if there are a lot of enemies in a screen
- No replay button

First real review so be gentle :3 If I made any errors in this review please feel free to add me or comment on it and I will make the changes needed.
After playing a little bit of DDE and from what friends have told me, I CANNOT recommend Dungeon Defenders Eternity. Long review so if you want to skip to the results then click READ MORE and scroll all the way to the bottom.
First of all DDE was made by Nom Nom Games. NOT by Trendy Entertainment. I'm not going to go beyond the line and say Nom Nom ruined Dungeon Defenders but in my honest opinion they did more bad than good. Someone said that Nom Nom Games is apart of Trendy but I don't know. All I know is that the main team that worked on DD1 did not work on DDE. Lets start out what DDE brought to the table.
Secure Dedicated Servers for anti-hacking protection: This means always online play, even in singleplayer. No more hosting games from your computer. Everyone has to connect to the servers and that means DELAY. if you log on to DD1 and do a map and switch to DDE and do the same map you will feel a major difference. In DD1 I barely saw any hackers and if i did I would kick them immediately.
Character Dye's: You could change the color of your character in the first game. Probably not on the level of DDE but it was still in there. This also ties into new Visible Armor.
Crafting System: While leveling I barely used the crafting system. Crafted items are slightly better than drops but it doesn't really add anything to the game. Really not that different from drops except you need random drops from mana chests in order to craft the item. If you get a good recipe you could probably craft and sell it to other players.
Pet Hatching/Growth System/active abilities: I really didn't care less about the Hatching/growth system. The active abilities seemed neat at first then I forgot about them and never used them. *shrug*
Dashing and mantling systems for better mobility: Dashing was a cool concept that i'm 50/50 on. More mobility but with the laggy servers its hard to use it. Also i didn't even know there was a mantling system... Never used it.
Weapon Swapping between two weapon sets: Didn't use this one either, i'm guessing it works just like how Series E.V. works where she has 2 weapons and you click your button and it switches to another weapon. The old DD UI was fine with swapping gear/weapons. Maybe its a little bit more convenient but I didn't use it.
Community Tavern: Forcing players to be social isn't always the greatest thing. I would much rather have my own tavern that showcases all my trophy's and items that I want to drop on the floor than have a big community tavern with random people that i've never met before and barely talk in chat.
Quickmatch: I never used this in DD1 and never used it in here. I play DD with people on my friends list and so I never had a use for it. I dont know why this is a "new feature" because DD1 had it as well.
New currency, Gold coins. Instead of using mana to upgrade and buy gear from other players and the innkeeper, it is now gold.
Yatta yatta yatta Cross platform play, *shrug* One DD account and that means you keep your progression on your android devices so that can be kinda cool if you have an Android device and you play DDE on there. 34 new equipable emotes that you have to purchase for REAL MONEY.
They seem to take away a lot more content from the first DD and then put in less content. I didn't get a chance to try the new content so I don't have anything to say on the new maps. New Rebalanced missions, I actually failed on Alchemical Laboratory on Normal with my countess but I played again and comepleted the mission.
Rebalanced stat system for a greater effect on late game, didn't get a chance to see this one either.
Survival Mode was revised and its shorter play times, constantly running around looking at loot drops because they disappear more frequently than DD1 and that can get you killed easily which means if you are playing on Hardcore, good luck. The shorter play times can be a bonus to some players but i loved going for long gaming sessions with friends, seeing how far we can get on a certain map.
Hardcore mode has better rewards but has Perma-Death. I can see it being fun but for a game like DD where you need to try different builds and see what works and what doesn't, i'm a bit iffy on that. I think they're reworking Hardcore so take this part with a grain of salt.
You do get all 12 Heroes, (Squire,Huntress,Apprentice,Monk,Countess,Hunter,Adept,Initiate,Barbarian,Series E.V.,Jester,Summoner. the original campaign including Lost Eternity Shards and 7 challenge missions, 5 bonus missions (Glitterhelm, Karathiki, Tavern Siege, City In The Cliffs, Tinkerer’s Lab) and Akatit Jungle, Palantir. and then the original DD costumes.
UI feels clunky and difficult to learn. DD1 had a much better UI and it felt more responsive and it was very easy to get the hang of it. Playverse, I just hate. Its just like Uplay. I don't need another thing between me and my game. I have steam and I love steam and I don't want anyone to get in the way of something that already works really well. You bring up Playverse by clicking F11 so it just feels disconnected from everything. Its difficult to invite friends and to join them and even talk to them. It feels clunky and id much rather use the steam overlay.
-------Results-------
I give Dungeon Defenders Eternity a 6/10. DDE wasn't needed at all in the first place and I bought it because it had Dungeon Defenders in the title, after playing and realising that it wasn't developed by Trendy, I felt cheated. Some of the new features are nice but there are more bad than good. For $15 you are getting a lot more content then if you bought Dungeon Defenders for the same price. However, if you are willing to spend a little extra for DLC please consider buying Dungeon Defenders, you will get a better gaming experience than if you would if you bought DDE.
Hopefully you found my review helpful and if you need more information feel free to add me and I will do the best I can to answer your question.

Dungeon Defenders Eternity is a revamped version of the original Dungeon Defenders. Owners of the original Dungeon Defenders can purchase this game for a discount, giving all the more reason to purchase this game. Upon hearing of it's release, I bought it immediately, despite the criticism it had gained over the first few hours of it's launch. I can certainly say that some of the complaints were justified, but most of the main problems have been patched out of the game, along with balance tweaks and more. Micro-transactions are contained within the game, but are only tied to cosemtic taunts in game, that do nothing to benefit the player, other than look cool. Dungeon Defenders Eternity also comes with most of the DLC from the original game, including all the characters, the Lost Eternia Shards DLC, and the start of a new campaign. It also contains the ability to transfer items to the upcoming game Duneon Defenders II. This game gets a solid 8/10, and is recommended to purchase over the original Dungeon Defenders, both to DD veterans, and beginners alike.

A 4X game worthy of your time, Stellaris is mind boggling awesome!
PROS
-Tons of alien races with their own portrait and ships. Create and design your own races!
-Diplomacy that actually works, where you have to decide what wars will cost you if you lose. Lose a planet, or become a vassal of an enemy AI?
-Enslave populations
-Different travel methods, FTL, warp, Hyperspace, allowing different play styles
-Random Research - NO game is the same! There's no direct path to get technologies, it's random which allows for new strategies. Don't have the tech to colonize new planets? Play your cards safe. Don't have tech to upgrade your power plants? Expand and mine more power from planets from the surface.
-Space battles are epic to watch with a light layer of strategy involved.
-Tons of dialogue about past and future colonies. Go on research missions, or gain tech knowledge by researching the wrecks of enemy ships.
CONS
-Learning curve
-Slow paced at the beginning, but you can fast forward to make things go faster.
-Turn off for many (even myself) at first glance. Need to give it a chance to fall in love with it.

For a long, long time, I had this on my "not interested" list. But finally, seeing it on sale for $3 and so, so many positive reviews, I thought I'd give it a shot to see if it might surprise me. And sadly, it didn't.
It's your typical rouge-like game, plus rhythm, and that's pretty much it. There's nothing to make it stand out other than the fact you have to move on the beat. And that completely turned me off from the game. Within a couple minutes of getting used to the controls, I was already getting tired of being restricted to whatever the tempo of the songs was. If you're traveling through the dungeon or have to backtrack, it's tedious; if you're trying to get to a good spot to attack an enemy and have to keep waiting for the next beat, it can be frustrating. There was absolutely nothing redeeming about the rhythym aspect of the game. The soundtrack was admittedly great, but it could have had a good soundtrack without forcing the rhythym stuff on you.
I don't know; maybe I should have listened to my instincts and not bothered with this, but with an "overwhelmingly positive" rating and two genres I enjoy, I thought, "Why not?" The thing about the game, though, is you get weak versions of both genres that is attempted to be carried by the novelty of combining the two, and that novelty swiftly wears off.

Since I don't feel like typing out F.E.A.R. every time I refer to it, I will now proceed to call the game "Mike". Mike is a gem of a first-person shooter that many games mimic now. Not only being a beautifully dark, depressing, shadowy world full of paranormal happenings geared to make your eyes bulge and your hair turn white while it stands on end. If you're interested in giving Mike a try, duct tape the hairs on the back of your neck down, turn on all the lights in your room, and get a cup of warm tea or coffee, because this game gets  super unnerving really fast. Not only does Mike get the Survivor-FPS vibe perfectly, but it also integrates bullet-time better than the original Max Payne, and has physics nearly as beautiful as Half-Life 2. After playing Mike for about an hour and a half, I'm finding it hard to find anything seriously wrong with the game, because when you get down to it, it's a hell of a lot of fun, no matter what your original opinion was before opening it up for the first time.

As pure an example of "style over substance" as it is possible to imagine.  This is a "journey" in the most basic sense of the word - you start at one place and end at another.
The game is a visual and auditory experience; if that is enough for you, then this may entertain.  The soundtrack is soothing and the design is colourful.  The fish are pretty and obviously a lot of thought has gone into programming their movements.
The art style is cell-shaded, which can work in some games, but this just feels lazy.  The design of the player character looks as though it probably took about 10 minutes.
The game lacks any context and is completely unapologetic about it.  The nameless, voiceless, clueless character awakens in the sea and starts swimming.  You find a little robot.  The robot helps you cut some seaweed.  You find some ruins, swim through them and are teleported to a different underwater cavern, where you cause some glowing coral to grow and spectral sea creatures appear.  Then an underwater lake rises up and you swim through a triangular door and swim with some fishes.  Sometimes you are rail-roaded through some sections and it looks like swimming through shoals of fishes collects them, or activates them, or something (they flash, you o a little twirl in the water) - but there's no indication if this is achieving anything, or necessary for your progression, or if matters in the slightest.  A shark eats one of your robots - am I supposed to be sad?  Worried?  I don't think it's possible to be injured or die, so I don't really know why I would.  You can see beautiful expanses of tempting, open sea but can't swim further than the game permits you before you're turned back by an invisible wall.
The gameplay is virtually non-existent.
I gave this game 39 minutes to prove or endear itself (much longer and I think I would have actually finished it, based on other reviews) and I was left feeling completely cold to the experience.  The lack of context, story or sense of purpose completely killed this game flat for me.

Deserves the 96% positive reviews and more.
Dust: AET is visualy amazing: lush, fresh and colorful, and surprisingly soft on requirements to run it smoothly.
As far as story goes, it's quite simple on the first steps but still manages to catch you despite the numerous cliches and makes many good turns (but also some really emotional ones) as it develops. As Dust, an amnesic individual recently awaken when the game starts, you set off to regain your memories... be them good or bad. Armed with the sentient sword Ahrah and Fidget, it's guardian nimbat, you start off by defending a village from monster attacks but soon start to see the big picture behind it all.
Soundtrack is captivating and really well composed. You'd find me quite often sitting around Archer's Pass just to listen the music there (and for some other reason you'll meet if you play).
Combat is fast, but stylish. Has enough variety of moveset to make more than some combos and rewards balancing the way of the sword and Fidget's magic. No block whatsoever, but sidesteps and parry move as defensive measures. Both aerial and ground combat are quite intense.
Leveling is quite simple and straightforward: Each level awards a gem to be invested in Health, Attack, Defense and Fidget. The first three are quite obvious, but improving Fidget makes magic and Dust Storm (an special attack) stronger as well as increasing the maximum capacity of gems for the rest of the stats.
And to boot it all there are plenty of secrets in the form of trials and cages that contain characters from other games (such as Kid, from Bastion, or Super Meat Boy), which provide bonuses as you free them. Some of them can be quite challenging to obtain / complete, but the result obtained greatly outweights the effort.
Expect some backtracking as some areas are unlocked way after they are first discovered, or blocked until certain ability has been obtained to move around.
Dust is certainly a jewel in any library. 100% Completion is quite a satisfying feat to accomplish, and by no means tedious.
Giving it a good review and a thumb up feels a poor recognition for what it is.
Edit: Update for nomination awards. Game is as amazing as it was.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game. It was a completely unexpected joy and probably my favorite game of 2015.
A ton of love, time, effort, and attention to detail went into the game and it really shows.The storyline, characters, voice acting, scenery, level design, depth, and combat, were all really well done. I have only a few quibbles, all of which relate to the art style. Now, I am not opposed to the art style and I appreciated the dedication to the look throughout. The backdrops were gorgeous and the levels all had their own unique vibe while being stylistically coherent. Even the characters, for the most part, were interesting, though I think they could have been a bit more diverse and refined. The most jarring character to look at, especially in dialogue sequences/cut-scenes, is Dust himself. He could have used some extra polish, especially since we spend the entirety of the game staring at him.
I also had an issue with the run/walk animations of most characters. The stiffness of the lower bodies clashed greatly compared to the fluidity of the upper bodies, again, especially with Dust.
My biggest quibble involves the cut-scenes. The drama and impact of the scenes were completely lost due to the lack of polish in animation. One set in particular, when the major crux of the story is revealed, was especially painful. There were literally two different animation styles used in cut-scenes back to back! On the one hand, I really liked the scene with the characters in silhouette with the environment animating around them. I felt that particular style really lent itself well to the mystery and drama of the scene and enhanced the impact. But that visual device was used only once and I feel it was probably the more effective of the two styles used.
In a perfect world, if the animation issues and style refinements could be fixed, this would easily make my Favorite Games of All Time list. I fully intend on playing through the game again to wrap up the achievements and give Hardcore a swing. I have staunchly recommended it to friends as it is definitely worth the price and the time.

Let me first start by saying this is a "No, for now", not a "No", as most of the issues I see are fixable and the dev team does seem to be involved in discussion.
Simply put, despite lots of apparent customizations, they fall absolutely flat. There is very little point to choosing a class as you can easily get the starting skills/gear of one class with minimal playing early in the game. The skill trees fall into 3 catagories: offense/defense/make money; there is no unique skill to be seen for skill development besides the ability to see what ores an asteroid will give you before you mine it, flying bigger ships, and I'll even count driving in reverse at an acceptable rate. It's true that there is some playstyle choices to be made here as to whether you focus on combat or money earning, but at the end of the day you'll still need combat skills in order to defend yourself, so there's no incentive to go for one specialization over another besides "I wonder if I can" (yes, you can, does it make any difference in the core gameplay? no.).
While character customization is flat, ship customization is concave. Choose from 1 of 4 weapon types, make sure you skill up the ones you want so you can use them, then find the 1 or 2 ship frames with decent stats that allow you to use them. From there attach passive items to fit your playstyle, and get the biggest shield you can. The stats from ship to ship are woefully similar, 95% of the time you're going to care about only 1 thing: does the ship support the weapons I wanna use? Armor, hull plating, cargo space, manueverability etc are for the large part similar providing it's a ship in the same class. It's not so much "design your own ship" as it is "find the one with the right weapon slots and put stickers on it".
The quests are the largest downfall for me here. Most of your time is going to be spent in autopilot taking object from station "A" to station "B", then report back to "A", or "go blow up this one bad guy and come back". There are a few exceptions, the fleet combat story missions are particularly noteworthy, and there is a cute quest about "hacking" which relies on actual programming knowledge to get through (non-required so no real penalties for failing, but refreshing to see a "click through" quest break the 4th wall in subtle way like this).
The hopeful part is this: There are ways to improve customization using what is already in the game. Expanded skill trees, class-skills (even if passives like aforementioned mining skill), unique story options are all tools that could be used to diversify character development. Ship customization can be expanded upon with additional content. There are already a few interactive bits of ship design with modules like the EMP, more active and less passive options would make it feel much more unique. More and far more diversified ship frames will open up design space and has potential to actually allow players to make meaningful choices about the paths they will take in the game.
Some of these fixes are already or will be made available through modding.
But I can't in good faith recommend a game that needs mods to deliver on its promise. So, "No", for now.

The basics are there but this project is still in its alpha stages at best.
Pros:
-Interesting concept (sort of like a more real-time FTL with ARPG-like elements)
-Attractive graphics and music
-Game works well within the 1st 25 levels
Cons:
-After a few hours in (or beyond level 25), you realize that the game has offered everything it possibly can
-Progress suddenly becomes repetitive and any updates are really shallow
-Lots of random crashes for a "finished product" and issues with reloading your last save.
-I found myself playing mobile games while I waited for my ship to make the many jumps from system to system (sometimes, you have to make as many as 13 jumps which can take up to 10 mins even with a highly-advanced ship)
-Wonky auto-pilot and path-finding algorithm that ends up killing you almost 50% of the time
-And when the auto-pilot kills you, you're teleported back to the very beginning of your path so you end up spending another 10 mins playing a mobile game!
-Poor combat system that I bet sounded good on paper. For good strategic combat, you're better off with FTL. If you end up playing as a trader or miner, be prepared for BORING REPETITION!
-Can't really see any replayability since most quests are procedurally generated and different character archetypes don't really mean anything except for the 1st few hours of gameplay.
It's an OK game for its price tag but it's got a long way ahead of it before it becomes as immersive and addictive as some other similar titles out there. Here's hoping the devs can iron out some of the kinks and spend some time crafting some more varied missions.

VoidExpanse is an arcade version of Escape Velocity.  It's a much shallower world, with a larger focus on action.  Pirates/hostiles aren't an anomaly, they’re scattered across every map like koopas and goombas, they’ll jump into any fight even when they’re horribly outmatched.
They have added XP for pilot leveling, and a skill tree to specialize your pilot, which is a nice improvement. Staying true to the more arcade feel, these rewards come fast and furious.  I’ve put in 5 hours (5 learning hours, so plenty of time reading tool tips and trying to figure things out) and am already level 35.
The ship upgrade process is also streamlined.  The hull is just one more slotted upgrade (although it does change which weapon slots are available), and there’s no weight attribute to balance things out.  So you never need to decide how to optimize one ship, while saving for another, you just grab an upgrade for whichever slot you can.  Not a lot of decisions to make, you just get the next level of your radar/fuel tank/grappler, and if you happen to switch out hulls, they stay with you.  Like the pilot leveling, these upgrades come fast.  You never really reach the limits of your ship, and set a goal for a better ship, you’re just constantly upgrading everything before you hit the limit.  I don’t know that I need a new generator, but one’s offered, so you upgrade it. You don’t really have any sense of accomplishment.
The factions are also very simplified.  There seem to be 6 total, and you're basically chosing between 2.  Pirates; Aliens that are trying to wipe out humanity; people that worship said aliens; neutrals; and then the two choices: Freedom or Order.  So far, it seems like progression of these quest lines are pretty much on rails.  Helping Order doesn’t seem to make Freedom like me any less.
There’s a nice dialog system in game, where you can ask anyone about any topic you like.  While the system’s nice, it doesn’t seem to be very fleshed out.  Most everyone just repeats the tutorial for most options, and there doesn’t seem to be much of a reward for being thorough or going deep.
Quests are fairly simplified, too.  There are bounty missions to kill one particular pirate in the system you’re in (and he’s marked on the radar).  You can do rescue missions to a piece of debris in your system.  Then there are escort missions and package deliveries, which go to different systems, but there’s no concept of time, so you can just pick up as many as you want and drop them off when you happen to get to the system. There’s a cargo quest I’ve been offered a couple times, but they warn you you need a lot of space (unspecified) so I’ve declined it.  The last generic quest I’ve been offered is a mining contract, which is always for the same amount of the same mineral.   Much like the dialog system, it seems like the quests really need to be fleshed out.
In true arcade form, death is only a minor inconvenience.  Your body’s cloned (the cost is equivalent to about 1 quest reward) and your ship, it turns out, is fully insured. You lose your non-quest inventory, and that’s it.
The ship to ship fighting has some interesting mechanics, different weapons having different tracking speeds, being able to assign different weapons to different firing groups.  I think it suffers for the camera being way too close.  If a ship comes in from the top of your screen, it’s already within range of your weapons, and is only ~8 ship lengths away. If things were zoomed out, so you could play with the edge of your weapons range, it opens up a lot more tactical dogfighting.
To sum up, it’s Arcade Escape Velocity, for all the positives and negatives that “Arcade” brings with it. I’d appreciate a bit more depth at a more deliberate pace, but VoidExpanse really leans towards the arcade feel.  Hopefully they expand on the dialog tree and quest options as time goes on.  And maybe at later levels you’ll actually know you want/need an upgrade before you’ve already obtained it.
Last note: I’m playing on a 5k iMac and even after lowering the video options it gets choppy in cruise mode.  It also requires a monoframework package install, and I’ve had a few freezes.
Holding out hope for improvements, but as is I can't recommend this game.

First impressions, after about 6 hours of game, and level 30 character.
While definitely worth the price, the game is still lacking compared to classics like Space Rangers, Drox Operative or SPAZ. It needs about 5x as much content as the current selection (5x as much mission types, module and ship types, random stuff happening, etc) to be a real classic. Still, the basics are all good, combat is fun, mining and trading is profitable, there is some danger in dying, so definitely a good start. Devs seem to be working on it with full steam, so that is also good.
+- It seems to have a more strict "storyline", with some "story missions", and the universe seem to be very static unlike Drox or SR. It is somewhat similar to SPAZ in this regard.
+- Visuals are okay, but nothing stellar. Personally I like this, but some people might want a prettier game.
+ Some missions can be solved multiple ways, which I liked very much. Fight, negotiate, or just betray the questgiver all count.
+ Mining is somewhat entertaining and can be profitable unlike most space games.

This game has literally no right to be good. But it is! It is incredible. I have now finished it about 5 times on different platforms. This playthrough I sat through and completed the entire game in one single sitting which took me about 3 and a half hours. Honestly one of my favourite games ever made.
So what is the premise of little inferno? Well you burn stuff. It's that simple. Burn everything you get given then buy more stuff to burn. So that sounds boring?! The real fun comes from making combos. Burning the right items together gives you a combo. You get a hint for each of these combos and then you have to work it out yourself.
What really builds this game though is the story. There a few different characters that build together a story throughout the game. They communicate to you only through 1 way, letters. Except somehow the developers seem to find a way to make you relate to these characters and gets them to convey a very wide range of emotion. The story is unique and really keeps you attached throughout the game.
The style of the game is incredible. What I mean by this is the graphics and the soundtrack. They both fit together perfectly. The graphics are cartoon like and everything is stylized incredibly well to fit the theme. The soundtrack is a mixture of tracks that are upbeat and slow and always convey the emotion of the scene. The main theme is great and they even have a nice little sing a long video at the start with a catchy but scary song (you'll know what I mean when you see it). It is definitely something I would be willing to listen to outside of the game.
So theres not really much more I can say about little inferno. The concept of the game is simple and sounds boring and terrible. But somehow it is incredibly fun. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone!

ATTENTION! THIS REVIEW IS ONLY A RESPONSE TO THIS BUNCH OF NEGATIVE REVIEWS AND A COMPARISON TO THE FIRST TITLE , IF YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT THE FIRST DUNGEON DEFENDERS IS LIKE, OR DON'T CARE ABOUT WHAT THE STEAM REVIEWS ARE TALKING, READING THIS WILL BE A LITTLE USELESS, BUT YOU CAN DO IT ANYWAY, I AM JUST A GUY WITH CAPS LOCK.
You know... this really surprised me. After i saw hundreds of negative reviews for this game i though that the game would be a disgrace to the humanity, and i will start by saying: Yes, it have its flaws, but it is not as much as Steam reviews are trying to convince there is.

The game uses the same gameplay style as the first one, and it is like you had all the DLC.
"BUT HEY! THE GAME IS TRYING TO SELL SKINS WITH REAL MONEY""
No, it is not, you have a whole pack of skins in your inventory, what they ARE selling is Emotes, that are basically animations that prove nothing. It is not only not required, but also, no one that buy them will be superior to you in any aspect, you probably won't even see anyone using these things.
"BUT THEY SHOULDN'T BE ADDING MICROTRANSACTIONS TO A PC GAME!"
Yes, that is true, but the same goes to the first game. Look at the DD1, look at the DLC quantity. There is a lot of them, and they are important things, like characters or missions. This one gives you all the previous game DLC included, comparing to that, selling emotes is almost a joke.
Anyway, continuing the review... The gear thing is awesome, you can have the most riddiculous equip possible, your character will still look amasing, the feeling of gearing up is incredible.
And about the new item types, there...
"THEY WERE TOTALLY CRAZY DOING IT! IT IS NOTHING LIKE DUNGEON DEFENDERS!"
Calm down... let me finish: Yes, the weapons ARE completely.. hm... peculiar. You still have the weapon types of the first game, but in this one, you have more. I already found a machine gun, a granade launcher and even a freakin' Flamethrower. Yeah. Completely not what you would search in a Dungeon Defenders game, but that is not necessarely a bad thing, i found it really awesome actually, these weapons are given a little "medieval" style, so it doesn't break immersion that much, and i found myself pretty badass while burning enemies.
Besides that, they indeed solved that hackers problem DD1 had.(even if they did in a strange way), they tried to add Playverse in-game, so they can have some feedback before DD2. Also they solved their first week probl...
"YOU COULDN'T PLAY SINGLEPLAYER OR OPEN A PRIVATE MATCH!"
Yes, yes... Stop interrupting. Even though they got that wrong, they solved really fast.
"HOW ABOUT THE WHOLE LOAD OF OTHER PROBLEMS WE TALKED?!"
Well. You can found online a chart the devs made showing the most talked problems with the game, and how were they handling it: First one was microtransactions, and they already pronnounced that every future mission will be free, and they will NOT sell level-increases or armor/items. The second and third were "no singleplayer" and "live texture streaming" things they already fixed.  Fourth was the confusing HUD and inventory system, what they said that it is a known issue and will fix it soon. Next on the list was that the game was a "portable device version of the original", and they already said that it is not (I didn't quite understanded this part, i have the DD second wave on my ipad and it is nothing like this game, and if they are referring to the way this game is presented, it obviously have something to do with mobile versions, considering it will launch to mobiles soon, with cross-plataform). And lastly on the list was the "must be online to play", what they are already fixing.
If there is something i do have to complain is the bugs, there are a lot of them, something small enemies glitches their ways into my defenses and stuff like that. Nothing game-breaking, but a little annoying.
Now the pros and Cons:

Pros:
+Classic DD1 experience.
+Gear showing up.
+Awesome new weapons and armor.
+Balancing fixes.
+Graphical Improvements.
+Devs are listenning to the feedback and trying to fix their mistakes.
Cons:
-Loads of bugs.              (may or may not be fixed)
-Confusing HUD.            (will be fixed soon)
-Must be online to play. (will be fixed soon)
-No private taverns.       (will be fixed soon i guess)
CONCLUSION:

Even by screwing up a bit, the Devs are giving attention to the feedback and improving the game. The game have all the features DD1 Had. It adds all the DLC content the first game had for free. It did rebalanced the game, fixed the hacker problem, added some cool new content. If you don't have DD1, i recommend you buy this game, if you have DD1, i recommend buying this game, but if you have DD1 with all the DLCs maybe it is not worth the full price, since it doesn't add much, you could wait some discount.

A 4X game worthy of your time, Stellaris is mind boggling awesome!
PROS
-Tons of alien races with their own portrait and ships. Create and design your own races!
-Diplomacy that actually works, where you have to decide what wars will cost you if you lose. Lose a planet, or become a vassal of an enemy AI?
-Enslave populations
-Different travel methods, FTL, warp, Hyperspace, allowing different play styles
-Random Research - NO game is the same! There's no direct path to get technologies, it's random which allows for new strategies. Don't have the tech to colonize new planets? Play your cards safe. Don't have tech to upgrade your power plants? Expand and mine more power from planets from the surface.
-Space battles are epic to watch with a light layer of strategy involved.
-Tons of dialogue about past and future colonies. Go on research missions, or gain tech knowledge by researching the wrecks of enemy ships.
CONS
-Learning curve
-Slow paced at the beginning, but you can fast forward to make things go faster.
-Turn off for many (even myself) at first glance. Need to give it a chance to fall in love with it.

I'm conflicted about giving this an up vote because while I did enjoy it I feel the difficulty level is so high that most gamers will quickly quit out of frustration.
It's a micro-managing strategy game in which you control planets that give you money and ships over time. The money can be spent on upgrades, attacks, or hoarded for a combat buff. The ships are sent out in streams to conquer enemy planets and defend your own.
This genre of game is not new, and variants of it can be found for free on sites like Kongregate. But this game has much better graphics and sound/music compared to the free versions.
There are various tech upgrades that you can earn and equip in a limited number of slots. There are different game types to keep things fresh such as Elimination (kill everyone) and King of the Hill (control a certain planet for a set period of time).
There are different kinds of planets and opponents to fight as well. For example, one planet is an "infested" planet which is covered with alien eggs. This planet will remain neutral while a timer counts down. When the timer reaches zero the eggs hatch and the previously neutral planet suddenly becomes a major threat. The player will have to weigh the pros and cons of destroying the infested planets before pursuing the main objective, or hoping to rush to victory before the eggs hatch and the situation becomes untenable.
The story is about an entrepreneur who goes looking for riches in an uncharted area of space while being hounded by intergalactic debt collectors. It was mildly entertaining but the ending left a lot of loose ends.
Multiplayer seems mostly dead, so I played only single player.
The controls are simple, actually a little too simple since there is no pause button I could find. Things get hectic very fast in this game with streams of hundreds of ships criss-crossing the map at any given time. A delay of even a few seconds in terms of not attacking or upgrading can spell defeat for the player. The AI is quick to notice any opening in your defenses and pounce.
I went into this game thinking it would be casual entertainment that wouldn't make me think. Wrong!
It starts out easy enough with some generous tutorial missions. After that the difficulty level starts ramping up exponentionally. By mission 10 I figure most casual gamers have been blown away. By mission 16 I figure all but the most die-hard strategists have been wiped out. I'm a glutton for punishment though, and I like a good challenge, so I toughed it out and beat all 30 missions of the single player campaign. Even the Easy difficulty level was ludicrously difficult. You have been warned!
If you're a casual gamer looking for an easy game, look elsewhere. If you're a hardcore strategist who isn't afraid of fast-paced micro-managing this game might be for you.

F.E.A.R. is one of the last challenging FPS games out there. The enemies don't linger in covers waiting to get shot like in mass effect 2 etc. Instead they are focused on smoking you out. You will often find your self being cornered into limited cover trying to find the time to load between kills. To make it worse, enemy AI often tries to flank you even more filling the game with intense firefights.
In the middle of F.E.A.R. is the creation and mass production of telepathic humanoidsoldiers, who obey a single telepathic leader. The project goes haywire as this telepathic leader, Fettel, learns about a few atrocities. As he has the controll of a formiable military force, he decides liquidate everyone responsible being quite effective in it. As there are way too many soldiers to be dealt with, the only sensible way to handle this is to find Fettel and eliminate him as fast as possible.
So while the story is excentric it is believable enough. The game even jokes about your department not getting enough funding because who would take the existanse of threats like these seriosly.
F.E.A.R. has a good variety of weapon have the real feel to them. Even the basic pistol carries the necessary punch in both sound & recoil.
Voice Acting & Music fit F.E.A.R well creating the eerie atmosphere it is supposed to have.
Highly recommended for anyone who likes high paced fps games. However, if you are more of a casual gamer, you might want to leave this one on the shelf.

As pure an example of "style over substance" as it is possible to imagine.  This is a "journey" in the most basic sense of the word - you start at one place and end at another.
The game is a visual and auditory experience; if that is enough for you, then this may entertain.  The soundtrack is soothing and the design is colourful.  The fish are pretty and obviously a lot of thought has gone into programming their movements.
The art style is cell-shaded, which can work in some games, but this just feels lazy.  The design of the player character looks as though it probably took about 10 minutes.
The game lacks any context and is completely unapologetic about it.  The nameless, voiceless, clueless character awakens in the sea and starts swimming.  You find a little robot.  The robot helps you cut some seaweed.  You find some ruins, swim through them and are teleported to a different underwater cavern, where you cause some glowing coral to grow and spectral sea creatures appear.  Then an underwater lake rises up and you swim through a triangular door and swim with some fishes.  Sometimes you are rail-roaded through some sections and it looks like swimming through shoals of fishes collects them, or activates them, or something (they flash, you o a little twirl in the water) - but there's no indication if this is achieving anything, or necessary for your progression, or if matters in the slightest.  A shark eats one of your robots - am I supposed to be sad?  Worried?  I don't think it's possible to be injured or die, so I don't really know why I would.  You can see beautiful expanses of tempting, open sea but can't swim further than the game permits you before you're turned back by an invisible wall.
The gameplay is virtually non-existent.
I gave this game 39 minutes to prove or endear itself (much longer and I think I would have actually finished it, based on other reviews) and I was left feeling completely cold to the experience.  The lack of context, story or sense of purpose completely killed this game flat for me.

Good enemy designs have always made video games interesting. They not only appeal to the eye and offer challenging opponents. Doom II does both very pleasingly. The level designs are not the most realistic by comparison to the ones of the games today, but they offer effective battlegrounds. The weapons remain unchanged, but the double barrel shotgun adds an impressive new tool. Getting to spray pellets over a large area gives players the chance to kill several monsters at once in a rather spectacular fashion, well rendered by the many spirits.
Doom II was among the first titles to introduce interactive three dimmensional objects and settings. They were still developing, but at the stage ID Software was, Doom II brought the seeds that would later blossom into the modern FPS shooters. It certainly presented some interesting concepts of physics, such as the BFG and the artificial goat's head that spawned living creatures from cubes.

Once upon a time I recommended this game and even posted a positive review here about it. But the more I played it, the more I realised how much of an unbalanced mess this game really is. Let's start with the AI shall we?
When this game first came out the AI was rather dumb so you had to crank up the difficulty so they'd put up a fight. Stardock released a patch that was supposed to fix it but instead pushed things too far in the other direction. I'll admit I'm not a strategic genius but when I'm on the easiest difficulty and it feels like I'm going up against SKYNET something's gone wrong. This isn't helped by a certain bonus the AI gets on every difficulty level: They pay no maintenance on ships. Zero military maintenance. So they'll sit there endlessly cranking out ships while a human player can barely keep a couple dozen ships in service. The AI recognises it's huge military advantage and........GAME OVER.
I could go on. I could talk about the weapon types, the useless ship defenses, the hit and miss map generation, the bugs and typos that still exist after so long...........And you know what rubs salt in the wounds? While this game sits here with more balance issues than a one-legged hippo Stardock are doing nothing but releasing overpriced, pointless DLC that nobody asked for. Do yourself a favor and buy literally anything else.

Each time I replay either FF8, FF6, FF9, or FFX I always think to myself "Wow, this is the best FF game.." because those four are amazing. This is a great port. My only complaints are the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ MIDI music and the slightly awkward controls (which is just how it has to be as a result of being on a keyboard.)
As for the super ♥♥♥♥♥♥ MIDI music, just download the mod Wine and Roses, and you'll be listening to Black Mages versions of the music even better than the original PS1 quality.
The junction system is very confusing at first, but its actually really sweet when you figure it out. Drawing does become tedious, but its almost unnecessary if you play Triple Triad and teach your GFs the abilities to "Refine" magic early. The CGI cutscenes that merge with the prerendered backgrounds are really one of the coolest things about FF7 and FF8, and they're especially awesome here (see the Parade sequence in particular.)
The story gets slightly convoluted, but nothing compared to the crazy nonsense that FF7 goes into (I also like FF7 so chill). The Laguna sequences make this game really stand out, and really make the world feel connected.
Overall, FF8 has always been one of my favorite games, and is quite possibly my favorite FF game.. I'd reccommend it in a heartbeat, but you're doing the game a disservice if you don't install a mod to fix the trashy MIDI music.

Years ago, I waited impatiently for the sequal to FF7.  What came out, FF8, was seen as a huge disappointment to many people.  However, years later, I now see what a gem FF8 truly is.  Sure, it doesn't have the memorable characters of FF7, but a part of me much prefers the junctioning system to materia.
Hear me out!  I didn't think it could be possible to love a game more than FF7!  But the secret to FF8 is the CARDS.  You not only have the card game, but the cards give you your magic!  And your tools!  And your limit breaks!  In the first 3 hours of the game, you can get to over 3,000 HP through junctioning Aero or Blizaga (refined from cards) to your HP!
This wasn't explained at all in the game and its tutorial system SUCKS.  But.  Replaying the game with an indepth walkthrough shows just how facinating the FF8 junctioning system is.
Replay this game again, letting go of FF7 and allowing FF8 be a game in its own right.  You won't be disappointed!

Stellaris in my opinion has some of the best features to date for a space genre 4X Strategy Game. It needs some refinement and adjustments for balance and such... but overall, a title worth picking up for those who like Deep Strategy/Campaign style games of galactic conquest. And the soundtrack... worth the extra $10! :steamhappy:
Does it need work? Yes. Will it take 10+ years to polish out those updates for a full-fledged gaming experience? No. Expect some DLC in the near-future to add more content and depth to the game.

Incredibly good strategy gameplay and interesting, lovingly crafted lore work together to create a wonderful gameplay experience.  The strategy seems to be just the right depth to challenge without completely overwhelming you, while the Traits, Ethics and Government Type do a fantastic job of bringing your freshly forged empire to life.  Staying with the theme, the techs are all incredibly creatively colorful and the "Random Draw" discovery style adds a lot of flavor lore-wise, making its self a refreshing take on the standard “tried and true” tech tree, adding immensely to the replay value.  The AI empire generator seems to have a knack for making interesting and logical empires as well, being so believable you can almost feel history being written as you interact with them.
My first Empire was composed of peaceful, knowledge loving otter-men.  They quickly came across a pre-sentient race of lizard people and, after promptly uplifting them to serve as foot soldiers, used them to solidify the empire among hostile neighbors.  Then, taking advantage of the peace, they developed into incredibly skilled genetic life-shapers, improving both themselves and all who joined their mighty empire, and I'm barely into the midgame.
All in all, I cannot recommend this game enough.  It is a must buy for anyone who loves a little strategy and  longs for the stars.

This game is something I was pleasantly surprised by. The soundtrack alone is amazing, but the dungeon aspect to it is pleasing as well. For those who don't know, Dungeon Defenders is technically a tower-defense game, where every map is essentially a PvE arena where you are protecting your central crystal. But, it has some fun RPG elements with the characters you choose.
There was a lot of negative flack about this editiion when it was first released. I think the negative reactions where kneejerk and misguided. The company has worked to get their servers more responsive. That has been successful. The game has also had some very needed balances corrected from the original and I can enjoy the weaker classes much more than before. There have also been a huge number of elements added to the game (e.g., crafting, dyes, outfits, etc), and more sophisticated play together UI. The negative criticism also was directed at a lack of single player, but really, you can host a private session with yourself or with any friends you want to bring along any time you want. Really, it's an excellent and incredibly addicting game. If it seems hard at first try a squire first, apprentice second. Those two characters are far and away the most powerful. But, the ranger, and most of the other classes have become far more playable. Summoner is a blast but requires some sophisticated play.
In any case, I recommend this game unreservedly, giving it about an 85% -- and I think it will continue to improve as the devs polish it further. Hang in and enjoy. It is a blast!

Short review: The idea is simple. Just RIDE. And it is executed brilliantly. Definitely recommended for all levels of bike enhusiasts. I do not own RIDE 2 but if i assume it has the same escence, you may probably go for RIDE twoo. (See what i did there :)
Long review:
Ride is a very content rich motorbike racing game. İt has lots of diversity and can be fun for all levels of players. The game has rider customization, split screen and multiplayer races, a quick race mode and a world tour. You just start riding bikes and making progress and money. And the rest follows along automatically. The game will direct and inform you at important points. You do not ahve to upgrade a bike to full level if you are impatient. Of course the game has riding aids like motogp games and a flashback mechanism. The worst thing about this game is that there is no real motogp circuits. This is probably because of licence issues or something. Nevertheless, the game is awesome. Here are pros:
- It starts fast and proceeds fast. You will probably never be frusturated because of monetary shortages (if you play on easy difficulty). There is a voice actor to enlighten and motivate you. He is doing a good job. Game starts the world tour with less poweful bikes so inexperienced bikers can easly adapt and learn dynamics and physic of the game. You can upgrade you bike all the way up or jump to other classes of bikes pretty soon. As i said before, Just RIDE.
- There will be new bikes that you can purchase in about every hour. Literaly, i have played 15 hours and bought like 15 different bikes :D The variety of the bikes is literaly exceptional amonf the bike racing games. There are weird street bikes, wild hog kinda bikes, electric bikes, legendary bikes, prototypic bikes and modern sports and professional bikes.
- There is a very detailed rider customization. You are able to customize you clothing and accesories, team name and riding style. This is where the customization gets deep. You can adjust the shoulders, elbows, hands, torso, legs and head position of your riders style. This style is just visual though, not effective in handling or physics. But it is clearly visible and exciting to see the rider is behaving the way you would like.
- Thw world tour starts very easy. There are single races, time trials, race day events (pass as many as you can), pass a certain number of opponents as quickly as possible race (can't remember its name), drag race (yepi good old fashion dragging), team races with you teammate, endurance races, all bikes free races and couple of more category limited races. Oh and elite trphies to win some locked bikes. The race diversity is plenty enough.
- There is an ingame music unlike Motogp games. Music is fine i guess.
- Physics is amazing. Every different bike has its own individual physics.
- Environmental visual quality is amazing. The nature surfaces your feelings of freedom, on your bike, riding to sunset... Damn :D
- Upgrading the bike is fun. There are engine, brakes, oil, visual tyres updates. Some categories have sub categories. You can even change the chain of the bike. The bike customization is also as good as rider customization. You will feel like you realy own the bike and feel the obligation to create your unique look.
Cons:
- Bike customization has no guide like in Motogp.
- Login failed to go online races.
- Optimization should have been better. My R9 380 was suffering at some tracks.
- The flashbacks are kind of short and does not overlap. It means if you crash and flashback, you should not crash for like another 10 seconds because the game will not let you flash it back again. This is weird and this is not an issue in Motogp 17.
I have played motogp 3, 14, 15, 17 and this game. I chose to be a hardcore racer in motogp (with helmet cam and manual gears on medium difficulty) and it is all fun, but in this game, i played on easy with 3rd person cam. That is also why this game was fun for me. The game is a bit expensive but an amazing game. Just buy it, install it and RIDE.

There have been plenty of rogue-like games in the last few years, but this is definitely one of the most unique and original. The concept is strangely brilliant, the art is great, and the music is awesome, so the whole package seems pretty stunning at first glance. However, when you look under the hood, it's not flawless...the concept may be amazing, but the execution is a little bit janky at times. There are times when I know that I'm 100% on the beat, and yet the game simply isn't registering that I'm on target, leading to my untimely death. I'm a musician, so I have a good sense of rhythm and timing - something seemed off here. There's just not enough precision to the mechanics, which can really sink you when you're facing a boss or going up against a  big room filled with tough enemies. There are definitely a few frustrations that you'll have to deal with to get into a groove here. I would defintely still recommend this, despite  whatever shortcomings it may have, because the idea is great and the development team has gotten pretty dang close to nailing it. There's also the ability to add in your own music, which is a fantastic feature...I pumped in some Tribe Called Quest, Wu-Tang, Biggie, etc., and then the game was really bumping and twice as fun. Get this on sale and it'll be money well-spent, as long as you recognize that there's gonna be a serious learning curve when it comes to getting into the game's idea of rhythm.

Not long after Half Life 2 Monolith came out with this gem with the intention of redefining the action in FPS games. And they succeeded! It's been almost 10 years and playing FEAR is still fun. Slow-motion is imperative for survival and it does make the gameplay exciting. All the particle effects accompanying this effect still stand out, even with today's standards.
While full of action, FEAR is mainly a psychological horror. Between the action sequences supernatural encounters are common and your main antagonist is someone of that nature. Your are keen on finding out more of this phenomenon you are after and the story has some surprises for you along the way.
Extraction Point was the follow-up expansion pack for the game which takes places exactly where the main story leaves us in the original game. Interestingly, the same studio that developed this expansion pack released another one two years later. Perseus Mandate was longer, more difficult and more action-packed - too bad the story was rather unoriginal and we already new a sequel would come out. Also, the story told by Perseus Mandate is not considered canon in this franchise.
Although lacking the multiplayer component (check the message on the game's store page), FEAR's single player content is still very original and can be entertaining in 2014. I recommend it to all people who adore the FPS genre.

Wow, it's really been nearly a whole damn decade since this came out?  I still remember looking at the pre-order box in the shop and saying "1GB OF RAM REQUIRED? ARE YOU INSANE!?" like it was yesterday.  But yep, next year F.E.A.R. will 10 years old.  So now is the time to sit down and ask: "Is F.E.A.R. still a good game that holds up"?  And the answer is "Yes."  Yes, F.E.A.R. is still a good game that holds up.  It sits firmly inbetween older fashioned shooters and newer shooters, not unlike its brethren (And at the time, competition) Doom 3 and Half-Life 2.  It's more linear, story focused, and the like than old school shooters but it still had navigational environments, a health bar, and other nice things that I miss.  For the time, F.E.A.R.'s technology was keen, and while aspects of it haven't aged as well as the previously mentioned Doom 3 & Half-Life 2 (Mainly the environments, plus some character models have visible seams down their faces and its weird.)  other aspects of the engine still remain pretty damn impressive and paradoxically, superior to the games own sequels and many other games today.  The bouncing particles, whizz-bang sparks, and the way each bullet creates light all around it still make for some damn cool scenes that please the eye.
The atmosphere is also pretty solid, and while the scares didn't get to me like they once did, I still got chills here and there and admittedly if you are a first time player the scares might get you good.  I've hardened to them mainly because I'm currently on my 4th playthrough.
The A.I. is also pretty spectacular, smart, and dynamic.  The weapons feel powerful and every bullet makes an impact on you and the enemies, and the combat animation is superb and packed with lots of satisfying bloodshed.
The story is also interesting, flawed, but interesting and it must have taken some talent to pull the story off considering that it was trying to be a Sci-fi horror story inspired by The Ring, The Matrix, and Kung-Fu movies.  Not a mix that makes a lot of sense, but somehow comes together surprisingly well considering all of those things are from completely different planets.
For 10 bucks, you get the original game and its expansions - and while "Perseus Mandate" is really only the quality of a fan made mod, it feels like its thrown in for free since the core game and "Extraction Point" are both pretty solid and will last you awhile.  And feel free to stop on by online, there's still folks playing - and its damn fun.
In short, F.E.A.R. has Guns, Grenades, Ghost Girls & is Gory, Grisly, Gritty, & Grim.  Mmm, alliteration.

First and Foremost, while there are a large amount of support staff, this game is largely the result one man's work.  Dean Dodrill did a phenominal job bringing this to life and while I'm usually not willing to give leniance to games simply because of they have a smaller dev team, I feel this game is worthy of an exception.
The game is quite pretty and you can tell that Dean's first love is animation.  There is beautiful detail in a lot of the work and the environments ooze character and personality.  It's the kind of art direction that a larger studio would never really get 'right' because Dust's art is the result of a singular vision, not designed by a committee.  While the artistic front is not as polished and as jaw-dropping as say, Ori and the Blind Forest, it's definitely a strong point and again, for a single person who kinda just wanted to do animation, it's nothing short of fantastic.
The combat is fluid, fair, and manages to feel pretty good.  The mechanics follow a lot of the standards that are expected in a action-combat game.  While the game feels pretty good to play, it lacks depth and has a lot of contextual actions that trade fine control for ease of combat.
I bought this game because I wanted to find a 2D Devil May Cry and I learned a something playing through Dust:  DMC is hard to make.
A game like DMC4 has systems are ultra tight and provide a platform for the player to do amazing things if you invest the time to learn them.  It has a skill ceiling that might as well be infinite due to the shear number of options you have as a player, and as difficulty ramps up, the game will expect you to use those options with a kind of fluency that takes hours and hours to master.  Dust does not have that kind of depth.  A lot of the combat systems aren't perfect.  Attacks in the air kind of auto-target anything close by, sacrificing player control at times when you'd rather not.  You can lock almost every enemy into an infinite loop of uninterruptable damage in a couple different ways, none of which are terribly difficult to perform.  Bosses have pretty predictable patterns that are easy to abuse and instead of fighting a dynamic fight that requires action and reaction, you are kinda stuck just doing 'the thing that works'.
There are a few other problems with the systems in place.  Attacks that would kill you will leave you at 1 HP as long as you have at least 50% of the HP the attack would do.  This means, that healing past that threshold is a mistake, and that max HP is effectively worthless.  You get bonus XP based on your combo, but you can farm combo with your secondary attack from your friendly NPC and since combo isn't damage, but rather hit count, it is in your best interest to keep her damage as low as possible while you just spam a screenwide AoE, allowing you to easily push your combo to several hundred with just a handful of monsters on the screen, which translates to easy levels.  There are a lot of counterintuitive systems that are ripe for abuse.
I was kinda hoping for a game with as tight of design as a modern DMC and I didn't really get that, but regardless, the game is a fine entry in it's own right.  Despite their flaws, the mechanics aren't frustrating and as long as you go into the game with the right expectations, You'll find an enjoyable experience.

Put simply, Abzu is a wonderful environment-focused adventure game. You control a silent protagonist who travels through the linear, yet highly detailed, underwater environment in order to fully explore the world. Why you are exploring is a mystery at first, but the beauty of the game is that it doesn't matter. The small details and inklings of the mysterious world are tantalizing enough that you feel like you almost have to discover more about it. And when the game does begin to introduce clear tasks for you to complete, the desire to move onward is intensified. Along your trip you'll discover the variety of creatures who inhabit your aquatic world, and gain insights into its history. The farther you travel, the greater the sites and experiences become; making the hours you've spent swimming feel all the more worth it. And once the ending arrives before you, the feeling of accomplishment is immense.
On a technical level, movement of your character is simple, but pleasant and smooth. The few times that careful navigation is required, it doesn't feel like a chore or an out of place activity. Visually speaking, the game is beautiful. It doesn't look realistic by any stretch of the word, but its art style works to its advantage and time after time I was awed by the scenes I was being treated to.
All-in-all, Abzu isn't a complicated game. You mostly just swim, look around, and can easily finish it in a single sitting. But the journey you take feels special and leaves you with a sense of hopefulness and wonder. It is an absolute treat.

Even though I loved Gal Civ 2, I am afraid I cannot recommend this game at this time.  Let me be clear: this is NOT because GalCiv 3 is a bad game.  It isn't; it has all the hallmarks of a good game in the making.   Rather, it is because despite this game being officially out of Early Access for over a year now, it very much feels like a late alpha or very early beta and NOT a proper v.1.0 (and certainly not a v.1.83!).
To begin with, as others have pointed out abundantly, this game is buggy as heck.  I am not what I call a "bug hunter," that is, someone who goes out of his way to find bugs and other oddities.  Rather, I just play the game and hope to have fun.  This is why it is so stunning to me that I find myself constantly tripping over bugs.  Take my last play session.  In the first 15 minutes, I discovered two bugs: the first involving my home planet disappearing(!) after being attacked by an enemy fleet, and the second involving a battle preview screen bug where the attributes of the enemy fleet (i.e., the names and stats of the enemy ships) were being applied to the drones that protected my planet (the drones were a result of one of my race's attributes).  In the play session prior to that, I discovered that if I send my survey ship through a wormhole and it emerges across the map in an area normally outside of its range, which is the point of wormhole exploration after all, that ship basically becomes trapped because every surrounding hex is considered as an invalid move location (in other words, the game still thinks your ship is in its pre-wormhole location and you are trying to give it a move order outside of its normal range restriction). The only solution is to lose control of your ship by setting it on auto-survey where it will make a beeline path towards home, something that ruins the point of distant exploration.  A game that has been released into the wild for over a year shouldn't be so bug-prone. I find it very telling that during my few months of owning Gal Civ III I have seen Stardock revamp more than a few systems already as if they are still beta testing ideas. Likewise, Stardock has announced a big expansion for next year that is going to revisit most aspects of the GalCiv III experience - another indication that this game still seems to be in pre-release development.  Did I mention that today's patch added in some HOTKEYS?!  Yeah, GalCiv III has all the hallmarks of an alpha or beta stage product that is still very much a work-in-progress.
The second problem is that Gal Civ III lacks some of the features of Gal Civ II, such as internal politics and espionage.  While I understand the decision to delay the incorporation of these features so that they can be better developed than they were in Gal Civ II, I still don't approve of it as a sequel should arrive with all the oringal content PLUS new content.  Needless to say, I will find it extremely slimy if Stardock locks the old-new features behind a paid DLC wall.  Having to make yet another DLC purchase for core content will leave a bad taste in my mouth, especially in light of the fact that Stardock has been pumping out way too much DLC already while the core game is limping along in its very rough current state.
So, for these two reasons I cannot recommend this game at this time.  At least, not for the casual player who just wants to feel like he is playing a finished product (if you are an alpha/beta enthusiast, jump on board because this is your cup of tea!).  Honestly, even though I got the core game and a bunch of DLC for roughly 45% off, I still feel kind of ill-used as the game is not really enjoyable in its current late alpha/early beta state.  I am hopeful that by this time next year (maybe sooner?) this title can be the game we all hoped Gal Civ III would be, but that time is not now.
