I've played every single iteration of Galactic Civilizations ... from the earliest days when this was one of the few games out for OS/2. I have enjoyed all of them. Until now. Yes, sadly.
Galciv 3 is as different from Galciv 2 as Civilization 3 is different from Civilization 5 as far as shift in game mechanics on the surface is concerned. There is only one problem with GalCiv3: it is as boring as Dante's Hell. I have not finished a single game. I have started a couple dozen times, and every time, 3, 4, 5 hours into a game I get so bored that I simply loose interest.
The map, zoomed out, seems busy, but really, there's little to do except monotonously scout scout scout and pop anomalities. The research has been revamped, but, in my opinion not for the better: it is obscure why the old tree has been changed like this, in a way that it makes less sense, and practically every thing has been recycled, only it's been put in a different place (and you now have to choose between options that were previously all obtainable, but ok, so what, life goes on). It doesn't add challenge, it just makes it less interesting compared to GalCiv II when you have logged several hundred hours on the latter. Even if you expand the research tree so you can see a little better where you're coming from and where you might be going to, it's counter intuitive and just 'bleh' compared to previous iterations.
Very hard to give your research direction now.
The new planetary maps .... um. Ok, the hex based system and the mutual benefits you can get from matching building types are different, and seem an enhancement. On the other hand, the ''trade goods' that you could previously research and then build are now relegated to being random pop ups on newly colonized worlds, without their influence on the whole empire being unclear. This way they've become more of an irritant than 'something to rush for' that they previously were.
Graphically - well, they have spent a lot of effort on this. Assuming you zoom in on things, you are in for a lot of chrome and glitz. Really, it is beautiful. But since I always play as far zoomed out as I can, I don't see any of that. Hey, it's a strategy game, and so I like to work on strategies, and that works best with the 'large picture'.
If you want a really good space based 4X, get GalCiv 2 - Twilight of the Arnor. Without a doubt, in my personal opinion, a far superior game.
Galciv III is a lame, somewhat aimless re-brewing of old tea leaves that makes me visualize a confused little old lady wandering around at night in the snow under the street lights, not being able to remember where she lives or what her name is. Very disappointing to me. I'll rather load up a game of the very dated Alpha Centauri Alien Crossfire, or Galciv 2, or Civilization 3 to Beyond Earth. Each one has no problems holding my interest with that 'just one more turn' factor that keeps me up into the wee hours. Galciv III just doesn't have that. As I said: a few hours into a new game I just want to turn it off and go watch paint dry.
Visually appealing, everything is so pleasant to just look at PLUS the controls are so smooth.

I knew about the Windows migration and have had Galactic Civilizations II on a couple Windows boxes, played extensively, and followed the development of this version.
Like the WIndows version being a substantive interface update over what I knew on OS/2, this updates the interface, but also much of the underlying behaviour has been improved. I still recognise the personalities of the various species, but the AI is more complex and unlike the previous situation where you cannot assume that personality trends for a species would automatically continue. Maybe over time I will get to find trends that will let me gain an advantage, but this has moved from being what could be a familar time filler to now being a new challenge.

Want to join the Order and fight the alien threat? Buy some weapons and start shooting rockets!

There are many paths that you can take and with a deep skill tree you will get many hours out of this game.

Slightly shorter then the first Witcher yet more satisfying. The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings expands off the first game evolving in many ways and creating a more enjoyable game. Ill cover some of the positive changes and some negative ones through the review while also covering the topics I generally do.
Story: Spanning over 3 chapters and a Epilogue you are continuing off the ending of the Witcher. Each chapter is perfectly paced, but takes a huge drop on the amount of quests. Compared to the first game having numerous contracts and side quests to contend with the main story, you only have 3-4 side quests each chapter. With the downside of lacking side material, the main story is involving enough for it to not really matter. Making you want to keep pushing the main story forward. Along the story you are presented with a handful of choices giving the series a boost to replay value.
Gameplay: Have to throw first mention to the combat overhaul. A completely different combat system to the first game, yet it infuriates me. Combat has such a difficulty curve from the start. You are presented with all these options of different signs but only 1 stands out above the rest and becomes the only viable option if you wish to push on. Shield and roll, roll roll roll and roll. You also have to be mindful when rolling because you can block yourself into a corner and be destroyed into oblivion. At one point I was fighting a golem and had it one hit away from death, a miss judged roll landed me into a corner and the stoned behemoth did a rush attack into me and kept me there. Slamming my face into the ground over and over again. Was not pretty.
Alchemy, potions, herbs, crafting. All that is present again for the Witcher to indulge in but you are restricted to a inventory weight limit. Things stack up quickly and prevent you from hoarding materials. Having to meditate before you can drink potions was aggravating. Couple of situations when I needed that vitality boost and couldn't use my stash in combat.
Arm wrestling = Stupid. Dice Poker = Fun. They also changed how the fist fighting works. No longer is it challenging and fun. It now switched to a simply one button command when prompted, removing any sense of difficulty. Granted the moves Geralt performs during the fights are entertaining to watch.

After playing Super meat boy, I started looking out for new games by the same developer. Edmund Mcmillen’s wonderfully strange imagination is an interesting thing to explore through his games, that’s for sure.
This game was not a disappointment. At first, I had no idea what to expect, the trailer was very strange but a tad intriguing. When I came across it there was next to no information about the game and the mechanics of it on the store page and back then there was no costumer reviews to go off of. Admittedly I never actually brought it to give it a go off of the information I was given, I ended up with it from a bundle and it’s the only reason I really played it. Although I wish I had taken the leap to try it because it is well worth it.
Binding of Isaac is a randomly generated dungeon crawler, one I have heard to be described as “Zelda-like” (I would have no idea about that, never played a Zelda game) you’re a young boy running from his demented mother. Who has been blinded by her hard-core Christianity and believes that the voice of god has spoken to her and told her to murder her son to prove her loyalty. So a very interesting concept, indeed.
A short cut scene plays on start-up, which expands on what I just described, you find yourself wandering through randomly generated dungeon floors, fighting monsters, picking up loot and items as you go along that changes how you fight, gives you different abilities and drastically changes Isaac’s image. At the end of each floor, you fight a boss, and move on down to the next floor. It being harder than before, with a bigger space to explore and more enemies to defeat.
There’s a large range of items to collect that when found for the first time is added to the “things I found” section in the main menu, so a lovely bit of collecting there to entice those OCD minded like myself, There’s new characters to unlock which vary in stats, challenges to complete and even some DLC that can extend your gameplay.
You are given one life and one life only. You can find hearts to heal, but once you are dead, that’s it, you start all over again. So throughout the whole game and especially when nearing the end, it starts to put a little pressure on and gets that heart rate going. I’m not one to be good under pressure so it gets me every time. I FINALLY managed to complete the game a few times over, again, admittedly, only after I gained some “top tips” from my way-to-good-at-games brother. There have been people that have completed the game 10 times over and still not gotten bored. I think that the randomly generated dungeon element to it keeps its replay ability intact. If it were to replay the same levels over and over when you died, the game would be a lot different and no doubt a lot less popular.
I have heard from friends that it is quite hard to complete without “doing your research” on the wiki or seeking tips from those nerdy minded like my brother who managed to figure all of it out themselves. I on the other hand find that kind of thing enjoyable, because it beats you every time and you work and research and try to understand the game more to finally get to that ending. I can quite honestly say that the first time I reached the end, my heart has never beaten that loud or that fast in a long time. And that sense of accomplishment you get from finishing a game, is a on a much higher scale when you work to complete this one.
The music is great, it fits the setting perfectly and is great to listen to. Rarely have I actually wanted to download a game’s soundtrack, I can give most soundtracks a thumbs up but not often do I actually want to listen to game music outside of gaming.
The art, as per usual in Edmunds games, is amazing. And I hear they are also looking to remake the game to have a more “retro” look, with possible multiplayer features. Which should be very interesting. For those interested you can look up “Binding of Isaac: Rebirth”.
All in all, it is a great indie game, which is both fun and challenging. Definitely worth trying, I am not usually the dungeon crawler type, but this game is a lot of fun. The only fault that I had with this game, which has bothered me quite a few times now, is that I have lost my save for no reason. The game is listed as having ‘Steam Cloud’ features, but it definitely doesn't work. I haven't uninstalled the game, I haven't touched it. But recently I hopped on and seen all the progress that I had made was gone. And for a game that has no real save points or ongoing plot to keep up with, your stats, unlocked characters and collection of things you have found is pretty much all you have. I was pretty upset to see it had vanished and it’s something I felt I needed to warn people about.
TL;DR : Awesome music, fun and engaging game with a slightly 'twisted' side to it. It's a challenge to reach the end and you can definitely end up putting a lot of hours into this. Addictive and awesome all around.

I gotta say, I was really skeptical going into this game, but all my skeptisim is gone. This game is amazing. I would recommend this to anyone I know who enjoys a racing game. For a long time I've wanted Forza and Gran Tourismo to incorporate motorcycles into the game, but now I no longer have that longing. This is the perfect mix of Forza and Need for Speed. It has all the good racing qualities of Forza with the awesome customization of Need for Speed. I've played other game, like Drive Club, that have motorcycles, and their rider dynamics are awful and unuseable. This game does a good job of providing different physics options to adjust for your comfortablility.
My one beef with it is that they don't do a good job regulating difficulty with the bikes power. They have different classes, but the classes are too broad. I found myself using an underpowered bike against more powerful bikes that were in the same class. It makes it really difficult to do well on a challenging difficulty. I found myself needing to turn down the difficulty to compensate for the bike's lack of performance, which is pretty unfortunate. They either needed to nerf the AI's bikes that are used when you're using an underpowered one, or they needed to make the classes more specific and bring the CCs of the bikes closer together. Having a class that's "Below 700cc" or "700-900cc" just doesn't work. You can't have 900cc bikes that make 140HP against 700cc bikes that make sub 100HP.
But besides that, the game is awesome and I hope they keep making them for the forseable future.

Before I mention what's good or bad about the game I think the reason this game was made should be stated.
The main reason this game was made is to hype up Dungeon Defenders 2 and to also test their playverse system.
So with that fact lets move to the pros, cons and they idk.
pros:
complete player reset, some wont find to this be a pro but this allows for new players to have a better multiplayer experience.
gear rework, they've managed to even out the gear progession so that becoming level 74 or higher doesn't make you a god in dungeon defenders with mythical etc.
New maps, who can complain about a few more maps and bosses.
visible armour, It's a small pro but its makes every character look unique which is always good
open tavern, Now this is a con if you prefer to be on your own but if you're like me a prefer to socialise it's a big plus.
loot rework, They've made it so the loot that someone sees is invisible to everyone else meaning that some of the more greedy players can no longer go around spamming e.
The ability to charge, I'm an extremely slow tower squire right now so the fact that I can charge helps alot for moving around the map it also allows you to leap backwards to dodge an enemy attack helping in close range combat.
You can also play at 4% allowing thos who can't wait for it to fully download to jump right in and play though you will experience slow loading times as 96% percent of the content hasn't even been downloaded.(Those of you who say It's 25% are wrong as the download to 25% is 51mb but the whole download is 1.61gb meaning It's 4%.)
Cons:
The enemy pathing is terrible I've noticed that enemies will not walk in the right path and will instead walk in circles at times.
The loot you find isn't always for your class, many times I've found a awesome sword to only realise it's a small monk weapon.
This may be a personal con but I hate the fact that the tavern keeper no longer sells weapons or armour.
buffs, agian this might be a personal thing but the fact that you can buy bombs etc makes it feel like the tower strategy has been made slightly easier.
For thos who have never bought Dungeon defenders have to pay 20 while I should be 15 euro out of sale(I'm from Ireland so I only have the Irish price.)
If you want to play a private game they make you wait through a 33 second timer.
They made the gui aimed towards phones making it akward to use. once you learn the shortcut keys it is slightly easier to use
The idk:
The fact that people can't host games is both a good and bad thing as It helps players find other players who want to play the same map but it also makes it very hard to setup a party of players who can work together properly e.g my first public game was throne room but  when I join my party was me and 3 barbarians luckily I could carry the team with my towers but if I had never joined that team was doomed from the start.
There is microtransactions but they are emotes and in all my time playing Dungeon Defenders I don't think I ever used an emote so I can't say they're a good or bad thing.
Conclusion:
This game is in a grey zone as you can't call it a cash grab from dungeon defender fans as It's 6 euro right now
but you also can't call it a new game as even though it has new things It's still the same game at its core.
If your a fan of dungeon defenders you'll probably buy it anyway but if your a new comer think it through before you buy it as I think the 20 euro price tag is too high for a game that was released 3 years ago.

Stellaris is a very mixed bag. It's very much like GalCiv 3 had a child with Europa Universalis or Hearts of Iron 3. It leans much more in the 4X genre than the grand strategy, however the grand strategy influence is there. You have to control and manage your fleets, spacestaions and directly controled planets yourself. It become quite cumbersome after a while and with no way to automate military assets, there is a lot of micro managing. Aside from that serious drawback, it is a fun and interesting game. No game breaking glitches on release (as far as I have encountered), which is usually a good sign. The reason you play (at least for me) is to grow and expand you fledgling empire into a dominant force and due to the scale of the game, you can really feel like you are making an empire. Mods are highly recommended as they really help spice the singleplayer gameplay. There are many pro and cons to the game but if you are patient or want to create a galactic empire and don't mind the micro in the game. This is the game for you.
-Pretty game
-Create your own faction works
-True sense of scale
-Modding support
-Great mods
-A lot of micromanaging during endgame
-No way to auromate your military assest
-No way to automate exploration
-Passive AI (can be fixed with mods)

There have been plenty of rogue-like games in the last few years, but this is definitely one of the most unique and original. The concept is strangely brilliant, the art is great, and the music is awesome, so the whole package seems pretty stunning at first glance. However, when you look under the hood, it's not flawless...the concept may be amazing, but the execution is a little bit janky at times. There are times when I know that I'm 100% on the beat, and yet the game simply isn't registering that I'm on target, leading to my untimely death. I'm a musician, so I have a good sense of rhythm and timing - something seemed off here. There's just not enough precision to the mechanics, which can really sink you when you're facing a boss or going up against a  big room filled with tough enemies. There are definitely a few frustrations that you'll have to deal with to get into a groove here. I would defintely still recommend this, despite  whatever shortcomings it may have, because the idea is great and the development team has gotten pretty dang close to nailing it. There's also the ability to add in your own music, which is a fantastic feature...I pumped in some Tribe Called Quest, Wu-Tang, Biggie, etc., and then the game was really bumping and twice as fun. Get this on sale and it'll be money well-spent, as long as you recognize that there's gonna be a serious learning curve when it comes to getting into the game's idea of rhythm.

I'll be honest playing FEAR is just wonderful, its a shooter that does so many things modern ones just don't and this might be the only game in the entire FEAR series worth playing. Decently spooky and scary (Got me shooting and wasting ammo whenever i could) Though said scary bits are heavilly scripted in a way so you can only really get spooked once and its not super organic (Sometimes you can just get distracted and not see the spooky thing like you'll hear a violin screech without seeing whatever creepy thing the creepy japanese girl de jour is doing.) Dust: An Elysian Tail is, simply put, a masterpiece. A modern classic, thoroughly humble in spite of its gorgeous presentation, it is a game that firmly stands among a gamer's fondest memories: Zelda, Metroid, Castlevania, Dust. But to say that this game is on the league of the classics from which it draws inspiration, is not enough. For Dust is, in many ways, better than any of those games, as it has learned and grown from them, not copied. Ocarina of Time, however wonderful our memories of it may be, is a game from the last century, and it shows. Not the case with Dust. This game runs in any resolution; it has hand-drawn high-resolution sprites; it is able of seamlessly changing between controller, keyboard and mouse inputs on the fly; it has charming and very well directed voice acting; great sound effects, graphic effects, cutscenes, dialogues, soundtrack. The technical details alone should be reason enough for you to try this game. Its wonders do not end there, however, for Dust is also a heart-touching story, unafraid of being naïve and juvenile, a fairy-tale in all the best ways — that manages to be mature where it counts. No wonder this is the work of a loving father: this is a game I'd raise my child with, confident that not only would he witness a great work of art, but that he would learn valuable lessons along the way.
If you are at all capable of enjoying platformers, give this game a try and allow it to enchant you.

Want to relax and contemplate and just generally chill? Do you have a love of the ocean and all of the animals that chill in there? Whenever you visit an aquarium, does it give you a chill feeling? Chill?
If you answered yes to any or all of these questions, buy this game! I got this game on sale, but it's absolutely worth the full price.
I've been dreaming of an ocean game like this. I got Endless Ocean for the Wii to try and fulfill that dream, but it fell short. This is a game that finally fulfilled that dream.
Without spoiling things, you essentially swim around with all the different types of wildlife in the ocean. You can latch onto animals as larger or larger than yourself and swim with them. You can tumble around. It's beautifully simple, and is a nice break from busy life. I feel scuba divers would really appreciate this game. I "beat" it in roughly 7 hours, but I plan on going back to this when I just need a zen moment of self reflection. I can see replayability simply in that regard.
My only dislike is that you can't really view the controls. I know why they chose this path, but as a dude who tries to play billions of different games with continually decreasing free time, it'd be nice to re-refer to the controls when I get back to the game days or weeks later.
Anyway, buy this game, totally worth full price, and enjoy!

Ah, good old Red Alert.
Nothing better than a RTS that is easy going with over the top plot and units and technologies. Comparing the three installments of this game the first one was the least over the top. It still had some seriousness from the original C&C, but had the basis for ‘over-the-top-ness’ with the idea of Soviet Union expanding into all of Europe. Oh, and there was time travel as well. The second RA didn’t disappoint and took a leap forward in ‘over-the-top-ness’ with Soviets assaulting the US and game being generally more colorful and cheerful. Now it is the other way around with Soviets eliminating key figure from the past instead of Allies as in RA 1 and events taking yet another direction with Empire of the Rising Sun coming out as a united threat.
The game is colorful, silly, over the top and most importantly much fun. This time the big new thing is a co-commander who can be a real person over the Internet or AI controlled. This is an interesting concept with sort of built in multiplayer, but I’m really glad they made the option of AI co-commander, helping me not deal with social interactions. On rare occasions AI glitched and never left its base, so all offensive had to be done by me. At least I didn’t have to worry about defenses. Overall having a co-commanders is very beneficial as they supply almost constant attacks on the enemy thus softening them up for my big armada, which is quickly reduced to almost nothing, because unit balance is made very well I think. In most cases you can’t storm in with dozens of Apocalypse tanks and win the level. Almost always you have to think about anti-air units since the enemy AI most often will use air units for defenses and offenses as well.
The best part from RA 2 is back – unit experience. There is nothing more satisfying than one or two units maintaining the pressure on the enemy or holding off what is thrown at you only because you previously cared and repaired them each time units were near death and now they have highest possible rank and therefore added defense and firepower. For me that was the best idea Westwood had for RA 2 and it is present in RA 3 as well
Overall I think it made a great transition from 2D to 3D and I loved the game just like the previous ones.

August 21, 2014:
After 4 weeks, a second look.  My original review (July 28th) was filled with optimism about the potential for the game to be all that was promised in the store listing:  the definitive version of an existing game, with all of the original content and expansions (plus additional missions), a fix for the cheating/hacking that existed in the original Dungeon Defenders, rebalanced heroes and towers and more new features. It concluded with:
"I enjoy the game despite the issues, and look forward to what it will be when the wrinkles are smoothed out a bit. My advice is to let it cook a bit more and come back in a month or two to see where it is at. It's a fun game, but despite being a rehash of a game released in 2011, it lacks polish and is incredibly buggy. I give it a thumb up, in that I do enjoy it and anticipate it to get significantly better as the current issues are resolved."
The problem is that to this point, none of that has come to pass.  Although weekly patches are released, there seems to be a fundamental component of the original game that is missing and/or broken.

For a game that really exists on the idea that you will kill attacking monsters to get newer and better loot or spend in-game currency to upgrade your existing equipment or some combination thereof, it is surprisingly hard to actually get that loot.  One of the issues is the existence of only so many 'objects' in the game at a given time.  Since DDE spawns both coins, mana crystals and loot during missions, if you aren't quick enough, there is no way to grab the loot before it disappears.  The rate at which items drop which are actually an upgrade is also extremely slow, and in my experience only occurs during the last wave of a mission (perhaps 15-20 minutes of gameplay for a standard mission, or in the last 5 minutes of 60 minute 'survival' wave).  While the original Dungeon Defenders had challenges you could complete and get rewards of equipment or pets, DDE has the exact same challenges, but with no reward at the end.  It's simply mission over, back to the tavern.
Hero and monster balance is incredibly flawed.  It is hard for me to criticize hero balance, since it is NOT my opinion that all heroes need to be on an equal footing or equally valuable.  However when a patch is released, where 'hero health scaling is changed by 108% for Huntress, 194% for Initiate, 66% for Monk and Jester" and so on, it is a sign that the game has not been playtested.  Again, for a game that is 95% a carbon copy of a 3 year old game, this is inexcusable.  It is not just hero health either.  Other massive, sweeping changes in their 'weekly patch' include Dark Elf Warrior jump attack damage reduced from 105 to 35,  Bowling Ball tower projectiles last 3 seconds (rather than 6), lowering all Huntress trap radius scaling from .039 to .0058.  The point is not that I am unhappy about a specific change, but that the magnitude of the changes are massive and demonstrate just how little testing the game had before release.
Summoner pets are altogether broken.  Imagine a class where the towers (pets) you create are similar to those of other classes except they are either severely underpowered, wander away from where you set them up, or simply don't attack.  These issues did not exist in DD1, so why do they exist here.  And why is it so hard to fix them?
In a multiplayer game, it is a common occurrence to find low level players join the game and idle, contributing nothing, but leeching xp to level up while away from their screen.  There is no way to remove them from the game, unless you make a new game session.  Worse than this though is the ability for any player to sell any existing tower or trap.  This comes in 2 flavors.  Those who sell everything to be griefers and those who sell everything because it does not confirm to the 'optimal' build for that map -- which seems to boil down only squires being able to build.  For me, unless I'm playing solo, the fun has been sucked out of the game.
The Playverse overlay/interface still remains broken.
Player levels remain capped at 60.  This was the cap in Dungeon Defenders before the release of any of the expansions.  There is no nightmare or higher difficulty level (it will be implemented at some future point). I have not reached the level cap (because I am not willing to put up with the buggy/broken release any further), but many have reached the level cap and have nothing else to play for due to the level cap and loot issues.
Other game modes are still missing such as nightmare and pure strategy.
I never thought I'd complain about the patching system, but I -have- to comment on it.  For one thing, the patches, when released, require a redownload of the entire game (5.25GB), no matter how large or small the patch is.  This is even more of an absurdity when a patch changelist can be as small as:
- Fixed the Barbarian pet bug issue
- Fixed the Hero Inspect window issue
I am fortunate to not have a data cap, but still, this is 20+GB of -patching- this month.
The second issue I have with the patching system is that you must run the game launcher and the launcher then downloads the patch.  There is no Steam integration with silent or background downloading of the patch.  The conspiracy theorist in me wonders if this was done to make it appear as if I am playing the game when I am really waiting for the 5+ GB to download.  Considering that the patches are released weekly, this adds up to a lot of time (my connection is 1MB/s download) of my 28 hours 'played' where I was not in fact playing.
And finally, I am not alone in my opinions.  The Dungeon Defenders community has slowly trickled away to other games as the patches have not fixed the core game.  At this moment, there are 626 players in game.  Six Hundred players, total (some of which may be patching, perhaps).
This is not a finished product.  It lacks polish, but more than that -- key features and key gameplay elements are missing while others (loot!) are broken.  If the game were feature complete and in need of balance tweaks, it could be called Dungeon Defenders beta.  This game should be considered Dungeon Defenders Eternity Alpha release.  I can no longer recommend it.

I played this game on the Playstation back when it came out and decided to buy the Steam version for old times' sake. Sorry to say that the PC port of this game is absolutely horrendous. It's not worth the purchase even on a deep discount.
The foremost problem is the controls: the button/key labels in-game are indicated using B1, B2, ... B10. Sure, you get shown the button meanings when the game boots, but it's not very useful when you can't remember the key combination for 'escape from battle' (required for the plot in the first game mission) and the in-game comments are useless. Also, don't bother with the controller support for this game. I attempted to use my wired 360 controller and found that the left and right triggers and the directional pad aren't detected -- you can't specify them in the custom configuration screen. (Also, there goes Zell's limit break.) On an aesthetic note, you should probably just mute the game instead of trying to tolerate the lo-fi, MIDI quality music. It's a shame, because the Dollet music mission is one of my favorites. Also, 'Magic Boost'? Seriously? Drawing magic was a HORRENDOUS idea to begin with, but Magic Boost is pretty much game breaking if you use it early on (it gives you 100 of the fire/thunder/blizzard, fira/blizzara/thundara, firaga/blizzaga/thundaga, all the status effect spells, and a few others... but fortunately it doesn't give you 100 of the top-tier spells like ultima, aura, etc) The game wasn't hard, there's no need for this kind of cheat.

This game is best played on a cold, rainy, or stressful day.
Little Inferno is a game for the pyromaniac burning inside you. With the click of your finger, a flame emerges. The flame hungers for fuel, so you feed it. You feed it more and more until the whole fireplace fills up.
Then nothing.
As a stress reliever, Little Inferno is at it's full potential for pyromaniacs going through a hard time or just need something to burn. Not much can be said here.
However, as a game, that's what i'm here for.
Little Inferno's way of storytelling is through letters, similar to Presentable Liberty, but less depressing. Characters range from a girl who also likes to burn things, and a weatherman who constantly flies around, telling you the weather. You will also fall into a deep connection to some characters, but to prevent spoilers, I won't detail who.
The game mechanic is simple. Click, and there's a flame. You can burn stuff with said flame. Burned stuff gives profit. Profit gives more stuff to burn. Burn stuff again. Repeat.
When I say it that way, it sounds boring, but the game has an excellent fire mechanic and interesting firestarters.
You don't burn wood, that's pretty boring, but the game gives you puppets, wood, blocks, toys, and various gadgets with different effects that turn on when it starts burning.
Overall, there isn't too much replayability but it's a sweet game with a charm.

Sure,this shooter may be old,but don't let that turn you away from a true great mix of shooter action and horror structure.One of my favourite horror games is FEAR,this is in my opinion the best of the series and ,whilst it does show its age,it's so much fun to play but at the same time can scare the pants off you.The game is told through first person,this brings you close to your environment and limits your view - plenty of times I spun around to check what may lurk behind me.The premise is simple,Alma is a creepy women who stalks you around all the time and is the origin of many jump scares.The story isn't great but it doesn't detract from the whole experience as it is simple and clear - not complex at all in my opinion..The graphics are dated,however the atmosphere is creepy and tense,the game supports this by giving you gameplay that is simple and straight forward - no packed HUD or mechanics to understand.The game isn't perfect as within the nearly 9 hour campaign there are several shooting sections that can feel a bit tedious.But this is simply a underated classic that any horror fan will enjoy due to its simplicity and ,most importantly; a perfectly balanced mix of fast paced shooter action and tense,hand-sweating tension that the horror atmosphere creates.

Stellaris is an amazing empire managment game.. it is advertised as a 4x game, and it is exactly that.
Starting off, you can completely customize your empire, mods support at launch makes customizing endless... ye endless spac---
ANYWAY, HERE ARE PROS AND CONS for Stellaris.
***PROS****!!!!!!!!!!!!! :D
Empire setting up--- Potentially limitless customization.
Visuals--- Its beauitful, well animated, great lighting, great portraits, lots of polish.
Sound--- It great, from the sound of different ships, to different weapons, to different worlds when you click on them, hearing a tropical from an arid, to a desert, very awesome.
UI--- some people said this is a nightmare, actually its great, there are few things hit and miss, but overall great start to a launch title! (please put UPGRADE ALL on controllable planets...)
AI--- the AI is good/bad/great, it really depends, some people say its dumb, no, not really. They declare war on you when you're a threat or they want something, really dependent on what and who they are. But if you see an empire with +14 approval, chances are they aint going to delcare war, as for fleets battles, they run away if they think they are losing, very sins of a solar empire.
GAMEPLAY!!!!!!!!!
--eXploring is the best out of all 4x titles, your exploring science ship has a leader you choose, who come with their own bonuses and levels, making exploring even better. By exploring you have chances to get technologies, artifacts, info on resources, discovering preFTL civs, other space empires, and giant space creatures. There are three types of FTL, Warpdrive, Hyperdrive and Wormholes, all are unlocked end game, each are better and worse than the other.
--eXpand is great, once you are past 5 planets, the game will suggest creating regions, AI managed areas to ease micromanaging, as 4x Vets know the micro hell. You can build stations that extend your influence as far as your FTL can take you. You can set up alliances, or federations with other friendly empires, vassal enemy empires or plain old conquer them to expand.
--eXploiting is also fantastic, resources improve your empire that you get from planets, suns, black holes, enslaved aliens/your own people, or dumb/sentient robots who can all rise up against you. Research is very expansive, with three different research areas that throw four-six different techs at you to choose every time a new tech is researched. It is randomized, and pretty fantastic, as it feels fresh every new game.  Ship designer is ok, it only lets you play with the inner workings, which some people may prefer.
--eXterminating is straightforward, build giant blob of ships, send ships to kill.
The combat is rock, paper, scissors... A, will be better than B, but worse than C, etc.
Its a good system. There are 6+ empire ship visual variations, more with mods now and in the future.
After you conquer an alien planet, you can choose to purge them. You have three stages of orbitial    bombardment, light, mid, full and the game responds in both audio and visually to the choices.
The game also has factions which develop in your empire, If left unchecked, can detach and create their own empire, and can be dealth with in numerous ways, PURGE!!!!!!!!.
Diplomacy is quite indepth and has different ways to dealing with an alien empire, alien empires interact with eachother and can if they all hate you, gang up on you.
**CONS**............... :(
Stellaris does 4x incredibly, but there are things that should be there, which are not...Otherwise I would be still playing. The game is, GREAT GREAT FANTASTIC, but the other side of it, is nothing, nothing, nothing. There is nothing bad about the game, its ridiculously well made, just needs more.
1-5 are required, as currently there are better 4x titles out there overall.
1.  No Espionage, none---- Huge empires that are pure evil, can only be dealt with an alliance of other empires, other games have this too, however with espionage, you can turn the tide of war.
2.  No Trade lanes/ships, none----- You can setup trade deals with empires that last 10-30 years, but no civilian ships, or industrial ships, flying around your empire, passively increasing relations and economy with alien empires. Without it, it just makes the game look, kind of stagnant, and not living.
3.  No more than two ways to get Influence, seeing how Influence is such an important resource in this game, you can only get it by rivaling an enemy empire, or upgrading your planets HQ... It needs more sources, making alliances with empires, federations, taking over an enemy empire and emancipating its slaves, etc.
4.  No automation, this is needed, badly, the automation starts at regions, and ends there. When you build a colony ship, it would be amazing to automate it to colonize a colonizable planet within the limit of its FTL... and automate a constructer to just build stations around the empire, and actually automate exploration and discovery... so it can let you focus on the true aspect of Stellaris, which is running your empires inner workings and dealing with aliens.
5.  No key binding change, you cant edit your keys, weird, very weird, Paradox fix this soon.. please.
6. No tools to make the game a bit faster.. I love my lengthy games, but as it is right now, its a grind, without a deep mid game like the early game, and more fleshed out end game, it is a grind to go through the pace Paradox wants it to be..
These must be put in, to give the game bigger legs than it has.
Below are just crazy ideas.
No massive ships, this is more of an addon to make the game even better, than something required. After building a battleship, build dreadnaughts, or a death star to blow up planets, like in Gal Civ 2, there is the terror star and blows up entire systems. I have seen a broken up planet around a black hole in Stellaris, and it was fantastic to look at, this is something that can be done, just to add more eXterminate to the game.
No visual variation between alien thrusters on the back of ships, this is tiny, and I think easily changed, but its annoying when there is an alien empire using something that looks very similar to your own.
No SUPER indepth terraforming or insane building, you can terraformendgame you should be able to terraform EVERYTHING, screw it, its set in space in the future, technology shouldnt be limited. I want to build rings like the forerunners, and from that have different visual variations for the alien empires, as well as technologically. And or building actual planets, artifically created living worlds.
No game changing resource/wonder, wouldnt' it be great if there was something that would change the war around immediately that you randomly found through discovery, something that allows you to either blow up planets or rip them apart for ridiculous amounts of resources.
VERDICT!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
If you're swayed by the prettiness, the polish, the Empire managing complexity, buy this game.
If the things that are missing bother you, Id say wait. Overall good game, in a year or two, it will be the defining 4x civ space game, and I will live on it, goodbye life, in 6months/year/two years.

Dust has a lot to like about it but it misses just enough notes that it falls into my "not recommended" bucket. If it were a shorter game, I probably would recommend it. It took me 10 hours to finish but after about 5-6 hours I felt like I was just grinding through it to get to the end. A couple of things contributed to that feeling: I'm not a combat prima donna but even I felt it was a little too simplistic and repetitive. I just used the ranged AoE in every battle and ran into very few challenges. The platforming is okay...but that's not the focus of the game. There are a number of side quests or unlockables. Some of them are the typical "you can't even get to this area because you don't have the slide/double-jump/super-jump power yet, so remember to backtrack to here once you do".
Only completionists will feel a strong desire to go after them all. Only 31% of players complete even 5 sides quests. 23% complete 10. 10% complete all 20. I did more than 10 (but less than 20) and still felt pretty overpowered by the end (I had no difficulty defeating the final boss by spamming my ranged AoE).
The game doesn't have any real flaws, to be honest. I just felt like it was a nice tight 5-6 hour game that overstayed its welcome.

Want to relax and contemplate and just generally chill? Do you have a love of the ocean and all of the animals that chill in there? Whenever you visit an aquarium, does it give you a chill feeling? Chill?
If you answered yes to any or all of these questions, buy this game! I got this game on sale, but it's absolutely worth the full price.
I've been dreaming of an ocean game like this. I got Endless Ocean for the Wii to try and fulfill that dream, but it fell short. This is a game that finally fulfilled that dream.
Without spoiling things, you essentially swim around with all the different types of wildlife in the ocean. You can latch onto animals as larger or larger than yourself and swim with them. You can tumble around. It's beautifully simple, and is a nice break from busy life. I feel scuba divers would really appreciate this game. I "beat" it in roughly 7 hours, but I plan on going back to this when I just need a zen moment of self reflection. I can see replayability simply in that regard.
My only dislike is that you can't really view the controls. I know why they chose this path, but as a dude who tries to play billions of different games with continually decreasing free time, it'd be nice to re-refer to the controls when I get back to the game days or weeks later.
Anyway, buy this game, totally worth full price, and enjoy!

I'm reluctant to post a negative for this game as I've been a fan of the Gal Civ games since the first.  But this game is an absolute unstable and buggy mess.  As of now I've put in 102.6 hrs (according to steam of course) to the game.
FIrst their DLC's are about as minimalist as they possibly can be.  Even ones that claim to "add a race" don't really do so.  For some you still have to either create them as a custom race yourself or download a mod where someone else already did just that.  As they are not added into the game proper.
As to the game itself, my PC meets the recommended requirements (above them actually) yet the game still has some hiccups as it carries on into later turns.  Crashes come periodically for seemingly no reason (It's crashed on me more than once just by clicking on something, be it a planet, ship, whatever.)
The Ideaology "perks" don't work properly with custom races, not giving you the bonus vessels they're supposed too (for instance choose the pragmatic one that gives 3 free constructors..great right?...nope you don't get them at all.)
And finally, the thing that completely breaks the game.  As you go on eventually the designer stops working.  Spend an hour or two on a nice design and go to save it? Oops, crash to desktop and you're now forced to FORCE STEAM to shutdown through the task manager as STEAM won't realize it's shut down and still has a couple processes going ape-crap.  Not only that but, at least for my machine, when this happens it slows down my PC until a full restart.
When it first started that it didn't happen until I was trying to make Large Hull ships.  But my most recent game worked fine until I unlocked medium hulls and tried to save one....CTD as stated above.
If you love the Galactic Civ game series stick with 2...3 is minimal, unstable, and performs as if it was still an Alpha during Early Access.

I have played Void Expanse before it was released on steam - bought it from dev's website last august. This is a very well done top down space arpg/sandbox game. I see a number of people comparing it to space rangers, but I think it is more like a slightly more hardcore Drox Operative (which was influenced by Space Rangers).
There are different character specializations and career paths, many ships and components to equip and use, factions to do jobs for, and a large galaxy to explore. The combat is fast and brutal. Once shields go down, it doesn't take much time to blow up an enemy(or to be blown up). The movement is much more like a real vessel moving in space than Drox Operative or Space Rangers- directional thrust provides rotation and braking. You can choose to use the mouse instead of the keyboard for directional control, but you still have to use keyboard input to move, unlike Drox Operative and Space Rangers where movement can be controlled by mouse clicks.
This is an excellent game with no glaring flaws or weaknesses in gameplay for anyone who llikes space games and arpgs.

When it comes to recommending this game, I would have to say I am more indifferent than yes or no.  I'm just saying yes because to me it can keep one's attention and, all-and-all it is not a bad game, though it has its as flaws, like any other game.
I'm not going to give a brief overview of the game, you want to find more official, better detailed ones, because I would probably miss a few important things, I'm just going to tell about my experiences and general opinion of the game.
So it has good art, the dragons and weapons are beautifully designed and look great.  The environment looks really good, for me I am not really picky about general looks, but this game has got it down.  The biggest flaw is that it can become tedious and often times boring relatively quickly.  In order to get more dragons, weapons and runes, you must have crystals, the in-game currency.  In singleplayer you get roughly 50-70 crystals a match and for multiplayer and pvp a little more, I can't really say I play singleplayer more then anything.  So let us say I played ten singleplayer matches and got a total of at least 500, at most 700, not bad, but dragons and weapons require a very large amount of crystals to purchase.  Runes are only 150 per pack so that is fine with me, but a 3 pack of weapons is 2500 crystals and a 3 pack of dragons is 5000.  So let us say I am very unlucky and I get 50 crystals per match, I would have to play 100 matches to get a pack, and each match takes about 10-15 minutes, which is quick, but that would take at least 1000 minutes or 16.6 hours.  That is a lot of time.  It used to be you could just buy a dragon or weapon for money, but they got rid of that and made one thing called a titan pack.  You pay 20 dollars and you get one of each tier one dragons, one of each weapons, all the avatar skins, all the dragon skins, Acts 2-4 are now playable (yes, you must pay money to play the story line), all of your rewards are quadrupled for a year, and you will get all new content(like a new dragons or weapons) for a year.  I gotta say, that is actually extremely good.  Before they did this if I wanted to buy all the dragons, weapons, and such it would be more than that, so to me that is an improvement, though now it you only wanted one dragon, you have to pay the whole 20 dollars instead of 3.99 so it can be a double-edged sword of some sort.  Gameplay is good, but it gets very boring, the storyline is okay, but it is more about the multiplayer function.
Going into the multiplayer function, I have only played multiplayer matches three times, but in those three times, the teams seemed to be a little lopsided.  But since you really can't have an overpowered dragon, you can increase certain things, but you can still be defeated easily if facing multiple enemies, so it depends on the players and their teamwork, and how well they use their skills too.
So in conclusion,
- dragons and weapons take a large amount of time to get
- multiplayer matches can be lopsided
- becomes tedious and boring quickly
- you must pay money to play acts 2,3 and 4
- you have to buy everything if you only wanted one thing, you must pay $20 if you only wanted to spend $3.99
but,
- the designs are great
- singleplayer is always fun, at least to me
- matches are quick
- you get free dragons from the acts, all three tiers of a certain dragon, though you need to have certain dragons and weapons to fulfill requirements
- you spend money once and you basically get everything
All-in-all, if you are a casual gamer, this would be a good game, you can put time and effort into it, and you only have to make one purchase and that is it.  I apologize if I left something out, these were the things that I noticed in the game.

Bigger, badder, more explosive than its predecessor. It's a good game, but it lacks some of the artful cohesion that made the original DOOM so great. The original game did a lot better at telling a story through its level design and gameplay. The levels in DOOM II, by contrast, feel much more abstract, and feel more engineered to antagonize the player than the original DOOM. That said, the mechanics are (for better or worse) exactly the same as the first game, adding one new gun and a host of new upper-mid-tier enemies. There's plenty of great levels here, all things considered, it's just a shame that the sequel to DOOM feels more like a fan-made expansion pack than a full-fledged sequel.
Presentation-wise, the Steam version of the game runs through DosBOX, which is serviceable, but feels a little low-effort. Fortunately, the game files are all there, so it's not difficult at all to find a source port to suit one's tastes.

I remember finding the Kickstarter trailer of the game in my recommendations box on YouTube right after the campaign ended. When it went into early access, I must admit - I sinned. I was playing a pirated version up to release. And finally, almost a year later, I got it on sale.
Boy, I managed to miss a lot despite trying to update my illegal copy.
And I regret none of the dollars I spent on it.
First and foremost - the game isn't something OUTSTANDING(c) in its terms. It is really good, indeed, but only to people who enjoy at least one of two parts this game consists of. By that I mean rhythm-game and roguelite-dungeon-crawler. The first part, just as the second, are by themselves rather simplistic. But together, they form a symbiosis of unparallelled polish, style and addictiveness. If it got you hooked once, you will keep coming again and again.
It has plenty of content - 4 zones, 3 bosses, 3 endgame bosses, multitude of enemies and upgrades. Before you know it, you'll be off single-zone and take on All Zones Mode and swearing at almost impossibly hard Aria, while your fingers twitch to the rhythm and your body wants to dance. Soundtrack, balance and combos are what makes this game shine - the more you listen to music, the more you like it, and obliterating enemies one-by-one with incredible weapons and equipment that will probably make your eyes shine when you get the taste of power you get with their proper use.
Now, this game is not endless. It can make you sick after a long while. But you'll keep coming back for another try at the Necrodancer's lair, because its style and overall quality make your heart bound to the beat.
Short recap: you like good music, rhythm games and/or fair dungeon crawling? This game's for you. If you are REALLY not sure about it, just wait for sales. I got the game at 5$, which personally, for my country, is a fair price, while for other people it'll be just a steal.
Oh, and also check out the Amplified DLC for full experience if you really like this game. It's totally worth buying even at full price of 5$.

RIDE is a motorcycle racing game, released in 2015.
The game comes with a huge variety of street motorbikes, all of them licensed. All of these bikes are either road-legal sport bikes or competition racing bikes, so you experience quite a lot of difference in terms of handling and speed throughout the game. There is also 2 fully electric motorbikes, which output a lot of power and feel different than the others, mostly due to the engine sounds being missing and a different way of accelerating.
You visit 15 locations and are free to ride them on one of 133 bikes (of which 20 come in the various DLCs). The tracks are quite detailed and nice to look at, but they could have more details such as more spectators and some background properties. Yet overall it's a blast riding in first person and watching the world fly by. Details aren't that important anymore as soon as you reach higher-tier events.
Technically, RIDE is a solid game for its time, the graphics look pretty good and it doesn't require that much of a beefy computer. The handling is adjustable and can fit a newbie's keyboard skills aswell as a pro's Wheel/Gamepad skills.
But all the nice stuff aside, the loading times are quite long (for me at least) and there is one thing that just kept preventing me from actually sticking to the game and staying until I finished every career event. And that's the fact that there's no long-time goal that the game tells you about. You pretty much only follow the career event lines, without any background of them. There is no personality for your character and all you have to do is ride and finish races. Achievements aside, I couldn't really find a point in the distance to lock on to and focus on reaching at some point.
Overall it's a solid game, and as many people say, a "Forza with bikes", which is quite true as the menus and HUDs do have a lot of similarities.
Recommended for every motorcycle enthusiast or racing game fan who doesn't care as much about storylines or background and just wants to enjoy a raw riding experience.

Call of Duty®: Black Ops is one of the best additions to the Call of Duty Series.
Treyarch has out done themselves with this one.
Very good graphics, Wonderful Zombie Mode Maps and has an awesome story.
My Ratings:
Campaign  = 7/10
Zombies Mode = 9/10
Multiplayer Mode = 6/10

STORY:
F.E.A.R. starts players off by putting them in the shoes of a faceless soldier that no one seems to like and also has 'very good reflexes.' Across a city that I don't believe is ever named, you and your squad run around killing soldiers that don't seem to have any real significance whatsoever, as well as seeing haunting images of corpses and this weird little girl that's just standing there all the time. If you play a game for its story, stay away from F.E.A.R. This game makes the Gears of War franchise look like a literary masterpiece.
GRAPHICS:
Though old and outdated, the game still looks fairly good. Character models stand out as the best moving visuals, but what really stands out are the bloodied, corpse-ridden halls and rooms you'll come across throughout your journey. The horrific sights of grissly murder stand out amongst the best of gaming's horror environments.
GAMEPLAY:
This part is more or less good and bad. The gunplay is clunky and awkward (luckily, it was significantly improved in the sequels) and you'll find many of your deaths due to the bad gameplay. However, the enemy AI are absolutely amazing. They'll react to your footsteps, so crouching in areas where they're unbeknownst to your presence is a good idea. If they see your flashlight, they'll react to it and dive to the sides, taking cover before you can squeeze of a shot. They'll flank, rush, and suppress your positions. The monster AI is lackluster in comparison to the human AI, however, and the jump scares in the game fall flat. This is more action than horror.
VERDICT:
With a terrible story, boring jump scares and awful gunplay, F.E.A.R.'s replay value is very low. However, environment eye candy, fantastic AI and subpar multiplayer (assuming you can find anyone online) give this game at 6.5/10.

TL;DR Summary: This is the game all you Master of Orion fans have been wishing for through all the disappointing other 4X space games since MoO2. It is not "Crusader Kings in Space." Also, get the Nova Edition for the arachnid species instead of just the base game.
Deep Thought Review:
I put in 50 hours before writing this because I wanted to make sure I wasn't just being an eager little fanboi and hopping on the thumbs-up bandwagon. I'm happy to say that it has met and exceeded all expectations I had, and, according to those more familiar than I am with Paradox, this game is only the beginning; free content updates in addition to DLC will be provided in the future. I have played Crusader Kings 2 for a fair number of hours, and while it is a fine game, I had no desire to own another CK2 that was just set in space. So, naturally, when a friend told me about Stellaris, I was less than enthusiastic. I am delighted to admit I was not only wrong in my assumption, but in point of fact, this is the absolute best 4X Space Game since Master of Orion 2. The only similarities it has to CK2 are the use of sectors (think vassals in CK2) and the jaw-droppingly beautiful artwork during loading screens. I actually regret not buying the super duper elite package or whatever it was that gave the art book, because it's that lovely. I did buy the Nova edition, however, and the arachnid species is definitely worth the extra $10 assuming $10 doesn't break the bank for you. I will now go through, topic by topic, to give an idea as to what to expect...
Graphics:
The best of any 4X Space Game so far. The procedurally generated galaxies are beautiful, the ship combat looks incredible. Once you get into some of the more unique weapons, it's really fun to watch them fight. As previously mentioned, the loading screen art is just amazing and is worthy of a coffee table book or a series of posters. It's better than most of the stuff on Digital Blasphemy.
Interface:
There's been some (admittedly meritous) grousing about certain aspects of the interface, however this should not be a deal-breaker for the buyer. The few aspects that do suffer from clunkiness or lack of features are already in the works for free fixes and upgrades by Paradox. Even the parts that need a bit of work are still navigable if one puts in the effort to learn the ins and outs. Minor problems aside, the interface is still much better than most other 4X Space Games I've played before (and I've played most of them), and in some cases, it's prettier. It's certainly a heck of a lot easier on the eyes than the Master of Orion 3 interface. You won't find a series of ugly spreadsheets, but rather an often intuitive collection of tabs. Almost everything you could possibly want has a mouseover explanation of what it is, what effects it has, and how much it requires in resources, and so on.
Custom Species Creation:
Yes. Not only does this game have it, but of all the species available, there's something like 20 animated sub-species to choose from for your critter avatars, each of which can be further customized for stuff like hair, feather, skin, color, clothing style, etc. The auto-naming schema presents you with several different options per species that range from the spartan insectoidlike names "Ika'Zre" to something that sounds like it strolled out of London "Reginald Davies" and follows suit for things like ship names, planets, etc. Not only can you choose any schema, regardless of your species, but during the game just about anything you own (from characters, to planets, to ships, etc) can be renamed if you don't like it. The same goes for the ship styles. You might have a mammalian species, but if you want to use reptilian ships, that's just fine and dandy. A wide array of different flag choices, custom colors for the flags, is a nice cherry on top. My only complaints are the limit of 4 traits that can be chosen, and what feels like a limited number of traits compared to Master of Orion 2. However, when you consider that in addition to traits, you also choose 2-3 ethos, and a government style, and leaders allow you to pinpoint further bonuses to government, ships, science, or what have you, then you begin to see just how rich the species creation process really is.
Learning Curve:
Stellaris has a very well-balanced learning curve. it's not nearly as hard to fathom as Crusader Kings 2, but still retains the richness of a great empire builder without being downright Civ-Rev in over-simplicity. Just when I think I've learned all I can about the game, something new clicks in my mind with regards to strategy, or outright suprises out of left field.
Gameplay:
The game plays like a pausable variable-speed RTS, much like Crusader Kings. One of the best differences from CK2 is, however, that you can wage war on someone without having to pursue casius belli first. And upon declaration of war you can set your terms immediately, should your opponent wish to surrender. Another lovely difference from CK2 is the fact that you can use this method to take over star system after star system without having to jump through an enormous number of hoops or luck rolls like with CK2. Combat is very easy to wage (though not necessarily easy to win, unless you have wisely chosen your fleet loadouts). Everything handles very smoothly overall. I would like to see some more uses for the strategic resources, but again, Paradox is already working on this, so I have nothing to worry about. As should be expected of any good 4X game worth its salt, Stellaris is infinitely replayable, and just seems to get more fun with each new game.
Multiplayer: Yep. It has it. And, unlike several games out there, you can use your saved custom species to play with, AND if someone is late to the party, they can join in (with the host's permission) after the game has already started. Otherwise, the MP experience is just like the SP experience, only your opponents are (hopefully) a bit more challenging.
The AI: The AI is nothing particularly noteworthy. It is neither terrible nor great. However, Padarox is also working on additional improvements to the AI, which is very encouraging.
All in all, you will find this game is worth every single penny, and will only become more so as Paradox addresses the few issues the game does have, and releases new content as well. If CK2 is any indication, this game is going to grow in scope a hundredfold before things even -start- to slow down on it. Two Thumbs, and Both Big Toes, UP!

Ok, so I've played through the campain a couple of times, and multiplayer for about 50 hours, so I have a few things to say.
The campains story is quite good, and much more developed than the other Call Of Duty games. At the end of the game I actually cared about the characters, and not not many games(especialy Call Of Duty games) can do that to me. the story makes you thnk are for fighting for something meaningfull, when in reallity it's all a hoax.(I don't want to spoil anything, so that's all I'm gonna say.) The gameplay is linier and involves quite a bit of scripted sequences. But I still find it very fun to play, especialy because most levels have some fun and redeaming gameplay usually at the end.(Wreeking havoc in a river boat, ripping ememys to shreds in an airplane maching gun, ect.) I also like the fact that some music is featured, including an amazing song from the rolling stones.
Multiplayer is usually a good experience. there's the occasional camper and grenade spammer, but this games maps are actually very good in preventing that. There are gamemodes and maps for almost everyone, from big path based runs, to tiny enclosed nieghborhood demolition. The hit detection is AMAZING in this game. I've done well with a ping of 400+, something impossible in other Call Of Duty games i've played. The unlock system is pretty good, You can purchase whatever atachments you want with call of duty points for your weapons once you reach level 5, But you do have to reach a certain level to unlock different weapons. The only thing I don't like about it is that some of the kill streaks are EXTREMELY OVERPOWERED. If an enemy reaches a 7 kill streak, consider your team screwed. I also hate claymores and think no game should use them ever. But that's just my opinion.
The visuals are okay, considering this game was released in 2010, but it seems a bit resource demanding for what is is. Make sure the textures are on extra, or it will look very ugly.
The way the DLC works is just plane sad, each being 15 dollars for FOUR MAPS. If you were to buy all the DLC, it would cost more than the actual GAME. And i have a problem with the games price, it was released in 2010, and costs fourty dollars. Battlefield 3 costs 20 dollars and was releas in 2011.
Anyway that's my review, I hope you found it helpfull.

Not only did I want to like this game, I TRIED, I REALLY REALLY tried to like it. I love Stardock and Sins of a Solar Empire is one of my favorite 4X games so I tried to give it a good shot. GL3 is one of the only games where I've tried to slog through the tedium, poor mechanics and bland unoriginality in the hopes that I was just missing something and this was actually a great game. Alas, after trying the campaign, tutorial and a straight forward, no strings attached game... I resigned myself to the fact that this game is just a really boring rip off of Civilization IV with worse AI.
Okay, the ship and race creation aspect is pretty cool, but it's basically aesthetic and adds little to the game overall. And in fairness they've also copied a few aspects from Civ V as well, like trade routes and city states. The only really original aspects of the game are space stations, which the computer pumps out constantly and will completely cover the map before you've advanced enough to stop them. Even if you're tearing them down with impunity, the computer can churn them out just as quickly as you can blow them up. The reason for this is that the AI is so diabolically bad that the devs have bolstered it with a series of cheats to stop AI races destroying themselves before the game even starts - like attaching robotic legs to a horse that died in the paddock so it can still run in the race. But they're not fooling anyone.
Apart from that, I was honestly having flash backs to a game released 10 years ago: diplomacy is identical to Civ IV, right down to the other races constantly nagging you for hand outs. Combat and troop types are similar, despite the ability to watch a little battle cinematic, and entirely pointless once you get to Corvettes anyway. The biggest difference in combat is that you have to send a troop transport to capture a planet, but then Birth of the Federation was doing that 17 years ago, so again it's hardly a game changer. The split tech tree struck me as a simplified version of Beyond Earth's.
The worst part is, I could actually forgive them for ripping off all their game mechanics from other franchises if it weren't for the fact that this game is just slow and boring. One of the great things about the Civ series is that, even when you're not doing a lot, you're always working towards something - you have a plan, or a series of goals or you're keeping your eye on a possible opportunity or building up to something. GC3 is mostly just a load of empty nothingness - habitable planets and resources are far between, conquest is too slow to be effective, economics yo-yo wildly with little discernible reason... It's just sloppy.
My overall impression is of a game made half-heartedly with the intention of copying a couple of successful 4X titles in the hopes of making some easy money. Stardock - I'm disappointed.
Meh. It's okay I guess.

I want to like this game, I really do. It's maddeningly addictive, and the customization adds quite a bit of fun to the genre.
But here's the thing, you can call it "open beta" or "early access", but if the game is developed enough to allow purchases with real money, it should be quite a bit more polished then Paladins currently is. They still struggle with balancing within the characters and cards. Sure, it's addressed on a bi-weekly basis, but there is still so much to do, and so many things ignored patch after patch.
The biggest problem to me is that they have no system in place to deal with hackers. Sure, you can report them, but there is no follow-up, and you have no way of knowing if anything has been done.
Worst of all, is that the casual matchmaking system is hopelessly flawed, and there seems to be little worry on the part of the Developers around fixing it; matches often end in complete blowouts because teams are so unevenly matched.
Until Hi-Rex takes a serious stance on actually fixing these matters, I can not recommend this game,

Fundamentally, this game can accurately be described as Hoard + Dota 2. It's pretty fun, in a simplistic sort of way, which I like. And it has good microtransaction policies, which is to say there are none. Which I like. There is only one thing purchasable in this game (aside from the in-game currency), which is a sort of season pass, and, honestly, it's very humbly priced and a good deal ($20 for all the content made thus far, the future content they make for the next year, and 4x money). If you like the game, buying that is definitely worth considering, and it's still not pay to win, for the developers seem adamantly against that sort of thing.
There is a good variety of dragons too, and it doesn't overwhelm you with the sheer amount like Dota 2 does. In this game, you play as the dragons (well, a guy riding them) and must protect the titans for the fate of the world. A lot more clear-cut than whatever story Dota 2 happens to have. Like, why the ♥♥♥♥ is a building called an ancient? An ancient is a really old living being, and those "ancients" are not living beings from what I can tell. They are buildings. And that word is mostly an adjective. Mostly. And on that note, there is a dragon that looks like a xenomorph!
But anyway, it could use some extra polish with the UI presentation, but it's not unsightly. Matches are quite short, which you may or may not like, but I think it is a good thing, personally. You can also really customize your abilities and strategy, since your choice of dragon nets you two abilities, and your choice of weapon nets you two different abilities. So you can mix and match. It also has a good tutorial, so I'd definitely say this a good introduction to the MOBA genre.

In its current state I 'can't' recommend this game, but do recommend "Dungeon Defenders" as a game, that would include DDE if it becomes as fully functional as I hope. This version is altogether broken and filled with so many poor choices it makes it hard to enjoy. This is sad because DDE is a fun game with creative elements but...
1. Mandatory online in order to play, whether solo or local. This is terrible for so many reasons. One reason is everyone starts in this small tavern hub and it's cluttered with people spawning and throwing spells around...its a mess. Shopping is difficult as you have to maneuver around to click the right spot not occupied by someone. The biggest problem of all is...I havent been able to play for an hour now as it won't connect. It keeps telling me matchmaking has problems...I DONT CARE, I DONT WANT TO PLAY WITH PEOPLE (outside my party and even then sometimes not at all). I paid to play a game not watch loading screens. mandatory online without ability to filter out people is just so strange and gives creedance ot those saying things like "mobile port", especially when in context of always online.
2. inventory and shopping is one of the other great detractors from fun. I played one match today and spent 45 minutes going through every piece of poorly indicated (stats) junk to find one or two better items. Multiple clicks to manage, lock/unlock items, then finding what is part of a specific set (from what I hear equipping everything of a set is a bonus), then guessing what each little icon indicates for stats/perks. If that wasn't a pain enough, to compare an item to an equipped you hover over it, everytime something happens (someone logs in, changes chars, chats...) the stats dissappear and you have to continue to hover....and only then do you get to compare it to one of the two weapons as it never shows stats for both. The loot drop system makes this even more of a problem because you collect sooo many items in one match, give us a few appropriate or decent items to choose from, we don't need 50 pieces of junk not worth much money or even useable by our characters every match.
New players be warned nothing is clear, not exhaggerating I literally mean nothing. It will not explain what anything means outside of the obvious, just make sure you play with someone who is in the know or good luck.
I kept the thumbs up in hopes this will be fixed, because the core of Dungeon Defenders no matter the version is fun and worth a play.

Stellaris is a good game that unfortunately suffers from the same mid to late game doldrums of other entries in the 4X genre.  I got my money’s worth from the base game and happy with it but feel that it is in need of substantial improvement.  No doubt most of the technical and gameplay issues will be remedied with future paid DLC’s and free patching as is Paradox’s way (rightly or wrongly).  In a couple of years when it has been patched and supplemented with DLC to the extent that EUIV and Crusader Kings II has, I can see it easily becoming the gold standard for the 4X genre that other games are measured against.  For now it is enjoyable, at least for the first few hours, if falling short in some noticeable ways especially later on.
Pros:
-A fresh approach to the genre.
-Several different ideological preferences, racial traits and planetary habitability makes for several combinations of unique races.
-Early game technology differences can make for different play styles and the lack of a tech tree makes technological research more interesting.
-The AI actually seems to behave in ways that are reflective of their traits.  I.e., Xenophobic species don’t like other species, democrats get along well with democrats and tyrants with tyrants and make alliances and federations along those lines.
-The graphics are pretty though the lack of variety in ship and stations designs is unfortunate (what an astonishing coincidence that all mammalian species design the ships that are almost exactly the same).
-Lots of random anomalies and event chains with divergent stories.
Cons:
-Diplomacy is shallow and interactions with other races are uninteresting or irritating.
-The Universe feels empty (yes, yes, I understand that the real universe is in fact mostly empty).  You can open the galaxy map and see a color-collage of dozens of empires, yet it still feels empty and lifeless.  Even your own planets seem to lack personality, uniqueness or any sign of life.
-Mid to late gameplay is weak and uninteresting.  Once the map has been explored and colonized, the game seems to lose any sense of purpose.
-A cap of five to seven directly managed planets seems too small and creating new sectors doesn’t add much to the game beyond correcting penalties fixed for having more than five to seven directly managed planets.
-Internal politics is useless except for the small perks offered by specific leaders.  Shouldn’t a democracy have a legislature with multiple parties?  Shouldn’t an oligarchy have a council and powerful aristocratic parties vying for control of it?  Even a tyrant wielding supreme power needs to keep some people happy.
-The economy feels simplistic and shallow.  EUIV had a lot going on in that respect and trade and economics is a big deal.  Not so in Stellaris.
