I'm not really a fan of the horror genre, let alone Japanese-themed horror T_T, but something about this game that makes it one of my all-time favorite shooters.
You play as the Point Man, a F.E.A.R. operative, sent to eliminate a group of super soldiers (replicas) and their leader, Paxton Fettel. You'd soon uncover that it was more than just a mission, it was a date with destiny.
I loved the concept of the story, but in my opinion, fell short on the story-telling factor. There were times that felt like fillers just to make the game seem longer and some times where I was confused at who was who. Even with all that, the story is pretty solid for an FPS.
The visuals are a bit dated today, but they did a damn good job at that time. The game doesn't rely on jumpscares to freak people out, but the way they build up the tension e.g. flickering lights, suspense music, things moving on their own etc. basically things that'll make your hair stand on edge, and the game did it well.
The gameplay in F.E.A.R. is honestly one of the funnest experience I've had in First-Person Shooters. Think Half-Life meets Max Payne with awesome ragdoll physics. The Slow-Mo ability partnered with the shotgun can be OP at times, but I'm not complaining :D I also love that it has a health bar, collectibles to upgrade your health and reflexes, and medkits which you can use to heal yourself at will.
Overall Experience: I love this game so much and is my favorite in the franchise. Plus, the ending is just awesome and will leave you wanting more. After beating the entire trilogy, I was kinda disappointed that the 3rd one took on a more generic approach. This game ironically managed to make me tolerate horror games, with the exception of Amnesia, Slender, Outlast and basically horror games that leave you defenseless T_T

This game was fun, HOWEVER, it felt like a huge knockoff of one of my all time favorite games, Journey. Now I realize that some of the people involved in Journey had a hand in this title, but that does not excuse it from being so similar that it borders on plagiarism. I wish I had more options than YES or NO for my recommendations as it isn't a bad game by any means, but since I don't, I favor the NO.
-Not really spoilers since you see this very early on, but if you're sensitive don't read on-
Strange, anthropomorphic protagonist? Check.
Shiny, bright way of travelling around? Check.
Hieroglyphics of a defunct civilization? Check.
Mysterious magical source that powers the world? Check.
The whole time playing this I felt that I had seen the moments, the shots, the environments, all done in Journey, and better as well. This WAS Journey, but underwater, with fish, and in my opinion, a LOT less soul. Although some scenes were quite nice and memorable, this game rarely got an emotional response from me, whereas Journey shattered me, stirred up the pieces, and put me back together. Everybody who says they cried playing this really needs to pick up Journey instead. Not hating on this game (okay maybe just a little bit), it WAS fun and I had a good time. However I'm very glad I got it on sale. This was just a slightly twisted carbon copy of a far superior game, trying way too hard to stir up an emotional response through weak metaphors and abstract images. Because this was so similar to Journey, I cannot recommend it. But if that doesn't bother you, it's still a charming game with wonderful art, ambiance and music to accompany. Good to kill a couple hours, but it won't bury itself in the cold husk that is my heart like Journey once did.

ABZÛ is a short but beautiful story driven exploration adventure. I wont call it a simulator, since I didnt feel being "simulated" into ABZU's underwater world due to the incredible immersion felt during the play. It's not an open world exploration, but that does not matter since you visit so many different places in a short term of time, that your mind gets flooded with fitting visual and audio effects and even possibly some emotions you might feel during the play.
I would not agree with people saying exploration games like this dont have a story - I am certain ABZU does and even though I can't know what the folks at Giant Squid (developer) wanted to tell us exactly, I got my own interpretation. My brain that normally functions in a more analytical and structured way, in ABZU, it took a more philosophical way. I will explain more in a spoiler section below, but before few more points about this rating:
you progress through the game in a more linear way with mostly clear targets. Besides that you have some smaller "ToDos" like freeing some fish pools, meditating or finding hidden sea shells that will make you explore the water world even more. Since the story itself is left to the phantasy of the player (you actually only perform actions to progress further and sometimes receive a visual effect as a reward), it is hard to rate the story, but I definetely enjoyed it.
Following part might spoil some of the "story" for you, it also might give you a completely different approach to this game, so decide carefully if you want to read it.
ABZU does not offer "combat" in its natural state, instead you "fight" for its world by progression in the game interacting with the world. It does offer a minimal challenge where you have to swim past some traps but it cant be considered anything serious since everyone will get past them fairly quick. The AI of the sea life is fitting the world, a lot of times following you but without disturbing your experience instead increasing the immersion provided by the AI.
This game has its beaty not in graphical detail for sure and offers rather a mix of "clunky" and "smooth" details. Still, there are places that looked incredible, not because of the details but the whole atmosphere made you dive in. The "drowned civilization" provided some mystical places, while the rest of the world is feeling alive with the plants and other sea life. The visual effects of interaction were in my opinion a bit overdone and could be limited. The only interfaces noticable during the gameplay were the few tutorial messages at the start.
The whole point playing ABZU is only to progress further in the linear world, leaving you not much room to play with besides exploration for fun and telling of the story. This game contained some really minimal side actions like swimming in a stream where you only had to control slightly the direction and try to interact with fish swarms on the way. Besides that the puzzles provided to progress in the game are absolutely simplistic and just to provide more visual impact on you. Another negative point about the progression in this game - it is absolutely short with ~2h story play time.
This is where the game absolutely shines. Exploring this beautiful underwater world while enjoying classic music is absolutely relaxing. Swimming with sharks, whales, octopus and other giant sea creatures, diving and turning with them is amazing. The sound provided from the sea creatures feels absolutely realistic. Still, in some more action filled chapters the music swifts and you get more tension to progress quicker, even though noone is chasing you. It is an amazing feeling to dive into ABZUs underwater world and immerse yourself with sea life while enjoying incredibly fitting music.
It is definetely worth to dive into this exploration adventure and immerse yourself into this sea world. Hopefully, you will also share some philosophical thoughts while playing ABZÛ.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

OK, 80 hours into the game, beat 3 full games, here's the review.
In a nutshell, Proton/Neutron torpedos + Vassalization = Snowballing to the end of the world, GG.
Early game is fantastic. Discovering aliens and sorting through anomolies really gives you the epic "Age of the Great Voyage in the Sea of Stars" kind of feeling.
However, Paradox needs to fix some serious AI logic, with FREE DLCs! Otherwise the single player game gets boring real fast, especially hurting when you don't have many friends to stay hours upon hours on multiplayer with.
1. AI like to build up shields when designing ships, which has no effect against Proton/Neutron Torpedos.
2. AI vassals send EVERYTHING to stick with your largest fleet when you go to war.
3. AI vassals never rebel no matter how "disloyal" or "dislike" they get with you.
4. AI vassals tend to go upfront and soak up all the damages with all the small ships they build. Invest heavily on battleships, vassalize 4-6 AIs, use them as cannon fodder, and you won't lose a single ship even against the ENTIRE Unbidden and beat them in one stroke.
The mid-late gameplay pretty much falls into this same pattern.

1. Get a fleet of roughly 12K strength, with battleships taking up at least 40% of it.
2. Load as many Proton/Neutron torpedos as you can.
3. Pick a neighbour equivalent in fleet size and crush him.
4. Vassalize him. Don't take his systems just so that he retains the production capacity.
6. Wait for a few years and let your vassal rebuild.
7. Pick the next target equivalent in fleet size to both you and your vassal combined....
8. A few more rounds, GG.
In the end, you'll just wonder when you have 100K combined strengths of 12 vassalized and very unhappy and disloyal AIs tailing your♥♥♥♥♥on your way to vassalize the 13th why they won't rebel all at once, crush your pathetic (literally) 30K worth of fleet, carve up and share your empire among themselves.
...what is this? why is this?

Final Fantasy VIII is a bit ridculous.
No, really - this game had a huge impact on me when I was 12 years old, so when I saw it up for grabs on Steam I acted fast. And you know what? Holy cow is this just goofy as hell. Of course, we should all be willing to admit that cliches are what FF is all about, and that's not a bad thing. It's just that VIII attempts to be a deconstruction and the story is frequently tripping and falling on its own "and now a twist!" approach that gets a tad bit tired by the "disc 2" segment. That being said, I do enjoy the  settings as they're consistently well-rendered and imaginitive. I'd expect nothing less of the team from this era.
The characters? Pretty damn bland. There's a certain backstory that ties in importantly, but it doesn't really explain why (with the exception of a couple) these characters are all so ridiculous. Only Squall, the mainest of main characters, has a degree of depth and even then it falls into borderline-woe-is-me nonsense. The models are certainly worth snickering at (to be fair, that's the age showing).
As for the gameplay itself - it's pretty fun! It's also pretty easy to manipulate if you know what approach to take with the juncitoning system. Putting the right spell on the right stat makes things so quickly breakable that it blew my mind how much trouble I had as a kid. Still, it's fun trying in mix and match what element you're going to smack what enemy with. And that Eden summon never gets old. Stuff like this is why I've avoided strategy guides ever since I turned 14. It's going to be fun if you don't know exactly what item does what function.
In summation, this is certainly a game that can be fun to play if you've never played it before... Just know your tastes.

I've played The Settlers since the Amiga original (Go go, Beau Jolly Collection!), and there's a very fine line between a good and bad Settlers experience. The core to it is whether you can easily see your Settlement growing, and whether there's interesting challenges facing you to overcome, either limited resources or enemy Settlers you must outpace.
Here... You have stationary, fixed enemy encampments that dont do anything. And confusing tutorials, badly defined mission targets and inconsistent translation. And long, long, LONG, LOOOOOOONG waits before resources come in.  There's literally nothing to do but click a few buttons, set up your construction queues, and come back later to see if you've enough resources to clear one more bandit camp or build one more item.
It's not a game, it's a system of timers masquerading as a game. I wasn't hit by the Level 7 bug, but you also can't see your Settlers consistently (they don't seem to carry resources from storage to production very often), the keyboard camera controls often don't work, right clicking even once brings up the Flash options menu that you can't easily get out of... for such a simple browser game, it's horribly coded.
There's a quest for adding people to your friends list. Of the 4 who have shared it with me, only one seems to have played beyond their first day in game, and even he might have quit by now... I've not, yet, because I'm a sucker for the Settlers and every now and I kind of like logging in now and then to set the little numbers rising; but I'm also not blind. It's a terrible game, and unworthy of it's classic pedigree.

It's like you're logging in to do your job, not playing to have fun.

This game really, really sucks, and I wish these types of games would disappear. Luckily, it's free, and you can get your requisite 3 Steam Trading Cards from it. I'm going to wait my 2 some odd hours for them, then uninstall, and never look at this game again.

So, from where should I start?
This game has good stuff, and TERRIBLE stuff.
First of all, the story: The ♥♥♥♥ is this? The ♥♥♥♥ is that? Why is that even possible? Does anything make sense?That's all you will tell to yourself while you play. Most of the main plot is just stupid. Not only that, the 6 main characters are in most part, not good.
Squall is emo, and won't say anything interesting until CD3. Zell only thinks about being important (Spoiler, he was only important in the Garden assault and when the Lunatic Pandora was ♥♥♥♥ing arround), Irvine is a Sniper who's afraid to shoot. Rinoa only thinks about Squall while Squall thinks how annoying she is. Quistis is only important at the start of the game, then she won't say♥♥♥♥♥♥ Selphie is...Weird. The only good characters are, infact, Seifer, and the Laguna Crew. And these last three, you will only play as them like 5 times in the entire game. I even dare to say that if they made the game about Laguna, and leaving Squall and the rest as side-characters, it would been way better.
Now, the battle system. Is broken beyond repair. The idea is okay, but badly done. There's magic everywhere, most monsters are weak but have a unlimited pool of spells you can steal and steam without stop, and those spells make you stronger. That's right, magic is useless in combat, but you can take those spells and apply them to stats. At the second CD, you can already get spells like Ultima (Shumi Village, I think it's called), and by grinding a bit, start dealing 9999 damage with Squall. IN THE SECOND CD. There are also way too many Summons, and making them free to cast is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You can spam them non-stop in the first and second CD because most monster will get affected by them, while in the CD3 and CD4, most of them are useless (The two only good summons are Devil and Eden).
Now, does the game have anything good? Well, it does. The side-quest are great. If you decide to ignore the main plot, and start searching the world at the CD2, you will find some interesting stuff that can be worth your time. Some places are well done, like the Tomb of the Unknown King, or the Ruins of Centra, both of them have one or two Summons hidden on them. The last CD, that is pretty much the final dungeon and battle is also well done, with a good addition: you lose the ability to save the game, or even use Phoenix down on a KO character until you defeat some hidden enemies in the castle. Some hidden bosses are also great, but with the broken fight system, turn out to be easy (beating Ultima Weapon in two-three turns seems like a joke).  Some people even say that the love story between Squall and Rinoa is the best one, but I think that's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Now, want to know the best part? Square Enix released the game with the same problem as FFVII in PC: Broken sound and OST. Everything sounds bad. Good thing the comunity made some patches for that, since Square Enix hasn't done crap yet. Lazy madafakas.
There are good things about FFVIII, but I don't suggest picking it up, unless you really liked it, and miss it. The ♥♥♥♥ man, the game even has cheats. WHO NEEDS CHEATS IN A GAME THIS EASY!? What I do suggest you, is save your money, and wait for Final Fantasy IX. Square Enix will make a port to PC, like this one at some point, and even though IX was a bit easy (but not broken as VIII), it's way better in pretty much everything.

Not sure why this is getting such bad reviews. This is everything Dungeon Defenders 1 was, and more! Player instanced loot and chests are an amazing addition, saving the grief from ninja looters in public games. Plus, currency is Gold instead of Mana, meaning you can spam your Mana in-game without having to worry about the cost. Blueprints are available as drops for crafting which is aother great feature. The micro-transactions in-game are strictly for cosmetic items, but that's to be expected in this day of Microtransactions. A lot of complaints were also targetted at the fact that you apparently can't create Private games, which isn't true. It may be a recent addition, but since I bought the game there is an option to create a private game just for you and your friends - You're not forced to play with random players. For £4.50 for Dungeon Defenders 1 owners, it's well worth it. It's just a fresh take on the game with some great additions, balance and bug fixes.
The negatives are the fact that the game features it's own Always-Online DRM, meaning you're relying on their servers for a good connection - I'm used to this having played Diablo III for a long time. Plus, the UI is a clunky and could do with some work here and there, but it's nothing game-breaking.
Don't let all of the overracting negative reviews put you off, I'm sure glad I didn't. The game has been out for 5 days, there are still some fixes they have to make and they're working fast. I have faith!
This game will definitely whet my appetite until Dungeon Defenders 2 comes out, and I'm pretty sure they have a few more features still to come!

DDE is what I would call the "game of the year" version of Dungeon Defenders. It constantly finds new ways to impress me as I play it, making the original DD seem obsolete in comparison. All the characters are unlocked from the get go, so you don't have to buy them seperately. Mana, chests, and all items are seperate to each player, so you don't have to fight over them. New item slots have been added like trinkets to use during combat such as Flash heal, Instant tower repair, and even a holy hand grenade to deal with pesky skeletons. A new currency has been added called coins, which is used to upgrade your items instead of mana. There are orb like items which grant you increased exp, loot drops, and loot rarity which apply for the entire map and for everybody, further encouraging team play. Towers now have stat numbers available, so you can see exactly how your skills affect them. There have been some downsides however, such as now your armor appears on your character at all times, which makes you look gaudy if your armor selection clashes. I would like the ability to turn this off. The summoner no longer has minion points but uses defense points like everyone else, however has been buffed to compensate. The tavern is a public hub, which lags everytime someone joins for a split second, making inventory management a bit irritating. Overall though, I would recommend this version over the original any day of the week. If you've already bought the dlc for the first one, maybe only get this for 5$ or if the new features really appeal to you. There is one last thing to mention, and that is the playverse overlay. I mention it last because it's barely worth mentioning as it doesn't really add anything to the game, and account creation takes a few seconds at best. Don't let it dissuade you from this awesome version of a good game.
EDIT: The mana that drops from enemies is not shared and is able to be picked up by anyone. I'm sorry for misleading you on that fact. Chests and items still remain as being unique to you and you alone

I'm not really a fan of the horror genre, let alone Japanese-themed horror T_T, but something about this game that makes it one of my all-time favorite shooters.
You play as the Point Man, a F.E.A.R. operative, sent to eliminate a group of super soldiers (replicas) and their leader, Paxton Fettel. You'd soon uncover that it was more than just a mission, it was a date with destiny.
I loved the concept of the story, but in my opinion, fell short on the story-telling factor. There were times that felt like fillers just to make the game seem longer and some times where I was confused at who was who. Even with all that, the story is pretty solid for an FPS.
The visuals are a bit dated today, but they did a damn good job at that time. The game doesn't rely on jumpscares to freak people out, but the way they build up the tension e.g. flickering lights, suspense music, things moving on their own etc. basically things that'll make your hair stand on edge, and the game did it well.
The gameplay in F.E.A.R. is honestly one of the funnest experience I've had in First-Person Shooters. Think Half-Life meets Max Payne with awesome ragdoll physics. The Slow-Mo ability partnered with the shotgun can be OP at times, but I'm not complaining :D I also love that it has a health bar, collectibles to upgrade your health and reflexes, and medkits which you can use to heal yourself at will.
Overall Experience: I love this game so much and is my favorite in the franchise. Plus, the ending is just awesome and will leave you wanting more. After beating the entire trilogy, I was kinda disappointed that the 3rd one took on a more generic approach. This game ironically managed to make me tolerate horror games, with the exception of Amnesia, Slender, Outlast and basically horror games that leave you defenseless T_T

Widely considered to be a true innovation of the series, this game tops the list of a lot of FF players - for good reason. Whilst not my own personal favourite, there is a lot here to love.
Although looking a little jaded by today's "modern" standards, back in the day the graphics were thought of as a technological breakthrough; VII is the first true 3D game of the FFs. It may be a little blocky now, but if you really take issue with that then there are plenty of nice-looking mods for the PC version.
At its heart, FFVII is an underdog story, telling the tale of a ragtag resistance facing a corrupt organisation (and later on, something even worse - a threat to the entire planet, coming from a villain who is without a doubt the most recogniseable of the series.) The characters are (mostly...I'm ignoring the existence of Cait Sith for the purpose of this review) a likeable bunch, with mixed backstories and rather good development. Cloud comes off as a little dull and bland to begin with, but he comes into his own later on. Occasionally the plot may take a little turn for the confusing and wacky, but it's largely resolved to a clean degree (anything that isn't is explained more in-depth through the spin offs.) The villains are very entertaining, and in some cases you really end up hating them - which is the point, naturally.
The Materia system is a nice touch - any character can equip any skill, and the more you battle the more powerful these skills become, and the more often you can use them. There is a real sense of progression and accomplishment.
Of course, as expected by now, the music is another accomplishment. This game probably has my favourite "standard" boss battle theme of the lot, except from maybe that of VI. The town themes largely have their own feel (an East Asian theme for Wutai, a tribal one for Cosmo Canyon, etc.) Also, "One-Winged Angel." Those of you who have played this before know that I need say nothing else.
This is the "entry game" for a lot of players, and it does give a very nice feel of what to expect from the other games. It wasn't afraid to take risks with both technological boundaries and storytelling, and should be admired for that reason alone. As I mentioned - not my favourite, but no less of a gaming classic.

This actually is a really great value. Not only does it have the first game, but it also has both expansions as well. Weird, as they don't really advertise it that well.
Storywise, I would say that the original and Perseus Mandate are the best. They have a good mystery, high stakes, but no characters you can really get invested in. Armacham Corporation tried to make military clones, their psycic (and psycotic) leader went rogue and now you have to clean up the mess. Then it turns out the leader, Paxton Fettel, is looking for something. Then he finds it, and HOLY CRAP WHAT THE F*** IS THAT AND WHY IS IT EATING MY SOUL?
If I said anything more, that would be spoiling it.
Backing up the story are the scares and the gunplay. The gunplay is, at its core, a very good tactical shooter, with bullet time stapled on. The reloads are way too fast in my opinion, but the marital arts moves and ability to watch grenades explode when they hit enemies in slow motion more than makes up for it. The weapons start off standard. Pistols. SMGs. Shotguns. Assault rifles. Oh! Dual pistols! Now I can pretend to be the hero in a John Woo film! Then, at around the second or third level, you find my personal favorite: The Penetrator. It is a weapon that staples enemies to walls. However, if that doesn't interest you, there's the 15-round rocket launcher that fires in 3-round bursts. Or the MP-50 repeating cannon. Or a laser that literally strips the flesch from an enemy's bones. The expansions have even more weapons that can get even more creative.
After that, you might have to ask "If it has all those weapons, how can it be scary? Scripted jump scares?" Well, there are some of those, and they are actually kind of good because they're combined with the right atmosphere. However, they don't just rely on those. Some of the enemies are actually pretty frightening, like these ghosts that drag you into hell and eat you alive. Then there are the sequences where the walls fly away to reveal new walls. Then monsters are everywhere. Then, you're falling into darkness. When you wake up, the villian has you locked in solitary. Or there's the scene that makes you afraid of ladders for all time. Even if you aren some kind of unscareable badass, you'll have to admit at the end that they did try.
There is some stuff that's kind of bad about the game. The art direction was horrible. I mean, look at the screen shots! Even when it first came out, I was never impressed by the graphics. Also, as its so old, sometimes you need to give it some help to get it running. However, it is all definitely worth it.

To be honest, this is one of the best games I've ever played so far.
Initially, I was rather skeptical of how this game will appeal to me as I was never a big fan of hack & slash games and the slow and mundane plot in the first few minutes almost confirmed my suspicion. Thankfully, things caught up quickly and soon I found myself lost in the world of Dust.
The artworks and soundtracks used in this game are top-notch from the start to the end. I thoroughly enjoyed the aesthetical aspects of the game and I applaud the developers for putting their efforts. The story as a whole was excellent and the characters are among one of the best written ones I've seen.
You'd need to play this with a gamepad though as playing on a keyboard may not be ideal in numerous fights and can give a different (or perhaps  a less enoyable) experience as a result. Anyway, there is also a pretty good variety of combat skills to choose from and you will be able to use them in various situations such as searching for treasures or going against different enemies. It's a rather big world out there so do try to explore all parts of the map.
The only negative I could think of were the lags during the cutscenes. I've already experienced it twice during my playthrough and I had to reload a save and complete the level/fights again to watch the cutscene once more. Not a potential game-breaker but they can be annoying.
In a nutshell, I highly recommend people to try this game out. I got it during the sale so it was definitely worth the money. However, even without any discounts, its price is still rather acceptable for a game of its calibre. An amazing game that will give you a whole lot to think about when you play it.

Doom 2 is a direct sequel to Doom, being released in 1994. Or you can count it as a stand-alone expansion pack. It doesn't change much.
Also, Steam version of Doom 2 comes with Master Levels, which should appear in your library. Well, at least this is what people say, I got whole bundle of Doom instead. It's quite a mixed bag of fan-made levels.
Now, about how Steam version of this old game was handled. As bad as Ultimate Doom. First, DOSBox was configured in such way that it casues heavy lag to many. It can be fixed by editing conf files in the game's folder to use "Opengl" instead of "ddraw". Doesn't enable Steam overlay for some reason though.
When you launch the game, it gives you a cchoice whetever to use classic control or WASD with mouse. Game also uses SoundBlaster instead of MIDI for music. If you want to configure your own control scheme or chooce another sound device, then tough luck, Setup.Exe was removed from files. Instead you will have to manually configure cfg files, putting numbers and figuring out which keyboard button corresponds to what number.
Now, as noted, Doom 2 feels more like expansion pack then a totally new sequel. It still uses same main base of game, same weapons, monsters, engine. Instead of changing what already was there, it adds more to it. And seeing that Ultimate Doom is awesome, it's not a bad idea at all.
What in general Doom 2 does is to buff up the challenge. It inroduces new enemies that fit "medium-tough" category that was lacking in Doom 1, including Reverants, skeletons who shoot rockets (some of which keep following you until they explode), Hell Knights, lighter version of Barons of Hell who were bosses of Episode 1 in Doom, mini versions of Spider Mastermind, who should be stun-locked in pain state with Chaingun, and even everybody's hated Archvile, who acts as occasional mini-boss. Few others as well, all bringing bigger variety and danger to otherwise weak common enemies of Doom 1. It also puts common enemies like zombies and imps into big crowds quite often. But it's all done because player got a new powerful weapon, getting buffed as well: Super Shotgun.
Super Shotgun isn't just alternative to Shotgun in a game, it's as good as becoming main weapon and replacement to shotgun, even taking over same slot. It delivers a wide pack of punch, with triple more damage than shotgun, being almost like a close-quarter rocket hit. The only small flaws is just slightly longer reload and that it uses two shotgun shells as ammo, but shells are so common in Doom 2 levels that it doesn't become issue at all.
All it means that you can easily take down crowds of common enemies which could be quite an challenge in Doom 1, changing balance. It also makes some other weapons, like Berserk fist, Chainsaw, Pistol and Shotgun pretty much useless by comparison, so much for balance between weapons. You sure would use chaingun only to stunlock Spiders and such.
And Doom 2 bring new, bigger and more complex levels, all 30 of them. More confusing too. Supposedly, the action now takes place on Earth, but seeing how level design is still highly abstract and non-sensial, you wouldn't be able to tell that. Outside of very few "city" levels, that are huge space with cubes. And well, to be honest, level design isn't on par to Doom 1, especially when it comes to looks. Doom 2 levels is mostly concentrated on being challenging and giving it "gotcha" moments, with many ambushes, they have more space to walk around too. And some of the ways that you are supposed to solve the puzzles aren't always obvious. You are supposed to shoot the door instead of using it, you know. Or having to drop down the acid to press the button that you probably don't see from above. It's not pleasent. And yes, it still has moments where game forces you to run over acid, making you take some damage. Or just teleport into small room with four imps from all sides.
Speaking of unpleasent, this game looks worse than the first Doom. The color pallete choice is quite ugly and the rendering of light doesn't help in this case. The usual variety of bright color (that was working excellent with lighting that was making them darker) is gone from most levels, after Map 4 you the only kind of texture choice you will be seeing is dirty ones. Black metal, brown wood, brown bricks. Even new monsters use brown as main color. And they say that WW2 shooters were the most brown ones. So yes, it looks worse.
As for music, it still delivers. Less memoriable pieces, but it does give give game soem personality. Exploration in hell of these brownness. But yes, music is excellent, not all rocking, but still, has some evil sound to it.
Secret levels also should be mentioned. Even back then iD Software started to reference to their older games, and thus all two secrets levels are Wolf 3D levels, even including blue nazi enemies from there, which happily get killed by mightier Doom guy. And yes, unlike BFG Edition on Steam, these ones weren't censored.
Mutliplayer doesn't seem to be implented in Steam version, so you should use Zandronum source port for that.
So yes, I can recommend this game, as it's still an awesome FPS. Compared to Doom, it's much more meaty, killing dozens, and core gameplay got improved with new enemies to challenge you in various ways. On other hand, level design, both in looks and maze-gameplay, took a hit and aren't on par with original.
But we talked about game itself, as there is another phenomena of Doom 2: Modding. Doom2.wad is a file that is often used as a base for almost every mod, and Doom modding is where most people go, making use of simple engine for their maps or even dream games
If you want to mod or enjoy them, then you should get this one for sure.
And then you will be able to play many various mods, whether it's Brutal Doom (that changes gameplay and then you have people thinking that Doom is about tons of gore and other teenager/new-school stuff), some other spammy mod, complete conversions or a multiplayer mods, like Zombie Horde (because zombies HAVE to be everywhere), All Out Of War 2 (Like that C&C FPS game, 1v1 me) or Ghouls Vs Humans...
Wait, GvH was good one. No shame in overplaying that one.

Eternity is a remake/remaster of the original Dungeon Defenders. While it's got some changes (some of which I'd prefer to have remained unchanged), the core gameplay is the same. The game is rebalanced, equipment generation has been rewritten, and a lot of complaints have been addressed. Only a few maps were taken out, and new maps have replaced those ones, and there's a new campaign to be discovered. I don't like how the tavern is shared now, and I wish you could still customize character color, but other than that, complaints are few and far between. It's effectively the Game of the Year edition for Dungeon Defenders, and those who loved the first game may not even mind starting all over from scratch. Especially since the new servers and the Playverse are all Trendy. So right now, in the beginning, is most likely the worst they'll ever be.
Edit:
As the game is being updated, I feel I should update the review. The game continues to be a fun and exciting experience, obviously better with friends. Apart from the occasional hiccup in server activity and a few glitches here and there, everything is running smoothly, and I'm very happy with the game. It's getting better, and I still recommend it.

J. Jonah Jameson was trying to blow up Moscow with a giant laser built into Theodore Roosevelt's head on Mount Rushmore, which wasn't good at all, because that would destroy my peace treaty with Doctor Frank N. Furter, whom I desperately needed on my side to help me defeat Lieutenant Sulu.
Red Alert 3 is an RTS game, set in an alternate timeline after the Soviets went back in time and rewrote history (again) by murdering Albert Einstein. It’s even more ridiculous than it sounds, and serves as a worthy sequel to my all-time favourite RTS, Red Alert 2. It’s fun, campy, and often hilarious, while still serving up slice after slice of the Command & Conquer we all know and love.
There are three campaigns to be played through: Soviet Union, Allies, and The Empire of the Rising Sun. Each campaign consists of 9 missions, and it took me about 23 hours to beat them all. When you’re done with that, there’s custom Skirmishes and the Uprising expansion to play through.
Between missions you'll be treated to good old FMV sequences starring well-known actors, including a couple of surprise cameos. These serve to convey the story, relay your mission objectives, and make you snort Pepsi out of your nose, especially when Tim Curry or J. K. Simmons is speaking.
The soundtrack is a blast, and Frank Klepacki, the musical genius behind the rocktronic compositions for the original C&C through to Renegade, returns once more for three tracks: Hell March 3, Grinder 2, and The Red Menace, which steal the show above the rest of the game's music. Pity he didn't compose the entire soundtrack.
But RA3 suffers from two flaws: Co-op, and hand-holding. These two elements work together to steal away your freedom. Each mission is designed to be played with a partner, but since EA have shut their servers down, you’re stuck with AI co-commanders. And before each mission, you’re given a step-by-step battle plan, telling you to go here and do this and move there and capture that.
Gone are the days of freedom to approach a mission in any way you see fit, which would allow for multiple replays and different experiences. Now you’re stuck with every step laid out for you, and an AI blundering alongside.
I used to find immense enjoyment in taking my time to complete a mission, as I slowly crept up the map, expanding my base, capturing all the enemy’s buildings, and then crushing him at the end. That’s no longer possible. Missions are too structured and linear, and my co-commander is always running ahead, blindly sending in troops and mucking up my strategy.
There were moments when my co-commander completed objectives without me while I was busy elsewhere. Why even bother playing when an AI is gonna do the work whether you want it to or not?
Then there were other missions when my co-commander failed abysmally at his task, and I didn’t have time to swoop in and pick him up before failing the mission. These were the hardest of missions, and it felt nice to have to actually work to complete them, even if there were only a few.
But at the end of the day, I had so much fun playing this game that I couldn’t help but forgive it for its shortcomings. Red Alert 3 is glorious and zany in all the right ways. What it lacks in strategy and challenge, it makes up for by simply being awesome, and it’s a fantastic throwback to past Command and Conquer games.
Now if you'll excuse me, 'I am escaping to one place that hasn't been corrupted by capitalism—SPHACE!'
TL;DR: Forced co-op can be a nuisance, and there’s too much hand-holding, but Red Alert 3 is great fun nonetheless.

if you've heard all about this game: it's as good as you've heard, you should get it and play it.
if not, ditto the second part.
what
does is skewer the "Farmville etc." business model of games that monetize on all of our need to have some casual game in our hands, our dependence on the screens that we carry everywhere, and most of all our willingness to pay real money to accelerate silly resource-farming in-game stuff that really is just an endless cycle of... whatever, more in-game stuff.
except the skewering is wrapped in a
game of that type: all you do in this game (till the very end) is throw stuff that you buy into a fireplace in various combinations, and burn the stuff; burning stuff gets you more coins to buy more stuff, and throwing in combinations unlocks new catalogues of stuff, etc. (see how it's satire?) But that action is pretty fun: the fireplace is fun, the combo-searching is fun, the
as things go up in flames is very fun.
then all of this is interlaced with an emerging narrative that pretty much just sheds light on what's clear from the start--that "something is very wrong here"; that this thing that you're just sitting there staring it isn't really making you happy or healthy. While that's not surprising, the narrative is very engagingly and tensely teased out, so that I found myself playing long after I was tired and the fun-action of throwing stuff into the fireplace had lost some of its luster, because I was really invested in the story. Which has, thankfully, an elegant and optimistic conclusion.
Lastly, the music is terrific; deliberately evocative and sweeping and terrific.
It's a great game that's a commentary on gaming and a great game in its own right. The whole thing will take you like 1/15th of the time you'll spend in a big AAA game, and you might get more out of it.

TL;DR Summary: This is the game all you Master of Orion fans have been wishing for through all the disappointing other 4X space games since MoO2. It is not "Crusader Kings in Space." Also, get the Nova Edition for the arachnid species instead of just the base game.
Deep Thought Review:
I put in 50 hours before writing this because I wanted to make sure I wasn't just being an eager little fanboi and hopping on the thumbs-up bandwagon. I'm happy to say that it has met and exceeded all expectations I had, and, according to those more familiar than I am with Paradox, this game is only the beginning; free content updates in addition to DLC will be provided in the future. I have played Crusader Kings 2 for a fair number of hours, and while it is a fine game, I had no desire to own another CK2 that was just set in space. So, naturally, when a friend told me about Stellaris, I was less than enthusiastic. I am delighted to admit I was not only wrong in my assumption, but in point of fact, this is the absolute best 4X Space Game since Master of Orion 2. The only similarities it has to CK2 are the use of sectors (think vassals in CK2) and the jaw-droppingly beautiful artwork during loading screens. I actually regret not buying the super duper elite package or whatever it was that gave the art book, because it's that lovely. I did buy the Nova edition, however, and the arachnid species is definitely worth the extra $10 assuming $10 doesn't break the bank for you. I will now go through, topic by topic, to give an idea as to what to expect...
Graphics:
The best of any 4X Space Game so far. The procedurally generated galaxies are beautiful, the ship combat looks incredible. Once you get into some of the more unique weapons, it's really fun to watch them fight. As previously mentioned, the loading screen art is just amazing and is worthy of a coffee table book or a series of posters. It's better than most of the stuff on Digital Blasphemy.
Interface:
There's been some (admittedly meritous) grousing about certain aspects of the interface, however this should not be a deal-breaker for the buyer. The few aspects that do suffer from clunkiness or lack of features are already in the works for free fixes and upgrades by Paradox. Even the parts that need a bit of work are still navigable if one puts in the effort to learn the ins and outs. Minor problems aside, the interface is still much better than most other 4X Space Games I've played before (and I've played most of them), and in some cases, it's prettier. It's certainly a heck of a lot easier on the eyes than the Master of Orion 3 interface. You won't find a series of ugly spreadsheets, but rather an often intuitive collection of tabs. Almost everything you could possibly want has a mouseover explanation of what it is, what effects it has, and how much it requires in resources, and so on.
Custom Species Creation:
Yes. Not only does this game have it, but of all the species available, there's something like 20 animated sub-species to choose from for your critter avatars, each of which can be further customized for stuff like hair, feather, skin, color, clothing style, etc. The auto-naming schema presents you with several different options per species that range from the spartan insectoidlike names "Ika'Zre" to something that sounds like it strolled out of London "Reginald Davies" and follows suit for things like ship names, planets, etc. Not only can you choose any schema, regardless of your species, but during the game just about anything you own (from characters, to planets, to ships, etc) can be renamed if you don't like it. The same goes for the ship styles. You might have a mammalian species, but if you want to use reptilian ships, that's just fine and dandy. A wide array of different flag choices, custom colors for the flags, is a nice cherry on top. My only complaints are the limit of 4 traits that can be chosen, and what feels like a limited number of traits compared to Master of Orion 2. However, when you consider that in addition to traits, you also choose 2-3 ethos, and a government style, and leaders allow you to pinpoint further bonuses to government, ships, science, or what have you, then you begin to see just how rich the species creation process really is.
Learning Curve:
Stellaris has a very well-balanced learning curve. it's not nearly as hard to fathom as Crusader Kings 2, but still retains the richness of a great empire builder without being downright Civ-Rev in over-simplicity. Just when I think I've learned all I can about the game, something new clicks in my mind with regards to strategy, or outright suprises out of left field.
Gameplay:
The game plays like a pausable variable-speed RTS, much like Crusader Kings. One of the best differences from CK2 is, however, that you can wage war on someone without having to pursue casius belli first. And upon declaration of war you can set your terms immediately, should your opponent wish to surrender. Another lovely difference from CK2 is the fact that you can use this method to take over star system after star system without having to jump through an enormous number of hoops or luck rolls like with CK2. Combat is very easy to wage (though not necessarily easy to win, unless you have wisely chosen your fleet loadouts). Everything handles very smoothly overall. I would like to see some more uses for the strategic resources, but again, Paradox is already working on this, so I have nothing to worry about. As should be expected of any good 4X game worth its salt, Stellaris is infinitely replayable, and just seems to get more fun with each new game.
Multiplayer: Yep. It has it. And, unlike several games out there, you can use your saved custom species to play with, AND if someone is late to the party, they can join in (with the host's permission) after the game has already started. Otherwise, the MP experience is just like the SP experience, only your opponents are (hopefully) a bit more challenging.
The AI: The AI is nothing particularly noteworthy. It is neither terrible nor great. However, Padarox is also working on additional improvements to the AI, which is very encouraging.
All in all, you will find this game is worth every single penny, and will only become more so as Paradox addresses the few issues the game does have, and releases new content as well. If CK2 is any indication, this game is going to grow in scope a hundredfold before things even -start- to slow down on it. Two Thumbs, and Both Big Toes, UP!

What can I say that hasn't already been said a bunch of times:  Just get the damn game!!!!!  Dust is what a fun 2D platformer is all about.
1)  It has a story.  It doesn't break new grounds, but most games don't.  With that said, it is told not only well, but at the right pace.  It doesn't drag, nor does it race along.  It has a well though out plot, and an ending that will stay with you.
2)  It makes you explore.  It isn't the most complicated map, but it has enough visit and revisit spots to keep those of us that like to find everything happy.   There are several spots on map and moving to and fro is quick and painless.  The places themselves get progressively more difficult to initially spot where hidden treasures are, but not mean spiritied or impossible like some games I could name.
3)  Voice acting.  It doesn't stand out at all and from me that is the greatest compliment.  I can't stand VA that is so over the top, or the opposite that is just so god awful that you want to turn the sound  off and read subtitles.  The VA meshes perfectly with the story.
4)  Artwork.  It is a nice blend of cartoonish hand painted with effects mesh.  It is also a perfect fit for the feel of the game.
5)  Combat.  Combat is easy to as hard as you wat to make it with the different combos, but definitely forgiving.  It's not meant to be a brutal test, but it offers enough of a challenge to be satisfying.
6)  Fun Factor.  So many platformers have zero replayability, especially story driven ones.  You finish and move on.  I played, replayed because I missed a couple of achievements, and then played again just to enjoy.  This is a game that will stay in your library as an old friend that you will just have to re-visit every once in a while.
Overall, I would say if you are looking for a hard game to challenge you this is not the one.  If you are looking for an absolute joy of an experience do not pass up this game.  I can't wait to see what's next from the dev's!!!!!  Cheers!

Dust: An Elysian Tail is an simple but fun beat 'em up RPG that pays high attention to detail. You can really see the amount of passion and dedication that went into this game.
1) Combat is a lot of fun. Dust is quite literally a tornado of death and it's really entertaning. Most enemies are just a matter of keeping up a combo and mashing buttons, but every one in a while you encounter an enemy that's a fair challenge and requires some strategy (the weird insects with razor legs in the haunted mansion come to mind). 2) The leveling system is actually very well done in that the choices make an
difference in gameplay. There's no "10% increased damage" B.S. here. Level ups sometimes
a stat early on so it feels worthwhile to take your time, explore, and gather xp. 3) The crafting and shop systems compliment each other well and are worth using. It's not just a matter of gathering gold and buying new items. You get blueprints from killing enemies and opening chests and then you gather materials from other enemies to craft items. However, rather than just having to grind for materials, you can buy them from stores, the catch being you have to sell the store at least one of the material first to add it to their catalog. I actually really like this mechanic. It makes you work for upgrades without making you tediously grind. 4) The animations and designs are just beautiful. The guy who made this game was primarly a designer, and man, does it show. This game has one of the best visuals and atmospheres of any game I've ever played. The environments are varied and really draw you into the world. This game is great as an art piece alone.
1) The lack of autoregeneration or any way to easily heal is quite frustrating, especially earlier in the game. At one point you're tasked with heading down a spiked cavern to unlock a sliding ability, and I managed to make it but with so little health left that I could not hit the spikes even once on the way up (and neither the game's autosave nor me had the foresight to keep a save before I had gone down so I could retry after buying more food for health). So I was stuck for like 2 hours trying to get out of the caverns without dying. Lack of autoregen can be done well, but the game needs more than one autosave file and possibly a place to heal back up. 2) Most of the central conflict revolves around the evil caused by General Gaius and his genocide of 'Moonbloods', but for how important the game makes this out to be it dedicates little focus, time, and information towards anything about the race or the conflict. Most of your time is spent exploring locations indirectly affected by the war rather than dealing with the actual problem. In addition, it's unclear who the enemies that you're constantly fighting actually are. The first boss sorta says that they're Moonbloods(?) but everyone else just calls them "monsters" and they definitely don't look or act like the Moonbloods that you eventually encounter.
This isn't so much a complaint as me being dismayed. I love that this game tackles mature themes. I love that the bosses you encounter and Dust himself aren't just black and white evil or good. But I'd be lying if I didn't say I would have enjoyed the game more had the developer taken the plot and characters to a more complex level, especially when it comes to General Gaius and the whole Moonblood conflict. However, I realize that this isn't a problem with the game but that it was designed to be kid-friendly and I'm just not the target age group. I could easily see this as one of my favorite games had I played it in my childhood.
While Dust: An Elysian Tail has some problems with its plot, it more than makes up for them in gameplay, setting, and design. Younger gamers will probably love this game, and others can still find much to enjoy. 8/10

I'm a bit biased, having played FF8 on PC when it first came out. But despite having a terrible computer that took 30s - 1 min to load between loading screens, I actually played it through to the end at that time.
This version is true to the original. Perhaps too true. The install size is huge (for a game this old). The original game came on 4 CD's, and the size of this release looks to be unchanged. I've noticed no changes in the actual game, aside from the chocobo world and magic boost that run from the launcher.
FF8 has an interesting story. It's not a masterpiece or anything, but it does make you wonder about what's really going on with the gardens and the political upheaval. Grit your teeth and bear with Squall. His attitude WILL make you angry for about half of the game. This is unfortunately something that most people won't do. I won't provide anything further on the story, just know that things get much more interesting once you get deeper into it. Just don't get bored with what used to be the first CD of the game.
The junction system is just as confusing as it ever was. Fortunately, with magic booster, you can save a TON of time and get your characters through the slow part of the game rather quickly. You'll get 100 of the core spells right off of the bat on every character in your party. This makes learning the junction system a bit much easier, and saves you a few hours of fighting monsters for hours just to draw 100 magic for every character in your party. The rare spells still require you to find draw points and strong monsters to draw from manually, so it hasn't turned into easymode.
There are a lot of GF's to find, and not searching them out will cost you a major advantage. Some can only be drawn from bosses before you defeat them. Always draw magic from bosses. There are some difficult side quests and powerful item and GF rewards for doing them.
This game gets harder as you get stronger. If you level all of your characters to 100 and fully outfit them with maxed GFs and junctions, the bosses will seem insanely strong. But they're still well within your power to beat. It prevents you from outleveling everything and barreling through the game. If you're lower level, they will be weaker as well. It's surprising how well the game actually adapts to your growing stronger.
TL;DR: Fun game. Slow start. Confusing junction system until you figure it out/study it. Plenty of play time, some pretty cool summons, spells and characters. Limit breaks are pretty sweet. Adapts to your level so it's never super easy to barrel through. Interesting story, if a bit slow at the beginning. Plenty of junctions, abilities and limit breaks to optimize your characters. You'll need to put some thought into your elemental and status offense/defense to make boss fights more manageable.

This game was released on my very birthday, yet over 20 years later would be my first time playing it.
Okay, so if you liked the first Doom, Doom II is basically everything Doom was, except bigger and better. The first thing I noticed about this game was that there were more textures, and a LOT more enemies. Levels have more depth to them, are much larger, and more often than not have well over 100 sprites onscreen. Sitting back in '94,this would've been pushing the limits of PCs, no longer being confined to small corridors and just a handful of enemies at a time. The only downside was the story, but the action-oriented gameplay perfected by ID software makes up for it, who seem to have had an everlasting obsession with the idea of being sent to Hell.
Doom II also added 2 player co-operative (not present in the Steam version) building upon the 4 player deathmatch mode, supporting up to 16 players on one server! Basically, this game gives you a whole lot more of what the first Doom gave you.
I'd give it a 9.5/10 considering the time it was made, it only loses points for story.
Small Disk Space usage and low CPU usage as well. I recommend this game for anyone that loves Strategy and Simulation game, and the point is this game is FREE TO PLAY.

A uniquely eerie experience of horror and rampaging violence.
F.E.A.R. is one of the best games ever made. Back in 2005, this game set the benchmark for high-end graphics and performance (I remember saving up my money from lawn mowing as a teen just so I could afford a $300 graphics card to play this one and only game, only to find out that I then needed a new CPU). Yes, at the time, F.E.A.R. was one truly ambitious beast. And for all of its ambitions, I believe it succeeded and even set the bar in some areas that have hardly been matched by anything in the gaming industry since.
The story might be a little ridiculous, but horror stories usually are. A little girl named Alma with abnormal abilities was horribly wronged years ago by Armacham corporation and so she is back from the dead and exacting her revenge on these people through her own horrifying supernatural powers as well as using Paxton Fettel (one of her sons). Fettel telepathically controls soldiers (Replica) of which you will spend a big duration of your time fighting throughout the story as you (a F.E.A.R. operative) investigate and try to suppress these supernatural happenings.
No, this not a game where you have a squad of guys to help you. This is horror. You are on your own. Not many games make you feel truly alone in the dark and fighting for your life quite like F.E.A.R. does and this is all thanks to several factors: the darkness, sounds, the masterfully grim soundtrack, dream sequences (you'll see what I mean). The settings are empty warehouses, empty office buildings, empty science facilities, all complete with gratuitous amounts of blood and dead bodies. You navigate your way through each interval with the constant gloomy ambience and the sounds of true silence. That is until you meet the Replica forces or when you start having nightmare sequences as reality comes back and puts you at another door. Sure the environments can get repetitive (as was one major gripe with the game people had back then), but this little complaint is overshadowed by that fear that something terrible is around the corner. The game does what a true horror game should and that is that it provides a dark, foreboding atmosphere that can leave you in the clutches of fear, and then it also has some jump scares (which seem to be the only "horror" element of today's games like Resident Evil 6 and Dead Space 3).
The firefights. Ah, the violence in this game is top-notch. It is bloodier than anything that came out in 2005 and the fights sure do escalate quickly (think Hotline Miami). Also, not only were the graphics praised as one of F.E.A.R.'s highlights, but the AI was as well. I will go on record to say that F.E.A.R.'s AI IS BETTER THAN 95% OF ANY SHOOTER SINCE 2005, even today as I write this much delayed review in the beginning of 2014. No other game had me more paranoid for where each enemy was at or where they were headed than this work of art. The Replica soldiers will not only take cover and pop up to shoot, but they will advance, throw grenades, and even go around obstacles to come up behind you.
It is quite an achievement for F.E.A.R. to have such intelligent AI that still plays as if it was developed yesterday. On the other hand, it is very sad that the games today still offer the same single player gunfights of computer enemies taking cover, popping up to shoot, maybe tossing a frag, repeat. It seems no progress has been made in developing thinking, reasoning computer-controlled enemies as F.E.A.R.'s vicious soldiers for today's FPS games, and this was almost a decade ago. But I digress. The AI is very smart and it does more than your typical Far Cry 3, Battlefield 3, Call of Duty simplistic copy and paste enemies do (and yes, I have played these other games and enjoyed them too).
Admittedly, playing this years later again, it does seem dated. The visuals are not the benchmark anymore and the scares can feel predictable now. But of course, this is only to be expected for a game as old as this, so really this is nothing to fear.
So overall, F.E.A.R. is a very unique and overwhelmingly satisfying shooter/horror experience that you do not want to miss (and if you like it so much, check out its EPs, Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate). In my opinion, the graphics still hold their charm (but this could be the nostalgia talking), but some may be put off by the old visuals in this graphics-demanding world. Oh well, F.E.A.R. is not for them. No, F.E.A.R. is a demanding game that will give you a good challenge while also throwing you through a rollercoaster ride of thrills. From the terror of wandering in the dark and listening to story-related voicemails in an empty, bloody office cubicle to the frights of seeing Alma as angry as the angel of death-F.E.A.R. delivers!

The worst problem is the handling. I think I figured out what the main 'cause' is, and this seems systemic of all Milestone bike games I've played:
The tyres float across the track. You can see this even when not moving. Just lean left and right and look at the back tyre, it glides right and left respectively across the surface of the track when it should remain in the same place. This effect only gets worse at higher speeds, with the tyres gliding left or right by almost a whole foot when leaning.
This isn't just the contact patch moving to the side of the tyre, its the whole tyre sliding as if there is no contact patch, and its not a power slide (it happens all the time), and it seemingly affects all 'modes' (pro and the rest).
Overall this make the bikes horrible to handle.
It's like there is no physics between the tyre and the track surface, as if the pivot point when leaning is somewhere in the middle of the bike instead of at the contact patch of the tyres. This is absolutely not a 'simulation', it's an arcade game (and, imo, a very flawed one at that).
Also, some of the rider animations/'physics' are super messed up (like a crazy 'superman' somersault your rider will do during endos).
And annoyingly there appears to be no practice or quali sessions, so to practice new tracks you have to go to Time Trials, which involves going through a bunch of slow loading menu screens.
The other issues I had are mainly UI related:
- Terrible loading screens throughout the menus.
- Split time between riders not shown in-game.
- Best lap time not shown in game.
- Being unable to change controls in-game (have to exit out to the main menu first).
- Being unable to un-assign controller buttons (so nothing is mapped to it).
- Being unable to assign multiple buttons to single actions.
- Unnecessary confirmation screens, like having to click proceed instead of backing out after a race, or having to re-confirm your bike (when you select a race your bike is already chosen, then get a loading screen, then have to choose your bike again - even if you only have 1 bike, then get another loading screen).
- Game trying to 'sync' and failing, causing an error message you have to confirm. You can switch 'sync' off, but it re-enables itself each time the game is restarted.
- Having to manually re-purchase enhanced oil after every single race.
- A second or two delay between model updating when changing visual stuff (like helmets, leathers, bike parts etc), making custimising a time consuming process.
- Key prompts always being for keyboard keys, even when using a controller.
Some of the above may seen like nit-picking, and it is, but each little inconvenience adds up.
Maybe some of the above has fixes and I missed it, but if I did its not obvious to me where it is.
A real shame. So close to being a great game, yet so far.

QUICK SUMMARY
Nice fun game. Not the prettiest to look at, but fun from start to finish. Some of the most amazing AI ever created. Probably worth $5 at most.
GRAPHICS 3/5
The game is from 2005 and it shows. However I believe they have aged well, especially if you crank up all the feature to the max, since it never really becomes bothersome, although a bit repetitive on it's color plate. Even when it was originally released, graphics where never meant to take the forefront though, so don't expect a big 2005 showcase. They are simply OK.
STORY 2/5
Again, for the time, mixing horror with military FPS was a bit of an inovation. The story also simply serves the bigger game picture, providing a good excuse to mow down clone soldiers, get a scare or two out of the player, and come up with some weird scenarios. However, you can't help but feel the story never reaches it's full potential, being content with only feeding you bits here and there. Even worse, a good chunk of explanations are left to audio recordings which are barely audible and force you to simply stand and listen when you are all pumped up and want to continue.
MUSIC AND SOUND 2/5
Not much music to talk about. It's creepy and barely noticible. Never stands out but subtly sets the atmosphere for either creepiness or action. Sounds simply fitts as it should, guns sound the way guns doo and some shrieks here and there can be chilling to the bone (but only the first couple of times).
GAMEPLAY 4/5
If anything, this is where the game shines the most. The controls are tight and the actual shooting is as satisying as shooting could be. The graphics, sound effects, animation and everything in general come nicely together so every shoot has the appropiate punch behind it. There's some good weapon variety and destructible stuff littered around to make firefights more flashy. AI is one of the best I've ever seen for a game though, and was years beyonf it's time. Enemies coordinate, use actual attack tactics and react as a human player would. So good is the AI that even at the lowest difficulty level, where enemies are weaker, have poor aiming and you can apparently take more damage, you can STILL be surprised by the AI and die.
REPLAYABILITY 1/5
Not much to do once you beat it except trying to do it again at a higher difficulty level. I'm not much for multiplayer so once I finished it I didn't touch it again.
If you like bikes, and bike racing, this is a GREAT GAME. Though you absolutely need a controller for this game on any kind of difficulty. Super fun, and quite accurate. TENOUTTATEN.

I do recommend this game: It's something new, the battle system is engaging and there's lots of neat things to do ingame. Many puzzles, the controls are nice and the art is good. Enough to keep you playing for some time.
Pros:
Lots of action
Engaging gameplay
Questing system
Many difficulty settings
Challenges to look forward to
Cons:
It gets repetitive, the enemies aren't strong, but there's TONS of enemies. Enjoy lvling up every other screen after killing 1,000,000 enemies.
Some places and enemies were put in the game just to annoy you. They don't offer any challenge, the challenge is to keep yourself calm and steady to get through the hordes of stupid enemies and hazards.
The story... is cool and all, but it's not that original.
Dialogue is uninspired. Really, this is a missed oportunity. It could have been so much better. Everything is a big cliché.
At the start, you're begging for some gold to get some health recovers. There's no way to heal outside of regen items (which you only get far into the game and even then it doesn't heal a lot) and, well, potion, or the assortment of random food items that drop from enemies an chests. At the end, you're swimming in gold and it's pointless.
Overall:
Yes, I did say there's a lot of bad things about the game. If you're looking for a masterpiece, clearly this isn't your game, but it's still fun to pick up and play. It's definetly a good game with some variety, lots of areas to explore, challenges and puzzles that will keep you playing and many neat things you can do. I would really like to see a sequel that improves upon the game and irons out the flaws.
Verdict: Buy it, of course. It's a good game for the price and it will keep you entertained for a couple hours. I've finished the game and it was fun. I don't regret buying it.

Given where FPS games are todat, FEAR is a nice refreshing dip into what used to make FPS games so good. With the original 10 hr campaign plus both expansion packs, you get your moneys worth with this game.
Pros:
+Challenging AI: The enemy soldiers won't just stand around and wait for you to play dentist and fill their teeth with lead, they'll come to you and try to bash yer fokin 'ed in m8. Plus, they are extremely accurate, even on Moderate difficulty.
+Good and Scary bits: Sometimes you'll have a vision on a genuienly spooky Silent-Hill esqe room which can definitely creep you out, and Alma appearing around corners or as soon as you climb a ladder can give you goosebumps or make you cry out and make your family wonder what exactly you're playing...
+Lengthy Campaign: Like I mentioned earlier, the story is around 10 hours long (or maybe I'm just bad) and has some challenging areas that require you to do some thinking to advance to the next area.
Cons:
-Not very "survival horror-y": I was hard pressed to find a moment in the game where I wasen't completely over-saturated with health kits and extra ammo (which is saying a lot since you can carry up to 10 spare med kits), which can take away from a lot of the horror since there isn't much of a scare of the player dying, just seeing something scary.
-Story falls apart at the end: Little spoiler alert here, Alma is referred to several times as a "powerful psychic being". But that doesn't really explain how she start calling forth GHOSTS toward the end of the game. Perhaps this is explained in a sequal, perhaps not. But there just isn't a lot of clarity on how she or the other villian have power that are completely non psychic related
But these are just a few water marks on this shining, beautiful window of a game. And as long as you stand at a healthy length, you won't even notice those water marks anyway.

Before you read this review, here's a bit of a caveat:
I'll begin by writing about one of my latest experiences, which is the one that stuck out to me the most. Not only did it exemplify everything that I enjoyed about this game, but it also drew everything I found wrong with it out into the light as well. I'll annotate it in a quote. If you don't care for that sort of thing, you can skip down to the actual review.
On to the actual review. I will say that, as someone who enjoys a mixture of sci-fi and strategy games, this was a very satisfying scratch on a long-standing itch. So many promises were made on that front within the last couple of years, but most ultimately fell short. That's disappointing, considering I like the idea of liberating myself from game elements involving a historical context and running wild with something that hasn't happened yet. This one made it - for me, at least.
Stellaris does a lot of things right. In the early portions of the game, and even some of the late, the game is crafting stories for your emerging empire. These stories change. From playthrough to playthrough, even if you're playing the same species, the context and history of your civilization will never be the same. The government, policies, and diplomacy will change with the dynamic climate this game can offer. That can be a very beautiful thing.
However, where this game falls, it falls hard - very hard. The mid-game slows to a drudging crawl. I would find myself involving my empire in other civilizations' affairs, such as separatist movements, just to try to keep the dynamic feeling alive.
Overall, I recommend this game to a very specific type of player. If you don't mind reading a wall of text from time to time, which would explain why you're reading this, and you have a passion for sci-fi and strategy, it is a
game. The devs have some work to do, but supporting them with a purchase isn't such a bad thing. The game is definitely worth playing, but from the drudging mid-game to frustrating AI and diplomacy, this game can be better - a lot better.

A stunning masterpiece, a truly magnificent experience.
You see, when I first saw this game I had just finished Ori and the Blind Forest so my expectations were a bit high I'm not going to lie but saying that I was blown out of the water is an understatment. This game excels in every aspect from rich atmosphere, immersive gameplay, heavy and well executed story telling, absolute stunning soundtrack and loveable characters that you can't not expect to fall in love with.
The story follows Dust, a warrior who lost his memories. He wakes up in a beautiful forest there he finds the knowledgable sword Ahrah and the adorable Fidget. The 3 of them set off on a journey to the memories of Dust's past and uncover some of the dark secrets behind said past, while also helping people along the way.
The way the story is executed is spectacular, it all starts seemingly simple but it all wraps up nicely at the end. On the way we meet many diverse and unique characters which all add flavor to the mix.
Combat is amazing, not once did I find it clunky or boring, just pure hack n slash through hordes with diverse weapons and combinations while maintaining a low level of strategy involved.
Art and Soundtrack are off the charts, the visuals never felt like a reskin of previous areas and each monster was different in its own way, Soundtrack is rich and immersive and really sets the tone for the adventures you'll face ahead of you.
I'll give this game a well deserved 10/10, while short it was a really beautiful experience and a game that I will treasure in my game library. Absolute masterpiece.

This game is incredible. Imagine a nature documentary about marine life with no words, with story elements similar to that of the game Journey.
ABZÛ is more of an experience rather than the traditional game if you ask me. Sure it has typical gameplay features such as achievements or collectibles, but those are only secondary. What makes this game stand out is the sense of wonder you experience as you explore these beautiful sceneries and creatures.
-You gently glide through the coral reef with curious colourful fish coming closer for a better look at you. Suddenly you see a pack of dolphins swimming by, chittering playfully. You follow them into a strong current which you swim along, the music score growing more intense and intriguing. Many fascinating and beautiful creatures can be seen hitching a ride, some of which are large enough for you to ride on like the humble sea turtle. The current starts to go upwards with you and the dolphins increasing speed. As the music builds up, you breach the surface. You're met with momentary silence before returning back to the water. A calmer melody starts playing and you've discovered a kelp forest with peaceful mantarays.
This is an example of what this game is about. The game is linear and has an interprative story with details scattered around the world. You are free to explore each area to your leisure and see the subtle but powerful interactions the sea creatures have with you.
Though the concept may seem simple this is by no means a boring game. ABZÛ takes you through a variety of areas with different experiences to be had. If you're satisfied with one area it should be clear where you need to go or what you need to do in order to progress to the next one.

Stellaris has been great fun so far. The sci-fi nerd in me absolutely loves the atmosphere and exploration in this game. It reminds me of the feeling the original Mass Effect gave me, an open unexplored unknown. With a great sound track to boot.
Civ V is the only other 4X/Grand Strategy game I've sunk a lot of hours into and you can draw a lot of comparisons between them. If you've played Civ the tile working system will just make sense, the income system will make sense and so will the technology + research system.
Stellaris does a great thing with the research system by randomising it. In Civ V you basically go down the same few routes every time. But in Stellaris it's mostly impossible with a randomised 3 choices for each tech type being generated. And what happens when two of those technologies you really want come up at the same? You have to make a tough choice. With the inclusion of specific researchers who have specialities and a finite life span you have to manage your leaders properly.
The custom ship designer is another awesome addition. You have to choose between rail guns, lasers, missiles or other weapons you’ve unlocked for your arsenal. You have to pick the right combination and then make sure you have enough juice to power it all. Deciding between extra shields or extra armour may depend on your neighbours and the kind of guns they’re packing. Combat can be as in depth as you choose to make it.
Overall Stellaris in it's current form is extremely fun and extremely varied. Currently there are only two victory types: Conquest and controlling 40% of the galaxy. But the journey to get there is exciting and different every time. Don't forget you can spend ages designing you own race from traits, personality, cosmetics and their home world. My review is only just touching on some of the best mechanics in the game, but there is much more on offer.
