Fight your way threw waves of monsters invading earth in this PC cult classic. Doom II has set the way for PC gaming since the 90's and it's still one of the most if not THE most cult classic PC game ever made.
Game play: 9 out of 10
Being a game from the 90's doesn't stop this game from having some of the best game play for it's time. It may not be Call of Duty, or Half-life but it has really solid game. Doom II is the “Guns! Guns! Even more guns!” kinda of game play. Doom II is a simple a first person shooter, you move, you shoot, you get keys, to unlocked doors and find hidden stuff. Nothing over the top. However back in the 90's it didn't matter. It how many guns can I use to take out these monsters.
While Doom has it fair share of weapons, It has a great design of monsters monsters and more monsters! Everything from your basic zombie soldier, to huge♥♥♥♥♥cyber demons ready to rip you apart at a moments notice. Each monster has there own style of game play. Some has simple things like a shot gun, or a melee attack, Some have more magical powers like fireballs or setting you on fire, while some are Cybernetic enhanced demons using rocket launchers or having a spider body with a chain gun on it. Whatever the case maybe this game doesn't sell you short on the fun factor.
Doom also uses the color key/door system. Meaning you have to search around from room to room finding these keys to advance in each level. In Doom II you do not have to really Aim at the targets it pretty much aims for you by using an auto aim system since you can't really look up and down and such. Pretty much means you can be standing on top of something and shoot something below you and not even be aiming or looking at it. There are ways to change this of course but please read blow for more info on that.
The maps are very well design, with each one having a different theme to them. However unlike games now of days one level leads into the next which leads into the next one Doom doesn't really have a set “level” design on how you go from one map to the next map. It's pretty much like an episodic tv show where you have the “flavor” or “theme” of the day. Here it's more so the “Flavor” or “theme” of the map.
There are a decent amount of power ups, You have Berserk mode, Radioactive suit, full map, and more. Each adds a little bit more to the game play element which adds even more fun to the game as it is.
Story: 5 out of 10.
Doom it's self has a good story... if you read the novels and such however the game it's self gives you a more simple smaller version of the story. There isn't much there to really work with. It's mainly about demons and monster that have came from hell that are invading earth and it's your job to stop it. Short and simple. This game isn't about the over all story as it is. It's mainly about kill everything that gets in your way.
Graphics: 9 out of 10.
Of course the graphics are pretty bad compare to games now but for it's time they where amazing. It's a 3D game with 2d rending sprites. Every NPC and items around the maps them self’s are 2D sprites that “follows” you. Pretty much whenever you step left or right it will turn and keep looking at you. While there are times when the graphics of NPC's and items can look flat by the way you are looking at them, but doesn't effect the game play.
The over all graphics are set to be more Gorey/ Horror themed with a dark gloomy setting. While a lot of maps focus on a certain theme for each one, you can get the over all feel they where going for.
Music: 10 out of 10.
This music in this game is amazing. For being midi files it is top notice. The music is midi version of song like Master of Puppets by metallica to other big named bands. The sound track will have to coming back for more. Doom has one of the best sound tracks in history for video games.
Extra: Mods and such:
Til this day Doom is the most modded PC game ever. People are still making maps, skins, game mods, movies, and more much. This show you have much love this game has gotten over the years.
Now there are some mods that I personally use that i recommend to people to enhance your game play better if you so choose.
The mods I use are as followed:
Brutal Doom
Zandronum (single player and online).
Brutal Doom takes the game and makes it even more Gorey and well brutal. This enhance the game play by adding more weapons, Alt fires for every weapons, Finishers, Harder mode settings, and much more. If you looking for one of the best mods out there for doom check out Brutal Doom mod. After installing this mod I can't go back to the basic doom game anymore.
Zandronum, is a mod that allows more enhanced game play to let you have free camra look, to allowing you to aim and not use auto aim. Allowing online play with friends or random people you meet or find on servers. There are a lot of different one like this out there. I use this one because it was recommended by Brutal doom for a better game play.
Other mods:
Skin mods
Maps
Guns
Power Ups
Game modes
These are some of the thing you can find, Skins for weapons, or NPC's. Maps from doom style maps to playing inside walmart or McDonalds. Guns, so when you get tired of the normal guns you can just add more! I mean who doesn't want the Rick Roll BoomBox gun Mod? Anyone? Anyone? Even more power ups and more game mods. There are so many mods out there that there are web sites dedicated to just that.
Cheat does:
There are a decent list of codes that can be use to give you powers like God mode, All weapons, Noclip and such. I don't recommend using them unless you have play this game so much that you're looking to spice things up a bit.
Cheat Engine:
This is a bit off for what I am reviewing. However I have used cheat engine to enhance my game play allowing more than what you can do in the game it's self. There are options in game that allows faster monsters, and respawning monster which is can be hard enough as it is. However I like to turn speed hack on and give myself x2 speed while giving the monster even more speed. It adds more of a challenge to the game and I don't recommend this to everyone unless your looking for a challenge.

Now, I have played motorsport racing games prior that not only include a Nintendo classic but MotoGP 13 as well. In my personal opinion, MotoGP 13 is probably one of the best racing games out there. I personally do not think Ride gives it a run for it's money but does have a few perks of it's own. Ride is a motorcycle racing game that entices players with it's various bike selection and decent
. The selection of bikes ranges from naked bikes, historical bikes to super bikes each with their own sort of feel (regarding handling) and power. I start off with this point as it's the most influential part of the game as all the big names from Triumph, Kawasaki, Yamaha to KTM are all here. The rest is give or take - alright at best.
The
scheme is decently immersive and accurate at certain times. There is the manual tuck that the player can choose to activate on top of other manual options (brake assistance and transmission settings). The braking system feature for example has two separate buttons for front brake and rear brake. Cool because that does make sense. The issue here though is the handling and braking throughout the turns (or before I should say). That "stiff" feeling of turning or tapping your stick to the right or left is still there. Instead of punishing the player for letting go of the left stick (turning control) too quickly, the rider slowly comes back to an upright position. Even if you're fooling around and tapping the stick left and right, it still has a choppy motion instead of a smooth movement.
I understand the player is flicking the stick but as I've said, the game should punish sloppy or quick movements that would break a trajectory. On top of that, the turning doesn't feel as rewarding as it should. In MotoGP 13, taking a turn at a high speed and keeping that lean was what made it epic. Here, it doesn't really feel like you're doing anything epic at all, just another turn so to speak. What I will give the game credit for though is coming out of a turn. This feels like it was done right especially with higher powered bikes. If the player begins to floor the gas (so to speak) the bike's rear tire will start spinning out of control and slowly start putting the player at risk. The effects of this are cool and do make for split second decisions in how to recover. Problem is even if you do sort of muck up, the rider will go through a small animation looking like he's falling then recover given you did your part. These animations feel stiff and don't move with the bike as well as are sort of misleading. The crashes in MotoGP 13 felt a lot better than they do here (according to my personal contrast)! I think the animations could have been more relative rather than putting the same one for every situation.
The
as I've mentioned are really good and the visuals and details on the bikes are quite excellent. Problem is games not only have to look good, they should also play well. The bike designs will make you stop for a moment and especially enjoy any modifications you've made to the bike (which can be seen). Then there are small things like nothing reflecting properly off the mirrors that could drive someone nuts. Some tracks it seems as though they put a repeating loop onto the mirrors. What is nice is that you'll see your player switching gears and letting go of the gas. The
are relatively good (not the best) but does give the player something different to listen to when switching bikes. Crash effects more or less sound the same and could have used a bit more diversity here (even though it's not the point of the game)! The music in-game is alright but I would argue the menus sound better.
So why MotoGP 13 over this game? I feel that overall the other game albeit doesn't have as many bikes as Ride, still provides for a better motorcycle simulation game than this. If they made Ride more of an arcade sort of racer and mixed some simulation points into the game, I feel it could have gone better. What is completely appalling is the fact there are SO MANY LOADING SCREENS! Why does it load to a confirmation screen to show my bike once I've already chosen which bike I want to use!? Makes no sense! If you want more diversity in bikes, you may like this game. I play MotoGP in first person when I race whereas here I find I'm stuck playing in 3rd due to things not feeling exactly right. The game does boast a nice career mode where the player can take part of many world tours with different sets of bikes. On top of that, the maps are pretty good and could give the MotoGP 13 maps a run for their money. Also,
. This can be disastrous in key moments. Additionally, the leader boards don't seem to work either.
I will recommend it but you'll definitely have to be a bike/race enthusiast to really enjoy it.

Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 is a real-time strategy game and obviously the follow-up to Red Alert 2. While I absolutely loved Red Alert 2 I can't say the same for this title.
First, there are some things Red Alert 3 does well. The storyline is as cheesy as it comes and that is what fans expect and love. It is also great that the game has actors like Tim Curry, George Takei and David Hasselhoff, who really seem to enjoy performing the B-movie-like storyline.
However, Red Alert 3 has many problems compared to its predecessor. The units have a cartoonish look to them and look like child's toys. Many of them look so over the top that it is just ridiculous. Also, the weapon's effects and sounds don't convey any impact, further reinforcing that impression.
The gameplay itself comes off as very hectic because units cannot take any damage, no matter the unit type. Even the biggest tanks and ships give off the impression of being made of paper. They get destroyed within seconds leaving no room for actual micromanagement. The problem is that the game wants the player to micromanage since every unit has some sort of special ability. There is not much room to use them however and I would have preferred not having them at all except the toggled abilites. The units' AI is also pretty bad. If the enemy has a slightly longer range they will refrain from retaliating and just get destroyed. Anti-air weaponry is extremely underwhelming in this game. Often building turrets don't seem to make no sense at all. Even if you have a solid turret setup there is just not much use in defending since there are so many units that can destroy your base from huge distances. If the enemy uses aircraft they will still destroy your base because there is no defense that will keep them from destroying at least one target in every run.
Red Alert 3 features a computer controlled partner in every campaign mission. This partner can be replaced by a human player and while I appreciate the idea of making the whole campaign able to be played coop it just doesn't work. The computer partner is highly unreliable in its performance. In some missions it will basically win the mission by itself with you struggling to keep up with the pace and in some missions it will be literally useless. During the last mission of the Rising Sun campaign my AI partner was actually unable to even defend its own base. When I didn't continually sent units there my partner would just be annihilated within a few minutes. All of this while I had my own problems, being hammered by airstrikes, superweapons and ground troops.
The campaign should come with a trigger warning (pun intended) because all missions are heavily built around triggers that you most of the time cannot see coming. However you need to be prepared for them because if you're not you have basically lost. There is no reaction time since the game is fast and units and buildings cannot withstand any damage. It's bad design if you can only win by being able to see into the future. If you have run your head into the wall a few times you will know the triggers and it basically becomes a minigame of avoiding those. One of the worst examples is from the Rising Sun campaign. At one point you will be confronted with a huge enemy fleet and have to hold out until your battleships arrive. When they arrive it is still not enough to destroy the enemie's base but you absolutely need to destroy all their shipyards. Why you ask? Because the AI will start producing an indefinite amount of aircraft carriers and since anti-air turrets are horribly weak you will lose.
Red Alert 3 is not a horrible game but is has so many shortcomings compared to its predecessor that I cannot recommend it at all.
P.S.: If you liked the Tanya from Red Alert 2 you will be severely disappointed.

One of the best Call of Duty games out there! It has an amazing campaign, great multiplayer, and amazing zombie maps!
Honestly I would have to say this: DON'T BUY THE DLC UNLESS YOU'RE INTO ZOMBIES! Don't get me wrong the Multiplayer maps are greta in this game. The entire game runs of dedicated servers for Multiplayer and most if not all the DLC servers run off the official Treyarch servers. So why is this a bad thing? NO ONE PLAYS ON THE TREYARCH SERVERS! It's sad really. If you're really that interested in playing the Multiplayer DLC maps then get it on console. Anyway, another problem with this game is that dedicated servers have a lot of stupid rules, a lot of Nuketown 24/7 servers, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ admins for the most part. Another big problem is that not a lot of people play the Wager Matches (Gun Game, Sharpshooter, etc). In general it's pretty hard to find a match of Multiplayer due to the fact not a lot of people actually play the PC version of Black Ops anymore. Which is a shame considering this is one of my favorite COD games!
Anyway enough of me talking negative, let's talk about all the postitives! For one thing, these have amazing and memoriable maps! They're pretty basic due to the fact the entire game is set around the cold war. Some maps you may recognize such as Launch, Nuketown, Firing Range, and Stadium. The guns feel great and are fun to use! And just about every server is a Ground War server so it makes it even more fun! The more people the better right? If I'm not mistaken, this is the first COD game to introduce controller support for the PC. I know. I know. Call of Duty: World at War had controller support by typing in console commands, (Honestly I'm not sure about Call of Duty: 4 Modern Warfare due to the fact I don't have the game as of making this review) but it wasn't as easy as Black Ops. Black Ops gives you the controller options right at the options menu easy as that. Sadly, if you played this game for a long time on console (not me) there is not auto-aim assist what so ever. It's easier to use the Keyboard anyway so whatever. One last thing I have to say is that this is the last Call of Duty game to allow mods. The mods are really fun in this game! There's a mod called Zombie Annihilation mod to pretty much you can play Infected in Black Ops, A reverse and Hardcore Gun Game, and many more! The mods are only for Multiplayer however and not for Zombies, but it's still fun to mess around with!
Overall this game gets a 9/10. I highly recommend it!

Given where FPS games are todat, FEAR is a nice refreshing dip into what used to make FPS games so good. With the original 10 hr campaign plus both expansion packs, you get your moneys worth with this game.
Pros:
+Challenging AI: The enemy soldiers won't just stand around and wait for you to play dentist and fill their teeth with lead, they'll come to you and try to bash yer fokin 'ed in m8. Plus, they are extremely accurate, even on Moderate difficulty.
+Good and Scary bits: Sometimes you'll have a vision on a genuienly spooky Silent-Hill esqe room which can definitely creep you out, and Alma appearing around corners or as soon as you climb a ladder can give you goosebumps or make you cry out and make your family wonder what exactly you're playing...
+Lengthy Campaign: Like I mentioned earlier, the story is around 10 hours long (or maybe I'm just bad) and has some challenging areas that require you to do some thinking to advance to the next area.
Cons:
-Not very "survival horror-y": I was hard pressed to find a moment in the game where I wasen't completely over-saturated with health kits and extra ammo (which is saying a lot since you can carry up to 10 spare med kits), which can take away from a lot of the horror since there isn't much of a scare of the player dying, just seeing something scary.
-Story falls apart at the end: Little spoiler alert here, Alma is referred to several times as a "powerful psychic being". But that doesn't really explain how she start calling forth GHOSTS toward the end of the game. Perhaps this is explained in a sequal, perhaps not. But there just isn't a lot of clarity on how she or the other villian have power that are completely non psychic related
But these are just a few water marks on this shining, beautiful window of a game. And as long as you stand at a healthy length, you won't even notice those water marks anyway.
*Non-analogy version*: Game iz gud, bai it.

+Game is a little aged, but it doesn't take long at all to get into the rhythm. Looked great in 2005 and it still holds up today, provided you're willing to overlook a few minor flubs.
+Guns all feel solid. The lineup is a little generic, between the standard pistols, automatics, explosives, and the token rifle/railgun, but for the most part it all holds up -- everything behaves, sounds, and shoots the way you would expect it to. However, the shotgun could definitely use some balancing and the lack of an option to go without dual pistols was a little disappointing.
+Story is alright. Nothing groundbreaking and it's hardly the focus, but it holds up without any plot holes.
+While the environments feel empty, the atmosphere is AMAZING. The soundtrack does a good job of sending chills up your spine, SFX cues are in all the right places, scenery is designed well and given all the right touches, and the game never does the same scary trick twice. I was left jumping and screaming on multiple occasions, and this is coming from someone who hasn't flinched at a scary game or movie in years.
++++The physics engine. Oh mah goodness. Chairs rotate when bumped against, lights flicker when shot, and there are even dangling wires that can be flicked around. The biggest moment for me was in a conference room with a projector hanging from the ceiling and, get this, SHOOTING THE PROJECTOR MADE THE IMAGE IT WAS PROJECTING JUMP AROUND AS WELL. HOW MANY GAMES HAVE YOU SEEN THAT DO THAT?! IT'S ALMOST AS GOOD AS WORKING MIRRORS.
-Environments feel empty. They try to cover this up by having blood dripping from ceilings and making it look like everyone there was already murdered by the time you got there, but it doesn't feel at all like a situation involving terrorists or whatever they try to cover the plot up with. It's excusable since it's an old game and they didn't have the memory to have such sprawling worlds, but you still feel there was a bit more that could be done.
-Enemies get old very quickly. You go from generic soldier to generic soldier to OH ♥♥♥♥ INVISIBLE CRAWLER to generic soldier WITH ARMOR, etc. etc. The only saving grace is near the end, which is largely a cinematic experience which is also a bit of a negative. The level design does a lot to mix it up and keep it interesting, but it's not totally foolproof.
-Shame about that sequel tho.
I just have to mention the reflex/bullet time mechanic as well. I feel it was largely inconsequential. You find plenty of powerups for it and all it was really good for was being a safety net, at least to me. You don't need it to complete the game, nor are you punished for using it or leaving it alone. It's a convenient way of explaining why the player character is such a bad♥♥♥♥♥and capable of dispatching an entire army of psycho-soldiers, but beyond that it's just there because bullet-time was a cool thing to have in 2005. It's not a pro, nor is it a strike against it, it's just there.
I'd give it an 8/10.

One of my favorite FPS games that I have ever played. It is a horror game, so expect a lot of gore, creepy moments, and jumpscares. The combat in this game feels and looks amazing. You have a slow motion ability that gives you the edge on your enemies. It makes the gunfights look very cool when you have bullets whizzing by your head and you are running up to things to deliver a shotgun blast into them and they explode into pieces. The grenade effects are one of the most amazing things I have ever seen in a game. When they explode (especially in slow motion), the particle effects from the blast look awesome. Try throwing them in a group of enemies with lots of destroyable objects around them and watch the eye candy.
The A.I. in this game is one of the best ever created. Your opponents will be constantly calling out different tactics to deal with you and then executing them in the middle of a gunfight with you. They constantly try to flank you, send multiple formations at you, throw grenades at you behind cover, and lots of other methods. Good thing you have that slow motion ability to deal with them.
The only negative thing I can say about this game is that it is a corridor shooter. You run through a lot of enclosed areas and a most of them are the same thing over and over while going through the storyline. The 'scary' moments are a hit or miss for people. I think it did a great job for the time that it came out in delivering a scary experience. Even after playing through the game multiple times, that 'ladder scene' still gets me every single time!
The main game is about 8 hours long, depending on how much you explore and listen to the audio recordings scattered throughout the levels. The Extraction Point DLC is worth getting too. It's about a 4 hour long DLC, that continues where this game left off. It still has all the great elements that made the main game so good. The only other thing I will say about it is, Holiday didn't deserve that :( Avoid the other DLC. It's terrible.

This game is fantastic. It's a firstperson shooter that has elements of stealth and, well, fear, and has a perfect amount of each. All the mechanics are well executed and while the control scheme may be a bit awkward at first, you get used to it. The story is fantastic, and the game offers some background you can learn optionally, but instead of reading a diary like in games like Resident Evil, you can listen to peoples phone messages and download data from computers and have someone from HQ read it to you. This helps with the flow of the game and makes it feel more real. One thing I found interesting was the SlowMo mechanic. By pressing control, you can trigger slow motion, allowing you to better focus your shots or avoid enemy fire. Throughout the game, you can find injectors to increase your total health and reflexes(time you can use slowmo). There are also health packs scattered around which restore 50 health. Unfortunately, the medkits are placed poorly, and at some portions of the game you'll find yourself with too many health kits, and at others none with low health. You can melee with MOUSE2 in three different ways: 1. A Bicycle kick 2. A standard weapon melee or 3. A slide kick. These attacks can be extremely useful in close quarter combat. As far as enemies go, you have your standard bad guys, which get more powerful as you go on, a heavy who carries a dart like gun or a rocket launcher, and robots. There are a couple different types of robots, giant missile-launching mechs and security turrets to name a few. You can hold up to three weapons at a time, and this can become a really fun issue. I hesitate calling this an issue, as it doesn't really feel like one, but the somewhat large and ever increasing variety of weapons at your disposal forces you to make sometimes challenging choices as to what you want to equip. The game is set up in multiple stages called "Intervals" and each one is loaded one at a time. Other than upon death, start up, and  interval change,  there are no loading screens, which really helps with the games immersion. The game is quite realistic despite the polygonal graphics, and this is helped by the stealth mechanics and difficulty. If you leave your flashlight on before you turn a corner, and there happens to be an enemy there, they will come shooting, and you'll  ruin your chances at a one hit kill by surprising them. F.E.A.R. also has a fantastic physics engine and almost anything in the game can me knocked over or sent flying by your melee. The horror that is present is provided by the eerie environment and sounds provided, as well as some perfectly executed jump scares. Not giving too much away, every once in a while you will be transported to a different area, where you move much slower and are occasionally greeted by strange, evil creatures coming out of black portals. This creates a great sense of tension that is not easy to achieve. There is also some other paranormal activity to remind you that those forces are still there. I found my heart racing at certain parts of the game, and sometimes even too afraid to peek around the next corner. Without a doubt, F.E.A.R. deserves its title.

If you're reading this review, chances are you're familiar with the roguelite genre and what makes them fun, so I'll just cut right to the chase and cover why I feel Unexplored creates such a great roguelite experience.
PROS:
Unexplored doesnt just generate random levels, it generates an entire randomized dungeon structure. Tilesets, level layouts, enemies, puzzles and pickups vary wildy each playthrough, while still forming a cohesive experience as you play. Each playthrough truly feels like an adventure where you learn to expect the unexpected!
Landing a blow feels like an accomplishment, and the game will regularly present unexpected combat situations where you have to think fast to get out of a jam, or carefully plan a strategy to get past a tough area.
Certain weapons/abilities are good in certain situations but not so good in others. You must learn to improvise and adapt based on your available resources to make the best out of each situation, and rely on your combat skills to survive.
CONS:
Everything has a sort of flat paper-like look to it. And the characters look pretty weird, I'm not a fan of the eyeball! I have spent, as of writing this review, about 1 hour in game. I have 6 hours on record, but about 3 of them were downloading, since the Steam download is essentially just the launcher.
What were the other 2 hours? Well, in all honesty, I've spent 2 hours collectively trying to connect to their servers. I got a single map in today. While trying to return to the tavern, a familiar "you have been forcibly removed from the game" message appeared. I don't even know what that means, but I'm guessing it's a way of saying the connection timed out designed to make the player feel ♥♥♥♥♥♥. When somebody's forcibly removed, you imagine some obnoxious guy getting kicked out of a store or club by security, not somebody that's having issues connecting to a server. That aside, I haven't been able to connect to a game since today. It's been like this since I got it. I get to play a little, then I'm forcibly removed from the game. Of course, if this were like the original Dungeon Defenders, I could just play single player if I wanted and still play the game at least, but nope, not an option. Between that, the addition of microtransactions in a B2P game, and the inclusion of a second type of log-in after Steam make me kind of wish I could just get my money back and leave this mess behind, and hope that when DD2 comes out, they make some improvements on this system they have.
All the complaining out of the way, there are some really great things here. The addition of 4 slots for consumables like potions or, which I prefer, amulets, are an amazing addition. The amulets give you little magical abilities at the cost of mana, like AoE lightning, of a fireball, or healing. The consumables have a variety of effects, ranging from potions of mana that give you additional mana, to holy hand grenades which just deal explosive damage. Before my last forceful removal from the game, I'd picked up a couple of pet eggs, which made the removal even more painful. They were drops after completing a level, and apparently you hatch pets in this game by putting them in one of your 4 amulet/consumable slots and getting exp. That was exciting to me, and I couldn't wait to see what I got.
Also, to their credit and to defend the second log-in, they seem to have included TwitchTV streaming. Or, at least, I saw an option that had a sign-in for it and a "start stream" button. That's cool, now there might be a good number of DD streamers to help bolster the community.
Overall, as the game is, it needs some work. Maybe buff the servers, or let there be an offline mode, even if it's completely separate from the online in terms of characters and loot and stuff. I'd probably recommend it if I could play it steadily, and since I can play larger games without connection issues, I don't think the problem is entirely on my end. I am prepared to edit my review, though, with future updates and any improvements they make, because this game has potential, and there are a lot of things I'd love to see from this game in DD2.

My favourite Final Fantasy game.
The soundtrack for this game is phenominal. The final boss is especially fantastic music-wise; definitely worth the wait. Nobuo really outdid himself.
The textures have been improved somewhat and it looks a lot nicer now; however the terrain in the overworld looks a bit dodgy but that's only if you take time to focus on the textures.
I've heard a lot of things about the FMVs not looking as nice as the original PlayStation version's but I really didn't notice this.
Another fantastic feature is the addition of the PlayStation Pocket minigame Chocobo World; which many westerners never got to play since the PocketStation wasn't released outside of Japan.
The only complaints I have about this re-release is that a) The midi versions of the music really isn't great so you may want to download Roses and Wine to fix that (it replaces the audio with the original PlayStation version's music) and b) The game's description isn't correct. Apart from that though, this is a fantastic version of Final Fantasy VIII.
And for all you achievement nuts (such as myself) the game features 45 achivements ranging from easy (Get Quezacotl and Shiva) to infuriating (Contrived Finish and Omega Destroyed - a secret achievement). Planets Under Attack (PUA) is one of those fast RTS that has a very simple interface, yet has more complexities hidden under the simple rules that makes things interesting.
You've probably played many games like this before: send "units" from one "base" against an enemy base, or send units from all bases. Bases are different sizes and controls their build rate. The bigger the base, the faster they build. The idea is to conquer all the enemy bases. Galcon, Spacecom, Archipelago, they are many variations out there.
PUA added several wrinkles to the game, as well as made things simpler. When you order an attack, ALL planets that's not in "defense mode" (which you can quickly toggle) will send ships to attack. However, your attack size are subject to your "budget", which controls how many ships you can send, and your budget only goes up when you are not busy sending ships. And planets can be upgraded (from level 0 to level 3) with the budget as well.
Then there are "space fortresses", which shoots down hostile ships that flies near it, but not fast enough to deal with a large fleet. When it's neutral it shoots everybody. If you capture it it shoots enemies, and upgrading them increases their firing rate (but still not enough to handle a large fleet).
Then there are different game modes, from simple conquer (kill all enemies) to king of the hill (hold one special system for 3 minutes against 1 or more opponents), to domination (hold special systems that generate domination points, first to 300 wins) to special conditions, like enemies that stays dormant for X minutes,
There are also alternate starting race. Instead of a human, you can play as robot with a very different starting rules.
Each "mission" can be played at regular, medium, or hard which yields 0 to 2 stars. Some missions can only be unlocked with X number of stars.
Some of the missions can get pretty tense. A king of the hill battle can be tense when you are trying to keep the two enemies fighting each other while you try to pick off the unprotected systems while keep both fo them equally weak and focuses on each other rather than ganging up on you, while making sure you can take away the "hill" before the timer expires to reset it. It will take a while to whittle them down and keep them weak enough for you to take the "hill".
The actual user interface is a bit weird. You can't set the exact number of ships, but instead you hold the mouse button until you got to the right number of ships, which is obviously not precise at all. Remember it's also subject to your "budget".
However, some of the missions are impossible, or at least not explained well. There's one about repaying the "loan" but I can't seem to find the button to replay, and I don't accumulate money fast enough to repay it.
Still, for people who enjoy this genre, the color graphics (slightly cartoony) and not quite serious attitude is a bit of fun. For more tactical challenges in a similar gameplay, you may be better off playing Spacecom instead.

My review only regards the single player campaign.
This game tries to have a hard core with a soft shell, specifically, it tries to be a challanging strategy game with a decent appearance and easy control which can attract hardcore and casual players alike. However, IMHO, it fails at both ends.
Firstly, I'd like to say that this game is actually decent in appearance, since its graphics and sound are nice for a casual game, the user interface is simple and friendly despite several small design flaws (like the planet moving at the edge of the screen or too close to another planet could not be selected, and you can't click the left mouse button to proceed the dialogue).
Nevertheless, appearance alone does not make a good casual game. I saw people complaining about unable to progress in the campaign mode after the first several missions, even at easy difficulty. Personally, I didn't have much trouble finishing the game in easy difficulty, but the higher difficulties really give you headache. Most importantly, some of the missions in the solo campaign need to be unlocked by earning enough stars through fulfilling conditions in medium and hard plays. Many player are not be unable to completely experience the story.
So if you are looking for a casual game, this one may frustrate you.
On the other hand, this game is not qualified to be a fine strategy game either. In the single player campaign, you control the human race most of the time, and the problem mainly lies in the inability to precisely control your ships which is practically the only move you can make in the game except for upgrading or changing the type of your planets: even the simplest operation such as sending your ships from one certain planet to another planet requires a unbelievably great number of click or mouse wheel actions, or else the computer will do this for you in a very unrational, non-optimal way (it seems that the planets are not weighted or wrongly weighted in computation, since it is very probable that a planet of full population very close to your target sends only half a dozen of ships while the planets across the map provide the majority of your required number). Moreover, since the game runs in real time and you can't pause the game, inputting the number of the ships to be sent by holding the mouse button seems to be a bad idea.
All of these flaws in control are magnified in higher difficulties by the fact that the AI can maneuver its troop exactly and simutaneously. Moreover, in hard difficulty, the population of enemy controlled planets is hidden from you, giving the AI better chance to cheat.
In summary, I do not recommend this game to hardcore strategist or casual gamer. You may give it a try during a large discount.

Another issue I have with this is how the AI racers seem a bit too rigid, and by that I mean they dont care if you're right in front of them, they wont bother braking and will just plow right through you if you happen to be in their way, it doesn't always happen but it does happen. Really this review just made me realize how much I want codesmasters to make this exact type of game on their engine, but until that day there's RIDE.

7/10 - Fun and aesthetically pleasing Platformer/RPG with an entertaining story.
While I recommend this game to anyone into the genre, as well as any casual gamer, it’s not the greatest game I've ever played. The story in my opinion was 7/10 - It was enjoyable, but felt too simple and unthought in certain areas. The companion on your journey is a little "Nimbat" called "Fidget," and he can be just as annoying as the name suggests. However, as you play through the story, you can't help but get attached to the characters and really care about your hero's plight. By the time it was over, the bitter-sweet ending hit me right in the feels, and it felt good.
Aesthetically, this game on my list of "prettiest." The art style is perfect for this game, and the animations and illustrations are just beautiful - you can tell that the artist was really invested in his work in this title. The controls and battle system are simple enough for anyone, yet didn't leave me wanting for more - well done, devs. I generally prefer more attribute and accessory customization in RPG's, but I do recognize that adding more elements like that would start to take away from the pleasant simplicity of the game.
TL;DR:
Some aspects of the game were a little lacking for my taste, but I loved the story and had a great time playing it, and I'd recommend it to anyone.

Dust: AET has one of the most engaging stories I've ever had the pleasure to experience. Characters are varied and all have some special quirks that make them all memorable. The dialogues in this game have these "quirks" just the right amount to make these characters seem more like individuals that you are interested in rather than just a squad of generic beings that you come across and smash A to skip the dialogue as fast as you can. Voice acting is great overall but at times could be heard that some of the voices weren't necessarily by a well-known professional, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but definitely noticable.
There is not much to say about the gameplay. Quite generic "smash buttons until baddies disappear". There is a special "move" called DUST STORM that you get quite early on and that is probably what you'll be spamming for the next 8 hours or so. I played the game on NORMAL difficulty and I would suggest NORMAL for this game if you're looking to play it for the story, since it has some of the epic moments of "Oh god. I'm gonna die soon but so is the enemy" but it also makes moving between areas easier and more relaxed since you don't have to spend 10 minutes per group of enemies.
This game isn't filled with a billion small particle effects or four tons of bloom and still managed to amaze me in nearly every area I went to. The cutscenes have a charming hand-drawn look to them that is beautifully executed and that makes them nothing to sneeze at.
Down right amazing. The music always fit the feeling I had while playing. Epic soundtrack. Can't say much more than that.
You'll most likely get 8-12 hours out of the campaign but will probably get 20+ hours if you plan to 100% everything and get all achievements (I don't know for sure, haven't done that yet) .
This is definitely a game that I will remember and will most likely play through again in the future. I'd definitely say this is one of the best games I've played recently, and even one of the best I've ever played. Even though the gameplay aspect becomes quite frustratingly repetitive towards the end, the story kept my interest in the game very high. I definitely suggest picking this up if you're looking for an engaging story-driven game with beautiful visuals that is not too hard for a casual gamer.

Even worse if you clash with an enemy attack, because that produces a giant blue/white spark on the screen.
I slog through. 'Okay', I think to myself 'Maybe that was just a terrible choice of color. Maybe it's just a one time thing." The next level is a snow level. Mostly white and blue....and the enemies are primarily white wolves, and some kind of goblins in blue parkas. And there's snow in the foreground. Again, I get to play a level mostly blind.
I play through to the end of the game to it's credit, but there's so many questionable design choices here. The combat ranges from boring and repetetive to plain unfair, with enemies blurring together to superior numbers and  getting extended periods of invulnerability for them as the game progresses. The story's a joke, the voice acting is ear grating, some of the control choices feel unintuitive.....
I wanted to like this game. It's a visual treat for the first couple of areas, while you can actually see anything. And the characters are endearing at first, in that cheesy overdramatic anime way. But once I was done, I wasn't excited to comb through for more treasure or finish any quests. I just uninstalled, happy that the game was over and out of my life. If I'd bought it full price, I'd have been extremely upset. As is, I picked it up for less than 4 dollars, and that seems about right.

A fantastic game. Fantastic.
I'll admit that I wasn't expecting to get so much this game. But it was full of quality gaming material with fabulous replayability. There are still many things I haven't managed to do and find, after 50 hours!
But finally, with Chethero the Thirty-Ninth, I brought the fabled Amulet of Yendor to the surface
!
For me, the overall level of complexity is just right. You don't need to learn a new language of terms to know what your enchanted gear actually does, and you won't have to look up a wiki site to figure out a good way to use your items. And yet, the game puts you in complex enough situations that you feel elated when you use gear efficiently and devastated when they go to waste. And in the end, your careful performance is what is going to determine how close you get to that famous, elusive amulet. Unexplored does a great job of creating that feeling of wanting to know what's behind that door, of the thrill of defeating a rare boss, and of that excitement of walking away with loot you've never seen before. And when you die, you may not mind losing it all, because you'll know the generator will cook up levels that were just as engaging as the last, and it's probably going to have a whole different set of challenges and aspects of progression. Who knows, maybe the next run will have that boss you need to kill for an achievement? Or maybe there'll be another chance at that secret room you locked yourself out of last time...
I feel that repetitiveness, which seems to be a dread among rogue-likes, is a very long time away. It may never come.
I still haven't earned all the classes, and there's only eight. Sure, it might be reflective of my proficiency, whatever. But they're meaningful classes, and your choice can hugely affect the way your encounters play out. How could it not, if you choose to enter the dungeon wielding a valuable pistol, such a difficult item to acquire inside? But what will you do when you run out of gunpowder and bullets; how will you ever find that? This game is full of considerations like this, and it's entertaining and thought-provoking.
Playing things out on a 2-D map in real time makes the experience active and immersive, but it is implemented in a way that still rewards good play and punishes recklessness like some great turn-based games do. One does not simply walk into the Dungeon of Doom, not even in casual mode. The game won't require extreme precision, but fighting perfectly can certainly be challenging. If in doubt, you can always pause and strategize. I think the best way to know what exactly the combat is like is to simply watch a video.
One downside is that I wish the game had richer visuals and better effects. I mean, the iron ore is nothing but a white pentagon. But the simplistic, somewhat cute design direction has its own appeal, and it's easy to look at. The soundtrack is good for creating the atmosphere and transitions well in-game, but it's probably not going to win any Grammy's. But really, I almost feel bad criticizing the presentation aspects when I know that in a game like this, it's all about the gameplay anyway. And the gameplay is remarkably good, so any shortcomings in the presentation aspects should be easily overlooked in light of it.
The combination of tactical execution and smart decision-making, leading to satisfying success. I think it's one of the great appeals of all rogue-likes, and this game nails it. You are 99.99999999% guaranteed to enjoy this title if you are a fan of rogue-likes and light action games.

I loved GalCiv2, and I was very excited for this new game (I was a junior founder, I bought in early). Now I am not so excited. I think it is the best new 4X game space game out there, but it frequently fails to live up to its predecessor, and it certainly doesn't feel like it has benefitted sufficiently from nearly a decade of advancement in gaming. This game has great potential, but after waiting a year for it to be realized, I'm beginning to lose hope. If you like space 4X, sci fi, or galciv2, you might try picking this up on sale, just to see if you like it. Don't get too excited, though.
Here's a short breakdown:
Con: Multiplayer doesn't really work well
Con: How long will the game keep making money and therefore being supported with limited multiplayer?
Con: The AI is not very good
Con: Worse, there are obvious exploits
Con: Someone with a knowledge of basic probability needs to go over the game mechanics... there are some weird bits*
Con: Only comes with a dozen factions. The rest are crowd-sourced on Steam, and they are generally lackluster.
Con: Only a slow trickle of "offical," complete new factions from the developer, and they seem to actively avoid adding them
Con: The first race they added in DLC is a species of super-aggressive squirrels that started in GC2 as a joke... seriously
Con: The movies use proprietary software, so it is much harder to add new ones
Con: Certain things, like lights for ships and faction map colors, are limited and difficult to mod
Con: Clumsy interface
Con:  The DLC is mostly weak and disappointing
Con:  The first expansion was similarly weak
Con: You can only design ships in-game, no independent shipyard
Con: The designer is terribly organized and harder to use than the GC2 version
Con: You can't just record a bug, you have to send them a video showing them something they could reproduce on their own computer
Con: And they will close a ticket if you don't get back to them very quickly (they are not so prompt themselves)
Con: You can't upload mods to Steam
Con: Some programming shortcuts make "obvious" mods difficult (not unique to this game, I'm sure)**
Con: But they are in an uneditable form outside of the game***
Con: There is no interface for editing factions, you have to start a game
Con: Large numbers of factions become unmanagable in an administrative sense: how do you find the one you are looking for with no search and no rational order to the listing?
Con: Odd choices in programming colors limits the customizability of ships, interfaces, etc.
Con: Game still doesn't include all of the factions remaining at the end of GC2 (Drath, Korath)
Con: Lacks, or nerfs, many of the features of GalCIv2, including spies (coming), asteroid miners (nerfed), terror stars (maybe someday)
Con: Major features that came with the basic GC2, like politics and political parties, are gone. United Planets seems to be significantly nerfed.
Pro:  The developer often throws new content into updates
Pro:  The developer is pretty clever
Con: There seem to be a lot of glitches/ "unadvertised features" that still haven't been resolved despite extensive documentation
* e.g., Class 8 and 11 planets are more likely to occur than an either 7,9, 10, or 12, and random planets cannot be class 17!
** Aquatic ability is hard-wired, adding new strategic icons...
** You can't get the text back out to, say, spellcheck, the the text boxes are too small, the formatting changes unexpectedly, the typing interface is glitchy, and you can't give custom factions everything a built-in faction can (mostly for Steam compatibility)

I have been hitting the rogue-likes and rogue-lites recently and this one is a bit of a gem.
I haven't really played a RPG style game like this before, where the items, enemies vary from game to game, and you sort of work towards "The next playthrough" Does the current play thru matter? It might not, you might be just trying to amass some arrows to unlock a class or maximise your gold to make next start easier.
Each time you play, your characters can't indentify scrolls or potions, so that adds to the fun ( sometimes its obvious when you dig some liquid from a well and it APPEARS to be creating gas = so thats obviously a gas potion.)
It is uniquely challenging and to be honest the random nature CAN be punishing from the get go.
Once you learn the subtle ins and outs ( right click stuff, its how you learn )
When you realise killing stuff ISN'T everything, you end up playing a bit differently.
Weapons are all varied and interesting, and you learn quite a bit about how the enemies function ( they are relentless sometimes )
I really enjoy how darkness, fire and the little sprites function. Fire can be handy and a pain in the bum.
Things I don't like, well occassionally performance seems to drop for me, and occassonally when I start it up, it does crash, but I haven't lost a save game yet, so I can't complain too much.
It's punishing, its fresh, it's fun and something just keeps me coming back.
I'd probably give this a miss if I was the sort of person who didn't like getting smash to bits. You will die, you will lose all that sweet sweet gear and you will rage. But whether this cuts you down, or gets you going again, will dictate if this for you.

Synopsis: This is nearly a perfect game with amazing music and very clever and rewarding gameplay, but the move-to-the-beat gameplay can feel terrible if your computer's audio latency is too high!  Blame the laws of physics for this, not the devs.
First off, the music is so good I would recommend this game for that alone, but along with the music you also get a great game!  It's very fast-paced especially in the later levels but all of the enemies have predictable patterns so when you make a mistake you know it's your fault.  Playing carefully and slowly will keep you alive but you'll lose out on gold and items if the song ends before you finish explore the level, it's a brilliant tradeoff.  It just feels so GOOD to play, possibly because I already play the drums so timing key presses to the beat was a pretty natural thing and I never had to deal with that initial learning curve.
YOU WILL WANT TO REDUCE YOUR COMPUTER'S AUDIO LATENCY FOR THIS GAME!  In most games you won't even notice if your audio is delayed by 200ms, but in Crypt of the Necrodancer it can ruin your experience!  I did lots of fiddling with my computer to find the lowest possible audio latency, and it turns out my onboard audio had much lower latency.  60ms  was as low as I got it and that felt pretty good to me.

At first look it seemed like a un-needed mobile-esque update to the original HOWEVER, and there is a however, after approximately 2 hours of playing my Series-EV char 'Clanketta' I realised that I was far more interested than I had originally thought, despite the odd UI in the item box and hero inventory the game is still capturing some of the original DD flare with new additions that are a huge plus to the experience.
The first thing that really caught my attention was the eggs, I love being able to fight through the horde to find, and loot a pet egg, look at its stats and try to guess what it will be. Having to incubate an egg by fighting with it equipt and waiting (im)patiently for it to be ready to hatch was a lot of fun, I have a seperate folder in my Item box for eggs and pets, I currently have a Shoddy Shroomite with 22 upgrade levels, which is great as you dont invest coin to upgrade them, but fight alongside them to get XP for them.
Secondly was the addition of visable armour, nothing surprised me more than noticing I had not only the witch kings great helm on, but a tiny little crown sitting atop it, not the most ferocious looking but still novel and fun, adding dyes to armours and skins was a interesting edition as I can finally get back into the customization of my character and I actually have to work towards it.
The game has enough new features to outweigh the current teething problems on the serverside with the occasional drops and inability to join games (sorted by hosting private and publicizing it). With responsive and active dev teams working on the community highlighted issues (such as the odd UI) I feel that given time DDE will be the true 'definitive' version we were promised.
Many negative reviews are given from the perspective of those who like DD and refuse to accept any variance from their accepted view of what is "right" for the series, however after logging several hours in both games I have found that most of the faults they find are all without any real impact other than the server problems which is common across nearly all new releases.
In conclusion, given time, this should prove to be more of a gem than people are giving it credit for.

Rating: 8/10
Budget: Worth it.
Replayability: I recommend spoiling the game for yourself, and reading ahead with a walkthrough to make the right choices. The game is simply too heavy for a casual gamer like myself to go through more than once. But what a journey!
Lenght: I'm ashamed to admit how long it took me to beat this game...
The Witcher II allows you to import your save from Witcher I, which is exactly as great as it sounds. Remember Mass Effect 2? Trying to start the game without importing a save from ME 1 always kinda sucked, because so many quests would be different - or gone.
The problems already start here. The best gear in Witcher 1 is basically junk equipment in Witcher 2. This is a bit ridiculous. Your powers and your level from witcher 1 seems to have no impact on how great you start out in Witcher 2.
Balancer, you say? I say no. Frankly, a few powers and some good gear doesn't make enough of a difference in the Witcher 2 for it to have mattered. What matters is practice, tactics and difficulty level.
I don't really care much for the gameplay of the Witcher 1 or 2. They're not even that similar. It's sort of a strange "dodge&strike" combat system, reminisce of console hack&slash games. Probably why it's popular with a larger crowd.
I don't care for this. I'm more into fps/third person direct control like Skyrim, Jedi Knight 2 or the up-coming Kingdom Come: Deliverance.
The style of gameplay in the Witcher is very popular though - just not with me.
The story is very rich, but I sometimes feel like the screenplay could use a bit more depht. Don't get me wrong, the story is masterfully written, the characters are intense and interesting and the graphics are very good for a game that is now a aged title, but the actual screen play, the over-used voice actors and character models...
I have unpleasant flashbacks to TES IV Oblivion.
Sometimes it also seems like the lines chosen by the people in the game are a bit... Artificial.
I'm obviously over-criticising the game at this point - It really is a great roleplaying game. But be warned, the only character custimization you can do is a hair-style and clothes beyond skills.
The reason I'm giving it 8/10 isn't because of my personal dislike of the combat system - I realize that the combat system is very good, and exactly what the company aimed for.
No, my issue is with the items that scale ridiculously in the game, in effeciency, and with the broken econimics of the game.
I HONESTLY recommend cheating in this game. You will have a much more enjoyable experience.
You're playing as a supernatural monster slayer who is a mutant with magic powers who works for several kings and the king's special forces. Your lover is a sorcerer who wields powerful magic, and you know pretty much everyone who is worth knowing, plus you already ♥♥♥♥ing saved the world once in the Witcher 1.
Why are you not rich? Why do you not have good stuff? Why are you not powerful when the game starts? These questions boggle me, and frankly I found the game much more enjoyable with a few cheats.
I even bothered to raise the difficulty a bit again, before I decided "Easiest" was the way to go when I found no enjoyment in the combat system at all.
Play the Witcher 1 first though!

Is this the best C&C game? No. Is this game as memorable Red Alert 2? No. Yet when this game goes on sale for $5, then it becomes very much a worthwhile purchase. To clearify - the game's story isn't bad, I personally find it to be fairly solid (although nowhere near as good as RA2) the campaign is has a decent length. The gameplay although fairly familair to veterans of the C&C franchise is a bit slower than that of the previous titles. In this game resources are gathered from a resource node - in eariler titles the way of gathering resources was to build refineries around a resource field. This change both slows the game while simultaniously makes the need for early expansion greater. But what this system allowed for is the advanced naval system. The system allows for a base to be built on either land or water - an interesting and surprisingly functional mechanic. But before I conclude, the biggest issue with the game is (this may or may not be resolved after this review is posted) that the multiplayer is not functional. When the game first launched it featured a co-op mode for the campaign (can be played singleplayer without a problem) but due to gamespy shutting down, there is no way to play multiplayer with anyone (LAN may be the exception but I have never tested it) Ultimately for $5 on sale, this is not a bad game to grab otherwise - I'd recommend either waiting or getting RA2.

I say without sarcasm or facetiousness that I do not understand why this game is popular. It isn't so much bad as it is unfinished. I don't mind poor graphics that come from a different era; Half Life, Cave Story, and Phantasy Star 4 still rank as some of my favorite games, not to mention Minecraft. I don't mind the occasional odd translation either; again Phantasy Star 4. I can handle cosmetic flaws.
What I can't handle is the lack of character and cohesive narrative. After playing through this game twice, I still don't feel like I really know any of the characters, or why they did any of the things they did, including the villain. Everyone seems to love putting Sephiroth on various sorts of Top Whatever Villains Ever lists, but I found him hilarious at literally every appearance. Presumably it's because he killed an important character, but I felt like I didn't know her. I was not sad, only confused, because the game never made me like her before it killed her.
After playing this game twice all the way through and using a few guides to make sure I wasn't just missing some bonus third of it somehow, I am left with a wanderlust that this game was supposed to satisfy, after being hyped to heaven and back by the rest of the world as some kind of classic. I am left with this, and questions. Questions like why was Sephiroth going to all the places that he was going to? Why did he attack that ship, or impale that giant snake? Why are there so many minigames that appear only once? What was the point of this or that chapter, this or that boss, and so on.
Nothing in this game world makes sense, but not in a way that I can even get angry at it for being poorly written. Like I said, it doesn't feel poorly written, it feels unfinished, like it's an abridged version of its own story, like it's the Video Game version of a book or show or movie that was poorly adapted. Phantasy Star 4 came out before this game and that game's story and characters kick this one's♥♥♥♥♥around the block and then steal their seats on the train.
Watch a let's play, and read Obstinate Melon's comic version on Deviantart, it is once again without sarcasm the better telling. Though unfortunately at time of writing this review, said comic remains unfinished.

No direction is given from the start other than a few control identifiers. You are otherwise left to venture and explore the depths of the ocean at your own leisure. Small challenges that offer up achievements give the experience a little drive, plus having to find your small robotic companion on each level enables you to advance through some locked areas. These small challenges and tasks are not difficult at all, they just give the player a little extra if they want it. Abzu is truly a relaxing experience and a beautiful journey. I give it a very high recommendation especially if its on sale!

Another cell game, but with arguably the worst UI / combat interface I have ever seen. Clunky, unwieldy and unintuitive. Imagine having the bulk of your army on a single planet and no way to send it out without manually switching every other planet to 'guard mode' first. One at a time. Oh, and there's no way to send ships quickly. You have to hold down the left mouse button on a planet, and the slider slowly goes from 0 -> 1 -> 2 .... -> 10 -> 11 ... -> 19 -> 21 -> 23 ... you get the idea. Sending medium sized fleets (only medium, mind you!) can require you to hold the LMB for several seconds, an eternity in action games like this. Wanna attack multiple planets simultaneously? Wanna get a bunch of planets to attack / defend a nearby planet quickly? Not gonna happen.
Conclusion: Bad interface. Very bad interface. Stay away. Even free flash games have better UI design. Check out Galcon 2 (which is free, even!) instead if you're into games like this. Now THAT's how this game should have been done.

Is it perfect? No, it has issues. But I've not experienced anything game breaking, and ultimately I found RIDE incredibly enjoyable. In a world where the last "Forza/GT but with bikes" came out 10 years ago, you have to overlook what I feel a minor inconveniences and enjoy a rare release. Having played a lot of Milestone's previous bike games (all the way back to EA Sports Superbike 2001) probably helps, as they have made incremental improvements to what I feel is a rock solid riding model.
Sure, its not GP Bikes, but there's a reason why no mainstream release has tackled simulating the weight shifting/countersteering that it takes to truly ride a bike, its an extra level of complication that would simply be a very large barrier for some people to overcome to find enjoyment. But all the right elements are there, braking points, lean angle and throttle application. A hold-trigger-to-go arcade racer its not.
The knock against Milestone is they barely supported this game, with limited fixes and some incredibly content light DLC, and seemingly they are moving on to producing a sequel. So I can understand peoples' grievances in this regard for a self-published title (where a developer would usually be subjugated to the whims of a 3rd party publisher)
I recommend this game with caveats; if you have a grunty system, and an affinity for bikes (or Milestones' previous bike sims). However I don't recommend getting anything more than the basic release, and if money's tight or you simply have a passing interest, wait for a sale.

This is one of the best games ever made.  So why don't I recommend it...
I think the 2 main points are:
- Extremely overpriced.  Even if you buy it in a sale (like me) for 7$.  It is nearly 20 years old.
- This new (Steam) version is very buggy.
Basically, if you wanna sell an old game for a ridiculous high price, MAKE SURE IT WORKS...
- Why it is so good:
You get an amazing story.  It's a fantasy story, but technology is present in the game.  You will fight fantasy monsters as well as robots, soldiers, other npcs, ...  (Tiny SPOILER following:)  It's set against a background of an all-powerfull corporation that rules the world, that loves to repress the common people.
A really cool fighting system.  It's somewhere between turn-based and real-time.  There are a lot of options and a unique magic system, that you can tweak yourself.  There are almost infinite combinations in which you can make the characters cast spells, become physically better, have extra attacks, attacks that inflict magic spells, or have extra battle-options (like steal or manipulate).  An important part of the game is about managing this system.
Next to it, every now and then you will be able to perform a super-attack with one of your characters.
Mini-games!  There are a lot of mini-games, that are funny (and sometimes annoying).  Some might take a few times to finish successfully and sometimes you will need to become very good in them in order to unlock certain items.  Those items are usually optional, but they will make your life easier.
No grinding necessary to complete.  However, if you want to unlock the certain items I was telling you about in previous paragraph, you will need to grind from time to time.  Also, if you want a fully-leveled magic system, grinding is necessary as well.
Choices are reflected in certain game aspects.  Some people might like you more or less, even from the pcs in your party.  You might miss out on spells, items, ... because of this.
There are an awfully lot of aspects in the game you need to manage for your pcs.  But not from the beginning.  This is build up very slowly and by the time it really gets important, you will have a good understanding how the things work.  How things are managed the best depends on YOUR playing style.
This game you can play for hours and hours and don't get bored (note: I get bored easily with most games).
Most important, when this game was released (back in the days when animals still spoke and optical mouses were pretty neat), lots and lots of gamers were playing this.  Even the ones prefering other game genres.  It boosted the rpg-genre and set an example of how a good rpg looks like.
- Why it is so bad
It didn't age very well.  You will look at pixeled backgrounds.  Sometimes the words displayed on this backround are important and very difficult to read.  It just looks old.
This version is anything but stable.  The game crashes from time to time.  Certain times, I could not go through certain places, unless I changed party-members.  Sometimes it just crashes.
This combined with a system that allows you to save on certain points only.  So if you have been fighting/playing for a long while, without the possibility to save and the game crashes on you, you won't be very happy.  Especially after long cut-scenes, or if you have been playing (for hours)  to get an item, just to see the game crash just before you got this (which has happened to me a few times).  Again, for a steeply overpriced game, this can't be tollerated.
Note: I do run it on a Windows 10.  Only windows versions up to 7 are supported.
The game needs to call home in order to run.  You will need to be online to run this game.  So let's hope the server over there stays up forever.
I never liked this kind of DRM (or any kind for that matter).  I usually wait until you can get a game on GOG, just for this reason.  The only reason I bought it here is because it's not available on GOG and I really love this game, I loved it when it came out, and I still love it today.
Recommendation:
I think this is a game that most people will like.  But you might be better off if you managed to get the original cd's (4 of them) and use a patch.  I haven't any experience with this, but even if it is flawed with a patch, so is this steam version of FF7.  It will be cheaper and the game won't need to *call home* in order to run.
Give it a chance!  You will be in for a unique game experience.

First and foremost:
This is NOT a pay-to-win OR pay-to-play game.
...the reviews that suggest so are flat-out lies...
The in-game currency is Crystal. You win Crystal by playing Single Player, Co-Op, or PVP Matches. You also acquire Crystal for free just by logging in each day, and collecting the Daily Reward. On top of that, as a Daily Reward - you get 6 free Dragons every 30 days; if you log in each day and collect the Daily Reward. Two of those Dragons will be Tier 1, two will be Tier 2, two will be Tier 3. You can sell the two Tier 3 Dragons for 5000 Crystal each, and buy two Dragon Packs; gaining 3 Dragons each. As a result, you can actually earn and keep 10 FREE Dragons each month simply by logging in every single day. You must eventually equip your Dragon with Runes, and besides Runes - you need to select a Dragon and Weapon for each Match; and you can upgrade (Forge) your weapons too. Eventually you'll upgrade all Dragons to Tier 4, upgrade all your Runes to Tier 3, and have all your weapons Forged - and you won't even need Crystal anymore; you'll have nothing to spend it on.
The funny thing is - I summed up the game in that entire paragraph.
I bought a Titan Pass for quicker Crystal income rate. I don't need it.

I have been holding off on Reviewing Stellaris because I wanted a clear picture of what the game is!
After having put more then 100 Hours into Stellaris I have found that I still can't answer that question reliably.
So I think I am going to start off with Broad Questions:
Is the game fun?  Yes
Is the game good? Yes
Would I recommend this game to others? Yes
Is it worth its price tag? Yes
So with that part out of the way I want it to be clear that I very much like this game BUT:
Stellaris is having a hard time claiming to be a Grand Strategy game!
It lacks Casus Beli's
The Game Pace is far too fast, it takes about as long as a Civ 5 game!
There is a complete lack of content for any playstyle thats not map painting!
Diplomacy is Abysmal
And Bug's are Galore
Basically I get NO Grand Stategy feel too Stellaris when I play it!  Infact it sometimes feels like it wants to be a Grand Strategy game but its not capable in its current form of grasping that role!  The game basically feels Naked with only two victory conditions that both involve lots of Pew Pew.....
So then I try to compare it too 4X games of new and old and well that leaves me in a similiar confused condition.  It just doesnt jive in my mind.  At times I feel some Masters of Orion or Galactic Civ like gameplay but by and large its so confused on its identity that it doesn't feel "4X" either....
So one of my biggest issues that I am having at this point in time is simply trying to classify Stellaris in my mind.  But whatever classification it finally evolves into its far from complete.  That is the one thing that really rings true when I play the game currently (1.0.2 - 5/17/2016 Only 8 days since release)  its not fnished.  Infact it often times feels like I am in a building with no walls just the 2*4 Frame and a roof....  There is a ton of work to do yet, its pretty obvious!
(Understand I am a Hardcore Paradox Fan who expects a Certain Level of product from Paradox)
The things I dislike the most:
Diplomacy:
-Very Lacking in options.
-The options you do have are again rarely if ever excepted by the AI unless you meet a very specific parameter.
-The AI itself fails to use the few diplomatic options that are currently in the game correctly.
Victory Conditions:
-An utter and complete lack of a victory type that doesnt involve Pew Pew??? You feel like you have more options playing as the Germans in Heart's of Iron then any Race in Stellaris....
Events:
- Severly lacking, this is the part I am most disappointed with, as all the short comings above I could easily ignore if there seemed like there was a credible effort put in to really make the world rich with events....  I really think the lack of events is what most makes Stellaris not feel like it has an Identity in my mind.  And then the events that are in the game are so MEH....  They almost feel like background flavor that has little relevance.
But with all that said,
Stellaris is a GEM its got a skeleton in place that has the potential to become a game thats better then Crusader Kings 2....   It has the potential to be one of the greatest of all time.  Its addictive, its flashy, its a must buy!  Even if its current state is filled with bug's and balance issues, and a Haven for Min Maxers....  Its addictive!!!

I would like to preface this review by saying this: this is a great game. If you see it on sale, buy it.
F.E.A.R., borders the line between horror, and action. And it does one of those well.
Now, I would not recommend F.E.A.R. as a horror game, because it simply isn't that scary. It is however, unsettling, and I did jump at least a couple of times. The atmosphere in this game is phenomenal, the eerie sounds, the oppresive nature of the environment, and the way you always feel like you're against insurmountable odds really come together to make everything just feel right.
Now, don't get me wrong, the game does have some genuine scares, but it really overall it just fits into the "2spooky4me" territory of "scary". The one enemy that did scare me were the phase-shifting ninja guys. You see a shadow when walking through a hall way from another room, so you look over and you see this... spider looking thing in the corner of the room... and it slowly turn its head to you to reveal its human form before jumping at you and disappearing and reforming on another wall. Sh*t, I just had to pause the game and take a break for a minute at that point.
The enemies are tough, smart, and they work together with each other in a way that I have never seen in any other game, so much so that you aren't even frustrated when you die most of the time, you are just like "well, I've been outsmarted".
The game still looks great, dispite being a 2005 game. The lighting effects are outstanding, and the slo-mo effect you can use makes everything much more dramatic.
The level design really is top-notch and made me actually think about what I should do before a fire-fight. You can see the shadows of enemy soldiers peek from around a corner before they see you, giving you time to hide or run to a place to ambush them. At one point you are climbing a ladder, and through the ladder you see an enemy placing mines in a hallway, so you know to avoid them when you pass through. It's just done very well.
Everything about it was really well thought out and made me realize you rarely see this kind of thing in modern FPS games. They just try to compete by having bigger explosions and and scripted sequences than the last, and yet this game has close to none and still manages to have a cinematic feel just by having the AI react to everything in a very human-like way. It's just GOOD.
GFX = 8.5/10 It is a game from 2005, but it still holds up. The lighting is great, and the effects look good.
Sound = 9/10 Eerie ambiance, music that sets the mood, and enemy voices all sound fine. No complaints.
Replay = 7/10 F.E.A.R. honestly doesn't have that much replay value to it, but it does come with its 2 expansions, so at least you can get some solid game time out of it. I have yet to play the expansions, but the base game took me about 6 hours to complete.
Story = 7.5/10 The story was honestly pretty boring until about halfway through, and you never really cared about any of the characters. This doesn't effect the enjoyment of the game much however.
OVERALL = 8.5/10 Buy it.
