These days, every hipster dev with a scarf and a macbook fancies his game a Roguelike. It means "unforgiving dungeon crawler with maybe optional perma-death, and what the hell, maybe it's actually about space ships" and that's fine, because definitions change, and I am not prescriptive with my linguistics (it is literally futile, trust me brah).
But there was a time when Roguelike had an exquisitely narrow meaning. It meant, and you might want to sit down... Similiar to Rogue*.
Okay, relax, I know that horse has been beaten to the point that it is effectively liquid, I mean I never thought you could drink a horse, but yes, it's pulpy but doable. But that's disgusting, and you should be ashamed. Horses are majestic. Good for your testosterone though.
But I digress.
Unexplored is an actual Roguelike, a love letter to Roguelikes, and should be considered part of the glorious tradition of Angband, ADOM, Nethack, Brogue and, why not, Dwarf Fortress.
There are many familiar elements, like dangerous equipment that has to be identified because it might bear terrible curses. The graphics are simple but interesting... There is a fair bit of Zelda mixed in to make it more skill-based. It has a tremendous amount of content and the devs continue to expand it and sand down the few rough edges that remain.
Unexplored is deep and unforgiving, and often has a tense spooky quality, because it implements permadeath in a way that conveys a sense of danger without being too punishing or grindy. And although it still has some bugs here and there (one of the devs fixed my save file and sent it back to me when I happened upon a problem), it is great, and I highly recommend it.
* Rogue was a text-based dungeon crawler where you died a lot. I never played it, Jesus kid, I'm not *that* old. But it spawned a bunch of presumably much better games, which, because of the primitive UI, were able to focus on churning out loads of content, and I did play some of those. A few are still fun today, if you can get past the UI.

Rating: 8/10
Budget: Worth it.
Replayability: I recommend spoiling the game for yourself, and reading ahead with a walkthrough to make the right choices. The game is simply too heavy for a casual gamer like myself to go through more than once. But what a journey!
Lenght: I'm ashamed to admit how long it took me to beat this game...
The Witcher II allows you to import your save from Witcher I, which is exactly as great as it sounds. Remember Mass Effect 2? Trying to start the game without importing a save from ME 1 always kinda sucked, because so many quests would be different - or gone.
The problems already start here. The best gear in Witcher 1 is basically junk equipment in Witcher 2. This is a bit ridiculous. Your powers and your level from witcher 1 seems to have no impact on how great you start out in Witcher 2.
Balancer, you say? I say no. Frankly, a few powers and some good gear doesn't make enough of a difference in the Witcher 2 for it to have mattered. What matters is practice, tactics and difficulty level.
I don't really care much for the gameplay of the Witcher 1 or 2. They're not even that similar. It's sort of a strange "dodge&strike" combat system, reminisce of console hack&slash games. Probably why it's popular with a larger crowd.
I don't care for this. I'm more into fps/third person direct control like Skyrim, Jedi Knight 2 or the up-coming Kingdom Come: Deliverance.
The style of gameplay in the Witcher is very popular though - just not with me.
The story is very rich, but I sometimes feel like the screenplay could use a bit more depht. Don't get me wrong, the story is masterfully written, the characters are intense and interesting and the graphics are very good for a game that is now a aged title, but the actual screen play, the over-used voice actors and character models...
I have unpleasant flashbacks to TES IV Oblivion.
Sometimes it also seems like the lines chosen by the people in the game are a bit... Artificial.
I'm obviously over-criticising the game at this point - It really is a great roleplaying game. But be warned, the only character custimization you can do is a hair-style and clothes beyond skills.
The reason I'm giving it 8/10 isn't because of my personal dislike of the combat system - I realize that the combat system is very good, and exactly what the company aimed for.
No, my issue is with the items that scale ridiculously in the game, in effeciency, and with the broken econimics of the game.
I HONESTLY recommend cheating in this game. You will have a much more enjoyable experience.
You're playing as a supernatural monster slayer who is a mutant with magic powers who works for several kings and the king's special forces. Your lover is a sorcerer who wields powerful magic, and you know pretty much everyone who is worth knowing, plus you already ♥♥♥♥ing saved the world once in the Witcher 1.
Why are you not rich? Why do you not have good stuff? Why are you not powerful when the game starts? These questions boggle me, and frankly I found the game much more enjoyable with a few cheats.
I even bothered to raise the difficulty a bit again, before I decided "Easiest" was the way to go when I found no enjoyment in the combat system at all.
Play the Witcher 1 first though!

What i have written down below is mostly my opinions and problems with this game.
I honestly feel like this remake is unfinished and has some really poor design choices.
The game still has a lot of glitches and bugs, i feel like im playing a beta sometimes.
So far the game has been more of the same with some little differences.
But its the little things that bother me the most, such as:
-Forced online taverns: I liked being able to relax in my own tavern, managing my gear, chatting with the other people i might have just played with, looking through my trophies, being able to change the music playing in the tavern ect, ect.
The new taverns are just chaotic and laggy, filled with usually 20 people in a small space.
I dont mind the option of public taverns, but i think the 4 man personally hosted taverns should still be available.
-Playverse: I know playverse isnt done yet, but it can be really buggy at times. There have been plenty of times the matchmaking servers havent been working or offline. And you need the matchmaking servers to be placed in a tavern. Which you need to be in to play solo.
-Glitchy: This game is advertised as a full finished game on steam, yet there are so many bugs and glitches and the general feeling of unfinishedness that the original didnt suffer from. If you are remaking a game you'd better make sure it works better then the original. Mostly the movement in multiplayer can glitch out pretty badly, the general collision between players and mobs feel wrong, not even talking about how much you can glitch the game when you start jumping.
-UI: Tower stats are now shown much better. Other than that most of the UI feels clunky and unclear. At least the original had a small tutorial explaining things. This one doesnt.
The moment you click play in the menu you are thrown into a tavern with no explaination whatsoever.
I had a lot of trouble finding out how the new dye system and crafting works, i cant imagine how confusing it will be for new players.
-small stuff i dislike: The 2 minute timer at the end of a map. I like staying a bit to collect mana/coins and chat a bit with people. But now you are brutely ripped away from it. You wont even end up in the same tavern as the people you were playing with. Also hardcore mode has changed to the degree where noone will risk it late game (if you die your character is deleted, rather then if you die you just dont respawn for the duration of the wave). Survival has also changed in such a way that it becomes a pain in the butt without a solid premade team.
But this rant has been long enough. I appologize for possibly butchering the english language, its my second laguage and thank you for letting me get this off my chest.

Not a terrible 3rd title in the Red Alert trilogy...
I was an OK fan of Red Alert 1. Then I became a HUGE fan of Red Alert 2. In fact I consider Red Alert 2 the RTS title that got me into RTS gaming.
I had high expectations with Red Alert 3 when it released. Was I impressed initially? Honestly, no. I was a little bit disappointed with the game and really didn't like the Empire faction. I thought it was pretty damn cheesy. I mean this is coming from a game that is loaded with cheese. But really, I preferred my mind whack job faction of Yuri from Red Alert 2. At least they had some Soviet in their style. The Empire faction gives up too much cornyness with their robot units that carry samurai swords and whatnot. I understand it's the theme, but let's be realistic here. You wouldn't be winning a war with swords in Red Alert.
For me, Red Alert 2 allowing you to choose from real world nations after picking either Allies or Soviets kept a more realistic approach to the madness and you could feel a lil more attachment to the story. Red Alert 3 is all over the place. BUT, not all is bad in the game.
I still do love the gameplay and minor enhancements they made. The graphics looking stunning even right now with the current gen games out. The Soviets and Allies are still great looking and have some really awesome units. Who doesn't love building a mass of Dreadnoughts to rain down dozens and dozens of missles? When the damage flies, it flies.
As I got this game on a cheap Steam sale, I figured why the hell not, and I'm happy for it. I stuck mostly with skirmish game matches where I could just have quick fun of building my base and laying waste to my opponent.
Where I didn't see much in this game initially upon launch, I found late in it's life thru Steam. At this point I recommend the game, but it will never be held to the standard I had with Red Alert 2.

Medium shows you enemy planet health, but no warning. It has 2 objective.
Hard mode hides enemy planet health and no alarm. It has 3 objectives. The objectives oftentimes serve as hints at a better faster way to finish the mission
On a side note as you progress through the campagin they unlock other things you need to worry about.
Money effects power and effectivness of ships. What kind of planet do you want? A bank? A cannon? A good old fashiond ship planet?
It makes for a very nice strategic experience.

I would not suggest this game to anyone who was a fan of the original Red Alert/2/Yuri's Revenge or even C&C Generals, EA and whatever is left of Westwood is long gone and dead.  This game does not have an enjoyable campaign, the units are basic and boring, and it is not fun thus defeating the purpose of it being classified as a "game".  The campaign is flat out dull and boring, the witty cutscenes that went hand in hand with good gameplay are no longer there, EA has seen fit to simply have bad acting encompass their bad game design just so they can say "look we remember what RA used to be too!"
The units are boring and made out of paper, the fun general powers from C&C Generals make a return but with None of the fun or innovation that the previous title put into it.  Factional units are cut and paste from each other with only some different looking models and alternate modes being the variation.  The units in general show the worst signs of AI that I have ever seen in ANY RTS title or game that I have played PERIOD.  They are extremely near-sighted; they always fail to return fire unless you give them a direct order and will just sit there getting blown away by everything.  Speaking of alternate unit modes, this game tries to do something different and fails utterly, the only thing that these abilities do is further complicate the most BASIC C&C formula and further hamper the gameplay and fun factor of the title.  Even when you have them built with attack at will rather then defensive they will consistently neglect to defend themselves even when the enemy unit is right on top of them, it is babysitting of the highest order and a huge failing of the “game” and its developers.  The “future” has shown that any C&C title past Generals or maybe the earlier 3D C&Cs have been a complete failure as fans continue to drop the titles in favor of something less driven by greed and fake innovation.
During the campaign you can either have a coop human player, if you can keep connection with EA’s trash servers (another quality sign of EA) or you can be aided by the in game AI, which is semi competent enough however the kicker is that for an RTS game you and your coop player share ore resources, which is absolutely ridiculous and a really poorly thought-out mechanic.  On the subject of the campaign again I will clarify further that it is one of the most boring three faction story mode that I have ever played let alone failing to bring me any joy from playing it.  I have to push myself in order to go back to it and attempt to finish it that’s how I consider the story mode and the game in general, boring and a CHORE, no game should ever make the player feel that way!  I am very glad that I never got this game when it came out for the full price and even then $10 for a 2008 title I still feel ripped off and the price proves that EA will never stop being a money grubbing parasite. To add to this, Steam needs to change the description of this game since as of now the Gamespy servers have been shut down indefinitely so the online Coop and multiplayer are no longer a functioning entity of this title.
The music of C&C has always been memorable this is especially the case with the Red Alert series.  However in RA3 they have yet again gone away from being GOOD and simply moved to the most repetitious garbage that I have had to listen to repeated through the ENTIRE CAMPAIGN.  You will hear a single song for the entirety of each an every single mission within the campaign as well as the multi and skirmish section, not ONCE is the famous Red Alert song played at any point within the game short of the menu, that is yet more proof that there is no longer a Command and Conquer series of RTS games at all.  They have simply screwed up on the entire game, which amazingly enough extends to even the music score which is unbelievable.
I am saddened that this title got such higher praises then I feel that it should have, as if the fans were so hopeful to the possibilities of the new EA Westwood titles that everyone seems to have given this game a pass regardless to how bad it truly is.  I feel sorry that the younger generations after me will never again know how good C&C titles used to be and that based on this, my last C&C title that I will buy, we will never see the good days again.

I loved the game at first, but the more I play it the more it irritates me.  At the lower levels, you can spend a few hours here and there having a blast, learning how to play and what dragon and weapon combination you can do the most damage with.  Unfortunately, leveling up too soon slows to a near halt, and you begin to realize just how unbalanced some of the types of attacks are.  An "update" early in 2014 added an auto-lock aim and the ability to strafe.  Add that to certain overly powerful attacks from certain dragons and you have inescapable death.  Seriously.  That's not an exaggeration.  It's impossible to avoid the attacks.  This kills the fun and often causes me to rage quit.  However, all that aside, I always end up going back to the game and trying again, with the (possibly foolish) hope that at some point perhaps I'll figure out how to defeat this foe, or the more likely hope that I'll get to play a few matches in which those particular attacks don't appear before I face them, die, and repeat the process.
Recommend w/ caveat:  If the devs fix the balance issues, I would absolutely, enthusiastically recommend this game.  As is, I recommend it only if you want to spend the money to buy the over-powerful dragons so that you can have the cheap thrill of hollow victories.  Or if you actually don't mind the occasional futile death match.

I have been holding off on Reviewing Stellaris because I wanted a clear picture of what the game is!
After having put more then 100 Hours into Stellaris I have found that I still can't answer that question reliably.
So I think I am going to start off with Broad Questions:
Is the game fun?  Yes
Is the game good? Yes
Would I recommend this game to others? Yes
Is it worth its price tag? Yes
So with that part out of the way I want it to be clear that I very much like this game BUT:
Stellaris is having a hard time claiming to be a Grand Strategy game!
It lacks Casus Beli's
The Game Pace is far too fast, it takes about as long as a Civ 5 game!
There is a complete lack of content for any playstyle thats not map painting!
Diplomacy is Abysmal
And Bug's are Galore
Basically I get NO Grand Stategy feel too Stellaris when I play it!  Infact it sometimes feels like it wants to be a Grand Strategy game but its not capable in its current form of grasping that role!  The game basically feels Naked with only two victory conditions that both involve lots of Pew Pew.....
So then I try to compare it too 4X games of new and old and well that leaves me in a similiar confused condition.  It just doesnt jive in my mind.  At times I feel some Masters of Orion or Galactic Civ like gameplay but by and large its so confused on its identity that it doesn't feel "4X" either....
So one of my biggest issues that I am having at this point in time is simply trying to classify Stellaris in my mind.  But whatever classification it finally evolves into its far from complete.  That is the one thing that really rings true when I play the game currently (1.0.2 - 5/17/2016 Only 8 days since release)  its not fnished.  Infact it often times feels like I am in a building with no walls just the 2*4 Frame and a roof....  There is a ton of work to do yet, its pretty obvious!
(Understand I am a Hardcore Paradox Fan who expects a Certain Level of product from Paradox)
The things I dislike the most:
Diplomacy:
-Very Lacking in options.
-The options you do have are again rarely if ever excepted by the AI unless you meet a very specific parameter.
-The AI itself fails to use the few diplomatic options that are currently in the game correctly.
Victory Conditions:
-An utter and complete lack of a victory type that doesnt involve Pew Pew??? You feel like you have more options playing as the Germans in Heart's of Iron then any Race in Stellaris....
Events:
- Severly lacking, this is the part I am most disappointed with, as all the short comings above I could easily ignore if there seemed like there was a credible effort put in to really make the world rich with events....  I really think the lack of events is what most makes Stellaris not feel like it has an Identity in my mind.  And then the events that are in the game are so MEH....  They almost feel like background flavor that has little relevance.
But with all that said,
Stellaris is a GEM its got a skeleton in place that has the potential to become a game thats better then Crusader Kings 2....   It has the potential to be one of the greatest of all time.  Its addictive, its flashy, its a must buy!  Even if its current state is filled with bug's and balance issues, and a Haven for Min Maxers....  Its addictive!!!

Little Inferno is yet another stylish creation by Tomorrow Corporation, the creators of World of Goo (which is a fantastic game in my opinion).
Just like World of Goo, Little Inferno has a very peculiar art style, which despite its oddness is rather aluring. The game revolves around the player burning different objects in a fireplace in order to both entertain himself as well as warm the house up. Lovely prospect don't you think? The objects that the player gets to burn are fairly varied, with more getting unlocked as the player earns money and completes special combinations. The combinations are simply 2 or more objects that have to be burnt at the same time. The game is fairly addictive, up to a point in which you realise that you're laughing while burning a school bus full of screaming children. Yup. That's when I realised that this game helped me develop a secret fixation with burning school buses.
In all seriousness though, this game is a great time consumer and actually does make the player question their sanity at times, as well as the consequences of their actions in game. I definitely recommend it as its both enjoyable and excellent at relieving stress accumulated on a bad day.

I grabbed Unexplored at random after hearing a synopsis from Austin Walker over on Waypoint radio months and months ago now. it sounded kinda clever and also, it was cheap. hundreds of hours later, i can easily say this has been one of the best entertainment purchases i've ever made in my life, and in a year as packed with all-star titles as 2017, it's easily in the top five releases of the year.
It's hard to exactly think of how to arrange my thoughts on the game so i'll go through whatever comes to me. First and foremost this sets a new gold standard for procedural generation in games. Not roguelikes; absolutely anything, at all. the developer's concept of cyclical level generation does what no game before has -- creating a rich, varied, and complex play experience each and every game, with levels, puzzles and traps that feel hand-crafted.
The game's ability to generate a holistic dungeon environment, implement backtracking and secrets in inteesting ways and create a consistend dungeon ecology from level to level creates a feeling of a hand-crafted dungeon delve on every playthrough (or nearly so). After more than 100 hours i'm still finding new surprises, getting caught off guard by unexpected situations and even seeing new bosses and items that i haven't encountered before.
More than this, JD has created a dungeon environment with enough variation and cleverly-programmed interactions between elements and items that a very rare thing emerges; you begin to realize that just about anything that seems like it should work, does. As simple as it sounds, this is a profound concept, and all the more impressive that the game manages it with a seemingly simple, top-down hack and slash style of play. Simple controls, a light but satisfyingly chunky stat system and a low fantasy, low-magic sort of setting means finding a single bundle of arrows, a potion of poison gas, a staff of disarming, can all be momentous experiences, defining a playthrough or giving you the key you need to escape doom at a critical moment -- aided, again, by the level generator's cleverness.
If you like roguelikes, zelda-style action adventures where your tools are your weapons, classical dungeon delves, or just want to see what should rightly be the new acceptable standard for random level generation -- grab Unexplored, give it a few runs, and watch it surprise you again and again.

F.E.A.R is a fun ride. The pacing of the game is pretty good but repetative in places. Nevertheless, it's an accomplished shooter with some really quite decent A.I who will flank you when they can. Mastering the 'lean' is advisable as it keeps you mostly in cover and can really save you at times.
The weapon set is not too big but is quite varied. Only being able to carry three weapons at a time (explosives not included) the game encourages you to make a tactical selecton that suits you best. The game supplies you with health, armour and ammo enough to keep the pace of the game flowing nicely.
But what about the scare factor i hear you say; well, for the most part it's just very eerie and there are some very creepy sequences early on. As the game progresses it gets a little more tense, but at times i feel the game wants you to feel scared so much it acctually detracts from the horror. That said however there are some genuine jump scare moments where ive just fired wildly in the general direction of what scared me and had a few minature heart attacks.
If you like FPS games this one's for you; the weapon design is well done, the shooting feels satisfying and theres lots of blood and ever dismemberment with a well placed grenade. If you're only after the horror or scary element defenatly consider it but its more a good shooter than a survival horror game so don't expect too much on that front. All in all i'd give this a very high 7/10.

The AI is tough, in that the soldiers will actively move around and try to kill you. In addition the main character is not too much of a super hero yet so you have roughly the same hitpoints as the soldiers you kill. It's fun, it's creepy, it's FEAR. The main game will run you 7-10 hours, EP 1 about 5 and I have not gone though EP 2 yet.
The expansions are deemed Noncanon by the company that went on to make Fear 2 and 3; Characters that die in the expansions continue to appear in the series. Though I was told if I ignore the deathes for the most part the expansions still apply.
Alma. That is the name of the creepy girl that you will see often throughout the series. Like any rage-stricken ghost her motives in the first game are completely nonsensical. Sometimes she kills good guys, sometimes badguys. Sometimes she makes things worse, sometimes better. Some times she wants to protect you, the next thing you know specters are trying to rip out your intenstines. In the first expansion pack she even seemed to be temporarily at peace after bombarding the player with hellish visions, what triggered the peace still confuses me as all the player does is traverse to the other side of a morgue.
I only have two complaints. Complaint one is: There is no contractor in the world good enough at his job not getting fired for the monstrocity that is the floor planning of every single building in Auburn. Kitchens become bathrooms become dining halls become maturnity wards and suddenly you may even drop into a sewer or elevator. This often left me disjointed and confused in terms of what direction I should be going even though I never seemed to get stuck enough to warrant a walkthrough. FEAR Obeys 90's shooter laws. Climbing into Vents is often a brilliant and eerily safe idea, side rooms typically have loot, and red valves are usable.
Second complaint. It's hinted throughout the game that the Point Man is more or less safe from Alma's outbursts. Of course she can and will kill you a few times but she has her reasons. But this seriously undermines her presence after completing FEAR and moving on to the first expansion.  The second expansion and Fear 2 have a different protagonist so this is more of a gripe about expansion 1's design.

Unexplored is a dungeon delver roguelike. It is centered in extensive exploration and harsh combats with a great variety of mobs to fight. It is pleasant, with great replayability and amazing depth.
Pros:
+Small decision you make affects your overall outcome.
+Achievement unlock possibilities for starts.
+Classes to add a little more flavor and make it even more awesome.
+The game is updated frequently.
+Pause button to take decisions and change equipment
+Great dungeon generation
+Grabbing and sneak options
+Humanoids also picks stuff from ground to use against you
+Replay levels by using their seeds
Neutral:
=Simple to play, hard to master.
=Fights are not beneficial, there is no xp, only loot from what mobs are wearing.
=Harsh scaling, the deeper you got the less powerful you feel, even with a ton of magic items.
=Undead really don't die.
Cons:
-Clunky Graphics
-A few bugs, sometimes you need to use the pray for help button
-Dumb AI, remembering skyrim's famous guards that forget you were there
-Some actions are too clouded, like grabbing, stealing and crafting.

Frankly, I love DD Eternity. I put a decent amount of time (173 hours) into the first Dungeon Defenders and loved it, but eventually stopped playing it. The fact that this game offers all the DLC together with the base game as a single package is just a bonus on top of the awesome gameplay.
A lot of the reviews around ♥♥♥♥♥ about being unable to play solo or the multiplayer taverns. Solo and private sessions have been promised, with the private sessions already having been delivered. And solo is fine too, all you have to do is start a private session without anybody in your Playverse party.
My only real gripe with the game is the new Playverse system. It has another overlay entirely on the game, which is rather clunky. I mean, in order to play with my friend, I have to make a party, invite him, and he has to make a party too before he can join? What?
Also, the game is a bit confusing at first. Tooltips and a tutorial, perhaps, would be great for newbies. I could barely figure out how to change my character's name when I first started the game up, since there were no tooltips.
Overall, while the clunky new overlay and lack of clear tips hinder new players and veterans alike, they don't particularly reduce the fun you can have with this game. I give it an 8.5 / 10, and damn is it fun.

RIDE has its flaws but there's no major problem not to recommend it to any motorcycle enthusiast. It does the job to render good riding sensation, the bikes selection is large, there could be more tracks but there's a pleasant mix of real & theme based (Japan, Wales, French riviera..) course.
As you probably know, there's no real competition for motorcycle racing game. Many reviews here refers to Tourist Trophy on PS2 (2006) and even Superbike 2001 (GP500 anyone?). Now if you're one of those that have not been convinced by MotoGP piloting model, i'd suggest you give this one a try.
Indeed it's rather close to Tourist Trophy in terms of sensation, bikes feels a little bit lighter and the speed effect is more convincing in RIDE. With all assistance desactivated, careful attention is needed on acceleration and braking. If you've never ride a motorcycle, it does matter to brake with the rear brake first then front (and also brake straight and never use the front brake when turning) and RIDE renders all of that.
Now the flaws. First it's not very beautiful, i mentioned speed effect and i'd add motorbike models are well done, the rest is outdated. Textures are blurry, background landscape is terrible, no wow effect here. Sounds are failed for 2 cylinders engine (come on guys you're developping from italy), and changing your exhaust doesn't help. Prepare your own tracklist as well. There's also the "AI" that goes from buggy to terrible, at first it's funny to see an AI going wheelie at some start, but the constant ramming is ruining the fun at times.
Recommended to all poor thirsty racers in need of something to keep up. After almost 10 years since Tourist Trophy guys, let's just hope it's not the last of its kind.

Review:
I bought this game while on sale, and with a coupon, which made it around $2-3. I figured that I would give it a try, and I am glad I did. Though this game can be very frustrating, especially when the difficulty increases a lot (Was stuck on levels 7-14 for weeks), it's a very fun game to play. It has multiplayer, skirmish, and campaign.
In campaign, your goal is to capture all of the planets, the enemy's home planets, or hold the 'flag' planet, using your force/army. You can upgrade your character/force, and gain money/energy.
In skirmish, you face 1-3 enemies and do the same as campaign, except here you can play as any character and can spend time practicing if you're having troubles on a level.
I have not played multiplayer on this game, but I plan to soon!
Overall, I would recommend this to anyone who likes a good, challenging game, and has patience and time on hand.
Pros:
-Multiplayer (haven't tried it)
-Challenging
-Good graphics and color
-Fun, upbeat music
-Multiple characters to play
-Campaign
-Skirmish
Cons:
-Difficulty increases a lot after level 6
-Robots are harder to play as
-Almost sure it's impossible to complete the campaign, at least for me

First of all I have to say that I like Stellaris. I like it a lot. Even though I haven´t played it a lot yet, I know that it will be a lasting classic for me. Especially in multiplayer.
That being said, it also has its problems. This is quite understandable considering the vast scope and complexity of the game. There are numerous reviews which cover the obvious weaknesses of Stellaris at the moment (AI, mid-game, diplomacy, combat) so I won´t list them here.
The one thing I would like to improve in Stellaris is the victory conditions. I like and play boardgames quite a lot as well and Twilight Imperium 3rd edition happens to be my all time favorite. One of the key elements of the game are the ever changing victory conditions and the fact that the largest empire isn´t necessary the winning empire.
I would suggest a quite bold approach on the victory conditions. Every race would choose their own victory condition as a part of their race creation. An easy victory condition will cost a lot and force you to create an otherwise weak race whereas a hard victory condition will give you lots of points to create a strong race. This will create a galaxy with even more different races and create a natural instability between them. Strong races naturally become empires whereas weaker ones create alliances and federations or try to say out of scope of everyone else.
This brings me to the next idea conserning victory conditions. In addition to every races starting victory condition, during the game races might get new victory conditions or their victory conditions might change. These can happen for example when creating alliances and federations. Alliances and federations would be classified to a certain type (dominance, defensive, scientific, mercantile etc.) and a race in a such alliance/federation would have an extra victory condition. For example if you´re in a dominance alliance your extra victory condition might be that the alliance must hold a certain percentage of the galaxy. New victory conditions or modifiers to existing ones could also emerge from tech discoveries, cultural events and simply when the game progresses long enough. So if the game goes on long enough, your victory condition might get harder to achieve (this will make it possible to win even in early game but balance the mid and late game so that meeting victory conditions isn´t too easy when you have lots of resources (planets, tech, fleet).
I know this would be a significant change to the game and create lots of challenges especially with the AI, but I think it would enhance the diversity and unpredictability of the galaxy, make it possible to win with very different races and approaches and just create an even more "alive" and beliavable universe.

Little Inferno is a great game, but it's important to know what it is. On the simplest level, it's simply burning things in a fireplace. What impresses me so much with this is that the physics of burning stuff is done quite well, and there's something satisfying just watching stuff burn (as there should be) and that alone was fun to play with for a while.
The next level is the combo system, whereby you get some extra perks by burning certain objects together. For the most part, these can be figured out with a bit of thinking, although there's a few of them that I think are not 'good' solutions. Or at least, I think there's more sensible solutions to it. There's 99 combos, and I'd say about 2/3rds can be gotten relatively easily, but the last few can be really tricky.
On the final level, there's a sort of plot-based undercurrent in here that I think is really interesting initially, but ultimately unsatisfying. It is sorta similar to how World of Goo had a similar plot that is introduced very subtly. I really wish that the plot had been a bit more fleshed out, I get hints of a larger message it was meant to lead to, but it feels indecisive about it.
Overall, the game's a fun 4-5 hours and I think there's a good sense of humour to it. There's some forced waiting in the game that I think could've been reduced so that late game was less tedious at points (particularly when trying to figure out combos). That said, unlike World of Goo, there really isn't replay value, unless you enjoy watching the fire. There's nothing to go back and try to earn once you have figured out all the combos so I do think it's important to know that buying this game is buying a 4-5 hour experience and not much more than that.

A surprisingly fun platformer, with good spritework, backgrounds, effects, and very engaging gameplay.  If you like that genre of game, you'll likely enjoy Dust, and so I wholeheartedly recommend this game.
But my recommendation does not come without a disclaimer. This game is held back from being truly good by three major flaws: character art, a major development issue, and length.
Firstly, what are otherwise interesting characters with some good humorous interaction is marred by the worst furry art in any video game ever seriously released on the market.  I have nothing in particular against furry art, but most of the characters in this game are really badly done.  The sprites are fine, but during the dialog the art is cringe-inducing.
Secondly, the last area and end of the game's story was cut due to development constraints, resulting in some odd plotholes and a replacement ending that does not meaningfully resolve the underlying story elements.  The replacement ending isn't bad really, but it was not what the game was building towards and kinda wrecks the story.
Lastly, the game is short.  I beat the whole game on hard and did every sidequest.  It took 11 hours and at least 3 of those were just the game being left on because I was too lazy to turn it off when I went out.
If those very real flaws don't discourage you, you will enjoy this otherwise very charming game.

Unexplored is a lovely real-time pausable Roguelike dungeon crawler.
The game has many game modes, some unlockable classes, and tons of variably generated content.
The dungeons are really interesting and procedurally made with unique puzzles, varied enemies, unique and magical items, and explorer notes used to figure out puzzles and hints throughout the game keep you engaged and paying attention.
The procedural generation is the best I have seen. Areas are unique, and you need to use that to do well, and be prepared for anything.
The combat is a fun skill based timing system with damage types, and even passive damage from making your weapon contact enemies without swinging them.
The UI is pretty clean, and it is easy to tell what things are, and what is going on.
The elements of this game come together to make something really wonderful but hard to express.
It is simple to get into, but hard to master, and the entire game is replete with charm and character.

I was introduced into the Witcher world starting with Witcher 3: Wild Hunt (if you havn't picked this up already, what are you waiting for?  It's one of the best games ever made).  After experiencing the incredible gift from the heavens that is Witcher 3 I decided to go back and play the first two installments of the franchise.
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings at first glance did not look particularly amazing(at least compared to Witcher 3), but after I got into it a bit, I realized that this game was quite good.
Here is a quick rundown of some pros and cons:
- Captivating and interesting storyline.
- Beautiful world
- Your choices matter!  (Even sidequests that appear insignificant can have a significant outcome on the storyline.)
- Awesome soundtrack
- Quite poor interfacing issues (detailed below)
- A so-so combat system (also detailed below)
- Annoying navigation mechanics
While this game is awesome as a whole, it does have its flaws.  One of its biggest flaws is its combat system.  The combat system is a bit difficult to learn, but once you have learned it, it shouldn't be as much as a burden on you.  The combat system could be accurately described as inefficient, to say the least.  When first starting the game, the game seems ridiculously difficult at times simply because it is impossible to find decent gear early on.  Later on, however, it is much easier to buy/craft better gear, which then makes the difficulty a bit more manageable.  The auto-targetting system can be a real pain at times.  In most games, when you face an opponent and press the attack button/key, your character attacks that opponent.  That is not the case in this game.  Geralt will sometimes attack a random opponent if you are in the midst of a group of enemies.  Also, dodging enemy attacks can become very difficult when fighting groups of enemies, not because it is difficult to avoid them, but because the roll mechanic often times will not roll you in the direction you are wanting to roll to.  Sometimes I would try to dodge roll backwards, and I would instead go forwards, and therefore be killed by a horde of enemies.  All of these flaws mentioned above CAN be avoided with a bit of practice.  It's a shame you have to battle the mechanics, but it is what it is.
The navigation system can become particulary annoying at times.  There were many points in the game where I asked myself, "Where in the world do I need to go next?"  Sometimes it would take me up to half an hour to find the answer to that question.  The minimap does show you where to go most of the time, but it does so with a single orange triangle, which is very small and sometimes hard to see.  For some quests, you will be required to complete a task with absolutely no assistance from the minimap.  These quests could involve finding a certain character or fetching a certain item.  This issue is somewhat rare so I didn't find it too annoying, but when it did happen, it took me forever to find what I needed to find to progress.
Overall, once I got used to the sketchy mechanics, I really loved this game.

Dear past self,
If this message gets transported back into the past, then beware, do not buy Crypt of the Necrodancer. The thing is I love rhythm games. I played the living hell out of Beatmania, Pop'n Music, Dance Dance Revolution, Guitar Hero etc. But why do I shy away from this. Well, I have a theory... The developers had a bit of a problem, the complete lack of content. If you took the assets and converted it into a standard Sega Genesis style platformer, it would probably be thirty minutes long. If you want to know the exact game style, watch ten seconds of a Youtube video. That'll be enough to get the gist of the game.
So what do you do when you lack content. Simple, increase the difficulty and make it a rogue like. Imagine you had to reset every time you die in Super Mario Bros., then Super Mario Bros. would be a 12 hour game per play-through easily. On top of that, increase the randomness and danger of enemies. In games like Dark Souls, even after you've mastered the difficulty, you'll still find a large amount of content to explore. Rogue-likes have become "cool" and contemporary with people with many becoming fans of the genre, so it's an easy sell. But the thing is other rogue-likes actually have a large amount of content.
So to sell the watered down content the developers had to shoe horn every little thing that is popular among the Indie gaming crowd. Pixel art graphics, chip-tunes, rogue-like, randomly generated maps, high difficulty etc. Even the inclusion of the female protagonist doesn't seem natural, but forced. Especially since the game was made during the "Tropes vs. Women in Video Games"/Anita Sarkeesian era, where it became the hippest coolest thing to shoe-horn a female protagonist in a game. If you want to see a natural inclusion of women in games check out Kings Quest IV, Metroid or Tomb Raider 1.
So now the developer force-fed whatever is fashionable for the indie crowd into the game. Another thing that is shoe-horned into the experience is the story. The story is presented through a slide-show that is rendered into videos. Every story cutscene, including the intro, totals to between 8 and 9 minutes of video footage. These videos can be watched by browsing the game folder or checking Youtube. The minimalist way Spelunky presents it's setting is magnitudes better. As a hypothetical example: Cutscenes of the Spelunker trying to find his dad between levels wouldn't actually add anything.
Another smaller gripe is something you see in pixel art games: the resolution changes to whatever is convenient. If you are making a pixel art game, stick with pixel art rather than include high resolution videos at certain points.
Regarding graphical assets: The first Kings Quest was released in 1984 and had a total of 48 160x200 pixel screens the player can explore. I don't think Crypt of the Necrodancer has 48 50x50 pixel tiles in total. There are five zones with only around 5 unique tiles per zone.
The one good thing about the game is the soundtrack which is definitely worth a listen.
Ultimately I think Crypt of the Necrodancer is contrived. I think if you are a hipster wearing a retro game t-shirt, lensless glasses and claim to be a classic game collector, then you'll like this game. The game sells a style that is popular among a certain crowd, however it doesn't sell actual content or substance.

This games premise is simple, so if your looking for something super complex it's not here. Strategy and tactics do exist though as taking which planet and when to attack and when to defend becomes extremely critical. One move can cost you a planet and sometimes if your not quick enough to react, the game.
The premise is your a certain colony of either humans or robots, and you start conquering worlds one by one. Some battles can take place with one or up to three AI's. Of course, each sector is it's own game, so don't look to go Star Wars and try to conquer an entire galaxy. You start the game, and you are able to choose linearly which sector to attack next. Once you are at the in-game screen, the battle begins. Planets can be upgraded and can be selected to either defend or allow for attacks. Some planets when properly upgraded have some self defense mechanisms... although I wouldn't highly rely on it. Game types vary (which is always a good idea in any game) where one game may be domination where you need to take ALL planets whereas another game may have to do with monetary means to win - meaning more money you have the more powerful your units are. Send an attack wave to an enemy planet though and watch your assets freeze as your at war. Small divot game-types such as these keep the game interesting and want you to play more.
This game is good, however NOT RECOMMENDED FOR EVERYONE! If you like space games and a casual indie territory take-over game this may be for you. If your looking for Star Trek Online keep it movin'!

I was faced with this game, The Settlers Online, when I was popping by Steam to pass some time. I thought, hey, I liked the Settlers back in the day, why not give this a try. Sure, it's an "online" game, and might be simple for the times, but I liked the old-school Settlers 2, so this can't be too bad... can it?
The game starts out with a simple tutorial, getting you through the basics. Or so it seems. I still haven't made it out of this tutorial after playing for an hour, and it is basically dictating my every move. Not much for open-world civilization-building. The tutorial basically holds your hand for the entire time, and actually punishes you for thinking individually. I started building more buildings than it required, and suddenly couldn't complete the next steps of the tutorial. The tutorial steps are required for advancing levels, and levels are required for building more buildings. I was stuck. This reminds me of public school teachings, which are often more focussed on regurgitating facts than actual exploration, learning, and fun.
In addition to being an inherently fun-spoiling "read-and-repeat" experience the game is generally lacking in quality. Settlers 2 had a more convincing atmosphere, even now, 19 years after its creation. This game looks and feels like a very bad browser game with unconvincing animation; roads that "do not improve" (their wording, leaving out the subject of the sentence); mediocre graphics; unconvincing copy; etc.
One example of unconvincing copy is this: a quest describes "Bandit camps" as such:
In addition, the quests regularly fail to notice that prerequisites have been fulfilled. For example, I had to restart the game to unlock the quests for level 4 (because it hadn't noticed that I had reached said level), and upon reaching level 7 was completely stuck. Restarts didn't help it unlock the next quests, for which I had already fulfilled the prerequisites. With no way of advancing, I was, again, stuck. This time for good.
I spent around an hour playing this game, thinking, "maybe soon it will let me out of the tutorial, and, you know, actually play." It didn't. Don't play this game. It is a waste of time. It is hardly a game.
At least the "quit" button has an instant effect.

This is a less shameful version of games like Dungeon Keeper Mobile: a "free-to-wait" game. My entire time spent in the game was either waiting for a timer to finish counting down or navigating a menu. There were no clear objectives, no stakes, no intrigue, and no challenge.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown had the tutorial done and the objectives set in less than 5 minutes, even shorter if you took the option to skip the opening tutorial. Battle Nations, an example of what I consider to be a free-to-wait game actually done correctly, handed you a battle to fight it out while you built up your resources and troops to take on a looming threat, all the while the premium currency can be earned and is entirely optional for one to have.
But this game? Nothing. Just "build buildings, stockpile resources". If one were to take out the timers, then this game might have a chance at building up a decent pacing. As it stands, I was falling asleep and I wasn't even a half-hour into it.
The only good thing I can say about it is that during said time I wasn't badgered into spending money on premium currency. But I have a feeling that this may have changed had I trudged further in.

Its been a long time since I played this game. I burned out on it and needed time away from it. As a founder I got DLC's, added to my downloads. I dabbled in the behemonth Terran return and it was a blast to use precurser tech destroying the Dregin threat. So now it was time to play again. I am playing the Terrans first voyage into space campaign. I have read many of the recent reviews and their comments. Some I will address with my spin of the game and I will also address areas of the game I feel are strange to me.
First the diversifications of the races not being apparent. The best advice I can give you is make a couple of custom races before you even pay your first game. Make your own warrior race, or trade race or fanatic race, look at the pluses and minuses. these numbers show the matrix of the race, that the AI will use to run it. these numbers are subtle but can steamroller you in the actual game if you dont know what they mean. When you meet a race in the actual game immediately go to the diplomacy screen and read up on the race and his key traits, also what he thinks of you good or bad and how untrusting or trusting it is to you.
what is your races strength, the Terrans diplomacy helped me and I have not been attacked or fired a shot and my game is now in the accension phase of the game. it has been very tricky to balance out the races opinions of the Terrans, I came close to war many times. but a gift of some extra credits here and there a trade route established at a critical time can avoid war. It is expensive to build a fleet to keep up with the Dregin or Alterion race, the global economics is quite robust and it works like a real world economy, a stream turns into a brook,turns into a river. do i do research or construction, do i do it system wide or planet wide. the difference in races those +1's and -1s now come into play. you should pick your race on your play style. the AI plays with those numbers. If you as a live player play as a terran you have to play the game using your diplomatic bonuses. Ripe for the picking can go up to i believe a minus 3 agrgession modifier I had to override it with 3 point of positive diplomacy. Early in the game hitting the diplomacy screen every turn and base your strategy of this information. This screen is your chessboard not the actual galaxy map.
Now your planets these are your economy engines and can spin out of control without you even knowing it until long into the game, every decision you make on each of your planets is crutial to a robust economy or a bleeding economy. the AI plays its economy very efficient, again playing the race pluses and minuses to the max.
If you decide to build ships you want to look at the opposing races ships and like in real life build your strengths to his weaknesses. if he uses beams you research shields, if he has no missle defence research missles. Each race picks a favorite and in the latter game you may have fleets made up to fight different races with your ships named that way. This means you must make custom ships, the Terrans core ships are to weak in many instances, you must make and outfit custom ships
Again like the real world accurate intellegence and planning is key to this game. If you pick up this game and decide to play the Terrans or any other race without understanding them you will get steam rolled in the age of war.
Meta gamers can break this game at this time. Many people have posted how so I will not go into detail.
This game is very deep, and like I said a move you did 30 turns ago can mess you up in your whole future game if you dont monitor your cause and effect factor.
Now some thing I feel need to be addressed.
Star Docks: they never improve they can never hold their own in a fight, you can put a hefty starbase near them but only the AI will attack that starbase first a human player will just bypass all your starbases and go for your spacedock. I would like to see a stardock actually being part of a starbase. taking on the starbases protection.
Starbases: I am using tons of starbases in my game, one thing I noticed is that no matter how many modules I put on the starbase, the base hitpoints never change, just the idea of the increase of mass brought about by the modules should increase the mass, making starbases being able to have possible thousands of hitpoints.
Also I think that as a starbase takes damage modules go offline, so a damaged starbase is not as effective as a fully functioing one.
also just like a space dock you should be able to move a starbase slowly to reposition it after placement.
Planet panel: in GC2 you could see in the planet screen if your planet had a stardock orbiting it. I miss this feature, as you scroll through your planet screens you can lose track of your planets that have a stardock built by it.
Ideology tree: To me is too powerful in certain areas, and as a general note can really hurt or help you in the early game.

So its been 3 years and I still haven't made a review of this game. However, due to recent times, I feel like I need to ensure what the player can encounter, and what I think you should help the betterment of the game. I both do and don't recommend this game for many many reasons. For the past 3 years of playing Garry's Mod, I've experienced nothing but cancer, but fun at the same time. Garry's Mod for these past years, has gone down this hole where very few unique servers actually become successful and people obtain a mindset that each server is just a copy and paste, so whatever you can get on one server, might as well stay on there as it most likely isn't the same for other servers. Sure there are unique successful servers, but what I'm talking about are unique starting out servers. Servers in which people have spent money on as if they were spending money on a game project, expecting you to play, only to come with unfortunate fact that you need staff before you even can start a server, and that's the only thing you need. However that alone is incredibly difficult due to the interests of most players being really short. This has caused me unparamounted wasted money, time, and resources all because I had put faith and trust that these staff members would be doing what I had requested for them to do. None had arrived, and like I said, it wasted money, time, and resources. Why should this concern you if you buy this game? Well think of it like this, there is a current issue in our triple-A market where there's a loss in quality, and even games that are essentially copied and pastes like Call Of Duty for example. This is almost exactly the same for Garry's Mod, and playing on these copy and paste servers isn't going to fix this issue. Now what I suggest is to give a gamemode a try, and look at a few servers. Take Star Wars Rp for example, look at a few servers, and then look at which ones are unique from any others that you've joined, and then look at how all the other servers are directly the same. Playing on those unique servers will help aid this major issue in the Garry's Mod development area, and it will start to fix this issue and finally get rid of copy and paste servers.
Now before I pretty much end it there, I included this in the review because I wanted to make a statement, and wanted to keep those who would get this game informed about this games community issues, but do note that this only scratches the surface of its issues, but also its greatness in this game.

It's cheap! It's good! It's fun! Basically, why don't you already own this?!
Binding of Isaac is one of the better "2D Top-Down Adventure Games". It has so many things to unlock. You could play this for hours on end and you still wouldn't even have the slightest of a chance of seeing everything that this game has to offer.
Oh, and did I mention it's a rougelike? No? Well, I did now. Every single time you press that tempting "Start" button, a whole new world is generated. Well, less of a world, more of a dungeon. That aside, even if you've unlocked every character, collected every item, done everything there is to do, you still haven't seen everything this game has to offer. Every floor is different!
The music. Oh, yes, the music... I'd just like to point out something. The best track in the entire game, in my opinion, is the Shop theme. All of this music is wonderful, but that Shop theme... Mmmh! So good!
The replay value on this is very high. You'll spend hours upon hours looking for everything.
The graphics aren't TOO good. I can't complain, though. It runs quite well, even on high, on this potato of mine. They're not eyesores, but they're not exactly eye-candy, either.
Now, let us delve into the world of Wrath of the Lamb. Basically, you have to go through Binding of Isaac as normal... And then on your next playthrough... There's a few extra floors! How wonderful!
There's new rooms, new enemies, new bosses, new music, new characters, everything a DLC could possibly offer, unlike SOME games that only add one new thing for every $15 worth of DLC.
The DLC is cheap and fun! Buy it along with the main game!
Now, if you're looking to buy this, and you can't afford $7 (not making fun if you can't, I couldn't get it either), wait until it's on sale. I managed to get DLC and BoI together for about $2.50!
Now, by the end of this review, your wallet is probably preparing itself to lose a bit of weight. Good! This game is worthy of purchase!

Of course, it was originally a ps1 game. The pc version has SOME enhancements, if you can call it that. running it at a higher resolution is pointless as the pre-rendered backgrounds are very low quality, and the new in game models are nice but for some reason the world map looks very bad. Dear past self,
If this message gets transported back into the past, then beware, do not buy Crypt of the Necrodancer. The thing is I love rhythm games. I played the living hell out of Beatmania, Pop'n Music, Dance Dance Revolution, Guitar Hero etc. But why do I shy away from this. Well, I have a theory... The developers had a bit of a problem, the complete lack of content. If you took the assets and converted it into a standard Sega Genesis style platformer, it would probably be thirty minutes long. If you want to know the exact game style, watch ten seconds of a Youtube video. That'll be enough to get the gist of the game.
So what do you do when you lack content. Simple, increase the difficulty and make it a rogue like. Imagine you had to reset every time you die in Super Mario Bros., then Super Mario Bros. would be a 12 hour game per play-through easily. On top of that, increase the randomness and danger of enemies. In games like Dark Souls, even after you've mastered the difficulty, you'll still find a large amount of content to explore. Rogue-likes have become "cool" and contemporary with people with many becoming fans of the genre, so it's an easy sell. But the thing is other rogue-likes actually have a large amount of content.
So to sell the watered down content the developers had to shoe horn every little thing that is popular among the Indie gaming crowd. Pixel art graphics, chip-tunes, rogue-like, randomly generated maps, high difficulty etc. Even the inclusion of the female protagonist doesn't seem natural, but forced. Especially since the game was made during the "Tropes vs. Women in Video Games"/Anita Sarkeesian era, where it became the hippest coolest thing to shoe-horn a female protagonist in a game. If you want to see a natural inclusion of women in games check out Kings Quest IV, Metroid or Tomb Raider 1.
So now the developer force-fed whatever is fashionable for the indie crowd into the game. Another thing that is shoe-horned into the experience is the story. The story is presented through a slide-show that is rendered into videos. Every story cutscene, including the intro, totals to between 8 and 9 minutes of video footage. These videos can be watched by browsing the game folder or checking Youtube. The minimalist way Spelunky presents it's setting is magnitudes better. As a hypothetical example: Cutscenes of the Spelunker trying to find his dad between levels wouldn't actually add anything.
Another smaller gripe is something you see in pixel art games: the resolution changes to whatever is convenient. If you are making a pixel art game, stick with pixel art rather than include high resolution videos at certain points.
Regarding graphical assets: The first Kings Quest was released in 1984 and had a total of 48 160x200 pixel screens the player can explore. I don't think Crypt of the Necrodancer has 48 50x50 pixel tiles in total. There are five zones with only around 5 unique tiles per zone.
The one good thing about the game is the soundtrack which is definitely worth a listen.
Ultimately I think Crypt of the Necrodancer is contrived. I think if you are a hipster wearing a retro game t-shirt, lensless glasses and claim to be a classic game collector, then you'll like this game. The game sells a style that is popular among a certain crowd, however it doesn't sell actual content or substance.

Pinning down precisely what makes the world of The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings so enthralling took me some time. It's not that the fiction is particularly "mature," though that's undoubtedly a term that will be tossed around until the next hyper-gritty fantasy game pops up. Think about it for a second: The Witcher, Geralt of Rivia, is a crag-faced, cat-eyed, gravelly-voiced mutant hardass who only stops screwing and fighting when occasion calls for a philosopher, at which point he dutifully duels scholars and monarchs with a tongue as sharp as either of his two swords. He is a character straight out of a 15-year-old boy's misused English notebook; the wounded warrior poet who, by the way, gets all the consequence-free sex he can handle, since he's totally shooting blanks, bro. And sure, he's stoic -- but he's also got a sensitive soul somewhere beneath that scar-laden chest of his, damn it.
No, what makes the Witcher's world so absorbing is an amazingly cohesive and consistent visual vocabulary that is -- and I know this is going to sound ridiculous -- far more logical than is typical for fantasy games. The impoverished fishermen of the riverside village of Flotsam shuffle around in nothing but ruddy underwear. Dumpy town guards patrol in filthy rags that still bear their national colors. Ornate attire is (for once) consigned solely to the upper class. Buildings look planted and properly dilapidated. This may seem a small thing, but from the first minutes of the game, it's clear how much effort has gone into researching how a society like the one portrayed would look; this medieval civilization, infused with -- but not dominated by -- magic and mystery (props to developer CD Projekt), is just awesome.
Similarly impressive: the degree to which the story changes based on your actions. Game makers (and publishers, and shareholders, and preview writers) love to crow on about choices and consequences. Hell, if you buy the PR spin, every single BioWare game in the past decade has been a watershed moment for cause and effect in video game storytelling. But frankly, the lofty language usually leads to a letdown -- the best we usually get are mundane tics on a morality slider that may or may not unlock a new dialogue tree, or perhaps a new companion somewhere down the road. I'd go so far as to argue that the only stable of games that's been quietly, consistently offering a serious set of genuinely game-altering forks-in-the-road for nearly a decade now is Acquire's Way of the Samurai series.
Not anymore.
While we have the underlying storyline of murder, intrigue, and (more stupidly) amnesia to which The Witcher 2 continually returns, the minutiae is wholly malleable. The allies Geralt makes on his journey and the enemies he combats shift with your mood swings; larger decision points alter the landscape of the world dramatically, but even minor events can cause repercussions much later in the game -- and how the whole thing ends is entirely your choice. Reading after-action reports from fellow players is like a game unto itself. Nobody seems to experience quite the same scenarios.
Not all is well in the Pontar Valley, however. Combat, for instance, is a serious problem made even worse by a poorly implemented, obscenely difficult and unhelpful opening segment. Plow into battle unprepared, and you might as well expect the worst: Even on moderate difficulty levels, this is not a game in which potential sources of aid can be ignored. Traps, bombs, magic, daggers, pre-battle potions... every tool in Geralt's arsenal is an absolute necessity.
Once I got the basics down, the extremely acrobatic, constantly active feint-and-parry style of Witcher warfare became seriously enjoyable -- just don't expect the prologue section to teach you much of anything valuable. And even when I finally felt like a proper monster-hunting mutant badass, I occasionally came across the rare room or fight so absurd that I had to wonder if CD Projekt understood the limitations of its own combat system. Geralt in a room too cramped to allow for falling back and trap placement? Battles before which you have no time to meditate and drink potions? No thanks.
Worse still, the user interface only exacerbates the combat system's flaws by forcing the player to keep an eye on everything but the melee itself. Geralt's vigor (read: mana) meter, health meter, buff/debuff indicators, and equipped spells/items are all scattered across the screen, which is a serious drawback when you're surrounded by screeching harpies.
But not even a terrible introductory sequence can take away from what is otherwise a fantastic game. Sure, the story is goofy, and at times the fighting is offensively clunky. The world isn't as colossal as the first Witcher's, and the ending is a bit of a tease. But in a time when I rarely bother to finish single-player games, I'm happy (and slightly embarrassed) to say that I'm already several hours into a second playthrough of Assassins of Kings. And I can't think of a better compliment than that.

Wow, what a game! -8/10
10 hours played
Motorcycle owner/fan
*MUST BE PLAYED WITH A CONTROLLER*- I can not emphasize this enough
There is no way to get the accuracy and finesse required out of a keyboard(at least using the most realistic physics). With a controller not only can you modulate the gas, brakes, and turning angle in a fluid way (which is extremely important to get a clean line), but you also get force feedback-which adds to the experience immensley. Every shift has a little rumble to it, you can feel when your tires are reaching/passing their grip threshold, and it's much easier to tell when you're close to the wall/another rider. I would not bother playing this game without one.
PROTIP FOR NEXT GAME- VR/steam controller native suppourt would be amazing.
Pros:
-Good graphics, Excellent detail in all of the bike models, all the way down to the proper speedo/tach layout.
-The tracks are fun and challenging, once again a lot of work went into making sure everything felt real, right down to the skidmarks on the road. Additional tracks would be nice, even as dlc(pikes peak pls). The crowds are your standard racing game low detail model but that really isn't why one plays the game.
-A decent amount of character customization and an excellent amount of riding style customization. I was amazed when I figured out how tweakable this was.
-The reverse function is super helpful when having issues with a certain corner. It allows you to reverse approximately the last 15 seconds and even change cameral angles to figure out exactly what the issue is. This feature should be in every racing game
-The first person perspective inside the helmet is very involving. The sensation of speed has been translated very well to a video game, even including accurate sounding wind buffeting, blurring of vision and helmet shaking.
-The mechanics, for the most part, are faithfully accurate to motorcycling. Using the brakes properly has been the hardest thing for me to figure out but I am starting to get it. *Big asterisk* There is no clutch control, which, while really only needed for starting, still removes a major component of a race, especially in drag races. This would be an awesome addition to subsequent games.
-Extensive motorcycle roster--includes basically every major production superbike and naked bike from 2015 - INCLUDING THE MOTHERF***ING LIGHTNING 218 OMGGGGGG. All bikes have all the main customization options that are normally changed. I wish the was a bit more variety of options in a few areas, namely tires and rims but that really isn't an issue.
-A decent amount of bike setup customization including, preload, spring stiffness, and preload with the top tier suspension, and full gearbox ratio customization with the top tier gearbox. *Things to add* Steering angle, more levels of gearbox and suspension customization, rear swingarm length, steering dampener settings, ecu timing and fueling, new throttle profiles, and EXTREMELY IMPORTANTLY, the ability to change settings on the fly to feel the difference and make it easier to experiment with different setups to find what works for you. It's annoying to have to go through three loading screens everytime you want to make an adjustment. A dyno would be nice too.
Cons, and there are a few big ones:
-THE BIGGEST PROBLEM WITH THIS GAME--Bike sound. While the sounds of different bikes vary appropriately according to displacment, engine arrangement, and exhaust, it's very obvious that not much money was put toward making the bikes sound real. When you're making a game with the sole intent of creating the most accurate bike simulator out there, this is hugely important. Does it do the job? Yes, I can shift at the proper time based on the sound. Does it add to the experience? NO. It most definitely removes from it. All the bikes have this wierd low quality synthesizer-esque sound that is just bad. I almost didn't buy the game because of this. The exhaust and intake systems should also have a more realistic effect on the overall sound.
-Controller integration, while superb with actual gameplay, does not properly transfer to the replay and picture taking functions. There is no way for me to save screenshots, which might be an issue with keyboards as well. Many of the main and contextual menus do not properly display controller buttons. Also, RB is reserved for the chat function which I'm sure most people will not be using--especially in the MIDDLE OF A RACE. Complete absurdity.
-No way to practice on a track in career mode-just an extra hassle and a few loading screens to switch to time trial but nevertheless annoying for something that is so essential to the game.
-No real sense of career progression at least in this point in the game. It feels like there's just a bunch of tracks that I will eventually win. The player should start out in low stakes, low displacement, public, ametur races and have to work their way up to the big leagues. The amount of money you get from even the lowest tier career mode races is enough to buy a new bike every 2-3 races. While it's nice to have access to the coolest bikes right from the get go it cheapens their value. All bikes should be available outside of career mode, but you should really have to work to earn them inside it.
-Mirrors do not function
Additional ways for the game to be improved:
-More extensive career mode. Sponsorship, factory and private teams, custom works parts, rivalries, greater acceptance of non-podium spots(to encourage playing on harder modes), qualifying, no restarts on official races(although I feel the rewind function to be neccesary to deal with the random crap that comes with the fact that this is a simulation and not real life), better integration of team members, multiple seasons, and more varied lengths of races are some ways to improve this.
-Tire, brake pad, slider, and chain wear would all be nice to see in addition to the already existing need to replace oil every few races (which is a nice touch)
-More bike customization options. Super/Turbocharging, Fuel injection system hardware, High-compression heads and forged pistons and cranks, different camshaft profiles, frame sliders, and more Colour options. Only being allowed to use the factory available colours is pretty crappy.
-Easier to navigate menus. Mostly evident in the bike customization menu, categories with many colour options are all one massive list. The different styles should be listed independently of colour selection.
-A drafting element
-A NFSU2 style free roam would be neat
TL;DR
A good game provided you can get past the sound. A lot of attention to detail even though this game doesn't seem to have been made on a large budget. Mechanics are good but must be played with a controller. If you like motorcycles and video games, buy it.

While clearly inspired by Galcon, Planet's Under Attack adds some much needed depth to the formula. Your planets produce units as in Galcon but attacking requires money. While you attack you don't generate money. Also, the closer you are to your money cap, the more powerful your ships are. Also, sending ships to defend a planet you already control costs nothing. This creates a wonderful risk/reward balance where you want to commit to attacks you can win, and only with just enough ships to take it.
Now add in 2 other races that each have modified rules for production (think the races in Starcraft 2 and how they are similar but unique in how they go about it) and you have not only a fine single player game but a great multiplayer setup. The campaign unfortunately only features the humans.
If you liked Eufloria, Mushroom Wars, or Blue Libra 2, there's definitely something new to like here.

I really want to like this game. It's cute, the story is interesting and touching. But unfortunately, the gameplay ends up hindering the story more than it helps. It's sort of a puzzle game, but the puzzle elements are limited to determining what combination of objects to put in the fireplace. It's fun for a little while. But after a while it just becomes a boring grind of waiting for the next thing to come and hoping you've solved the developers' next vague riddle. On top of this, the delays in objects arriving tend to bog down gameplay for no real reason. You'll often find yourself staring at an empty fireplace with nothing to do while you wait for the clock to tick away on your next item.
The world is interesting and the riddles are basically a word game hidden behind a narrative driven mechanic. If the story and puzzles were delivered in a more straightforward method, I probably would have been happy to play through it. But as it is, it's bogged down in the game mechanics. It disappoints me to see such an interesting world get bogged down in a mechanic, but that's exactly what has happened here. The reward of burning the correct combos of things (or anything at all you throw in the fireplace) is to give you more things to burn that behave in exactly the same way as the last set of things you could burn, you just need to wait longer and pay more for them (not that money is ever an issue in this game, since literally everything you throw in the fireplace gives more than it costs). It could probably do without the money element at all, as it just serves to force you to grind out some cheaper items if you repeatly fail guessing an expensive combo. No new mechanics or challenges are introduced. Just more waiting and more burning.
Good content, needs better music and some sort of campaign other than selecting tiers.
