First of all I have to say that I like Stellaris. I like it a lot. Even though I haven´t played it a lot yet, I know that it will be a lasting classic for me. Especially in multiplayer.
That being said, it also has its problems. This is quite understandable considering the vast scope and complexity of the game. There are numerous reviews which cover the obvious weaknesses of Stellaris at the moment (AI, mid-game, diplomacy, combat) so I won´t list them here.
The one thing I would like to improve in Stellaris is the victory conditions. I like and play boardgames quite a lot as well and Twilight Imperium 3rd edition happens to be my all time favorite. One of the key elements of the game are the ever changing victory conditions and the fact that the largest empire isn´t necessary the winning empire.
I would suggest a quite bold approach on the victory conditions. Every race would choose their own victory condition as a part of their race creation. An easy victory condition will cost a lot and force you to create an otherwise weak race whereas a hard victory condition will give you lots of points to create a strong race. This will create a galaxy with even more different races and create a natural instability between them. Strong races naturally become empires whereas weaker ones create alliances and federations or try to say out of scope of everyone else.
This brings me to the next idea conserning victory conditions. In addition to every races starting victory condition, during the game races might get new victory conditions or their victory conditions might change. These can happen for example when creating alliances and federations. Alliances and federations would be classified to a certain type (dominance, defensive, scientific, mercantile etc.) and a race in a such alliance/federation would have an extra victory condition. For example if you´re in a dominance alliance your extra victory condition might be that the alliance must hold a certain percentage of the galaxy. New victory conditions or modifiers to existing ones could also emerge from tech discoveries, cultural events and simply when the game progresses long enough. So if the game goes on long enough, your victory condition might get harder to achieve (this will make it possible to win even in early game but balance the mid and late game so that meeting victory conditions isn´t too easy when you have lots of resources (planets, tech, fleet).

Like some have said before me, F.E.A.R. stands out in my mind much like the Half-life series. Granted there should be certain expectations going into this game series - The two first and foremost being that your enjoy FPS games and like the idea of a horror/sci-fi twist to them. Since well, those are the two main elements to the games, especially in the first (and argubly the best) game. You will either a) Be shooting at bad guys with guns, stormtrooper types, that sometimes consist of tougher enemies like Mechs or b) You will be putting up with creepy and horror-esque paranormal events - usually in the form of Alma who of course you learn about as you progress.
Now, if that sounds appealing to you; then odds are you will like FEAR. Dealing with Canon/Non-canon b.s. aside, all of the renditions of FEAR have at the bare minmium been decent in my opinion. However because of this Canon/Non-canon bull, things do get confusing if you care about the story at all.
Both the expansions for the first game are considered Non-canon. Extraction Point being the one that clearly is, though oddly enough is the one with more favorable reviews. Perseus Mandate seems to get less love, though honestly I view both of the expansions as one in the same - they simply add "what ifs" and more FEAR gameplay, if you like that idea then you probably won't mind the expansions.
I will say this though - FEAR is by no means the "scariest" game ever, it has scares much like you would expect in horror movies - and a lot of the panic or spooky moments are built around the linear game design. You are pretty much being led along, killing bad guys or avoiding/putting up creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥as you go. There are moments where you can divert from the main path, which usually involves some sort of paranormal sighting in order to get an easter egg; be it an item like the health/reflex boosts (which you want btw), or a rare weapon or even just one of the many phone messages left in the game.
All in all, if you like FPS games with healthy dose of sci-fi and horror - then by all means pick this game up(and maybe the series).

It's cheap! It's good! It's fun! Basically, why don't you already own this?!
Binding of Isaac is one of the better "2D Top-Down Adventure Games". It has so many things to unlock. You could play this for hours on end and you still wouldn't even have the slightest of a chance of seeing everything that this game has to offer.
Oh, and did I mention it's a rougelike? No? Well, I did now. Every single time you press that tempting "Start" button, a whole new world is generated. Well, less of a world, more of a dungeon. That aside, even if you've unlocked every character, collected every item, done everything there is to do, you still haven't seen everything this game has to offer. Every floor is different!
The music. Oh, yes, the music... I'd just like to point out something. The best track in the entire game, in my opinion, is the Shop theme. All of this music is wonderful, but that Shop theme... Mmmh! So good!
The replay value on this is very high. You'll spend hours upon hours looking for everything.
The graphics aren't TOO good. I can't complain, though. It runs quite well, even on high, on this potato of mine. They're not eyesores, but they're not exactly eye-candy, either.
Now, let us delve into the world of Wrath of the Lamb. Basically, you have to go through Binding of Isaac as normal... And then on your next playthrough... There's a few extra floors! How wonderful!
There's new rooms, new enemies, new bosses, new music, new characters, everything a DLC could possibly offer, unlike SOME games that only add one new thing for every $15 worth of DLC.
The DLC is cheap and fun! Buy it along with the main game!
Now, if you're looking to buy this, and you can't afford $7 (not making fun if you can't, I couldn't get it either), wait until it's on sale. I managed to get DLC and BoI together for about $2.50!
Now, by the end of this review, your wallet is probably preparing itself to lose a bit of weight. Good! This game is worthy of purchase!

Tl;dr - Galactic Civilizations III is an awful game that appears to exist only to pay off Stardock's legal fees (they were copyright trolled). But the customization is quite good.
Galactic Civilizations III is a great writing prompt and a miserably bad game. If you enjoy making custom ships, writing backstories for custom factions, modding, and the like you'll find plenty to enjoy in GC3.... at first. Which of course is by design. If you could enjoy the game after spending a long time with it, there'd be no reason (that the developers could concieve of) to buy their 11(!) DLC packs. For more money than the game itself costs. In the hopes that you'll finally have the 'complete' game this time.
The game's balance is a mess since shields only work for energy damage, armor only works for conventional cannon attacks, and you have to install jamming devices to defend a ship against missiles. All of which take up a lot of space, so you'll have to leave most of your ships undefended against one or two types of attack throughout most of any given round. Starbases don't so much defend planets as sit around waiting to be taken out by whichever militant AI's forces happen to be near enough to do the job. And it's one of those games with a culture/loyalty system which has to be overpowered pretty stupidly in order to have any value at all, so it is. That having been said, though, at least you can play as a diplomat or economist and win the game. There's a culture victory too... which will always be either way too easy or way too hard, depending on which patch it is.
There's a morality system, but it's incredibly expensive in the early parts of a round to deck out a planet in whichever building(s) represent/produce your chosen morality. Just in case you wanted to focus on that instead of, say, military production or food output - don't. The bonuses it gives are generic and manage to usually be either useless or overpowered. And you'll probably get tired of having the same Sophie's Choice about hapless natives on planet after planet once you've played the game for 20 or so hours. And your interactions with the other factions do literally nothing for your moral alignment. You'll only get morality points by building structures and clicking on a text menu that pops up for new colonies. But admittedly the alternative would've been a nightmare to impliment, and this game's already loaded down with severe implimentation problems.
Overall GC3 is a poorly constructed Skinner Box that attempts to be a turn-based strategy game sometimes. And usually fails in those attempts. If you want to get the definitive GC3 experience, wait fifteen more years and get the complete edition (if the DLCs have stopped rolling out by then) at a steep discount. Or alternatively you could just buy a much better strategy game.

This game is a worthy tribute to one of the best roguelike games "Brogue," and in a way it is also its worthy successor by choosing to be realtime instead of being turn based. It has its own unique flavor and personality so that it does not feel like a rip-off at all -- on the contrary, I'd say Unexplored is how a contemporary roguelike game should be like.
The game is hard, and has permadeath, so do not expect to easily beat this game, especially not on the first couple of tries. But it is a good thing, because this way your achievements will actually mean something for you. You'll feel like you have truly achieved and conquered something even if you could not complete the quest at that time (and you can re-try as many times as you want). Since the environment is procedurally generated and Unexplored has a lot of content, replayability is essentially infinite, which is not bad for a game that can be purchased for a limited amount of money. :)
Regarding technology, I really like the visuals which is presented in a 3D top-down view. The environment and the characters are made of sharp, vector-like shapes, and cleverly and dynamically applied shadows and lights make everything feel alive and dangerous. The soundtrack is also nice as well as the sound effects. The menu system (including the in-game inventory) is simple but effective and works well.
I recommend this game for anyone who likes to explore and wants to experience a modern roguelike, even if its realtime game flow might be strange for some -- it works and it's fun.

tl;dr? This is an actual negative review of Isaac. The story is unnecessarily dark which leads to only polarizing its audience more so than just the game would. The actual game has no controller support, which is dumb. It personally seems repetitive to me regardless of the rouge-like elements and got boring fast.
The Binding of Isaac's story is highly juvenile but just the fact that I’m seeing people call the story good is making me scratch my head it isn’t good. The dark themes in this game are highly unnecessary for what the game really is; a rouge-like dungeon crawler. The game sure has the Newgrounds feel to it, but what it’s missing is the humor, instead of having a dark comedy vive like how I thought it was going to be, it seems to be a lot more focused on the DARK part of that. The story is almost like it’s both trying to be taken seriously and not at the same time in the same parts which makes it both not funny and laughable at the same time.
Of course, you’re probably wondering why I’m harping on the story so much when it’s obviously not the purpose of the game. Reason is, because of the way the story it seems to only polarize its audience with one side either not caring about the story, or liking it because they’re hard-core atheists who like anything anti-religion; and the other side being people who aren’t comfortable with the story, or feel it’s distracting to the game. Again, this polarization seems very unnecessary since the story is a very minor part of the game. I feel like the game could have still had its own unique identity with a different story.
The Binding of Isaac really has nothing too wrong with it mechanically, though. Other than the fact that it has no controller support (some people don’t want to download a separate program just to play the game with a controller) and the game really is a controller game, the keyboard controls feel awkward as all hell. Besides, it might just be me, but even with the rouge-like elements the game feels very repetitive and it bored me pretty quickly.

Pinning down precisely what makes the world of The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings so enthralling took me some time. It's not that the fiction is particularly "mature," though that's undoubtedly a term that will be tossed around until the next hyper-gritty fantasy game pops up. Think about it for a second: The Witcher, Geralt of Rivia, is a crag-faced, cat-eyed, gravelly-voiced mutant hardass who only stops screwing and fighting when occasion calls for a philosopher, at which point he dutifully duels scholars and monarchs with a tongue as sharp as either of his two swords. He is a character straight out of a 15-year-old boy's misused English notebook; the wounded warrior poet who, by the way, gets all the consequence-free sex he can handle, since he's totally shooting blanks, bro. And sure, he's stoic -- but he's also got a sensitive soul somewhere beneath that scar-laden chest of his, damn it.
No, what makes the Witcher's world so absorbing is an amazingly cohesive and consistent visual vocabulary that is -- and I know this is going to sound ridiculous -- far more logical than is typical for fantasy games. The impoverished fishermen of the riverside village of Flotsam shuffle around in nothing but ruddy underwear. Dumpy town guards patrol in filthy rags that still bear their national colors. Ornate attire is (for once) consigned solely to the upper class. Buildings look planted and properly dilapidated. This may seem a small thing, but from the first minutes of the game, it's clear how much effort has gone into researching how a society like the one portrayed would look; this medieval civilization, infused with -- but not dominated by -- magic and mystery (props to developer CD Projekt), is just awesome.
Similarly impressive: the degree to which the story changes based on your actions. Game makers (and publishers, and shareholders, and preview writers) love to crow on about choices and consequences. Hell, if you buy the PR spin, every single BioWare game in the past decade has been a watershed moment for cause and effect in video game storytelling. But frankly, the lofty language usually leads to a letdown -- the best we usually get are mundane tics on a morality slider that may or may not unlock a new dialogue tree, or perhaps a new companion somewhere down the road. I'd go so far as to argue that the only stable of games that's been quietly, consistently offering a serious set of genuinely game-altering forks-in-the-road for nearly a decade now is Acquire's Way of the Samurai series.
Not anymore.
While we have the underlying storyline of murder, intrigue, and (more stupidly) amnesia to which The Witcher 2 continually returns, the minutiae is wholly malleable. The allies Geralt makes on his journey and the enemies he combats shift with your mood swings; larger decision points alter the landscape of the world dramatically, but even minor events can cause repercussions much later in the game -- and how the whole thing ends is entirely your choice. Reading after-action reports from fellow players is like a game unto itself. Nobody seems to experience quite the same scenarios.
Not all is well in the Pontar Valley, however. Combat, for instance, is a serious problem made even worse by a poorly implemented, obscenely difficult and unhelpful opening segment. Plow into battle unprepared, and you might as well expect the worst: Even on moderate difficulty levels, this is not a game in which potential sources of aid can be ignored. Traps, bombs, magic, daggers, pre-battle potions... every tool in Geralt's arsenal is an absolute necessity.
Once I got the basics down, the extremely acrobatic, constantly active feint-and-parry style of Witcher warfare became seriously enjoyable -- just don't expect the prologue section to teach you much of anything valuable. And even when I finally felt like a proper monster-hunting mutant badass, I occasionally came across the rare room or fight so absurd that I had to wonder if CD Projekt understood the limitations of its own combat system. Geralt in a room too cramped to allow for falling back and trap placement? Battles before which you have no time to meditate and drink potions? No thanks.
Worse still, the user interface only exacerbates the combat system's flaws by forcing the player to keep an eye on everything but the melee itself. Geralt's vigor (read: mana) meter, health meter, buff/debuff indicators, and equipped spells/items are all scattered across the screen, which is a serious drawback when you're surrounded by screeching harpies.
But not even a terrible introductory sequence can take away from what is otherwise a fantastic game. Sure, the story is goofy, and at times the fighting is offensively clunky. The world isn't as colossal as the first Witcher's, and the ending is a bit of a tease. But in a time when I rarely bother to finish single-player games, I'm happy (and slightly embarrassed) to say that I'm already several hours into a second playthrough of Assassins of Kings. And I can't think of a better compliment than that.

Garry's Mod is some of the most fun I've ever had, period. Playing this game with friends has been an absolute blast and I firmly believe that all Steam users should own a copy. Even though I've only clocked in a measly 90 hours, I plan on bringing that up to 900 or more someday (and it will happen, mark my words). GMOD shows how perfectly unperfect the Source Engine is, and abusing its physics can lead to some choatic good times. I'm also really proud that the community hasn't given up on this game yet years after its release, and I doubt it will anytime soon.
Without the modding aspect, this game would be hot garbage. Good thing it's there, because some of the mods I've gotten are crazy. Many playermodels, maps, vehicles, weapons, and gamemodes that people have made are truly amazing. I even made a list of my addons that you can check out on my page (too lazy to link it here). Of course, not all the addons are winners. Most of them are just random things that some kid stuck together in the game rather than actually make something. The good news is that you'll usually know which addons are bad and which ones are good just by looking at them.
My main problem with Garry's Mod isn't even with the game itself; getting together enough friends to play GMOD is suprisingly difficult, because it all depends on the time that they all have. If you're currently in school and want to play this, I strongly suggest that you play it during the summer (obviously). When you can't get together people to play with, and you really should try to because it's more fun that way, then there are thousands of servers and game modes you can join in with anyone. It's still more fun to play with your friends, but this option still works great.
GMOD is one of, if not, the best game on Steam (in my opinion!) that you should buy if you haven't already. While not perfect, like all games, the experiences and memories I've gotten from this game are hilarious and unforgettable (that may be a bit of a stretch...).
Final score: 9/10

Honestly, if you're not already interested by the description "rhythm dungeon-crawler" I don't know what else to tell you.
I can say every single thing about it stylish as hell, it has one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard from any video game in my life, and the two genres blend together shockingly well. It's not a hugely innovative roguelike, you just explore a randomly assembled network of rooms and tunnels full of monsters and gear. And it's not a hugely complex rhythm game either, you just take every step in beat with the music. But putting them together REALLY transforms the experience of both. Having to work out your own "dance" to outmaneauver enemies and traps as you come to them makes the rhythm game feel clever and engaging in a way they're usually not. Putting that dance into every little thing makes the busywork of a roguelike feel satisfying and just GOOD in a way I've never felt before.
This is one of those mashups that sounds pointless when it's described to you, and after actually trying it, you don't understand why there haven't been games like this since 20 years ago.

Ride is probably the best motorcycle video game since Tourist Trophy on PS2. There's been many MotoGP and WSBK games, but not many that use real-world motorcycles. I do enjoy riding some of the lesser known, or less racing-orientated bikes, its unusual.
The gameplay is good, not amazing, but good. Sometimes the rider can be a little sluggish, almost like a deliberate input lag of sorts. Its most noticeable when switching directions quickly in a chicane, the rider will be noticeably delayed in swapping his body position on the bike. Sometimes the 'simulation' style of gameplay where excessively hard braking or hard acceleration causes the bike to squirm or slide aren't particularly smooth or realistic. There isn't that many tracks in the game, the selection will get repetitive after a while.
The graphics are ok, the bikes and tracks look fair enough but the riders standing helmetless next to the bikes in the menus look ridiculous. 10years have passed since video game characters looked this simplistic.
The audio, where do I start? Its terrible. Truly aweful. The bikes noises are appalling, I turned them off long ago, like some weird electronically generated whine. The best motorcycle engine noises in a video game ever, are in Burnout Paradise. And bikes are a side show in that game! Come on! Get your act together.
Summary:
Pros:
- Great Selection of bikes, even some older 80's and 90's calssics.
- Fast access to decent bikes, no need to spend hours riding slow bikes (unless you want to).
- Decent on-bike graphics.
- Decent controls.
- Bike customization is limited, but still relatively well implemented. A tuned bike is still noticeably faster than the standard version.
Cons:
- The sound is abysmal. Bikes sound dreadful.
- Some glaring omissions as far as bikes are concerned.
- Helmetless riders look ridiculous, very dated.
- Controls can sometimes feel delayed.
- Some occassional dodgey slides where the physics don't add up.
- Bike customization could have been better. Custom paint jobs, maybe even workshop support for cutom graphics kits etc. Why can I remove all the mirrors and indicators on some, but some leave the indicators when you choose this option? Where are the race fairings with no lights?
- Limited number of tracks.
Ultimately if you like bike racing games, this one is great, I may have been critical, but it can be very fun and its nice racing around on something that isn't necessarily a fully fledged race bike.

What more can be said for ABZÛ that hasn't already been praised to no end?
Aesthetically, I believe this to be the most beautiful game ever released. Graphics can continue to become more refined and realistic, but you'll be hard-pressed to find a game with as striking a visual present in this game. There are so many moments in the game where you have to stop moving for a while just to soak up all the beauty to be seen, it's truly an experience to just float around in for a while. I believe this game took what Journey did for visuals in gaming, and amped it up beyond any expectations. It's just incredible.
The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard, and adds nothing but pure bliss to the experience of the rest of the game. There are points where the music and gameplay blend together so seamlessly that you can't help but smile. This game provides something that I've never seen from another title before, and while I can't quite describe what that feeling is, I can guarantee that it's not something to be overlooked.
There is symbolism present throughout the entire game - none more poignant than the moment you descend with a Great White - and I encourage anyone to seek out more information after playing, but if that's not your thing, it doesn't matter. ABZÛ is strong enough aesthetically to stand alone as an experience and nothing more. It's really quite the feat.
At its simplest, I hope as many people as possible play ABZÛ and enjoy their time with it. At its most complex, I hope it envokes enough empathy in people to understand that we need to treat our environment with more respect before it's too late, and will hopefully push more people into making changes in their own lives to make a more positive impact on the world we live in.

One of the best space strategy games I've ever played and I've been playing since MOO in the 90's. It strikes a great balance between micromanagement and AI. You can setup zones as your empire grows that are indirectly owned and setup govenors to manage those zones. As your empire grows the story of your empire, which is unique with each play, grows, changes, and becomes more colorful. Characters (leaders) have a lifespan, advantages and disadvantages, and a personality of their own. It makes the game feel more rich and story driven even though it's a generated galaxy each time. There is a lot of waiting early on but you can speed up the game when there's a lot of waiting so that doesn't bother me all that much. On my Mac it does crash somewhat often with the last set of patches, and that's annoying but I have confidence they'll fix that.
The only thing that I really don't like that much is the way you have to setup war goals or war goals are setup against you. I feel like if you invade a planet you should be able to cede it to your empire at will. When someone goes to war with me I haven't found a way to negotiate them out of it. So, this ends up with long wars where you want to negotiate your way out of it but there isn't an option. I also haven't found a way to encourage other empires to go to war against your ememies without creating an alliance. I find that a bit of an annoyance. Still, it's absolutely the best space empire strategy game I've ever played.

text:
Dust: An Elysian Tail is a side scrolling beat em' up with beautiful 'hand painted' backgrounds, and an exciting story about an amnesia-stricken warrior fighting his way through many unique environments to try and remember who he is.
Though the game starts off with a Shadow the Hedgehog vibe, and the dialogue can be sorta cheesy (At least Fidget's, who fits in as the over-excited side kick who doesn't stop talking), it branches away from the "edgy furry confused with the world" as the prologue progresses, and Fidget sorta grows on me.
Update:
After finishing the game, I can safely say that it was amazing.
I didn't finish all the sidequests/get all the treasure yet, but I have about 14 hours on the game. Pretty good amount of gameplay for the money I spent on it. (On sale for $3), but even if I bought it at normal price, it would be worth every penny.
The combat in the game is pressing either the right and left mouse buttons, or J and K. All of your attacks will be done with these keys, and you can with dodge/dash forward with Q and E. I've seen people complain how the combat gets stale, but that's not true. Each enemy is designed to be fought a certain way, and you're forced to think strategically when fighting many of them at once. One enemy can be killed with simple melee attacks while the another enemy will parry all of your attacks, and you must strike him right as he's about to attack in order to land a blow on him. This can prove difficult in the later rounds, but it also keeps the game interesting.
My only real complaint about the game is the boss difficulty. In Normal Mode, the bosses are not that hard. The first boss is one of the easiest intimidating bosses I've ever fought, so I was a bit disappointed, especially because he's a key part of the story. You'd think he'd prove more difficult to fight. Each boss, obviously gets harder to fight, and the final boss fight is very satisfying in terms of difficulty. But the difficulty in general seemed too easy, but perhaps I'll just need to replay the game on Hard mode.
To conclude;
The story is great, the designs are great, and while many people will ignore the game solely because of the animal characters, I'm glad I gave this game a shot. The combat is exciting, the enemies are unique, the environments are beautiful and the story is compelling. While some bosses are too easy ( or I'm too good :^) ), the Final Boss stands as quite a challenge, and defeating him rewards you with an ending that truly settles the dust.
I'd give it a 9/10, I highly reccomend it.

Lighting is decent and so are textures for the time it came out. The only problem is the damn color palette. Every room and corridor are painted grey. Grey walls, grey floors, grey guns, grey everything. Atmosphere is great but that damn grey makes me wish they used more color in the game but its not a game breaking issue. In summary, the game has great FPS gameplay, atmosphere and AI. I feel the game is more focused on shooting and less on horror but that shouldnt prevent a horror fan from picking it up, especially if they enjoy first person shooters.

I've been playing this for 3 hours yet I haven't even been able to play yet. Why? Read on below.
I bought this game because it looked cool and you could build your own ships and make your own faction. I also like these big games like Civilization. However, I have found some very big problems that I am currently not fond of and have prevented me from playing this game.
First off, I began making a new faction. Nothing wrong with that except that it wouldn't let me put spaces when typing out the descriptive description for my faction. It was a slight drawback.
Secondly, I began playing the game and tried making my own ship. I decided to come back to that later.
Thirdly, I made another faction and began playing as that one. I went about 10 minutes into it and tried designing a capital ship once I researched weapons. I spent an hour trying to figure this out. Everything is there, but it seems very unfriendly. For one, I don't notice any sort of light when designing. You're basically designing in the dark and it's very hard to do. So I quit trying.
Fourthly, I went to the campaign. When the cinematics began, it was too quiet to hear so I raised my SFX volume to hear it better. Restarted the campaign again. Still very quiet. I raised my SFX volume to 100% and started the campaign again. Still, quiet. I raised my MUSIC volume to 100%, started the campaign and what do you know? Cinematic volume is based off of music volume. Very inconvenient for me since I always put my music settings to 25% or lower.
With all that being said, the game seems really good from what I've explored, but the third and fourth points make this game incredibly annoying.
I'd like to mention that I also didn't complete the full tutorial because it was very boring and lacked the "helping" feel to the game. I spent about 10 minutes doing the tutorial to learn barely anything new that I already know about 4X games. So fifthly, the tutorial to me was garbage.
I can recommend this game to people who like 4X games, but these small things make it very difficult to recommend it for newer players. I got it on sale for 66% off. I'd recommend to get this on sale too.

So far I am really enjoying this game, however, there are still some issues that need to be ironed out in my own opinion.
Essentially it is a reboot of the same game, with a few additional maps, better scaling and quite interesting graphic and unlockable options, however, as it is early days there are some things that the developers need to address quite fast:
1 - Time waiting for a private game. Mostly, I prefer to play my own games, especially at low level just to get a feel for my own playstyle and have a bit of fun without some rather nasty folks getting in my way. Yet even with a private game option, there is still a long countdown to the game start...no need to wait for other players if you're not expecting (or wanting) any.
2 - The tavern needs some serious revamping. I can see where they were going with creating a community hub, but what they have really created is a lagfest extravaganza, not to mention, a headache. I would love to be able to comment on the purchaseable items and the changes in pet levelling, but I simply can't because I lose my mind after more than 4 minutes of looking in my itembox because Monk 56 wants to mess about with Aura's all over my bloody screen and the squire has created a dozen harpoon turrets that have rapid attack speed.
3 - The timeout at the end of each level needs to be discontinued, or at least replaced with a 'Select another level' screen. Also, where on earth did the retry button go? You have to zone back in to the headache zone in order to try another level. And you don't get 'dwelling' time where you can inspect the drop items at the end of the game, you have a limited time to look at them and get out. Forcing you in the larger maps especially, to collect 10 tonnes of crap in your item box.
4 - This is the big one. Why do I have to sit in an ever changing queue to play the game at all? So far I've spent a few hours playing the game, and more than double that waiting in a queue for a 'session' from the server. And the queueing system is pitiful, with me so far being 4th, 12th, 18th and 1st in the queue, but still not actually getting past the menu. More annoyingly, is that this doesn't seem to be a global issue. Only a few forum posts exist about it, and none of the guides or publicised material by Trendy make any reference to this. It is annoyingly bizarre.
Overally, the bits that I have seen so far have been really grand, its just these very strange features that I can't seem to understand why they were created in the first place.

I wanted to like this game so damn much--especially since I enjoyed the first Witcher a lot--but I just don't.
I also tried very hard not to compare this game too much to the first one but it's impossible, especially since the story picks up almost exactly where it left off in the first game.
I know a lot of people complained about the combat mechanics of the first game and they tried to fix it here, but this new system is much worse. I only have one nice thing to say about anything combat related, and it's that Quen is a bit more useful this time around.
The minigames are also worse now--the dice game is now **** in a box, the punchups are no longer fun as they're all quicktime now, and the arm-wrestling game isn't great.
Despite clearing the minimum requirements for the game by a long shot, the game still chugs and at times will take ages to load its textures. I also had to deal with the Steam startup bug, which took me quite a while to fix.
Somehow even the save system works worse, the world is uglier despite the better engine, and the characters from Witcher 1 have flatter personalities now. Didn't think Dandelion could get even more annoying? Boot up the second game. The new major characters are at least somewhat intriguing, however.
Common theme/tl;dr: the only reason anything entirely new in #2 seems great is because they ruined all the old things from #1 and it shines in comparison. Everything they tried to reinvent here didn't work at all.
I managed to get this game for $2.49, and I'm only pushing myself through it for the sake of continuing the story and carrying it over to Witcher 3, which I'm relieved to hear many good things about. Pay any more than this and you'll feel ripped off. This is not a great game, it's an endurance trial.
P.S I'm glad Bloom lighting is not really a thing in more recent games.

A good game ? Yes. Better than the original ? No.
DD-E is basically the same game with a variety of details changed, some for the better, some for the worse - And probably which is which is based on taste. My love for DD has always been its tower defense part and the long progression system, while running around and shooting stuff for hours was never my thing.
Anyways, to the good and the bad based on my taste:
Good:
Every map and mode needs to be unlocked - I love this mechanic, it gives you a feeling of accomplisment as you unlock stuff that yesterday were too hard for you.
Balanced better than the original - I can only speak for how far I am at this point.
True hardcore mode - Perma death, although I wouldnt dare it till I have backup armor sets and a character to take over.
Crafting - nice addition although I have seen nothing I would like to actually craft yet.
No longer shared loot - no need to fear others picking up your Ultimates.
Re-learning tactics, classes and everything - Just pretty fun process especially in a game that is still the best TD/Defense/FP cross genre game to date.
All classes, most maps, even a few new maps - All for a fair price.
Bad:
No pure strategy - My favorite mode.
Based too much on co-op - I do love co-op, but I the mindless shooting monsters for hours is boring, and with so many maps requiring those 3+ players doing just that to finish them.. Unfortunately this is the direction DD2 is also taking but owell its their game.
Clunky UI - Or rather some stuff took me long to find out how to work, for example bulk selling, hatching and then click info and hatch again to make the pet useable.
Too many consumables and combat things I will never use.
Coins - Unnessesary. I preferred the mana system, one currency for all.
Still way too many drops, and it still dissapear pretty fast if you don't pick it up.. One of the things I think they should have improved while at it.
Having to download 1.5Gb every time you start (after a reboot) the game - This is utterly stupid, period.
Details:
Mobs getting stuck (for example in City in Cliffs) don't always time out and making that particular map mostly unplayable.
Tower placement areas have changed, some towers require less space, but all in all good because it forced me to re-think tower placement tactics.
Summoners now use DU.. I am not sure if this is good or bad but it removes the need to always have a summoner.
Better anti-cheat, moot point. In DD playing trendy net I didn't experience it as beeing a problem, infact in my 800 hours played I have never seen a duped item for sale.
Although the original DD is a better game, this is better prices and lets face it, with this release the original will die, so move along and embrace the future, good and bad.

One of the few games I truly love. The game have a pretty funny story and not very serious at all. As an Age of Empire 2 lover I also want a change of pace and fight with something like tanks and laser cannon rather than bows and swords. And better yet, fight by commanding an army of robot! The unit types in this game counter each other to the point that a lowly infantry can withstand a blow from the main gun of a tsunami tank (but not its tread of course). The King Oni shoots laser beam from its eyes are vulnerable to infantry (yes, infantry) without its secondary ability. King Oni can finish off buildings and armored vehicles and blow them up to oblivion, but gaze that scary glowing eye of yours at a Conscript, for example, and congrat comgrades, experience how lame you can be.
It pretty much like rock paper scissor. In short : the unit strengths and weaknesses are enhanced, and heavily amplified. Get the right units and you will raze their base to the ground, get the wrong ones, and totaloo, your base will be razed to the ground, oh and your pride as a RTS strategist, too, if you have any.
The pace of battles is very fast for me, the outcome of combat is decided pretty quickly, and you better put your godlike microskillz to use, else, screw micro managing, just right click your way to victory.
The differences of three forces: Allies, USSR, and Japan Empire are very diversified. The Allies has Air superiority, the Japan Empire, of course, master of the sea. Finally the USSR prefers to fight on land (yes, LAND WARFARE) basically if you confront them head on, and they are not hindered by your navy or air force, then you are dead my friend; the Red army will mow you down, they loves using brute force.
There are lots of tatics and tricks that can be used, thanks to the special ability of some units.
Joking aside, to be honest, I bumped onto this game when it was on sale and it was the best bargain I can get with just $5.

Honestly, if you're not already interested by the description "rhythm dungeon-crawler" I don't know what else to tell you.
I can say every single thing about it stylish as hell, it has one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard from any video game in my life, and the two genres blend together shockingly well. It's not a hugely innovative roguelike, you just explore a randomly assembled network of rooms and tunnels full of monsters and gear. And it's not a hugely complex rhythm game either, you just take every step in beat with the music. But putting them together REALLY transforms the experience of both. Having to work out your own "dance" to outmaneauver enemies and traps as you come to them makes the rhythm game feel clever and engaging in a way they're usually not. Putting that dance into every little thing makes the busywork of a roguelike feel satisfying and just GOOD in a way I've never felt before.
This is one of those mashups that sounds pointless when it's described to you, and after actually trying it, you don't understand why there haven't been games like this since 20 years ago.

What an incredible dungeon generator.
Don't be fooled by the art style. This game is a challenging, in-depth experience that adds substance and significance to every single run. It is so much more than a bunch of room pieces put together with some random enemies. Each dungeon is created in a way that transforms it into a cohesively structured chain of action, puzzles, quick reflexes and strategic intelligence. Rarely does anything feel out of place within the mini-story that each run writes through its gameplay. You'll likely find yourself wondering in amazement how some of these moments are not hand-crafted. It is simply (or not so simply) an effect of the dungeon generator, and the incredible work that was put into it.
On top of this, the game has been updated on a quick and consistent basis since release, with a lot of significant new content that has already made the game so much better since its February release. There have been a few stumbles with bugs along the way, but most of the issues have been fixed already.
It's a gem that will only get better with time, as it is expanded further. Highly recommended for those looking for a challenging roguelike with cool dungeons.

Before I purchased this on Steam I had hopelessly waited forever for this game to come out. To me it looked almost identical to Forza Motorsports for motorcycles. Kind of a simulator but designed to have arcade abilities to enable less experienced sim folk to enjoy. Well I eventually give up after a year of watching everyone else get it . Time goes on and I build a PC and sure enough here it is. I get excited and make my purchase. I am ready to delve in to deep upgrades and competitive racing enjoying the real sounding and feeling machines so I thought.
What I will complement them on is the 3rd person view and graphics in most cases seem pretty decent but it ends there. Upon starting the game for the first time I realize that the amount of options to enhance graphics or disable depending on your build was absolutely pathetic. The online doesnt work at all despite it telling you you have created a valid account. It just keeps telling me "failed to authenticate" which is dismal to say the least. For the sake of a short"ish" review I will move on and not get too hung up.
Now I am in the game and buy my first bike. The sound is nothing like the real thing and obviously it looks like a stock bike so I head on over to the garage to upgrade and maybe see some info on my bike. By the way the dealership completely sucks. It has no interaction or detail. Its just 5 bar stats going from 0-10 and basic specs. Well inside the parts list I realize there are only oil change, port work in two stages, two brands of exhaust (and obviously Akropovic paid the higher dollar to have their exhaust used here because their exhausts give way more power which is completely wrong in the real world) and wait for it.......... two brands of air filter. The supposive "customize your machine" is a load of crock also. You can change brake lines, remove fender eliminator, and pick between usually two to three factory colors for your machine. Not even a paint shop on this game its so plain and empty.
The mechanics of the game seem to be very similar to MotoGP while on the track excluding the tire slippage and spinning are lacking in a realistic way. There is no clutch option at all. The tuning is also a joke. Its pretty much a slider bar for five basic catagories of suspension and a few on and off switches for TCS . I think you are stuck in ABS on .  The boards become old quickly because there isnt many and the ones that are there are just the same things. I also noticed a stock bike on the drag strip is just as competitive as a "completely modified" version. Everything costs the same for each bike also. I did notice the prices of the machines are around real world price but because the game gives you money so quickly you are in a top notch machine in less than an hour and no real feeling of any campaign or point system outside of a fake "world ranking" they give you that basically moves up a couple spots each time you win a race. The AI is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and bounces off walls or you and loves to cut you off frequently.
Overall guys this game looked to be something huge so my hopes were high and I was completely let down. This felt far more like a demo or BETA than an actual game. I cant believe I paid 65$ for this. I doubt we see a Ride 2. Trust me by taking your money and going back to MotoGP and deal with no real upgrade system. At least then you get real simulation feeling and competitive racing. Overall 5 out of 10.

tl;dr Game doesn't have any technical issues for me (though I advise doing your own research first), bikes are absolutely beautiful and a joy to ride. Get it if you're a motorcycle fan.
Full review:
Doesn't honestly deserve the flak it gets.
Encountered no save game issues, and the game runs buttery smooth on my rig. The bikes are beautifully modelled and rendered, and the engines sound fantastic on headphones. The tracks pass by fast enough while I'm riding that the supposed lower quality details do not stand out at all.
Riders are believable and very well animated, and the amount of control finesse you can get over the bike is huge, from extremely hand-holdy assistance to letting you have full control over the brakes individually, and shifting gears manually.
The attention to detail is appreciable especially in the first person helmet view available, it even muffles the engine sound, simulating wearing a full-face helmet.
Though no game can really ever come close to capturing the physical aspect of actually riding a motorcycle, RIDE does a respectable job of it. A solid purchase for motorcycle fanatics and riders, in my mind.

This is not a game, it is a new myth for a post modern world. It is made of sacred geometry and love of the beauty of nature and it tells the One Myth that has always been used to help people reach a true understanding of themselves in the world to unlock their true power.
Unlike most games it relies only on your pure joy of being in the moment to move you forward and punishes you for almost nothing. There is no real bad guy or critical plot requirement, you dont get to pilot a giant missile and laser spewing war machine, you wont have to practice combos to get through it.
ABZU is beautifully simple thus, it depends solely on the beauty of the environments and your curiosity about whats really going on in the plot. For me the outcome was amazing. I lived in Hawaii for a few years and this game took me back to my best times snorkeling and spearfishing there and into my wildest diving dreams while reminding me of all my psychological, religious and mythological studies along the way.
The game only takes a few hours to "complete", even if you do everything, but you will find yourself wanting to relive it over and over again.
Great game to introduce people to quality gaming with, my girlfriend who had never picked up sticks loved it.

This game is ok, not perfect, not horrible just ok.  The last few levels are really REALLY frustrating with the scaling of difficulty being off.  I believe the fifth level to be harder than the sixth.
Controls are pretty good, I am able to freely control my character wherever I need to except you can't manipulate your jumps in air so if you make a bad jump, you can't correct yourself and it's back to the begining of the stage with you.
The levels are ok but some are panfully long and if you mess up at the very end, you have to start all the way at the beginning of the stage except for the last stage which is broken up into segments.  If there were checkpoints in the stages, I wouldn't be so upset about dying over and over to something over and over again.  Also when the enemies die, they leave segments of their body lying around.  THIS can lead you to get stuck and take unintended hits from other enemies which can kill you and force you to start the stage.  This is highly apparent in Test 8 where you can't jump over any of their body segments and when there's ten plus enemies on your butt, then it gets really frustrating when there's nothing you can do to prevent yourself from dying.  Again, checkpoints would be great for the long stages.  Another additon that would make the game better would be a sprint option.
Your movement speed is kind of on the slow side and for some reason, when you look up or look down, your movement speed is decreased.  Why is this I would never know but it's stange and can lead to you getting swarmed by enemies because you can't move fast enough to get away from them.  If there was a sprint button, then you could get away from swarms and feel safer but also risk running into obstacles that could instantly kill you as the risk vs. reward option.
Although some of the stages are really long, the game itself is really short.  I beat all the stages in less than two hours and that's with Alt tabbing out of the game to check some other things while the game was running.  While dying over and over again can be frustrating, what isn't frustrating is the soundtrack.  The soundtrack is really good on the ears and can go well with what is being thrown at you in the stages.  Beating the game gives you the sound test so you can listen to all the songs at your leasure.
For the price (under  one dollar at the time of this review) I believe you're getting your money's worth.  The game is harmless and can be fun but at the same time really frustrating.  The game is worth it in my opinion because it's really cheap and you're getting a decent, although somewhat frustrating, experience in the long run.  If anything it's worth it for the soundtrack alone.
Pros: Smooth control
Awesome music
Cons:  Frustrating enemy design
No checkpoints for really long stages
Short (Only nine levels)
Score: 3/5  Bare in mind you get what you pay for.

First of all, to make things clear — Stellaris is by no means a bad game. However, reading the community reviews here one would think that it is the "promised game"  of the strategy genre, some people describing it as the "best strategy game" and such. This surprises me. In my experience, Stellaris is a fairly bland game that doesn't bring much (or maybe even  anything) new to the table. Its definitely playable and even enjoyable, but it gets boring and tedious fairly quickly. I wouldn't know if it has a lot of depth, as others often claim about it. It certainly has a lot of "breadth" though, in form of modifiers that affect all kinds of stuff as well as small micromanagement minigames. One needs to learn all that stuff in order to be successful. At the same time, the sole purpose the minigames seems to keep the player occupied.
Take for instance the planet management. Its still the basic old assign-props-to-tiles-and-build-improvements minigame we know from many games before, made slightly more 'complex' by adjacency bonuses. Yes, it gives the player something to do and it seems to offer a 'choice' — but this choice is merely an illusion. In the end, optimal tile development is a linear optimisation problem (what gamers often refer to as min-maxing), an additional puzzle game within the larger game where the player is rewarded by playing the puzzle well and punished by playing it badly. I never understood why I have to play puzzle games of this sort when I want to play a 4X strategy game. Now, while Stellaris generally is quite micromanagement-heavy (planetary survey being one of other annoying things), it also attempts to cut down on micromanagement by introducing sectors, which are basically "AI" assistants that take over management of planetary systems. However, they do it spectacularly badly. The funny thing is that the planet development minigame can be solved by the computer optimally. This is not a particularly difficult problem and algorithms to solve it have existed for decades. Not within the Stellaris universe apparently. Other things that disappoints: the diplomacy system, trading and don't get me started on the leader system. First of all, leaders/heroes have a limited life span, which sounds like a neat feature on paper but is incredibly annoying in practice. Second, leaders can be elected president, which immediately stops them from doing what they are doing and essentially removes them from the game. You need to manually(!) look through all your leader assignments, find out/guess which slot now became empty and hire/find a replacement. Combat is ok, even though quite basic. Some more control of fleet tactics would be nice (such as ordering sniper ships to at least try keep their optimal distance from the opponent).
All in all, in my view at least, Stellaris is mostly a combination of old and not very exiting ideas in a new package. Now, there are some things that are quite neat, like the heavy utilisation of random events (storytelling, research, etc.) which do offer meaningful choices. But the tedious micromanagement and non-exiting gameplay are still big downers in my book. I would have wished for the game to try more advanced/novel solutions instead of pushing the player into the old boring micromanagement minigames.

Absolutely classic run and gun game play with light horror themes and near-future weaponry. Pick it up if you like shooters, you won't regret it. The later installments are a bit iffy from what I've read, but the game that started the franchise still holds up today as a solid experience.
When FEAR was new, it changed up the classic arena shooter formulas by introducing melee attacks (jump kicks, slide kicks, etc...) and limiting the number of weapons you could carry to 3, but the biggest feature was the bullet-time mechanic which has been used in a lot of games since. I'm not going to get into a long discussion here, but hitscan (projectiles you can't dodge in mid-flight, as opposed to say a Doom imp's fireballs) weaponry is difficult to implement in games because you can't dodge it, you can only either soak the hits (unrealistic) or hide from it behind chest high walls (not fun). FEAR neatly solved this problem with bullet-time by allowing you to move so much faster than your enemies you could dispatch them without needing to soak up hits or hide for very long (only if you ran out of bullet-time).
If you like this I highly recommend the two expansions, Perseus Mandate and Extraction Point. They are full games and essentially more of the same, but there is nothing wrong with that when the game play is this good.

This was one of my first childhood games so I am a little biased, but I do love this game. The story is good. Sometimes you want to slap Squall around for being such a little♥♥♥♥♥♥but he has a personality, and a character arc. All the characters have these things. The owner of a pub in Dollet has a backstory and he is not even in the main story. The story works, and makes sense, while still leaving a little to be read within the lines. It understands subtlety. For instance, Ultimacias final line. It was cut short for a reason, to make a point words could not convey. That was poetry. Like darksouls it takes a little sleuthing to work out some finer details, but they are there.
Now the gameplay, while at moments satisfying, falls into farming alot. The magic booster in the PC booster attempted to address this, but instead of giving 100 of a few choice spells I thought it would boost any spells found to 100, eliminating unnecessary farming while still leaving explration and progression. I am also glad chocobo world was included because it's nice to know what I was missing out on as a child. It allows the item farming to do itself, I just had to edit the hex file to make it go faster. Farming like this did eliminate alot of the challenge that I faced during my original playthrough, so I suggest not bothering with chocobo world; it's a terrible game anyway.
I like the junction system, it makes you choose what stats to focus on, what to be immune to, and how to flavour your attacks. It also fits the aesthetic of the game, which is more industrial than other Final Fantasies. It still does have its own fantasy mythos, but grounded in a world of science.
This is an old style of RPG that rewards busy work, but if you are willing to put up with it there is plenty of exploration to be had.

Forget "for the price tag" or "for an indie game", Dust: An Elysian Tail is an amazing experience which really reignited a passion for gaming that I wasn't sure if I had any more.
This is not an 'artsy' game, although it does sport some of the best artistic direction that I've ever seen in a videogame, accompanied by a brilliant soundtrack. The story and characters, whilst kept behind gameplay in priority, are likeable and easy to follow. A few inconsistancies here and there, but an enjoyable experience with enough sidequests and secrets to keep you playing for 20 hours, easily.
The mechanics are tight -- if you die, most of the time you're going to feel like it was your fault rather than the game cheesing you out of a death. I only played on hardcore mode, because I found the difficulty on this level was at the perfect point between challenging and tedious.
One of my few gripes about the game is that the save spots could have been more considerately placed. I often found that after dying, I was re-doing tedious but simple parts of the game. The save spots should be after the tedious but simple parts, not before them. I want to re-do the part I died on, not the three screens before it (here's to you, Sorrowing Meadows).
I did run into two possibly Linux-only issues, one was some sound distortion in certain areas of the game which required me to reduce the volume, and another was an issue with one of the secret rooms not displaying correctly. I e-mailed the developer about the latter issue and within an hour, had a response saying it is being looked into this week.
The game's difficulty curve is brilliant, introducing new concepts and abilities as the game goes on so as not to overload the player with one of those half-hour tutorials which most of us skip. The first area is easy, and the final boss will challenge all of your mechanical abilities. I suggest starting on the highest difficulty level and working your way down if it's not enjoyable, it feels like Dust was designed to be played on hardcore.
There is plenty of endgame content, as I'm finding with over 20 hours played that I still find things to do and treasures I haven't found yet. I have thoroughly enjoyed this game, and struggle to recall the last time I had this much fun playing a videogame.
Thank you, Humble Hearts. I look forward to the next one.

I definitely recommend Stellaris. The setting is fantastic and it is hugely enjoyable, it offers enough depth and customisation to get you truly hooked.
There are some things you need to know though:
-If you're playing a large game, there's a significant amount of lag end game making it near unplayable. I believe they are working on a fix for this.
-Mid game is sorely lacking.
-You can cheese the game currently with vassals.
-Diplomacy is lacking.
-There are only 2 victory conditions: Conquest - Conquer or vassalise all factions, Domination - hold 40% of habitable planets.
-Research is RNG, this is good and bad.
-You can't realistically play a small empire and be able to comete with bigger ones. You have a higher chance of forming alliances but the beneifits of expanding are much greater.
-Fallen empires can massively disrupt your progression.
Sure the list is fairly large but the nice things Stellaris does outweigh them and Paradox will definitely work on some of them and improving the game overall. This ranks as one of the best space strategy games of all time for me.

Dead Bits is about a block guy who gets kidnapped by aliens. In order to escape, he must go through 9 of the alien leader's tests. The game is just a generic FPS where you shoot at random enemies until they die. Enemies are slower than you and you never have to reload, so all you need to do is run away and shoot. No effort required.
Despite the combat being incredibly easy, the game still has ways of making itself difficult. For starters, the game will go into a black and white slow-mo effect at random when you shoot at enemies. This feature is as annoying as it sounds, and gets old immediately after the first time its used (and no, it can not be turned off). For a few levels, you need to kill every enemy to unlock the next level. So if you're at the end of a level but forgot just one enemy, you'll have to go all the way back.
On top of this, jumping is really awkward. Whenever you jump, you are basically locked into that animation, so if you stand still and jump, you will always go straight up even if you try to move in the air. In a regular FPS, this wouldn't be that much of a problem, but in one that relies heavily on platforming such as Dead Bits, it often leads to many accidental deaths. Also if you die, you always get kicked back to the level select screen.
The visuals do not bring the game any justice either. The game is composed entirely of blocks, making the game look like some random Minecraft mod. The music is basically just generic dubstep. Everything in the game from the text to how you start each level in mid-air feels like some sort of mod and lacks any polish (the button you click on the menu to go into level select is always titled "new game;" think about that for a second).
Yes, I am aware that this game was apparently made by one person. I can get past the graphics and the music, but the monotonous gameplay and other faults are what keeps this game from being a decent experience. If you really want to try it out, it's only $1 so knock yourself out. Otherwise, save your precious dollar for something better.

Have you tried survival horror games? Maybe it's time.
F.E.A.R. is a FPS game, but more importantly a survival horror.
Playing as the Point Man, part of a First Encounter Assault Recon team, your job is to locate and eliminate Paxton Fettel, a psychic able to control a battalion of Replicas. What seems to be a classic spec-ops mission will actually turn into a nightmare, that will put your enhanced reflexes at heavy use.
Through this game, you fight smart enemy soldiers, you dig into Armacham's story, you help funny and frail survivors... But you can't expect how good this game is at scaring you, nor how bad things can turn to.
I find this game a good choice in order to begin survival horror games, specially if you are used to FPS ones. I suggest continuing with its first DLC, Extraction Point, which starts right when the main game stops, and puts you in an even worst nightmare than before.
I also suggest stopping before the second DLC, Perseus Mandate. Though the universe is the same and gives some good scares, it's a lot more focused on firefights and is a lot more difficult.
Be advised though: the game engine is far from optimized, so don't be surprised if you can't run it with highest details, even if you can with recent games.

This game is not what I was hoping for, but it was better than what I was expecting. I have been on something of a quest looking for a spiritual successor to Space Empires IV and it would seem that quest must continue.
Galactic Civilizations 3 has a beefy ship construction system, but with little actual instruction on how to use it it can be cumbersome and frustrating to get the hang of. The game itself plays almost painfully slow for the most part, with many an idle turn spent simply ending the turn. This makes it feel like either the game needs more to do or the time it takes for things to build/research needs to be reduced simply for the sake of expediency. It is actually somewhat easy to get bored with the constant ending of turns.
The camera is also frustrating, as you have to click and drag it around and cannot simply move with the WASD keys like nearly every game allows you to anymore.
The combat is based around a Rock/Paper/Scissors weapons system where lasers are countered by shields, missiles are countered by point defense, and kinetic weapons are countered by armor. Simple enough, but the game lacks any kidn of tactical combat whatsoever, instead allowing you to auto-resolve battles or sit and watch them. The psuedo-cinematic battles are amusing to watch, but again the game is lacking in the "something to actually do" category.
You do have the option to build your own race, which is nice. It will even easily let you load in your own images for a faction leader, and coupled with the ship builder can let you have a pretty good time there.
The campaigns are somewhat frustrating in that each "episode" starts you in a default position instead of letting your previous accomplishments carry over, which means you can easily restart one if you lose without saving, but means that what you accomplish goes away at the end of each session, leading to more long waits filled with clicking the end turn button. There does appear to be multiple option to free-play, which may add some actual longevity to the game, but it isn't enough to make this game great.
In all honesty this is a mediocre game with a pretty great customization feature. If you are looking for a simple and straight forward sandbox gaming experience on a galactic scale, this isn't too bad. It does have quite a lot of DLC, which if you are dying for a touch of story with this game then by all means, go for it, but otherwise I would strongly encourage you to start with just the base game to see if its worth investing in all the rest.
I purchased the full package while it was on sale, and honestly kind of regret it. I think if I had only bought the core game I would have been happy with what I got for the money, but as it stands I am a touch disappointed, really.
Going to go ahead and thumbs up this only because it is just good enough to make me want to spend a few more hours in it, but I feel it is one that will eventually drift into that forgotten place where old games go to try and collect enough nostalgia to get you to play them again.
Seriously though, buy the cheapest option before investing into all the DLC's and expansion. Plunging straight into the whole kit may well lead you to regrets.

Other than that I'm enjoying my time, I think I'll wait until the connection issues are fixed and I can actually host a public game and/or tavern to remove the complaints I talked about above.

+ Great pacing, story, overall a story I was drawn into and wanted to know more about.
- Somewhat borrowing from other lore (LOTR, Warhammer 40k, etc)
- Characters are good, but not great. While CD Projekt Red makes incredible games it's a well-known fact that Geralt is a pretty boring protagonist.
+ Voice acting is very consistent and believable. Not like TW3, but still very good.
- Animations are clunky and often need triggers. Feel very last-gen.
- NPCs will often mirror animations, sometimes up to 10 at once. Again, a CPU restriction from the XB360/PS3 I wish wasn't there.
- Killcam/finishing move cutscenes (think Skyrim) appear to be premade and are executed in a completely different area of the map than where you are fighting the NPC - which makes zero sense.
+ Immediately recognizable, classic controls
- No automatic controller detection, have to go into the settings and switch it.
- Looking around/picking up items is very 'stiff' with the default controller profile. I haven't tried to change this, I think I might just need time to adjust.
- Getting to your character ugprades/inventory/leveling system is in the same menu as the save/load/quit menu (accessed by pressing start on the 360 controller) and that's a pretty stupid design decision.
+ Much less demanding than The Witcher 3 (~25% CPU, 60% GPU on an i5-6600k and GTX 970)
+ Wealth of graphics options
+ Very scalable, will run on older hardware. I'm talking laptop hardware here. If you can't run witcher 3, this is the game for you.
+ No crashes yet!
- Cutscenes max out my 970 for no reason and drop my framerate. (this only happens in cutscenes and I think it's the DOF setting not being optimized AT ALL.)
- Supersampling is stupid and no card can run it. You'll need an SLI/Crossfire setup to use this, and even then it's a ridiculous setting.
- Cutscenes often have a very (read: VERY) overdone DOF filter that not only looks weird, but destroys what is otherwise a very well optimized game. I'll probably be disabling this.
- While it does have a lot of settings to change in the launcher, you're usually limited to 'Enabled' or 'Disabled' - not a lot of versatility there.
If you like RPGs, The Witcher 2 is a must play. If you like LOTR, a must play. Open world games? Play it. It's leaps and bounds better than Skyrim and doesn't require heavy -- or any -- modding in order to enjoy. It has a lot of rough edges that CDPR was clearly aware of, as they are nowhere to be found in The Witcher 3. CD Projekt Red takes pride in their games and this is no exception, it's a masterpiece and the fact that the graphics have held up for so long is testament to that. Buy this game.
Look at how many hours I've spent on this game. That one statistic tells you everything.

I love this game. Unexplored takes Zelda style action, mixed with random treasure finds, random dungeon generation, and randomly generated puzzles to make something wonderful. I won't comment on if this is a roguelike/lite as I know the semantics of that get some people worked up. I will say it is very much influenced by that genre. Potions and scrolls are unidentified until used and there are altars to a few gods you can sacrifice items on for a boon. The dungeon generation in this game is astounding. The entire dungeon is generated so you can find clues to later floors in books/notes. The dungeon isn't linear either, some floors lead to multiple other floors on the same level. There can be more than one "level 3" depth dungeon for example.  Lots of little details in the environment, great layouts with puzzles to solve that seem to flow naturally from one to the other. The weapons and shields mechanics are really awesome, each weapon has its own little advantages and attack styles.
Traps, monsters, magic, mayhem. If you like the genre or the gameplay style, try it and I think you will like it.

No, its not Unstoppable Gorg, but it is interplanetary warfare from an RTS angle.
PUA offers more than just a tower defense rehash. You get to go on the offensive against other planets in your solar system; taking them over and reaping their resources for your own benefit.
There is no individual unit control here, but a more overarching system of command, simplified all the way down to a couple of mouse clicks. Dont expect the keyboard flurry of micromanagement that comes with starcraft, red alert or the like. This game is aimed squarely at casual gamers who will come back for more in short bursts.
No story, simple controls, but enough achievements and a steep enough learning curve to make casual gamers feel rewarded.
recommended for tower defense / real time strategy fans.

Ok I don't usually do reveiws of games I've played..... but this game is somthing that has really raised the bar on my expectaions from both adventure and beat'em up games. You play as Dust in an Anthropomorphic world(Animal people). He awakes not knowing where or who he is. Then you are greeted and named by a floating talking sword called Arah. The sword's pint sized gaurdian Fidget shows up next. After a short exchange you sent off on an adventure.
Pro's:
1.This game has a very well executed combat system that  results in Dust flying across the screen throwing out blows, casting magic spell, and using the Duststorm to rack up combo's and cause massive destruction to anything on screen.
2. Exploring never feels like a chore and you are ecouraged to come back to area's you have been through before to reach new areas to get loot and face challenge dungeons as you gain new abilities.
3. The RPG elements put into the game allow you to specialize Dust skills, but it will restrict you a bit only allowing a one skill to get so high allowing your others to catch up. Here is what I mean. The game has four base stats Attack,HP,Defense,and Fidget(magic/duststorm). Your have reached level five and you have put all your skill points into Attack. The skill tree will not allow you put a fifth point into atack until your other skills have all been brought up by one. This kind of system is put in so the player doesn't suffer from a handicap farther along in the game when enemy's are tougher.
4. The story will keep you engaged and the world that is it's setting is beautiful. Which bring me to my next point.
5.The entire game, except for a few enemies and your sword, is hand drawn. This type of graphical choice in a game is always refreshing and is something that many Triple A title's never do. (exept the current Rayman game)
Con's:
1. I had very few problems with this game. One thing I wish would have been better is the map. It needed to be a little more detailed. A few labels here and there wouldn't hurt and the terrain should have been displayed. They didin't need to save space to prevent the game file from being too large. This could have been inpimented.
2. Sometime with all the crazyness going on on screen you can somtimes lose track of yourself in a mass of enemys. It doesn't happen often but it could result in you taking a hit ending your combo and loseing extra EXP. There is no way to fix that your character is already brightly colored. It's not much of a problem but it is there.
Verdict. This game is a good 12 hrs long if you play it how it is meant to be played. Doing a few side quest and exploring. This game is must play. 95/100.

This is a difficult game to review. It has many wonderful things to recommend it, and it pains me to give it a thumbs down. The fire physics, art direction and music direction are all absolutely fantastic. The game has simply incredible atmosphere. But the ending is so bewilderingly incoherent, and so utterly fails as a payoff to the build up of tension throughout the game that that negative experience ultimately cancels out all the rest of the good that went into crafting this experience. I played through the game twice trying to find some form of actual choice or controls that the player could make to influence the ending and make it make some kind of sense, and after nine hours that now feel completely wasted I have given up trying to find meaning in this experience. In short, none of the implied mystery of the setting is explained or expanded upon, and the story inexplicably reverses events that clearly happened with no justification for no clear reason in a way that feels as though it invalidates the actual experience of playing through the game.
It's possible that the game is just buggy- there are hints throughout the game that saving items or finding combos will influence what happens, but after my second very frustrating run in which I hobbled myself holding on to every unique item I was sent and then ground through all ninety-nine combos and still got the same ending, it does not appear that there is anything reasonable that I can do to make the game make sense. The apparent inability to go back and redo the ending on a given save file doesn't help; I can't justify another hours-long playthrough just to try going through the ending dialogue trees in a slightly different order to see if it will have any effect. Again, trying to play the game has become a very disheartening and exhausting experience.
The game appears to be totally on rails, and in fact the second run hammered in how completely pointless everything the player does actually is- what mastery of the fire physics the player may pick up over the course of the game has essentially no impact whatsoever on anything- the sole exception being helping time burns to make sure that combos are counted. But since combos don't seem to have any effect on anything, that still doesn't matter. I feel now that the entire game could have simply been a video with no interaction and still had the same amount of meaning.
Please don't buy this. You will only waste your time and your energy and your emotions, to say nothing of your money.
