The game is a marvelous piece of art. Although the storyline is relatively straightforward and perhaps predictable, its gameplay makes it up for it. As a Metroidvania, you are continuously being challenged of revisting areas once you have unlocked new skills. However, this doesn't mean you can't try it without acquiring the skills. The majority of hidden secrets and/or treasures in each level is designed that it can be visited when not having the right skill. Having the right skill does make it easier on the other hand, but less of a challenge.
Had enough of visiting areas? You can always try to think of practicing your skills by chaining your combos. Besides its gameplay, the soundtrack is extremely well done. Each piece of music fits the moment making it a great enjoyment for the ears when walking through the same area again due to backtracking.
However, the game does suffer from a couple of small glitches. Interaction windows popping up while being far away from the shops or savepoints and in battle does hamper the game a bit. While not necessarily gamebreaking, it might be experienced as a nuisance when trying to chain a combo hit.
For a game that has been written, programmed and drawn by one single person is an amazing feature. Even more amazing is that all elements in the game fit perfectly together: the gameplay and the OST are very well thought and executed.
However, it doesn't mean the game doesn't suffer from some minor glitches. Interaction windows that unexpectedly pop up might be a bit annoying, but are not necessarily gamebreaking.
+ Great OST
+ Amazing art work
+ Challenging gameplay: difficulty can be adjusted when necesary
+ Good level design: majority of the secrets can be reached early in game for a bigger challenge. Having the adequate skill later in game facilitates reaching these secrets
- Game suffers from minor glitches at times
- Storyline is a bit predictable

A fantastic game, that genuinely has been given unfairly bad reviews.
The game is genuinely a unique ride, from start to finish. I've clocked in my fair share of Draconic combat, and thus far, I've genuinely enjoyed myself. There are most certainly aspects of it that are less than enjoyable, such as certain dragons feeling unstoppable, but in truth, every dragon can be beaten, but it's a matter of how well you play your own Dragon, and work with your teammates.
For a free title, the game has quite a massive selection of unique Dragons and weapons to choose from, though they are unlocked via random bundle packs that are purchased via in-game currency, called Gems. 3 dragons per hatching pack, 3 weapons per weapon pack. It certainly adds an air of eagerness to earn more Gems to try and unlock more dragons, as well as trying to get lucky to obtain a weapon you may have your eye on. The controls take a short bit of getting used to, but once you're used to them, they're surprisingly smooth, and let you maneuver your way through the skys fluently, while breathing various elements at your enemies, to deter them, as well as throwing out interesting techniques, unique to each dragon.
Is this game perfect? Definitely not. Is this game fun? Most certainly. Is it worth the asking price of 0 dollars? It got me to buy a founder pack, so hell yes it is. It frankly is a game worth trying, before passing judgement, and I don't regret any of the time I've spent in it so far.

Great for people with infinite time who'd really love to dive into a complex but ultimately pointless game.
Not so great for anyone else, such as those who would love to see a game in this genre with a strong story, immersive graphics, or player involvement that's more exciting than being an accountant.
The campaign, at a mere 3 missions, is unforgivably short, and it is a real missed opportunity to turn the beautifully complex game engine into something meaningful and engrossing. I'm not sure what Stardock has against campaigns in their games, but to me, single-player story is the main reason to play a game. It's fun to escape to and get drawn up in another world for a while. It's not fun to click and be bored for a few hours, then be left with not even a few fond memories to show for it.
I tried and didn't particularly care for Gal Civ II, but I thought I would give III a chance anyway -- surely they made some improvements, eh? Nope. Same boring game. Slightly more polished graphics. What should be the most climactic parts of the game -- epic space battles -- are still rather akin to watching football games after the season is over. You know the outcome of every battle before it starts, and they're not that visually impressive to watch, so what's the point? Limited fleet sizes also contribute to this problem, as most battles have only a handful of ships.
To some degree the game does appeal to my OCD side, in that Stardock grants you the opportunity to control every last detail. But without some grand goal to strive for, sinking your time into doing so feels pointless. It doesn't help that you're almost entirely on your own in terms of learning the game. The tutorial is essentially just another map with a few videos to explain the basic controls that are easy enough to figure out anyway. The game does not attempt to clarify what precisely the dozens of different modifiers for the 4X axes do, so turning to the manual or Googling everything is mandatory.
I'll give Stardock kudos for writing really-quite-funny text for most things in the game, but since everything humorous or fun is plopped unceremoniously onto the screen amidst the grind of remembering what planet to go manage next, and since nothing ever alters the pacing of the mind-numbingly even, persistent, calming background music, everything that would otherwise make the game charming or interesting falls rather flat. Relax. You're a Galactic Civilizations III player now. You have nothing else to do and nowhere else to be. Go ahead and click Turn. Don't listen to that screaming voice inside your head begging you to quit and do something more meaningful with your life that you'll remember tomorrow. Go ahead and choose your research again, even though you've made this same choice at some point in every game. Maybe the next turn is when something cool will happen.
The fact that this game managed to replicate all the boredom but none of the fun of Civilization V in space aside, it's also somewhat buggy. I've twice had it crash, once when loading an autosave, and again after a campaign mission ended due to victory. It really makes itself hard to recommend. The intricate game engine clearly required a lot of craftsmanship, but I don't think they built enough on top of it to make this game worthwhile.

I have played the Galactic Civilisation games since the first one. It is one of the few 4X games that has really kept my attention for as long as it has, and I have really enjoyed the entire series. GalCiv 3 has been no exception and is a great, fun game to play (as my hours played will attest).
There have been incredible (and much needed changes) from the earlier incarnations, and it just keeps getting better. There are numerous aspects that are great about the game and very few problems; however, those problems are fairly irritating.
The most annoying thing about the game (and all of them have had this feature) is the alignment system. You are occasionally faced with a decision that contains three answers (one for each alignment) and you have to choose one of them. I understand that no game can possibly cover every permutation involved in this situation, but GalCiv 3 has some really bizarre and nonsensical outcomes. As a generic example: Your race discovers a weapon of immense power, and you are presented with three choices. The Benevolent option says "Let's break down this weapon to make a building that can defend a colony really well", the Pragmatic option says "Let's figure out how this works and make our missile weaponry inflict a little more damage", while the Hostile option says "Let's mount this baby on our most powerful ship and kill things with it". Any alignment could argue for any of these choices, so you're occasionally forced to choose between the option of maintaining your alignment or choosing the option you want (of course, real life is very similar in this regard, but it is rarely this absolute).
GalCiv 3 introduced a point system to go along with this; essentially, choosing any of the options gives you points in that alignment, which can be spent to buy bonuses such as additional trading licenses, extra gold, &c.  This means if you are playing a Benevolent or Pragmatic race and choose a Hostile answer, you gain Hostile points. You have to earn a lot of points to buy the bonuses, which means you have to focus on one alignment in order to buy bonuses at the expense of the choices that would really help your race (when each of the options could be theoretically applicable to all of them).
Other than that, the rest of the issues are quite small and hardly problematic. It is still a fun game and I love playing it, but here's to wishing some improvements in the next incarnation, which I will surely buy as well!

Doom 2 is a classic that maintains its fun to this day. At first glance, it looks very similar to Doom 1, using many of the same graphics, the same gunplay, and the same arsenal (plus the new double barrelled shotgun). Where this game differs from its predecessor is in the level design and overall flow of the combat. Whereas Doom 1 was very mazelike and encounters were more personal with a handful of enemies, this game frequently drops you in huge, open areas and sometimes throws dozens of enemies at you at once. The double barrelled shotgun changes the fight dynamics a great deal. Where the Pink demons were a challenge in the first game, they can be dispatched with one blast, and other enemies that were difficult to deal with are similarly cut down to size. To compensate for this, Doom 2 introduces a handful of new, more offensively focused enemies, such as the mancubus and revenant, which shoot rockets at you, and the archvile that catches you on fire and resurrects the dead. The effect that all of this has is that encounters in Doom 2 are usually more intense and challenging. As is the case in every classic Id software game, the level design is brilliant and encourages a kind of exploration you just don't get in today's FPS games. The levels are large and sprawling, but the clever design gives each level a sense of direction and flow, so you generally know where to go next. I can think of exactly two spots where the way to continue was overly obtuse (for those interested:
). Still, two bad spots in a campaign that lasts about 9 hours total isn't bad at all. Visually, this game is very obviously old, and yet I still find it pleasant to look at. If you really must have modern graphics, there are plenty of mods to accomplish that, but the aesthetic of this game is so well realized that it's beautiful to look at thanks to the downright surreal and creative art direction.The singleplayer experience of Doom 2 stays fun for the entire duration of the game and is an absolute joy to play.
Even though this game is 20 years old, the multiplayer scene is surprisingly strong thanks to the fact that iD software released the engine's source code for free, allowing people to create programs such as Zandronum and ZDaemon (both of which I reccomend highly for multiplayer) that allow players to connect with ease. The deathmatch mode of Doom 2 is hands down one of the most fun deathmatch games I've ever played. Everyone moves ridiculously fast and you will initially find yourself getting lost in a volley of rockets and shotgun blasts. The deathmatch gets so chaotic that it can become almost incomprehensible at times, but I find myself getting used to it after a few rounds and eventually making sense of it all. There are no perks or killstreaks here, just pure reflexes and strategy. Knowing which weapon to use in which situations is key for survival and the game is surprisingly accessible for new players as long as you just practice (despite playing singleplayer Doom games for a long time, I just started playing Doom multiplayer this year and generally hold my own in matches and manage to win every now and then). Co-Operative modes are also very popular and even though I prefer deathmatch, there is tons of fun to be had in co-op (one defense-based mod in particular gives you money for every demon you defeat, which allows you to purchase buildings for a base you have to protect, which is pretty fun).
There are a ton of user-made mods and maps available to try out as well, so purchasing this game (although I would really encourage getting the whole series as well) is a great investment as you will get acces to a great amount of content.

The story in Witcher 2 is interesting and mostly filled with well written characters. There are some short segments that you get to experience from the viewpoint of different characters or VIPs from the game world, which is a huge plus, althou they are mechanically simplified. Without mentioning spoilers, if you want to get the most from the story in w2, make a safe before a critical decision at the end of act I. At that point the story branches dramatically for the rest of the game and is most certainly worth a 2nd playthrough from that point on.
From the get-go Geralt, our professional monster hunter, has all his sword styles, gadgeds and signes available, which makes perfect sense, but can feel overwhelming at first. Still it is nothing too scary and you will get used to it by the end of Act I and once you have the dynamic combat becomes really fun. DO NOT set your expections for the game based on the tutorial/prolog, it has so much gimmics and quicktime events in it that almost put me off from playing the rest of the game, but oh boy am I glad it didn't.
The game still look amazing at high-ultra settings even by today's standarts.
Crafting system is easy to understand, but most of the stuff from it you will never use. Still there is a stash in the game so you can hoard all your crafting materials there until you needs them. It becomes available at the inn in Flotsam.
At first I considered the game a bit on the short side with regards as to how long it took me to complete it, but after experiencing the difference from the above mentioned choice, I'd say it is in a good place - not too long, not too short.
One last thing I'd like to mention is to play this game for what it is. Do not make your decisions based on what MIGHT be there or not be in the Witcher 3 (I'm currently on my 2nd go at w3). The only decision really worth considering in this aspect is the very final one, imo.
When all is said and done, I fully recommend this game to all who like the dark medieval fantasy setting with added political intrigue.

DOOM II's gameplay is much the same as the first game with very few changes.
The super shotgun is a fantastic(ally overpowered) addition.  It's satisfying to use, does as much damage as a rocket, and uses pretty common ammo... except most of the levels (Petersen's, so you know who to
blame) are huge, have long sight lines, and are swarmed with monsters that do not drop ammuntion.  The variable lighting from the first game is less present this time around, too.
On the note of the level design, I'd like to cite Map 10 in particular:  the only seemingly reasonable way to do this map is to kite every enemy on the map to the entry hallway and gun them down as they catch themselves in chokepoints...  which is what I did, after several failed attempts at running and gunning my way in (since all of the rooms had enough hitscan enemies to make that impossible).
The new enemies feel gimmicky and most have very simple strategies associated with them:
The giant skeletons will try to punch you if you get near them, but cannot punch and move at the same time
The flying meatballs will not spawn skulls (or attack in any way) if you are touching them
The archvile's flames will go out if you hide behind a wall (of any width!)
Many of them just feel annoying and I'd compare the meatballs to Satan if they weren't already demons.  Fighting them is like stepping on Legos.
Granted, I haven't finished the game yet, but I don't think there's much left that could change my mind at this point.  The level design of the first game was probably the best thing about it (although it had a lot going for it), and the second game's level design really does not play towards the game's strengths.  Is it fun?  On the better designed levels, yes.  Is it as good as the first game?  No.  Play DTWID if you want more of the first game.
Rip and tear me a new one if you like.  /opinions

Final Fantasy VIII is arguably one of the more polarising FF games, particularly in the UK. Many gamers' first taste of the now near-staple console JRPG was Final Fantasy VII, and as such the departure that FF8 presented appeared to be a shock. The Junction/Draw system for magic remains hotly debated, many who cut their JRPG teeth on FF7 preferring the Materia/MP system used there. Personally, I cannot see the issue - they are both distinct games that have their own mechanics... it would be like criticising FFII (and by FFII, I mean the Japanese FFII, not the relabelled-for-the-US-market FFIV) for its system of levelling up, where you had to use a stat to improve it. While they are all part of the same series, direct comparisons are somewhat unfair. I have enjoyed pretty much every Final Fantasy game I have played (although admittedly the recent ones I have been on the fence about) and it is always best to look at a game from its own merits, rather than why it isn't something else.
To this end, this Steam release of FFVIII is along the same lines as the earlier release of FFVII. There is no disc swapping. It allows the game to work on newer hardware and OSes without the need of patching, tweaking or sacrifice to the emulation gods. More specifically, it removes the need for "8-bit palletised textures" which was a feature that every card supported when FFVIII was released on the PC, but has since (Red Dwarf reference incoming) "gone to Silicon Heaven". It has improved resolution support - although it must be noted that the pre-rendered backgrounds are the same as always, and while some still look impressive, others are showing their age... any with people in the pre-render look pretty awful - and is still in the same aspect ratio as always, although the launcher does list a variety of resolutions; up to and including triple monitor, which I have not tried for lack of need when the backgrounds are 4:3.
The story is the same as it was, however it must be noted that whoever wrote the short text description up for the Store page really needs to check their facts - they have got the initial part of the "box synopsis" so horribly wrong it's embarrassing. I will not spoil the story for those unfamiliar with it, but to me, aside from a few moments, it remains one of the more enjoyable FF stories. I like most of the characters, where even the antagonist is a person I can form an emotional connection with during the course of playing. This is a vast improvement on many more recent outings for the series where I actively dislike characters that you are supposed to feel a connection to.
The music is, as has always been the case, well composed and well suited to the situations that it accompanies. Nobuo Uematsu's work has been left as it was from the original PC version, which while many would say is inferior to the Playstation music... I can't help but feel that if you find some MIDI music difficult, you really don't want to go back and play the original FF games, where the synthesiser capabilities were more limited. The Opening Theme, "Liberi Fatali", is an orchestral and choral work of art that never fails to rouse. The Ending Theme, Brahms-ian in its composition, leaves me ambivalent for all the right reasons upon hearing it – a glorious end… but still an end. Faye Wong singing “Eyes on Me” I will not discuss in great depth, as I tend toward preferring instrumental music.
A few brief words on the re-release specific features that don’t focus on graphics or modern systems. The “Magic Booster” I have not used, but looking at the description of the magic that it gives you, it’s close to useless. The Achievements, if those are your thing, really won’t be too hard to get if you complete the game. The only one to really be particularly difficult will be the “Contrived Finish”, which will mostly be because there is very little leeway to keep Squall’s level at 7, its starting value.
All in all, if you like JRPGs in general or Final Fantasy in particular, a worthwhile purchase.

It’s come to this: you’re having a torture-induced flashback to a time when you were told a story by a guy who is himself having an exposition-induced flashback to a time when he was shooting some people behind crates, following an NPC, and calling-in mortar strikes. This is what happens when Call of Duty tries to do a psychological thriller.
You’re Alex Mason, a protagonist completely unrelated to Red Faction: Guerrilla hero Alec Mason, though he does happen to have the same square jaw, grubby stubble and gormless stare. In story terms, that means you’re a hardened agent of a Special Operations Group carrying out classified objectives for America’s interests around the world in the 1960s. In game terms, it means the NPCs you follow into battle are shouting “Get on the machinegun, Mason!” instead of “Get on the machinegun, Ramirez!”
CoDBlOps, we’ll call it, is by Treyarch rather than Call of Duty creators Infinity Ward, but it wants to be a film just as desperately as their Modern Warfare games. The upside of that is several properly spectacular scenes: some of gaming’s most exciting Vietnam vistas, slowmotion breaches through plate glass windows, base jumping off snowy cliffs, and various heavy things very nearly crashing into your face. Its set-pieces are as colourful and varied as Modern Warfare’s, and frequently a little nuttier: you’re sometimes given control of the vehicle involved, and the stealth ops motif lends itself to sillier gadgetry.
The downside is that it punishes you any time a scene doesn’t play out as the director intended.
Your team is fleeing an avalanche. An enemy with an RPG pops out, so you shoot him. No dice: he’s invincible, because he hasn’t played his part in this scene yet. So he fires his RPG at the walkway you’re on, beneath the guy in front of you. That guy’s in front of you because if you try to run ahead of him, you’re blocked by an invisible barrier. So the guy falls through the gap, and so do you. And if you weren’t near the gap, you’re teleported there to make this scene work.
Your friend is lost but you manage to pull yourself back up onto the walkway, on the wrong side. If you take a run-up to jump across, the game ends with the message “You failed to stay with your team!” You have to jump practically on the spot, or you’ll be too far behind your comrades for the next scene to work, so the game simply ends.
For every great set-piece, there’s at least one unforgivable mess of mis-scripting. One mandatory stealth section expects you to run out into the light and kill a guy in a potentially exposed area, without prompting. If you don’t, even if you stay in perfect darkness next to your guide and no one sees you, it claims you’ve been spotted and guards pour in until you’re dead.
All of the last four Calls of Duty have taken this attitude, but HakeBlips is barely interactive. It’s like being in an action movie, certainly, but one where the writer won’t tell you the script, the set designer puts perspex cubes in your way if you don’t go where he wants, and the director yells “Cut!” every time you fail to read his mind.
Here’s an idea, guys: make a ♥♥♥♥ing film. Get it out of your system, and come back to games when you’re ready to give the player even the illusion of control.
Never fly in a vehicle that is mostly door.
Between the set-pieces, SharkBlimps is exactly the same shooter we’ve played through twice already in the Modern Warfares: short, controlled bursts with interchangeable assault rifles at B-movie baddies who tuck themselves behind crates, then sprawl theatrically across the floor when you finally clip them. You’re taking hits! Duck down until the jam clears off your eyeballs. A grenade! Press G to fumble with it uselessly until it explodes, or move slightly and survive. We have fire support! Press 6 to target the gunship/ artillery/airstrike. A door! Wait for an adult to open it for you.
The only tweak is that the assault rifles are marginally less interchangeable now: apparently every goon, guard, trooper and agent has been a contestant on Pimp My Piece, so whatever rusty slugchucker they were packing turns out to have a scope, custom mag, silencer or Sellotape reloading system. It’s almost like RPG loot, and it’s fun.
You get incendiary shotguns, explosive crossbows, chunky revolvers. It’s just a shame all this gonzo technology, and the whole black ops theme, doesn’t relate to what you spend most of your time doing. The bungled stealth sections are brief lead-ins to the same shooty/shouty all-out war that’s been getting increasingly lifeless with each game in the series.
Second worst way for a Castro lookalike’s career to end.
If all its bits worked, PrawnFlaps would be worth about 75%. They don’t. It’s the first game since Elemental that I’ve had to install on three different PCs to progress. On one the game simply hangs during a certain cutscene, on another the very next mission roots me to the spot at a checkpoint. And restarting the level set me two levels back – ones I didn’t much enjoy the first time.
It’s worse in multiplayer. Server disconnects, lag spikes on good connections and total lock-ups are so frequent that it’s unplayable for some of us in the office. They’re only occasional on my main machine, so I’ve played enough to see that the technical problems are a real shame. Without them, this could be the best multiplayer Call of Duty in the current generation.
The game uses a currency system to let you choose which upgrades, equipment and perks to unlock as you progress. Having more choice, and a steadier flow of upgrades, ties the item system more tightly to the general business of deathmatching.
You get to fly and shoot in this section. So who’s that guy?
The items themselves have a spirit of fun: the explosive remote control car is as hilarious to flee as it is to use. And while they’re sadly restricted to wager matches that cost in-game currency to play, there are some nice new game modes. The best, Sticks and Stones, gives every player a crossbow with explosive bolts, projectile knives and a throwable tomahawk: get tomahawked and your score is reset to zero.
It’s still grossly unfair, of course. CoD online is a great game waiting to be let out from the wreckage of Modern Warfare’s disastrously stupid bit of design: giving the players who already have the advantage of skill and experience the added advantages of better guns, more damage, more powerful perks. And – when they inevitably achieve a streak of kills – a ♥♥♥♥ing helicopter to kill everyone on the map for them.
What saved the last Call of Duty, Modern Warfare 2, was its brutal co-op missions. FlounderChops doesn’t have that – instead it revives the incongruous zombie defense mode from World at War. It’s a slow, unsatisfying attempt at a genre that’s been done masterfully by both Left 4 Dead and Killing Floor; nothing like as tense or exciting as just playing a Call of Duty game in co-op.
If Treyarch’s goal with their Call of Duty games is to imitate Infinity Ward, they’re finally doing an impressive job. The shooting is as dull, the scripting claustrophobic, and the set-pieces try just as hard to distract from both. But without a great co-op mode to back it up, without a startlingly fresh setting, and interrupted by regular technical screw-ups, Call of Duty’s bluff and bluster has never felt so hoarse.

An excellent game with an attentive developer and superb level generation - something deserving merit in its own right: it's not just built out of unique 'chunks' or totally random individual dungeon levels, but built from the ground up so that the entire dungeon interacts - a masterpiece of procedural development - and better, one which feels totally natural while exploring the unexplored!
Not to mention - the worlds within are gorgeous. You can feel the chill in the icy winds, be stunned by the verdant life in the teeming underworld or move through the silent, echoing halls of the long-dead and above all, the sounds: hear the whispering sounds of dead gods in forgotten corners, your own footsteps and the shuffle of things moving behind walls: 'atmospheric' doesn't cover the half of it.
In addition to this, the game gives endless replayability, I would also add a solid- and terrifyingly dangerous - world: the monsters, all the way from the standard bats and rats up to the big scary stuff later on all feel unique, and are all potentially dangerous, even when you know their foibles: all it takes it one bad curse or mistep to remind you you're not invincible.
For all that though, there is a definite gratifying progression - you start off living off your nerves and twitch reactions, and you get solidly geared up and down your first-dozen strength potions with a healthy supply of life and healing potions and you think you're all set - and you can wade through anything!
...right up until you find whatever new horror the dungeon's got lying in wait to trip you up.
The attention given by the developers on the forums is also excellent - regular additions of new content and bug-fixing come day-by-day. On which subject, the one area I have a few issues with - bugs. Most people seem to be able to run the game without problems - great. I'm not so fortunate, sadly. That doesn't mean I dislike how it stands, but it is a bit glitchy - and again, I hasten to point out that most people don't have any issues!
None the less, every issue I've raised has been dealt with as speedily as one could expect, and I've rarely experienced the same issue for long - and each version is smoother and cleaner with less of the issues showing.
I still remember my first great run - I was doing swimmingly well, geared up, health and strengthed up. Only then I came down to a dark level - so switched my shield out for a torch - of which I had a good 4 or so - so far, so good. Only I was surrounded by a
of giant rats. 'Ha! Rats!' I thought, and strolled through them as they parted round my light in a wave.
Three rooms later, still surrounded by them, I began to wonder if I'd lose more than a few torches exploring this particularly ingenious labyrinth of switches, dark holes and
...
Undeterred, I continued until I realised I'd burned through 3 torches. That got me a bit worried, so I decided to speed it up a notch and continued. As my last torch was guttering, I realised I was down to just the light of one sprite, couldn't use my shield while holding it and hadn't bothered clearing out all the rats - and now, I was stuck in a corner cause if I moved, the rats would get behind me too - and I'd left it too late to retreat up a floor.
My run ended there, and I forever learned my lesson: never
underestimate a swarm of rats :P

"Planets Under Attack" is a strategy gem: very simple concept, yet has just enough depth to the gameplay to make it not just addicting but weirdly satisfying, especially after playing tug of war with the AI over a planet for what seems like forever and finally ripping it from their hands at the same time you attack their last planet.
A quick summary of the gameplay: you start with usually one planet in one of multiple gametypes, including a deathmatch type, king of the hill type, and a gametype where you vie for control of specific planets ( the first to control all the marked planets wins, regardless of how many planets the other players have). You click on another planet and hold the mouse button to determine how many ships you want to send; neutral planets/your own planets dont cost any money to invade, but enemy planets do--at least for the human race, the only race i've played as so far, but i've read that the robots play differently--and you go from there, upgrading your planets to increase taxes and building up your defenses by transferring ships to increase the population. Again, on the surface, simple, but a game can quickly dissolve into chaos requiring quick thinking and quicker clicking to turn the tide.
Definitely recommended if you get a coupon, but for $10, its a great strategy time killer that also has a fun multiplayer. Check it out.

-There are only 2 victory conditions: Conquest - Conquer or vassalise all factions, Domination - hold 40% of habitable planets.
-Research is RNG, this is good and bad.
-You can't realistically play a small empire and be able to comete with bigger ones. You have a higher chance of forming alliances but the beneifits of expanding are much greater.
-Fallen empires can massively disrupt your progression.
Sure the list is fairly large but the nice things Stellaris does outweigh them and Paradox will definitely work on some of them and improving the game overall. This ranks as one of the best space strategy games of all time for me.

DOOM II is a worthy sequel to a classic FPS, which I've
if you somehow didn't know about it. This gives you 32 generally great new levels, a new weapon (the Super Shotgun - a double-barreled shotgun), and adds a number of new monsters that serve to elevate the gameplay even further.
And...that's it. It's honestly more of an expansion than a sequel. But trust me when I say that the game is all the more better for it, because pretty much every addition is an improvement. Doom fans view this as the pinnacle of classic Doom, and custom level designers have generally used it in lieu of the first game since it came out. Not that the first game is bad; with the
of Doom II's new features it becomes an experience all its own. But if you get the first one, you'd do extremely well to grab its sequel as well.
Just don't play it with the included DOSBox emulator. What you're paying for is DOOM2.WAD - the game file itself. If you want a high quality experience, download Chocolate Doom if you want the closest thing to pure Doom, ZDoom if you want to easily play custom levels and mods, or Skulltag if you want to try multiplayer. Given how many of the aforementioned mods and custom levels there are, how many are still being made to this day, and how many
ones there are of varying types and stripes, you'd better believe it when I say it's worth it.

F.E.A.R. is essentially the horror equivalent of Half-Life: a FPS that manages to revolutionize the way we perceive shooters. But whereas Half-Life made an impact in the narrative department, F.E.A.R. made a mark in the combat department. Simply put, the gunplay in this game is INSANE: pieces of shrapnel fly across the screen, enemies exhibit some of the best ragdoll physics ever seen courtesy of the Bullet Time mechanic, guns feel powerful and unique, the enemy AI is still THE best AI you'll ever see in a game... The list goes on and on. Also, F.E.A.R. also sports some of the most chilling atmosphere in a game to date. Only S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and Half-Life 2 achieve a similar level of excellence when it comes to ambience. But what I like the most about F.E.A.R. is the fact that it hailed from an era that saw PC games become dominant once more in the gaming market: the mid-2000s gave us some truly unique PC experiences such as Doom 3, Far Cry, Half-Life 2 and of course, F.E.A.R.. To say that F.E.A.R. is a great shooter would be a colossal understatement. F.E.A.R. deserves your attention because it manages to be consistently memorable and incredibly fun to play. And the fact that you also get two expansions alongside the main game makes buying this game all the more enticing.

Okay, so let me get this out of the way: Yes, I play Overwatch. Do I see the similarities, hell- even the BLATANT character knock-offs? YES.
But the question is: Does Paladins do enough to separate itself from Blizzards Hero based team shooter?
YES IT DOES.
This game is awesome. There are still a lot of kinks and seeing as it's still in beta I can forgive that. I'll separate this review into a couple different chunks.
TECHNICAL:
1. Okay so I have yet to have Paladins straight crash on me. I run an i7 4790s, 12GB RAM and GTX 1060 6GB. The game runs fairly well. However, my roomate runs an AMD FXsomethingsomething (octo core is all I know) and a GTX 1070 and his game crashes CONSTANTLY. It can get pretty annoying and sometimes just makes him quit altogether. I don't know if it's because of the AMD processor or what have you, but that's pretty much the only difference we have in our builds. So, I'd have to say the game is more optimized towards Intel builds.
2. Framerate is good. Again, this is based off my build. I play with all settings maxed out and I'm getting my full frames - no dips or anything like that. It runs off a 32bit directX9 engine and I can see how that would help a F2P game be playable on many different builds.
3. There are small hiccups - like sometimes I can't put down a spray, sometimes I can only spray on the floor, sometimes only on the walls. Weird but not important enough to annoy me.
4. Some characters are much more effective in their classes than others. I love playing Ash [Tank], but if there is a Torval [Tank] on the enemy team, I'm done for. She just doesn't put enough damage in.
5. PLEASE PUT THE CHARACTERS CLASSES IN BEFORE THE CHARACTER LOCK IN SECTION. I'm new to the game, and there's no way for me to tell that certain characters are Healers or Front Lines or Flankers because the game won't even let you hover over those characters to tell what they are because somebody chose them. It would really help with team composition.
GAMEPLAY
(The classes go as follows: Front Lines [Tanks], Flankers [MOBA-like assassins], Damage [Offense based] and Healers [ahem... they heal]. All of these characters can mostly hold their own. And the cool thing is that the healers can actually do a lot of damage compared to OW. I know, the comparison to OW is going to be annoying but you have to understand that these games are very similar in nature.)
1. The characters kits are fantastic in Paladins. I have so much fun playing every hero. These characters play a lot more like MOBA characters than Overwatch. The Ultimate abilities can really sway the tides of battle because of the MOBA-like skills. For example, there are characters who produce MASSIVE knockbacks and can win the match based on that alone, or others that completely blind you (save for like 3 feet in front of you). It keeps the game interesting and honestly - it can be much more tactical than OW.
2. I like the gamemodes, but they are similar to Overwatch's gamemmodes with the exception of Onslaught (which is basically king of the hill and only lasts 1 round). Otherwise, you're pushing a payload after capturing the point.
3. The hitboxes in this game are very large compared to other FPS's. Sniping is much easier to do, but it still requires a fair amount of skill to do well in. You don't have to have precision aiming to be effective at most heroes and to me, it helps with the fun factor.
GRAPHICS
1. There is definitely not as much shine in this department, but again - it's because of the way the devs tried to allow many different types of builds play. Especially lower budget builds. Nothing wrong with it though as I like the art style.
2. [THIS MIGHT TRIGGER SOME OF YOU BUT IT NEEDS TO BE SAID] Some of the character designs kind of look stupid and are blatant copy and pastes of other games. Like Ruckus looks like Bolbi Stroganofski from ♥♥♥♥ing Jimmy Neutron stuffed into D.Va's mech. Viktor looks like a Guns of Boom character had sex with the brute from TF2 and plays a lot like Soldier 76. Sha Lin is Hanzo without the dragon ult. Drogoz is Pharah with an ult that auto-kills one hero. Bomb King is Junkrat. Even the ♥♥♥♥ing Ultimate is Junkrat's except that YOU are the riptire. Kinessa is Widowmaker with a different ult. And don't even get me started on Barik. I mean, he shoots LAVA out of his gun, builds TURRETS and sounds JUST LIKE TORBJORN. Fernando is Reinhardt with a flamethrower.
PLEASE UNDERSTAND THAT EVEN THOUGH THESE CHARACTERS ARE SAMEY, THEY CAN PLAY AND MUST BE PLAYED VERY DIFFERENTLY, AND THAT'S WHY I'M NOT ANGRY ABOUT IT.
Overall, Paladins is a fun game. It's balancing needs to be addressed and matchmaking is hit-or-miss. I've been playing this over OW and I'm having a blast. Don't let that ruin your enjoyment for an overall great game that deserves praise as well.

I will be making comparisons to the original Dungeon Defenders, so I apologize to those who have not played it as this review will be difficult to understand. Do note that this review is solely based on how the game is in its current state (
). There will be changes made as the developers iron out the bugs.
This is essentially Dungeon Defenders 1.5, so if you enjoyed the original, you will enjoy this even more (assuming you can get over the fact that you have to start over). However there will be certain exceptions. Although there have been some MAJOR improvements when it comes to the loot, leveling, stats and gameplay in general, it comes at a cost. This game REQUIRES you to be online, at all times. Not only this, but you must also have a decent connection in order to be able to play without monsters lag-warping all over the place. While this issue does not really affect the tower-defending portion of the game, it will hinder some players from being able to properly fight mobs up close. This game also contains its fair share of bugs, and requires you to sign up for a Playverse account (relatively painless however).
While many people will say that it contains every DLC from the past game, there are a few noteable exceptions. In the game, the maps are divided between Campaign, Lost Shards Campaign, the new Campaign (only one map in it so far), bonus maps (Glitterhelm, Palantir and such), challenge maps (Raining Goblins, etc.) and another grayed-out tab that has crossed swords as an image. I found that most of the combat-oriented maps are missing, the Presidential PvP map, the two-team tower defense, the Assault maps and other similar maps. However I speculate that the grayed-out tab has something to do with that.
While most of this that I mentioned in my review here is already mentioned on the store page, I feel that it helps to repeat these as they are important factors when it comes to deciding whether or not you wish to purchase the game.
I enjoyed this new remake of the old Dungeon Defenders, however I was one of the lucky who were able to get the game to work from the start, and have no issues with connectivity so far. I've also been lucky enough not to suffer from the hardcore glitch (they have disabled hardcore mode until they fix it) which causes you to suffer the consequences of hardcore even if you haven't died. I know not everyone will be so lucky, so you could take this as a warning.

Planets under Attack offers a surprising depth of gameplay, while its intuitive controls allow even casual gamers to pick it up and feel comfortable immediately. In addition to the addicting gameplay, Planets under Attack is an obvious labor of love. An exciting and memorable cast of characters exist perfectly in this artistically beautiful world. From the ships to the planets, everything has an essence of its own, with a memorable soundtrack and comical sound effects breathing life into the visuals
The goal of this challenging space adventure is to conquer a galaxy of planets, while undertaking a multitude of special challenges. Take control of your mighty space armada, and wreak havoc across the cosmos, but choose your targets wisely! Conquered planets will net you income to expand your forces, but you must carefully weigh the pros and cons of attacking each planet, as timing and available resources are critical to victory. Above all else, you must keep a cool head. Enemies race to capture your territory as you hone in on theirs and multiple battles will rage on all fronts. You must make tactical decisions at every turn, from scouting your enemies and deploying units, to shoring up your planets’ defenses and knowing when to attack and when to defend. Strategic multi-tasking and a keen military mind will lead directly to unrivaled glory…while careless play will reduce your army to space dust.
The Campaign mode tests your military might with 32 thrilling levels, each with varied planets, tasks and game modes. Defend a planet until reinforcements arrive, fly into uncharted space, conquer planets and set up defenses before rivals attack - the list goes on and on, as there is no shortage of objectives in your struggle for interstellar dominance. Start out as a novice and learn the ropes, or ramp up the challenge with three levels of difficulty. The longer you play the more experience you’ll obtain, allowing you to unlock new technologies, changing the way you play and ensuring you’ll keep coming back for more!

EDIT: As a Paradox fan going back as far as the very first EU, it's difficult to put a thumbs down here, however their recent pricing policy to reflect the "increased purchasing power" of several countries in recession sounded like something straight out of the PR office at Ubisoft or EA. I accept that this game is still supported, but increasing the price of a ten year old game like Victoria II (conviniently just before the steam summer sale I might add) exposes this for the con that it is.
In the beggining, there was Master of Orion 1, the greatest 4x game ever made, and only surpassed by the messianic arrival of the sequel MoO2. Many years would pass, computer power expanded exponentially, wars were faught, generations lived and died, and dozens, if not hundreds of 4x space games were developed in imitation of the progenitors, yet none could surpass them. We don't even talk about MoO3. (Distant Worlds is maybe the one exception to this, buy it). Until (possibly) Stellaris. Stellaris is a contender.
What made these games such masterpieces, unable to be devoured by their own offspring? In my opinion, the core gameplay mechanics (exploration, technology, expansion, and combat) were incredibly strong, and the parameters allowed for infinite and flexible replayability. The imitators failed in delivering the strong core gameplay of meaningful decisions that aggregate into a larger strategy of interlocking parts. Stellaris doesn't have all the parts yet, but it has enough of them in place to make me confident that when fully expanded, this game will take the best elements of paradox game design, and marry them to a true spiritual successor to the MoO series that focuses on strong core mechanics and replayability.
The core mechanics of exploration, technology, and expansion are all quite developed and engaging. You star trek all over the galaxy finding interesting things, the tech system is solid and expansion feels rewarding. The scope of the galaxy and the interface tools given to manage it are quite impressive. The sector system seems to prevent late game slog as intended.
As the 3 (or more) expansions roll out for the game, I think they should focus on developing the rest of the neglected core mechanics that made the MoO series great, namely combat. At present, the combat in stellaris is not particularly compelling, although it is kind of interesting to watch.
What makes this game great are the many small design touches. The way black holes are actually spheres of negative space, the way you enounter new species of aliens hours and hours into playing, the way many standard issues with the late game are resolved are all excellent examples.
I never buy games at retail price. Why do that when you can just play MoO or MoO2 until they go on sale? But I bought this one at $40 on launch. $40 is a perfectly reasonable price for the INSANE amount of content here, even Paradox skeptics can be assured of that. I respect Paradox greatly for setting this price point, they want people to give the game a shot and go for the expansions if they like it. This is the kind of confidence that produces good customer-dev relationships.
I highly recommend Stellaris as a master class in strategy game design. Everything from aesthetics, interface, multiplayer, gameplay, and mod support are made by people who care about those systems working well, and working together. With the current direction of the MoO reboot, it looks like Paradox has stolen yet another beloved pc strategy genre out of the back pocket of a complacent industry (ala cities skylines). Kudos Paradox!

So, Little Inferno is a strange game...Of course, if you're reading this, you probably already know that. I went back and forth, but ultimately I'm giving it a thumbs up, though a tentative one.
First, you've probably realized that Little Inferno focuses on burning stuff...And the fire effects are AMAZING. Burning things in the fireplace is an odd but substantial pleasure in itself. And things don't just burn; some of them move, or spit out other items, or explode, or any number of actions, all powered by a polished physics engine. It really is a joy to play with!
Also, Little Inferno has the same whimsical, borderline-grotesque art style as World of Goo--not to mention the same satirical edge!
Unfortunately, the game is kind of short. You can probably play through it in a day, maybe two. There are various "combos" to hunt down, but as far as I can tell there isn't much benefit to being completionist; unfortunately again, there are no achievements. Also, after the 'main story' there's an ending sequence that sort of goes on too long. In my opinion, it's just gilding the lily.
Even with its flaws, though, I'm glad someone actually followed their vision and created this crazy thing. There are definitely a few "WTF?" moments that make it worthwhile!

How to quickly win in GalCiv3: (1) get Prominence III on the Benevolent ideological trait tree (a.k.a. "Enticing," which allows for all planets and starbases within your Influence to switch to your ownership) as you (2) save up a lot of cash.  Then, (3) buy a planet (and any Starbases) from the AI player and then (4) do this for all AI opponents.
Nice job, Stardock.
Besides that, the rest of the game also feels "mailed-in" - it feels like the game's developer (Stardock) was resting on its laurels from the previous two smash hits.
Here are some reasons below as to why I do not recommend that you buy Galactic Civilizations III:
1)  For starters, the DLC isn't worth a nickel.  If you never bought those, you wouldn't miss much except for a few planet types that are hardly interesting.  Really, almost all of their "expansions" and DLC need to be included in the base game.  Of particular note is that you cannot use any of the newer DLC in the Map Editor, which is itself a feature you must pay for.  The expansions and DLC are major rip-offs, and the "Mercenaries" expansion pack is one of the worst I have ever seen in all video games I have ever played.
2)  The "wiki" is a laughable joke.  You will not benefit from it because (i) it does not contain any specific details on most things you can't figure out on your own and (ii) you can figure out the basic stuff on your own.  So why is it there?  It's just a picture book; you will get no strategy or useful information, such as what an Aquatic planet's stats are once you've researched Colonization Focus - but the wiki will indeed tell you that the tint of this planet type is blue.  Good luck.
3)  Some of the worst mods on the Steam Workshop exist for this game.  You will be amazed that you cannot find one decent modified race/civilization or map on the Workshop.  The best you are going to find are pictures of women in bathing suits as civilization leaders.  I guess the dweebs have taken over.
4) The combat in GalCiv3 is almost a pathetic joke.  You wouldn't believe that a professional game designer would let that out into the market on purpose.  The opening salvo of attacks is pretty cool, but once the two sides "clash," the starships sort of do these slow loopedy loops and curls as they pass by each other, firing their weapons in nonsensical directions, and floating around stupidly.  Absolutely pathetic.
5)  Managing your Fleets in GalCiv3 is cumbersome and sometimes pretty lame.  The biggest nag is that if you add a unit to your Fleet, the Fleet gets renamed.  Besides that, looking at the Details page for your Fleet is hardly helpful - names are not alphabetized, and you cannot decipher clear information about individual Fleet units.  Sort of the opposite of a Details Screen, eh?
6)  When trying to Upgrade your ships, you won't have a side-by-side comparison to see what you are getting yourself into; you will only see the attack and defense stats of your current build, while you can hover over the upgrade-to unit and get the information you want.  The best you get to work with is the nomenclature.  (Eg.: Marauder M5 going to Marauder M7.)  You will likely be cancelling-out of the Upgrade pop-up so you can hover over your unit so that you can compare adequately (from memory).  Cumbersome.
7)  Oh, you wanted an easy way to manually determine your research, revenue, and manufacturing spending on an easy-to-use slider, eh?  You don't get that in GalCiv3, even though it is a major component of playing a 4X-genre game.  You get this odd triangle pictograph around which you have to aggravatingly drag a cursor.  It is very hard trying to get the percentages how you want them; you can't just type in what you want.  Ridiculous.
8)  If you want to sort your Planets List by Class, you can't.  If you want to sort the list by Manufacturing output - a number you can't see on this list - then you can.  Huh?
9)  Do you like spam?  Me, neither.  Here are some "intriguing" messages you will receive constantly throughout your GalCiv3 games: "Our mutual trade continues to strengthen our relationship" (from the same civilization, ad nauseum); "Be wary as you explore the stars.  What is new to you is ancient to others" (from the same civilization, ad nauseum); and other useless gems where you can always provide only one type of clickable response: "We will take your words into consideration."  That's it.  Useless information just to tick you off; no other reason for Stardock to program that poop into GalCiv3 whatsoever.
10)  The United Planets screen, like all the myriad spelling errors in this game, is just one more show of "We don't care about our game like we should" from Stardock, the game's developer.  Leader portraits overlap, blocking each other in a scrunched-up, offset fashion; the message pane at the bottom covers multiple leader portraits (so you can't see their portraits or their votes); your own leader's portrait is not even presented on this screen; you will never know how many votes you have or how many votes were cast for the various U.P. propositions.  GalCiv2 provided all of this information.  Why does GalCiv3 suck so hard?
11) Try scrolling down most lists in GalCiv3.  You will notice hover-over pop-ups blocking your view of the list underneath.  Annoying as heck and defeats the whole purpose.  Also, Stardock's lovely "free update" recently included having another list on your main screen letting you know what events are active.  Just one more absolutely stupid decision by these people.  Completely shameful.
12)  Remember terraforming planets in GalCiv2?  Man, you could almost do whatever you wanted in that game.  In GalCiv3, the highest you can start with is a 26-class planet, taking it between Class 32 and 34 for most planets, and maybe Class 37 for only one planet (with a certain civilization feature).  Also, the buildable terrain on these planets is rarely connected: you will mostly have two unconnected sides of a planet to build on instead of a wad of tiles in one bunch so that you can build planets how you want to.  This is another key ingredient of a 4X-genre game (building your planet how you want to) that GalCiv3 was made to thwart.  If this was just some form of balancing for the game or a challenge or  whatever, then it would be fine if and only if the rest of the game were better.  But it is just one more stupid thing about GalCiv3 that makes it so much worse than GalCiv2.  On top of all that, throughout the game you are given six "buildings" to change/terraform unusable hexes on a planet into usable ones.  I have had several planets on a map where I simply could not use 5/6 of these terraforming "buildings" because the strips of usable land on these planets were not connected or not large enough to allow me to add usable hexes!  So my terraforming "buildings" just sit there in the planet's building list with nothing to do.  How stupid is that?  I have 5 terraforming buildings that I cannot use?  STUPID!
13)  Do you like being in a state of war and not knowing that?  It might be exhilirating, but it is certainly not 4X genre.  Welcome to GalCiv3.
14)  I counted sixty three (yes, 63) modules for what is known as a "Military Starbase."  63!  After all that time and effort, these "Military Starbases" are easily destroyed by low-level enemy ships.  Asinine.
15)  So you destroyed a civilization.  Neat!  Now their tens of Constructor ships turn into unarmed, non-Fleet Pirates that roam about space, slowing down your computer for you to find and destroy individually.  Stardock don't care.
16)  You don't know how to mod this game.  The few that do either (i) don't or (ii) make stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥
17)  Memory leaks galore.

REVIEW OF RECENT GAME CHANGES by ALVARAKK, 16/01/2014 (updated 09/09/2014)
MY BACKGROUND
I started playing DnT with first released on Facebook about one year ago and I have been playing regularly since. I was admitted to play-testing group and granted access to the developer's test-server. I am a pro-player, with some 5,000+ ranked PvP matches and reached top 3 ranking position consecutively in the last three PvP seasons and last stats show me at highest KDR (Kill-to-Death Ratio) in the game. I am currently ranked #9 in PvP season 4.
Trust me when I tell you, Dragons and Titans is NOT WORTH your time or money. .
* The game patch of 01/04/2014 introduced lock-on auto-aim which drastically changed the movement controls in the game, made several dragon combos obsolete, and completely removed the need for players to learn and master their maneuvering and aiming skills. In the recent months Wyrmbyte carried on to dumb-down the game in hopes of attracting more players -- ultimately failing in that too as player numbers in Multiplayer PvP at peak times of the day stand at around 400 now (compare that to DOTA2 or LOL where you have tens of thousands). They reduced the competitive aspect of PvP into a witless and uninspired routine of holding down the fire button and moving your mouse back and forth to control the firing range. Teamplay and coordination have been rendered obsolete in lieu of a contest where players compete only on who can dish out more damage fastest. The advantages of precise timing and tactical thinking have been stripped out of competitive PvP and matches have descended into routine of blindly rushing the opponents in the hopes of out-damaging them. Outcomes are primarily decided on what combos individual players picked up, which is random and unpredictable.
* The update of 10/06/2014 continued the steady decline changing the mechanics of the matching-system.
-Teams are now truly and completely random and unpredictable. The most shocking change is that the pre-match setup stage was removed, which is where you used to be able to get a minute's worth of chat with the 4 teammates the game picked up for you and discuss combos and tactics. Now, you are plunged directly into match with no opportunity to plan and prepare.
-To make things worse, players can not choose or predict what map is going to be played (there are 3, each a completely different mode of play), so they don't get can't pick a suitable combo and enter matches blind and ill-prepared.
- The other drastic change was that the restrictions on selection of dragon and weapons was removed. In the past players could only pick a weapon and dragon that was not already in use by one of their teammates and generally whoever was first to click it, got it and mostly refused to relinquish it. Whilst this caused a lot of heated pre-match bickering and some truly foul behavior between teammates, it also forced players to think about what combos best supported and complemented that of the rest of their team. This is no longer the case and players have foregon support roles and invariably stick with the cookie-cutter combos that give them the biggest DPS advantage. This change has also taken away from the formerly enjoyable variety offered by DnT 's myriad of choices, and along with it the need for new players to familiarize themselves with all weapons/dragons and take time to learn their strengths and weaknesses. To illustrate the point, most matches now include a bland carbon-copy selection of combos, with most players equipping Winter Floe and Skyburst and riding either an Imperial or Gemtalon.
- In the same stroke, Wyrmbyte hammered-in the last nail to DnT's coffin by preventing players from teaming-up with more than one player. Thus, they dashed all hopes of players being able to form into clans or guilds and fighting it out in Full 5v5s. We are now left to suffer matches that are little more than a frustrating lottery and where skill and experience have scant impact on the outcome.
OTHER ISSUES
Disappointingly, Wyrmbyte continues to ignore feedback from their play-testers and experienced players alike, resulting in a completely unbalanced PvP and proving to the gaming industry that their diminutive team is just too amateurish and does not have what it takes to deliver an enjoyable gaming experience. Also characteristic of Wyrmbyte is their complete inability to improve and fix their game code, where the blight of bugs seems completely out of control. Major bugs that have been in existence at the early stages of the beta testing, persist still with no indication from Wyrmbyte as to whether they have any plans to sort them out. The introductions of STEAM client failed to stem the constant flow of speed-hacking cheaters that continue to abuse the game and take all fun out of it for genuine players. On top of that, new game issues and exploits are cropping up at an alarming rate and each new game update from Wyrmbyte is a guaranteed source of new and persistent problems.
CONCLUSIONS
Somewhere along the way Dragons and Titans drifted off-course and lost all sight of becoming a balanced and challenging 5v5 arena and is now being precariously carried-away into the chaotic waters of a mediocre free-for-all. The spectacular dragon themes and above-standard quality of art alone fail to sustain player interest and unsurprisingly their numbers are dwindling daily. This game had promising potential in its early life, which was however ultimately squandered by Wyrmbyte who failed time and again to improve and polish their product.
RECOMMENDATION
This game will disappoint and frustrate you. Stay away from it.
There are better free MOBAs out there.
UPDATE
As of 09/09/2014 there is still no option to choose map or predict which one will be played. No pre-match team screen to discuss tactics. Speed-hackers continue to dominate the game and the cheaters are completely out of control. Whoever in Wyrmbyte is making decisions on game development should hang their head in shame and just leave the gaming industry forever. So much fail.

This game is like a Director's Cut or Definitive Edition of the original Dungeon Defenders.  It takes everything that was great about Dungeon Defenders and adds new features such as consumable items, permanent enhancements and reusable amulets.  There are several new maps and challenges, including what appears to be the start of a new campaign.
The Tavern has been converted to an open lobby with a personal trophy room at the back.  Survival Mode has been modified from the original 3-5 hour binge to a 1 hour timed single wave survival and the loot curve has been balanced for proper advancement.  Players will also find that all loot and chests are player instanced so you can loot all you want.
In the original Dungeon Defenders, mana was used to summon traps/towers and level up weapons.  A few changes to this system make it more friendly.  Mana is now only used to summon traps and towers.  Weapons are leveled using gold coins and pets have their own separate experience pool.
I would recommend that you buy this if you enjoyed the original Dungeon Defenders and are still interested in playing. If you have already burnt out of the original Dungeon Defenders this game will not offer much to keep your interest since the innovations added do not offset the lack of new content.

Okay, so let me get this out of the way: Yes, I play Overwatch. Do I see the similarities, hell- even the BLATANT character knock-offs? YES.
But the question is: Does Paladins do enough to separate itself from Blizzards Hero based team shooter?
YES IT DOES.
This game is awesome. There are still a lot of kinks and seeing as it's still in beta I can forgive that. I'll separate this review into a couple different chunks.
TECHNICAL:
1. Okay so I have yet to have Paladins straight crash on me. I run an i7 4790s, 12GB RAM and GTX 1060 6GB. The game runs fairly well. However, my roomate runs an AMD FXsomethingsomething (octo core is all I know) and a GTX 1070 and his game crashes CONSTANTLY. It can get pretty annoying and sometimes just makes him quit altogether. I don't know if it's because of the AMD processor or what have you, but that's pretty much the only difference we have in our builds. So, I'd have to say the game is more optimized towards Intel builds.
2. Framerate is good. Again, this is based off my build. I play with all settings maxed out and I'm getting my full frames - no dips or anything like that. It runs off a 32bit directX9 engine and I can see how that would help a F2P game be playable on many different builds.
3. There are small hiccups - like sometimes I can't put down a spray, sometimes I can only spray on the floor, sometimes only on the walls. Weird but not important enough to annoy me.
4. Some characters are much more effective in their classes than others. I love playing Ash [Tank], but if there is a Torval [Tank] on the enemy team, I'm done for. She just doesn't put enough damage in.
5. PLEASE PUT THE CHARACTERS CLASSES IN BEFORE THE CHARACTER LOCK IN SECTION. I'm new to the game, and there's no way for me to tell that certain characters are Healers or Front Lines or Flankers because the game won't even let you hover over those characters to tell what they are because somebody chose them. It would really help with team composition.
GAMEPLAY
(The classes go as follows: Front Lines [Tanks], Flankers [MOBA-like assassins], Damage [Offense based] and Healers [ahem... they heal]. All of these characters can mostly hold their own. And the cool thing is that the healers can actually do a lot of damage compared to OW. I know, the comparison to OW is going to be annoying but you have to understand that these games are very similar in nature.)
1. The characters kits are fantastic in Paladins. I have so much fun playing every hero. These characters play a lot more like MOBA characters than Overwatch. The Ultimate abilities can really sway the tides of battle because of the MOBA-like skills. For example, there are characters who produce MASSIVE knockbacks and can win the match based on that alone, or others that completely blind you (save for like 3 feet in front of you). It keeps the game interesting and honestly - it can be much more tactical than OW.
2. I like the gamemodes, but they are similar to Overwatch's gamemmodes with the exception of Onslaught (which is basically king of the hill and only lasts 1 round). Otherwise, you're pushing a payload after capturing the point.
3. The hitboxes in this game are very large compared to other FPS's. Sniping is much easier to do, but it still requires a fair amount of skill to do well in. You don't have to have precision aiming to be effective at most heroes and to me, it helps with the fun factor.
GRAPHICS
1. There is definitely not as much shine in this department, but again - it's because of the way the devs tried to allow many different types of builds play. Especially lower budget builds. Nothing wrong with it though as I like the art style.
2. [THIS MIGHT TRIGGER SOME OF YOU BUT IT NEEDS TO BE SAID] Some of the character designs kind of look stupid and are blatant copy and pastes of other games. Like Ruckus looks like Bolbi Stroganofski from ♥♥♥♥ing Jimmy Neutron stuffed into D.Va's mech. Viktor looks like a Guns of Boom character had sex with the brute from TF2 and plays a lot like Soldier 76. Sha Lin is Hanzo without the dragon ult. Drogoz is Pharah with an ult that auto-kills one hero. Bomb King is Junkrat. Even the ♥♥♥♥ing Ultimate is Junkrat's except that YOU are the riptire. Kinessa is Widowmaker with a different ult. And don't even get me started on Barik. I mean, he shoots LAVA out of his gun, builds TURRETS and sounds JUST LIKE TORBJORN. Fernando is Reinhardt with a flamethrower.
PLEASE UNDERSTAND THAT EVEN THOUGH THESE CHARACTERS ARE SAMEY, THEY CAN PLAY AND MUST BE PLAYED VERY DIFFERENTLY, AND THAT'S WHY I'M NOT ANGRY ABOUT IT.
Overall, Paladins is a fun game. It's balancing needs to be addressed and matchmaking is hit-or-miss. I've been playing this over OW and I'm having a blast. Don't let that ruin your enjoyment for an overall great game that deserves praise as well.

An old game that if, released this year, would be my favourite. It is what fps should be, not what they have now become. It is sometimes hard to review an older game as its graphics and sound are of such a lower quality, however at the time of release it was the best graphical game out there. Besides that let’s get into it. The map design is nice and allows for a limited, but still present, multiple pathways systems that help you beat enemies and find hidden items, like med packs etc. However the environments are sometimes repeated to often and enemy spawn and triggers become quite obvious. The story, although hard to follow and riddled with holes is still interesting enough to keep you interested in the main story. One way to fix the holes is listening to phone messages and finding laptops which give you, sometimes vague, insights into the story. The gameplay is actually the best part of this game. Guns feel responsive and enemies take damage well and ragdolls are fully utilised, the wide array of weapons also helps this. The slowdown time ability is the funniest and fun thing in the game. The ability allows you to slow down time, so you can enter a room in slow motion and kill everyone without getting damaged; it leads to fun and creative gunplay. The mood of this game is creepy and horrifying, but doesn't fully rely on jump scares to create this mood. The game constantly creates an eerie and scary mood that follows you throughout the campaign and keeps you on your toes. The vivid hallucinations created by the main villains are creepy and horrifying. The game blends horror and combat well; however it is quite obvious when the game quickly changes tone from a fast paced shooter, to a horror. The game also comes with two expansions packs which should be entertaining and practically the same. The game also lacks the multiplayer that the original game had.
8.5/10- An incredibly fun game with great combat and horror elements that blend well together. The story is interesting although filled with plot holes and the environment is creepy and eerie....have fun.

I’m gonna say something controversial here. Witcher 2 is the best in the series, even better than 3.  Kinda like how Empire Strikes back is the best Star Wars movie.  Yes, even better than Witcher 3, which was also fantastic.  But let me explain why.
What really makes Witcher 2 so brilliant to me is its plot.  Geralt is not trying to save the world from generic universe destroying bad guys, nor travelling around finding the magic-mcguffins.  He’s not the chosen one, nor is he fulfilling prophecy or banishing the ancient evil that’s just reappeared.
‘He’s not the messiah; he’s a very naughty boy!’
It’s almost like a medieval fantasy cop movie – you’re out to get the rascal who framed you for regicide, and your quest to clear your name leads to a search for truth that sets you into a web of conspiracies and betrayals.  It avoids all the clichés, and becomes something truly wonderful for it – unravelling a mystery yet not knowing who to trust is much more capticating then saving the world YET AGAIN.   It’s the kinda game Guy Ritchie or Martin Scorsese would make if that had to produce a fantasy RPG.
And this story thrives in its non-open world. While these big open worlds give you huge breadth of exploration, the trade-off is often a focused, driving and compelling narrative.  This is where the Witcher 2 succeeds.   There’s a real sense of urgency and dynamism to the game, which is constantly driving you to make progress, and I was just dying to see how it would all unfold.  Likewise, a smaller cast of characters that are almost always with you lets you know them better and relate to them more.  Plus, the branching story lines which let you play the same story from two different sides is something that I’d like to see a lot more of.
Thirdly, although the game only really has 5 large areas, they all left a lasting impression on me, much more so than the 5 million identical small villages in the Witcher 3.  From the opening bombast of the epic castle siege through the festering hole that was Flotsam, through the gorgeous dwarvern town of Vergen to the chilling elven Ruins of Loc Muinne, every single place had strong personality and atmosphere, I felt like I had experienced these wonderful diverse places, rather than rode through identi-kit wooden villages.
On top of that, even though its aged slightly, the game looks GORGEOUS, with striking use of colour and very atmospheric lighting and shading, and the gameplay is almost exactly the same as Witcher 3, so it’s pretty brilliant.  And finally, unlike 3, the game actually has nice-looking armour (seriously, aside from the starting set and the Witcher armours, 3 had you in get up worse than a BBC historical drama from the 1960s).
Now, I realise that most will disagree with me here, but I felt 2 was fresher and better than 3, and it remains the definitive Witcher experience for me.  I wish more game developers would make rpgs like this instead of the stared ‘chosen one saves the universe’ guff (Yes Bioware, I’m looking at you).  If you still haven’t played it, now is the perfect time.

As a fan of roguelikes, this scratches the itch without becoming incredibly tedious to start over like ToME or DC:SS. Gold from one run carries over to the next, and achievements unlock new classes and equipment available for purchase with all that carried over gold (which does not carry over twice - so spend it!).
Play style is simple but not shallow. The game is completely controlled with WASD + L/R-clicks, with about 1000 ways to pause the game/enter inventory. It does away with much of the tediousness found in turn-based roguelikes by giving you the option to throw/equip items while paused - so no menu delving to switch your loadout or use a scoll/potion. This also means you can change playstyle on the fly.
Item selection is nice and interesting, though a few more variations and combinations especially in magic wouldn't be unwelcome. There is a bit that can be added in future updates that I would like to see, like a more fleshed out deity and crafting system. More variation in puzzles, and more secret/hard to reach rewards that require certain effects (like fire resistance, flight/levitation, etc) would also add much to the game I think.
Overall, I've had a ton of fun and can really get into playing half a dozen runs in a row trying to get just that ONE MORE achievement. Solid 4/5 that is well worth the low price.

I know what you're thinking.  "Farming sim? Who would want to do that?".  Well, that's a good question Billy.  Let's sit down and figure this one out, shall we?  I would say this game appeals to a side of me where you start out with very little and you have to work to improve what you have.  Games like Minecraft, Harvest Moon, The Sims, etc.
Now I'm not saying you are going to dig for diamonds and fight zombies and creepers, nor am I saying this is exactly like Harvest moon or whatever.  I'm just saying that in those games you're started off without much and you have to work to make your world grow.  Likewise, they start you off with a single field and a few tractors and a bank loan, and from there you have to pay off the loan, plant your crops, figure out the best time to sell your crops, and in general keep finding new ways to make money.
If you want to be lame, you can buy windmills, and solar panels and a bunch of other easy money-making items.  These items require very little to no maintenance and you earn money every day.  There's no challenge in that though.  You might want one so that you have some steady income while you're working 5 fields at once and hiring 2-3 workers to keep things moving as you jump from tractor to tractor.  You don't want to be able to just walk away and come back 8 hours later to find you're filthy rich though.
There's plenty to do in this game.  You can play the original map (in Germany?) or now with the Titanium edition, you can play the same game with a more American theme.  There's cows for milk, sheep for wool, chickens for eggs, and several crops to plant (some of which require special machinery). You also need to learn where to sell your eggs and wool as well as how to feed your cows so your milk output is at its best,
When you feel like exploring there are some hidden items in the map that  you can collect (it doesn't really affect the game so you can ignore it if you like) and occasionally there are some side-jobs you can take on for extra cash.
The only thing that's missing in single-player is an actual economy.  Prices will go down if you flood the market with a certain type of crop, but other than that, demand seems to be purely random.  There are no competing farmers for your crops so you merely wait for the best time to sell (except maybe in the early days when you have the loan to pay off).
Fortunately, you can play this game online so it doesn't feel so empty...and it's a lot of fun to cooperate with farm work, though you'd need mods to get "paid" for your work in an online game.   If this game had a neighboring farm that you could cooperate with and/or compete with, and if there was an actual economy that was reflected in the prices (instead of price changes to simulate an economy), this game would be perfect.
Still, as you can see, I've spent a lot of time playing this, and that was mostly before the titanium edition.  I've only just begun a game on the new map.  If you enjoy the satisfaction of building up a farm (or an empire or whatever) this game will have a lot to keep you interested.  It can also be relaxing to just chill out as you are taking care of the farm business.
