Dust is a really fun combat/platformer in the "Metroidvania" style, with a lot of charm to boot.  Don't let my play time fool you, I have a platinum trophy for this game on Playstation Network.  The basic gameplay mechanics are solid.  Dust controls very well, and pulling off combos is a breeze.  The platforming also feels tight, which is a huge selling point for me as I have always loved 2D platformers.  They have successfully combined combo-based fighting and platforming, to the detriment of neither aspect of the game.  Ripping combos for hours on end can get a bit tedious by the end, but that is one of the few criticisms I have of the experience.
The art speaks for itself.  This is a cartoony, but beautiful game world, and was a joy to explore. The characters are fun and interesting, and the voice acting is mostly very good.  Fidget is my favorite, with the right amount of humor to avoid becoming annoying.  The world offers a varied selection of environments to explore, and many different enemy types to battle.  This is a really fun experience, and does not take very long to get through for those of us who no longer have time to complete massive 50+ hour games.  I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys "Metroidvania"-style exploration.

Okay, so let me get this out of the way: Yes, I play Overwatch. Do I see the similarities, hell- even the BLATANT character knock-offs? YES.
But the question is: Does Paladins do enough to separate itself from Blizzards Hero based team shooter?
YES IT DOES.
This game is awesome. There are still a lot of kinks and seeing as it's still in beta I can forgive that. I'll separate this review into a couple different chunks.
TECHNICAL:
1. Okay so I have yet to have Paladins straight crash on me. I run an i7 4790s, 12GB RAM and GTX 1060 6GB. The game runs fairly well. However, my roomate runs an AMD FXsomethingsomething (octo core is all I know) and a GTX 1070 and his game crashes CONSTANTLY. It can get pretty annoying and sometimes just makes him quit altogether. I don't know if it's because of the AMD processor or what have you, but that's pretty much the only difference we have in our builds. So, I'd have to say the game is more optimized towards Intel builds.
2. Framerate is good. Again, this is based off my build. I play with all settings maxed out and I'm getting my full frames - no dips or anything like that. It runs off a 32bit directX9 engine and I can see how that would help a F2P game be playable on many different builds.
3. There are small hiccups - like sometimes I can't put down a spray, sometimes I can only spray on the floor, sometimes only on the walls. Weird but not important enough to annoy me.
4. Some characters are much more effective in their classes than others. I love playing Ash [Tank], but if there is a Torval [Tank] on the enemy team, I'm done for. She just doesn't put enough damage in.
5. PLEASE PUT THE CHARACTERS CLASSES IN BEFORE THE CHARACTER LOCK IN SECTION. I'm new to the game, and there's no way for me to tell that certain characters are Healers or Front Lines or Flankers because the game won't even let you hover over those characters to tell what they are because somebody chose them. It would really help with team composition.
GAMEPLAY
(The classes go as follows: Front Lines [Tanks], Flankers [MOBA-like assassins], Damage [Offense based] and Healers [ahem... they heal]. All of these characters can mostly hold their own. And the cool thing is that the healers can actually do a lot of damage compared to OW. I know, the comparison to OW is going to be annoying but you have to understand that these games are very similar in nature.)
1. The characters kits are fantastic in Paladins. I have so much fun playing every hero. These characters play a lot more like MOBA characters than Overwatch. The Ultimate abilities can really sway the tides of battle because of the MOBA-like skills. For example, there are characters who produce MASSIVE knockbacks and can win the match based on that alone, or others that completely blind you (save for like 3 feet in front of you). It keeps the game interesting and honestly - it can be much more tactical than OW.
2. I like the gamemodes, but they are similar to Overwatch's gamemmodes with the exception of Onslaught (which is basically king of the hill and only lasts 1 round). Otherwise, you're pushing a payload after capturing the point.
3. The hitboxes in this game are very large compared to other FPS's. Sniping is much easier to do, but it still requires a fair amount of skill to do well in. You don't have to have precision aiming to be effective at most heroes and to me, it helps with the fun factor.
GRAPHICS
1. There is definitely not as much shine in this department, but again - it's because of the way the devs tried to allow many different types of builds play. Especially lower budget builds. Nothing wrong with it though as I like the art style.
2. [THIS MIGHT TRIGGER SOME OF YOU BUT IT NEEDS TO BE SAID] Some of the character designs kind of look stupid and are blatant copy and pastes of other games. Like Ruckus looks like Bolbi Stroganofski from ♥♥♥♥ing Jimmy Neutron stuffed into D.Va's mech. Viktor looks like a Guns of Boom character had sex with the brute from TF2 and plays a lot like Soldier 76. Sha Lin is Hanzo without the dragon ult. Drogoz is Pharah with an ult that auto-kills one hero. Bomb King is Junkrat. Even the ♥♥♥♥ing Ultimate is Junkrat's except that YOU are the riptire. Kinessa is Widowmaker with a different ult. And don't even get me started on Barik. I mean, he shoots LAVA out of his gun, builds TURRETS and sounds JUST LIKE TORBJORN. Fernando is Reinhardt with a flamethrower.
PLEASE UNDERSTAND THAT EVEN THOUGH THESE CHARACTERS ARE SAMEY, THEY CAN PLAY AND MUST BE PLAYED VERY DIFFERENTLY, AND THAT'S WHY I'M NOT ANGRY ABOUT IT.
Overall, Paladins is a fun game. It's balancing needs to be addressed and matchmaking is hit-or-miss. I've been playing this over OW and I'm having a blast. Don't let that ruin your enjoyment for an overall great game that deserves praise as well.

I forgot how much of a great game the original F.E.A.R. was. I played this game way back in 2005 when it was first released, and I had an absolute blast playing though it again. It has a nice mixture of fast paced game play with some horror tossed in it. And it’s not cheesy "American horror" either. None of those lame sudden movements or gore that tries to gross you out. The game's horror was heavily influenced by Japanese horror movies, like the original "Ring." F.E.A.R. does an excellent job in making you wonder about what is going on all while keeping you on your toes as you progress through the story.
The game is a visual treat as well. F.E.A.R, being a game that first came out on PC back in 2005, has definitely aged but it has aged well. Some parts of the game just look fantastic. The designers have done an excellent job of using the lighting to their advantage. The shadows and overall dark environments of the game help to enhance the atmosphere. Even the small things, such as lights flickering, lights of a phone that has a voicemail on it, and empty offices where the only light source is a computer monitor just help to make it that much creepier. You’ll find yourself constantly using your flashlight, and dread walking through long dark hallways.
I highly recommend this game, even if you're not a big fan of first person shooters. It’s definitely a must buy if you don’t have it already, and a great game to add to your collection. It goes on sale constantly on Steam, so don’t hesitate to pick it up if you’re interested. F.E.A.R. 2 was also a pretty great game. I personally liked it a lot, but I found the first one to be a bit better. The expansion packs for the first game were just pretty average. I have not played F.E.A.R. 3, but I’ve heard that it’s the least well received of the trilogy.
You’ll be perfectly fine with just the original F.E.A.R.

I have been a huge fan of Dungeon Defenders for a long time and have very fond memories progressing through the game playing with friends and solo. That being said Dungeon Defenders Eternity has turned my once loved go to game into disappointing waste of time.
While Trendy has recently patched the game to include online single player it has clear balance issues when played as such to the point of my avoiding it completely. This has caused my motivation and excitement when I saw the release into a strong aversion and dislike of the game in general.
While the original had its own problems in regards the inventory management and loot distribution/progression this game has taken a severe step away from fixing these problems. When using said inventory I feel as if I am trying to smash a square peg into a round hole and leaves me only with a bitter taste in my mouth as this should be one of the simplest tasks considering the clear focus on the new progression and loot system Trendy has recently made.
Playing with my group of friends has now become a challenge and lesson in patience with the addition of playverse dedicated servers and the poor interface for inviting and creating a party. This interface should be a seamless and painless procedure but falls far short of the mark. Being forced to return to the shared tavern after every level instead of just continuing the play through of the campaign has me frustrated and confused as it takes away from experience and fun of the main story by a rather large margin.
The shared tavern itself seems to be only a cost saving measure and serves only to create chaos as I attempt to manage my characters after a level. I find my screen flooded in spam from players leaving and joining said tavern while my senses are assaulted by other players firing wildly testing their DPS or checking out what some new item does on use. As you attempt to compare current gear with recent loot the tool tips frequently disappear by players joining and dropping from the tavern further adding to my frustration.
The gameplay itself has remained largely unchanged aside from a pointless crafting system, texture pop in and balance issues.
If you own the original there is little to no point in purchasing this new version and strongly suggest you avoid it until some large changes are made and maybe not even then. Hopefully Dungeon Defenders 2 won’t leave me with such a bitter experience.

If you're a fan of rouge-lites, Unexplored is a true hidden gem on Steam.
As a general rule, I'm not a fan of procedural generation. It typically feels like one long hallway with boxes (rooms) randomly attached on either side.
But there's something special going on here. If you had told me the maps were manually designed I wouldn't bat an eyelash. I think it also helps that the entire dungeon is created from the start, so you'll read notes specifically referencing content in deeper levels, as well as equipment to deal with puzzles further down the line. It lends a sense of purposeful design to the entire experience .
I found a short dev video on YT giving a brief explanation of this unique approach to randomization.
Anyway, I'm absolutely loving this game so far. Movement and tactical, timing-based combat feels dialed in and tight. Audio/visual design is top notch. No XP* so there's a great sense of risk/reward with every enemy encounter.
* You do keep Gold currency between dungeon runs. As well as unlocking new starting classes and pre-dungeon shop items through and Achievement-like system.
It's all pretty sweet, to the point where Unexplored is likely earmarked for a spot on my GOTY list.

EDIT: As a Paradox fan going back as far as the very first EU, it's difficult to put a thumbs down here, however their recent pricing policy to reflect the "increased purchasing power" of several countries in recession sounded like something straight out of the PR office at Ubisoft or EA. I accept that this game is still supported, but increasing the price of a ten year old game like Victoria II (conviniently just before the steam summer sale I might add) exposes this for the con that it is.
In the beggining, there was Master of Orion 1, the greatest 4x game ever made, and only surpassed by the messianic arrival of the sequel MoO2. Many years would pass, computer power expanded exponentially, wars were faught, generations lived and died, and dozens, if not hundreds of 4x space games were developed in imitation of the progenitors, yet none could surpass them. We don't even talk about MoO3. (Distant Worlds is maybe the one exception to this, buy it). Until (possibly) Stellaris. Stellaris is a contender.
What made these games such masterpieces, unable to be devoured by their own offspring? In my opinion, the core gameplay mechanics (exploration, technology, expansion, and combat) were incredibly strong, and the parameters allowed for infinite and flexible replayability. The imitators failed in delivering the strong core gameplay of meaningful decisions that aggregate into a larger strategy of interlocking parts. Stellaris doesn't have all the parts yet, but it has enough of them in place to make me confident that when fully expanded, this game will take the best elements of paradox game design, and marry them to a true spiritual successor to the MoO series that focuses on strong core mechanics and replayability.
The core mechanics of exploration, technology, and expansion are all quite developed and engaging. You star trek all over the galaxy finding interesting things, the tech system is solid and expansion feels rewarding. The scope of the galaxy and the interface tools given to manage it are quite impressive. The sector system seems to prevent late game slog as intended.
As the 3 (or more) expansions roll out for the game, I think they should focus on developing the rest of the neglected core mechanics that made the MoO series great, namely combat. At present, the combat in stellaris is not particularly compelling, although it is kind of interesting to watch.
What makes this game great are the many small design touches. The way black holes are actually spheres of negative space, the way you enounter new species of aliens hours and hours into playing, the way many standard issues with the late game are resolved are all excellent examples.
I never buy games at retail price. Why do that when you can just play MoO or MoO2 until they go on sale? But I bought this one at $40 on launch. $40 is a perfectly reasonable price for the INSANE amount of content here, even Paradox skeptics can be assured of that. I respect Paradox greatly for setting this price point, they want people to give the game a shot and go for the expansions if they like it. This is the kind of confidence that produces good customer-dev relationships.
I highly recommend Stellaris as a master class in strategy game design. Everything from aesthetics, interface, multiplayer, gameplay, and mod support are made by people who care about those systems working well, and working together. With the current direction of the MoO reboot, it looks like Paradox has stolen yet another beloved pc strategy genre out of the back pocket of a complacent industry (ala cities skylines). Kudos Paradox!

I'm really bad at Rogue-likes (Rogue-lites? Rogue-like, likes?), but I am addicted to them. Earlier this morning, after putting over 40 hours into Unexplored, I finally made it out of the dungeon with the Amulet of Yendor. It was super satisfying. This game has the best level generator I have ever encountered. While playing I died hundreds of time. That sounds frustrating, but it never was. Every death was fair. Every time I was killed I knew exactly went wrong. In fact if you explore properly you'll  always have a decent idea of what's coming next, allowing you to strategize before each battle. Strategy only goes so far though. You still have to win the fight. Hotkeys help a lot.The combat itself feels great. It took me awhile to get used to the way you swing your weapon, and how to properly use other equipment. Oh and I blew myself up while trying to brew potions without finding a recipe or testing out an unidentified staff more times than I can count. But it's all fair. I know the Cyclic Level Generator® or whatever it's called has been hyped quite a bit and for good reason. I remember reading an interview where the creator said he got the idea for it by watching his kids play in a friend or relatives house. Apparently their house had a layout where you could run around the ground floor in a circle. He saw how much more fun they had playing there than at his own home which lacked a circular layout. That's pretty brilliant. I grew up in a house like that, and I have a niece and nephew that are taking advantage of it now, so I understand how intuitive it is. And it's not just the layouts that are cyclic. The puzzles and clues follow a similar route. It's pretty amazing. My favorite game so far this year.

TL;DR: A bit too casual in some respects, but at other times I feel like I should have read a guide. Note that most of the positive reviews show playtimes under 20 hours.
NOTE: I have hundreds of hours in ToME and many other Roguelikes (including Rogue), so don't assume this is just another "I DONT LIEK ROUGELIEKS" review. Also, credit where it's due, the devs seem very active, which I respect.

Reminds me of Binding of Isaac meets Mines of Moria. I hated the control scheme of the former, loved the depth of the latter. Unfortunately, this particular recipe doesn't work for me.
Control scheme aside (as this is more a personal dislike), I was surprised by how hard it was to die. Several health restoration options kept me bumbling along for much longer than I expected, and I don't really consider that a plus. To be fair, it may get harder further down.
Very little in the way of explanation as to how anything works...alchemy tables and forges? No clue. Why do some doors stay blocked unless I wait for a while (at which point, despite my literally not moving, they open)? Perhaps I missed the visual or audio clues that would explain this, but I also wasn't really told to look for such things. Speaking of which...
Puzzles? In a Roguelike? This would bother me less if I understood the rules the game was functioning under (hey I can push or pull this torch thing, but it's kind of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get it where I want...am I SUPPOSED to do that, or is it just here for flavor or... what?). Sometimes there are floaty lights...are they part of a puzzle, or just ambiance? What do these glowy gems do, and why are there sometimes indications of wind blowing in a certain direction? Is any of this relevant? Can I interact with it in some way? PLASE HALPS.
I can see many people love it, and I'm certain I'll be downvoted, particularly since I only gave the game about an hour before walking away. There may indeed be a deeper game here, however, I was left feeling frustrated and wasn't impressed enough to go look up some guides (playing the tutorial didn't help much). It's only $10, so if it looks fun to you, jump right on in, however I'll stick with Roguelikes that are actually like Rogue (back to Caves of Qud I go!)

Dust is a pretty looking 2D platformer. That is just about the only positive thing I can say about it.
It has annoyed me greatly and I'm going to drop it. I have better ways to spend my free time than with a game that pisses me off.
Annoyances:
#1 - The writing is awful, and the cutscenes cannot be skipped. Yes, you can hit a key to jump to the next line of dialogue, but only after the previous line is about half through. In order to rub salt in the wound, the game makes you watch the same crappy cutscenes again and again every time you retry a boss fight.
#2 - The controls are bad. want to turn around on a platform to look in the other direction? Too bad. Pressing a direction key will always make Dust take a step in that direction and fall off the platform, blunder into a trap or whatever. You can't really choose how high to jump either, how long you hold the jump button makes almost no difference at all.

First, a caveat...I actually do enjoy this game, at least some of the time.  Now, onto business...
Pros:
+ Potentially expansive universe with what could've been nearly endless options.
+ A notably unique storyline with interesting details, and races at least some of which don't seem quite "cookie cutter".
+ A ship designer such that, to this day, no other 4X game has.
Cons:
- Maps typically end up more like Battle Arenas than strategy maps, for a couple of different reasons, but the most important of which is that even truly beefy computers are greatly taxed trying to run an Insane map of any kind.
- Far too short a campaign, that could've been entirely epic.
- Too little variation between how each race plays.  Essentially, there's only one winning strategy, and the tactics each race uses to follow that strategy are only mildly varied at best.  The game had a lot of potential for a lot of unique mechanics for each of the races that would have actually drastically changed how they play, but this wasn't done.
- Ship designer somewhat clunky and unintuitive. Great variety of parts to choose from, but missing a good selection of truly simple, universal "core" parts.
- The AI is abysmal.  There simply is no other word for it.
- There are still far too many bugs, and far too little polish, for what was supposed to be a top-shelf, finished game.
- Excessive emphasis on DLC rather than actually improving the base game.
Summary:
This game could've been one of the best 4X space games of its generation, if not of all time.  It could've been better than even Stellaris (though I haven't played that yet, so I could be wrong).  Enjoyable as it is, some of the time, it's just not quite enough on its own to earn a recommendation.  Coupled with how much potential it had but missed out on, I just have to flat-out not recommend it.
If it goes on a decent sale, however, I wouldn't fault you for picking it up anyway.  It can be really fun in small doses.  But it just doesn't carry the kind of epic grandiosity that one reasonably expects from a game about conquering (or liberating) the galaxy.  It's unfortunate, but here's hoping that they did well enough in sales, and are willing enough to learn from their mistakes, that a Galactic Civilizations IV will happen, and be better than ever.

If you can get past the old textures (see below if you don't), F.E.A.R is still a good horror-FPS that holds well to modern standards while keeping a lot of the "older" FPS elements like rewards from level exploration.
How's the gameplay ?
The weapons, while beign quite standard, have a good feel to them and are pretty much balanced depending on the situations. This, coupled with the slow-mo makes gunfight quite tense and enjoyable.
How are ennemies ?
There are very few bulletspongy ennemies and the AI manages things quite well. Its able to flank you, use grenades to push you out of cover and aims decently. There are enought scripted ambushes and other unsuspected situations able to push you out of comfort zone and keeping you away from borederom.
How's the level design ?
The level design is quite linear and dosen't offer a lot of different approaches and somewhat lacks variety, but its not bad and serves well the claustrophobic atmosphere of the game, there are some hidden powerups that'll be grealtly helpfull, forcing you to explore a bit.
Is there stealth in it ?
From what I've tried, "stealth" works in this game, ennemies can spot you by sound but also because of your flashlight, walking and crouching to reduce your noise can allow you to surprise ennemies or seldomly knock them down without beign noticed.
What about the story and the athmosphere ?
Its quite a decent story for an FPS I guess, it builds up slowly and gives you clues as you progress and the final is quite memorable. The horror aspect is very efficient for a first run, less on a second but sucessfully goes beyond beign just a jumpscare fest. There are whole levels made up to build up the tension and the line between reality and illusion isn't always explicit.
What are the known issues and possible improvements on modern systems ?
- If you have a logitech keyboard like a G110, you might come accross a hudge frame drop. There's a workaround on the steam forum about it, there's also an utility online for this fix, but I'd suggest you do things manualy, safer and probably more effective.
- If you find the textures too ugly, know that someone is working on remplacing them with HD textures here :

Time to review this with a Pros and Cons list...
CONS:
1. Public Tavern = People everywhere whining and asking things like, "How do you play?" and "Why does this game suck so much?" And there is always a hoard around the forge and tavern-keep that makes walking around hard.
2. Requires constant internet connection = All file are on their servers, not your computer. This means if your internet goes out, you can't do a thing. And it means long wait screens while it downloads the map you just tried to enter. If you have slow internet or frequent outages, this game is not for you.
3. Summoner = The Summoner no longer uses his own pool of Defense Unit points (Minion Units). Instead, he draws from the same DU as everyone else. This makes him a character that is now a builder like any other except that he can't attack. Two pets doesn't really make up for this and minions are not good at being the only thing on the field. He is most pointless now that he costs other builders their points.
4. Costumes = Completely pointless. Armor is visible and that cannot be turned off. So what you look like under all the cool little helmets and masks and shields seems almost pointless by the end of even the first level.
5. Eternia Crystals = The crystal is now no longer customizable. Only look it has is the default look. Sad. Really, really sad.
6. In Game Store = Yes, there is a store in the game that costs real money. Yes, it is just for cosmetic items when you are playing on Steam. Yes, it still stinks. In-game stores that use real money on a game you already paid real money to buy is dumb. It's tied on annoying level with Release-Day DLCs for me. I already gave you money to buy the game and now it's "Oh, wait, you wanted the entire game? That'll be an extra $20."
7. Perma-Death = Perma-Death in Hardcore??? Why? Just why? Never playing that mode.
8. Two friend systems = o.O If you play on Steam, please note that there are two social systems in the game: Steam and Playverse. This gets confusing fast... "Wait, I just added that person, how do I have a friend request from them. Oh, this is Steam that is Playverse." "Why aren't they showing up in my friends or this group?..." Etc.
9. Tooltips = There are none. Happy button-guessing folks!
10. Tutorial = My sister had not a clue what to do as a first time player and I had to show her everything. A tutorial to do that would have been really nice...
11. No Split-screen = I used this all the time on the old game and I have actually already missed it. Please patch it in.
12. Box System = They made it worse. I didn't know that was even possible. It's like an apps touchsreen now with a bad PC overlay on it.
PROS:
1. Single or Multiplayer Missions = I can play with random people or just my friends. A welcome early patch that was really, really needed. Works great now.
2. Visible Armor = This is awesome. Sure, for most of the game you will look like you covered yourself in hotglue and rolled around in a junkyard... But once you hit max and get a real set of armor that all matches: You will look awesome.
3. Dyes = They now sell dyes of different colors at the Tavern-keep's place. And most items have 5 to 6 dye slots for colors on it you can change. Yes, for people who like micromanaging every little detail of your character (aka: people like me), this is awesome. They are low in price so you can change colors a lot. :)
4. Pet hatching = You get eggs and weight for them to hatch as you run around and do things. AKA: Pokemon eggs. It is actually quite fun to see what will pop out of each egg. Awesome system.
5. Coins = MANA IS NO LONGER MONEY!!! You no longer have to try and use Mana for everything and worry about lost Mana all over the map. Gold coins enemies drop last longer than Mana and you don't have to feel bad burning through thousands of Mana a battle in the later stages with you skills.
6. All DLCs built in = ...need I even say why this is nice and awesome?
7.  Dashing = You can dash! ...four times... ...than your meter needs to recharge over-time...
8. Two weapon slots = Switch out to a different weapon quickly when they are resistant to your main one. Very, very nice.
9. Graphics = Slow to load, but once they do, they are awesome!
10. Fun = The first Dungeon Defender was fun, this one is fun. They are the same game though.
11. Co-Op Awesomeness = Grab a few friends and go to town. Just plain more fun with more friends.
12. Loot system = Fewer drops of better quality? Individual loot? Both very nice.
OVERALL:
This really just seems to be you paying money to help them test PlayVerse...

If you enjoy fantasy RPG, this game is in much the same vein as the Elder Scrolls series. The setting is similar, but what makes the witcher 2 stand out is how the choices you make affect the game. The Witcher 2 at first felt more linear and confining that an open world rpg (Witcher 2 is more like open section than open world), but this led to a focus on character choice (comparable in some ways to Mass Effect), and a more focused narrative. The best part of the Witcher 2 is how the consequences of decisions you make won't be felt until much later in the game and in the case of some decisions even in the next game (Witcher 3). This element of gameplay really makes it feel as if your choices actually have real consequences, since by the time you see the result of your choice its too much later to go back and reverse course. Although some players might end up stuck with decisions that they regret (I was), I love the realism of the system. Anyone who is a fan of fantasy RPGs and wants to see what a massive RPG game where your choices carry heavy and not immediately seen consequences, the Witcher 2 is for you

Long time Dungeon Defender players may raise an eyebrow or two at Dungeon Defenders Eternity. At best it seems like a light DLC at the current discounted price for previous owners ($6 USD). It includes a few new maps, a new consumable system, rebalance of classes (summoner being one of the bigger changes), and a new patching system which requires an online connection to play single player. Players can also play crossplatform with this version. There's also a built in cash shop in the game and for the time being, it only contains cosmetic things for $1 USD for a costume. The developers have said they intend to keep it cosmetic only and not pay to win. Currency is also changed from mana to in game coins creating a slower climb to currency becoming trivial. DDE includes all of the original's DLC minus some of the holiday maps (for now).
As of this writing, there are many bugs that plague this new version from summoner pets jumping off cliffs to hotkeys being unbound with every map. The bright side of this is the new patching system is far better than before. Like Guild Wars, they can patch small things with minimal downtime server-side.
The UI is far more suitable for mouse and keyboard in this iteration, albeit a bit clunky at the moment. It's still more customizable than the original DD. Controller support on the other hand is clunkier on this version. Hopefully these quality of life things will get ironed out with time.
So for those who own the original and enjoyed it DDE really only offers a chance at a fresh start with less hackers, a few new maps and a promise of easier distribution of content with the new software for the future. For $6 USD, it could pass for DLC-lite for prior owners. For those who haven't tried the original DD or don't own most of the DLC for the original, even the normal price of $20 USD is a worthwhile investment. However, for normal price, prior owners who own all the DLC might want to hold off picking this up until there's more meat on the bone.
I really wish there was a way to just post a review without a recommendation. For DDE, it's less black and white and more 'depends'. There's potential in DDE as something to hold out until DD2, but for now it's only for those looking for a fresh start or those who haven't tried DD, a fantastic tower defense game. The tech behind the patching system is a very solid foundation for future content, hopefully TrendyNet will support DDE with more content before the inevitable DD2 hits the market.

After many, many hours in the first game, many of the improvements of it in Eternity shine through. In public matches I used to run into hackers a lot, as well as having a hard time getting over the hump of level 75. This game fixes all of this, and that alone makes the $6 worth it in my eyes. I have to guess that the reason it's a standalone game is because the engine and coding for the first was badly optimized, or they couldn't do much about people who already hacked the game, which I understand. With a fresh start, the game feels much more balanced and the introduction of consumables is neat.
So, after playing for a while I noticed that boosters started to drop from enemies, for completely free. Experience, loot quality, loot quantity and what not. I thought that was really cool seeing how they aren't sold via micro-transactions. In fact, when I checked I was surprised that it's only taunts which are being sold, and the possibility of skins and heroes, which I find are fine seeing how that's what they did with the first game, nothing wrong with that. I also noticed that they are expanding the trading feature over Steam, which sounds great.
Leveling does not seem to slow down at any rate as long as you're playing at correct levels for your character, it's been smooth leveling for me and my Initiate, who is level 46 currently. I used to have trouble leveling up in the first game as it forced you into Insane mode at around this point, but now I can ease in instead of having to deal with tough enemies. It also feels like I have less pressure of being a complete DPS or complete Tower hero with the new array of stats to level up. Although since I am an old player, I tend to stay towards just leveling up in towers since that is what I am used to.
The UI can get a bit confusing but I get caught up to it after using it for a while. Some buttons are in weird places, and it seems to be a bit messy. I also had trouble loading in sometimes due to the streaming way of downloading the game, and textures sometimes bugged up for me. As far as I know though, both of this issues have been addressed and/or fixed, so that is good to hear at least.
If I had any complaint of the game, it would be these: I would love an option to individually hide the armor pieces from your character. I hate seeing my Initiate having a pink peice of armor that looks like a brain on top of her general cap. (I used the sky captain skin.) It looks rather silly, but the rest of the armor seems to be okay to me at least. Maybe even add an option that Terraria does, having a vanity slot so you can place over weapons/armor and have the gear you like in terms of look. Another problem I have is the matchmaking. Not so much the DRM, but I'd love to find which matches would need a DPS hero or a Tower hero. This way I know I am needed in the mission and I am not pushed aside or unneeded for the task at hand. It annoys me to find another aura monk already building, so I have to either be sorta useless in terms of damage or leave the match.
Aside from the problems, I find this game to be great. It is a nice change from the original, and for cheap, too. I suggest if you are a hardcore veteran of the first game like I am, to pick it up. Or if you haven't, enjoy it while you can before Dungeon Defenders 2 comes out! Overall I'd give this game an 8/10.

This game is absolutely amazing and underrated. I love roguelikes - I've clocked hundreds of hours on TOME, and recently got my first 4-rune win in DCSS - and this game absolutely scratches that itch. Every frustrating death is almost immediately followed up by the compulsive need to try again.
Pros:
+ Great value for money - hours and hours can be sunk into this
+ In a related point, great replay value. Play-throughs will be defined by the stuff you find. Fireball staff? Mage run.
+ Surprising depth in terms of item combinations - forging, as well as in terms of how potions and such interact with the terrain
Con:
- Probably to flavour, but I find it frustrating that so much of the game is deliberately made unknown (and there isn't much out there - trust me, I've googled). I love the game, but when you don't have unlimited time in a day it would be nice to know what's going to happen when you combine sigil x with weapon or item y, rather than have to experiment endlessly.
- Some runs are terminated by horrific bad luck. In one, I walked out the starting door to find a plain of grass. Hidden in the center was a fire trap. The world immediately turned into a burning hell and I died. I have no problem with dying, but I would rather mistakes of such a minor kind - e.g. walking in the center of the room - not be punished by death.
100% must-buy if you enjoy roguelikes. An interesting sidenote: after playing Unexplored for a while, going back to DCSS felt incredibly relaxing because it wasn't real time and I wasn't desperately mashing keys to equip daggers to throw at bosses or swap weapons in and out.

Call of Duty; Black Ops is the Vietnam themed installment of the franchise, known for revitalizing the tired formula of the World War and Modern War installments.
Call of Duty Black Ops has too many problems: Terrible, weightless gunplay, uninvolved announcer system, broken hit registration and interpolation lerp, hamfisted campaign, boring lacklustre level design, rigid movement system and an overall unsatisfying perk system in the combat when playing online multiplayer. Not at all challenging due to how all the guns react and function (extremely low spread rifles and SMG's apart from Sniper Rifles which are the worst weapons in the game due to their low rate of fire and lack of real openendedness in the level design), a campaign that is lukewarm at best due it's rigid and linear structure, uninvolved cast of characters, cliché action-hero, poor "artificial intelligence" node design/scripting and nasueating voice cast that tries far too hard to sound serious instead comes of as unintentionally hilarious. Narrative of the story which has Mason (main character) consistently tries to play off his delusion of his friend Reznov, a character you played as in World of War
as complex insight of
but merely comes off as irritating to the player as it invades the majority of the plot around Nova-6 the experimental gas that is designed to be an extremely potent neurotoxin that would win the Cold War.
On multiplayer's awkward perk system and horrible networking quality is combined with outdated graphics, from the Modern Warfare 1 era and gameplay mechanics that are not consistent (such as the insertion spawn system, lack of said spawn protection, poor spawn positions etc.) makes COD;BLOPS an incredibly mixed response from me. Only worth the purchase if you're aiming to find yourself losing ranks constantly, getting spawn-killed frequently and grinding a useless prestige system and one of the worst "hitboxes" this side of Battlefield Bad Company.
Black Ops' engine running off a modified IDTECH 3 enigne which was not only horrendously unoptimized on lower-end systems and buggy on release and it still contiues to show freezes and framerate dips and micro-stuttering back from 2015 on a decent rig. EDIT: As a Paradox fan going back as far as the very first EU, it's difficult to put a thumbs down here, however their recent pricing policy to reflect the "increased purchasing power" of several countries in recession sounded like something straight out of the PR office at Ubisoft or EA. I accept that this game is still supported, but increasing the price of a ten year old game like Victoria II (conviniently just before the steam summer sale I might add) exposes this for the con that it is.
In the beggining, there was Master of Orion 1, the greatest 4x game ever made, and only surpassed by the messianic arrival of the sequel MoO2. Many years would pass, computer power expanded exponentially, wars were faught, generations lived and died, and dozens, if not hundreds of 4x space games were developed in imitation of the progenitors, yet none could surpass them. We don't even talk about MoO3. (Distant Worlds is maybe the one exception to this, buy it). Until (possibly) Stellaris. Stellaris is a contender.
What made these games such masterpieces, unable to be devoured by their own offspring? In my opinion, the core gameplay mechanics (exploration, technology, expansion, and combat) were incredibly strong, and the parameters allowed for infinite and flexible replayability. The imitators failed in delivering the strong core gameplay of meaningful decisions that aggregate into a larger strategy of interlocking parts. Stellaris doesn't have all the parts yet, but it has enough of them in place to make me confident that when fully expanded, this game will take the best elements of paradox game design, and marry them to a true spiritual successor to the MoO series that focuses on strong core mechanics and replayability.
The core mechanics of exploration, technology, and expansion are all quite developed and engaging. You star trek all over the galaxy finding interesting things, the tech system is solid and expansion feels rewarding. The scope of the galaxy and the interface tools given to manage it are quite impressive. The sector system seems to prevent late game slog as intended.
As the 3 (or more) expansions roll out for the game, I think they should focus on developing the rest of the neglected core mechanics that made the MoO series great, namely combat. At present, the combat in stellaris is not particularly compelling, although it is kind of interesting to watch.
What makes this game great are the many small design touches. The way black holes are actually spheres of negative space, the way you enounter new species of aliens hours and hours into playing, the way many standard issues with the late game are resolved are all excellent examples.
I never buy games at retail price. Why do that when you can just play MoO or MoO2 until they go on sale? But I bought this one at $40 on launch. $40 is a perfectly reasonable price for the INSANE amount of content here, even Paradox skeptics can be assured of that. I respect Paradox greatly for setting this price point, they want people to give the game a shot and go for the expansions if they like it. This is the kind of confidence that produces good customer-dev relationships.
I highly recommend Stellaris as a master class in strategy game design. Everything from aesthetics, interface, multiplayer, gameplay, and mod support are made by people who care about those systems working well, and working together. With the current direction of the MoO reboot, it looks like Paradox has stolen yet another beloved pc strategy genre out of the back pocket of a complacent industry (ala cities skylines). Kudos Paradox!

This game, is a real shame. It had such an oppurtunity to be a fantastic game, unfortunately, it's fallen flat on it's face.
Let me explain, now, Ride, as you might guess is a production motorbike racing game. Something I have been wanting for ages.
The problems start at the thing the game is about, motorbikes. Or the lack there of.
***CONS***
- Now we have some bikes on here for sure, don't get me wrong. But we are missing some essentials. Hayabusa, ZXR1400, etc. The bigger bikes.
- The sounds of the bikes. Some are pretty good, others? Crap. I mean really, really bad. The 2 strokes? They sound like a smaller 4 stroke. Annoying.
- Stuttering, low FPS around corners. It runs at 60FPS constant until it suddenly decides to dip to around 10. Usually happens when going around corners.
RIG:
Intel i5 4670K
GTX 690
8GB 1866Mhz bla bla bla
- Sometimes you come off for no reason. It just happens. You'll be flung off your bike, for apparently no reason. No idea why, but you do.
- Menu's are not good. Pretty ugly, slow, not very well laid out.
- Small one, but very annoying for me, changing your exhaust doesn't effect the sound of the bike at all.
- The AI seem almost impossible to knock off, where as you come off very easily.
- The walls can sometimes just push you off your bike even if you aren't touching them.
- You cannot practise, or even qualify for a race. You are straight into it. This is so annoying.
- Not much customization for bikes. When you first play it, it seems like a lot. But then you realise, most of it is the same for every bike. I'd like more exhausts, own decals, racing fairing, that sort of thing.
But now the good bits.
***PROS***
- The ability to change your ride style. How far you lean, how far you tilt your head, the lot.
- Being able to change your kit.
- There is nothing else like it. The closest is Tourist Trophy back on PS2.
TL;DR
I don't like it.

Memories... So many memories of childhood remembered from playing this game... This game, when we look back from the present, is a masterpiece. It's not always these days that a game developer would decide to bring and remake an old game for the present to enjoy. And sometimes, it can truly be depressing. We don't respect the old games at times, and we go for the new ones. What do we get these days? What do people decide to improve? Graphics, graphics, and more graphics. But I say a huge NO to that. Sometimes, people get too carried away on the graphics of games that they lack the most essential parts of games. The gameplay. The story. These two have been carried on by Final Fantasy in an astonishing way. They truly have created a game worth celebrating for years to come. We should not care only for graphics, but also the gameplay. Anyway, this FInal Fantasy, compared to other Final Fantasies, is still a masterpiece but I think Square Enix is starting to lose some of their touch as they progress onto the new ones such as A Realm Reborn. But I think they should always remember that the gameplay is most important, not the graphics. Excellent graphics but bad gameplay is still a bad game. I suggest Square Enix to look back at their previous titles, and keep up their previous great work. FInal Fantasy VIII is great, however I think it is too focused on one character, which is the protagonist, who is Squall. Final Fantasy VII did a great job in not only focusing on one character, but gives every character in the party a role to play, side quests, secrets, and many other things that makes the game truly worth playing and exploring every corner for. But a positive point I would raise up is the character development in this game. Square Enix explains in detail how Squall changed, but in an indirect but very detailed way. Squall, from a very unexpressive, lonely person, becomes an expressive, social person from just spending time with Rinoa. And that development is throughout the whole game, with 40+ hours of playing. Square Enix truly did a great job with this game. I reccomend this to anyone who likes RPG games, especially old school gamers who miss their old school games. If you're not one with RPG, I suggest you try it too, as you will find yourself slowly drawn into the Final Fantasy world with the story slowly engulfing you.

You already know what this is. If not, and you don't think turn based JRPGs are archaic, then you're in for a wild ride. FFVII is still arguably one of the best JRPGs within Squaresoft's golden age. You can't go to a forum or Facebook post about gaming without it being mentioned. It's literally iconic, and not that B/S self-proclaimed iconic you get from Ubisoft. FFVII is what traditional JRPGs are all about because it redefined the genre in the 5th generation. It might not have aged well, but the cinematics and usage of both polygons and pre-rendered backgrounds redefined immersion in the 32-bit era. No matter how many people crap on it these days, it's still relevant almost 20 years later. So if you got 50-70 hours to spend, do yourself a favor and see what the fuss is all about.
For FFVII Veterans:
Not exactly the best port and not the worst either. But at the very least it runs smoothly. Still has the midi format of the original PC version too, sadly.  Also, you'll go through hell modding since Tifa's Package runs off of the original PC version's compatibility and you'll lose any achievements after installing. But let's be honest, if you've played FFVII before, you come from a generation that doesn't care about achievements anyway. You're required to sign up for a S-E account, but at the very lest they don't require online-only DRM, so thank goodness for small favors. At the end of the day, it's still superior to any console version and comes second to the original PC hard copy. I'd give it a 10/10 but I'm taking a point away for the required sign up and outdated sound format. So 8/10.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a stunning game, real proof that video games are a form of art. No matter where you are, in the mountains or deep underground, you are surrounded by colour. Everything is bright and full of life, immersing you into the world. The multi-layered backgrounds mixed with the pseudo-3D character cutscene animations gives way to interesting visuals that work to the game's benefit. The audio of this game is fantastic, just the fight sounds alone are amazing. You can tell that Dust is putting his heart into every swing of his sword with his grunts as his blade makes contacts with his enemies, and a loud *woosh* if he misses. Over the fights, there is an amazing soundtrack that pulls you into the game and really captures the overall feel of Dust's struggles, his triumphs, his and Fidget's whimsy. The voice acting for most of the characters are very well done, and you can tell actors care about their personas and feel a connction with them. Each character has a voice that perfectly fits them, especially Fidget and Dust. Fidget has an adorable (possibly annoying) voice that has hints of guilt, as she tends to get into mischief and cause a little bit of trouble. With Dust, aside from him saying it a lot, you can tell he is troubled and confused about his past, yet strives to put others before him. You can hear his anguish when something goes awry.
From an audiophile's standpoint, this game is a handsdown must buy. And oh yeah the gameplay is incredibly smooth and the story is quite intriguing

Another day, another zombie game. This time, in glorious 2D sprites, courtesy of RPG Maker VX Ace and the creative efforts of a debutante two-man dev team. I’m pleased by what Animakemu Games have achieved with their first Steam project and I accepted to play and review this title, mainly because I haven’t played a JRPG-style featuring the undead apocalypse theme. All genres need to integrate zombies eventually, right?  Now where are my undead-themed sports games?
Focusing on the task at hand, I can assure you that despite the generic theme, Story Of the Survivor still managed to surprise me at times. Not with the main plot, but with its crazy side missions and the few but friendly NPCs around. Seeing people who are more self-aware about the zombie impending doom, was a breath of fresh air. In most movies and games, you have oblivious characters who never heard or seen an undead reference in their life. Hard to believe indeed and the devil’s in the details. It’s always the small things in the indie titles I review, that can hide the most interesting facts. This game ain’t no State of Decay, but it doesn’t want to copy or emulate other zombie survival/crafting titles that came before it. Story Of the Survivor wishes to carve a name for itself and remain as original as it can.
The protagonist in this tale is an average Joe. A former cook called Thomas. As the undead began to walk the streets, he remained indoors, caring for his sick mother. Once the supplies ran out, he could wait no longer and began scavenging for food and medicine. The basic needs are nicely simulated in-game via counters for hunger, thirst and level of inebriation. But you’ll stick to good ol’ water, right? No need to drink yourself to death, when it’s already knocking on your door in search for brains. Ironically or not, you will have to use that brainpower if you are to survive.
Thomas might not be the bravest hero around or the sharpest tool in the shed, yet he must fight for his survival against all odds and seek out a new meaning to life when he's only surrounded by death. He even becomes sort of a leader for a ragtag group which will constantly accompany him. Remaining on the move seems like the smartest choice in this type of scenario. If you’ve seen enough TV series and films about zombies, you certainly realize by now that the biggest enemy to human survival is infighting encouraged by none other than our human nature. Even when money becomes useless, you can still count on the oldest form of greed to keep on bashing skulls. The insatiable hunger for power over others.
I already mentioned RPG Maker and the game looks as good as it’ll ever get on that graphics engine and assets provider. The one thing which really bothered me though, was the lack of Steam Overlay support. I don’t understand why games using this graphical medium, have to eschew the auxiliary system which Valve implements for its users. The Overlay is more than just an in-game frame rate counter and screenshot linking method. I use it predominantly for those two features though and I don’t regard kindly, the Steam games which don’t even allow me to share my screenshots of them, on my Steam profile.
It’s even more upsetting since the game looks nice, it has nothing to hide or fear. I played “dollar bin” games on Steam which allowed me to take Overlay screenshots, showcasing them in all their abysmal glory. Story Of the Survivor is anything but abysmal, yet it has disappointed me, perhaps more than the games I used to write negative reviews about.
I understand that the game engine and genre itself, leaves little room for sound diversity, but it was still a far too silent experience. Forcing me to play my own “creepy soundtrack” off YouTube, doesn’t leave much room for interpretation. Story Of the Survivor lacks all but the most basic sound effects. Not good at all, Animakemu Games.
At least the gameplay itself washes away some of the “shame” or more precisely, bitter taste that the audiovisual limitations left me with. I enjoyed the pacing, the action and intrigues. The combat sections felt a bit weird since the game insists upon a real time method instead of the tested and proven turn-based fighting which also makes use of the JRPG party system. Devs attempted to stray away from the classical formula but the results are underwhelming, to say the least.
The crafting system is the saving grace since it offers numerous possibilities and you couple that with the constant scavenging for new resources. You can assemble or take apart pretty much anything you can pick up in your inventory. The dev team clearly emphasized on this, but I feel like it’s still not used to its full potential. Plus the party of three (out of which you may switch to a “main” character at will) doesn’t really help as much in RTS mode, as they could have in TBS. Don’t try to fix or change what was never broken in the first place.
I couldn’t rate Story Of the Survivor any lower than this, since the game doesn’t deserve the “honor” of a negative review from me. It didn’t annoy me (despite denying me screenshots) and it’s far from a dysfunctional gaming experience. As a fan of survival games using post-apocalyptic settings, I still found enough redeeming points to this title. It won’t bore you with useless conversation between NPCs, the fetch quests don’t feel like a chore and the antagonists are abstract enough to avoid repetition. I’d say that the game is also priced accordingly, but perhaps the developers may add Trading Cards as well, in a future update. That would really convince all Steam collectors, that Story Of the Survivor is fully worth it.

This game is going offline here pretty soon thanks to EA dropping support for the "less than 1%" of their playerbase across over 50 of their titles. Regardless, this is a RTS game that would still remain fantastic to play in singleplayer OR co-op with a friend, as everything does work with Hamachi and if you have a disc version, Gameranger works too. The game has an extensive list of tutorials that for the most part a seasoned C&C player can entirely ignore and figure the new stuff out themselves, but as far as features go, this game is the closest thing to a Westwood C&C styled game that has come out since their demise. No squad system, extreme countering-style units, extreme diversion amongst the factions (the fast-paced allies, the turtle-heavy soviets, and the...asians), diverse base construction (finally bringing walls back) and a ton of lighthearted and extremely amusing missions and dialogue from units and the campaign with rocking music featuring Tim Wynn, James Hannigan, and of course, Frank Klepacki from the westwood titles helping to soundtrack as well. That said, the campaign is absolutely fantastic by ANY standard - FMV cutscenes that add up to somewhere around an hour in length and use top notch actors such as J.K. Simmons and George Takei.
As far as how well this game can bring in new players to the series, it's extensive campaign and the fact that 1 of the 3 campaigns (Soviet one) is almost explicitly designed to ease players into the gameplay makes this a FANTASTIC entry point for newcomers. The tutorial itself consists of 6 amusing tutorials that really don't feel tedious despite totalling about an hour in length to explain the game mechanics, and are entirely skippable for anyone who's familiar with certain aspects of C&C or basic RTS controls to either see newer features or try to figure it out themselves. And for those not particularly happy with the soviet campaign style of easing players in, the allies campaign as well as empire campaign are notably more difficult right off the starting line and clearly designed with veteran players in mind. The campaign endings are lackluster so don't expect anything amazing, but the story throughout each campaign is rather intriguing. And yes, I keep going back to the campaign - that is really where the most work went into this game, clearly. The campaign at all points in time gives you an AI partner of a certain personality, each personality having a different playstyle. If you don't want an AI partner, it's possible to have a friend play with you instead in co-op, replacing the AI partner. The AI isn't particularly bad, however, and you are capable of issuing 4 basic commands (Strike area, strike target, plan (build up and launch) attack, don't attack) to your AI companion in an attempt to order them around like you would with another player.
As far as skirmish goes, it does provide a lot of replayability as once again, you can call in these AI personalities to fight with or against you. Likewise, in multiplayer which will be limited to LAN-based hosting services or just straight up REAL LAN if anyone still uses that, other players can join you and you can still add AI or remove them at will. The limit to 6 players at maximum, however, is upsetting, and the map editor for this game does not work with the steam version as far as I can tell, but there's already plenty of community maps worth downloading and playing.
For a $20 asking price, you are more than getting your money's worth. Compared with the considerably less westwood-like C&C 3 Tiberium Wars game asking $30, you are far better off getting this game and will undoubtably have more fun with it alone or with friends and it is by far the best entry into the C&C series as a whole for new players.

It was around 1994. The Internet wasn't as widespread, there was no Facebook, Twitter or Google, the mobile phones weren't common, had no eye candy UI and the connection to the Internet. Many people still used DOS, setting up its environment in autoexec.bat and config.sys, and started Windows using the command "win" from the text mode prompt.
In this time, where text mode applications like Lotus 1-2-3 or WordStar were still used, there was this game, with its striking loading "screen", with white and yellow text on a red background, behind which was a menu with a skull for a selector and a gunshot menu item activation sound. The game was entirely set in a 3D virtual environment. (It actually uses 2D sprites, but who cares?) It had a chainsaw and a shotgun as weapons. It had green imps shooting fireballs and biting your character. It had your character's face in the status bar, showing how bruised he is when he is hurt. It had a player versus player multiplayer mode called "deathmatch". People competed in how fast they can complete levels, and shared recorded games - "speedruns". This game had the world in its grip. Few games today can compare to the level of excitement DOOM (and what would today be called its "expansion" - DOOM II) evoked around the time of its release.
And now it is on Steam.
P.S: This Steam release uses Dosbox to emulate DOS environment for the game, but its default setup is not optimized. You will either need to tweak the settings yourself, or download a "DOOM source port", to which you feed the DOOM data files (.WADs).
If this is a problem, go back to whatever modern shooter you are using.

An excellent all around shooter. The F.E.A.R. has great pacing and its firefights are cleverly done. Even though the majority of the enemies you face are identical, the A.I. is so well done that each encounter play out differently each encounter. The enemies will even try to distract you while their cohorts get behind you and unload their weapons into your unsuspecting back.
The reason I would call the pacing excellent is because of how the enemies are placed. I've beaten the game twice and still make sure that all my corners are cleared before going into rooms because I'm still paranoid that there are enemies somewhere in the room, silently waiting for me to get into their field of fire. Quite a few deaths have been because an enemy had the audacity to quietly hide in a corner while I mowed down his allies and then confidently walked into the room, not noticing the weapon pointed at my skull.
The bullet time in this game feels incredible too. Unlike most games with bullet time, your movement, look speed, and firing speed slow down just like the enemies', keeping the playing field fairly even, although you are still slightly faster than they are. It also doesn't reduce damage at all, unlike some other games I've played, so keep an eye on your health, since it will be whittled down nearly instantly if you try and run and gun all the time.
One other hugely important aspect of this game is the sound design. My original playthrough was on some mediocre laptop speakers, so I never really heard everything in the game. I'm currently playing through on my desktop using a combination of my, still mediocre, but passable speakers and my Corsair headset. The game becomes far scarier and more atmosphereic if you can hear all of the noises right in your ears. So when you're playing this game, I would highly recommend using decent sound equipment to get its full, and wonderfully scary, effect.
The story is actually fairly decent if you really pay attention. There's a noticable lack of spoon feeding of information like most games do now. You are given information through your environments and left to your own devices to figure out what it all means. Sure the overall feel of the horror is a well traveled path, particularly in games (thanks old school Silent Hill for your greatness), but FEAR's take on it is genuinely interesting, seeing as there's a nice little detail or two at the end that has been hinted at from the first minutes of the game.
I also have to say, make sure to watch the credits, there's a little gem of a post credit scene that helps cement the story and make FEAR 2 a reality.

Little Inferno has a lot going for it.  It's original, visually appealing, and tells a wonderful story.
Unfortunately, it's also incredibly boring and repetitive.
Game-play can be boiled down into a few simple sentences.  You buy things from a catalogue, wait for them to arrive, and then burn them in your fireplace.  The goods you destroy always return cash, and since the reward is always greater than what you paid for the object in the first place, you're able to buy pricier and pricier goods to sacrifice to the flame.
And that's it.  That is the gist of the game.  Buy, burn, and repeat.  Advancing through Little Inferno is simply a matter of working your way through the catalogues of flammable objects.  As you progress, you'll receive letters from various characters that hint at the state of the games world beyond your fireplace.  This is actually where the game gets interesting, when it starts to question the reasoning behind the pyromania, gradually moving towards the grand reveal.
It's just a shame that you have to spend two and a half hours burning things over and over again just to get that pay-off.

The game tells the story of an anonymous operative known as Point Man, who is part of a team, called First Encounter Assault Recon, sent in to investigate the goings on at a site in the Auburn district, with reports of gunfire in the area. It isn’t long before the player is thrust headlong in to the midst of a paranormal nightmare, as all of his squad mates are slaughtered in the blink of an eye by some unexplained malevolent force. And this is only the beginning of the game too – the pace picks up from there as there are many action-packed gunfights (enhanced by slow motion) with extremely intelligent and intimidating enemies to be had, and supernatural creatures – some that can’t be killed by conventional means – to face off against, and not to mention there are plenty of scares.
This isn’t a Doom 3 type game where there are monsters hiding in a closet waiting to pounce on you. This involves the player embarking on a dark, twisted, psychologically tormenting journey in to a brilliantly crafted world where they will strive to put the pieces of a much larger story together.
There are several inspirations evident in F.E.A.R. as it draws from famed horror films such as The Ring, and by extension the Japanese film it was based upon, Ringu. This is easily the best in the series, and Monolith shows its mastery when it comes to the horror genre.
The only real gripe I have with the game – and it’s a very minor one at that – was perhaps the sound effects, particularly the weapons, which I found to be a little flat sounding, although there is a wonderfully fitting soundtrack composed by Nathan Griggs that more than makes up for it.

If you enjoy fantasy RPG, this game is in much the same vein as the Elder Scrolls series. The setting is similar, but what makes the witcher 2 stand out is how the choices you make affect the game. The Witcher 2 at first felt more linear and confining that an open world rpg (Witcher 2 is more like open section than open world), but this led to a focus on character choice (comparable in some ways to Mass Effect), and a more focused narrative. The best part of the Witcher 2 is how the consequences of decisions you make won't be felt until much later in the game and in the case of some decisions even in the next game (Witcher 3). This element of gameplay really makes it feel as if your choices actually have real consequences, since by the time you see the result of your choice its too much later to go back and reverse course. Although some players might end up stuck with decisions that they regret (I was), I love the realism of the system. Anyone who is a fan of fantasy RPGs and wants to see what a massive RPG game where your choices carry heavy and not immediately seen consequences, the Witcher 2 is for you

Dungeon Defenders Eternity is a bit of a surprise to most. A game that changes up the multiplayer aspect of the original Dungeon Defenders game to better protect itself from cheating (which was apparently a huge concern for the original game) is now caught in ethical crossfire as to whether or not it should be a free update or what-have-you regarding those who owned it.
In the end it doesn't matter. A game stands at $19.99 for a redeveloped online-only release of Dungeon Defenders using the same back-end that Dungeon Defenders 2 will use. Is it fun? Very much so. Just like the original game I've found myself addicted to the game and found it even cutting into sleep these past few days.
Build Towers, defend crystal, level up, get stats, fight again with a harder map or difficulty. DDE supposedly improves this aspect by making a rebalance pass on items, making it a little more fair when it comes to upgrades. While I didn't have trouble in the first game, it is nice to know things were looked at a second time.
As far as items go, you now have them actually displayed on your character. Get a helmet for your summoner? Shows in game. All these items can also be dyed, which in turn gives a much more personal touch on the game as you play through.  Pets also have a new mechanic that allows you to find eggs and hatch them. While so far it feels like an extra step to the process of obtaining gear, I have a strong suspicion that there is more to it than first appears.
Some new content has also been added. Challenges and maps that are supposed to be a bridge from Dungeon Defenders and it's sequel while allowing you to earn gear for when Dungeon Defenders 2 comes out. This is interesting as I personally can't wait to see what challenges there will be.
Since the game is online-only, there are some issues with performance. Server latency can impact the game as can disconnects in the newly tuned Hardcore mode.  This also means those with poorer quality connections may have trouble with this version of the game, however this was done with the intent of keeping all user data server-side to prevent tampering. For those that were frustrated about the cheating going on in the first game, this may be the solution (though admittedly it may cause a bit of grinding teeth since it isn't a patch.)
If you haven't played Dungeon Defenders before, now is a great time to get into it. $19.99 and you get almost all the content that was released in the first game, plus a little more in a secure environment. For those who owned the first game and its DLC, it becomes a much more difficult decision. Did you want a safe environment to play, or did you stick to solo or private matches in the first place? Where you frustrated with balance issues in later game modes?
At $10.99 it's hard to recommend to existing players if they truly didn't have issues with the first game. However, at a lower price (like at the time of this review) it's much easier to make a compromise and move up for $5.99 instead.
I like the game and while some of this business leaves a bad taste in my mouth, it's hard to not enjoy what time I have with it.

As someone who played the Original DD quite a bit I was wary of a new version that had to be purchased seperately and  featured much of the same content as  the first title.  Having now levelled a new character into their mid 20's I can say that this version is better than the Original.  Players no longer fight over crystal chests each round; the loot system has been tweaked for a smoother experience and the dlc from the first title has all been included and rebalanced for a better levelling experience. The UI does  have some issues with not being very intuitive on how to manage your inventory but the developers have posted that UI changes are being looked into.  As far as price goes even at its full $19.99 tag, this version is a better deal than purchasing the first title with all the dlc; so its a no brainer for anyone who hasn't already purchased the first game.  With the game servers being handled entirely by the developer, instances of cheating will hopefully be far less prevelant or nonexistent compared to the first DD.  Overall I'd say this title has some rough spots to work out as far as its UI is concerned but overall I would not tell someone to not give it a try and enjoy one of the best action/tower defense games available.

Or run like hell from those stupids bees? Whatever I'm doing, I feel like I'm taking a real adventure. And, without a doubt, this game is addicting - right after I die, I so badly want to go back and see what genius dungeon I get to explore next.

Didn't like the first fifteen minutes at all. The rest of that hour grew into 'OK'. Now I'm convinced that it's a pretty amazing game. You'll be surprised at the sheer breath of content there is, or how surprisingly deep a game gets with trap systems, different terrains, gasses, different magics and literally dozen and dozens of weird armour/weapon enchantments.
Seriously.
If you've ever played Brogue, Nethack or Dungeon Crawl and wondered 'how would this look like with graphics, in real-time, top-down?' then Unexplored is it. Since there's a pause that lets you manage your inventory you don't even have to be all that fast, precise or good - you get to plan your moves, just like in a roguelike. Fall into a pit of spiders - take a breather.
No early-access trash, none of that tomfoolery - just an obvious love for roguelikes and dungeons.
There's one negative aspect that still strikes me as unfortunate, but perhaps nessary - the backtracking. The game rewards backtracking quite heavily - there is crafting stations, altars and similar places where you can turn found resources into powerful equipment and consumables. This means that you'll most likely have to run back two, three or even four entire floors sometimes, since the game is *hard* on the hardest difficulty. This'll only happen once or twice per successful character, but it's annoying and takes a fair few minutes - ten, maybe fifteen with especially complex floors in the way.

After playing my first FF game (7), I was eager for more.  Luckily, FF8 was released on Steam as my cravings reached their peak.  Having never played 8 before, I was excited to experience another FF game.  My inital reactions were mixed.  The game looked great (considering its age) and after I installed the original PS1 music, it sounded fantastic as well.  However, the whole junction/GF system coupled with the odd level scaling system initially made me apprehensive to continue.  Despite this, I continued with my playthrough and found it to be one of the most engrossing games I have ever played.  The junction system turned out to be fairly simple once I got the hang of it, leaving me to always search for new magic to strenghten my abilities.  In regards to the story, I found it to be quite enjoyable.  The main character Squall's character development is pursued fairly well and his relationships with the other characters do not seem as artificial as some RPGs.  The supporting cast seems a bit off-to-the-side at times, but this is largely a non-issue.  The villain(s) in FF8 are very individualistic, though I wish their motives were made a bit more clear.  All-in-all, I recommend this game to anyone who has the patience to learn its strange mechanics and find the story underneath.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a stunning game, real proof that video games are a form of art. No matter where you are, in the mountains or deep underground, you are surrounded by colour. Everything is bright and full of life, immersing you into the world. The multi-layered backgrounds mixed with the pseudo-3D character cutscene animations gives way to interesting visuals that work to the game's benefit. The audio of this game is fantastic, just the fight sounds alone are amazing. You can tell that Dust is putting his heart into every swing of his sword with his grunts as his blade makes contacts with his enemies, and a loud *woosh* if he misses. Over the fights, there is an amazing soundtrack that pulls you into the game and really captures the overall feel of Dust's struggles, his triumphs, his and Fidget's whimsy. The voice acting for most of the characters are very well done, and you can tell actors care about their personas and feel a connction with them. Each character has a voice that perfectly fits them, especially Fidget and Dust. Fidget has an adorable (possibly annoying) voice that has hints of guilt, as she tends to get into mischief and cause a little bit of trouble. With Dust, aside from him saying it a lot, you can tell he is troubled and confused about his past, yet strives to put others before him. You can hear his anguish when something goes awry.
From an audiophile's standpoint, this game is a handsdown must buy. And oh yeah the gameplay is incredibly smooth and the story is quite intriguing
