Dead Bits is an action, FPS. It was developed by an indie company, Microblast Games, it was published by the same company. This was their second game and being so cheap to purchase, was bought a lot. This game isn't unique and looks like a couple of sprites and voxels thrown together whilst they were bored. There are many other types of games like this out there and Microblast didn't out do themselves, yet again. It is singleplayer and can be bought for £0.75/$1.08, there are steam trading cards so when this game goes on sale you will make your money back.
The good side: Dead Bits can be entertaining for about an hour. It has a slight challenge to it so you do come back. The game looks quite funny and the sound track is okay but can become irritating. There are 5 different types of weapon in the game 1 melee and the rest guns. It has some variety between missions and they do get progressively harder. The bugs in the game do make it slightly funny when you can B-hop and then just go flying across the map and it is fun to watch the blocky enemies explode once you've killed them. You can scope in on the weapons in the game making it easier to aim and I like that they added that feature. It is very colourful and the colours do usually go well together so it is easy on the eyes.
Although there are a lot of negatives. The game is insanely buggy and can feel almost unplayable at some points. The weapons don't really work properly and the hit boxes for the enemies are broken. The actual firing of the gun looks weird and when the bullets leave the gun they glitch and sometimes just disappear meaning that when firing at the enemy it won't make contact and they can kill you. The death scene once you have died is very irritating and the same every time no matter how you die, it lasts for a long time and doesn't even make sense. The art looks copied and it repeats the same objects to fill in things. Like a platform will be used as a wall and a lot of the enemies are just shrunk down versions or re-skins. The menu in the game is awful, navigating it is easy but it's just been made lazily, everything is repetitive in this game which makes it very boring after an hour. The developer chose not to make the game easy to play and it kind of strains your eyes because of the FOV.
Overall I'd give this game a 4/10 just because it's so irritating to play. The bugs in it just make it to much of a task to enjoy yourself properly. I wouldn't purchase unless it's on sale and you want to make some money on steam.

The soundtrack really does fit the atmosphere they were going for. The crafting aspect of the game is also good enough to keep you involved.
As far as the story goes. There is no voiceacting involved but the story does a good job of pulling the player into the midst of this zombie infested world. The story starts of slow but when you keep playing you find out that it leaves the slow story telling behind and puts you into way more action than you find in the first hour or so. I will not spoil anything but the 2 developers did a pretty decent job writing a good story and making the game with RPGmaker.
Overall I was quite supriesed by what the 2 developers brought us with RPG maker, I have not reached the end yet but so far so good. It runs well and it plays well. To keep it short. In my opinion it is well worth the pricetag of $5. It offers enough playtime and content for that price and overall it is a decent game.

TL;DR: WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR!? JUST DO IT! JUST BUY THE GAME!
Dust: An Elysian Tail is a very well made side-scroll beat'em up/Metroidvania/Platformer (If I were to give my own opinion on the genre). The game itself features amazing animations and great fighting moves which connect to eachother with grace.
The story is VERY elaborate and memorable with great character development and a plot that really makes good use of paying attention if you're all about the lore.
The quests are well balanced, with the primary one that progresses the story and a lot of side-quests of which none are quite like the others. On top of that, the maps and areas feature a lot of potential for backtracking if you want to add more power to your arsenal (I highly recommend this, as the game is really punishable on higher difficulties).
The soundtrack isn't the most appealing feature, but it's still fitting and does its job well. The voice actors for this game (yes, it has voice actors) are actually really good. I was blown away by that as I expected less from an Indie game. Here and there it may be some flaws where it could have been done better, or that the volume might be unbalanced, but that's fully acceptable with the regular impressive performance by the voice actors.
The enemies aren't the most interesting, but they feel appropriate and they get the job done. They may not have your advanced moveset but they'll hit hard if you let your guard down (REALLY REALLY hard on higher difficulties). The bosses are challenging though, may it be the first of an introduction of an enemy, or a story-made boss, it doesn't matter as they make powerful opponents.
Conclusion: amazing game, great story with smooth gameplay. Should you get it? Yes. You can really understand how much love and devotion that went into this game by the creator, whom did pretty much EVERYTHING on his own. I finished the game in 12 hours (played offline some), and then I didn't complete it 100%, and you could probably get a few more hours to get everything done.
May it be sale or the regular price, it's without a doubt worth it.

Everyone will tell you that this game is a continuation of the wacky shenanigans that happened in RA2, but I really don't remember the game being that wacky and silly. Case in point, in Yuri's Revenge, there was a building that ground up troops for resources all while using slave labor.
Mind you, this was also a game where you fight dinosaurs and hollywood stars were actually commandoes, but I can also say that with the combination of frank klepacki's unapologetically metal soundtrack combined with equal amounts ridiculous and awesome units and set pieces, RA 2 worked on a level that couldn't be replicated.
That being said, RA3 is in no way the game that anyone was looking for. See, what sets RA2 above other RTS games is the idea that a gamebreaker should be countered with a gamebreaker. Just remember the chronotroops and the psychich commandos, its a game with glorious power creep that encourages you to out-do your opponent.
That being said, not only did EA make a pathetic attempt to balance this game, nothing feels as crazy or nearly as fun. Or as balanced.
A focus on naval warfare means that Rising Sun in theory should have an advatage, but with no viable anti-air until at least 2nd tier dock/factory, and to be honest I never used it. Everything feels squishy and underpowered, and nothing is as interesting as it was in RA2, and although Klepacki's soundtrack is fun, its not nearly as engrossing as it was in his other works.
If you're really jonesing for a CnC game, get tiberium wars/wrath of kane.

What is F.E.A.R.? It is the name of a video game I designed in school. And then the name was used by some other dudes a year later. But my game would have been way scarier.
F.E.A.R. (♥♥♥♥ing Evil Aliens Rising) Na not really, is more or less a generic FPS, with some horror thrown in the mix. You are a silent dude who can go Slow-Mo and do karate kicks, running through warehouses and offices, shooting up marine-type guys and a few robot guys. It's like Call of Duty. You run in, the bad guys go "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥", you shoot their asses down. It's nothing new, apart from being able to slow down time and do some meaty headshots, and a few weapons that don't exist in the real world.
Oh and, through all this there is a creepy little girl / an older version of herself, and a cannibalistic ghost scatting about the place. It is freaky, for a while. But if you've played Amnesia or Outlast, the jumpy bits in this become a bit.. meh. Basically you turn a corner, one of the ghosts is standing there, the screen goes blurry and flashes, the ghost disappears. You walk down a corridor, the room changes, the ceiling is covered in blood, the ghost chats ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t about how you're going to die, then disappears. The game slows down and goes blurry, the ghost chats more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, then disappears. Rinse and repeat.
So if you're looking for scares, go for Amnesia or Outlast as I said, or Dead Space. F.E.A.R. serves it's purpose as a meaty run -and-gun shooter with a good story, nothing more. And the expansion packs, forget about 'em, they are Copy/Paste jobs. Get 'em if you're not already satisfied with killing hundreds of soldiers.

To put it simply, this is a disgusting mess.
To be fair, all the new stuff is great. The new gear system, the modified progression, the consolidation and simplifying of all the DLC... all of that is really nice. The problem is the unholy layer of oily grime and garbage it's all buried underneath.
The UI is beyond clunky. It actually feels like it's even working against the player at times. Doing even the simplest of tasks requires navigating menu upon menu, where the original game has everything right there waiting for you. And it's all just so slow.
The new tavern system is atrocious. Gone forever are the charming personal taverns, decorated with trophies and awards. But the really important part is how you are now forced into a crowded, public tavern. It lags, it's loud, and all the while the chat is popping up over your menus you're trying to navigate. Be prepared to inspect multiple players instead of opening the forge or shop because the tavern is so overcrowded. What used to be a place of relaxation between missions is now just as chaotic as the missions themselves.
Even the tavern itself is a mess: The Tavernkeep is still behind the counter for all your shopping needs... but the new crafting guy is on the balcony above him. This places every single useful aspect of the tavern as far away from each other as possible, leaving you to run around all over the place when all you want to do is get set up for the next mission. Also, for some reason some of the practice dummies have been removed. Want to test your new weapon? Well get in line, because so do the other dozen people in your tavern!
Customization seems to be a mixed bag. Your character wears their gear now, which is neat, and you can even dye it with a wide selection of colors. (This is extra fun with the Jester/Fool, who like to just kinda slap the gear onto their bodies wherever they'd like.) However, you can no longer customize your crystal or your character's base colors on creation. They gave some, but they also took some.
One of the big draws is the usable items, like the amulets. They're kinda neat, but really, I feel like they're unnecessary and just serve to dilute the diversity of the character classes a bit. Also, the pet eggs are weird. The game gives you a pet, but you must carry it in an item slot and watch it do nothing for a while until the game decides you may start using it. This is somehow considered fun and a positive addition to the game.
Speaking of "fun," there's also a crafting system. Maybe this is a personal opinion, but I've never seen the appeal to these things. They jsut seem to be this weird fad game mechanic that everyone puts into their games nowadays. I've never heard of anyone saying "Wow, a crafting system! I am so excited for that!" Honestly I don't see the draw of the game giving me a weapon, but telling me I can't use it until I collect an arbitrary number of useless doodads.
Finally, there's the biggest elephant in the room... the always online system. This is another one of those cases where, if you want to play your game, you're at the mercy of the servers. No offline play at all here, not even for single player. (There isn't even a single player mode. You just have to make a private room and not invite anyone in. But you still have to deal with the public tavern.) And someday, when the servers die forever, so too does your access to this game. While on the other hand, the original game is all on your computer, meaning you'll always have it.
So, in short, this is a good... expansion? Remake? I don't even know what to call it. But whatever it is, it's good. It just needs a LOT of buffing and scrubbing before it's actually servicable. I'd STRONGLY recommend just playing the original version. The updates here are nice, but ultimately not worth the tradeoffs. Only get this if you've never played the game at all and don't have the cash to get caught up on all the DLC.

I started the game expecting this to be super complicated and hard to learn (and I can see how it could be for novice strategy players perhaps) Luckily this game has a good tutorial.
The 'Tutorial' is a little A.I. Assistant that is well voiced and even a little funny. He will describe the process of running an empire down to the little details, and after only 2 shortish games I was ready to play with limited help, and on the third game I turned the tips off. I was constantly immersed in this massive (if you choose it to be) galaxy, in which I interacted with species ranging to Xenophobic Zealot snapping turtle people, to Democratic Crusader parrot people who detest dictators . In my second game I was surrounded on my left and right by xenophobic spiritualists who wanted nothing more than to destroy my military republic, luckily I used a preemptive strike to vassalize the empire to my east, and with our combined forces I vassalized the empire to the west becoming the most powerful species in only an hour and a half of gameplay!
Gameplay mechanics:
On your planets you have to build on the various tiles of land masses. These can range from mining stations to collect valuable minerals, to power plants to collect the all important energy.
In order to build and maintain a large fleet you need to have a large amount of minerals and energy coming in or you will find yourself with no money to spend on planet development. You also need to balance out the research buildings to advance your empires technology level.
You can create custom ships by picking different modules, such as a module with 4 small guns or a module with one big gun. Ships in your navy range from corvettes to massive battleships.
You can choose to equip your ship with tons of armor, or high powered shields, Lasers, Missiles, ECT.
Ship combat is fairly average at worst. Reminds me a bit of RISK. With your fleet strength measured in a number over their heads.
Sometimes if you have very good missile defense systems on your ships and fight an enemy fleet that only uses missiles you can absolutely tear them a new one without any losses, but the strategy does not really get much deeper.
Planet Combat:
Planet invasions are pretty simple. You can build an army ranging from simple soldiers to freaking Xenomorphs (not kidding thats what they are called in game). Which is pretty cool. You orbitally bombard the planet to weaken their defenses and then land your troops, if you have a better army you win and control the planet. Easy.
There is so much in this game I can hardly describe it all, so I will get on to the bad stuff
-Game runs poorly on my computer late game
My computer is not a beast but with an i3-4160 and an AMD R9 270x, that should be more than enough for this game which leads to my next problem-
-NO GRAPHICS OPTIONS
Besides multisampling and resolution there are no graphics settings in any menus. You can do some stuff in the command menu in game, but it should be in the options.
-Combat is pretty meh. Planet invasions are pretty lame especially with the cool armies you can make.
You just watch a small icon of your army land on a picture of a planet. A little dissapointing after I started getting cool stuff like Xenomorphs and Gene Warrior armies (Basically Spartan Super soldiers). Imagine Spartans riding Xenomorphs into battle who wouldnt want to see that??
Overall I rate this game a good 8.5/10 I very much look forward to expanded content and some sweet mods.
P.S. You can change alliance names and federation names by clicking the icon in the lower right hand corner :)

A fantastic and unexpected mix of roguelike top-down dungeon crawler and rhythm game, in Crypt of the Necrodancer every step, every attack, every action is made to the beat of the background music; failure to do so greatly reduces the coins gained from enemies, and those coins are vital to purchasing the gear needed to survive, since in classic roguelike fashion the player starts off incredibly weak.  Everything about the game shouts out polish.  Enemies seem simple and predictable by themselves, but in a swarm of other “simple” enemies it gets harrowing fast, and there’s no time to think; the beat must go on!  The graphics are vivid and fun while taking advantage of a retro sprite style to avoid visual clutter and make everything pop out at a glance.  Controls are tight, responsive, and simple so the player can devote all their focus on planning their movements while still keeping the beat.  The music is of course phenomenal, a melange of rock, metal, and techno with driving basslines throughout.  Not enough good things can be said about Necrodancer, and no matter how long this review could get it wouldn’t do it justice; play it for yourself and experience the magic.

Firstly, keeping in mind that this is only a $5 game and the reminder that appears every time you begin the game that only two people worked on it, I won't tear too much into it, but I want to give a few words of advice for the future in case they decide to patch it up or make a sequel.
1) Hunger-In the game, you get hungry (as any real survivor simulator) the meter goes from 0 (not hungry) to 100 (hungry). Solution: It makes more sense/logical to have it go the opposite direction from 100 (full) to 0 (hungry).
2) Debuffs/Icons/Text/Guide-Also, there are debuffs in the game with icons (there's a bleeding icon, a headaches/migraines icon, a scared icon, etc.) but I couldn't find a guide that clearly indicated what these icons meant, you had to figure it out for yourself. I bring this up because when you're trying to treat a debuff/ailment with food or medicine, it does show you the icon of what the food/medicine treats, but it doesn't tell you in text what it treats or what it means. Solution: Have a page or simply indicate in text what the buffs/debuffs are and what the foods/medicine treats.
3) Water-You can't drink tap water from the sink because the game tells you that the government advised against it because its toxic (even though you can still drink "dirty (bottled) water" which raises your toxicity levels like in Fallout 3. So your other options are a) find dirty bottled water with toxicity and drink that, b) find (fresh) bottled water and c) drink from a water cooler. When I tried to refill my water bottles from the water cooler, it said I needed empty water bottles despite having empty water bottles in my inventory after using/drinking the bottled water. Solution: Be able to use the empty water bottles that you finished drinking from, to refill water from the water cooler. Also, be able to drink and refill from the sink water, just like in Fallout 3. If toxicity levels go up, that's ok, that's what the medicine is for.
4) Dark/Night time-There's day, afternoon and night time. You can hit a button to tell you the time of day it is. Problem is when it's night time, it's almost too dark to see what's going on. I tried adjusting my computer's settings and even the color settings in the game and it was still a little too dark to see. Solution: Lighten the night/dark so people can see what's happening more clearly. You can still indicate to the player that it's night time without having the screen be so dark.
Note: The first two are very minor things in the game, but none of these make the game unplayable, even together. I beat the game in about 8 1/2 hours, taking my time, not even rushing it.  To be honest, I thought it was going to be longer, but I was left entertained after all of it was over. And the music, for a game like this, is really good. To me, it was on the level of Resident Evil for Nintendo 64. Was it worth my $5? Overall, I say it was worth $5. No regrets.

Story of the Survivor is made by two people, Kamil Szczepanik and Bartosz Zajkowski with a passion for video games who wanted to partner together to create a passion project. The game draws its inspiration from The Walking Dead games and television shows. I know what you’re thinking, ‘another zombie game made by newbie video game developers’ but this one may in fact be well worth checking out especially if you’re not someone who is instantly put off by the RPGMaker engine.
The story begins relatively slowly as many RPGMaker games have a tendency of doing. However, what is immediately clear between the art assets both created and selected from those already made and the game’s soundtrack is that the developers have established the necessary tone and the aesthetic required to immerse players into their elaborate game world. As the story gains pace  so too does the tremendous action. Although I have not reached what I am certain is going to be a mildly interesting conclusion it has been a very reasonably written one as far as RPGMaker games go and one that serves its inspirations well. The story does a solid job of conveying the feelings and emotions of a world in the midst of a zombie apocalypse.
I enjoyed the crafting aspect of the game which is available from very early on in the game. It is something that you will need to be constantly thoughtful of as some of the items that are available to be made from your crafting items can play important, if not vital, roles in progressing further into the game.
I know that there are perfectionists among us so if I was to pick out a negative it would be that the English isn’t the very best. However, in my time with the game I found it to be definitely passable. There weren’t any sections of the text that I felt as though I couldn’t understand what was being conveyed. There’s a few words here and there that I feel are incorrect. However, keep in mind how far traveled the language has become and the different ways in which people speak it and I’m not merely talking the difference between American and British English here. I find it interesting listening to someone from Europe speak English with someone from Southern Africa for example. At times it can seem as though they are speaking two very different languages yet all of the worlds are noticeably English. The dialects of the language are fascinating and so what the writers may have implied may be purely correct from one perspective and not from another. There’s only very few misspellings.
Would I recommend Story of the Survivor? As the devs themselves wrote in their Steam Description, if you’re a fan of The Walking Dead or other zombie-related media, then is the game for you!

you know how game making kits come with tutorials? you know, the ones that help you slowly put together a game using basic code and free assets? dead bits feels like a game made from some of those tutorials, which might explain why it's so awful.
bloody hell, where to start? everything that could go wrong has done so in this game. it's a game where your health is measured with a single number.
to begin with, it looks awful. bright colours thrown onto squares, and the devs claim it's "pixellated". no doubt this is riding on the minecraft bandwagon, but if you're going to copy something popular, copy it right. at least minecraft has consistency and a colour pallet that doesn't make one want to cry.
the story is practically non-existant. a guy gets kidnapped by aliens and has to do tests. there's really nothing to say, asides from the fact that you're at least making super mario brothers jealous in terms of writing.
the gameplay is bare bones and entirely uninteresting. in my playtime i found three weapons; a shotgun, a machine gun (both of which i'm willing to bet are free assets based on how they don't look anything like the rest of the game's art style - or lack thereof), and what i'm guessing is supposed to be a metal pipe, but in reality is an untextured bar. none of them have any interesting functions, any ways to modify them, or even a bloody ammo counter. just hold down lmb and watch in amazement as your horrid pixellated block monster "enemies" shatter into fragments.
on the subject of enemies, they're a joke. they walk towards you. that's it. they don't try to dodge and their only attack is walking into you, which does as much damage as either a ping-pong ball or a bowling ball. what enemy deals how much damage is up to chance. some do this really weird bullet time effect that slows down the game and places a grayscale filter over the screen, which becomes obnoxious after one showing. they're also able to walk across gaps because i don't know video games??????
the level design is... jesus christ. whether it's hallways of enemies or obstacle courses where almost everything is a one-hit-kill, you're guaranteed to have fun! and by fun, i mean murderous impulses. levels four and five in particular are laughing stocks; long tunnels stuffed to the brim with enemies one can kill in a single hit. it's boring as hell.
hey, developers, filling rooms with the same enemies one has killed before does not make the game harder, it makes things more irritating. how about you develop an enemy with a unique attack? and just to let you know, levitation does not count. sorry.
in short, this thing is an atrocity. it's amusing for five-ten minutes tops just from how shockingly bad everything is, but after that it leaves a horrid taste in your mouth, like when you drink a coke and there's that awful aftertaste that lingers for a while; you know what i mean.

This is not really a game, it's an experience... Or is there something more?
The game is tagged as 'Story-rich', so I was a bit bewildered when I started the game, and found no story at all.  We're in the water, and we're told how to interact with the environment, and that is all.  ie. Here's how to dive, click button X here... So where's the story?
It took me a while to realize that I needed to slow down, to take the time to really look at my environment, to just... relax.
This game is a dream come true for someone like me who loves to just enjoy the surroundings and take lots of screens - there are PLENTY photo of opportunities!
Some of the things you can do to really connect with the environment:
- Swim and explore
- Latch on to larger aquatic life and "ride" with them - you can even steer them!
- Flip, twirl, and glide through the water as you swim
- Meditate
Ahh, I should explain how the
works, shouldn't I.  There are "meditation statues" scattered throughout the regions you will explore, and when you get close, you can sit on top of them and just... meditate.  When you do so, you take on the perspective on a fish or school of fish, and just see what they see.  You can jump about from one species to the next with ease, and take on new sights as you do so.  Once you've unlocked a meditation spot, you can access it from the main menu if you'd like to
the area.
In addition to enjoying the environs, you can also pursue:
- 12 Achievements
- 12 Meditation Statues
- 20 Hidden Pools
- 19 Secret Shells
As you really delve into the depths, you'll find that there's more to the game than just relaxing and enjoying, but I don't want to spoil anything for you.  As I mentioned, this is an
.  I will tell you that there were a couple of shocking moments, and a few moments of the purest awe for me.  The way I felt when I was swimming with the
was indescribable. The majesty of some of these creatures was truly humbling, even in game form.
Once you finish the game, you can replay any chapter you wish - especially nice if you want to find the things you've missed without replaying the whole thing.
In the end, I discovered that there really IS a story to all of this, and I love that it wasn't at all what I was expecting.  This is a game to take your time in and just enjoy.  It's not a terribly long foray into the deep, but it
a beautiful and moving one.  I'll definitely be revisiting this one.  Highly recommended!

Farming Simulator 2013 is one of the purest and most focused business simulations I’ve ever played. You own a farm in a country town, and your only goal is to grow crops to make as money without any “final objective” to chase. There are no scores, storylines, cosmetic money sinks (such as new player skins or houses), or other long-term goals. You simply choose a crop from four possible seeds to start your career, plant it in your field, harvest it, sell it and put that cash back into the farm. It’s almost impossible to damage your crops unless you’re not paying attention, so it’s difficult to fail or find yourself in a no-win situation.
Still, you should harvest as much as you can because of the sheer number of investments you can make into your business. There are dozens of licensed vehicles, forty plots of land (of which you only start with one), and additional buildings such as solar collectors and greenhouses that you can sink your money into. As you increase the number of fields you own, it can take more than a dozen tractors and tools to coordinate all the work and minimize downtime. It could take hundreds of hours of work to afford everything, but you have complete freedom in how you accomplish your goal and what your priorities are. Livestock, more or bigger fields, and faster machines are all available, so you’ll have to think about what best suits your particular play style. More valuable crops take extra work and extra machines in order to maximize your profits, so you need to decide whether you’re willing to make the investment or stick to simple but low-value crops. The entire system gives you a tremendous amount of freedom in how to best approach your business, although that first week will be fairly slow-paced.
The most unusual aspect of Farming Simulator 2013 is the complete lack of competition. In a single-player career, there is only you, the farm, and the AI townspeople who wander around but can’t be interacted with. Even in multiplayer, all players work together on a single farm. In both modes, the game will not fail you for slow production or even no production at all. As a result the gameplay is incredibly peaceful, though possibly a bit daunting for newcomers to the series. Admittedly, the act of virtual farming doesn’t sound like it would require a complex series of steps to perform, given that most of your job involves jumping in a tractor, attaching a tool, and slowly driving in straight lines. However, there are subtleties that are under-mentioned or completely undocumented that require some practice to master. AI-controlled workers can be hired for most tasks, and watching how they perform can teach you techniques to use when you get behind the wheel. Hiring those workers is the key to running a successful and profitable farm, especially when you’re trying to manage a half-dozen fields or more at once.
Those aren’t the only presentation missteps. To help keep you busy during those slow early days, you’re given regular “missions” to earn you some extra cash. There is no punishment for failing a mission, and they pay really well when you’re starting out, but they’re executed poorly. There are only two types of missions that ask you to mow some grass or move heavy equipment across the town. The problem is, you don’t have the equipment to perform either mission when you start off with a new career, so you’ll be forced to decline the mission unless you spend all your first-day profits on the machines. Further, the mission types seem a little strange… no missions for delivering certain crops to certain houses? No scrambling to save a field from a pest outbreak? How about a mission where you have to drive your water trailer to assist the fire department to help extinguish a burning building? While reward money is good, mowing grass is incredibly boring, and the mission system simply doesn’t feel rewarding enough.

Have you ever played a game thats still fun reguardless of how old it is? Or how many times you've beaten it? Well FEAR is without a doubt, one of those games. This horror FPS classic is still one of my personal favorites.   Anything from the atmosphere, graphics, soundtrack, story, enemy AI. FEAR devlievers that in an excellent way.
True, the game's scares may not shake you up the second time around. But, it doesn't ruin the atmosphere. You have that sense of someone watching you even when the room is empty. (Or littered with the bodies of the soldiers you shot to pieces.)  FEAR also has that sense of helplessness. Like no matter how hard you try, the bad guys are always one step ahead. So it moves away from the typical hero formula of where the hero always wins in the end.
The AI does the enemies in the game justice. Have you played a game where the enemy was supposed to be a "professional" killer? Or something similar? But, they were dumb as bricks? Well this is not so for FEAR. The AI is quite intellegent. The soldiers will actually work as a squad to take you down. For example, say you were in cover against a sqaud, the squad members will attempt to flank you or flush you out with a grenade. But, while you're trying to get out of harms way. The soldiers are waiting at the ready to gun you down.  (and believe me, it can be easy for them to do so.)
Overall, I recommend this game to those that enjoy good creepy shooters/ supernatural games. Being a firm believer in the paranormal, this game is even more interesting to me.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings. Developed by CDPROJECKT RED and being a sequel to the first Witcher game, which was based off the writings of Andrjez Sapowski "Wiedźmin" series, The Witcher 2 is the more ambitious game from #1, which has the problem of having aged terribly. The game was ambitious and got a bunch of acclaim once it came out, though sadly I wasn't interested in video games at the time and when I was my PC was♥♥♥♥♥♥and I already packed away my 360, so I had to wait until my new PC. I finally installed it and booted it up, then started playing. Well what did I think? Well, I guess I'm going to tell you.
STORY: Your name is Geralt of Rivia. After King Foltest is killed on your watch after the siege of a castle, you are accused of murdering him. You didn't, and you convince your allies enough to get them to help you escape the dungeon to clear your name and kill the man who did so. Along the way, you are forced to interfere with the politics of the Northern Realms, initially with a minor trading settlement but eventually with a whole kingdom and all of the realms. Someone once called the Witcher series as the Game of Thrones of video games, and that's a pretty good comparison. The political talks are deep near the end of the game, there's a lot of killing, there are boobs and sex, I'm surprised George R.R. Martin doesn't have a writer's credit on this. Like Game of Thrones, The Witcher 2 handles these pretty well. The story is interested, it keeps you going and you want to conclude the story. Very well put together.
GAMEPLAY: 3rd person perspective, use swords as weapons. You have two swords, one silver and one steel. The steel one is good for killing humans, elves, and dwarfs, while silver is better for monsters and wraiths. You have a light and heavy attack for either, with the usual differences. You can parry attacks or just move out of the way with a spin dash (for lack of a better term to describe it coming to mind). You also have 5 magic abilities: Igni, which lights your enemies on fire, Yrden, which traps enemies down, Axii, which has enemies fight for you for a small period of time, Aard, which pushes your enemies back and sometimes gives you an opportunity to instakill them, and Quen, which surrounds you with a protective barrier. All of em are useful in their own way, though Axii isn't very effective half the time and I only used Yrden for boss battles that required me to. There are also some bombs, daggers, and traps in the mix. You can brew potions or apply oils to your sword to increase damage or give you extra benefits. And there's a skill tree to level up yourself up and give you extra stuff. Deep enough, kind of hard if you have no idea what you're doing or just try to button mash, but if you take a few steps back and breath, you should got it.
GRAPHICS, WORLD DESIGN, AND PERFORMANCE: Ran it on Ultra, and goddamn it looked beautiful. Ran pretty well, 60FPS, some drops but think it might be Windows 10. There was an annoying thing that whenever I died later in the game, it crashed, though that turned out to be an issue with having too many saves since I'm a bit of a frantic saver. Had to turn steam cloud off to get it to work normally but it worked just peachily once I turned that off and deleted some older saves. If you have an issue like that, it's probably because of that. World design is varied, you go to 4 different places through the main story and they're varied enough, look nice.
CHARACTERS, VOICE ACTING, AND AI: AI is a bit derpy sometimes, sometimes when an enemy charges it just stays there and let me get backstabs, though that only happened once or twice so I guess I can excuse it. Voice acting is pretty good, Geralt is well done, one of your possible allies Vernon is done well, your love interest for this game Triss is good too, some of the NPC VA's are kind of lame but overall it's top notch. Character design for NPC's is kind of redone, with different colorations varying a few NPC's if there is one, but for the main guys it's good and varied enough.
SIDE ACTIVITIES: You can arm wrestle, fight, or play dice poker wherever you go. This is fun enough, and you get money that you can use to buy weapons, armor, potion materials, sex, and the usual stuff. There are a lot of side quests, some just being monster contracts while others have some more depth into them. I'd recommend you do them to get some more money and XP to level up, since it makes everything easier afterwards, but it's up to you, is it not? :P
FINAL THOUGHTS: Phenominal game. Try it if you haven't. 9.5/10, worth a look at without a doubt. At this point it goes on sale for 2 or 3 bucks, and that is an absolute steal. You run out of excuses every day to not play this game, people. Just get it over with :P

Okay, so I've been playing this game for a while and here is what I have to say.
It's pretty damn good, the visuals are nice, the various dragons keep matches interesting and I can assure you, you'll have a hard time finding only one you like.
A lot of people tend to compare this to something like League of Legends, or DOTA. I honestly don't understand that comparison, I've seen LoL and I've played DOTA. And while all three games are MOBA, they're all unique in their own way. So with that out of the way, let's get onto the pros and cons of this game...
Pros
Oh yes, there is quite a selection to choose from, with lots of dragons and weapons the choose from. Each mixing together in their own way. Some for better, some for worse.
The community for this game is usually rather friendly and welcoming, I believe a major factor to this is the smaller player base in comparison to something like DOTA.
Although the game is rather standard when it comes to MOBA maps and gameplay, they aesthetics stand out from the rest. While most MOBAs have you going toe to toe in some sort of arena, forest, etc. This game takes it up a notch, you're flying on the back of these magnificent beasts high in the sky, fighting on various planes to free your Titan as the battle between light and dark wages on.
Besides the "Lore" tab on all of the weapons and dragons, the game also has a single player story mode, something I've never seen in this kind of game before. In which various events call upon you to help. Whether it's bringing the Myre Bog back to peace, or fighting through Magekeep in a desperate struggle for power. Most of the story is rather interesting, albeit with some problems.
Another thing I find rather unique to this game. You will get various gemstones throughout your playtime, those are used in the Forge to buff your weapons, giving it various perks such as shortening the cooldown for abilities, the mana cost of some abilities, or even just a flat out increase of damage.
Cons
The maps are your typical MOBA style maps, although usually with some sort of twist. The problem being there's only four maps as this is being written. Chaos Unleashed, Baliste Alley, Nethergate and Towers and Titans. It's a shame, alongside the fact all multiplayer matches use the same map. The maps rotate on a vote system every thirty (30) minutes.
Don't get me wrong, the community is lovely, and most have a really good attitude. But the issue is how small it is, as it can lead to long queue times. Other than that there's not much to complain.
So in conclusion, Dragons and Titans is nice little MOBA with new aspects to it, while still keeping it familar to fans of the genre. And if you like it, a Titan Pass is only 20 USD a month for a year's worth of content.

I've seen way too many bull reviews, so here is a review with the information on BOTH sides. Hopefully this will actually help someone make the choice on if they want to get this or not. This review is admittedly mostly aimed at those that have played dungeon defenders in the past and are thinking about buying this one as well. As you have looked below, I'm sure you see the wall of text; don't worry, I will be putting bullet points at the end.
[PROS/CHANGES]
Let me start off by saying I do really enjoy both dungeon defenders, and Dungeon Defenders Eternity. As for all the wonderfull changes that are made, there isn't a single one that I don't enjoy.  We have two stats replacing the skill stats, such as the joust for countess, as Ability Offensive and Ability Defensive. They act just like they sound, with Ability Offensive helping out the offensive skill if you have one, and defensive helping the other. These two stats do play into more, but I'll get to that later. The next new thing is that you no longer only have a helmet, chest plate, pants and gloves. Now you have all those, plus greaves, belts, masks, shields and each one of those items has stats associated with it, as well as actively change the way your character looks. A nice change to actually see your equipment change your character, besides just your weapon. There is also now a crafting system, where you can randomly come across blueprints for items from monsters. From chests you gain crafting materials, and you just take those and go talk to a shroomite on the 2nd floor of the tavern, and if you have the necessary materials you can make said item. The really nice thing about this is that you actually know the stats the items is going to have before it's made, but the bad thing is that I believe once you make it once, you'll have to get another one to make it again.
Another really nice thing that falls near the same catagory, is artifacts. From beating certain bosses and challenges, you obtain artifacts that you can use (you can only use that specific artifact on that specific character once, but are not limited to only one artifact used on that character,) to give a permanent bonus toward stats, such as tower attack. Some do have level requirements as well, such as a demon one requires your character to be level 15 in order to use it on it. There are also boosts you can get that are consumables that can increase the quality, quantity and rarity of items that drop on that stage. At least, until you're done with the stage, then it reverts to normal. That being said, getting a bunch of rare items with really good stats isn't something I can complain about.
The next really big change, is in a completely new catagory called "Active Items." These active items can be potions, bombs, distracting traps, eggs, and ability amulets. Yup, ability amulets, such as "Thunderstorm Amulet," that give you new spells to use. Remember those new stats I spoke of? Well, say your Thunderstorm does 70 damage every .33 seconds base. Not only does your offensive ability buff your Joust, or whatever base class ability you have, but it ALSO buffs the item abilities. So, instead of doing only 70 damage every .33 seconds, now you're doing 100 (70+30). That's just an example, mind you, so no real formula's were used. As for the eggs, it's a new way to gain pets. While your out slaughtering hapless orcs and whatnot, an egg can sometimes drop. All you do is put that egg in the active item slot, and wait until it get's enough xp to hatch. Doesn't seem to be too bad as far as the amount necessary. You already know the stats of the pet before it hatches, but not the type, so you can take an educated guess on if you want to hatch it or not. Speaking of types, pets now have a passive ability as well as active. Take a hawk, for example. It still has it's peck-like attack that does damage that it will regularly do, but it will also have a swoop active ability (On a 15 second cooldown,) that doesn't cost any mana that adds a bleed effect to anything hit by it.
Next up on the list is how things have been rebalanced, and the UI changed. If you place a turret down, say a ballista, you can still cursor over it and check it's stats - such as how much damage it does and fire rate. However, if you open your radial menu and select the tower out of that, then it will actually show you information such as the ballista's base stats, and how much YOUR stats add. It also gives you information on if certain stats, like tower speed, will affect it or not. Kinda neat, and somewhat helpeful! On the topic of rebalancing, I don't have any direct examples, but I can definitely say that after 712 hours or so of Dungeon Defenders this one definitely feels more fluid and even. Another neat thing is the dodge mechanic. You get 4 charges that replenish quite quickly, assuming you don't use them one after the other, and it gives you a horizontal leap in whatever direction your moving in. This is great for avoiding projectiles, jumping ledges, getting around the map faster or dodging that assassin that just jumped over you and is about to eviscerate your head.
All in all, lots of really, really nice changes in my opinion.
[CONS]
Nothing is perfect, and dungeon defenders eternity is no exception. The game does suffer currently from some nasty bugs, some of which I've noticed particularly with Summoner. I've had orcs moonwalk through walls off the level and dissapear. I've had ogres decide they don't like where they are and relocate to a different spot, or go suicide in pits. I've had the kobold lit fuse running at you about to explode sound looped on my headset until the round was over, even though the last kobold had died a while ago. I have teleported to my cursor's position while selecting something from the radial menu three times, though I have been unable to purposefully recreate it.
There is a ... cash shop... shudder... I place this under cons because it invites the "Pay to win" aspect in games. No better example then the original Diablo 3. Thankfully, as of right now, all it contains is Emotes so hopefully their plan is to only sell cosmetic items through it. If that is the case, then I can remove this off [CONS] and place it in a [MEH] slot. As of right now, the tavernmaster pretty much only sells those emotes for cash, and some dyes, dye removal and respec potions so he's pretty much unnecessary at the moment which makes me kind of sad.
While the thought of  having to start completely over from scratch does not personally annoy me or anything, I understand why it does others. It especially hurts if you played 100% legitimately, but still... It's understandable, to me, due to all the other changes. Once again though, I do miss my stuff and I know that others do as well, so leaving it here under cons.
[  -----THIS IS THE BIG HITTER----
You have to be online to play it, since you have to be logged into their trendynet servers. Even if you're playing solo, just like Diablo 3, you have to be connected. Also, the tavern is now a... well... tavern...  You no longer have a private tavern all to yourself, as now it is a hub for all players. The bright side is you get to see lots of people running around doing stuff, but the bad side is that you're constantly being spammed by "SUCH AND SUCH HAS JOINED," and "SUCH AND SUCH AS LEFT." This wouldn't be so bad, except it plays that same noise as when someone would join your tavern in the original every single time, and also removes the tooltip if you're, for example, trying to compare two pieces of loot. When I have tried to figure out if I wanted to equip something, I've had to jump into a game just to keep it straight so I could actually compare them.

I started the game expecting this to be super complicated and hard to learn (and I can see how it could be for novice strategy players perhaps) Luckily this game has a good tutorial.
The 'Tutorial' is a little A.I. Assistant that is well voiced and even a little funny. He will describe the process of running an empire down to the little details, and after only 2 shortish games I was ready to play with limited help, and on the third game I turned the tips off. I was constantly immersed in this massive (if you choose it to be) galaxy, in which I interacted with species ranging to Xenophobic Zealot snapping turtle people, to Democratic Crusader parrot people who detest dictators . In my second game I was surrounded on my left and right by xenophobic spiritualists who wanted nothing more than to destroy my military republic, luckily I used a preemptive strike to vassalize the empire to my east, and with our combined forces I vassalized the empire to the west becoming the most powerful species in only an hour and a half of gameplay!
Gameplay mechanics:
On your planets you have to build on the various tiles of land masses. These can range from mining stations to collect valuable minerals, to power plants to collect the all important energy.
In order to build and maintain a large fleet you need to have a large amount of minerals and energy coming in or you will find yourself with no money to spend on planet development. You also need to balance out the research buildings to advance your empires technology level.
You can create custom ships by picking different modules, such as a module with 4 small guns or a module with one big gun. Ships in your navy range from corvettes to massive battleships.
You can choose to equip your ship with tons of armor, or high powered shields, Lasers, Missiles, ECT.
Ship combat is fairly average at worst. Reminds me a bit of RISK. With your fleet strength measured in a number over their heads.
Sometimes if you have very good missile defense systems on your ships and fight an enemy fleet that only uses missiles you can absolutely tear them a new one without any losses, but the strategy does not really get much deeper.
Planet Combat:
Planet invasions are pretty simple. You can build an army ranging from simple soldiers to freaking Xenomorphs (not kidding thats what they are called in game). Which is pretty cool. You orbitally bombard the planet to weaken their defenses and then land your troops, if you have a better army you win and control the planet. Easy.
There is so much in this game I can hardly describe it all, so I will get on to the bad stuff
-Game runs poorly on my computer late game
My computer is not a beast but with an i3-4160 and an AMD R9 270x, that should be more than enough for this game which leads to my next problem-
-NO GRAPHICS OPTIONS
Besides multisampling and resolution there are no graphics settings in any menus. You can do some stuff in the command menu in game, but it should be in the options.
-Combat is pretty meh. Planet invasions are pretty lame especially with the cool armies you can make.
You just watch a small icon of your army land on a picture of a planet. A little dissapointing after I started getting cool stuff like Xenomorphs and Gene Warrior armies (Basically Spartan Super soldiers). Imagine Spartans riding Xenomorphs into battle who wouldnt want to see that??
Overall I rate this game a good 8.5/10 I very much look forward to expanded content and some sweet mods.
P.S. You can change alliance names and federation names by clicking the icon in the lower right hand corner :)

A fantastic and unexpected mix of roguelike top-down dungeon crawler and rhythm game, in Crypt of the Necrodancer every step, every attack, every action is made to the beat of the background music; failure to do so greatly reduces the coins gained from enemies, and those coins are vital to purchasing the gear needed to survive, since in classic roguelike fashion the player starts off incredibly weak.  Everything about the game shouts out polish.  Enemies seem simple and predictable by themselves, but in a swarm of other “simple” enemies it gets harrowing fast, and there’s no time to think; the beat must go on!  The graphics are vivid and fun while taking advantage of a retro sprite style to avoid visual clutter and make everything pop out at a glance.  Controls are tight, responsive, and simple so the player can devote all their focus on planning their movements while still keeping the beat.  The music is of course phenomenal, a melange of rock, metal, and techno with driving basslines throughout.  Not enough good things can be said about Necrodancer, and no matter how long this review could get it wouldn’t do it justice; play it for yourself and experience the magic.

At this price, you can do no better.

So I'm one of those people who scoffs at the term roguelite. I love roguelikes, but the mass ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of them from the past few years has been sometimes difficult to watch. Except unexplored. This game is a real roguelike. Its tough, and deep, and fair, and fun, and exciting, and brilliant. Only now after 15 hours, writing this review do I understand the brilliance in the name even. Being a roguelike the dungeon is, of course, perpetually unexplored, but I like to think that the title is referring to the game itself. For you, the new consumer, this game is unexplored. It has so many treasures and secrets and brilliant discoveries and exciting bits and pieces to experience. So go explore it.
I heartily recommend this game.
That being said, be patient with it. It just launched a couple weeks ago, and its obvious from the incredible depth of the game that it is a painfully complex engine. I was going through a rough time in my life. My parents were fighting constantly, I had no friends, and everyone I met hated me because I was fat. I needed something to prevent me from suicide. I could not find anything I really liked. I tried buying toys, but the store clerks always prevented me from buying anything because I was overweight. I tried making a vlog on YouTube about my troubles, but I was banned from youtube for supposedly impersonating Gabriel Iglesias. Google fined me all of my money until I only had $1.10 left.
The only things I had were things necessary for my survival. I was fed a potato every other day and also given water in a shot glass. Sometimes I forced myself to use the water as a way to bath instead of drinking it. I was locked in my room every day cuz my parents were busy fighting about which console to play on. Well, not entirely.
I had this netbook, one my parents got me for my birthday when I was 12. I used it for school, mostly, until now. I was also lucky enough to have a charger, and all the stuff you need to use the netbook. I decided, maybe give video games a try. No one would judge me there. I was unable to play the f2p games because A. They took too much storage and B. I would be banned whenever I joined a multiplayer game. I remembered the $1.10 I had left.
I knew I had to find something that gave me a reason to live. I looked through the steam store. Jesus almost nothing was $1.10! I was about to give up and just end my life when I found this game. Dead Bits . 99 cents, without 10% tax. It took up all the space on my netbook. After waiting for it to download, I opened up the game. Upon opening it up there was a well made launcher with many options. Once I opened up the actual game, I heard a sweet soundtrack, and saw some badass looking aliens and a cool human. Was this what I needed to continue living?
It was. I am proud to say Dead Bits saved my life. The characters were deep, had personality, and I was able to connect with them. The story was unique, suspenseful, and I shed multiple tears. The graphics were revolutionary, and the soundtrack was the first good thing I had heard in awhile. It, in a way, provided everything I needed to live. The characters were my friends. The game was like a good parent. The game was easy to fap to. I could have just played the game for my entire life. It was amazing. It changed me. Here I am, sitting in my room, now infested with bullet ants and bees, starved half to death and with my throat about to dry up. But you know what? I do not care. Because I have Dead Bits. And I will always have Dead Bits. This game is my life now. I am finally happy. I am finally free. I know now the meaning of life. And only because Microblast games spent their time on this godly game.

Excellent game, highly replayable.
I think the thing that stands out for me the most as how it brings the fun back to gear identification. It's a concept that's been watered down over the years, to the extent that in something like Diablo 3, it's almost entirely pointless (and I say this as someone who loves Diablo 3).
In Unexplored, every magical item starts off undentified. They can only be identified via two methods; a scroll of identification or, and this is the fun part, by using it. Unidentified weapons reveal their true natures after killing a certain amount of enemies, armour by walking a certain distance, scrolls by using them, and potions by drinking or throwing.
And the limited inventory space means that at some point you will be forced into trying out something unidentified. This is where it shines, as you end up with something gloriously beneficial or hilariously unfortunate. It's so good to play a game that understands what this concept was originally meant to be. A true risk/reward mechanic.
In addition, it's so good to play a game that rewards skill and intelligent use of equipment and the environment rather than simply grinding out more power levels. Sure, occasionally it means you'll have no tools available for an encounter, but you can always run away. With there being no experience points to worry about, retreat is ALWAYS a valid tactic.
Highly recommended, especially now. When I bought it back in February, it was good, but buggy, resulting in me shelving it for a month. Now however, it's a lot more stable. It can get a little rickety after a few hours of play, but it's quick enough to save and restart that it doesn't matter too much.
An absolute steal for the money.

Unexplored creates interesting and varied procedurally generated dungeons to delve. Not only are these dungeons stocked with a variety of enemies, bosses and obstacles, but there are a great many puzzles, often with multiple solutions. Rarely have I played a game with so much random generation, but that still felt like it had been created by someone in a level editor. Many of the items you find, though they're drawn from loot tables, often feel like they've been hand placed because seemingly found loot is actually a tool for completing a puzzle. Most surprisingly to me was finding that many of these puzzles were spread over multiple levels.
Though the graphics are bare bones polygons, there are a variety of environmental interactions, such as poisonous gas that can be burned off with a torch, or maybe simply explode and setting you on fire, along with vegetation, furniture and all sorts of other terrain with which to interact, offering many surprises.
The sounds are rather disappointing, but functional. The soundtrack isn't bad, though at twenty hours I was done with it.
The enemies, and most of the objects in the Dungeon of Doom, can be clicked on to bring up a description, often giving clues about them. Additionally, clicking on any object in your inventory pauses the game. Your inventory can be fully manipulated and your character re-kitted, all without missing a beat. The seeming twitch game play can be slowed down to allow for a full consideration of the situation, which I appreciated.
I generally enjoyed combat, though much of melee is dependent on understanding the exact ranges of your weapons and how far they may make you move. It took a little while to get the hang of positioning (at least for me). Once I got into the swing of things, though, I found it generally responsive and rewarding.
Unexplored also includes unlockable character classes, three difficulty levels, and options to add even more bosses and puzzles to the game, along with a daily dungeon and a weekly dungeon (with leaderboards for the competitive), adding replay value to the game.
I did experience some glitches that dumped me out of the game.
Also, there were moments that I found myself locked in a room, one that was described as a potential death trap by a clue I'd found. Upon using the escape mechanism that the procedural generation had left for me, I found myself in an even worse situation. Occasionally these unexpected events would spiral out of control, leaving me feel cheated. I expect in rogue-likes to die, but in the good ones there are (perhaps in hindsight) clear choices that I could have made for a better outcome. Sometimes the complicated puzzle and map generation of Unexplored would combine to spit out something that felt unfair.
Those negatives are small compared with all the interesting scenarios that this budget priced dungeon crawler can spin, yielding hours of fun.

Dead Bits is a colorful first person shooter which features environments and enemies, which are made out blocks. It is about a creature named Quilly who is abducted by an alien and has to fight hoards of blocky enemies to regain his freedom.
The game features nine unique levels which all provide unique challenges. This may sound like if the game is a little bit short and it indeed is. I managed to finish everything in two hours and some people can certainly do it even faster. Although the levels lack in quantity, their quality makes up for it. Every level is very distinct from one another, so no level feels the same. Although they provide variety in challenges and difficulty, they are fairly linear, so there is no point in exploring them.
There are four weapons in this game, a submachine gun, a shotgun, a bat and an alien blaster. They come with unlimited ammunition and no reloads, but are otherwise pretty basic. Shooting is not the only thing you do in this game, though, there is also an emphasis on platforming. For the most part it handles pretty well and the levels are designed with that in mind, but sometimes the jumping can be slightly delayed and Quilly is unaffected by moving platforms so these have to be handled with caution.
The graphics are very simple by the nature of the pixelated blocks, it still looks fine though especially with added lighting effects on higher settings.
This game is accompanied by a dubstep soundtrack which cues in and out depending on level progression, and every level features one or more distinct songs.

+  Nice difficulty curve
+ Smooth and stable gameplay with no glitches
+ Pretty lighting effects
+ Very high variation in level themes
+ Large soundtrack

- Platforming can be a bit awkward
- Very short
- No pause feature
- Linear level design
Dead Pixels is a basic game, which does nothing new in the FPS genre, but is crafted pretty competently, so that the gameplay is still enjoyable. With the low asking price of 0.99 USD in mind this game can be recommended for someone who wants a short distraction from life.

FF8 is quite possibly the most discussed FF due to how the public percieves its story and what it really means.
I'll explain this game a little for players who missed this gem from back in the day. It is quite confusing to someone who's never played it before for the first time.
The game uses a GF system (Guardian Force = aka Infinite Use Summons in Battle with outside of battle skills)
Now you need GF's equipped on a character to use basic actions like using Summons, Drawing Magic from Monsters or using items.
It's important to realize that there is NO MP at all in this game. Think of Magic like Items. Only way to gain magic is from draw points on the world or Draw it from Monsters in combat.
With Magic you can Junction it onto your characters to give them a boost in Stats to greatly increase their capabilities, like putting Fire on STR to boost Damage, or stack Cure onto HP to give your characters a boost in Max Health.
The more of a certain Magic you have while Junctioned onto a stat, the greater the bonus. So you'll get more STR bonuses from 100x Fire rather than just having 15x Fire. The same goes for the Level of Magic too. So you'll get even more bonuses to stats for Junctioning Higher Level Magic onto your Stats rather than Low Magics. (Like Cure vs Curage. Curaga gives much more to bonuses)
Now everyone should take note that the Limit Breaks in this game are different. You don't get a limit Meter. As such it can be abused to hell if you really want it to, just leave your characters in Low (Yellow) HP and watch your Limit Breaks wreck everything for you, making the game considerably easier.
This is a game EVERY JRPG player should experience once in their life. The music is top tier. Boss battles are blood pumping with the music, the story is pretty good and the Superbosses are really fun. Not to mention Squalls and Irving's limit breaks at endgame can completely wreck any boss in a matter of seconds.
To sum it all up. This is by far my favourite Final Fantasy, besides Tactics of course.

Have you ever played a game thats still fun reguardless of how old it is? Or how many times you've beaten it? Well FEAR is without a doubt, one of those games. This horror FPS classic is still one of my personal favorites.   Anything from the atmosphere, graphics, soundtrack, story, enemy AI. FEAR devlievers that in an excellent way.
True, the game's scares may not shake you up the second time around. But, it doesn't ruin the atmosphere. You have that sense of someone watching you even when the room is empty. (Or littered with the bodies of the soldiers you shot to pieces.)  FEAR also has that sense of helplessness. Like no matter how hard you try, the bad guys are always one step ahead. So it moves away from the typical hero formula of where the hero always wins in the end.
The AI does the enemies in the game justice. Have you played a game where the enemy was supposed to be a "professional" killer? Or something similar? But, they were dumb as bricks? Well this is not so for FEAR. The AI is quite intellegent. The soldiers will actually work as a squad to take you down. For example, say you were in cover against a sqaud, the squad members will attempt to flank you or flush you out with a grenade. But, while you're trying to get out of harms way. The soldiers are waiting at the ready to gun you down.  (and believe me, it can be easy for them to do so.)
Overall, I recommend this game to those that enjoy good creepy shooters/ supernatural games. Being a firm believer in the paranormal, this game is even more interesting to me.

C&C: RA3 is one of those very much so rare games that even though all competition from newer RTS-titles, still have managed to remain just as fun to play at the current as back when they were initially released.
With this IP, EA Los Angeles introduced to us (the players) one of the very best of gaming-experiences ever crafted, let alone one which one could ever have asked for. EALA gave us players lots of additional features and tools both advanced as simple that made and still makes this game from the bigger rest.
The Developers gave us the very best, with features such as the fantasticaly simplictic hosting-system of which still runs as smooth as ever and in which one didn't need to set up a entiere f*****g home-based server in-order to do so.

The Witcher 2 tries harder than the original Witcher in every regard, but it ends up in the same place, only for different reasons.
The graphics, writing and performances are mostly solid. I found it a bit backwards that the places you visit most often are also the most colourless, but the rest certainly make up for it. The only thing that is actually broken is the decision tree, where some quests can break if you don't do things in the right order. In addition, very often you will hear dialog with references to things that didn't happen or that the character shouldn't know about.
The one thing that the Witcher 2 excelled at, and perhaps the only reason why one should play it, is the extraordinary focus on treating you as if you are the protagonist himself. It is all about choices, but not in the way that you might be used to. Other RPGs assume you have a fetish on choices and running errands. NPCs costantly give character-breaking quests, like picking herbs, and choices, like deciding for an NPC if they should marry. Why would anyone ask a warrior to do those things? Luckily, there's none of that nonsense here.
Instead of assuming you are using your character as the means to shape this virtual world, the Witcher 2 assumes
the character and it lets you
to shape the world. None of your choices have clear consequences. Most choices don't have consequences at all. You are given those choices, like to be honest or to try lying, not because it will change the outcome, but because that's what your character is considering. Your character doesn't actually have any power and is constantly in fear of what others might chose to do. All you have is a set of skills, which you use to earn some infuence over the people who get to decide things. Sometimes you'll get what you aimed for. More often, you'll find that nobody waits for you.

Many of these reviews revolve around the game's commentary. Yes, there is a refreshing commentary on vidya and how we use it, but let's explore some other aspects of the game;
The narrative is good. The story isn't spectacular, but it's good. Takes about 3 hours to work your way through it.
The execution of the narrative, however, is astounding. Beautifully constructed and emotionally gripping, perfectly compensating for the raw story's imperfections. Everything from the soundtrack to the use of the fireplace as a story-explorative platform worked perfectly.
Also, it's fun. It's just plain fun. The whole process of buying and burning stuff is just simply enjoyable.
There's a freeplay mode if you like it that much.
Lastly, the puzzle-aspect - the finding combinations - is great fun and embellishes the sandbox with some much-needed direction. More items and puzzles would be a great step forward, providing a fun sandbox with a bit more direction, but in its current state, any buyers will absolutely be getting their money's worth.
In conclusion, buy the game. At the time of review, it's about 2 dollars. You won't regret this.

TL;DR - Simple rating: 5/10
Pros:
+A solid story continuation from W1.  It might not stand so strong on its own, but so be it.  It's a sequel.
+The game is quite pretty, especially for when it came out.
+Sex is sex not...playing cards.  If you understand, you understand.
+Combat is much improved (visually speaking).
+It's short.  A positive in this case considering I found it a bit painful to play.
Cons:
-Combat mechanics....sigh.
-The importance of one's potions was EXTREMELY diminished, and made inconvenient when the player did want to use them.
-Bestiaries were split in two very separate sections and filled with more lore than practical use.  Lore's not bad, but I do need to know how to prepare.
-The map was a little unwieldy and on the same note, some quests were too vague.  Obscure is okay, needing to leave the game screen and use the internet to find out something about the game, is not.
LONG version:
The Witcher 2, while it got high praises, and there's no denying the story was intriguing, you can tell the game was a bit of a lab rat and stepping stone to Witcher 3.  This installment introduces many new mechanics, "theoretical improvements", and honestly in many places they were just unnecessary.  The combat looked more real, the graphics present in this game show the direction the company wanted to go with 3, and it was a good direction.  Finally CDProjektRed got braver about nudity and the story was great.
But that's about all the praise I can grant the game...
The flaws I see in it may be biased since I played the game on Dark mode, but the finer mechanics of the game seemed...incomplete or maybe more fairly, seemed experimental.  Fights weren't balanced for difficulty as much as they were "this is what we want the boss to do, as for how you fight it?  Meh, not important," at that level.  Boss fights with suspense filled lead-ins became repetitive motions.  Enemies followed incosistent rules (some might argue that as realistic, but the journals and literature in the game fails to even mentioned these differences, or provide much of any practical information at all).  Some quests (read NOT all, most are fine) have absolutely no indication in the game of how they might be completed.  A 3rd party guide should not be needed to complete a game.  I don't like having my hand held.  A good brain teaser is great, but no quest markers, or at least large quest general areas higlighted, on cacoons the same color as the surrounding flora?  Come on.  If you think that type of searching is acceptable, then okay but add more to the world in that case.  Traversing through emptiness while doing so with no indications of any kind, broad or specific, was a little boring.  Finally, I simply didn't like any part of the new potions system, from effects, to preparation to consumption.  Just...I am glad it's changed again in the third, that's all I can say.  In fact I'm glad many of the new things introduced were either re-thought a third time, or reverted in the newest release.

The Aprillia RS250 sounds like the various speeds on a marital aid as you go up through the revs, the Suzuki GSXR1000 K5 sounds muffled, as if you've got your ears plugged and all of the V-Twin Ducati's just sound boring. One of the most significant things about a motorcycle is that they resemble what hell would sound like, not what a hairdryer sounds like. The menu's however are not. Sure, the backgrounds are pretty, but the text and text boxes are just bland. Navigating the menu's is like trying to force spaghetti up a cat's backside. I have spent a good 3 out of my current 16.7 hours playing this game sidescrolling left and right, be it trying to choose/upgrade a bike, pick an event or simply change my character's helmet. However, ironically, when you're about to purchase yourself a new motorcycle and you go to pick a manufacturer to choose from, all of said manufacturer's are laid out in a nice, easy to navigate grid menu, yet once you pick your desired motorcycle manufacturer you go back to the slow, dimwitted sidescrolling mess that they call a  menu, it's like being stuck in a world of Soup with only a fork. Why is that simple, easy to use grid menu not implemented in ANY OF THE OTHER MENU'S?
So in conclusion, if you manage to make it through the seven levels of menu hell and start a race, you will enjoy yourself. Hopefully they'll improve the engine sounds because right now they barely resemble anything that combusts.

You know all the games that call themselves 'roguelikes' nowadays?  Most of them are at best roguelike-like-likes.  Well, not this one.
is real time, but apart from that, it is a true roguelike, of the hacklike family, to be precise.
I just beat the game, and I am on a bit of a high, so the review is going to be glowing.  So be it.
has everything that I like about a roguelike.
- Compex combat, with varied equipment that really matters, where different enemies are handled in a completely different manner.
- Upgrading and crafting of equipment, using limited resources to produce specifically what your character needs, as opposed to mass producing the same stuff everytime
- Intricate levels which are a pleasure to explore
- Varied enemies who start as deadly unknows, but once you understand what makes them tick, can be handled in a manner than makes you feel smart and skilled
- Awesome interactions between items, creatures and the environment.  Find a blank scroll, copy an
spell on it, use it to learn that the potion you have is
, drink it to bypass a bridge behind which waits an ambush, fill the empty bottle with water, douse a torch near the ambush, and take out the ambushers.
- Multiple ways of handling problems, be it brawn, stealth, using the environment, etc.
Does the game have problems?  Yes, a few:
- There are still bugs, but the developer is great about fixing them as they are reported
- There are still some interactions that are needed, if only because you get used to things making sense, and want to be able to do things you would never ask from other games.
- The level generator will sometimes paint you into a corner, but once again, the developer is actively hunting down those situations.  Mostly it happens when you fall or teleport down a level, so just avoid that as much as you can
But the game is a lot more fun at its normal than it is frustrating at its worst.  At its best, when you have filled a room with flamable gas, and toss a torch to burn a crowd of dangerous enemies, it is awesome!
Well worth the 10 bucks... If I had spent double that, I'd still think it was worth it.
