Grand galactic strategy games has a particular allure to fans of strategy games in general. Stellaris certainly manages to offer up a scale and scope that should satisfy even the most discerining connaisseurs of the genre. If you want, you can take on a densely populated galaxy with a thousand star systems and dozens of alien races in a single-player game and basically pre-book all your free time for weeks and months to come!
Performance seems to be excellent on my "middle-of-the-road" i5, 16GB ram, 970 GTX on a 28" monitor running full 4K resolution. I've had a couple of sizeable space battles with dozens and dozens of ships on each side and it seems to resolve itself well, visually. But the maneouvering of the fleets and ships in large engagements are a horrible mess, looking much like the fights in a Peanut comic. Considering how much detail they put into the ship models, it's a shame that they all end up clustered together as if they were in a dog-fight, even though the smallest ships are corvette-class and the largest are capital Battleship class behemoths.
Overall there is, to me at least, a discrepancy between this different ways the game presents itself. You have a beatifully rendered galaxy with many kinds of cosmic phenomena - different type of stars, black holes etc. and their constituent planet, planetoid and asteroid variations in attendance. They all look fantastic, are animated and almost worthy of a "Cosmos" episode. The interface is suitably sci-fi and a lot of effort has clearly gone into trying to make all this available to the player. And then there are the alien races, which are rendered as cutesy low-fi modestly animated cartoon portraits - and that is just jarring as heck. The whole "suspension of disbelief" aspect goes down the drain and you are abruptly reminded that you are in a game.
Any of you people out there know of the writer Isaac Asimov and his Foundation series? This game screams to be treated with the same seriousness and fidelity as those books. I don't know if it's a budget issue, but this game should have taken its' clues from the Foundation trilogy (including the writing, which is also a little pixie-book-ish at times) with visuals inspired by  Chriss Voss' designs (book cover artist for the Foundation trilogy of books). Had that happened, it would have been possible to "stay" in the universe of Stellaris and never have to come out of it.
However, considering how good the game is, perhaps it is better for everyone's health that it isn't perfect in that sense.
For what it is worth, I wholeheartedly recommend this game, if you have time to spare. It's a solid 8/10 for me - had they just polished it off with better species types/factions and some serious writing and this could have been the galactic strategt game to end all galactic strategy games.

This game is so, so good. It's a roguelike in almost every way, so it has unidentified stuff that can kill you, and the difficulty is high, and there's a lot of learning how the game works, so you can succeed no matter what the random number generation throws at you. Even the graphics are, let's say, functional. I'd like more color, But like an ascii roguelike, at a certain point you realize that you see what they are trying to do, and the graphics become beautiful in a utilitarian sense. You even spend a lot of time fighting from doorways.
The only way it's not a roguelike is in its real time presentation, but even there, it's not a twitchy click fest. It's a more of a thoughtful thing, and really worth a look because it adds something new to the genre.
Also, the dungeons are excellent, and there's a lot to see here. I've played over 200 hours, and I still haven't seen everything it can generate, there are a bunch of things I've only seen once, and almost every playthrough has some novelty. And yet, it all hangs together (unlike, say, Nethack)

While there are other credible contenders (like Quest for Infamy) -- and more to come in the next couple years as Hero-U and Mage's Initiation wrap up development -- Heroine's Quest not only the best Quest for Glory game in the past 20+ years, but in some respects the superior of the games that inspired it.
First, let me get the shortcomings out of the way. The production values are not as strong as in the Sierra originals (the animations are a little choppy, the VO is a little amateurish, and the music is not as memorable) -- but those were commercial games made by seasoned veterans with a considerable budget. Heroine's Quest, unlike our Primordia or the majority of other AGS games you find on Steam -- is free, so it couldn't even theoretically recoup paying professional voice actors or the like. More fundamentally, the game seems to lack a little bit of the smoothness of the original QFGs: the grinding feels a little more grindy, the exploration a little too slow, the world somewhat less open and more driven by a linear plot. But to be clear, this is a *relative* comparison, and it is in relation to what I consider some of the best games of all time.
Having cleared that underbrush, let me now sing the game's praises. Most fundamentally, it achieves what I consider the game developer's greatest duty: generosity. That comes through not just through the price (i.e., free), but through the sheer quantity and variety of content. Everywhere the developers could give us more, they have, optional solutions and little Easter Eggs aplenty. That generosity is conveyed through the timeless and sadly underutilized QFG marriage of RPG and adventure game elements. The challenge of that kind of gameplay is that it requires a lot of art, a lot of alternate paths, and careful balance and testing. Heroine's Quest succeeds in all those things.
Earlier, I mentioned that the game exceeds QFG, and the way in which this is so (in my opinion) is the use of the Norse mythology and foklorica. It's not entirely consistent, and sometimes it mixes in modern fantasy elements or interpretations of the source material that don't quite work, but I found overall that it drew more deeply and broadly from this lore than did QFG, where individual elements were often cherry picked without their contextual elements.  (For instance, QFG introduced a whole generation to Baba Yaga and her chicken-legged hut, and what a gift that was, but she is hardly surrounded by other Slavic elements -- instead you encounter a hodgepodge of Greek mythological creatures and D&D monsters in a quasi-German setting.)  Heroine's Quest has greater consistency in this regard, though it suffers from the fact that Norse folk lore is more familiar so the characters feel less like "discoveries" than did, say, Baba Yaga.
Anyway, the bottom line is that this is a charming labor of love, shared for free, which leaves you with the warm, full feeling of a childhood feast, for those who grew up on QFG, or will serve as a pretty good entry point to genre to those unfamiliar with it. Three cheers for, and many thanks to, Crystal Shard!

So... I really owe this game a positive review, at least. I must admit i wasn't expecting much. Just a small adventure game. This is really a nice, fully fleshed out game. F.E.A.R is a classic FPS game for the PC in which you star as "Pointman", a soldier with a mysterious past being flung into a situation to hunt down a psychotic madman known as Paxton Fettel, who has hyjacked a rogue army of psychically controlled "replicas", which are to say, super soldiers. Oddly, they act like normal people, they even swear and feel pain, but somehow don't.. have a mind of their own, because they'r- okay, forget it. That's the theme of this game, forgetting. Wade tries to forget Alma, Aristide tries to make the world forget Alma and "bury the dead", and you try to forget the expoisition you just heard or the bit you just experienced because nuh-uh-uh-uhhhhthing is going to make any sense at all unless you go to the F.E.A.R wiki and read it all for yourself.
Apart from the confusing storyline, there's the dissappointing characters. Whilst Alma herself is a boss and is rightfully the main focus of these games, the other characters you meet along the way are somewhat more dissappointing. Perhaps with the exception of Wade.
SPOILERS INCOMING
The fat guy (I will not remember his name) never dies, he just sort of.. dissappears. He's never mentioned again. (EDIT: He is mentioned again in the next expansion, extraction point. How he got out, how he recovered from a bullet wound and how all the blood miraculously dissappeared is not explained. Also, what then happens to him isn't explained.) Ms. Wade, whilst we have some attachment to her because we had to spend some time with her, still has a lackluster death. There's no rhyme or reason to it. Instead of killing her and eating her perhaps in the apartments or immediately after finding her, they do it in the facility - and her death is only mentioned when you kill off Fettel, the primary objective of the game since the start. If you don't pay attention, you'll probably miss her bloodied corpse on the ground altogether and believe that it was a loose end. Underplaying a little much? And lastly, Fettel. You shoot him in the face. That's it. No bosses, no catching up to him, no getting him by surprise, he traps you in a hallucination and then somehow, for some reason, you're able to shoot him in the face after a few waves of weak enemies. Primary antagonist of the game, folks.
Wade's death was a bit more appropriate, and although we're given very little insight into his character, his death still seems appropriate. Perhaps not in the way that he died, but the fact that Alma kills him. Fact that he shoots fatty, and that he brings about his own death, directly, because of the guilt that he can't FORGET.
SPOILERS OVER
That all said, the game is overall, pretty fun in bursts. You get an arsenal of weapons of which you can only pick 3 to carry at any given time, mechs and tougher enemies tend to serve as bosses, you're not only limited to grenades, you have mines, remote bombs, the unreal 2 engine delivers dynamic lighting, big explosions feel BIG and your guns feel appropriately powerful. Enemies will explode into little giblets if you hit them with enough force, with I've often been able to do with the shotgun. Enemies respond appropriately to being shot (okay, somewhat, they are supersoldiers, but they're also human, so it's a half and half thing) and their AI is decent enough to sometimes flank you and sometimes, outright kill you. You're constantly upgrading yourself via the use of health boosters and reflex boosters, which allow you to go into slow motion for a select (usually kinda one-sidedly long) amount of time. There's also a variety of types of enemies, giving some true difficulty to the game as it goes on. The controls are good but require some rebinding for modern tastes and Pointman feels like he has some weight to him.
Oh, and, F.E.A.R is not scary. Not even in the slightest. There's a few true scares, but, it's usually not adequete of the "horror" title. It's more appropriate to call it horror "themed". There's the "theme", but it's really just an FPS.
I'd recommend it, but, I'd prefer F.E.A.R 2 to it. You don't NEED to play F.E.A.R 1 in order to understand F.E.A.R 2, either.

TL;DR - Simple rating: 5/10
Pros:
+A solid story continuation from W1.  It might not stand so strong on its own, but so be it.  It's a sequel.
+The game is quite pretty, especially for when it came out.
+Sex is sex not...playing cards.  If you understand, you understand.
+Combat is much improved (visually speaking).
+It's short.  A positive in this case considering I found it a bit painful to play.
Cons:
-Combat mechanics....sigh.
-The importance of one's potions was EXTREMELY diminished, and made inconvenient when the player did want to use them.
-Bestiaries were split in two very separate sections and filled with more lore than practical use.  Lore's not bad, but I do need to know how to prepare.
-The map was a little unwieldy and on the same note, some quests were too vague.  Obscure is okay, needing to leave the game screen and use the internet to find out something about the game, is not.
LONG version:
The Witcher 2, while it got high praises, and there's no denying the story was intriguing, you can tell the game was a bit of a lab rat and stepping stone to Witcher 3.  This installment introduces many new mechanics, "theoretical improvements", and honestly in many places they were just unnecessary.  The combat looked more real, the graphics present in this game show the direction the company wanted to go with 3, and it was a good direction.  Finally CDProjektRed got braver about nudity and the story was great.
But that's about all the praise I can grant the game...
The flaws I see in it may be biased since I played the game on Dark mode, but the finer mechanics of the game seemed...incomplete or maybe more fairly, seemed experimental.  Fights weren't balanced for difficulty as much as they were "this is what we want the boss to do, as for how you fight it?  Meh, not important," at that level.  Boss fights with suspense filled lead-ins became repetitive motions.  Enemies followed incosistent rules (some might argue that as realistic, but the journals and literature in the game fails to even mentioned these differences, or provide much of any practical information at all).  Some quests (read NOT all, most are fine) have absolutely no indication in the game of how they might be completed.  A 3rd party guide should not be needed to complete a game.  I don't like having my hand held.  A good brain teaser is great, but no quest markers, or at least large quest general areas higlighted, on cacoons the same color as the surrounding flora?  Come on.  If you think that type of searching is acceptable, then okay but add more to the world in that case.  Traversing through emptiness while doing so with no indications of any kind, broad or specific, was a little boring.  Finally, I simply didn't like any part of the new potions system, from effects, to preparation to consumption.  Just...I am glad it's changed again in the third, that's all I can say.  In fact I'm glad many of the new things introduced were either re-thought a third time, or reverted in the newest release.

I played The Witcher 2: Assasins of Kings Enhanced Edition and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt in 5 days.
In this part of my review I will be going to concentrate on the Witcher 2.
The game is a story driven RPG where you play as Geralt of Rivia, a witcher. The world is vivid, colorful and full of life. There is alot of additional dialogue and small bits of information of the lore hidden everywhere. (perfect for someone like me who skipped the first one, a big mistake).
Graphics still hold to this day, even tho it's already 2016 and we are used to eyecandy. Ubersampling still totally destroys my 390. There is alot of graphical settings, which is good. There is most likely some combo to get it running smoothly on pretty much any system. To me, audio means atleast as much as graphics. The audio is topnotch, I really like the dialogue and ambient sounds.
Combat system is just tad bit buttonmashy, it really isn't a problem for me. It spices things up with a sign system, essentially spells. There is also potion and oil system which is essential for higher difficulties. As a witcher you carry two swords: one made of steel, the other one out of silver. The silver one is for salying monsters. I really like this mechanic and it ties some of the story together aswell.
Conclusion: A amazing story driven RPG where you play as a professional monsterslayer, with an amazing story to back it up. This game still excells in graphics and audio.

TL;DR - Everything Dungeon defenders orignal had + All DLC for the original + new DLC & game restructure, combined for a tiny fraction of the price. #worth
Firstly, for those who don't know, This game includes everything from Dungeon Defenders Original + all their DLC released for that game. That totals to a value of £40 (~$67). This game also adds new maps (at least 4) and with the promise of more to come. They also have many new features that run throughout the game. They are only selling it for £15 (~$25) full price, with the game being on sale at the moment + the added discount for anyone who bought the Original game it is currently 70% off so it only costs £4.50.. what an absolute bargain.
At first glance you might think, "How can they sell this as a new game? Is it not the same as the original?". In short, No.
Here's why, the main reason this game is sold as a seperate game, is because they are trialing their new secure server system for DDII. The reason behind the servers is to intercept cheaters trying to modify any loot or equipment that they get. This was and still is a huge problem in the Original Dungeon Defenders game. The problem got so bad there that cheated items were being sold everywhere, mana could be generated and had no value, people were trading with items only obtainable from end game challenge maps. The cheaters essentially ruined the economy of the game as well as cheating and ruining the fun.
There are also several new features that run throughout the core of Dungeon Defenders Eternity (DDE). There is a new currency, "gold coins" they drop in game, from minions and from selling loot to the shop (or letting drops auto sell after waves). Many ignorant reviews of this game popped up as soon as it came out saying this was a pay to win item mall. It is not. The only items in the shop that appear to be sold for real life money are Emotions / Actions, which are costume specific animations a character can do ingame.
Another new feature that runs through out this game, is the visual update to every piece of equipment your character is wearing and the new models for them. With this comes a selection of Dyes to recolour the equipment (bought with Gold coins not real money).
The game feels so fresh and crisp, the characters have been rethought about and rebalanced so they scale appropriately. Text isnt continuously spammed in the center of your screen when certain minions arrive (a noise prompt is still there for those that relied on that). The minions have been rebalanced and they now have levels for easier understanding of their strength.
There is a new pet system, involving eggs and hatching them, with the new pets comes pet abilities! Also characters have slots for amulets that also give you abilities to use to help defend. Consumables are sold in the in game shop (for gold coins not real money) and they can be used in game to help you defend on the tougher maps. The same consumables and Dyes etc also have a chance of dropping in game, during waves from minions. Nothing about this game is pay to win.
Trendy is a very intereactive developer and will listen to the community and respond, this game is evidence of that. On the first day of release people were upset there was no Private lobby (unsure as to why, probably and oversight) and on the same day as they released the game they patched it adding Private lobbies and refining the match making system. They continue to strive to make their games the best experience possible for the user.
There's alot more I could go into about how much I enjoy this game over the original, but if you havent been persuaded by what has been said already then I guess there's no point going on. I would suggest ignoring any bad review with a play time length under 1-2 hours. As I am posting this review I have played 15hours+ and I have enjoyed every minute.
TL;DR - Everything Dungeon defenders orignal had + All DLC for the original + new DLC & game restructure, combined for a tiny fraction of the price. #worth

((Review reworked 24/7/14 - yes, this could be considered 'in constant development'.))
...is my personal motto for this review, because I've heard a lot of bad things about this. Like, a lot of bad things. Like, seriously, this game had severely negative reviews when it first launched and I can't blame them. It is supposed to be the definitive Dungeon Defenders experience, and while it may be shaping up to be one, I can't help but feel... well... annoyed, and somewhat disappointed.
Now, first things first, this game is basicaly DD1 with a new engine, there's no two ways about that, the game has been rebalanced and tweaked and looks better in some ways, looks worse in others. It still plays pretty much the same: Build towers, kill monsters, collect loot. The upside to this is that DDE has all the heroes and their costumes unlocked for you right out the gate, well, whatever was in DD1, anyway, who knows if they'll offer costumes as a microtransaction.
The game plays just as well as the original, with a few QoL tweaks like client-side mana and equipment (thank goodness), the fact that the currency is replaced with gold coins so that you no longer feel the need to leave mana out on the field, the ability to AUTOMATICALLY JUMP OVER SMALL OBSTACLES (10/10! GotY!) and the fact that there's more equipment slots plus the ability to weapon swap in the middle of a wave even if you're not Series EV (which is her gimmick back in DD1, although it seems useless now because her towers are pretty good for support.).
The UI is decent enough to fuss about with, it's not terrible, but it sometimes feels a bit clunky like the item box interface. No idea how crafting works, and my hotkeys get reset everytime I go back to tavern. There's not much of a tutorial to figure anything out if you're a newcomer, although some veterans reportedly had some trouble with it as well.
Taverns are now public... that's something I'm not too sure about, sure, it's nice to see other people in the tavern but some people don't like to see strangers running around, spamming attacks, towers, and so on. I tend to ignore such things, preferring much to get out of there as soon as I can.
When this game first released, and this is going to be an understatement, there was a terrible fuss over how the game was missing some of its advertised features. Single-player and private lobbies? Patched in after the fact. Cards and Workshop? I dunno when that came in, but they're there now. Third-party accounts? Not advertised at launch, but there now. Always-online DRM? Not what most people were expecting. Cash shop? Bluh.
However! The company seems to be putting a small effort into fixing a few things if what they've been doing didn't tip anyone off, so at least they're trying to make things work.
So, acknowledgements of missing things at Day 1 and general fussery aside, what's the problem here?
The servers breaking in the first few days of launch doesn't really come as a surprise to me, these days. It's probably just me, but I just don't really expect any company to handle their launches very well, but perhaps I've been jaded by seeing so many online games releasing and then buckling under the pressure of people coming onto the server and breaking them. When I first played this, they were fine, although it was after the initial surge, I believe, or I was playing at a quieter time.
The cash shop in a paid game kind of rubs me the wrong way, although they're selling cosmetics right now, so that kind of mitigates it, it's still a cause for concern. Right now, I don't feel
strongly about it, but I would feel wary about it, just in case.
All in all, this is not a bad game, but it's been sullied by how it was handled right out of the gate, and that doesn't put a lot of trust in their customers. The price for this is questionable, but having a hefty discount for owning the game plus the initial release sale at this time of writing brings it down to a price I can somewhat agree with. Sure, I'd prefer it to be more or less free or be a patch for DD1, but if they insist on it having a price, then so be it, but the initial asking price right now for a small upgrade doesn't fit the bill, perhaps when it is more fleshed out then the price would have more worth to it.
Anyway, it is up to you as to whether or not you should buy it. If you don't particularly care much for Trendy's antics and want to play Dungeon Defenders, this
be a good pickup for what it's worth since it has the Eternia Shards levels packed in with it. However, if registering a separate account on Playverse and having a game that requires you to always be online irks you, but you still want this game, I suggest you go pick up DD1 over this.
Side note: I honestly wish there was an undecided option for reviews on Steam whenever the reviwer is unsure on whether to recommend it or not, like in my case. Honestly, what happens in the future can tip my view on this game in whatever side's favour.

The art style of this game is absolutely beautiful, the characters are very likeable, and it actually has a pretty good story.  One of the big criticisms of this game is it has too many "furries". I grew up watching cartoons so, I'm not sure why it's ok for one thing and not the other, but whatever. This game is actually pretty long for an indie platformer, it took me about 15 hours to finish, which for me is impressive especially since there are AAA titles that aren't even that long. This game in some ways is a little bubbly as with a lot of Anime-style games, but trust me, the game has a little more serious of a tone then you would expect. Seriously there is so many things to like about this game, one of the biggest highlights that are shocking to me is that this game was made solely by ONE MAN, Dean Dodrill. From story writing, to hand drawn art style, to programming, EVERYTHING (minus voice acting obviously) was done by him. It is truly an impressive display of talent. If a Hack and Slash, Metroid-Vania, platformer with a basic but viable upgrade/leveling system, and a decent little story sounds appealing to you, I definitely recommend this game.
+ Well-written, heartfelt story
+ Beautiful art style
+ Awesome Soundtrack
+ Lots of replay value
+ Cool little easter egg/cameos from characters in other indie titles that you might know
+ Flat out, fun and challenging Action-RPG
- Mediocre voice acting (Not terrible)
Seriously, if you can't get past a little comic relief and bubbliness, its a shame because you are truly robbing yourself of such an amazing experience. Seriously, F*** the haters, its a great game.

My two favorite roguelikes are brogue and DCSS.
Until now, I didn't think a real-time roguelike belonged in the ranks of those two games... but Unexplored does.  This is one of those games that's hard - you don't feel like a newb playing on easy-mode... you are proud if you make progress on easy-mode.  This is an actual roguelike with hundreds of pieces of loot; you will need to use everything you find in strategic and creative ways.
The level generator is amazing.  Make sure you choose 'Randomize' everytime you play and I guarantee every game will offer a new experience.  You will unlock new classes via achievements.  It isn't easy raising your stats - since each class starts with unique gear and abilities, they all feel strong in unique ways.  For example, the rogue class always starts with a cloak of stealth and 2 daggers.  It doesn't sound like much but as a rogue you won't worry as much about range fighting and traps.
It's a rare thing finding a "roguelike" game that's worthy of my time these days... With so many pretenders on Steam containing the word rogue somewhere in their descriptions, it's difficult to find a game that actually has some resemblance to the great game of rogue.  If you're a true rogueliker, you won't regret getting killed in Unexplored dungeons.

Do not dismiss this game for its simplistic aesthetics. Unexplored is a rather classical approach to the rogue-like genre, that happens to be bundled with one of the best seed based dungeon generators I've seen. Heck, it's probably better than Daggerfall's. *cough*
Joke aside, it's really good. It will generate huge-ish, interconnected levels, with interesting puzzles, and after 30+ hours spent in it, I've never found a level that wasn't solvable. I've encountered a few bugs, but that was a couple of releases ago and the devs seem to have committed to update the game regularly.
The loot is great and can be plentiful depending on the seed, and while there is no character leveling per-se, there is character progression by the way of potions and magical items. So that's good. There are several character classes to choose from, although you'll have to unlock them by performing diverse feats during gameplay.
The graphics, while not exactly breath-taking gorgeous, serve their purpose efficiently in that  everything is clearly presented and you'll have no problem identifying an enemy, a trap or a piece of treasure. The sound design is of the same vein, with a special mention for the musics, which manage to support the ambiance, building the tension when there's danger around, slowing down when you're in a peaceful place, all the while sounding pretty good, in my opinion. I get tired of in game music really easilly in most games, and after 30 hours, I still haven't turned them off. That must mean something, however subjective music tastes are.
But I digress... game is great, definitely has more to it than meets the eye, especially at $10/10euros. I definitely recommend it.

Retro games rarely pull me in like the original that they draw inspiration from, but this one did.
I am a big believer that things change, and trying to re-create the atmosphere of the 90s is a bit of a futile effort. This game proves me wrong. What got me most is that they managed to blend the classic point-and-click adventure style with the classic FRP seamlessly: You can - of course - look at/talk to/walk to/run to/handle anything. But the cool part is that you can also bring up the spell menu at any time to cast spells to see what will happen - not even a classic like Simon the Sorceror had that.
Second example is about your first task. Your first task is finding food in a harsh environment. (By the way, I love a decent amount of realism in games, so I loved this start.) I had opted in to play with the Sorceror among the three basic classes, so I had a few extra points in my herbalism skill. But that meant that I could actually collect herbs - I am guessing that a Warrior would have had to hunt.
So thiry minutes into the game, it feels like it recaptured the 90s feel for me.
I enjoy these types of games. No suprises, exactly what I thought it was.

For a game written in 2005, FEAR holds up remarkably well.  Playing at 1080p with all the options maxed, it really does not feel that old.  There is a noticeable squareness to the environments but this feels more like deliberate art direction than a limitation of 8 year old technology.  There is a beautiful simplicity to the gameplay too - compared to a modern game such as Far Cry 3, this is a tightly-focused stripped-down elegant shooter where the only thing that matters is blowing bad guys away.  While the environments are fairly linear, this fits well with the horror theme.  Like the classic bad dream, your only option is to walk through the door at the end of the corridor even though you know you aren't going to like what you find there.  The story is so-so but largely superfluous. The environment builds tension on it's own.  The horror is less the visceral in-your-face variety of, say, Bioshock, more the subtle psychological horror of Silent Hill. Instead of chainsaw-wielding maniacs leaping out of cupboards at you, there are flickering lights, unexplained footsteps and phantom photocopiers. The concept would be good, but the game has a lot of flaws. And by that, I mean, a LOT.
First of all, let's begin with the tutorial. It's one of the worst training levels I've ever seen. You will also get bored of it really quickly.
Then, I'd like to get into the controls: it's sometimes unclear, and some of the moves have two or more alternative functions aswell, meaning, that we may perform a specific attack without intention. Also, it's a mouse-cursor-following control, which is perfectly fine for games such as Diablo, Space Hack, Magicka or Path of Exile. For this game, I'd be more happy, if I got keyboard-controlling option.
The other thing is the characters/abilities. Basically, we have 3 dragons to select (you have to buy the others by real money, but I'll tell more about it later), that has only 2-2 abilities. Then, we have a selectable item, which will provide us 2 more. For a game like this, it feels too few. I know, Awesomenauts also has 2-2 abilities for the characters, but it is still much more fun, and it doesn't feel like if it would need more. Also, as I said before, because of the controls, we may activate an ability by accident.
The difficulty: (I'm going to talk about the botmatches) Well, the tutorial isn't really helpful, and the bots can♥♥♥♥♥♥you very quickly, and then win the moba gamemode. To compare with another game, Dota 2 is also hard, but it doesn't feel that bad.
The gameplay: It feels empty and blank. You will get bored in really short time.
The largest fatal flaw: One thing, that the game is pay to win. But it really got carried away with it. This is not just "Pay to Win", but "Pay to Do Everything" or "Pay to Breathe". I mean, that you have to buy characters/items for real-money, if you just want to finish a single "quest". And the reward just doesn't worth it. You will feel, that you just wasted your time (and money). If it's "F2P", then players shouldn't be limited down this much. Maybe if we would pay for some exclusive things/quests, I'd say, "OK, let it be, I will still have fun with the rest of the game", but this is like a cruel joke. If you handycap the F2P players that much, then make the game "Pay to Play" each month, and much less players will be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off.
Summa summarum: Dragons and Titans is a huge disappointment. It is a pity, because it COULD have the potential to be a great game. Unfortunately, they didn't make it.

Being a big fan of the 1st game along with a really good sale of this one i decided to get it, and dont regret it.
i'm not going to go through a whole list of positive things about the game as their are so many, though i'm going to have a little moan about things they got right in the first game and so wrong in this 1.
Private Taverns: i dont want to be lumbered with no escape from a bunch of other players spam attacking dummys and skills in the tavern, me and my mate play mainly at night till early hours in the morning due to being busy during the day, and to have a private tavern to talk about the items picked up and the next fight and tactics and stuff was perfect, now we're dumped in a zoo of 20-30 other people going mental.
User Inteface: The UI in this game feels rushed, trading is useless unless you wish to spend an hour looking for the item you said your mate could have when you picked it up, as the icons are so small in the trade box and you cant tell the difference between a staff and a sword.
An added filter for class would be great, their are a few filter choices to help you look for specific items in your inventory, but their is no filter that allows you to look for specific class items, if you have a few characters that you would like to progessively level and gear up, this would be a huge bonus.
Their are a few other issues with the UI but you get the idea.
Loading times: The loading times are starting to annoy me a little. Because i'm so used to the game loading instantly in DD once a level is picked and now this whole countdown waiting for player stuff has been implemented it needs to be tweaked slightly. Add a check box that allows players that are ready to tick, and if all players have loaded and ticked, they can begin instead of waiting for the whole countdown, me and my mate have monstrous gaming pc's, 95% of the loading time is us waiting about.
Trading: i know the game has its reasons for having our own client side loot, and it is great i enjoy not fighting over loot anymore, but it would be nice if i could just right click an item in my inventory and click drop and it becomes server side, when playing with more than 2 friends its time consuming clicking trade on each person when if a "drop" feature was implemented everyone in the game could mouse over the items i dropped to see if they are better and take them, if not ill scoop them all back up, i miss that.
These are just a few of the problems in this game in comparison to the first, it bugs me when developers seem to lose a lot of good aspects to a game that were in previous versions, this should be every good thing from the last and much more, which in most cases it is, just these little things let it down.
I'm a massive DD fanboy and i do love this game, i could spend all day pointing out the amazing points of the game which is why i chose to just dig at the negatives a little hoping it would get some feedback out there and hopefully eventually sorted.
highly recommended game guys, if you loved the first you will love this one more!

***BE WARNED*** This "Definitive" version does not have local co-op. That is my biggest disappointment on this game. Note to Trendy: When you use the marketing word "Definitive" it will lead people to believe that it doesn't lack any of the original features. I think local co-op was a core feature in the original Dungeon Defenders. I now know that the store page doesn't specifically say the game has "local co-op" but that's something sort of like finding the hidden fine print. I feel duped in that sense.
Nevertheless, the game does offer a lot of interesting changes compared to the original game. I'm going to assume a lot here but based on what I can tell so far, the online multiplayer isn't via peer-to-peer connections anymore but rather each user connects to the playverse servers. I used to lag frequently when connecting to other people's games in the original dungeon defenders. But now I'm not. I can't confirm this at the moment though.
With those two things being pointed out, I'd conclude that this game is heavily focused for online play and you should only buy the game if you enjoyed playing online with other people in the original DD. If you are like me and enjoyed playing this game on local co-op with your family, YOU WILL BE DISAPPOINTED. All of the other new and neat features just wouldn't matter because you can't play with the people that matter.
PLEASE TRENDY. I would like nothing more than to play this version of the game in local co-op with my wife and kid.

Grand galactic strategy games has a particular allure to fans of strategy games in general. Stellaris certainly manages to offer up a scale and scope that should satisfy even the most discerining connaisseurs of the genre. If you want, you can take on a densely populated galaxy with a thousand star systems and dozens of alien races in a single-player game and basically pre-book all your free time for weeks and months to come!
Performance seems to be excellent on my "middle-of-the-road" i5, 16GB ram, 970 GTX on a 28" monitor running full 4K resolution. I've had a couple of sizeable space battles with dozens and dozens of ships on each side and it seems to resolve itself well, visually. But the maneouvering of the fleets and ships in large engagements are a horrible mess, looking much like the fights in a Peanut comic. Considering how much detail they put into the ship models, it's a shame that they all end up clustered together as if they were in a dog-fight, even though the smallest ships are corvette-class and the largest are capital Battleship class behemoths.
Overall there is, to me at least, a discrepancy between this different ways the game presents itself. You have a beatifully rendered galaxy with many kinds of cosmic phenomena - different type of stars, black holes etc. and their constituent planet, planetoid and asteroid variations in attendance. They all look fantastic, are animated and almost worthy of a "Cosmos" episode. The interface is suitably sci-fi and a lot of effort has clearly gone into trying to make all this available to the player. And then there are the alien races, which are rendered as cutesy low-fi modestly animated cartoon portraits - and that is just jarring as heck. The whole "suspension of disbelief" aspect goes down the drain and you are abruptly reminded that you are in a game.
Any of you people out there know of the writer Isaac Asimov and his Foundation series? This game screams to be treated with the same seriousness and fidelity as those books. I don't know if it's a budget issue, but this game should have taken its' clues from the Foundation trilogy (including the writing, which is also a little pixie-book-ish at times) with visuals inspired by  Chriss Voss' designs (book cover artist for the Foundation trilogy of books). Had that happened, it would have been possible to "stay" in the universe of Stellaris and never have to come out of it.
However, considering how good the game is, perhaps it is better for everyone's health that it isn't perfect in that sense.
For what it is worth, I wholeheartedly recommend this game, if you have time to spare. It's a solid 8/10 for me - had they just polished it off with better species types/factions and some serious writing and this could have been the galactic strategt game to end all galactic strategy games.

Milestone set out to succeed playstation 2's Tourist Trophy as the modern motorcycle racing simulator. It however falls very short of that goal. Graphics are last generation quality that somehow taxes modern video cards. The only positive things I could say about the game is it's selection of bikes and gear. But it falls short from there. It feels very shallow and geared towards the casual gamer/racing fan.
Short-comings in on track riding is what ruins the game the most. It is the same arcade style simulation (an oxymoron) engine as the previous MotoGP games. Trailbraking deep is ridiculous and offers no feedback when the front wheel is at it's limit. The reactions of the bike to too much throttle is the same for every bike. Turning into the first corner is always the same even if the race just started and the front tire is still "cold". Then there are the small missing details. No clutch lever use even on the older bikes. The throttle hand works but the brake lever is never used, never mind the rear brake pedal on the right foot. There are ZERO braking markers for non-track circuits. Only occasionally is there a reference point like a tree or a fence, but the rider is left with nothing to judge the approach most of the time.
Then there's the ridiculously aggressive AI that has no qualms of ramming passed you because somehow collisions only penalize one bike. The AI will insist on it's line even if you're in front of it and worst of all will not brake if you plan on braking earlier than it. The AI is also on a very suboptimal line
The set up of the game progression is obviously an afterthought to Milestone as there is NO QUALIFYING SESSION. YOU ARE ALWAYS 8TH. Leaving you with having to deal with the 7 AI-controlled bikes that will slow you down. Then there's the classification of the bikes into races. Some are beyond lazy such as grouping the MT07 with Ducati Monsters and Triumph Street triples because they are all below 700cc. WHAT?! That's a very ignorant way to classify a class race. The MT07 MAY have a corner speed advantage, but that advantage is completely blown away on circuits with straights. Why even bother having that bike? There was no beta testing for this game.
Then there's the customization for looks and performance. The biggest mistake Milestone has in this area is completely ignoring the significance of a rear shock. The whole customization is an insult to any enthusiasts who love to customize their motorcycle's performance capability. Front forks are all stock upgrades. No chance of changing oil, springs, or even valves. Seat height, wheelbase, sprocket size, rotor size, handlebar vs clipons, removal of DOT required parts like lights.
Milestone also only includes a very small amount of tracks despite having the license rights to the tracks in MotoGP15. None of those tracks appear in this game. Some tracks are ridiculously unfit for racing. Miami circuit being the most obvious because the street is too damn narrow .
All in all RIDE is a game made by a casual company  meant for the casual gamer. If you want a game that shows the dedication to the sport like Tourist Trophy did for the Playstation 2, you will be very disappointed.

I'm a bit late to the party, however I feel the need to write a review for this game anyways, considering how much I've enjoyed it. Despite my seemingly immediate praise of the game, that doesn't mean it lacks actual flaws.
With that said, let's start with the game's two biggest strengths, the first being it's asthetics. The game is gorgeous, even with the settings set to minimal it remains a rather great looking game graphically and is well optimized, the game is capable of running in a good margin between 30-60 fps consistently and the only real instance of lag is mostly when I spam Fidget's enhanced attacks, even then it still runs very smoothly. It also took me a while to notice the subtle mixture of 2D and 3D rendering which makes the game look nice and detailed. However the background and foreground can blend in too much which can make platforming rather annoying (Then again platforming in Dust can be tricky at first to begin with), also sometimes you can lose track of Dust durring large battles.
The gameplay is where the game truly shines, I will admit that Dust's gameplay is the most satisfying I've ever experienced in a long time, to the point it's still fun treating underleveled enemies like ragdolls. Platforming as stated prior, can be tricky at first, particularly the climbing vines, though you'll get the hang of it quite easily. The one and only thing I can say that's remotely negative about the gameplay is it's difficultly, as in the game is radically easy on Normal and below, granted Dust is a character who's rather squishy when low leveled, take the time to level him up and he practically have became something akin to a demi-god. Ironically I actually would recommend playing Hard instead for your first playthrough, solely because of how easy the game naturally is.
Finally the story... before I state any criticism about the story, before playing this game my expectations for it's story was rather low after learning about a several cuts this game have went through (Apparently the true main villain was axed from the final game as well, and frankly despite how epic and climatic Gaius' fight was, I personally did not consider it Final Boss worthy, I will explain why soon). I will say I was still surprised despite my low expectations, as in I was expecting something worse, however that doesn't mean these cuts weren't obvious. The story had a great set-up, setting and characters have indeed interested me, in fact I will admit that in the very least I was attached to the main characters. Sadly despite the great introduction and rising action, the story sharply falls flat at it's climax, and honestly lacks a proper conclusion anyways, all because of lack of proper exposition. There's a frequent amount of "info-dumps" which strangely left me with more questions, for example
, could've been written better if it still didn't feel so ambigous at the moment it was revealed, in fact alot of things in the world of Elysium felt rather ambigous even till the end. The character I disliked was Gaius, and this is mostly because it was fairly obvious that he wasn't meant to be the actual Big Bad to begin with, although as a villain he have done many horrible things, such as genocide, the thing is that just telling the player he did these things honestly don't have much a impact, even down to his design I knew, the moment I saw him, that he would be a disappointing final boss.
In short, the gamplay is amazing however the story feels rush and honestly convoluted (perhaps my opinions towards the story may change if there's any other content that might explain things alot better, with that said, I will be lenient towards the story nonetheless).

Overall this game just doesn't hold up.  While playing it I considered that as a 'free to play' it might be acceptable... but the more I played the more I realized that even then it's a game that's more irritating than fun.  I play AdVenture Capitalist and Clicker Heroes and Swarm Warp, and those are all terrific examples of free to play time eating games.  The thing about each of them is, I can get involved, or I can walk away and let them run and stuff keeps happening in the background.  But this game... this game unfortunately both requires your attention for things to progress, but also has what I feel is a completely unnecessary imposed time limit on its item orders.   I'm not sure why that felt like a necessary addition in a game this simple and straightforward.
To begin with the positive, I like the design, it's very nice, and there's an interesting little story development with the neighbor - and this is a case where the game introduces a time-eating element that actually works - the letters reveal very little at a time, but it's not irritating, because you're still getting something out of it (letters, items, mild amusement at the letters - if you've ever watched Tiny Toons, don't be surprised if you find yourself reading her letters in Elmyra Duff's voice).  There are also some fun animations with the burnings - I especially liked the marshmallows and the opera singer.  And the idea of combinations is fun.  Unfortunately all of that was just "mildly entertaining" and therefore not enough to overcome the rising irritation of waiting to continue playing.
So, the negative: picture sitting at your computer for an hour with several episodes of "okay, now stare at the screen for 2 minutes", that's what this game is.  As someone else pointed out in a positive review, it's not enough time to do something else, but it's enough time to be annoying as you stare at the screen waiting for anywhere between a few seconds and 2 minutes to pass for *each order* so you can burn something else - it gets more annoying the more combos you're looking for, especially with a limit of 4-ish items at once, which can be *slowly* expanded by spending money for more slots.  But you can only buy one.... slot....at...a...time.  Everything about that just seems like "we don't feel like our game's long enough to ask for money for it" but honestly the time wasting elements are exactly what make me not recommend this game.  Earning slots and new catalogues would both be acceptable, without that added time on each and every package you order (and letter/weather forecast/etc you get).
If this game ever gets rid of the time limit, I would absolutely pick it up again and recommend it as a fun casual game.

All the initial backlash to this game was blown way out of proportion.
The online DRM is there but it actually works incredibly well. The UI seems kind of pasted on to the game but I've been matchmaking with 1-3 other friends and parties work fine and I've had no connection issues with about 5 hours of playing. The login is painless, doesn't require an email confirmation or really much of anything to get it to work. Steam remembers the information and you don't have to input it everytime you want to play. I saw a comparison of it to GFWL and almost laughed. It works great and even has Twitch integration (which I'll never use, but it's there).
Singleplayer is present and works fine. This was not the case at launch but was fixed the day of release, mainly due to people being upset about its absence.
As far as complaints of it being a ported mobile game I don't see this at all. I admittedly haven't played the original DD in about 2 years but the graphics fidelity is perfectly fine and doesn't seem any worse or better than before. I haven't done a side by side comparison, but it looks really good.
My biggest complaint is the convultued inventory and character screens. Their messy and confusing and use icons for stats rather than just saying what it does. Locking and unlocking items is bizarre and crafting seems promising but I don't really understand it too well yet. Once a wiki comes out I'm sure it'll be easier to get it all down.
As for the gameplay itself, it's a tweaked and polished DD. It's fun, it's intense, it's colorful, and it just works. I don't know what DLC is or isn't included, but I didn't own much in the original and there's definitely plenty of content for 6 bucks (what I paid) or the 15 or 20 it's going to be for new players. Definitely worth it.

Grand galactic strategy games has a particular allure to fans of strategy games in general. Stellaris certainly manages to offer up a scale and scope that should satisfy even the most discerining connaisseurs of the genre. If you want, you can take on a densely populated galaxy with a thousand star systems and dozens of alien races in a single-player game and basically pre-book all your free time for weeks and months to come!
Performance seems to be excellent on my "middle-of-the-road" i5, 16GB ram, 970 GTX on a 28" monitor running full 4K resolution. I've had a couple of sizeable space battles with dozens and dozens of ships on each side and it seems to resolve itself well, visually. But the maneouvering of the fleets and ships in large engagements are a horrible mess, looking much like the fights in a Peanut comic. Considering how much detail they put into the ship models, it's a shame that they all end up clustered together as if they were in a dog-fight, even though the smallest ships are corvette-class and the largest are capital Battleship class behemoths.
Overall there is, to me at least, a discrepancy between this different ways the game presents itself. You have a beatifully rendered galaxy with many kinds of cosmic phenomena - different type of stars, black holes etc. and their constituent planet, planetoid and asteroid variations in attendance. They all look fantastic, are animated and almost worthy of a "Cosmos" episode. The interface is suitably sci-fi and a lot of effort has clearly gone into trying to make all this available to the player. And then there are the alien races, which are rendered as cutesy low-fi modestly animated cartoon portraits - and that is just jarring as heck. The whole "suspension of disbelief" aspect goes down the drain and you are abruptly reminded that you are in a game.
Any of you people out there know of the writer Isaac Asimov and his Foundation series? This game screams to be treated with the same seriousness and fidelity as those books. I don't know if it's a budget issue, but this game should have taken its' clues from the Foundation trilogy (including the writing, which is also a little pixie-book-ish at times) with visuals inspired by  Chriss Voss' designs (book cover artist for the Foundation trilogy of books). Had that happened, it would have been possible to "stay" in the universe of Stellaris and never have to come out of it.
However, considering how good the game is, perhaps it is better for everyone's health that it isn't perfect in that sense.
For what it is worth, I wholeheartedly recommend this game, if you have time to spare. It's a solid 8/10 for me - had they just polished it off with better species types/factions and some serious writing and this could have been the galactic strategt game to end all galactic strategy games.

If the tone of Jak and Daxter met the gameplay of DMC with the art style of a Philipps CD game gone Super Saiyan 3, you get something pretty close to Dust.
This game hits it out of the park on so many levels. The visuals  are what I always wanted every Phillips CD game to look like (though not a single one ever did,) and the gameplay is a straight homage to every grand beat'em up from times of old. Ther are combos from DMC, Cancels akin to to God Hand, and stats that are versatile enough to allow you to fight the way you want to. I wouldn't go as far as to say the item and level up systems are dense, as if anything they are thin and stale, but the primary point of the gameplay is to have the player racking up insane combos by controlling space and using the the crouch attack to cancel into anothr combo or 2 or 3 or 4 or wait a second, was that combo for 1000 hits?!?!?! In that regard, I would say the items and levels give more than they take away. The game does feel rushed and  stale by the final chapter. It almost felt as if they made the last chapter first. The gameplay became much more choppy and the mechanics they introduced became somewhat irrelevant in comparison to the rest of levels. The last chapter made me feel like I was forced to try one or two gimmick tactics over and over, while the rest of the game seemed to invite creativity and unique combos. That being said, I would reccomend this game to any beat em up fan. Overall, It's a blast and a half even with the downsides.

Command and Conquer does it again with another great installment onto the Red Alert series. Although not as good as its predecessor C&C: RA3 continues to offer no need for builders and no worry of controlling population.
Unlike past Red Alerts I only played about one skirmish as I did not find the AI as enjoyable as the predecessors. This Red Alert offers some interesting new teams and resource harvesting concepts which seem different than before. Like in the past Red Alert games the Russians and Allies are pretty much the same basic strategy type, while the third team offers a fresh new tactics. Similar to past Red Alerts to expand bases (when playing as either Allies or Soviets) you can build Mobile Construction Vehicles. But, unlike past Red alerts they have also added the ability for Prospectors (allied ore miners) to deploy into Command Centers which allow you to expand to nearby areas mitigating large costs. The USSR can build “Sputnik” which can also deploy into a command center. Both of these units allow for cheaper base expansion. This is different for the Japanese whose buildings are built by transforming vehicles into buildings and thus are not limited to base parameters.

The campaign took me about 21 hours to complete (that includes Allies, Russians, and Rising Sun missions). Interestingly the campaigns intertwine and in some instances you play the same missions but just as the opposing team, which I sort of liked. In the case of this game the missions are not exactly gripping, but that is the case with all strategy games. The campaign offers a great composition of actors which make you laugh, gasp, and reminisce in the old days when you first sat down and played Red Alert. Some of the missions are very quick and last no time at all while others can last a couple hours.
If you are expecting something just like the second Red Alert then you will be disappointed. There is only one Yuri and his revenge was an epic adventure that could only be told once. If you are interested in playing a strategy game that brings Red Alert on a new adventure then this is a game worth checking out. With an amazing intro song to boot and epic campaign cut scenes that you won't forget. Red Alert 3 really takes Westwood’s dream into action: hot babes who flirt with you throughout your entire game and keep your spirits bolstered with cheesy lines.
Pros:
+Great campaign with fun dialogue and amazing cut scenes.
+New Empire of the Rising Sun team which brings all new tactics to the game
+Campaign missions that don't just require you to continually build a base over and over again, but rather test you through a variety of scenarios.
+Epic main menu music that just makes you want to jump right into the Russian campaign.
+It has been 18 years and Tanya still hasn't aged over 30... a mystery? Or did someone use the chronosphere?
Cons:
-Its not Red Alert 2 (that game already existed, if you want that game you may want to go find the disk from your shelf)
-Some campaign missions can run rather long, while others last about 10 minutes. (Some missions took me up to three hours).
-Poor movement AI can cause units to not exactly act how you want them too.

A realtime Roguelike strongly reminiscent of Nethack. And just like Nethack I'm not very good at it, but have great fun trying neverthless.
The art style took a little adjusting but is clean and simple, occupying the eye without being cluttered. The interface is well thought out with drag and drop and click functions, and a simple twinstick control scheme. For those who consider options menus a concern, there are the expected basic resolution and fullscreen/window options, separate sliders for music in audio, and remappable control schemes. You can also switch between absolute and relative movement, which is a nice option to have. Ambient sounds and combat are well done and provide useful info to the player, the soundtrack is good but not particularly memorable (good background music).
The gameplay is where it's roots show particularly strongly - a core game focused strongly on randomised dungeons, puzzles and items, with a simple but technical combat style. There are options catering to more combat oriented players (by generating more bossfights and combat heavy dungeons) and for more puzzle oriented players; not to mention your regular easy/normal/hard difficulties. You can also just leave it at stock standard for a balanced game.
There is permadeath and you'll quickly find yourself on Rodney XV but that's part of the experience for roguelikes. There's a successor based progression system in place rather than leveling up, which may put off some but helps make the game more approachable, as stats and more advanced concepts don't matter quite as much until you've got a few dead adventurers under your belt. The achievement system gives you actual in game rewards in the form of unlockable equipment - for example killing 20 enemies with the same dagger unlocks the option to buy an extra dagger at the beginning of each run.
Overall an enjoyably frustrating experience, where dying is generally clearly your own fault, and with enough variety to keep you coming back for more.

When F.E.A.R first launched in 2005, people were blown away with the technical level of its graphics. Unfortunately for the gamers of today, Monolith Productions forgot to implement any art style or set pieces what so ever. The most fearful thing about this game is how cold and sterile the world seems, rather than its imitation of Samara from The Ring. Thanks to said girl, the game was also commended on living up to its name, thanks to scripted sequences involving corridors of blood à la The Shining, and cheap jump scares. I’m not really sure what all the fuss was about, considering horror masterpieces Resident Evil (2002) and Silent Hills 1 (1999), 2 (2001) and 3 (2003) had long been on the market. The ‘spooky sequences’ played out as little more than a predictable ghost train, and couldn’t actually harm the player. Sure, they broke down the repetitive battles, but to any seasoned horror game fan, they felt shallow. Condemned: Criminal Origins (2005) did a far greater job of striking fear into players in a first person perspective, and using the very same engine as F.E.A.R.
My other major complaint about the title is that while starting out solidly enough, the cliché story becomes vague and muddled throughout the campaign, and although their back stories are vaguely revealed, the characters entirely fail to develop.
Yet despite these major flaws, I would recommend this game (or it’s first expansion pack) to fans of the FPS genera in a heartbeat, thanks to some of the best gunplay I have seen in games, even to date. Whilst the weapons might be neither realistic nor visually interesting, the kinaesthetic feedback from a firefight is uncannily satisfying. Be it a pistol, shotgun, smg or rifle, the ricochets, plaster chips and dust clouds that get kicked into the air are immensely satisfying in a way that the game’s sequels never managed to replicate. In addition to this, the enemy AI is still some of the best I have seen, so gunning down waves of clones as they squeal in fear over their radios  never out stays its welcome, despite the frequency of battles.
If you enjoy shooing things from a first person perspective and have any interest in games that predate a couple of years, you owe it to yourself to play F.E.A.R

To put it short, F.E.A.R. is an excellent game. Why? Because it does right the one thing it has to do right: shooting. The weapons are fun and feel good, there's enough different weapons to keep interest. It feels great seeing the damage your weapons do: enemies bleed when you shoot them, certain weapons can even nail them to walls, and whenever your bullets hit walls, they leave a mark you'll surely see. Overall, gunplay feels the way it should.
Not only that, but gameplay is made even more fun by one of the best AI's I've seen in a shooter. The AI can, naturally, take cover when necessary, but what really sets it apart is its ability to move. The AI doesn't just camp behind a wall, it actually moves in a sensible way and it actually tries to flank the player when it sees a chance for that. The AI works outside direct combat as well: It gets confused in ambushes, and it can lose the player, in which case it will actively search for the target. Tired of dumb AI? Try out F.E.A.R.!
F.E.A.R. isn't only a shooter, though. There's also the horror side to it. It's not all that scary but for a person that's easily scared (like me), it's pretty good. The game is generally paced so that shooting and horror parts take turns. The game also has a decent storyline which should keep your interest for one playthrough. Make no mistake, though: You will not be playing the game just for story.
Graphically, the game still works. By todays standards, it's nothing great but it works and it has aged surprisingly well. Nothing looks antique, and the game really benefits from its dynamic lighting. Style-wise, the game is pretty boring. It's office complexes, gray corridors, and then some more gray corridors. Gray is the color of F.E.A.R. along with black.
In addition to the things mentioned above, there's not much to tell about F.E.A.R. It has a multiplayer component which went free some years ago. It felt pretty good but I don't think it has any memorable gamemodes to keep interest. You can pretty much forget the multiplayer for this game. Sound effect are decent for both shooting and horror, with the typical static radio chatter and all. Music must not've been very memorable as I don't remember any.
Overall, F.E.A.R. is a good game. You won't find a great horror game in it, but if you're a friend of shooters, you will definitely want to try it out thanks to its solid gunplay and excellent AI.

MOBA based on dragons, weapons and elements.
Choose to either play the campaign or jump into games VS real people or bots. You pick a dragon of your choice, being different from each other and depending on its element, will give you two unique abilities - Q and R. Q is your main attack, it cost little mana and normally has a small cooldown, W is your secondary attack, usually if your dragon has an escape or damage reduction ability, its situated here.
Now for the weapon, you get to pick an item of your choice to wield into battle, giving you the other two abilities, your E and R. Depending on what type of build you wish to play, these items will give different skills. Example is a mace that gives massive mana regen as a passive, your E, while the R is a dmg ability. Some items are strickly support, some are healing, some are damage and some are a mix of both. This allows you to play the same dragon with different weapons to create completely new builds and playstyles.
There are no items in this game, the gold you collect from killing enemy players and minions is stored on your person and requires you to return back to base and dump the gold in a pile. This then gives you experience depending on how much gold you had stored away.
Three different gamemodes, ARAM, normal MOBA with three lanes and a zone capture gametype.
You begin the game with 3 random dragons and 3 random weapons, so if you don't get what you want, you will need to play a bunch of games for crystals to buy the desired items or pay real money for bundles.
The objective of both the ARAM and normal 3 lane MOBA is to destroy the turrets linked to a statue, then destroy the statue to deactivate a forcefield that weakens your dragon and slows down his speed. Do this several times until you reach your titan and release it from its prison, (attack the main objective, like the nexus in LoL) and the game is over.
I play League of Legends a lot of the time, so that satiates all my MOBA needs, but I do recommend trying it out, its free and pretty fun if your willing to get the hang of it.

Storyline missions and battles only give you around 20-60 each. Don't think you can complete tutorial objectives to speed this up as you start out either, how about a 50 reward for a task that requires you spend 150.
So you either want to pay or you're in for the hard slog for that shiny gold dragon you set your eyes on.
This game also doesn't have much to do when it comes to the matches in multiplayer and from what I've seen there is only one map per game-mode, making it rather boring after a while. After playing around with the level for a bit, I can definitely say that Lost Coast is a complete success. It's not available seperately, but it is available in the Half Life Complete Pack (which is on sale right now). Here, you play as Gordon Freeman, as you come across the tiny town of St. Olga, whom is under attack by the Combine with a gun that launches headcrabs into the town. The 14-Minute Tech Demo shows off what the Source engine can really do, and as a result the game looks beautiful. It's almost like a work of art.
The level is paced very well here. You start by heading upwards on a cliff, where you encounter quite a few Combine soldiers blocking your way. The level has little cover here, so you must be aware of enemy positions and use your grenades well here. You are given a few other weapons along with the Gravity Gun to boost your arsenal. Once in the courtyard, you are allowed to take a small break and take in your surroundings as the game shows off the High-Dynamic-Range Rendering (or HDR Rendering).
You then enter a church, and one small puzzle later more Combine soldiers enter. You are not allowed to leave until you defeat them all, which is something that wasn't really explored in the original Half-Life or Half-Life 2, so it's nice to see some different gameplay elements here (along with the aforementioned cliff). After you defeat the enemies, you are led outside where you confront a chopper in a very confined area. After that, the level is over.
Overall, the game succeeds in the one thing it was meant to do: be an excercise in level design and act like a tech demo. This level is the very reason many maps in games such as Team Fortress 2 or the Source Counter-Strike games look so good. However, it's length really shows it's a cut piece of content (cut from Highway 17) and, being a demo, you wish for more. Then you go back to playing regular Half-Life.
9/10
Pros: A sweet, short level with brilliant level design that looks good in the proccess
Cons: It's length is short compared to other levels in previous games in the Half-Life franchise

If you have the original, steer clear of this one. Always-online DRM (seriously?) with their own overlay (Uh, hello? Steam? You know, that thing you're selling your game through?), no offline/LAN options whatsoever (there's "singleplayer" sure, but that's it), and literally unplayable without a constant internet connection.
There are also a few costumes inexplicably missing from the original, which I'm assuming will be patched in later. Too little, too late.
It's not even funny how much better the original version was just because of the fact that it did NOT have the always-online DRM/overlay... thing, proper singleplayer/LAN support (clicking "play" and being dropped into a lobby designed for 4 players with 20 other people in it is not my idea of "singleplayer", and if that's all I want to do, I should NEVER have to deal with that OR the online overlay/DRM thing). I can never stress this enough: Always-online DRM is NEVER a good thing. For anyone. The punchline? Pirates crack these games too. Some people even take it as a challenge, this one doesn't even really look particularly hard to crack, and coming from someone with zero programming knowledge that should say a lot.
I think my last complaint would have to be that the original version pretty much had full support for everything this has to offer. They just decided to mislead their consumers to get more money on the way to the sequel. Wasn't the whole point of having offline saves and trendynet in the original that one would be secure? Well good job keeping that secure and showing support for it by just completely giving up and making an entirely new thing that might as well be Uplay or Origin. Granted, it's not THAT bad... Yet.
There ARE a select few positives I didn't quite explore: Equipment is (allegedly) visible on your character when equipped. There's something like six new maps. The dedicated servers are (allegedly) more secure than the old trendynet (would it have been so hard to let people make a local copy of their trendynet saves and force a restart on that one after implementing actual security measures?), though there's also supposedly some noticeable latency, so all things considered... That's two positives, one iffy and a whole lot of terrible ideas and execution.

I still have a few issues with the game, namely a lack of developer support and little individuality between the bikes (they all feel like the same bike with different handling, braking, and power stats, there are no handling quirks to make them interesting beside some bikes being more wheelie prone than others), but overall I think it is a fun enough game to recommend to anyone who likes bikes or racing.**
I really like this game. As someone who races motorcycles IRL this is about as close as you can get to the real thing (apart from the ridiculous amount of trail braking you can do) with a screen and controller while still being fun to play. The bikes will slide, wheelie and stoppie in a similar way to their real life counterparts, but the game is more forgiving which makes it much more enjoyable. The tracks are well designed even if the environments are a little repetitive, and the bikes look good and there are some interesting options, even though the bike list is lacking in some areas (very few small bikes, no super motos) and they sound a little flat. Over all I would say if you have even a passing interest in bikes you will find joy in this game.
With that said the reason I am giving this a negative review is the saving issues. With 8 hours play time I have had my save corrupted twice, and one of those times the game created a 84GB junk file which maxed out my hard disk and caused all sorts of problems with my computer until I found it and deleted it. Even now that I have started a new save I am still having issues with it, the game has given me the starting bike and 3000cr but is still saying I have already won the races I completed on my previous save, meaning all the races my bike has a hope of winning pay out  a measly 2500cr instead of the normal 10000cr for a first time completion. There is no point in playing the game if all I am able to do is complete the same races on the same bike until my save is corrupted again and I have to start all over. It's a shame because I really enjoy the game itself, but with the current  issues the fun isn't worth the frustration, especially when I payed full price for it when it was released.
I'm not saying this will be your favorite game of all time... But it was mine.

Abzu is not a challenging game- you'll never get stuck for long or find something incredibly hard to beat.
It is not a long game- I was taking my time and beat it in about 2.5 hours.
It doesn't have a ton of gameplay features.
Are these the only criteria to take into consideration when evaluating a game?
Never.
Abzu is one of the best games I've played, and is one of my most cherished media experiences. A video-game is, in its most fundamental form, an interactive experience, and I think there are few games that nail this as well as Abzu does. You'll feel utterly immersed in its world despite there being little to no text in the game. You'll be moved by the story despite a complete lack of dialogue. You'll be confronted with all of its complexities even when it's so simple.
This is because Abzu is the undisputed king of visual (audiovisual?) storytelling in the video game industry, and that's saying a lot. Furthermore, this game came out about a year after the groundbreaking The Witcher 3, and a year before the revolutionary Breath of the Wild, but I think that when people look back on this era in the history of video games, with any luck, it is Abzu that will be best remembered, and stand out as a historic title that defined the era.
I've deliberately refrained from technical details on what makes this game so great. It can run on anything, is on sale all the time, and isn't a particularly large download, so you have very few reasons not to find out for yourself. Go try it out.
Verdict: 11 out of 10- a rating reserved for games that set the barrier.
