Well I've had this game for a while now and this is my two cents on this title:
This is a fun game both solo and with others. There's quite a bit of content, more so given the maps fromt he workshop if that's your cup of tea. All in all I enjoy playing alone and with others from time to time. It's something different then your normal MMO type game, such as swtor, maplestory, etc. If I had to name what game this reminds me of, I'd have to say, torok, DinoiCriss, those kind of games. (forgive me if the spelling is a bit off, it's not one of my strongest subjects)
However there are a few down sides I've noticed. First there is the ability to join players even when they picked solo. That to me is kind of pointless, here's why. If someone clicks solo they did so to play alone not to play with others. I've done that a few times pre-prelude, meaning back when it was still dino horde. There wasn't a way to make it private or put a password on your game, at least not that i ever found. That is the frist con I have found with the game. However this has been fixed from what I've seen as now you can name a server you create and lock it with a password, make it private, and truely play alone. So that con has now been outdated with the release of prelude.
My next issue is more of something I've managed to do and I do not fault the game's play ability for it. I have just managed to get to lvl 55 on one of the classes. Now mind you I did this using an xp grind map from the workshop, but using the new prehistoric settings found in prelude sdkbeta. The issue was found after I hit lvl 50 and is still going on. My frame rate drops to the point that the game freezes. This could be the map, even though theres not much of anything on it, could be how fast I've been killing the dinos, could even be that it's a bug that happens else where in the game. I have done nothing to fully test this lag/frame rate drop. That is why it's more of a personal issue since I can't blame the game without knowing if it's happening to a lot of people. However there is a warning sign before it starts getting really bad, while in first person, you will see your body move around in front of your point of view. In 3rd person your body just rotates while your crosshair and bullet lines still seem to be aimmed where they were before the body starts to rotate. This maybe a small matter on my end or witht he map I was using, but it is troubling that it's only started doing this at lvl 50 when I'm using the prehistoric difficulty setting.
Other then all of that I give this game a 9 out of 10, the 9 is simply because I have yet to play all the maps that come with the game normally. Still one of the best games I've played involving dinos that is a 3d enviroment. Keep up the great work, and I'll keep recommending this to my friends. ^w^

The Witcher 2 is...interesting. I generally enjoy games with heavy narrative focus, a developed lore, and challenging combat. Witcher 2 has all of those. It's a great game, even. But it misses the mark ever so slightly, at least for me.
As far as gameplay goes, it looks much prettier than is plays. While the highest difficulty level can push it to near Dark Souls level of difficult, it's rather unfulfilling. Combat is a very dominant strategy style ordeal, while using runes and belt items are enjoyable, nothing beat the effectiveness of simply mashing your light/heavy/block buttons, with an occasional dodge roll to spice things up. It's especially eggregious on easy and normal, where you can just mash your light attack brainlessly and still win versus a whole horde of opponents. Most rune signs felt novel and niche, useful in specific fights, where in the other 70% of the game Aard and Ignis are really all you need. Traps are basically useless, as your swords are more reliable damage, and the Yrden sign is a free, infinite use trap; even then, I only found the Yrden to be mandatory in exactly two fights in the game.
I think this partially stems from the way the skill tree is set up. Don't get me wrong, I think the skill tree is actually really awesome, it makes me think of games like Path of Exile. You get one point in a node to travel it, and can invest a second in a node to increase it's effect, and sometimes gain a bonus effect as well. You can also throw in items you find killing monsters called Mutagens on specific skills, which add a little extra "oomph" or give Geralt a small stat boost. But the problem, at least for me, was that, with my sword being the single most effective and reliable tool the game afford you, I found myself only pumping the Swordmaster section of the tree once it was unlocked. I'd only invest in nodes from Magic or Alchemy for extra health and stamina. Perhaps it's just a fault of how I generally like to play games like this, but it made me feel like the majority of those skills go to waste. It might also be due to the fact that levelling up is beyond slow - the real xp is from quests.
It's not typically a bad thing that quests are where your big xp rewards are hidden, especially when you're a very narrative-driven and lore-focused game. The Witcher is definitely that type of game. But the problem is that means while only the basic honest witcher contracts you find on town notice boards (these are generic "slay x of monster y" quests, which happens to be the protagonist's profession) are your standard fare, every other quest is about five times longer than it should be due to different outcomes based on choice you make. Your decisions actually do affect the world the game exists in, but at the cost of really dragging things out. In fact, whoever you side with at the end of chapter one, completely changes the entire middle portion of the game. The downside of that being you need to replay the game to see the other half. Similarly, it does the same at the end of the third chapter. This results in a few plot points only directly integral to this specific game to slip by the player, necessitating a replay, or a trip to youtube.
The main narrative is just excellent. It's deep, multi-threaded, and you are given a full "curtain is pulled back" moment in the epilogue, which wraps up all the loose ends except for three keys points that set the stage for the next game in the series. I figure that those you enjoy Game of Thrones would enjoy it the most as it is primarily a story of political intrigue, but anyone you enjoys a fully fleshed-out world and complex narrative will have a good time.
For me, in all honesty I force-fed myself this game in 3 marathon sessions just to know what's going on so I could enjoy Witcher 3. I've not read the books or seen any of the television shows that this series is based on, but the game makes me wish I did. Because then I'd get the story and world lore without the drawn out quests and somewhat boring gameplay. Still, it's an undeniably solid game, and an excellent deal, especially on sale. Think Game of Thrones by way of Dark Souls with a light seasoning of Skyrim.
I just wish I had a horse to cover all the distance poor Geralt instead had to leisurely jog while back tracking. And a nickel for every time I heard either "plough" or &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; used by an NPC.

There are not that many games that I can say have sucked me in as much as this one eventually did. The combat can feel clunky at times, and the difficulty is pretty outrageous at first because you are exponentially weaker than when you are mid-game.
Still, the world is beautiful, the dialogue is well thought out and you do feel as though every decision you make has at least some sort of consequence later on. I've had small decisions I thought were absolutely meaningless turn out to make things alot easier for me at some later time.
The downside to this game is that it is very linear, and the inability to fast travel can be very, very aggravating. Save often, save early, and make sure that before anything big happens you save because most fights take a few tries and nothing makes you desire to play less than having to go through 20 min of content each time you die because the auto-save option is sometimes ill-fitted for regular play.
If you haven't played this yet, but are playing Witcher 3, play this one too. The story acts as a general prequel, and a good amount of the things mentioned in the third installment are more enjoyable when you've played this.

The short version:
BOMB KING! The Sensational Character Find of The New Millennium, And The Best Thing About This Game By Far! Play This Game, Peasant!
The long version:
So at first (and second, and third through tenth) glance, this appears to just be a lazy F2P ripoff of Overwatch. That is, basically, what it is. But it is actually quite good.
Let's get the rest of the negatives out of the way first. Overwatch is by far a more polished, spectacular, more fully-realized game. Obviously both Paladins and Overwatch devs are coming out with new content constantly, so that's a wash. Basically Paladins is a scrappier, lower-budget game and it lacks some quality-of-life things Overwatch has. A good example is how in Overwatch there's a distinct "you're about to get killed" effect, a visual screen thing and a distinctive gasp. Paladins--I think--has a similar thing but it's barely noticible and it's easy to lose track of how hurt you are.
Another facet of this rudimentaryness is the unlockable costume options, which are incredibly lazy. But screw hats, anyway.
And the creative bankruptcy here is pretty legendary. I don't know who first invented these concepts and who stole from who, so I won't say it's a blatant "ripoff," but pretty much every iconic Overwatch character ability is given to someone in Paladins more or less one-to-one. Thing is, there are quite a lot more abilities that make Paladins feel unique.
So on that let's segue to why I think this is a good game--not necessarily better than Overwatch but worthy of standing alongside it.
It plays very differently. Well okay that's not really true, the core gameplay is very similar: arena shooter with ults and cooldown abilities, capture points and push carts. But it takes much more after DOTA 2. You choose a champion and you're locked in for the match, so team comp matters. As the rounds progress, you purchase "items", which are more like permanent upgrades that can themselves be upgraded, using money you earn by playing well over time. You can move faster, ult sooner, have shorter cooldowns, reload quicker, lots of stuff, and this adds a lot of depth to matches. Pick and counter-pick to respond to the enemy team's composition and their own item picks. For instance, shields (which can be very powerful in this game) can be destroyed by Wrecker, which makes your shots deal way more damage to shields. If the enemy team is shield-heavy, one or more of your champions better go Wrecker or you're gonna have a bad time.
But the customization doesn't end there, far from it. Each champion you unlock can be customized with a bewildering array of loadout cards, which can radically alter how each champion actually plays in matches. In that sense it feels a bit like speccing a character for PvP in a MMORPG. Like the sniper character? Like getting sick headshots? Build that card loadout. Like the sniper's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Oppressor Mines that slow people down and annoy them? Buy the right cards and you can throw like 8 of them and be a useless burden to the enemy team AND your own team.
The gameplay structure is different, and in a lot of ways better. The best and most ubiquitous game mode involves first fighting for a king-of-the-hill point, which then spawns a cart you must push to the enemy base. You score 1 point for winning the point and 1 point for finishing the push, but you also get 1 point for defending a push successfully. First to 4 wins, but you cannot win by scoring a point defending a push. Therefore, if skill levels are mismatched or you pick a horrible team or you have trolls or whatever, you will quickly lose a 4-0 stomp and get to try again without having to quit and incur an abandon penalty. But you can have interesting matches that are very long and involved and come down to 3-3, and whoever caps the point this one last time wins it all. Even the longest matches aren't that long, certainly nowhere near as long and stressful a comittment as DOTA. The fact that you can't win just by defending means there's less inevitability and comebacks are more feasible. There aren't that many super-turtley characters at all in this game, actually--there's only one real builder character who isn't that big a deal. There are very durable tank characters, but they can be outmaneuvered or counter-built against.
The final point for me: it's free to play, yes, and grind to win. But by the time you've got the hang of the game you'll be able to buy a character or two to try, and might be tempted to buy into the game and get every character for...$20, half of what Overwatch costs.
So, basically, if you like Overwatch and/or DOTA or at least would tolerate a bit of DOTAness, there is no reason at all not to try it for free. You'll be surprised. Just be prepared to put up with rough edges (which might one day be smoothed by the devs) and a really rather hilarious amount of "hey look it's the guy who looks like a Taiwanese knock-off action figure of Hanzo that you'd see in a blister pack with Spider-Man and Shrek."

unexplored is the very best of the recent crop of 'roguelikes'... i put that in quotes because most games that call themselves roguelike dont even pass for 'rogue-lite' but this one is the real deal. its true, it might not meet the strictest definition since it is real time and not turn-based, but this is a rare example of a roguelike that isnt, in my opinion, disqualified by it.
unexplored feels very much like a graphical version of Brogue (and if youre a roguelike fan, this alone should be reason enough to insta-buy). it has a similarly pared-down set of mechanics, eschewing the complexity of more common roguelikes for a more streamlined experience that keeps things simple without sacrificing the strategic depth that keeps a roguelike interesting.
there is no experience, no leveling. your character is developed through a combination of strength potions and equipment choices, again along the lines of brogue. strength allows you to use a wider variety of equipment, and equipment allows you to enhance the various attributes of your character through enchanting, forging, and lucky drops. each run will have its share of high-powered equipment, usually locked away behind some combination of puzzles and challenges, as well as a scattered mix of items with lesser enhancements, and this will largely determine how you go about approaching each run... one run you might get a lot of fire-resist gear that might lead you to hoard fire-starting potions and items with an eye towards burning out most of the monsters... another might find you with a lot of speed and stealth gear encouraging hit and run tactics. also, monsters can frequently use the same equipment you can, sometimes to great (or hilarious) effect.
dungeon and level generation is where the game really shines, with a nice variety of layouts that sometimes require real thought or skill to navigate, as well as branching paths and multi-floor puzzles. in many ways the dungeon itself is the main adversary, and almost every run features at least one floor or set of floors that makes you just pull your hair and want to scream at the screen.  it is at times hard to believe the floors are randomly generated, since the generator does such a great job at really putting you in some sticky situations with some devious combinations of traps, layouts, switches, and the like... and does an especially good job of continually forcing you to make the risk vs reward decisions that are a core part of every good roguelike.
unexplored is very hard, but for the most part very fair. when you die, its pretty much always your fault. you know that somewhere down the line you made a mistake that cost you the game. im pretty experienced with these kinds of games, and reasonably good at them, and i still havent managed to win a game yet (although i HAVE managed to get the magical macguffin at the buttom of the dungeon).
in fairness, there ARE bugs, mostly with the level generation... for me, it often fails, usually forcing me to restart. this is frustrating, but the lead developer is super responsive with fixing these bugs and rolling out updates, so i am confident that in time these issues will all get worked out.
bottom line, if youre a fan of the genre, this game is worth every penny, and i can recommend it without hesitation.

The way in which the levels are laid out feel like they were hand crafted  and give you a great feeling of exploration.
The game feels more like a zelda game than a roguelike in some ways especially if you find yourself replaying dungeons. There is also alot of fun emergent gameplay to be had with throwing items to set off traps, burning down forests and diving off cliffs.
The combat is very different than anything I've played before. It mixes the 'bump' to attack of roguelikes with zelda style sword and shield combat. There are also a decent number of different weapon types that can be duel wielded and all change the style of play.
Something has to be said about the very simple user interface and controls which lets you focus on the game rather than tripping over your controls and menus. It feels really polished.
I'm looking forward to playing more and seeing what else this game has to offer because right now I've just scratched the surface.

Well, I gotta say... this game absolutely came out of nowhere for me.  Apparantly showing up in August, yet I'd never seen it even once until Steam randomly threw it at me recently (stupid overloaded store...).  And that's a bloody shame: I buy alot of different games pretty often, but of all of them I've gotten this year, this is probably the one that deserves the most attention by far.  Hopefully, perhaps this review can help to convince some more people to buy it.
Unexplored is an action roguelike (as in, real-time) that creates a very detailed and interesting world for you to explore, as you control your amorphous one-eyed blob of a character (???) throughout an extremely intricate dungeon full of traps, monsters, exploding things, and all sorts of junk that you'd expect to find in a horrible dungeon of doom.  The Amulet of Yendor (which apparently is like the greatest thing ever, according to roguelikes) is your goal, which needless to say is at the bottom of this horrible death pit.
And that horrible death pit is one of the big draws of this game.  Possibly the game's most striking feature is the dungeon itself.  Using something called "cyclic generation", the game creates all sorts of amazingly complicated floors that tend to feel hand-crafted rather than purely random.  This fascinates me to no end, and it ensures that each floor is INTERESTING.  But it goes a bit further than that.  For example, the idea of a lock and a key... pretty familar, right?  Well... not always.  The game takes the idea of a lock and key and abstracts them (is that the right word?).  The "lock" might be a hideous room of death turrets.  The "key" might be a potion of invisibility that you found elsewhere, allowing you to bypass the turrets safely.  Or perhaps you're in a dungeon floor filled with chasms, and you find out that the exit is COMPLETELY blocked off in it's own seperate room... you cant get in there.  However, the game has been handing you a bunch of ropes, which can be used to climb down into the abyss and onto the next floor.  And from there, if you find the stairs that go back UP to the exit you couldnt reach, you might find a powerful item in that closed off room.   These are just a couple of examples of the fascinating situations that the game will create for you.  There's all sorts of interesting stuff that can happen.
And going along with this, there's all sorts of interesting items to get too.  Many items are relatively familiar... you've got your equipment (armor, weapons, magic rings), your potions and scrolls (often unidentified when picked up, but not ALWAYS... and this aspect is soooo much more managable than in things like Nethack), magical staves, and all sorts of things.  The game tends to encourage you to actually USE these things.  Not just to get through those "lock" situations, but for any situation you might find yourself in, chances are you have some tools that can help you.  Even negative items (bad potions for example) can help you... that horrible potion that produces a poison cloud could wreck you if you actually drink it, but instead of doing that, you could open a door into a room filled with monsters, fling the potion in, and close the door, letting the room fill with gas, slowly killing everything inside; needless to say, this sort of thing is entertaining as heck to do.  Speaking of gas: there are various types, many of which can be ignited, and some of which do funky things.  This game being as amazingly detailed as it is, there is even wind that can blow the stuff around.  There's also water to wade through and swim in, which can really change up a situation fast (particularly if it's murky water... beware of the hard-to-see Bog Worms).  The environment and area types really add to any situation that may already be there in what is already a very complicated dungeon.
And it's a dangerous place, too.  Monsters and sword-wielding jerks everywhere.  This game has quite the enemy variety... there's tons of different monsters.  Combat with these foes is rather slow, careful, and calculated.  Each individual enemy is it's own unique threat... this isnt the sort of game where you're going to dash through a room, guns blazing, killing 20 monsters in the blink of an eye.  You have to be careful here... time your swings/stabs properly, watch the enemy's movement, keep track of your surroundings, and make sure you're using your items well, as most foes can mess you up pretty badly if they get the best of you.  You have many methods of attacking your foes, as well as defending against them, and combat can get pretty tactical.  It gets especially loopy if there's a number of foes around at once... in a game where a fight with just one enemy often is careful and calculated, you REALLY dont want to be surrounded by 5 axe-wielding orcs, or something like that.  You need to keep track of your surroundings, and plan your movements.  Get the drop on the enemy (there is a stealth system!), dont let them get the drop on you.  Combat, overall, is pretty darned fun and satisfying, and the sheer enemy variety combined with everything else keeps it that way.
One nice quality-of-life bit is your health potions:  You dont have to worry about forgetting to use these.  When your HP gets super low, one of them will automatically fire off for you.  This is a good thing, as you already have a squillion other things to worry about.  Dying simply because you didnt click your health potion would be stupidly irritating.
And did I mention the traps?  All sorts of horrid things.  Turrets, gas vents, you name it.  Deadly things, all of them.  Exploring the level though can sometimes find you switches that shut down traps in key positions... offering you even more reason to explore this detailed world.  Be warned: this is not an easy game.  You will die, sometimes in hilarious ways (dont drink exploding potions... just dont).  There are, however, multiple difficulty options to choose from, a rarity in roguelikes.  And the game is never unfair... it always gives you the tools, you just have to figure out the best way to use them.
And detailed it is.  There are even books you can find, written by previous adventurers, which may mention things like a secret room containing a Cloak of Movement on the 6th floor, giving you a clue that you can use later.  This is a very polished game filled with tons of things both major and minor, and even the smallest bits shine with quality.
There's even some crafting, if you find things like forge or alchemy stations.  You can make some useful stuff here... IF you have the right items.
Now, it is worth noting that the game IS still in early access as of this review... but it's so very polished and just outright good that it easily outdoes tons of completely finished game.  And the developer is very helpful and interacts with the community, and clearly cares about the project and the people playing it... so that helps even further.   I can say though that I have not run into many genuine bugs in this game; this is a very stable game, despite being in EA status.
All in all, I've been playing this one to death, and this might really be my "game of the year".  And considering the sheer number of games that I buy, that's quite the feat.  But honestly, it's THAT good, and I'm just having that much fun with it.  I cant recommend this one enough.  The early access label doesnt matter this time... this is more than worth it, and can only get better from here.

Unexplored is the game all roguelite fans have been waiting for. Traditionally roguelikes visually display the world with characters on a black screen. These kind of graphics don't appeal to everyone, so I was overjoyed when I found this game. It has the depth of a traditional roguelike with a much improved visual interface.
Your goal is to find the
in the
. A mythical amulet that has the power to destroy the world! As a greedy adventurer you immediately depart to get your hands on the mythical amulet. You descend down the stairs and enter the first floor, you proceed to kill all its inhabitants who have been living peacefully here for many years. You leave behind a trail of blood, dead bodies and probably your own bones. In the first few runs you will die a horrible death. As you get better at the game you will understand why you died and slowly make progress.
Along the way you will encounter many enemies, puzzles, traps and bosses. They will all try to brutally murder you in their own unique way. When you manage to reach floor 20 an unspeakable horror lurks in the dark. Red menacing eyes stare at you guarding the amulet of yendor. But this horror is nothing compared to what happens next.
The game is very expansive, you will not be able to get all the achievements in your first run. You might beat the game but you will be far from having seen all the content that the Dungeon Of Doom has in store for you. The game offers an infinite replayability that will keep you amused for many hours to come. Each dungeon offers a unique set of floors that will challenge you in different ways! But don't get to attached to your character, death lurks around every corner. The learning curve is steep but flattens out once you get the basics of the game down.
All in all this game has a lot of potential in it's current state. I would definitly recommend it if you enjoy playing roguelikes.

It seems this bears reiteration upon reiteration:
Disregard the majority (though never all) of the negative reviews and sentiments for Dungeon Defenders Eternity. The vast majority are based upon misunderstandings, misconceptions or factual errors, and are therefore inapplicable to the actual product.
Dungeon Defenders Eternity is NOT:
* A mobile port. It is based completely on Dungeon Defenders, with added code and assets. From whence this idea comes, I know not, as there is NOTHING to suggest mobile roots.
* Laden with IAP. The in-game shop ONLY sells cosmetic items, a standard not only of the genre (in as far as DD can be categorized), but a new paradigm for the games industry as a whole. And it is one of the most harmless and fair ways for developers to increase their profits (which is often not about quick cash grabs, but about staying in business and making new games, especially for indie developers).
* Visually downgraded. This fallacy is based on the new streaming texture mechanics, where textures are streamed upon first launch, thus allowing players to get into the game faster. That this would make 50+ reviewers believe that there has been a graphical downgrade only shows that customers will jump to conclusions within SECONDS, and never challenge the legitimacy of their own preconceptions, or double check their initial findings. I first launched Eternity on a 1 MBIT/S TETHERED SMARTPHONE CONNECTION, and the textures for the tavern loaded within one minute.
* More demanding than the original edition. The two Steam apps put almost the exact same strain on my processor, GPU, etc.
Dungeon Defenders Eternity IS:
* Significantly improved. The list of new features include manual dodging, a whole crafting system, consumables and spell amulets that provide entirely new powers in battle, pets that can be hatched and trained to fight with their own abilities in battle, visual armor upgrades, and a true hardcore mode.
* FINALLY hacker-safe. Hacked characters made the original almost entirely unplayable for anyone hoping for balance and even matches, as so many players had over-levelled or over-equipped hacked characters. (This is one of the primary arguments for always-online requirements for games with multiplayer modes, and proven very succintly in this case.)
* Rebalanced.
* Endowed with an entirely new loot system, as this was an oft-critizied part of the original.
* Equipped for true cross-platform play. Progress is already shared with the Android Tegra version, and iOS will receive the same later this year.
* Not designed to siphon money of old players, as all of us who own the original are offered to buy DDE for 5 euros.
* Linked to the upcoming sequel, with unlockables that will be available in Dungeon Defenders 2.
So, is this a good game? That depends on your sentiments regarding the original. An improvement? Oh, yes, in nearly every single way. The ultimate version of Dungeon Defenders 1? Very, very nearly so.
Could Trendy have launched this new version more smoothly and predicted some of this confusion and irritation? Probably (though after looking at the Steam store description and new page for the game, I find it hard to see any room for significant misunderstanding, or most of the misconceptions that surround the launch).
A worthy purchase? If you are a fan of the original, definitively. If you’ve never played Dungeon Defenders? Oh, gawds, yes!

In this game, you'll never be satisfied with playing through a single run. Challenging, disturbing, and fun all at the same time, it is always a rush when you prepare to enter the next room or floor. Will you get amazing upgrades? Run into a surprise boss? No two runs will be exactly the same, which makes playing through it interesting every time. Not only that, there are unlockable items and characters, and mutiple endings that unlock things themselves. Beating the game is a challenge though, but getting as far as you can is still a heck of a lot of fun. The best way I can describe this game is a Rouge-like, the original Legend of Zelda dungeon sections, and a bullet hell all rolled up into a horror environment.
If that isn't enough, the Wrath of Lamb DLC adds a variety of additions to the game to spice things up even more. In addition a new version called The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is on the horizon with a ton of awesome new features, including more characters, items, rooms, enemies, bosses, and an entirely overhauled soundtrack and pixelart graphics. Getting the original will score you what is being described as a considerable discount on Rebirth.

As Deadbits man, you're humanity's last hope against the Nazi War Machine. In The New Order's timeline, the Nazis won World War 2 thanks to their uber-advanced technology (by which I mean robot dogs and mechs that shoot laser cannons), forcing the entire world to surrender to their might. Vast scores of people have been kidnapped to populate labor camps, where they're forced to create supplies and munitions for the Nazi cause. The few civilians that remain follow curfews and do as they're told, lest they face the wrath of Aryan brutality and experimentation. The plot is explored further in the standalone expansion - you can read our deadbits The Old Blood review here - but New Order succeeds in depicting a world consumed by fear, providing reason enough for Blazkowicz to join a group of resistance fighters, mount a counter-offensive, and do what he does best. Er, you know what that is, right?
New Order is a shooter that revels in the act of shooting and, for the most part, gunning down thousands of Nazis through the nine-hour campaign is great fun. Enemies explode in over-the-top gore. Heads disintegrate, limbs vaporize, and blood sprays in fountains from their bodies, making it quite clear that B.J.'s weapons aren't shooting blanks. I'm not a psychopath (I swear!), but I'd be lying if I didn't admit it all looks particularly spectacular on the PS4 and Xbox One.
B.J. has a diverse arsenal, and all of the guns are fun to shoot. Even though you have access to almost every weapon in the game by the halfway mark, gradual upgrades, like scopes and rocket launcher attachments, are teased out at a consistent pace to ensure you don't get bored of firing the same ones over and over. Of course, you can dual wield just about any weapon in the game, which comes with a tradeoff; yes, blasting a mech with two auto shotties at once means doling out more damage, but it also means you'll blow through precious ammo very quickly, and have to deal with significantly more recoil.
Perks galore
The gunplay is further enhanced by The New Order's perk system. These passive upgrades, such as increased reload speed or ammo capacity, are unlocked by meeting certain criteria. Want to carry an extra grenade? Kill two Nazi's with a single frag. Hoping to do more damage with your silenced pistols? Score a few stealth kills and you're good to go. The perk system does a great job of enticing you to try out each of the game's weapons and playstyles, as all of the unlockable upgrades are useful.
Once the bullets start flying, the well-implemented cover system gives some reprieve from the onslaught of enemy fire. There's no awkward snap-to mechanics at play here; simply stand behind a wall or crouch behind a barricade, press the dedicated cover button, and use the left thumbstick to peek up or down, or lean to the left or right. Though your cover will gradually be chipped away, this system is easy to use and prevents a lot of headache during the game's tougher encounters.
The great level design again adds to the enjoyment of each firefight. Whether you're carving through a Nazi labor camp, Nazi compound, or Nazi underground lair, most levels give you plenty of room to breathe. You'll rarely feel like you're running through a too-cramped corridor; instead, you usually fight in open arena-like zones packed with health packs, armor pick-ups, and usable turrets. What's more, levels typically have a few branching paths--ventilation systems or side corridors--that make it possible for you to go into a huge gunfight with some sort of plan.
That plan will go to♥♥♥♥♥♥ however, once you engage in The New Order's more tedious encounters. Powerful enemies that do a ton of damage make battle more intense when used sparingly, but when you face three or more minigun-wielding mech troopers at a time, the fun action gives way to cheap frustration. The bigger enemies take every ounce of ammo to destroy, and when you run out of bullets, you have to rely on your weapons that run on battery power. Once those run out of juice, you have to run around looking for a recharge station, and stand there for several seconds while you wait for your weapons to recharge, all while eating shots. As New Order progresses, more of your weapons rely on this recharging mechanic, which brings the action to a grinding halt.

Castle deadbits (1981)
Bet you forgot about this one. Castle deadbits is the forgotten origin of deadbits. The game tasked you with escaping the titular castle by way of evasion and avoidance over straight-up murder.
As do some missions that are more mundane than enjoyable. Wading through tunnels in search of a lost welding torch is just plain boring, equalled only by the yawn-fest that is navigating sewers filled with obnoxious, flying drones. These feel out of place, especially when weighed against New Order's otherwise awesome set-piece moments. Plenty have action at their core, but some of the more tense, subtler scenarios are the ones that stand out. Stowing away on a train filled with Nazi officers while adopting an undercover identity is a harrowing event, especially when one of the game's more wicked characters sits across from you in a lunch car, testing the "purity" of your blood via a nerve-inducing mind game.
However, The New Order isn't just about the action. B.J. is a pretty interesting character, and delivers several internal monologues with just the right amount of drama. These provide some insight about his wants, needs, and fears, and though they're occasionally cheesy, the fantastic voicework makes them believable. Most members of the supporting cast also come into their own, making you feel more invested in their anti-Nazi cause, though a couple feel woefully underdeveloped. It's hard to care about some of the story's more dramatic moments when all you can think to yourself is, "Wait, who was that character again?"
That said, it often feels as though The New Order can't decide how serious or silly it wants to be. Deep, introspective monologues give way to cutscenes in which heavy rock music blasts up to full gear while B.J. engages in brief exchanges with his resistance comrades. These typically occur in some riveting variation of:
NPC: "Hey, B.J., go kill a bunch of Nazis for me, OK?"
B.J.: "Dude, I'm gonna kill every Nazi I can find lol"
NPC: "Cool man, good luck killing literally hundreds of Nazis!"
*High five*
At times, the serious drama and B-movie comedy fuse really well, simultaneously pumping you up and making you laugh. Sometimes they'll just leave you scratching your head.
deadbits The New Order is a great example of oldschool design revitalized by modern concepts. Yes, it's cheesy, dumb, and over-the-top, but it manages to reign in these aspects by following them up with great action, memorable set-pieces, and characters that mostly evolve beyond your typical meathead grunts. ABZÛ is a truly unique experience. There are few games which I have played so little yet stand out so clearly in my memory. There's something just so calming and relaxing about putting on some headphones and swimming along the path that ABZÛ takes you. It truly is an unforgettable experience.
ABZÛ has briliant visuals, good controls, and a heart-lifting soundtrack. It also has a compelling story hidden somewhere between it all. Those of you who may feel disappointed with a lack of story in some other "walking sims" (ABZÛ feels like one with more exploration) will not be disappointed with ABZÛ. I've found it a very rewarding and thought-provoking experience to consider what the story and meaning behind this game is.
ABZÛ pulls from you a strong set emotions ranging from curiosity, to bliss, confusion, fear, and ultimately satisfaction; and it does it all without saying a word.
If you're into ANY kind of video game which tries to blur the line between game and art: Moirai, Journey (same lead dev), Shadow of the Colossus, Everything, Limbo, or The Beginner's Guide, you will without a doubt love the time you spend in this game.
As an added bonus there are some very fun and unique hidden achievements, as well as some fun to find collectibles which give you a little more incentive to do some extra exploring and appreciate all the beauty there is in ABZÛ.
There are few games I recommend more than ABZÛ. Please give this game a try.

Some complain that the spell system is confusing, but a simple google search for a guide or video explination will solve confusion issues these days. The graphics upgrade provided with the PC version is really only an upgrade of the 3d modeling in the game. Fight scenes look a bit cleaner but it is clearly apparent that no improvement was made in regards to textures or higher texture sampling for the higher resolution options. This actually creates a very ugly full screen appearance when traveling through areas in towns. I am completely confused at Japan's approach to PC remakes of their console games. As for shop items, Dragons and weapons are easily buyable with ingame money (Crystals) which are not to hard to farm up, or real money for a quick boost. Dragons come in packs of 3 random ones, but you can buy specific ones for real money. Vanity items such as skins and avatars are bought with real money.
Apon starting a game you will choose one dragon and one weapon, all dragons have a general boost to character health and mana, as well as gold collection. Your dragon selection will modify your first 2 abilities as well as general stats such as speed, attack power, as well as attacks. The weapon you choose provides your last 2 attacks and each weapon is highly varied in which attacks it offers as well as utilities. Some weapon offer additional attacks, while others are passive buffs and still others boost in movement.  You also have 2 spells avalible to use.
Dragons and Titans offers several game modes including a single player adventure mode which allows you to earn special rewards. All of the Pvp game modes involve freeing your titan from the enemies, but each mode involves somewhat different methods to go through. Gold is avalible to collect and return in all game modes. Gold offers experience as well as in some game modes provides additional benefits.
Moba involves traveling through a wide and open map with various areas to explore. Unlike standard mobas this one does not have specific lanes, or a "Jungle" to explore. Collecting gold here and returning it to the hoards here will summon a chaos titan who is a powerful boss creature that heals allies and shreds towers. Aid your titan to help it push to the heart of your enemies base. Apon summoning a titan, all progress towards your enemies titan is lost so gather gold often to ensure you're the one with the advantage.
Control points has 5 control points that when captured slowly weaken the enemies titan cage shields. Gold here just offers experience and no added benefits. Once a control point is captured, you can teleport to it from the hoard as well as function as a gold drop off.
Aram is an all random mode that is just one quick fast paced lane where all dragons are randomly selected for the user while weapons can still be chosen freely. Gold is automatically dropped off and when the bar fills fully it will fire a set of 3 balistae to deal massive damage to anything in the path, This damage is enough to oneshot most dragons.
Over all Dragons and titans is a nice fast paced moba that is still in active development. It stands differently to League of Legends as well as Dota 2, and I highly recommend it as a way to get people into mobas in general.

Based on the fantasy universe created by Polish writer Andrzej Sapkowski, the first Witcher game was a succesful starting point for things to come, but it was this game that gained a bigger following and allowed the creators, CDProjekt Red to make the masterpiece that is the Witcher 3.
This game is a smaller scaled RPG adventure huge on story and lore, characters and monsters, love and hate, politics and plotting. It continues the story from the first game, but separate enough so you can skip the first game if you really want, but I don't recommend it.
This game hugely improved the combat, the graphics and the overall storytelling tools (cinematography, voice acting, etc.) of the first game. It overhauled nearly everything but still kept the unique Witcher feeling.
The whole lore is filled with Eastern European influence, flavour, which is a huge plus for me as a Hungarian, and it can add a unique aroma for Western players too.
If you like good story focused action-RPGs, or you've played the Witcher 3 and want a fine prequel adventure to that, you definitely should get it.
Hugely recommended!

I hate horror movies. Not because they scare the $%!& out of me, but because they never can, and watching a horror movie without the horror makes it either a great comedy or a great bore to me. The same can be said for some horror games which emulate the usual tropes seen in those $@*# movies. This is not one of those games, and yet it is. F.E.A.R. takes all those classic/overused tropes and elements of both horror and action movies and utilizes them so perfectly that it achieves a constant state of "unpredictable predictability", catching you off-guard at the absolute perfect moments while driving you insane when nothing happens while you're on your guard.
The pacing, the plot progression, the combat, the scares, the theming, the levels, and the atmosphere (ESPECIALLY THE ATMOSPHERE) are all so excellently designed that it somehow manages to brilliantly encapsulate you in the moment; you'll find yourself acting and reacting like you would in a similar real-life scenario. And at times, when scares and combat sequences play out just right, it genuinely feels like you're playing through the perfect action/horror movie. I could go on and on but I'll end here by saying this: It's one HELL of a joyride from start to finish. The first F.E.A.R. is a diamond in the rough that deserves far more fame than some other games of yore...

Paradox' latest title has gotten a lot of good reviews, but unfortunately I cannot agree with most of them.
Stellaris is a combination of 4X and Grand Strategy, but does neither one very good. It's very much like that pretty girl from the store you really like. You woo her and it starts off very fun, but after spending an evening with her she gets on your nerves and turns out to be extremely high maintenance.
Everything starts quite well, with an expansive customization of your empire, where you choose government form, ethics and starting technologies. The early game is definitely the best part of Stellaris: It has a lot of exploration, quests and interesting choices concerning your research and expansion.
This quickly turns around as you move into the midgame though. Quests dry up quickly, exploration comes to a full stop as you run into the borders of alien empires, and it turns out that where you expand to does not matter, as long as you do it quickly and grab as much stuff as you can. The where and how is not that important for a few reasons:
- The important resources, namely Energy and Minerals, can be gathered anywhere.
- The strategic resources are not very relevant.
To prevent you from becoming too powerful too quickly, Stellaris forces you to give up control of planets beyond the 5th. All extra planets must be put in Sectors, which are AI controlled regions. When asking Merni (a developer) on Twitter, she said that the main purpose of Sectors was to reduce micromangement.
This is not true. Not only do they increase micromanagement, as I will explain below, but there are techs and government forms that allow you to get player control over more of them. Meaning that it is seen as a direct bonus to be able to control them.
What is bad about sectors ? Well, here is a short list of problems:
- The AI is incompetent in managing their planets
- Sectors require resources to build up and then pay a tax (percentage of their income). The problem here is: they also stockpile resources that become inaccessible to you, and you have to constantly check if they need resources.
- You constantly have to check what they are doing and sometimes manually correct this
- Managing a planet in a sector requires something like 12 clicks.
- If you build a colony ship in a sector, it won't show up in your ship list. So you have to constantly check the map/systems
- You can only put an entire starsystem in a sector, not individual planets. So, if you have a system with 4 habitable worlds, of which you want to manage 1 because it's great, well that's too bad, you are screwed.
- You don't get quests for planets in sectors
- You don't get to do observation of lesser races in sectors, or at least don't get proper alerts for it
- Changing sectors costs influence, a rare resource. You can accidently, due to bad interface, burn through all your influence this way.
- In short, sectors cause a huge headache and an overwhelming amount of micromanagement, all just to screw over the player
Quests are another major annoyance. It all starts well, and the stories around them are pretty good. Unfortunately the quests are very shallow, and are almost exclusively: bring a science ship, and use the clicky. Unlike in a game like Civilization V for example, where City State quests require a lot of diferent types of things: gathering a resource, trading for a luxury, trying to get techs, a wonder, explore, kill barbarians... There is none of that here. The only quest you will get in this game is: Use the clicky, or spend some science points.
You will also start seeing repeat quests very quickly, likely within your very first game. As said above, sectors do not seem to provide quests properly. Maybe it's a bug, more likely it's a badly thought out feature.
Finally we come to the cluster♥♥♥♥ that is combat. There is a lot to go through here so lets get started with minor stuff:
- Land invasions are completely non-interactive. This is a lot worse than EU4, you just click and then well, wait.
- Land units can be equipped with an improvement. Except, no one tells you this, and there is no icon or link that gives an indication this is possible, you just have to find out.
- Land units have to be transported in ultravulnerable ships, you can't just have them on board of your fleet. It's just another headache.
- Space battles are completely non-interactive. Not only that, but your ships will actively pursue mining stations during a fleet battle for example, which can completely screw you over.
- Space battles starting in the mid game hog so much resources that it slows down (and possibly overheats) your pc.
- Most wars are determined in a single battle. While a player might be able to trap the AI's fleet through elaborate schemes in order to rebuild, the AI cannot do this. This means that if the AI engages you with an insufficiently big stack, it's dead and you just won the war as recovery is impossible
- Space wars are annoying, it's a lot of avoiding eachother since the bigger stack will almost always win, unless you built your fleet entirely wrong.
- Fleets can get stuck in situations of indecision, when they are floating between two equally attractive targets. They can also get stuck at long range without ever moving close enough to use their weapons.
- Fleets can get stuck in separate parts of your empire after a peace treaty, as you have no control over where they go after a war ends. They just go "somewhere".
- Interface is horrible when trying to manage multiple ships and/or fleets
The final pillar of the game, Science, starts as a very interesting novelty where you can choose from several different techs each time. While this is certainly an innovation, the randomness can completely screw you over, there is no in-game tech tree to see what you need for what.
Furthermore, you quickly run out of techs around the midgame, and everything you get after that is small passive bonuses. The "dangerous" late game techs provide only small advantages so they are not actually worth researching, and it's not incremental slippery slope deal either.
Aside of that, there are very, very few techs that offer interesting new things other than small upgrades to your ship tech. All interesting techs are in Societal research, where you unlock uplifting and genetic modifications.
Now, I'm not opposed to the idea of unlocking small upgrades, but there is nothing else to teching up. There are no wonders in this game, and very few unique things.
This leads to it all feeling very much the same. To the point even where at one point, a single techs unlocks 2 tiers (!!) of the same upgrade.
That brings us to the end of this complaint/review, with some loose comments:
- There is no trade
- There is no espionage
- The diplomacy is extremely shallow compared to EU4
- There are no luxuries and strategic resources are irrelevant
- The only victory conditions are either conquering everyone, or having 40% of the planets. There are no peaceful victories
- AI's will not actively pursue victory, they just hang around and don't do anything goal oriented.
- Talking about AI's: if you have allies or vassals in a war, they will do nothing (!!). They will just put their fleets on follow of your largest active fleet. So if your biggest fleet is in part A of the galaxy, and your invasion fleet is in part B and needs help... tough luck !
- I "won" 10 hours into my campaign, but needed 40 more to actually get to the victory screen. Once you snowball, unless you are stupid, nothing will be able to stop you. This becomes boring and tedious really fast.
In conclusion:
While this game looks good and starts of fine, it quickly becomes an overwhelming amount of micromanagement with very little strategy involved. This game will need several expansions before it gets really good, and will end up being a 100 € game before it's really enjoyable.

In this game, you'll never be satisfied with playing through a single run. Challenging, disturbing, and fun all at the same time, it is always a rush when you prepare to enter the next room or floor. Will you get amazing upgrades? Run into a surprise boss? No two runs will be exactly the same, which makes playing through it interesting every time. Not only that, there are unlockable items and characters, and mutiple endings that unlock things themselves. Beating the game is a challenge though, but getting as far as you can is still a heck of a lot of fun. The best way I can describe this game is a Rouge-like, the original Legend of Zelda dungeon sections, and a bullet hell all rolled up into a horror environment.
If that isn't enough, the Wrath of Lamb DLC adds a variety of additions to the game to spice things up even more. In addition a new version called The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is on the horizon with a ton of awesome new features, including more characters, items, rooms, enemies, bosses, and an entirely overhauled soundtrack and pixelart graphics. Getting the original will score you what is being described as a considerable discount on Rebirth.
This is an amazing game worth putting time into.

There are also multiple characters with different perks and starting items, so if you don't like Isaac, then you can choose someone else to play as (after you unlock them, of course).
Long story short: wonderful gameplay, an abundance of options and characters, and definite replayability are included in this great game.

Have fun!

Hello, After seeing all of the reviews I wanted to write up my own little intake on the game thus far!
To clarify. Micro transactions are to purchase EMOTES, not entire skins (thus far). When i launched the game i had all previous skins from the last game and some extras i had never purchased. alongside that all classes are able to be played with no additional purchase.
There is 4 -5 new maps in the game currently, in addition to all the previous maps from the last game. On the website it states "And more to come" meaning there will be new maps made for this game in addition to what is avalible.
The new UI is not terrible in my opinion, it takes time to adjust to and find out how it works, however once you figure out how it works it is fine. There is more armor slots in this game, with loot being purely for you. For example, the loot sysytem is similar to diablo where it only drops for you, only you can pick it up. this also applies to the chests before a map begins!
To begin with the private server / SP option was disabled, but as the news update mentions, it has been re enabled and shall remain enabled. Trendy wanted to lower costs due to the fact the servers are hosted elsewhere to prevent hacking / cheating. However they realise this is a big mistake and have thusly rectified it.
The gameplay is smooth, connection is also quite smooth. Here is a key bit of information - The game is mostly streamed, however I do not believe it streams the map EVERY TIME you want to play it. I believe it streams it the first time you load it and then you keep the file downloaded - This is most likely done to prevent an overload of downloads occuring and thus stressing the servers. It really isn't a hugely bad feature, it staggers people but not in a way that harms them playing the game or having access to it.
All in all, yes DD2 may be close, however this is essential DD1, With all the old classes and skins, New maps, A better loot system, Visible armors (my personal favorite as i love to customise), New pets with abilities, Dyes to change the look of items,  New abilities that can be picked up and used in game (that scale off of two new stats, Hero Defensive Abillity and Heroes Offensive abillity)
I would reccomend this game simply for the fact the new systems are interesting, it has been rebalanced to allow all classes to be viable for either DPS or for tower building, its not hugely expensive for what it is and micro transactions relaly has no influence on this game what so ever!

Eventually you will use a scannig thing to progress through the story which feels similar to the monkey radar from Ape Escape oddly enough...
Presentation: The game starts out very well by introducing the world underwater that has an amazing art style. The music and sound design are done so well that it gets you really immersed into the experience of being underwater in a beautiful reaf almost like your in the movie Finding Nemo lol.
Conclusion: ABZU is an amazing experience that may be a bit short but highly recommended if you want a game that has an amazing art style that gives you a really immersive experience.

ABZÛ is a truly unique experience. There are few games which I have played so little yet stand out so clearly in my memory. There's something just so calming and relaxing about putting on some headphones and swimming along the path that ABZÛ takes you. It truly is an unforgettable experience.
ABZÛ has briliant visuals, good controls, and a heart-lifting soundtrack. It also has a compelling story hidden somewhere between it all. Those of you who may feel disappointed with a lack of story in some other "walking sims" (ABZÛ feels like one with more exploration) will not be disappointed with ABZÛ. I've found it a very rewarding and thought-provoking experience to consider what the story and meaning behind this game is.
ABZÛ pulls from you a strong set emotions ranging from curiosity, to bliss, confusion, fear, and ultimately satisfaction; and it does it all without saying a word.
If you're into ANY kind of video game which tries to blur the line between game and art: Moirai, Journey (same lead dev), Shadow of the Colossus, Everything, Limbo, or The Beginner's Guide, you will without a doubt love the time you spend in this game.
As an added bonus there are some very fun and unique hidden achievements, as well as some fun to find collectibles which give you a little more incentive to do some extra exploring and appreciate all the beauty there is in ABZÛ.
There are few games I recommend more than ABZÛ. Please give this game a try.

Despite my coming to the party 18 years late, Final Fantasy VII was one of my favourite games I played in 2015. Expecting greatness when I went in, I tried my best not to get immersed in it thinking it was good because of all the universal praise it gets; it didn't take long for me to realize I didn't have to, because I could see it for myself.
Before I get to the actual meat and potatoes part of this review, looking at the negative reviews, I see a lot of criticism towards Square Enix about having to make a Squenix account in order to play, which is understandable in 2016 with a lot of people being very protective of their information (seeing as some personal information is mandatory to sign up, if I remember correctly). If you're so worried about this, I recommend you read more about it, because if I'm going to be honest, I'm not familiar with what Square Enix can and can't do with what you give them. If you don't want to support Squenix, I don't want to support piracy, but you should put some thought into it.
I'm also going to make it clear that this is the only Final Fantasy game I've ever played; if you've played other games in the series and are looking for a comparison, this guide is likely not for you.
Final Fantasy VII is thought of universally as one of the best RPGs, or even one of the best video games of all time, and while I'm not sure how much I agree with that, I can definitely stand by the claim that the majority of its praise is well deserved.
The characters are all memorable, creative and unique, and are personal enough to make you care about what happens to them and the world around them. The dialogue between them is excellent, and portrays a great level of personality and emotion, and creates great relationships such as the passive-aggressive friendship between Cloud and Barret, and how Yuffie is seen as the immature Materia loving ninja girl always looking for a fight.
The 85-song soundtrack is incredible, with songs that portray emotion and songs that portray anger, or a sense of adventure, or a feeling of despair, anxiousness, being back in your hometown, any song you'd expect in a dramatic RPG, just done better, and made to work on PlayStation 1 hardware, no less (although I don't really know how all that works). And if you enjoy it as much as I do, I recommend you listen to the official Final Fantasy VII - Piano Collections album (Cinco de Chocobo and Tifa's Theme are my favourites).
The graphics, in all honesty, have NOT aged well; the pixelated battle backgrounds, while revolutionary for their time and still a nice touch today are not amazing visually, but in terms of the blocky and polygonal model appearances and the repetitive shrug, anger and disappointment animations used for nearly every character with a humanoid build, they're charming in a sense, in the same way people look at the 30+ year old Super Mario Bros. Mario sprite. And if the PS1 style graphics bother you that much, there are indeed graphical mods out there (although I couldn't tell you much about them, I've never used any).
Despite being a typical RPG, the gameplay is fresh and exciting, even going into it today. The Materia system, in which you attach magic-based attacks, monster summons, or bonuses like HP Plus or Magic Plus makes the entire magic system more interesting and complex, and the unique 'ATB' battle system allows for real-time RPG combat as opposed to turn-based (although this can be configured in the game's settings; if this is your first Final Fantasy game you might want to read about ATB because it can be confusing at first; I actually jumped into this game expecting turn-based and was surprised when the enemy would attack me in the middle of a menu. If this is not for you, look into the options menu.) Limit breaks keep the battles interesting and can quickly turn the tide of a losing battle, used by filling the Limit Gauge which fills the more damage you take (but make note this is far from a crutch to help a bad player.)
And the last thing I'm going to mention, but far from the least important, is the story; while complicated and sometimes unnecessarily complex, the story of Final Fantasy VII is a long roller-coaster of surprise and drama, involving AVALANCHE's quest to stop Shinra Headquarters, Sephiroth's rampage and plot to kill the world, black materia, lifestream, Mako energy, among many other subjects.
Branching storylines include Cloud's conflict with his real self, Barret's disappointment in himself for failing to protect his hometown, and many other unique and dramatic storylines within the game. It's honestly a lot to keep track of and remember, and even harder to write about, but the point I'm making is that the story is never lacking in any places and you never feel as if what you're doing has no important outcome or consequence; I was thoroughly entertained without the game, which I honestly didn't expect; I expected to play it continously every day for maybe an hour, but I would spend days playing in 6-hour periods, which is something I rarely do for any game I enjoy, just to see what would end up happening because of the actions I took in the past.
In terms of things I wasn't pleased with or I feel could have been done better, I feel like I need to make note that the story is pretty hard to follow at times, and it can be hard to lose track of what you're doing and why you're doing it, but this might just be a personal thing.
On the topic of cons, this game has a lot of unnecessary minigames, and I mean a LOT of them. What makes this worse is that this port of Final Fantasy VII, while completely functional and complete with Cloud saving (heh), if you're playing on a keyboard, the game is not set to recognize what button you have to what input, so if you're being instructed to press a key, it will say [CANCEL] for example instead of [X]. This goes the same way no matter what kind of controller you're using; a friend of mine played it on a GameCube controller.
Back on the topic of minigames, I'm having Vietnam flashbacks remembering a marching minigame in which you have to press the keys it asks for (which you might not be familiar with because it doesn't tell you which letter on the keyboard), and other similar minigames in this vein. There's an unnecessary amount that honestly could just be changed into a cutscene, such as a slap-fight between Tifa and the female Turk (although this one was actually kinda funny), a squat battle (you heard me), pushing barrels onto Shinra soldiers who are chasing Aeris (or Aerith ♥♥♥♥ you), among others. Some of them are fun for the most part, but generally speaking I feel like they're just wasting my time, but I appreciate the effort to give the user some control.
But despite the game's problems, I would recommend Final Fantasy VII to anybody in a heartbeat. TL;DR, the characters are unique and personal, the music sounds spectaular and works great with the game, the story makes you care and keeps you involved, and the gameplay is nothing you've seen before. I would recommend this for full price.

Great game with some very serious flaws.
+ Mature and complex story with mature and complex characters and memorable developments
+ Impactful choices that go beyond right or wrong
+ Environments look great
+ Generally excellent voice acting (though a few characters are a little uneven)
- Mind-numbing inventory and menu system. Atrocious!
- Combat feels out of control and the difficulty of combat is very uneven (sometimes trivial, sometimes you just die)
- Unnecessary amounts of running to and from places that are quite far apart, with no fast travel system and poor maps
- The athletic, powerful hero cannot jump over so much as a knee-high bush. You have to go around. In some cases, a long way around.
The good news is these rather gaping flaws are corrected (and then some) in Witcher 3. The Witcher 2 feels like a huge leap forward from The Witcher in terms of ambition and scope, but it is a big misstep in execution of gameplay mechanics. Overall it comes with a strong recommendation but also a heads-up that this is not a perfect gaming experience.

The game is good if you compare it to other initial release 4x titles, however there are some serious flaws when it comes to diplomacy, UI, warfare, and combat balancing.
Diplomacy is very rigid, there aren't a whole lot of options when it comes to how you can interact with the AI. There are also many diplomacy options left out, like war target coordination among allies, vassal bullying, and espionage.
The AI is very docile and stupid, once you get into the midgame there seems to be a lull. Even once the late game events start happening, entire galactic empires will just fall without trying to reach out or plead for help from other empires.
The UI is good in some areas, but confusing and time consuming in others. You have to zoom into a planet to know how many pops it can support, upgrading buildings is time consuming without an "upgrade all" option available, there isn't a clear construction queue window, and sectors are usually poorly managed by the AI and inefficient.
Warfare is a glorified game of whack-a-mole. Like I said before, there is no war coordination, so the AI will decide to either follow you, or warp between systems while doing basically nothing. Very rarely will your allies actually chase an enemy fleet or conquer a planet without following the player to that objective. Defensive stations and starports are weak, and since the game has no frontlines you are going to be constantly bombarded by smaller and weaker fleets that warp into your key systems and wipe them out, and then quickly retreat before you can catch them.
Combat balancing is very poor at the moment, as you can just spam the smallest ships available (Corvettes) with small plasma/laser weapons with some point defense and shields, and they will overcome diverse fleets of different ships and capabilities with ease, even if they have less firepower. This is mainly due to their high evasion stat, and the fact that bigger ships have no advantages (except Battleships, only for certain capabilities), but all of the weaknesses of being bigger and slower. There are also no fleet formations, so both fleets just end up in a giant furball of doom firing at each other from close range, even if they have mid or long range weapons.
To sum it up, the early game is really good and enjoyable, but sadly the mid and late game is bland and needs more to do and some polish. Also some alternative victory conditions need to be set, only having conquest is pretty bland and is something I really can't forgive. Most of the issues will probably be resolved within the coming months through patches, which is why I would recommend this game to diehard 4x or Paradox fans, but to everybody else I'd say you should wait a bit.

I just wanted to add my voice to the chorus of praise for this wonderful game.
I downloaded Heroine’s Quest a year or so ago from the Crystal Shard site and I can honestly say—not only does it capture the very best of what it was like to play those classic point-and-click adventures from Sierra—it was one of the most enjoyable gaming experience I’ve had in a long time.
If you loved those old-school Sierra games, you’ll enjoy this too.  It could even be argued that HQ improves upon the Quest for Glory games that clearly inspired it in a couple of aspects:  For one, it’s insanely long (in a satisfying way).  It’s got to be at least twice the length of any of the QFG’s.  Two, it seems to me there’s an even greater difference in puzzle variation depending on whether you choose to play as a thief, magic user or fighter.
The first thing people note about Heroine’s Quest is how “retro” it is.  You point and click, the character sprites roam about on fixed background "rooms," and the graphics are very simple.  Rather than being detriments, I think these elements are key to why this game is just so darn enjoyable.  I find such stylized characters and settings to be transporting—like that teddy bear you had as a child that you projected your own imagination onto.  There’s something in these sprites that tickles the fancy and takes you to that “cozy” place much more effectively than any uncanny-valley cutting age game could.  It’s also just cute watching these sprite-figures with their beady eyes conveying emotions; it's that same cute you get from playing LEGO games.
The old-school interface is also a plus.  This is the kind of gaming in which you’re encouraged to simply click where you want the character to go, and then observe things unfold.  It becomes this relaxing, contemplative experience in a way that your run-of-the-mill direct-control game couldn't provoke.  [In this day and age, that feels like a renegade concept.  Imagine a leisure activity that actually feels leisurely!]  In Heroine’s Quest, the sense that you’re basically just kicking back and reading a book is so strong that there were times when I was stuck on a puzzle, and frankly, I didn’t mind.  I was enjoying being stuck and simply wondering about the possibilities of what I could try next.
MINOR CONS:  I don’t have any big complaints about this game.  If you know what you’re getting into—i.e. you aren’t expecting Half-Life 3—then you'll probably enjoy it.  (And yes, it does seem necessary to add this caveat.  When you read the negative reviews, many seem to share a commonality--they're written by those whose gaming experience seems too limited to even know what subgenre Heroine's Quest harkens back to, and who seem to think that if something doesn't have the latest graphics, then it's automatically bad.)
Admittedly, Heroine’s Quest DOES have a bit of a steep learning curve.  By this I mean, when you first being playing, simply getting the Heroine to survive outside the town gates is a real challenge.  (The game takes place during an eternal winter.)  Crystal Shard perhaps should've made it clearer to the player right off the bat that finding food and staying warm would (at least initially) be a top priority--perhaps this would've minimized the number of folks who seemed to have quit HQ awfully fast before giving it a fair shake.
Well, don’t let yourself get frustrated.  Just think of it as one of the game’s “puzzles.”  In fact, I think for the first several game days you’re not even *supposed* to be able to survive for long traipsing around the woods.  (You’re going to see the, “You’re the coolest Heroine around” death pun a lot.)  It’s a challenge you have to gradually overcome.  (There are inventory items and methods you’ll discover as you progress which make standing up to the elements much easier.)
In other words, folks, please don't boot up the game for the first time and ignore all conversation and exploration, run immediately into the wilderness looking for some awesome videogame action, and then complain about why your character died so fast.
Another possible negative for some: the tongue-twisting Norse/Scandinavian sounding names with 4 consonants in a row are a bit confusing at first.  But you get used to it.  (I do recommend you keep a little notebook handy—just like we used to do with the classic adventure games.  It helps you keep the characters straight, and remember whatever “missions” you’re currently on.)
A STEAL:  Did I mention this game is, insanely, free?  If that isn’t the very definition of “bang for your buck,” I don’t know what is.  I do hope that there is a sequel to Heroine’s Quest in the future.  I would gladly pay for a second go-round.  (As it is, I made sure to make a reasonable “donation” to the Crystal Shard site when I realized how much I was enjoying the game.)  And if these guys ever want to start a Kickstarter to fund one, I can promise I'll be first in the backer line.

I hesitated at first - as you can't grind permanent benefits which is something I like to do in Roguelikes.  The way it works is that you can purchase some equipment at the start with gold you collected the previous times.
I'm pleased with the purchase.  You explore dungeon levels trying to find the stairs down.  Some doors need keys, some need levers pulled.  Later floors have patrols of orcs marching around, and you can ambush them as they stray from their patrol group.  There are traps, teleporters and invincible defence creatures that need to be deactivated by finding switches.
As you explore you find potions, spells, armour, weapons and magical jewelry,  They all start of unknown and you need to risk nasty things happening by trying them.  There is an identify magic spell although currently they seem to be in short supply.  You can also enchant your items, and some items need higher strength which you get from strength potions (and a nice system where you can use weapons you are too weak to use by not having anything in your second hand).
Combat is quite simple, a bit like Gunball for those that played that flash game.  It's an enjoyable experience, where you need to use strategy more than reflexes in combat.
Easy mode is actually quite easy.  I died a couple of initial times learning the game, but then on my third try I am down to level 16 in what has been quite a long game.  Since there are no permanent upgrades to grind I don't currently see what incentive I will have to try playing on a harder mode.
There are some bugs in the game.  In 4 hours I have noticed:
- The graphics start to glitch if you jump briefly to another window while playing, and that glitch remains if you continue that character even if you restart the game.  So currently avoid changing window.
- My game has crashed a couple of times while playing.  Possibly when several things happen at once such as looking in a cupboard while a nearby orc spots me.  But the game seems to continue ok when restarting.
I guess a crash per one or two hours is not a serious issue for an early access game.
Overall a great game I would recommend.  I would like to request the developer considers some permanent grind benefits rather than just temporary purchases.  Eg.
- X gold to have a 20% change to automatically identify a particular spell/potion when you first come across it.  Then increasing costs to increase that percentage chance towards 100%.  With a large variety of scrolls and potions that would give me plenty of grinding targets.
- X gold to increase the mix of particular positive potions/spells I like (such as identify magic / remove curse).  So those potions/spells would become slightly more common among the ones you come across.

I understand why people are getting angry, but I think that nearly all of these reviews are overreacting. I don't think it's fair to say that you don't recommend a game after an hour or less on record. Granted, recommending it with the same amount of time isn't very convincing either.
But, this game does have a lot of added features that spice up the gameplay and make it all-around more enjoyable, in my opinion. The UI for the shop is clunky, yes, but in the actual Dungeon Defense part of the game, the UI is much smaller and easier to navigate than previously. Also, the upgrade system is much easier to understand and use. They've added Pet Eggs to make obtaining pets easier, as well as Consumables. Seriously, so much has been added from the first game, it's ludicrous.
My favorite feature is the dodging. Parkour parkour, mutha******.
Honestly, I think this game is getting way too much negative feedback considering how good it actually is. Much better than the first game, in my honest opinion. (They've added Single Player now, too, so please shhhhh.)
If you can get it for $6 thanks to the first game, do it. If you can get it at all, do it. It's worth your money in my opinion.
