The public taverns are utterly painless, and remove the hassle of closing your game every time you want to look at your inventory. Nor will you need to politely decline the companionship of players 5 times your level while they hop around on the bar.
Everything else seems pretty much the same to me, though I don't doubt that those of you who've put in hundreds of hours will find changes to the math you'll find pleasing or not so pleasing. The biggest change I see is that you won't need to derp around the game listing, wondering if you belong within the weird level range of the various games that have been running for heaven knows how long. You quite literally press go and get dropped into a game seconds later with people around your level. It's honestly pretty nice.
As a side note, the numbers on the negative reviews here paint a picture of an angry little brigade putting in an hour or less before writing the game off on bugaboo grounds. There are serious reasons to find fault with this game - there always have been - but they certainly aren't in play here. These people are upset about specific disagreements they have with the direction the franchise has taken, NOT with the actual quality of the game.

This is a very promising real-time roguelike. It is very accessible, but also has all the classic "accidentally-drinking-a-fire-potion" fun and requires proper solution-based thinking. The combat mechanic is unique and interesting, a sort of "aim and point" system combined with cooldown management, yet the game can be paused at any time. They've put a lot of attention into the dungeon generation, and it shows. No boring dead ends, but solid, interesting level constructions.
If you like games like brogue or powder, or are looking for a friendly way to start exploring some of the more hardcore roguelike mechanics, this comes very recommended! UNEXPLORED hits a nice level of difficulty where you'll die terribly for sure, but it's definitely a lot more friendly than most.

I quibbled for a while to decide if I was going to recommend this or not.  I do recommend it if you're a fan of Journey or just like the idea of swimming around the ocean without the need for special training or equipment.  The soundtrack is beautiful, the environments are majestic, and the critters are friendly, so it's an enriching experience if you're looking for something a bit artsy.
On the other hand, no game is perfect.  There was not a moment of this game when I felt fully in control of the diver.  Fiddling with the controls did little to mitigate this.  Also, although the ocean is a vast place, and you're experiencing some of the most amazing parts of it Abzu somehow manages to make it feel small and linear.  There's no possibility of you becoming lost, and while I understand that from a game design perspective, it really ruins the joy of discovery and exploration to have your character turn around because you're going off the map.
Overall, give it a try if you're a fan of watching fish swim around, or want a safe way to explore the ocean.  But don't expect an open world experience or precise controls.  Also, play Journey.  It's basically everything that's great about this game with exactly none of its issues.

For an indie game, it was pretty sweet I won't lie. The action is explosive (literally in many cases), the platforming is pretty precise, the art is gorgeous, and while the story isn't necessarily a stirring epic that will bring you to tears, the characters are likable and provide a good framing to motivate you through each set-piece to see it's end.
It isn't without it's problems. The RPG aspect is really weak, you don't really get many new tools to play with and the only new tools that you get belong to Fidget, and function largely the same way. Combat feels smooth, ducking and weaving around amidst a barrage of attacks along with the insane agility that you get from your whirlwind attacks feels really satisfying. But the combat never really evolves past that either, you don't really get any new attacks or combos outside of those that you start with. Crafting is bare bones and doesn't feel particularly rewarding to delve into as well.
Sometimes the shops and saves will bug out as well, leaving you either entering a shop or saving every time you press W even when far away from the shop/save point. It's also a bit annoying how your only option is to spam "skip" during cut-scenes if you died and are re-trying a boss, especially because in many instances you'll have to skip several sections of a cut-scene.
My last complaint is that sometimes the action can get to be too much of a gang bang when the action calls for a lot of precision outside of spamming your enormous aoe fidget attacks. This is particularly true in the climax where there is so much on the screen at one time that you can't easily discern who is attacking what, and the animations for the soldiers can be very sloppy so it can be very frustrating when trying to tell when someone is gearing up to attack you.
With all of this being said though, I enjoyed the game. The characters play off of each other well and are very likable. The art direction is awesome, everything feels really crisp and the animations are very detailed for the most part. It's a very straightforward story, but it holds up well enough to motivate you to keep pushing forward to the next plot point. While the main baddy is cartoonishly evil, some set pieces are VERY loosely tied together and don't really build towards the main plot, and the plot twists are kinda out of left field, I didn't feel compelled to skip anything as the VOs are solid in their delivery and the plot good enough to keep me at least interested in seeing it through.
All in all, a solid platform/action game that you should pick up if you are interested in buying it. If you aren't as into the action/platformer aspect, then it probably won't shatter your expectations.

Despite my coming to the party 18 years late, Final Fantasy VII was one of my favourite games I played in 2015. Expecting greatness when I went in, I tried my best not to get immersed in it thinking it was good because of all the universal praise it gets; it didn't take long for me to realize I didn't have to, because I could see it for myself.
Before I get to the actual meat and potatoes part of this review, looking at the negative reviews, I see a lot of criticism towards Square Enix about having to make a Squenix account in order to play, which is understandable in 2016 with a lot of people being very protective of their information (seeing as some personal information is mandatory to sign up, if I remember correctly). If you're so worried about this, I recommend you read more about it, because if I'm going to be honest, I'm not familiar with what Square Enix can and can't do with what you give them. If you don't want to support Squenix, I don't want to support piracy, but you should put some thought into it.
I'm also going to make it clear that this is the only Final Fantasy game I've ever played; if you've played other games in the series and are looking for a comparison, this guide is likely not for you.
Final Fantasy VII is thought of universally as one of the best RPGs, or even one of the best video games of all time, and while I'm not sure how much I agree with that, I can definitely stand by the claim that the majority of its praise is well deserved.
The characters are all memorable, creative and unique, and are personal enough to make you care about what happens to them and the world around them. The dialogue between them is excellent, and portrays a great level of personality and emotion, and creates great relationships such as the passive-aggressive friendship between Cloud and Barret, and how Yuffie is seen as the immature Materia loving ninja girl always looking for a fight.
The 85-song soundtrack is incredible, with songs that portray emotion and songs that portray anger, or a sense of adventure, or a feeling of despair, anxiousness, being back in your hometown, any song you'd expect in a dramatic RPG, just done better, and made to work on PlayStation 1 hardware, no less (although I don't really know how all that works). And if you enjoy it as much as I do, I recommend you listen to the official Final Fantasy VII - Piano Collections album (Cinco de Chocobo and Tifa's Theme are my favourites).
The graphics, in all honesty, have NOT aged well; the pixelated battle backgrounds, while revolutionary for their time and still a nice touch today are not amazing visually, but in terms of the blocky and polygonal model appearances and the repetitive shrug, anger and disappointment animations used for nearly every character with a humanoid build, they're charming in a sense, in the same way people look at the 30+ year old Super Mario Bros. Mario sprite. And if the PS1 style graphics bother you that much, there are indeed graphical mods out there (although I couldn't tell you much about them, I've never used any).
Despite being a typical RPG, the gameplay is fresh and exciting, even going into it today. The Materia system, in which you attach magic-based attacks, monster summons, or bonuses like HP Plus or Magic Plus makes the entire magic system more interesting and complex, and the unique 'ATB' battle system allows for real-time RPG combat as opposed to turn-based (although this can be configured in the game's settings; if this is your first Final Fantasy game you might want to read about ATB because it can be confusing at first; I actually jumped into this game expecting turn-based and was surprised when the enemy would attack me in the middle of a menu. If this is not for you, look into the options menu.) Limit breaks keep the battles interesting and can quickly turn the tide of a losing battle, used by filling the Limit Gauge which fills the more damage you take (but make note this is far from a crutch to help a bad player.)
And the last thing I'm going to mention, but far from the least important, is the story; while complicated and sometimes unnecessarily complex, the story of Final Fantasy VII is a long roller-coaster of surprise and drama, involving AVALANCHE's quest to stop Shinra Headquarters, Sephiroth's rampage and plot to kill the world, black materia, lifestream, Mako energy, among many other subjects.
Branching storylines include Cloud's conflict with his real self, Barret's disappointment in himself for failing to protect his hometown, and many other unique and dramatic storylines within the game. It's honestly a lot to keep track of and remember, and even harder to write about, but the point I'm making is that the story is never lacking in any places and you never feel as if what you're doing has no important outcome or consequence; I was thoroughly entertained without the game, which I honestly didn't expect; I expected to play it continously every day for maybe an hour, but I would spend days playing in 6-hour periods, which is something I rarely do for any game I enjoy, just to see what would end up happening because of the actions I took in the past.
In terms of things I wasn't pleased with or I feel could have been done better, I feel like I need to make note that the story is pretty hard to follow at times, and it can be hard to lose track of what you're doing and why you're doing it, but this might just be a personal thing.
On the topic of cons, this game has a lot of unnecessary minigames, and I mean a LOT of them. What makes this worse is that this port of Final Fantasy VII, while completely functional and complete with Cloud saving (heh), if you're playing on a keyboard, the game is not set to recognize what button you have to what input, so if you're being instructed to press a key, it will say [CANCEL] for example instead of [X]. This goes the same way no matter what kind of controller you're using; a friend of mine played it on a GameCube controller.
Back on the topic of minigames, I'm having Vietnam flashbacks remembering a marching minigame in which you have to press the keys it asks for (which you might not be familiar with because it doesn't tell you which letter on the keyboard), and other similar minigames in this vein. There's an unnecessary amount that honestly could just be changed into a cutscene, such as a slap-fight between Tifa and the female Turk (although this one was actually kinda funny), a squat battle (you heard me), pushing barrels onto Shinra soldiers who are chasing Aeris (or Aerith ♥♥♥♥ you), among others. Some of them are fun for the most part, but generally speaking I feel like they're just wasting my time, but I appreciate the effort to give the user some control.
But despite the game's problems, I would recommend Final Fantasy VII to anybody in a heartbeat. TL;DR, the characters are unique and personal, the music sounds spectaular and works great with the game, the story makes you care and keeps you involved, and the gameplay is nothing you've seen before. I would recommend this for full price.

"The hardest tracks are ones you most lack confidence and the easiest are ones you are most confident/comfortable with. Because when you lack confidence you tend to go slower but if you're comfortable you go full out because you know how to handle the track. You don't hold back since you're not afraid of crashing and all the adrenaline/excitement rushes in because you can go full out. You dominate the race and are ahead of everyone else. Yet, you get the feeling that you want to 'overtake' every section of the track itself. It's no longer about beating the competition, you're the competition" -Me on Ride gameplay.
I was foreign to the world of motorbikes because I never able appreciated riding one. I played one of the first motogp game in around 2000 and I loved the game very much though. Recently, I tried Milestone's MotoGP14 and despite the lack of support for the game I loved it! I still think riding a motobike is a dangerous and risky business but I can appreciate the thrill and freedom of bike riding.
All this brought me to RIDE. I almost passed on buying until I saw a youtube video clip showing a tuned bike excellently ridden.
Now that I have tried RIDE, I want to share my opinion of the game to help you decide. Overall, the game is good especially if you're a motorbike lover. However, it still lacks tracks to race in in my opinion. The game forces you to start with one of 3 naked bikes and I thought it was rather uncool to force you to start with a specific type of bike. That being said, the progression until you buy a new bike that you like is quick and I now have realized that naked bikes aren't that bad actually.
The game allows you to buy parts for your bikes from aesthetic parts to performance enhancing ones. It also allows you to customize your rider avatar's face and gears (apparel) as well.
The game feels easy to play even with pro physics and no assists especially if you compare it to MotoGP 14. It could be because the bikes are slower than those in MotoGP. But this brought a more arcade feeling to the game than Milestone's MotoGP 14.
Other than the lack of tracks the only other gripe I have is the inability to select the number of laps in any race we participate in (with the exception of online games).
Do note that there's no weather in game neither is day/night setting. I think every track is set to certain pre-programmed time setting. Milestone has a habit of giving you just good enough game without trying to make it really superb.
Online is enjoyable too with stangers or even more with friends.
UPDATE 2 APRIL 2015
Now that I have spent more on the game I have more to share.
The difficulty of the game increases as you upgrade from lower powered bikes to higher ones. Riding a supersport bike may be too easy compared to riding a motoGP bike in Milestone's other game but riding a modern superbike is not so easy. In fact it can feel a bit too difficult. That is until you adapt to the changes.
Wheelie and stoppie happen a lot when you ride a bike with respectable horsepower unless you turn anti wheelie option to full (modern bikes have that tech actually!). Wheelie forces you to go easy on the throttle thus slowing you down despite  the bike's increased power rating. Opening up on the throttle aggresively will slow you down as your bike performs unintended wheelies.
Furthermore, the game has its fair share of bugs and performance issues. Custom bike settings are not remembered forcing you to load your bike setting before every race which is annoying.
Stutters can happen if you set the VRAM to auto which is the default setting.
The game crashes to desktop when you try to  exit and sometimes when loading it just freezes although the likely occurence of the later is not that high.
Perhaps one of the most annoying bug is that rewind doesn't always work and when it doesn't it costs you the race thus in-game money, prestige and REAL free time
UPDATE 3 April 2015
Just want to add that many people mention the sounds of the bikes are not that good but to me ithey are decent enough. When you use helmet view, sounds are muffled a bit which is very nice and thoughful. You could also hear the whizzing of air past you....which is also muffled if you're in helmet view. Each bike sounds distinct enough although you can't quite immerse yourself in the feeling of raw power when hearing your engine purring and roaring as you race. But the sounds are decent enough.
One of the best things in Ride is the inclusion of older bikes. These are a thrill to ride and race. You get to understand the advancement in motorbike technology as you try bikes from different eras. Most of the older bikes are from the mid 1990s and all throughout the first decade of the 21st century. Bike lovers will understand that they are riding not to show off or to indulge their prestige/ego by riding an expensive sport bike but for the enjoyment and thrill of riding it. Thus, being able to race these older bikes is awesome.
Overall, this is a fun game and that's all that matters. Yes it is easier than Milestone's previous MotoGP 14 game but it's way more fun.
UPDATE MULTIPLAYER
The multiplayer part is a blast in this game. It's made in such a way that your own riding is not affected by the ping response to the host. Your fellow players may rubber band if you have bad ping to the host but your experience of the race is flawless. This made it such that your result is almost not affected by the quality of your ping to the host's pc.
It's a lot of fun playing with other people. And way safer too. ;)

This is a great tech demo for HDR lighting (Yes, this is a tech demo. Get that through your head before you write a review, please.) in my opinion. If you're intrested in the source engine and got this with Half-Life 2, its a must play (must expeience?), I think.

The little bit of gameplay that comes with the demo also entertained me while I marveled at the lighting. It isn't hard and not to easy, like most of the puzzles in the other Half-Life games. The whole product is a cut chapter from Half-Life 2, where you must deactivate a combine cannon that is firing upon a close village. While you travel to the cannon, you are attacked by combine soldiers. It also has a brief cliff-side part, which reminded me of the cliff-side trek from the original Half-Life. After you have de-activated the cannon with the mighty power of physics, you must fight another small group of combine and then take down a combine helecopter, and then find your way back down to the ground, then, the experince is over.
The Dev Comm tells you about the HDR lighting and why the location of the chapter is what it is, while giving you nice visial references. The all mighty Gabe also talks. Twice.
Takes you through the game and calculates your average FPS (Frames Per Second), which could be helpfull to you in the future, so you know if you can run a certain game at good frames before you buy it. You can also send your results to Valve. Do it, there isn't really a reason not too.
This is a tech demo for HDR lighting in the source engine. It has some nice gameplay thrown in, and there isn't really a reason not to play it, since it comes free with Half-Life 2.

So far, I've got o say Ride hit the mark on a niche role that the MotoGP games weren't filling.
Pros:
-Over 100 bikes
-Over 400 different paint jobs
-from 390-1200cc bikes
-Naked bikes/sports/supersports/superbikes/track bikes/prototypes
-The actual gameplay feels smooth (when you use correct graphic settings)
-Can change things like fender eliminators and mirror elminators, tires, lever colors, triple clamp colors.
-Rider gear can be custumized from helmet (they even have my skin of the AGV K3), gloves, boots, suits, pants, and jackets
-Riding position can be made custom, and that's really cool little feature for me personally
-You can REALLY feel the difference in bikes. Went form an R6 600cc bikes to the Ducati Penigale 1199s, and it took about 5-8 races for me to actually get used to the feel of the Duc. I power wheeied up several times, hit the throttle too hard out of corners and slid out. Things I was doing that aren't always good practice (powering early out of turns, opening wide up in lower gears) were fine on the R6, but on the Duc, double the power it was very clear that I had to race much cleaner.
Cons:
-I feel the "Racing Line" they have is a tad off at times, there's definitely points where I can clearly break after it tells me to/lines that are more optimal to take wide/short. Looking at you Road America
-The racing line isn't always clear on when to lean, Often times I can go early to get a jump on the apex. While other times if I turn when it wants me to I'll come up short on the turn.
-The starting bikes are incredibly lopsided. I went with the 636 Monster, and it was a clear loser to the speed triple. I struggled very much to even finish on the podium with the Ducati. But when I started over, with the triple, it was a walk in the park to finish top.
-I don't feel the tracks are varied enough in world tour mode. I've seen Road America, Imola, and Miami plenty of times. I've only seen Wales once, and yet to see Sierra Nevada.
-I wish they did more with the salt flats track, It's a big relaxer to just drag it up, but I think they could do a little more with it. Maybe a mode where you try to beat your top speed?
-Bike damage is nonexistant, I'd like to see a hardcore mode.
Overall, I think Ride is shaping up to be the niche motorcycle riders, enthusiants, and race enthusiants are looking for.
However, there are minor tweaks that need to be made, and some content as far as tracks go I'd love to see added (Isle of Man TT [PLEASE, even if it's just a segement of the track] , Leguna Seca, Catalunya, Mugello).
For now, I'd give it an 8/10, hopefully Milestone actually sticks with this to provice patches, and new content.
For $40, I'd say it's definitely a save bet for any motorcycle rider.

Choplifter HD is a sidescrolling shoot em up where you shoot yourself trough tons of enemies and rescue people.

Final Fantasy VII has not only an above-average story, but a great turn-based combat system that has won over many a fans since the game's release 20 years ago at the time of writing this.
Lemme just start off by saying the soundtrack is awesome, and it is on par with that of Final Fantasy VI. The spell animations are really good, and it went on to inspire many games later on, one being Planescape: Torment. The story, while not being as great as FF VI's in my opinion, is still stellar and much better than a lot of other games.
The materia system is very good, and it can be used to make an incredible amount of playstyles with diverging tactics with nearly limitless capabilities to the things you can combine other things with, for example making one of the more buffy characters who uses a gun and then make him a full-fledged mage with highly destructive spells. Or make one character a god or make all of your characters share equal powers, theres just a lot of things to consider when applying materia to a character, and I didn't even mention the long list of stats in the process to consider too.
The turn-based combat system is only necessary for the materia combinations to take place. While you can't have as much party members in combat like you could in the older games the level of customization and variability has been stepped up to make each one absolutely essential to your success in battle. The bosses require strategy and caution, as they aren't as simple as the normal enemies, every boss has their strengths and weaknesses to consider on the fly, and you will have to experiement with your attacks a little before figuring out the most effective way to take it down. In fact it might be my personal favorite combat system in a game.
But unfortunately most of the joy only comes to those who play past roughly around the part where you get out of Midgar to the part where you secretly enter Rufus' boat. If you're willing to get past the slow bits at the beginning where there isn't much to be had in terms of gameplay, then you're good to go and you will find the parts beyond that to be very fun and at least a 40+ hour experience.
Whenever you get stuck on something, don't be afraid to look up the walkthrough the part you're stuck on. Games back then weren't known for being all that friendly to newcomers like nowadays and because of that they are prone to have some times where you question what you're supposed to do next in the game.
Definitely my 5th favorite game of all time, it really is a masterpiece. While it may be overrated slightly, it definitely deserves a lot of that praise and you can't deny the influential impact it had on the industry for the better years after it was even released. I still find myself playing through this game once a year and I never get bored of what it brings to me over and over again.
Also can't wait for the remake. Don't screw it up guys, please.

The Witcher 2, even before entering the main menu, shows us maybe the best CG intro ever in a video game. After the shocking ending of The Witcher leaving us with a cliffhanger, The Witcher 2 starts shortly after the predecessor. Geralt of Rivia, after saving King Foltest of Temeria, works for him now, as a personal bodyguard. Hunting traitors, Foltest sieges a castle and “invite” Geralt to help his army. Something shocking happens in the action-packed epic prologue, and now Geralt must prove he is saying the truth, and have his vengeance, seeking a mysterious man. The Witcher 2 storyline is more action-packed than the first one. It’s epic, it’s complex and have a lot of politics involved. Also, you have to make dramatic choices, that even before the half of the game, show a totally different perception of the entire story, making it almost two in one. (Beat the game two times for the full experience!) Personally, I prefer the first Witcher story, but the second one is really better in showing it’s themes and involves a lot of more things happening in the world, with decisions that matter even in The Witcher 3, drawing to one possible conclusion, showed in an epic CG. The ending does not disappoint and put another cliffhanger that serve as a promise for the epic The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, the conclusion of the saga. Character development is very good and you will possible love two characters, Saskia and Ioverth. They’re amazing and shows a good background. But… it’s The Witcher! Everyone have their own personal story and unique quests, everything in the world have something behind it. The game’s campaign is shorter than the first one, because is kind of divided in two, but its more action packed like I also said and includes even more epic Boss Battles, that I bet will surprise you. Besides the campaign being smaller, the game itself is bigger, have more quests, bigger areas to explore and more content! The graphics are impressive, as still of today. The darker style of the game shows beautiful scenarios and regions, and well done animations, a problem from the first game. Alongside the epic soundtrack and sound effects, it all boils down to the amazing fantasy atmosphere the game shows you. The movimentation is more fluid than in the first game and you can even climb some obstacles. Combine this with combat that also shows an amazing innovation. Maybe the worst aspect of the first game, turned in one of the triumphs in The Witcher 2. The combat combines the Signs again, but now it’s not a totally combo-based like the first one and have a lot of movements and sounds like more a hack’n’slash game, with truly epic fight scenes with all kinds of monsters, that are now bigger in number than on the first game. Contracts are back as always and you have to clean monster nests and destroy them. As this is the enhanced edition, it features better graphics, bugs correction, and all of the released DLC, so you may find trolls in the game world with some interesting stories, and there is also the special Arena mode where you fight waves of enemies. Talking about the game itself again, there’s a lot of weapons again, and this time, a lot of armors, something I found lacking in the first. You can breed potions as always that help you in combat and sometimes is even necessary for quests. The world feels alive and you have a lot of romance options, but this time with no romance cards, but explicit scenes, even more than its successor, including specially one with Triss…There is also a crafting system for the armor and weapons which gives you the best ones in the game. Now you can meditate (to pass time and brew potions) anywhere if there’s no enemies, so it’s more practical than the predecessor. Dice poker is present: you can play a game with almost everyone and it's very fun and have quests related. The perk and level up system is cool and works well. The bad aspects for the game includes some bugs, random crashes that make you lose your progress and even lose your save in some cases (do a lot of them) and the lack of “RPG interactions”. The first one had a lot of food, drinks that you could eat and an animation was showed. This one does not feature all of that and no animations are present. Ok, that's a minor thing but...my opinion. Another thing is the game can be too punitive at the beggining, not stimulating someone into proceeding in. After you level up a bit it becomes fun, however. Mini games are present in boss battles. And they are annoying. The inventory menus are kind of chunky for me, also.

Stellaris launched as a skeleton for DLC and, as a result, has very little in the way of meaty content. The game is an ostensible fusion of Grand Strategy and 4X, featuring massive scale, intragovernmental management, POPs, strategic resources, government types, etc. While it has the makings of the 4Xs and a smattering of strategy, it fails in both regards. I cannot recommend it in its present state. Having played Utopia, this includes that present state as well.
The game utterly lacks any deep systems outside of population management; there is no intergalactic economy to speak of, no trade routes, no logistical considerations for war (no fuel or ammunition), very limited options when declaring war (you can only conquer/liberate/vassalize planets/systems/empires, respectively; you cannot enforce government types, abduct citizens, execute leaders, or claim unsettled systems), very little in the way of planetary management (the sector system ensures that you'll rarely hold any more than 10 planets in a given game, whereas the galaxy can contain several hundred; on top of that, it's basically a similar version of GalCiv2's planet management screen with clunkier automation - you develop tiles and place people on them, that's it), very little control over research, and no espionage. You do a lot of clicking to affect little direct change.
The leader system, where you can recruit extraordinary citizens from available populations in your empire, boils down to nothing more than a bunch of timed, growable modifiers. Leaders have no personality whatsoever. They do not trigger trait-specific events, and they have no effect on interactions with other empires unless they have traits that do. There are no feuds between two God-Emperors, no presidents detested by embittered rival empires, no events dealing with leaders of other empires, or anything of the sort. Contrast with CK2, where the characters of your leaders vastly affects the composition of your realm, even in vanilla.
What depth there is remains inconsequential in most playthroughs. It's not like CK2, where you have to learn the ins-and-outs of managing vassals to have a shot at governing a large empire. The new faction system, while a good source of flavor and short-term objectives, feels neutered. I haven't even bothered with gene modifiation since I'm doing just fine without that kind of expensive, time-consuming optimization.
Everywhere you look, it feels like something is missing. Interactions with other empires boils down to conquering them or allying with them and conqering them later. POPs management consists of spamming certain resources/actions/other POPs when factions get unruly and colonizing certain planets with certain species. War is a Kinetics-beat-all spam-off where cruisers dominate the meta. Dealing with primitives involves picking one of four options and waiting, or just invading them like you would an AI - except it's even easier. Research consists of crossing your fingers and waiting for the game to generate the techs you want. Managing planets stays the same all throughout the game since anything beyond your first few get relegated to self-governing, inefficient sectors. There's just nothing worth engaging with, mechanically. Even exploration, the best-executed feature in the game, becomes worthless once you're either boxed in or you've already gathered data on other systems via map exchanges in a buggy, antiquated trading interface.
Buy something like Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion instead. At least that game has compelling combat.

This is Dungeon Defenders 1: Complete Edition.  Without hacking, with some extra content.  As such it gets my full endorsement.  As someone who came to the party late, there was no point in playing public multiplayer due to the hacking.  This game finally allows me to play the original as it was meant to be played.
Despite early reviews, this is not:
1) A mobile port (this is a complete misunderstanding of the cross platform service launching later)
2) Full of microtransactions. The only thing you can (currently) buy are useless Emotes for $1 - all skins and dyes are earned as usual, as are all weapons, armor, etc.
3) Dumbed down or DLC deficient - the gameplay is identical, and the UI is largey the same or slightly streamlined
4) Lacking single player or private matches (both were added with a day 2 patch)
They did add a uPlay-like launcher to the game that might annoy some, but I found it to be seamless.  They need the overlay to offer cross playform play later on, which steam cannot do.
Drawbacks:
- You cannot import your characters.  This is to prevent item hacks from exploiting this game also.
- They added too much bloom.  Hopefully a patch will allow you to turn it off.

In my opinion, the leveling system used in FF8 is probably my least favorite, but this is mainly because I feel that it is overly complicated. Although, this does allow a depth of customization that is only achievable in FF10, but even more so than the sphere grid.
The music in this port isn't perfect, but those that are saying that it is unplayable because of the music must be some serious audiophiles because it isn't THAT bad.
The game looks decent enough, but it is clear that it hasn't aged terribly well, albeit better than FF7 has due to the physical representation of the characters on and off the battlefield, but that doesn't change the factt that the foreground is. . . well. . . abysmal. That being said, the first time I summoned Shiva and watched her perform Diamond Dust, chills of nostalgia washed over me. (No pun intended)
Having to sign up through Square-Enix's website is definitely a downside but mainly because it's just an added inconvience that shouldn't be necessary.
Gameplay wise the only problem I have encountered is the ability to run away. The button combination didn't seem to work on my 360 pad and I couldn't remember for the life of me what the keyboard controls to run were, so I ended up fighting a dinosaur with 15k hp within the first hour of the game. The added magic booster feature makes the game absolutely trivial and you may as well be using gameshark codes, but if that's your thing then by all means, cheat away.
If you have never played this entry into the Final Fantasy franchise and have no other means of doing so other than this port, then I would definitely recommend giving it a shot; however, if you can get your hands on the original, own a PS3, or something similar, then I would say to pass on this title. It's not the games fault that the port is poorly done.

I bought this game out of Nostalgia for the countless hours I spent years ago payling the old Civilisation games, because it was cheap and had great reviews.
In short I don't quite understand how this game managed to get such rave reviews. The game mechanics have (bare few improvements far from revolutionary) not evolved one bit since the old civ games from over 10 years ago. Managing your units fleets and city hours into the game is an absolute chore. There is nearly no macro management option.
A few examples!
- No fleet management: Good luck finding that specific ship by scrolling through the list of your 150 ships. Have fun organising your fleet,
- Nearly no planet management tool. Granted there is a table view where you see key data for your planets in a mostly readable form, but it stops there. By your 50th planet, having to decide tile by tile what you build gets seriously tedious. Oh, there's an auto-govern feature, you can chose a profile and let it do it mange your planet automatically, excepts it's so stupid as to be useless.
So basically, when you notice that there's something wrong with 20 of your planets, you'll just have to go to each one, one by one, scroll to a list of improvement, select one, and rinse and repeat for each planet.
- There's so few "events" narratives that you will get the same "surprise"  several time in one hour of play time, there's some humour into these, but same jokes all the time wear thin fast
- The bonus you find on the map don't evolve over time, so even 4 hours into a game where you just want to burn a vodoo doll to finish a turn, you will still be stopped by a popup window letting you know that you found a treasure of .... 1 credit, awesome.
- same thing as above for the "ideology" choices that give you points to unlock ideologic abilities , there are so few of those "dilemnas" that you will stop reading after a few hours and just click on a choice depending on the abilities you want to developp (benevolent, pragmatic, malevolent)
- The turn by turn mechanic is basically the same as in the first Civilisation game that came out in the 90s, again, on large scale map, it gets tedious really fast.
-The ship designer is cool, so there's that. I use it mostly to build exploring vessels that don't totally suck. (long range, many moves, large vision radius) because exploring the galaxy with the normal ones is just an absolute bore.
- Exploring: see above. Couldn't there be a hubble telescope or something ?
All that said, this is still somehow addictive, and I still find myself putting many hours into it ... just one more turn... so I can't really say it's a bad game, I just see so much potential for innovation and so little of it, and I really don't get the hype. It's kinda cool, but it's basically a civisilation in space with all the same default as the old turn based classic and little in the way of novel game mechanics.

This game improves from the sequel. If you have not read my review on that then please read it before you read this. This review will make more sense if you know my thoughts on the first game of the series and see how Witcher 2 has fixed these problems.
Lets start with how they fixed my biggest complaint from the first game, the combat. When I started up Witcher 2, as soon as I tried the combat, I threw my arms up in joy to see how improved it is. They switched it from the three styles and clicking on the enemy to attack into what we are probably more used to now adays, one button being a fast attack and another button to do a strong attack. I cannot say in words how exactly this made me feel, you'd just have to see the differences for yourself. I will say that I suggest using a controller for at least only the combat cause I find it better that way.
The graphics have improved drastically as well and I felt like they hold up pretty well. The environments are beautiful and great to look at. The character models, like the combat, is improved so much as well. There is no scary character models unless you are meant to be afraid of them.
If you read the review on the first Witcher game, you might remember how I said that I felt like I didn't need to change my weapons for most of the game. They fixed that by adding a lot more options of swords and they get stronger as you level up and find them. You can only carry two weapons though, but like I said I only used the steel and silver swords anyway in the first game.
The characters are still quite memorable in Witcher 2 as they were in the first game. You even see quite a few familiar faces from the first game. I still meet these characters and I love to hear more about them and seeing all the different personalities.
Finally, lets get to the quests. The main story always stayed with the story and didn't feel like it went off rails like in the first game, but maybe too much so. I felt like it was a bit too linear. However, I actually felt like I was doing main quests and was going closer and closer to the ultimate goal as I did each of them. You do need to keep in mind that once you finish a level, there is no coming back, so if there are some side quests you wanted to do, you'd need to do them all before you finish all the main quests in the level.
The story itself was pretty good. Believe it or not, but I felt like Witcher 1's story might be a bit better, you know, around the end. The saved data even transfers from Witcher 1 to Witcher 2, and Witcher 2 even transfers to Witcher 3. I'll try not to spoil too much when talking about this. The main enemy was pretty cool as a nemesis, but for a video game character, he's kind of a let down. I think this because he's just a big strong guy and in the end you get to pick whether or not you want to kill him or not. I chose not to kill him because I already fought him earlier in the game and the fight would barely be any different if it's different at all. I think I forgot to mention that there are multiple endings to Witcher 1, but the same goes with Witcher 2. All your actions have consiquenses (not sure if I spelled that right, I'll check later), and you'd have to deal with whatever course you go with.
I hope you enjoyed my reviews on the first two Witcher games. I'll write a review on Witcher 3, but I am having so much fun with it, it'll take me a while to finish it.

While sectors sound like a neat way to remove the tedium of a large empire in most 4x games, the Stellaris sector implementation actually introduces extra micromanagement rather than removes it.  This is largely because of missing UI elements and very poor AI.  No way to quickly get to starports in sectors for building stuff, no way to see colony ships that you build at a sector starport without hunting on the galaxy map for it.
Then there are enemy AI's that start right next to you with the same territory color creating border confusion.
Victory conditions are mostly about conquest:  conquer or subjugate all other empires, or colonize/conquer 40% of all planets.
End game galaxy threats are very very buggy and the enemy AI doesn't treat them as serious threats and sometimes just ignores them while getting slaughtered.
Once the game has had a few major polishing patches and/or DLC, and some *real* achievments added for Ironman, I'll revist the game and possibly change my thumbs-down to a thumbs-up.  If you're on the fence about buying the game, I recommend waiting for a while and checking it out again in the future, or when it's on sale.

This is the first time I have ever felt compelled to write a review, so apologies in advance if I ramble.
Firstly, let me say that Stellaris is a *wonderful* game with scads of potential.
But if you're buying Stellaris expecting “EU4-In-Spaaaaaace”, then I would advise caution.
Stellaris is its own game. Not simply a re-skin. There are some recognizable UI elements and Paradox Grand Strategy tropes, but that's it. Many things are handled differently: resources, vassals, armies (in both creation and customization), and research - just to name a few.
However, as I mentioned above, the operative word is potential. It’s not there yet. Stellaris has a long way to go before it’s on the same level as EU4 or CK2. I don't mean in terms of story or setting, I mean in terms of gameplay and UI.
There is a surprising lack of map modes for a Grand Strategy game. Not having a way to easily see who’s allied to whom, or who you are sucking up to, is particularly missed. The trade map mode is missing as well, but then again, so is trade. In this way Stellaris reminds me more of Civilization. No managing trade nodes. No way to steer trade or use your mercantile strength in your favor, it simply happens via trade deals with other empires. No sneaky-sneaking either. Intrigue is non-existent against other space faring races (though you can infiltrate pre-space age peoples and supplant their government with your own).
Those are just some of the issues I’ve run across in 20-or-so hours. Now, I have no doubt that Paradox will positively inundate Stellaris with DLC content to flesh it out. But that's the rub. If you’ve ever played a Sims game at launch you’ll know the feeling. "You gave me pools last time EA... where are they now? Seriously? Five lamps and a wall sconce?" Except here I was asking for deeper trade, easier ways to access information, more options to flex my diplomatic muscles, a more succinct and intuitive UI - in short, a greater range of ways to conquer the galaxy. I know you can do it Paradox! You've done it before!
Doesn’t paint a pretty picture does it? So why would I recommend Stellaris?
Because even with its flaws. It's good. Really good. And it will only get better.
There are too many positives to list. There’s creativity here; quality too. This wasn’t half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it needs some polish. That shouldn't be a big surprise really. This is a big departure from what Paradox normally puts out, Stellaris needs time to acclimate, room to figure out what works and what doesn't. If Paradox’s track record is any indication – it will get there in time. Just temper your expectations for now.

TL;DR
This is one hell of a game. It’s not for everyone. If your liked EU4 or CK2 then this is an automatic buy. If you want a 20 min. quick match then stay clear.  If you have never played a paradox game, but the idea of playing the same scenario for weeks on end sounds appealing then this is as good a title as any to dip your toes in. The graphics, game play and shear complexity will have you logging aver 400 hours easy on this title. Go ahead add it to your library, you won’t regret it.
Summary
Stellaris is a “Grand Strategy” game released by Paradox Interactive. What that means is essentially it’s a massive complex tangle of military, political, and economic strategy components all rolled into one large game. It’s kind of like playing SimCity, MOO, and StarCraft all at once. But even that doesn’t give it justice. It’s complex, on a level that conventional wisdom says should not be fun.
However it is a lot of fun. Be prepared for a “long game”. I mean a single map for months or more in daily 2 hour sessions. This is not a 20 min. random match. Playing multiplayer is very fun, but unless your with a dedicated group of friends it’s unlikely your going to “finish” in a traditional sense. Usually a session is about setting a specific short term goal, that helps bolster your long term goals. For example, I want to conquer Steve. could take weeks of work. Tonight’s goal may be so small as “get my energy credit production to +30 so I can expand my military later”. Tomorrow’s goal may be to get mineral production up.  Then you may spend the next two weeks getting allies, alliances, and chipping away at his allies. This is not a game where you conqueror the entire map. This game is about guiding an empire among other empires. Simply put, you are not alone, and you never will be.
Under the hood
If you have played other of Paradox’s games, you will feel right at home. Stellaris uses the Clausewitz engine. Which means it plays a lot like EU4 or CK2 (among others). It also means you will, at first, be lost in a sea of numbers, and information. Once you learn how to read this info though, you will be hard pressed to find a better, more concise way to  present it.
Game Play
At the start, you have 1 planet, and a few ships. If you enable the tutorial (which I recommend the first few times) you will get a scripted set of events to guide you threw the process of exploration and expansion. The tutorial barely scratches the surface of the game, but it’s a nice “here’s your next step” that will keep you from being lost. What the game effectively comes down to is making a series of decisions. Every decision feels important and  even when you don’t know all the consequences, you still have an immense feeling of weight when you make simple decisions. The way tech works helps with this. Essentially your presented with three choices of what to research. What ever you choose the other two choices are not, usually, going to be available the next time you get to make that choice. There are some important exceptions that will come up till you choose them, but make no mistake, this game is more then willing to let you fail.
As you transition in to a more exploitative phase, you will run into aliens. Sometimes, they will research you and be able to communicate with you, some time you have to research them. Taking the time to research them will pause your current empire research, so make sure you really want to spend the time.  You will spend a good bit of time, exploring and growing, learning and researching. Eventually, however, you will transition smoothly into a solid mid-game.
This transition is smooth. Your not thrust into it, there is no key tech to unlock that advances you to it. Just all of the sudden, you will find a goal, that is beyond your reach without making friends, or enemies, or both of your neighbors. Now the game transitions into a higher level of play, where you spend your influence, power, and military might in order to reach your goals. You can have a huge number of goals. From “protect my border” to “take over that black hole”. There is no limit, and the goals are things you mostly set your self.
Graphics and Interface
The interface presents you with a lot of information, and it will take you some time to learn how to read it. Once you do however, you will find your self wondering if real government officials have an interface like this.  It’s not always intuitive, but after 50 hours or so, you will be hard pressed to come up with a better way to display and access everything. There is an in game  browser to help you out with direct in game wiki access.
The graphics themselves are clean and neat, nothing to make your jaw drop, but beautiful, and powerful in their own way. The game simply looks amazing though there are no “look at those awesome shadows” moments that some games provide.

If you loved Quest for Glory, download right now.  It's free.
My single gripe was that I did not like the harsh 'warmth' meter, but if you look around, you can find things that keep you warm.  Boots, scarves, cloaks, fur pelts, or even a bottle of warm water are all things that slow the meter to a very bearable level.  Also common sense can dictate whether it's a good day to go out or not.  Snowing outside means you lose warmth faster, night makes you lose warmth as well.  If you really want, you can turn the game to easy and I believe it stops the warmth meter.  If you're curious what happens when the warmth meter runs out, you start to lose stamina.  When your stamina runs out, you start to lose health (just like Quest for Glory).  Once all meters run out, you die.  So it actually takes quite a while, and it takes longer and longer as you gain more hp and stamina.
So, at first glance, the warmth meter was annoying.  But, it's really not that bad when you progress through the game and acquire things that make it trivial.  Other than that, it is a great modern Quest for Glory homage.  There's nothing else I could say was a turn-off for me.

Ever since Paradox announced Stellaris I was anxious to try it out.  I had such high hopes for the game however the game hasn't lived up to what I had thought it would.  Originally I played for about 90 minutes and found myself very turned off with the game so I got a refund.  Then I had a number of people say that I should have given it longer so I picked it up again.  I really wish I hadn't because the game still continues not to be my cup of tea.
Compared to other 4X space games that I own Stellaris (at least for me) ranks near the bottom.  It just doesn't have that one more turn sort of feeling.  Every minute I spent playing Stellaris was a minute I spent thinking about how much I like the new MoO.  I don't know exactly what it is that Stellaris is lacking for me but it just feels so incomplete.  I will try to write up an actual review so this is just a place holder but I wanted to just throw it out there that the games is very meh.  It isn't horrible but it just doesn't have the soul that I had hoped it would, something that is strange because Paradox strategy games almost always have a ton of soul to them.
I will most likely play another couple hours before I do my actual full review but as of now even after getting a refund then deciding to try again I wish that I had just left well enough alone and hadn't bottered with the game.  Maybe like some people have suggested the reason the game feels lacking is that Paradox left out a bunch of things to sell via DLC.  If so it is a shame because you have to have a good game before you can "enhance" it with DLC.  EUIV and CK2 are great examples of having a great base game first then improving with DLC later.  I just feel that Paradox released a stripped down game instead this go around.   Once again I personally enjoy the latest MoO many, many times more and it is still in early access.

The base gameplay is clicking to create fire, and buying this from a catalogue to burn them. Unfortunately, you have to wait real time in order for the toys or electronics or whatever to arrive. This mechanic in the game is a massive downside, because some items in the later catalogues take a full 2 minutes. I see that the Dev’s wanted to make the game last longer but it's an annoying amount of time. Not long enough to alt tab and do something else, but long enough for the player to be annoyed. This time can be finished but using stamps, which can be collected by burning certain combos of objects. The list and what items required are online so this can be figured out easily. The gold coins you use to buy the objects to burn, are earned by, you guessed it, burning things. Its almost impossible to go broke in this game, with profiting from burning most things, and random spiders coming down and providing $ from their burnt corpses.
Burning combos, at first, seem to be the only objective. After a little bit of time someone in the next room sends you a letter, befriending you. Her and “The weatherman” start to produce a legitimate storyline, making the game more appealing, drawing the player to play more. After grinding out the combos the player is handed a combo that is very easy to do, implying said player has a good memory. After that combo is completed a whole new world and story is added to the mix. The story is added in gradually but soon becomes the full focus. Its not only a well told story, but it's also a grasping one.
The graphics of the game fit the game alright, but the music in-game make the world around you feel so much darker and lonely, suiting the game perfectly.
Little inferno does some things right.
The sound and music is amazing
The story is one of the best i have ever seen out of an indie game
The combos, are witty and require some thinking, making it more immersive
The fireplace looks good, and get to annoying to look at
The objects you burn are rather comical
The ability to toss burning objects around your fireplace is good fun.
Little inferno does some things wrong too.
The lack of achievements and playing cards make the game a time killer, lowering their audience
The story although great, is slow to get started.
The repetitive nature could leave some players bored after an hour or two
The combos are both hard and easy at the same time, depending on the player’s skill
The combos are really easy to look up shortening the game time and lowering the fun
Little inferno, although a compelling story and a good time killer, isn't really worth the $10.99(CAD). With the lack of achievements and playing cards, it seems almost like a narrative interactive book, then a game. The price aside, i think people who love a great story, or even just wanting a few hours to go buy, should pick up this game. If it's ever on sale, get it. This is the weatherman, signing off. We’re all going to be okay.

TL;DR Review:
Red Alert 3 is a beautiful, terrifically fun game that also does some interesting things with the RTS genre.
Long Review:
The Red Alert series has some defining aspects - alternate histories, time travel, trained animal units, psychic powers - but its most obvious trait was the cheesiness of its cutscenes.  The Red Alert developers realized that trying to do "serious" FMV for these games usually ended up producing something nigh-unwatchable, like Command & Conquer 2.  So they decided to just turn the cheese knob until it broke off, and Red Alert 3 continues this tradition with pride.  It combines time travel and crazy inventions and Tim Curry to make a wonderful, fun mess of a storyline.  And the best part is that the actors are into it - they understand that the scenery here is meant to be eaten.
But look past the cheese (and cheesecake) and you'll find a fun, very playable RTS.  The three sides all play differently, with the Russians being the simple bruisers, the Empire having the coolest (but most difficult to use) units and the Allies having the most useful commander powers.
Plus, the game has co-op.  The "single player" campaign is actually designed to be played by two people at once, each controlling a different commander.  Since co-op multiplayer is the best multiplayer, it was nice to see this finally come to the RTS genre.  And don't worry - if you don't have anyone to play with, there are nine different AI commanders to help you out, each of whom has their own play style and personality.  As the story progresses and you move to the next campaign, AI commanders that used to be your allies could become your enemies and vice-versa - an excellent touch.
The game is also beautiful, with some of the best water I've ever seen. Models are detailed, textures are rich and of good resolution and special effects are excellent.
In short, Red Alert 3 may have disappointed fans who were eagerly awaiting the next "real" Command & Conquer, but if you take it for what it is it's a blast.

This is a fantastic game. I did not expect it from a game I've never really heard of, but it was cheap and looked cute so I bought it on super sale.
The game is a classic rpg with pixelated graphics. The game takes place in a vikingstyle world with a lot of mentioning of the norse gods and myths. You paly as either a warrior, a sorceress or a rogue and your goal is to wave the world from Ragnarok.

Little Inferno is a very unique Indie game created by Tomorrow Corperation. The nonsensical, comical game style makes the game highly enjoyable and addictive. The objective of the game is to burn various items in your fireplace in return for coins, with which you buy more items to burn! When you burn certain items together you will unlock combos, these give you extra coins and when you get ebough you are able to purchase a new catalogue containing new items to burn!
When put like that the game does not sound very enjoyable, however the way in which the items react just makes you want to see more of the game.
Tomorrow Corp also add in another couple of characters who you get to meet and develope relationships with as the game progresses including an annoying but lovable neighbour who circums to a tregedy later on in the game.
The game play is very responsive and you do not need a good computer to run the game. The colourful design gives the game a very positive atmosphere, which seems to be uncommon in newer games.
The only down critisism that I have for this game is that it does not take a long time to complete, if you do not focus on unlocking all of the combos you could complete the game in little over 2 hours. But, if you wish to piece together all of the clues than you would have to spend a lot more time on the game.
To conclude:
Little Inferno if a brilliant and unique game, it includes a lot of fun puzzles to solve and will keep someone entertained for a number of hours. It's relaxed game style means you are able to play it without having to stay and "finish this bit" as it saves the game as you go.

As someone who's put hundreds of hours into the base DD game, all of the negative reviews of this one were very concerning to me. I decided to go for it anyway, and I've been pleasantly surprised. I've put several more hours into the game since my first review, and I figured I'd update it a bit with what I've observed now that I've made it to 60 on a few characters. I've come across a few annoyances, and there's definitely a few more cons, however my final verdict is still a 'recommend.'
Aside from the general pros, this review assumes you're familiar with the first DD game. If not, watch a few let's plays on Youtube to get a feel for the gameplay; it's a combination of tower defense and action game, and it's hard to describe in words what is way easier to show on video.
General Pros:
+ Very fun mix of strategic and action based gameplay.
+ Good character/gameplay variety (8 classes, multiple character build options in each class)
+ Great to play with friends
+ Leveling up and finding new gear is very satisfying. Finally perfecting a map build is insanely satisfying.
Pros vs. the Original Dungeon Defenders game:
+ The game is VERY MUCH Dungeon Defenders 1.9, lots of little things that make the game more enjoyable.
+ Everyone gets their own drops. No more people running around stealing all of the drops while you keep the defenses running!
+ The four slot amulet/consumable system where you can add four extra abilities to your character- instantly heal a tower, amplify elemental damage, heal other players, curse enemies, summon a giant storm, etc... It definitely makes you feel like you have more options and allows for some cool new character builds (like a 4 tower repair amulet + hero speed + hero health to quickly run around the map healing defenses).
+Pets now have uniqe abilities and drop as eggs that you equip in your amulet slots to hatch over time. You can see the stats before you hatch them
+There are consumable items that let you boost exp, loot quantity, loot quality, and loot rarity. Especially useful on survival runs to get some great gear
+ Items, Maps, and Hero are balanced much better
+ Item value is tied to the rarity, not the stats; crazy weapons don't sell for an insane amount any more
+ Currency and Mana are separated. It's very satisfying to run around picking up huge amounts of gold.
+ All of  the DLC Maps, Characters, and Costumes are unlocked for free. There's some new maps that aren't in the original game
--
Cons:
-Rollbacks. This is almost enough to not recommend the game. Three times now I've completed a survival game only to return to the tavern and find all of my items/exp/money reset. Extremely frustrating and totally unacceptable. It happend twice after Trendy claimed it was fixed, but it HASN'T happened since the latest patch. I'll take this one off the list if I go a few more days without another rollback.
-Game UI: The UI is awful. When I say awful, I mean really, really, really bad. The item box is clunky and other than the ability to filter by rarity and item type, there's no sorting or ability to rearrange items at all. Folders are clunky. The only way to check an item's stats is to hover over it (why not a table view that shows each item on a row along with its stats?). There are random numbers and symbols everywhere with no explanation. Crafting is incomprehensible until you actually start finding blueprints and realize that it takes blueprints.
- Playverse UI: Stupid Javascript/Twitter Bootstrap overlay that's used to make parties and... I guess stream to twitch? There's a buch of useless buttons on that thing, and it feels totally out of place. Definitely needs to be replaced with ingame menus that acutally fit with the rest of the game. Right now if feels like they just copy+pasted a web page as an overlay and called it a day.
- Server Lag/Always Online: I understand why they went to server-side only, and I'm mostly happy about it. However there is occasional lag and rubberbanding. I'd rather than then hacked items, though, so it's not a huge deal for me. If you have an unstable internet connection, DON'T BUY THIS GAME.
- Bugs: Summoners are broken, some towers are broken, Dark Elf Warrior Ninja ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are broken. This stuff can all be fixed with patches, but it's still a pain in the butt. The Dark Elf Warriors will oneshot you on insane, then turn around and wreck your defenses. I refuse to believe that the insanity of the DEWs on endless spires on insane during the last wave are NOT bugged.
- UI: I know I said this one already, but seriously, the UI really sucks.
Misconceptions:
Cash shop: Now that I've played more, I realized that the cash shop is literally JUST emotes (at the moment.) It's not even outfits, it's just an animation that you can buy for a dollar. The concerning thing is that the infrastructure exists if they decide to sell more than just cosmetics, but they promised to keep the cash items cosmetic only.
'Mobile Game Port': Yeah, there's a dungeon defenders game for Android that's very close to the PC version, but I'd call that an exceptionally good Android game, not an exceptionally bad PC game. Controls are fine, video options are fine, gameplay is fine. I'm never in a place where I say "Wow, if this wasn't a mobile game port, X would be easier/better." If I never played the android version, I wouldn't beleive the game could even be ported to android and still work the way it does on PC.
In the end, I'd contine to state that if you like DD, you'll like DDE, especially if/when they fix the remaining bugs.

As someone who's put hundreds of hours into the base DD game, all of the negative reviews of this one were very concerning to me. Even then, I got enough enjoyment out of the base game that I didn't mind supporting the devs a bit more.
I don't know if I'm playing the same game as the people who played for .2 hours before downvoting it, but I'm beginning to think I'm not. From what I've played so far, it looks  like they took major steps towards fixing a lot of little annoyances from the base game- mana is no longer currency, everyone gets their own chests and gear drop, and hardcore mode is actually scary (when you die you lose all of your levels and gear!) They added consumables, new pet abilities, two weapon slots, and it looks like all of the paid map DLC from the base game is unlocked for everyone.
A big problem with the first game was hacked in items, a problem that appears, for the moment, to be solved.
I'm going to address a few concerns I've seen brought up.
In App Purchases: From what I'm seeing, the ONLY thing bought with real money is costumes which are purely cosmetic. I have no problem with that model, and usually nobody else does either.
Blurry Textures: If the reviewer played for more than a few minutes or read the on screen tips, he would have seen that the game downloads super low res textures to get you playing, and then continues the download of the rest of the assets in the background.
Mobile game port: I'm not sure if the game started out as a port from a mobile device, but it feels like a full featured PC game: tons of remappable keyboard shortcuts, graphics options, and controls that work well.
UI: This is the only place where I see problems. Creating a private match was simple enough, but the friends system took a little while to get used to. It appears to be a (Twitter Bootstrap Based) Javascript/HTML overlay that you get at by hovering over the top right corner. It feels really disjointed from the rest of the game's menus.
The bottom line is that if you like the original Dungeon Defenders PC game, you'll like this too. I feel like a ton of the negative reviews are by people that haven't put any time into actually playing the game.

Choplifter HD is a fun little game.
You fly your helicopter out on missions to rescue stranded soldiers, civilians, and even the odd media personality (you have to rescue a TV reporter, with his cameraman, on most levels).
Along the way you fight soldiers, insurgents - and even zombies!
It's a bit of an old-school side-scroller, which looks like it was based on an old helicpter rescue video game, circa 1980, but which has been updated to the year 2000.
But if you don't mind that, it can be a good game.
The little comments made by your co-pilot can be amusing, such as:
"Time to pin the bullet on the terrorist".
"Walk towards the light" (after I killed an armed insurgent).
"This is a chopper, not a battering ram" (a comment made after I crashed the heli a bit).
"I know if I had half a brain, I could be a reporter too".
He also refers to one dead terrorist, killed by rocket fire, as "Napoleon Blownapart". Nice one.
There were a few light-hearted comments made whilst fighting the zombie hordes:
"I think I dated that zombie".
"Can a zombie be a vegetarian?"
"I can't believe it, that's my Uncle Ted!"
"I wonder if zombies think people are ugly".
I would have loved it if this game was 3D, but you get what you pay for - and this game is a bit dated.
My only real complaint is that the shooting can sometimes be a bit off, with the aiming being a bit jerky in places.
Nonetheless, it's a fun game.
If you don't mind helicpter flying games which are a bit old, then I recommend that you get this one.

Amazing game. I have played this game for the first time and beaten it shortly before writing this review. So my opinion is non-biased on nostalgia.
The game is older, so the graphics, and art style are nothing compared to what is out now, and may be a little jarring at first, it was for me. This game has a lot of charm and tongue-in-cheek goodness to its tone, not taking itself too seriously. That said, I just couldn't get used to the turning controls. You have to push Q or E to rotate the chopper one way or the other, and I it's a crapshoot as to whether I hit the right button or not each time. Also, in one mission, a horde of enemies comes running from the "north," and you have to rescue to men on the bridge that horde is running south on...but you cannot turn "north" in this game, so the two guys get killed every time I see them.
New helicopters are locked behind getting more stars. Of course, to get more stars, you have to do better on missions. What's really annoying in the point system for me, which is what is used to calculate how many stars you're awarded, is that each killed civilian costs me 1,000 points. It doesn't matter if I kill the civilian or if someone else does. So on one mission, I saw two optional civilians. I could have just left them and they would have died, and it wouldn't have cost me anything. Instead, I risked my fuel, armor, and time to save the two men, and some random machine gun fire hit the chopper, killing one of those two fellows. So if those two men get killed by random bullets coming at you, then you just lost 2,000 points in additiona to the points you lost for the time you could have turned in for finishing early. This is counterintuitive. The risk of losing time is the gamble, and that's fine, but costing me extra points if they die? Really? =/
I do enjoy the humor of the game, though the scoring system is a bit too harsh for me to be able to make much headway, and turning the helicopter "south" is almost always a disaster for me. I really don't like the enemies being in the foreground, requiring the pressing of additional buttons to turn to shoot them. If you can get the game for $5 or less and don't care if you'll ever finish the game or not, and don't mind the potential to have trouble with the turning controls, you might enjoy this game. Anyone not terribly skilled should probably avoid the game, though.

Some years ago I saw a friend making his first steps in FEAR, now I give it a try of my own. My feelings are generally positive, though I probably should not have played all the three games in the package (the original and the two expansions) at once: when FEAR itself was over, I was excited, after finishing Extraction Point I was interested, and by the end of Perseus Mandate I was exhausted.
It's my first thriller, and I'm certainly not disappointed. The expansion packs deserve separate recognition: they are quite the way such additions should be. Perseus Mandate, for example, is in fact a yet another game, as lengthy as FEAR itself, and having a slightly different approach to storyline (which is, I dare say, generally better than the original).
There's mostly nothing to complain about, except for some issues with walls, doors, and other obstacles (especially corners): it's very, very annoying when you are completely covered by these, but bullets sometimes still go through and hit you. Except for that, the game gave pleasant experience.
Take caution if you have weak nerves. There are rivers of blood and many fearsome visions inside the game. Even I was frightened once or twice, though I'm very resistant to such things.

This game improves from the sequel. If you have not read my review on that then please read it before you read this. This review will make more sense if you know my thoughts on the first game of the series and see how Witcher 2 has fixed these problems.
Lets start with how they fixed my biggest complaint from the first game, the combat. When I started up Witcher 2, as soon as I tried the combat, I threw my arms up in joy to see how improved it is. They switched it from the three styles and clicking on the enemy to attack into what we are probably more used to now adays, one button being a fast attack and another button to do a strong attack. I cannot say in words how exactly this made me feel, you'd just have to see the differences for yourself. I will say that I suggest using a controller for at least only the combat cause I find it better that way.
The graphics have improved drastically as well and I felt like they hold up pretty well. The environments are beautiful and great to look at. The character models, like the combat, is improved so much as well. There is no scary character models unless you are meant to be afraid of them.
If you read the review on the first Witcher game, you might remember how I said that I felt like I didn't need to change my weapons for most of the game. They fixed that by adding a lot more options of swords and they get stronger as you level up and find them. You can only carry two weapons though, but like I said I only used the steel and silver swords anyway in the first game.
The characters are still quite memorable in Witcher 2 as they were in the first game. You even see quite a few familiar faces from the first game. I still meet these characters and I love to hear more about them and seeing all the different personalities.
Finally, lets get to the quests. The main story always stayed with the story and didn't feel like it went off rails like in the first game, but maybe too much so. I felt like it was a bit too linear. However, I actually felt like I was doing main quests and was going closer and closer to the ultimate goal as I did each of them. You do need to keep in mind that once you finish a level, there is no coming back, so if there are some side quests you wanted to do, you'd need to do them all before you finish all the main quests in the level.
The story itself was pretty good. Believe it or not, but I felt like Witcher 1's story might be a bit better, you know, around the end. The saved data even transfers from Witcher 1 to Witcher 2, and Witcher 2 even transfers to Witcher 3. I'll try not to spoil too much when talking about this. The main enemy was pretty cool as a nemesis, but for a video game character, he's kind of a let down. I think this because he's just a big strong guy and in the end you get to pick whether or not you want to kill him or not. I chose not to kill him because I already fought him earlier in the game and the fight would barely be any different if it's different at all. I think I forgot to mention that there are multiple endings to Witcher 1, but the same goes with Witcher 2. All your actions have consiquenses (not sure if I spelled that right, I'll check later), and you'd have to deal with whatever course you go with.
I hope you enjoyed my reviews on the first two Witcher games. I'll write a review on Witcher 3, but I am having so much fun with it, it'll take me a while to finish it.
