This review in a nutshell: Singleplayer was added, games now 500x better. Dont believe me?
You should. All the negative reviews on this page are before they added singleplayer in.
When you first log in, I will admit, its nuts. Have you ever been to a spawn town in a busy MMO, or gone to New York? Thats it. The tavern is a hub that EVERYONE uses. So, sometimes crazyness happens. But don't you worry, little girl, this is the only time your little loner side has to show like a sore thumb. Ignore the people. Go join A PRIVATE GAME. Dont join a public game if you dont want to join muilitplayer. BOOM! Your alone!
The gameplay hasn't really changed, other than you now get less mana. Or so it first seems... in singleplayer this doesn't really matter, but in muilitplayer, people used to NOT share chest, and made it so people couldn't even do anything because there was no mana to go around. They changed it so every player can open every chest. So, 3 people can touch the same chest and it wont go away for the forth person. So, every player gets the same amount of mana. Otherwise, in singleplayer, this change sucks, because your getting less mana.
The games pretty. Nuff said.
They added some new missons to the main campain. It will feel a bit fresh to older players.
The GUI, is uh... really, well ugly, acually. Its new. Does it feel rushed? Completely, acually. Its not something you can't get used to, mine you, but its odd.
Coustumes are now items, so only 1 person can wear them. Yea, it kinda sucks. You can see your armor though, so who knows what you'll look like in the end anyway.
2nd to last, the crafting system. Cool! At the time of this review I couldnt test it out, but I'm sure that i lets you dupe items for crafting ingredents you find on quests.
Finally, the shop system. Lots of people don't like the whole spending real money thing, but its only for cosmetics, so its okay. The new system goes like this. Instead of using mana, it uses coins, witch is found the same way mana is. Its a bit more rare, but you wont cry because you only got 5 peices in a run. The money can buy lots of new items that are consumed on use. These items do a varying amount of things, but an example is a mana collector. Place this bad boy down, and collects mana for you? Easy! Nice! Theres also mana potions, health potions, bombs, lots of awesome stuff.
So, yea buy this game. If you havn't bought dungeon defenders go buy this. Its worth it. If you have bought dungeon defenders, its up to you. Its a plunge your gonna have to take, but the new changes and others things I didnt take about in this review, You might be happy. Remember that you have a big discount because of you owning the game already.
Remember though, I'm a dude on the internet. I like DD a lot. I bought this game (before singleplayer) knowning it was bad. I bought it anyway, because I love DD. I'm not gonna make you use your wallet. (If you have it anymore after the steam summer sales!)
Oh, and all DLC carrys over. Nice!
If I write anything else, I'll start writing a novel. You get the idea. Check out more reviews, NOT THE ONES BEFORE SINGLEPLAYER, before you spent your money.

Wonderful love letter to the Quest for Glory series, and 100% FREE to boot. I was an old member of the Hero6 scene back in the day and remember the first screenshots of this game. Wonderful to see it finally released years later.
Great things:
+ Old Norse setting really adds to the game, with appearances by Loki, the valkyries, Sigurd, frost giants and tons of lore that will make you want to read up on viking mythology.
+ RPG stats really do matter, much more so than they did in the Quest for Glory games.
+ Combat system is fairly deep in the spirit of Quest for Glory 2; true, eventually you get strong enough to just click your way through most battles but each enemy has certain "tells" that you need to watch out for and dodging attacks takes practice. There are also many more enemies than I expected.
+ TONS of sidequests, and many are optional. Rogues, since they can steal stuff, actually have the option to bypass what feels like 80% of the side stuff in this game, making the replay value really substantial.
+ For a free AGS game, Heroine's Quest feels remarkably "alive", more so than some commercial releases. All of the characters have their own schedules and say different things when they're in the presence of different people. Some might find this annoying, since it can be hard to find a character during a certain time of day unless you know their schedule down to the hour, but I felt it added a lot of life to the adventuring experience.
Not as great things:
+ Main character is bland. I realize she's a blank slate like the hero in Quest for Glory (who was also bland but at least silent), but since the devs made the decision to make her talk, I felt they could have added more spice to her dialogue. She could have been as memorable as Roehm from Quest for Infamy.
+ I know quest logs aren't a traditional feature of adventure games, but this game could have benefitted from one since there are just so many side quests to keep track of.
+ Sometimes things veer into infamous "adventure game logic". Occasionally items that can be picked up are not obvious on screen and certain puzzle solutions seem illogical. I used the official walkthrough more than I would've liked and certainly would not have guessed that Rogues need to escape the blizzard with Heime by combining a certain two items.
+ Speaking of Rogues, it's REALLY easy to get caught by guards when thieving in this game. A few warning messages like "That was a close call! You really shouldn't try robbing that house again." or "Do you REALLY want to pick his pocket?" might have been appreciated.
Neutral:
+ The food/rest/freezing mechanic definitely won't be liked by all! At the start of the game it's so hard to pass out from the cold...this really makes the first few in-game days tough since you're constantly retreating back to town for warmth and worrying about food. I didn't mind this, since it really makes you feel like a badass at the end when you're just running through the forest with your stamina barely dropping. But I also "cheated" a few times by dropping the difficulty to zero when I was in danger of freezing/starving, lol...
Anyway, nitpicks aside - a lovely game! This came out the same time as Quest for Infamy, so I know a lot of people are wondering which of the two are better. Well, this one's FREE, and you can't beat that, but they're both good. In the end, Quest for Infamy is funnier and has a slightly more epic scope, but Heroine's Quest provides a tighter experience with better RPG mechanics and lore. Play both if you're an old school QFG fan.

This game improves from the sequel. If you have not read my review on that then please read it before you read this. This review will make more sense if you know my thoughts on the first game of the series and see how Witcher 2 has fixed these problems.
Lets start with how they fixed my biggest complaint from the first game, the combat. When I started up Witcher 2, as soon as I tried the combat, I threw my arms up in joy to see how improved it is. They switched it from the three styles and clicking on the enemy to attack into what we are probably more used to now adays, one button being a fast attack and another button to do a strong attack. I cannot say in words how exactly this made me feel, you'd just have to see the differences for yourself. I will say that I suggest using a controller for at least only the combat cause I find it better that way.
The graphics have improved drastically as well and I felt like they hold up pretty well. The environments are beautiful and great to look at. The character models, like the combat, is improved so much as well. There is no scary character models unless you are meant to be afraid of them.
If you read the review on the first Witcher game, you might remember how I said that I felt like I didn't need to change my weapons for most of the game. They fixed that by adding a lot more options of swords and they get stronger as you level up and find them. You can only carry two weapons though, but like I said I only used the steel and silver swords anyway in the first game.
The characters are still quite memorable in Witcher 2 as they were in the first game. You even see quite a few familiar faces from the first game. I still meet these characters and I love to hear more about them and seeing all the different personalities.
Finally, lets get to the quests. The main story always stayed with the story and didn't feel like it went off rails like in the first game, but maybe too much so. I felt like it was a bit too linear. However, I actually felt like I was doing main quests and was going closer and closer to the ultimate goal as I did each of them. You do need to keep in mind that once you finish a level, there is no coming back, so if there are some side quests you wanted to do, you'd need to do them all before you finish all the main quests in the level.
The story itself was pretty good. Believe it or not, but I felt like Witcher 1's story might be a bit better, you know, around the end. The saved data even transfers from Witcher 1 to Witcher 2, and Witcher 2 even transfers to Witcher 3. I'll try not to spoil too much when talking about this. The main enemy was pretty cool as a nemesis, but for a video game character, he's kind of a let down. I think this because he's just a big strong guy and in the end you get to pick whether or not you want to kill him or not. I chose not to kill him because I already fought him earlier in the game and the fight would barely be any different if it's different at all. I think I forgot to mention that there are multiple endings to Witcher 1, but the same goes with Witcher 2. All your actions have consiquenses (not sure if I spelled that right, I'll check later), and you'd have to deal with whatever course you go with.
I hope you enjoyed my reviews on the first two Witcher games. I'll write a review on Witcher 3, but I am having so much fun with it, it'll take me a while to finish it.

The game is good if you compare it to other initial release 4x titles, however there are some serious flaws when it comes to diplomacy, UI, warfare, and combat balancing.
Diplomacy is very rigid, there aren't a whole lot of options when it comes to how you can interact with the AI. There are also many diplomacy options left out, like war target coordination among allies, vassal bullying, and espionage.
The AI is very docile and stupid, once you get into the midgame there seems to be a lull. Even once the late game events start happening, entire galactic empires will just fall without trying to reach out or plead for help from other empires.
The UI is good in some areas, but confusing and time consuming in others. You have to zoom into a planet to know how many pops it can support, upgrading buildings is time consuming without an "upgrade all" option available, there isn't a clear construction queue window, and sectors are usually poorly managed by the AI and inefficient.
Warfare is a glorified game of whack-a-mole. Like I said before, there is no war coordination, so the AI will decide to either follow you, or warp between systems while doing basically nothing. Very rarely will your allies actually chase an enemy fleet or conquer a planet without following the player to that objective. Defensive stations and starports are weak, and since the game has no frontlines you are going to be constantly bombarded by smaller and weaker fleets that warp into your key systems and wipe them out, and then quickly retreat before you can catch them.
Combat balancing is very poor at the moment, as you can just spam the smallest ships available (Corvettes) with small plasma/laser weapons with some point defense and shields, and they will overcome diverse fleets of different ships and capabilities with ease, even if they have less firepower. This is mainly due to their high evasion stat, and the fact that bigger ships have no advantages (except Battleships, only for certain capabilities), but all of the weaknesses of being bigger and slower. There are also no fleet formations, so both fleets just end up in a giant furball of doom firing at each other from close range, even if they have mid or long range weapons.
To sum it up, the early game is really good and enjoyable, but sadly the mid and late game is bland and needs more to do and some polish. Also some alternative victory conditions need to be set, only having conquest is pretty bland and is something I really can't forgive. Most of the issues will probably be resolved within the coming months through patches, which is why I would recommend this game to diehard 4x or Paradox fans, but to everybody else I'd say you should wait a bit.

Combat is definitely less clunky, and I would recommend playing with a controller. Combat feels like a mid ground between Dark Souls and the type of combat used in games like Batman Arkham Asylum, or Shadow of Mordor. Some people dislike it, but I think it works well enough. It is very punishing difficulty wise however. One wrong move could cost you your life. Once I got used to the combat, I came to appreciate it, and enjoyed the challenge. Over all, The Witcher 2 is an excellent game that you won't want to miss.

Galactic Civilizations 3. Is a direct evolution of Galactic Civilizations 2 ( hereout Galactic Civilizations title will be shortened to GalCiv). While not revolutionary, and only offering some great new graphics and a few new features, it does run like a charm in comparison to its predecessor. The on screen battle videos are much better entertainment. I find myself cheering for my ships as they duke it out.
For those of you new to galciv games. These are a turn based strategic 4x set in a space galaxy, either via campaign or sandbox. Galciv games are highly modable. The mods are often hosted on
. In galciv 2 i played both star wars vs star trek mod (self explanatory) and the Babylon 5 mod (also self explanatory). These offer a great measure of replayability in comparison to other 4x strategies. You have civilzation building elements like in most of 4x. These take place on a planet to planet basis. So yes, a lot of colonizing. In this iteration of Galciv, in fact, you can chose to do an insane amount of colonizing. Playing a single game that spans over 100 hours of gameplay. No two games are alike either, as you can choose who your openents are. Did i mention multiplayer? Yes they've got that also. One flaw is that unlike some other 4x games there is no hotjoining. So you have to make some friends to play multiplayer. Yet don't let that discourage you, single player is fun. You have other elements such as starbase building that work quite different than most 4x. Starbases can be economic boosters, military boosters, influence boosters or relic harvesters. Which bring me to relics. Relics are a feature from Galciv 2 ( haven't played 1). They provide bonuses to your civilization such as better research, production, influence. Now what is this influence stuff? It works much like culture off of the Sid Meier's Civlisation games. With one major exception. No great people. Influence expands your territory and can even flip enemy planets. There is also an influence victory option in sandbox.
One last thing I'd like to mention is customizability. Galciv 3 is custumizable with its randomly generated sandbox maps, and custom race creation. Due to this I hardly ever play the same map or the same race twice. It also has difficulty levels for all gaming levels. From complete noob to the ultimate 4x player.
Things I do not recommend for Galciv 3 are, buying the dlc without checking the reviews carefully. The dlc may or may not be worth the price for you. It's your choice but don't regret it.
In summary if you like 4x you will like Galciv 3. You may not love it but you will have fun. Isn't that what games are for. I give Galciv 3 8/10

Summary: Quest for Glory in Midgard
Multiplayer: No
Completion: 16 hrs
Cards: Yes - must craft or receive boosters, buy from the market or trade to obtain
Cloud: No
The Quest for Glory series by Sierra were basically adventure games with RPG character development and combat tacked on. Imagine King's Quest but with the ability to fight foes in actual combat instead of dying every five seconds to the environment. Heroine's Quest takes much of its inspiration from these series of games and adds a few mechanics of its own.
Right away you'll notice the generous use of norse mythology, even hinted in the game's subtitle. The decision to have this set so directly in norse mythology feels somewhat odd to me. Rather than creating its own mythology that's inspired by real life mythology, this one references it directly and loosely retells those stories. It's not a bad thing - Disney does that all the time. But this one feels a tad out of place.
There's some good humor here and there. The squirrel is great. I enjoyed the Tetris game over. I feel it could use a few more laughs though. Roughly 80% of the characters are intensely serious, and they don't quite gel in a world that has silly characters like Aurvandel.
The art and music is fantastic. The game world feels somewhat barren, but this is more a fault of the genre, as many adventure games tend to include many screens with little interactivity. I would have liked more items sprinkled on the ground that you could pick up.
The hunger/survival mechanic is strange at best. Adventure games generally reward you for exploring. Heroine's Quest instead punishes you for straying too far, or taking your time. Because of the survival gimmick, the puzzle-solving seems to take a backseat because you're always pressed for food and warmth. Thankfully you can shut this feature off, but I did try to play it as intended and did not find it increased the fun factor at all.
The combat system is pretty simplistic. It's one-on-one real time combat with menu inputs, much like the QFG1-3. Nothing special, and not irritating. It's just there.
Most of the game is voice acted, which is rare for indie adventure games. Huge thumbs up for that! Most voices are good, though Hervor sounds curiously tired and disinterested. I get that there's a deadly winter, and everyone is at their wits end, but I would have liked a more likeable character to wake up to first thing than her.
The map is greatly appreciated! This also gets a huge thumbs up. That is definitely something missing from just about every adventure game.
Perhaps the most striking feature of this game is the fact that it is free! Try it out. You've got absolutely nothing to lose but time. The sheer amount of work that must have gone into it cannot be understated. I enjoyed it enough that I believe it deserves a donation. I give this game a 8/10

Final Fantasy VIII is a wonderful throwback to the multi-disk, open world RPG's of the Playstation Era. It has an interesting (albeit somewhat convoluted) story, multi-dimensional characters that have compelling motivations behind their actions, and a world full of incredible environments and enemies.
No game is without fault. The experience system of the game is flawed in that it actually rewards the player for NOT leveling up, and the Draw system (which allows you to stockpile enemy magic for junctioning) can become tedious at times, but with the inclusion of the Magic Booster modification and playing enough Triple Triad (the trading-card minigame within the FF8 world) you can bypass the more tedious parts of the game.
Final Fantasy VIII, like any other Final Fantasy game, has 100+ hours of playability, is chock full of quests and side missions that take you around the world, into outer space, and deep, deep into the dark ocean depths. For veteran players looking for a nice piece of nostalgia or players who want to experience a classic RPG, Final Fantasy VIII is certainly a good buy.

A pretty game in the style of the Journey that somewhat fells short of it's spiritual predecessor.
There is no way to review this game without comparing it to the Journey. It's pretty much the same premise. There is not much game in a game - it is a very calm, beautiful experience that focuses on the journey of the main character rather than any particular story or puzzle solving.
Starting off with the setting. You're a some kind of diver travelling through an underwater world. So here's the first thing you need to know - the whole game is an underwater level. That gives you some additional movement directions but you're going to be swimming all the time. The good thing is the swimming does not feel sluggish like in some games and is pretty enjoyable. This however puts some limits on the level design. The areas need to be enclosed and because of that they feel more like a series of lakes or pools rather than open waters - although there are instances of that but are rather rare.
The graphics are stunning - very colourful and alive. Sometimes it feels like there's too much going on at the same time, but still it sets a very good relaxing feeling. Accompanied by a superb soundtrack it's a game to just chill and feed your senses.
The game however lacks a bit in the meat of the game. When played there's very little aside the visuals and great music. When playing Journey I had the feeling of going somewhere, discovering different ruins, wall paintings gave a sense of discovery and progression. There was this mountain in the distance I was going to reach and on my way I learned about the world through environment. This is missing here. You just swim from area to an area. Touch an underwater thing to release some fish. Swim with fish. Activate some underwater drone that will cut open a net in the way and swim again. There are some triangular things floating in the water but somehow they lack context. I never felt intrigued. Just swam from one area to the next.
Overall I kind of enjoyed the game. Though it felt a lesser experience when compared to Journey. It's definitely pretty and worth picking up if you know what you're getting into. If presented with choice - go for Journey.

*FINAL REVIEW*
Contrary to it's namesake, I find F.E.A.R. to be far from scary in the slightest. To me, any horror game worth it's title does not have a shotgun and instead leaves the player feeling helpless and hunted.
Not to say that F.E.A.R. isn't good, the game has an addicting combat system, very dynamic gore and a wide range of enemies to keep the pace flowing.
The game's combat system is simple in theory, you are given three weapon slots which you can fill with any weapons you come across during the game, allowing the player to mix and match any combination of shotguns, assault rifles, grenade launchers, even spike launchers and particle rifles. The player also has access to a skill called "reflexes" which allows the player to effectively slow down time to either initiate an assault on a fortified position, allow an escape from a dangerous situation or to simply take in the hilarious ragdolls from a dated engine. Exploration of the maps gives the player opportunities to find boosters to increase their max health and the size of their reflex bar, making them a greater threat to their enemies.
F.E.A.R.'s gore system, given the game's age, is very impressive and hardly any games I've seen recently come close to comparing to it. From simply dismembering enemies by shooting off limbs/heads to reducing them to red mist or a charred skeleton to even sawing them clean in half with a mothertrucking shotgun. Not many games I've seen can allow you to turn your enemies into a red puddle by blasting them point-blank with a buckshot. SMOD is the only other game I can think of, and it's only a mod for Half-Life 2.
Enemies in the game start off as the tried and true generic gas-mask soldier, the likes of which have been seen in other games like Half-Life 2 and Mass Effect 3. As the player progresses new enemies are added to the mix, forcing the player to adapt their strategies and keep the experience fresh. You might be doing an amazing push when suddenly a heavily armored tank soldier wielding a rocket launcher comes at you, forcing you to fall back and lay the path with grenades. Or a group of invisible ninja-esque soldiers can appear forcing you to go on the defensive.
The game's story I must admit leaves a bit to be admired, the characters feel two-dimensional and are difficult to care about, and the player will often find themselves annoyed by the slow-paced Alma scare scenes meant to advance the story. But if you have the capacity to pay attention to the story then at the end of the credits you'll be rewarded with a twist and a cliffhanger for the sequel.
F.E.A.R. also suffers from some irritating bugs caused by all the recent updates to Steam's UI. By simply holding down the W key, Steam takes a screenshot every 2.5 seconds, resulting in a flooded screenshots folder than needs to be cleared out regularilty. It's like playing Pokemon Snap on the N64 with the A button taped down.
In conclusion, despite it's software compatability hiccups and it's forgettable storyline, F.E.A.R.'s gameplay is unique and highly enjoyable. If you have the capacity to work around the screenshot bug then I definately recommend this game.

Having this and FFIV been long-term games of mine since I was very young, old enough to read the lines of dialogue on screen (even if just barely... pronouncing "innocent" as "in-connect" at that time), I can admit that to an extend, I do suffer from nostalgia bias. I've gone from the six-year-old getting his butt stomped at every major boss fight to a teenager who finally, barely beat it... to a young adult who dominated it in every way he cared to.
Having said that, and given it some time between the now and the last, victorious playthrough a few weeks ago, I think I've stewed on it long enough to give an honest review.
Is this game good?
Yes, it is. Granted, it's dated... noticably so. But it's aged fairly well over the past two decades, to the point where it's enjoyable both nostalgiac players and new ones.
What do I like about it in particular?
I like that, as a person who's been digging into the FF franchise most of my life, I can say that the newer FF games are among the first to ascribe literary thematics into the story, actually trying to tell a tale that can be summed up in terms more complicated than "an epic adventure".
Previous FF titles had simple premises, seemingly designed solely for children... "take a cause, fight for it, BBEG appears, pursue them, save the world". An actual story is attempted in FF7 and beyond, each with it's own thematics that make each story worth reading through, which I believe is essentially for modern RPGs. Tones of personal identity, environmentalism, and the threat of human greed play forefront roles in the story.
I also like the Materia system, to an extent. I like to grind in my games... whereas when I was young, an RPG was merely an interactive story-telling experience laced with action, I've since come to appreciate character/stat development, and while each individual doesn't level up in any exciting way (get exp/levels, use/learn/use again Limit Breaks) Materia picks up some of the slack.
You find/buy Materia that grants magic/summons/skills/advantages/etc., you equip it and AP farm, you master the Materia to where it buds off into a new, unseasoned Materia in addition to the last one, and on and on it goes. The benefit of this is that, given time and sufficient work, You can switch Materia between characters as desired, and if you're very careful to grab and master all Materia as you find them, you can fuse all like-colored maximized Materia into singular ones that possess abilities from them all.
After buying this game, and about a hundred hours later, I had three battle-hardened, super-wizard characters who could stand proudly on the corpses of the game's toughest enemies, including the sadistically hard Superbosses it possessed.
What do I dislike?
In terms of story-telling, I don't care for it's environmental tones. That's not to say that caring for the environment isn't important, but in a game, it's rather impersonal. I for one enjoy stories that connect to the human experience, and in such a way that the players can identify with. Unless you're an environmental activist or something similar, tales of a dying planet might not connect with you personally, the way later FF titles would, like in FF8 (love, and the things we do for it), FF9 (life, and the ability to ascribe value to it), and FF10 (hope, despair, and the role faith plays in them).
I also dislike the blocky graphics of the game... granted, this was Square's first 3D endeavor, so it's not going to be an easy transition, but I'm not going to pretend that I enjoy having Lego characters take up the majority of the game in all but the most important of cutscenes.
Overall, it's fun for me. There are many things from my childhood that I revisted as an adult and came to hate. We tend to look upon the past through rose-tinted glasses, and when exploring it, we often find ourselves quite disappointed. I'm glad to say I wasn't disappointed with this game.

Choplifter is a sidescrolling arcade game, in which you pilot a rescue helicopter which must save civillians in warzones while fending off enemy troops. Choplifter was an old favorite of mine when I grew up; I played it often on the Commodore. When I saw the remake, I just had to get it.
The game both succeeds and fails in a number of ways. It does a good job of replicating the gameplay of the original, and while they've added some more features, including multiple weapons, a speed boost, limited fuel and different chopper types, it's similar enough that the game feels very nostalgic.
There's also more enemy types, including AA guns and RPGs, and the various stages show off mediocre, but visually pleasing environments from cities to deserts and jungles. Furthermore, there's some mildly humorous comments from your co-pilot and the various people you pick up during the game.
Unfortunately, you have to deal with aiming controls which often don't work properly (you can aim in an arc around your chopper, and if often doesn't recognize your mouse unless you're in a sweet spot), and AI which often spoils your fun. It's not uncommon to fly in to rescue a civilian who then promptly runs in under your chopper and kills himself, or takes forever to figure out how to board the helicopter. These issues aren't severe enough that you'll hate the game, but you will be annoyed by it occasionally.
CONCLUSION:
If you're a fan of the original, it's worth taking a look. Even if this is your first encounter with it, it has the appeal of an addicting flash game - kind of entertaining, but very difficult to put down once you start playing. It probably doesn't have too much lasting appeal and it's still kind of broken, but if you wanna kill time, it does the job.

Doom II is the sequel to one of the most innovative, important and legendary games of all time. Doom II is, in all senses of the word, a better game than the original. While it doesn't add a whole lot, it does add one of the greatest FPS weapons of all time, the Super Shotgun, and some more enemies, and thrity-one new open and fun levels, two of them secrets.
Today however, it can be a bit hard to get into Doom II, seeing how the engine is twenty years old and that can take some getting used to. There is no vertical mouselooking, meaning you cannot look up or down with the mouse, only left and right, and moving around in general can be awkward as moving the mouse forward moves the player forward.
That doesn't make it something you shouldn't play through though, it's an important piece of gaming history and is still fun to play if you're a fan of old-school styled FPS's like myself. It's still a joy to run through these classic levels pumping demons full of lead. Just put yourself in the right mindset and remember that Doom II is an old man now, and you'll enjoy your time with it.

So I'm gonna preface this by saying that I am a massive fan of paradox strategy games and I have many many hours into Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis
Stellaris is 4x space exploration game In which you command a species that has just managed to create some form of faster than light technology and is ready to explore and colonise the stars, as you expand you will find other similar space faring empires with whom you can form alliances with or wage war. You can also research technologies in a quasi-random manner (explained later) and design your own vessels from scratch in the ship designer.
I want to start this review off by stating clearly that Stellaris feels unfinished and needs polish. There is room for improvement everywhere from the combat, diplomacy, to the management of your empire. I have over the course of my playthroughs noticed fairly commonly assets appearing where they shouldn't such as the center of the galaxy being a missle, some assets not dissapearing such as the visual effects from the ships FTL drives which at one point lead to me to believe during a war that my opponents fleet was in a entirely different place than where it actually was. Speaking of war, AI is a bit strange during war, allies tend to rush to you and stick to your fleets instead of doing independent activities which is annoying because It means you'll probably have to guide their navies around or they'll end up losing. During lategame crisies such as Invaders from a different dimension the AI doesnt really care to send their fleets to attack their home system, meaning that if you are playing singleplayer you'll probably have to fight them all off yourself and the sectors that you can use to automate parts of your empire really need more options.
Now that I've explained that to you lets begin.
The planet management I'll go over firstly, planets are based on tiles and citizens work these tiles, some tiles may have a bonus to a certain type of resource like maybe one tile gives +1 Food even though nothing is built upon it, It's very Civilisation like in this manner, requiring a surplus of food to get new citizens and then being able to build farms, mines, research labs, military acadamies ect ect, the number of these tiles depends of the planets size, the size meaning how many there are. There Is nothing particularry wrong with it but there is one minor gripe that I have and that is that planets don't differ in how much minerals they have or how fertile they are. A barren planet is just as good at producing food as a tropical one is which is a bit strange, I first thought that the "habitability" of a planet was how fertile it was but actually it's just what the maximum happiness is but aside from that minor gripe I have, I actually had a bit of fun min-maxing planets to do certain goals like minerals or research.
Species and empire creation is suprisingly indepth allowing you to create a species and an empire from scratch. You create a species select their appearence from a wide variety of options and give them traits for example one of my games I was playing as a Avian race that was industrious and dilligent at work but were weak at ground combat, then you create their government. You can select their ethics which is basicly what their society believes in. As in, are you millitaristic or pacifists, Spiritualistic or Materialist ect ect. Normally most of the time Empires have 2 ethics one of which is a extreme version of one (EG: Fanatic Pacifist and Individualist but you can have 3 at maximum (Pacifist, Materialistic and Induvidualist to give an example) these change the options during events and give bonuses. Once you have selected your ethics you then select a government type that Is based upon those ethics, So If I picked militaristic I can be a Dictatorship, or  Moral Democracy If I picked Pacifist. There are quite a large number of different government types and I was really surpised by just how many options there were, I mean you even get to choose what the cities look like which are only ever seen when you are looking at the planet overview menu.
There is no real goal that the game sets for you to accomplish which is similar to other Paradox titles, instead you set your own goals and try and accomplish them, I personally enjoy to role-play who I am playing as. Which Stellaris lets you do very nicely thanks to it's ethics system, I think the way that ethics work is great for people who like to role-play and I enjoyed playing as a Fanatic Collectivist and Xenophobic hivemind hell bent on the continued existance of my species and mine alone regardless of the cost.. The ethics sytem isnt just good for roleplaying though, as AI empires are randomized It meant that every time I played I never found the same nation or species twice. One game my neighbors were federation builders who wanted to create an alliance with me, the next I was surronded by millitaristic expansionist empires and constantly fought wars and had to prioritize millitary research tech as I tried to survive. I never felt bored when I was starting a new game and I was never in the same situation twice which I absolutely love as it make the game very replayable, although It is worth stating that if you are not role-playing you may end up feeling restricted by the ethics system as It means at certain times you can't do certain things and It may even be a detriment at times.
Now research is a bit weird. I mentioned earlier that you can research technologies in a "quasi-random manner" and I'm gonna simplify it a tiny bit If you want a indepth explanation then check the Stellaris wiki page. Now. In Stellaris you have 3 areas of technology, Physics, Society and Engineering, now Stellaris doesn't really have a tech tree instead once you have researched a technology 3 new ones appear at random for you to select, at the start of the game some techs are coded to always appear for example the tech that allows you to build colony ships will always appear at the start but past that it is all random but some techs are weighted to appear more than others. Now personally I'm a bit 50-50 on this system because while it does mean that there is alot of varience in terms of what different empires are good or bad at, It meant that quite a few times RNG utterly screwed me and I didnt get any of the techs to build bigger ships which eventually lead to a war and then I entered a death spiral which eventually left me defeated. However you can reduce this RNG through reverse engineering, after a battle, destroyed ships turn into debris and researching it does two things, firstly is adds a percentage of research progress to whatever technology the ship had on it like better missles or shields and secondly makes those techs always avaliable to research, untill they are researched which is a good way of balancing out the RNG aspect.
The ship designer is pretty good, you create a ship based on modules called sectors these sectors have inside them differing numbers of slots of differing sizes and It also varies the look of the ships depending on what sectors you have selected for them which Is a nice touch. In general you can add stuff to you ship such as shields, armour, weapons and power supplies. There is only one main issue with the ship designer and that Is that the auto-generated ships tend to be rubbish so It's probably for the best that you design the ships yourself.
Apparently I've hit the character limit so here is very brief conclusion.
Steam needs neutral reviews. I personally utterly adore Stellaris as It scratches an itch that I've had for a while but at the moment it needs polish and a lot of it. If you want to buy It but are even the slighest bit unsure then wait for the patches and DLC to come in a few months and then determine if it's worth it.

The whole MOBA concept as we know it now is highly overrated as it's seriously flawed by a number of issues, such as too long matches, repetitive game play with same builds, and community harassment. I've played DOTA and LOL pretty extensively but eventually left both. As for DaT it has addressed a number of key issues of the concept while adding a nice twist to it. The game plays differently unlike any MOBA you've played before, but the new control system seems to work pretty nice since you cannot lose your character in the middle of the fight, which often happens with inexperienced players in other MOBAs, designers have put a lot of thought and imagination in the dragons and the main map feels better that a regular "three lanes" map. The matches are usually 10-15 minutes long, so even if you're stuck with a bad team, it doesn't hurt you all that much, hence no harassment. The flaw with repetitive builds was fixed with weapons that are chosen before the match: they give you two abilities along with the two provided by your dragon. This gives you an imaginable number of variants that will keep you from getting bored for a long time
All in all, this game won't replace DOTA2 or LoL but will have a consistent player base that will grow over time. As for those claiming it to be "P2W", those players don't understand the whole concept of this model. DaT is a free to play title since no other player will get an advantage over you that you will not be able to get eventually, it does require some grind, but when you enjoy the game you don't really notice it. The only flaw I've come across - the game needs some polishing, but I believe it will get there eventually.
And the game still holds well after all that time.

Why is this game called Dragons and Titans?
You're a dragon lord, who rides dragons into battle. Now, why this is cool is you get a dragon with it's own unique abilities, and your rider can use a helpful weapon, so rather than filling inventory with objects and potions you're using abilities you specify as you progress. Once you reach enemy base, you find YOUR Titan is trapped there, and once you break the cage, you free them.
Now for the negatives I noticed.
If you are just trying to practice to get a feel for the game, you will want to go and do the prologue and the acts. That's fine and dandy, but the learning curve is harsh even on Easy (because yeah, when I'm new, I'm going to hit Easy, k?) So you will find yourself frustrated time and time again with going through the entire thing after losing 4 lives (4 total, you get 3 hearts, and once you die after that, you have to start over).
The biggest, most horrendously awful thing about this game:
Sometimes, those acts bug out. Mobs will not come on que as they should to progress, leaving you looking around frustrated until you decide to quit. The good news here is that if you quit "the match" (again, this is an act, not playing with others) you will be able to try it again and then the enemes spawn accordingly.
I don't know about you, but that seems almost game breaking to have to QUIT just to play the damn thing. I'm genuinely hoping this is addressed and repaired.
Aside from that, I do recommend this game, it's fun, the music is fantastic, and you feel like you're getting somewhere (when things aren't wonky).
===Edit===
Also, some people are complaining that this is a pay to win game. As of 3/15/2014 this game actually gives you freebies for doing tutorials and stuff. Free crystals to buy a pack of dragons and weapons. No, you can't specify which ones you get, but I'm not complaining x3

I personally like the game, but like others, are a bit jaded on the details of what is new or included. I'll break it down best I can.  The game is basicly a GotY edition of Dungeon Defenders, including the DLCs from the original, but also including changes and new levels.
- You share one tavern.  I assume it has a cap, so there are several taverns.  To those who never played the base game, the tavern is where you prep before going into a game, sell items, and can goof off.
You will be paired with like, leveled people.  You still get to choose what level and difficulty you choose to play on.
- Your item drops in a game are yours.  You don't have to worry about someone taking an upgrade because of the matchmaking.
- Yes the game looks bad when you first load, as many reviews have said.  This is due to the game streaming textures and whatnot the first time you need them.  It only downloads once.  That's why the download for the game through steam is quite small.
- Everyones favorite thing to hate.  Currently (June 22, 2014), the game only has emotes as microtransaction items.  A bit overpriced, but they are cosmetic only.
- It just dumps you into a lobby, the tavern.  No character creation, no explaination of controls.  Ask in chat and someone will probably gladly point you in the right direction.
- They decided to use their own matchmaking system, with its own friends list, party making and trade system.  The reason probably stems from cross-platform play with phones/tablets.  This can be seen as a good thing if you plan to play on your phone or tablet as well.
- This shortcoming is already being fixed tonight; seems like an oversight by them.  I think they were hoping to have a bustling matchmaking system, instead of a bunch of private games.
- You'll be starting at level 1 again.
- Pets now have abilities you can activate.  You'll find pet eggs you can hatch.  And there are items you can use in combat, like health potions and bombs, as well as buffs.  Also they added a dodge ability.
Despite my short list of what I liked, I really enjoyed the original, and look forward to leveling up and seeing how the end-game has changed.  For people who haven't played the original, this is the version to get.  If you have the original and are debating getting this one for the discounted price, look at the things I highlighted.  Comment on this review if you have questions or want clarity.

I want to start out by saying I'm somewhat apprehensive about leaving a 'not recommended' review and that there is a good chance that this review will be revised in time to a positive review.
Here is, in my opinion, the biggest problem Stellaris faces: It tries to be a 4X and a GS game at the same time, but does neither particularly well. The viewpoints of both crowds can easily be found in the various gripes of online forums and reviews but to summarize: The tactical options and style of aggressive play do not suit the competitive 4X/RTS gamers while the simplicity and limited scope [and even absense] of numerous elements pertinent to grand strategy games will annoy or disappoint the GS gamers.
That's what is wrong with this game in a nutshell.
On the flip side, it does a lot right:
Unfortunately, numerous annoyances remain:
Overall it's a great start and a good framework for something that could truly be made into a game that stands apart from everything else out there. But until many of these problems are rectified and the game is fleshed out that's all it is: framework.
If you're on the fence about buying, my advice would be to wait a couple of months and see where the project goes. Given Paradox's sales numbers for this game, I think it is going to be supported and updated for some time to come. Check back in six months or so.
Another patch or two and maybe another solid DLC pack are still needed for me to flip this review positive. It is improving though!

My old review was literally me saying that I was playing as a race of robots enslaving Space penguins. I will now make an actual review. Keep in mind I will mention Mods alot because I mod every game I can and they become part of a core experience to me, Like modding fallout or skyrim or something like that.
Stellaris is a very fun Strategy game were you manage and soon to be universe scale empire. You start out with making your own race, You choose their portraits, ships, name, traits, goverment and ethics. I really enjoy this system and because its a paradox game with amazing mod support you will get a ton more of all of those things i listed with mods.
You start out with just a science ship, A construction ship, and 3 corvettes. You need to scan the surrounding solar system and other systems with your science ship to learn about the local resources and plants that you can occupy. Once you have probed around you can construct a frontier outpost and eventually colonize the area to get a permenant foothold, I really enjoy this, But I also don't like the beginning game if I get a slow start. IMO I wish we had the option to choose a "Starting tech level" Like how you could choose an era for the game to start in Civilization games.
War. War is very enjoyable and I love making my own ships and choosing their loadouts and naming their classes and such. I also just feel like a badA$$ during war, Like "Glassing" a planet then laying down troops for a ground assault to finally take over those dirty space fish. It just feels cool. Also forcing them to be your vassal, Thats pretty cool to.
Im sorry if this review is all over the place, but i really enjoy the game and recommend it to anybody who likes Strategy games or wants to try something new. 8/10.

With a fair learning curve, manipulative save system and genuine fun factor, F.E.A.R. not only goes the extra mile as a game, but as an example to all future first-person shooters.  The original game-play mechanics, namely slow-motion, bring a satisfying flavor that some future games have failed to reciprocate (properly).  Being a survival-horror game, there are points where the game offers jump scares and the occasional plot twist that works against the protagonist, giving players a chance to feel, if just a little, genuine fear.  Despite these elements, there's clearly a greater emphasis on action and strategy over story (though that alone has never kept a good game down).  While F.E.A.R. and it's expansion packs do offer a fun, memorable experience, the primary issue with this game is poor optimization for PC's; players may be forced to unplug and re-plug their mice and keyboards in order to keep their USB ports from flooding, which creates unplayable lag on any machine (for more info, go here:
.  The fact that the game hasn't been optimized for resolutions other than 4:3 and the loss of it's (supposedly) strong multiplayer support also testifies to the game's failures in standing the test of time.  Technical shortcomings aside, F.E.A.R. offers dedicated gamers a game that's not only fun to master, but philosophically engaging.

Fans of the classic adventure games by Sierra will be right at home when playing this. Taking heavy inspiration from the Quest for Glory Series
that was released throughout the 90s the game doesn't fail to live up to it's high standards.
The story is pretty straight forward and once again pays homage to the Quest for Glory series. Like in the older title you are a hero(ine) who is suddenly stranded in a foreign land and then forced to deal with impending doom. The story takes many twists and turns along the way and is intricately crafted to keep you on your toes.
The gameplay is equally inspired. You have a choice of three character classes to chose from when you start. Each class has their own unique traits and skills. The enjoyable part is, much like the classics, each obstacle you face can usually be solved in different ways. Magic, brute strength, or sleight of hand can be used to accomplish each task differently.  Conversational options can also change the required task. This creates the chance for a varied play through and replayability.
The combat is the Quest for Glory series was never it's strong point and it's not the strongest point of this game either. It does get the job done though and isn't a turn off.
The music and sound effects and crisp and enjoyable and fits the atmosphere of the current screen well. The voice acting is excellent if somewhat varied in it's quality.
The artwork is amazing. It represents the 90s game style perfectly. Backgrounds that look like they could have been hand painted fit together well and make the world feel well put together. The sprite work is clean and well executed. The portrait pictures for the characters are interesting and give a face to what would otherwise be a handful of pixels.
All together the game is simply amazing, especially  for something that is offered for free on Steam. If you're the person who feels adventure gaming hit it's peak in the 90s and misses the feeling those games give you this one will be exactly what you want. It feels like a game that was made by Sierra in that era and simply unearthed later.
If you've never played the classics then I still recommend you give this one a shot. Then after you complete this one I recommend you check out some of classics that inspired it and run through the entire Quest for Glory series.

Pros:
- Fun gameplaying
- Humorous
- Combos to solve
- Freaking creepy/awesome story
Cons:
- Gets old quickly
- Have to wait for purchases
- Short game
- A bit pricey
In short, you burn a whole ton of stuff. You pyromaniacs out there, this game is for you! Each item has a special event that occurs when you burn it (like setting a credit card on fire releases a bunch of dollar bills) and there are 140 things + the mail you receive to light up! So there is a lot of variety. This game also has the Tomorrow Corporation sense of humor (which I find hilarious), so it'll make you laugh! There are also "combos" to try to solve (burning certain items together), but they are pretty easy. There is actually a story in this game and it comes from the letters you receive, which explains the atmosphere. You can get a glimpse of it in the trailer. I absolutely loved it! It was very simplistic, but had this eery tone to the letters that kept me on edge. If you've played any other games by Tomorrow Corporation, you'll know what I'm talking about :) The two problems I had with the game were that there is a waiting time after you order an item, so you spend a lot of time waiting for your purchases (well, by a lot I mean around a minute on average). The other thing is that it can get old pretty quickly. You burn stuff. That's basically it. I get tired of it after about an hour or so of playing. Then I come back another day and have fun again. In conclusion, I had a fun time with it, and would recommend it to people. Just get it on sale :)

Just a few words: Absolutely beautiful!
This is what was going through my mind as I played through this game.
----BEGINNING: "This game looks great! this is a nice little time-waster"
----Beginning-Middle: "Oh man, this just gets better and better. I wonder what does what? This is so neat! The music is PHENOMENAL!"
----Middle: "Oh my gosh... things are getting good! I don't quite know what is going on here, but I am liking it."
----Middle-End: "Oh man... that was so sad. Why oh why?! And everything just keeps getting better and better play-wise."
----Almost-End: "The story, it is unfolding before my eyes. What seemed like nothing but a time waster is so good!"

Alright, here we go. This'll be a fairly short "review" after a rough playtime of seven hours and much, much regret. First off - I did not enjoy myself, but the people I played with had a significant resistance to nonsense and wanted to see if the game is even beatable in its current condition.
In case you're wondering: Yes, it's indeed beatable. Out of the... roughly 42 games we played, we've won one. All on easy, with roughly 3 people on average total. It didn't feel like a victory though, since all it boiled down to is sheer luck.
My main gripes with the game is probably what makes it so appealing to the eyes of the developers: the time limit, the lack of guidance and the disappointment of how much more useful the chalk could be if the only option you had wasn't a simple "x". Let's quickly go through these: the time limit is absolutely ridiculous. Even on easy, the maze is big enough so that you'll never be able to "map it out" even once anyway and that's assuming you
get lost, which you will, all the time. The only person that has partial immunity to getting lost is whoever is lucky enough to get hold of the chalk at the beginning, but even so, it boils down to marking dead ends all the time which, if you're unlucky, might not even have been dead ends in the first place since the first lever you need to pull removes one of the walls in front of the exit! (What a fun idea!) There will be games where you won't even find a single lever in 10 minutes, then there are some where you start out close to one, but still don't manage to find the other - it's a ridiculous predicament. Talking about randomization for a second, this shouldn't be a thing. If you have a team that sort of "knows what it's doing", then success or failure should be fairly consistent as a result. I don't expect to win everytime, but right now, whether we even find a single lever is not up to our skill, but to a roll of the die. Similarly, the developers expect you to make choices on whether it's smarter to sneak or hide, rather than run, but in practice, there is no choice: You always make a run for it. There's simply no time to waste and most enemies can be avoided so easily by just... running, that it's pointless to do any more anyway.
Secondly, the lack of guidance is just ridiculous. Sure, it's supposed to be this gigantic maze where you just get lost and if that's the kind of thing the devs wanted to accomplish, then congratulations, it worked! It's just not fun - there is nothing you can go off, no clues, no hints, nothing. Perhaps it's easier to clarify, I'm talking about the sorts of hints that could give you slight sense of direction, perhaps there are markings on walls, or you could see faint light *above* the levers that you can see even when you're a tad farther away. Sure, it doesn't help you get there at all,  but at least you know where you're attempting to go! As I've mentioned before, right now, there is absolutely no way to know which way is correct. enemies can be anywhere, the people you're looking for are camping the levers for the most part (especially fun in dead ends!) and there's nothing you can do apart from marking every single dead end and slowly making your way through maybe a third of the labyrinth  before the time runs out. On easy. I'll talk about the strategies my group attempted to use a bit later on, so bear with me.
The last point I want to speak about a little bit are the items. They're god awful, but why? Two of the items serve a very specific purpose: stun a very specific monster. The stick is alright at doing its job, but mostly because the creature it protects you against is very vicious in the first place. Now if there was any point in sticking together, that'd be a cool feature, but right now, when you don't have a stick and encounter one or two after turning a corner, you're pretty much done if you haven't saved up stamina or are just plain lucky. Now for the flashlight: it's completely pointless. While you don't see much in the dark, that usually doesn't matter at all and the enemy it's supposed to protect you against is easier dealt with by just running away. It literally cannot kill you as long as you're running and it's not really giving chase either. It's just a very pointless piece of equipment to begin with. Now on over to the general-purpose tool, the infinite stone bag. It pretty much helps against every single monster appart from the ones that can only be beaten by the stick and redirects them towards the impact point of the stone for a few split seconds, if even. This is useful in a variety of situations, so not much to complain here. As for the last item, the chalk, it's ridiculous. Since you can only place "x", there's only one real function it can serve: marking dead ends. And that's about it! Why wouldn't we be able to draw arrows, or different signs, if feasible even free drawing for more useful, customised notes to potentially mark pathways we *wanted* to take, but couldn't just yet, or ones that might have a crossroad we haven't fully explored? It would make a very mediocre item that much more useful, but apart from that, it'd be neat if more than just one of the group could have it. The reason being, that literally everyone who doesn't have the chalk will get lost, eventually, while the chalk player happily creeps along at a snail's pace, but can still get lost when chased, which is fun, but rarely happens.
Before I finish this quick (...intended) nagging off with some pointers that *could* potentially be implemented, allow me to say what we did and why I arrived at the previous conclusions. Our group of 3-4, once comfortable, had just one strategy. Everyone grabbed an item, (with three people, whoever got the flashlight also had the chalk) and we made a run for it. At every crossroad, we'd split up to quickly search for dead ends that if found, could be marked down with chalk. Now while this sounds like a pretty insane strategy (just sprinting around the maze the entire time) it's currently the only feasible one. You simply don't have time for strolling about or building any sort of atmosphere, you just run. Enemies get ignored (you can run away from most of them anyway, even without a fitting item) and the only time where cooperation becomes sort of necessary is when one of the levers is in a dead-end. It sounds simple, not necessarily fun (it really wasn't, just a grind to maybe one day getting lucky, which we did once) but it lead to the result of beating it once. The ending really has no impact either, but at least it's there, so that's good.
Is Sleeping Dawn a bad game? Maybe. Is it worth buying? Not right now except for when you have a high tolerance for the kind of situation where RNG completely decides over win or loss, even with a full party of agitated rabbits, but that might change in the near future.

Ok whre to start. This Game is quite different from the usual Dotalike games. Its faster and round are shorter with usally more kills.
The movement system is one of the biggest differences. There is no klick to move to location. Instead the dragon moves forward by either pressing shift or right mouse button. And it is always facing the mouse coursor. Space is used to move the dragon backwarts. There is no sideways movement.
Most skills are skillshot fiering in a specific pattern from your dragon. For example dragon btreah usally fires out of the fron (duh)
It less complex than other titles because it doesnt have items to buy in a match as you collect gold. Instead your skills will be determined by dragon and weapon choice for a total of 4 skills (two from each) and 2 additional spells like it it done in lol.
There is a huge selection of Dragons (about 30) and weapons (about the same amount) all of which play somewhat differently. You get 3 random dragons and weapons permanently as part of the tutorial. Other than that you have the usual rotation of free dragons and weapons.
The forced tutorial is one of the worst parts of the games. You have to go through serveral singleplayer mission + one match against the AI (a quite short one, just explaining the dota like mechanics) if you want to have full access to the multiplayer part. This should take about 45 minutes of gameplay and could be a letdown for some people.
The game is somewhat pay to win. You can pay for dragons  and weapons(randoms or specific ones) and only radom weapons ad dragons can be bought in ingame currency. Dragons can be upgraded by using 3 Tier1  or tier 2 dragons of the same type. They get some slight bonuses for it. Like 8% less mana cost and 4% more speed. Something about that line. It is achiveable by just playing but it will take quite a long time and you have to be lucky to get the right random dragons. Buying a tier 3 dragon costs about. 45€
There is a forging system which make weapons a bit stronger (something like 5% more damage, less cooldown, less mana cost) which can be payed for to get it as lot quicker.
And there is a rune system. which you can buy runes for with real money. (only random) Of couse tier2 and tier3 runes are available for non paying players too but they take a long times to craft it seems. (about 3 days for one tier 3 rune and one day for a tier 2 rune). Sadly i cannot asses how strong tier 3 runes are in comparison to tier 2 and 1. Here could be the part where the real pay to win could lie.
In total i would reccoment the game though. Its free and has dragons and it seems quite balanced and knowing the game is more important than bought 20% performance. You have to endure the tutorial though. Which isnt actually that bad.

After buying Stellaris and playing it for a bit I wanted to share some of my thoughts as the one true ruler of the Glorious Empire of Man. Humankind...People of Terran Ancestry...err anyway once we sort the naming out I'll get back to you.
My brethren followed while I led them on a noble quest to scan our local planets (The heck - I didn't see Pluto...WHERE DID PLUTO GO?!). From there I scanned local star systems, and settled some of the scruffier humans (They claimed they were "Individualists" - but look...showers were invented for a reason people...) on distant worlds.
In an inspired moment I promptly declared war on some local gang of rednecks claiming to be a Fallen Empire. I think it went well, I mean it did offer our scientists a nice close up view of a death ray, which really helped our theoreticians...
Errr..yeah don't do that. Anyway this game really sucks you in, I had just bought DOOM and it's just been gathering the digital equivalent of dust once I started playing this. I like how leaders (scientists, fleet admirals, planetary governors, generals) actually age – and die (make sure you keep some influence in reserve to buy new ones).
The way the game handles tech is...different. There isn't so much as a tech tree as a choice of semi random technologies to pursue.  This can be a little frustrating when a tech you didn't choose to research in the past doesn't show up again. Certainly makes you think about tech choices in a different light. As my empire grows I am beginning to see how managing a larger and larger empire takes more and more time, although I suppose this is true in most 4x games.
That said, I heartily recommend this title.

This was a massive let down. I bought it because I figgured "hey, for how much I played the original, I could get $6 worth out of it". I was wrong.
One of the features listed is cross platform play. One of those platforms is Android. Basically this means you are playing an awkward phone version of Dungeon Defenders on your PC. The graphics took a noticable downgrade and everything feels a lot slower paced and clunkier. Not to mention the new interface manages to be even more awakward and unhelpful - I don't think I can see what a pet does without first equipping it and swapping into an entierly different menu.
It's a shame too, because some of the new features ARE pretty interesting looking. 7/10 - The game still has problems, but its fun to play either way.
Pros:
- Fan of the previous games will enjoy the visual update and update from the older version.
- Love the new ideology aspect and constant moral choices which need to be made and the upgrades given with them. I love being evil and taking the benefits over peoples lives and the greater good etc.
- Prototype ships & parts that are tied with space mining. This gives a huge improvement to starbases and trade resources. This gives so many ways to play the game. (You may have better research, but it means nothing when my ships all have extremely powerful prototype weapons thanks to my mining empire) LOVE IT!
- Anomolies can now have varying levels of defence which is great. This aspect still needs work, but it is still good fun to rush some precusor anomolies for advantages.
- Bazaar in the Merc add on. Love the unique ship types and the bonuses, great addition.
Cons:
- Anomoly defences are far too predicatble. Laser weapons and all with the same attack on each. Extremely predictable which is no fun. Would be great to run into an anomoly which had 36 missle dmg and 36 armor, that would crush my survey ship which normally only has shields (since they always have laser weapons).
- I feel like the tech tree could use alot of work. Nothing feels unique and it is more going through the motions.
- Still need to add "auto" options. There is alot of tedius micro-management, if I am at war, I really dont want to control hundreds of fleets to attack each turn. The larger the empire, the more tedius micromanagement is needed.
- There are many features and unique things which appeared in Galactic Civ 2 which have not been added to the new games. I hope they will look to add these in the future.
Overall, it is a very fun game. I have yet to finish a game though. I always make my empire so large that it becomes irritating to manage so many ships turn after turn (which is why I need the auto features).  BUT I have enjoyed every moment of playing, which is a good sign.

Choplifter HD is only recommendable to people who don't mind a severe "old school" challenge. Everyone else will probably find the game too frustrating, even on the lower difficultly levels.
Like the 1980s original, Choplifter HD puts you in control of a helicopter and tasks you with rescuing people and bringing them back to safety. Enemies dot the levels and they'll take shots at you; if your helicopter takes too many hits you'll blow up. Likewise, if you run out of fuel, you'll crash. Choplifter HD becomes a game of risk management; do you have enough fuel to make it to the next person who needs to be rescued, or should you turn back to refuel and repair first? The clock is ticking...
All of this is fine, and is keeping in the spirit of the original game. Where Choplifter HD veers off-course is in the difficulty: this game is tough as nails. The first two or three levels are easy enough, but the difficulty spikes severely from that point on. Levels are jam-packed with enemies that can take your health down in a flash and many of them re-spawn after a short time, meaning you have to deal with them over and over. Enemies with RPGs and EMP rifles that stand on rooftops are very hard to spot, and later on you'll have to avoid missiles fired from jets as well as incoming mortar fire. There are even tanks and AA cannons that can take you out in a couple of hits. It's almost impossible to avoid taking damage in Choplifter HD, so get used to restarting some levels multiple times before you finally conquer them.
If the campaign becomes too much to take, Choplifter HD also has a zombie mode: here, you fly back and forth across a besieged city, shooting zombies and rescuing people. It's fun for a while.
One other thing worth mentioning: the awful voice-acting. Throughout Choplifter HD, you'll be treated to poorly-written and voiced jokes and one-liners from your chopper's crew. None of the jokes are funny, and they're repeated over and over. Some of the dialog is surprisingly tasteless too. Turn your speakers off.
If you're one of those people who think that modern games have become too "casual", then Choplifter HD is for you.

I want to start out by saying I'm somewhat apprehensive about leaving a 'not recommended' review and that there is a good chance that this review will be revised in time to a positive review.
Here is, in my opinion, the biggest problem Stellaris faces: It tries to be a 4X and a GS game at the same time, but does neither particularly well. The viewpoints of both crowds can easily be found in the various gripes of online forums and reviews but to summarize: The tactical options and style of aggressive play do not suit the competitive 4X/RTS gamers while the simplicity and limited scope [and even absense] of numerous elements pertinent to grand strategy games will annoy or disappoint the GS gamers.
That's what is wrong with this game in a nutshell.
On the flip side, it does a lot right:
Unfortunately, numerous annoyances remain:
Overall it's a great start and a good framework for something that could truly be made into a game that stands apart from everything else out there. But until many of these problems are rectified and the game is fleshed out that's all it is: framework.
If you're on the fence about buying, my advice would be to wait a couple of months and see where the project goes. Given Paradox's sales numbers for this game, I think it is going to be supported and updated for some time to come. Check back in six months or so.
Another patch or two and maybe another solid DLC pack are still needed for me to flip this review positive. It is improving though!

short version: graphics and gameplay hold up pretty well. atmospheric, creepy..
long version: if you've never played it, it holds up well. the graphics are basically doom 3, maybe a little better. the level design is weird, so expect to get lost a couple of times. you'll spend most your time in industrial facilities (like half life), and offices.
they're generous with the "bullet time", so even if you use it up, you'll find more to spare. you can increase your amount of bullet time by finding hidden needle thingies throughout the levels. if you jump and melee, you'll do a bicycle kick. this takes dudes out instantly, and feels kinda cool. you can also do a slide kick, but i forgot i had it. when i re-discovered it, i didn't use it much. mostly i used melee to creatively break glass. they give you remote-controlled grenades, and proximity mines, in addition to regular grenades. these are pretty situational, so i ended up throwing out, for example, a proximity mine like a regular grenade because my inventory was full. you don't fully regenerate health, but if you're below 25, it'll recharge. it recharges faster if you don't move. i appreciate that kind of nuance. i mostly used the shotgun. the assault rifle and submachine gun go all over the place, and the tracers look out of synch with the sound. you can kinda aim down the sight, but it's actually just a slight zoom-in. it's still tactically viable. in the end, i stuck with the shotgun as my primary weapon, particle beam as my secondary, and rocket launcher or repeater (which is...a grenade launcher?).
about half way through the story grabbed my interest. i even went out of my way to hear "bonus dialogue" you find on laptops. it ends on a cliffhanger, though. i like the atmosphere, but some of the ambient music is on a short loop, which hurts it for me. it's good at creating tension, and most of the jump scares worked, but it's nothing like amnesia. i thought doom 3 was a little scarier. maybe.
will also mention the AI doesn't seem extremely smart, but i did find myself playing with it often. it's better than mindless legions of soldiers running at you with assault rifles. more than better. they'll try to flush you out with grenades, which leads to you having no other option than running straight in and gunning/meleeing everyone down. that's how i approached it. you always know what they're doing, and you can plan accordingly. if they didn't say anything, maybe...well, it's still fun.
leaning is outdated, and it's awkard to hold down Q or E while moving. i guess you're not supposed to. i ended up binding them to 2 of my 6 side mouse buttons, and it worked well for me. you'll probably want to spend some time making comfortable keybindings before you get too far into it.

My general impression is that the game is okay and that in itself disappoints me. The reason why is that I find Paradox makes great games then they become greater with DLCs. This game is the opposite, it is an unfinished game that needs DLCs to make it great.  Stellaris is a basic game that laid the ground works for customability and more in-depth. Everything from diplomacy, technology research, AI management and combat feel unoriginal or even outright basic compared to other Paradox games.  After one play through I feel that there isn’t any replay-ability. As for the game play it is fairly stale midgame: the AI is very passive; ships are unbalanced (corvettes swarms ftw) as are defense stations (its too easy for small enemy fleets to destroy your spaceports as they don’t scale with technology improvements – the only way to stop a fleet is with a fleet); micromanaging your plants is clunky and feels outdated (especially with sectors); internal politics is lackluster (imagine a CKII scenario where governors have loyalty but this isn’t the case); and diplomacy is very poor (and you can’t do anything with a xenophobia race). Its disappointing that their isn’t culture victories, diplomacy victories, spiritual, or even economic (like your corporation have their presence on all the habitable planets and everyone is buying your products – its a shame you don’t even have corporations).  Also when you do go to war its all too easy to win then annex or make the opposing empire your vassal. The warscore system is broken.  Conquer a few planets and now they surrender giving you a new vassal.  I expected more or better based on previous games by Paradox. I wouldn’t recommend anyone to buy it at this stage and maybe wait for a few dlcs to come out and buy them on sale (a very significant discounted sale).  I could go on about the inefficiencies of this game and frankly I feel that I have overpaid for an early beta access. This game isn’t a complex strategy game it’s a basic "who has the best fleet swarm will win the game".
Edit: there is an endgame but that point I'm already bored out of my mind.

7/10 - The game still has problems, but its fun to play either way.
Pros:
- Fan of the previous games will enjoy the visual update and update from the older version.
- Love the new ideology aspect and constant moral choices which need to be made and the upgrades given with them. I love being evil and taking the benefits over peoples lives and the greater good etc.
- Prototype ships & parts that are tied with space mining. This gives a huge improvement to starbases and trade resources. This gives so many ways to play the game. (You may have better research, but it means nothing when my ships all have extremely powerful prototype weapons thanks to my mining empire) LOVE IT!
- Anomolies can now have varying levels of defence which is great. This aspect still needs work, but it is still good fun to rush some precusor anomolies for advantages.
- Bazaar in the Merc add on. Love the unique ship types and the bonuses, great addition.
Cons:
- Anomoly defences are far too predicatble. Laser weapons and all with the same attack on each. Extremely predictable which is no fun. Would be great to run into an anomoly which had 36 missle dmg and 36 armor, that would crush my survey ship which normally only has shields (since they always have laser weapons).
- I feel like the tech tree could use alot of work. Nothing feels unique and it is more going through the motions.
- Still need to add "auto" options. There is alot of tedius micro-management, if I am at war, I really dont want to control hundreds of fleets to attack each turn. The larger the empire, the more tedius micromanagement is needed.
- There are many features and unique things which appeared in Galactic Civ 2 which have not been added to the new games. I hope they will look to add these in the future.
