I haven't been playing it for long, but my mind often drifts to it. It's one of the few games in recent years I almost played through twice (my Steam library grows almost daily, so that kinda means something) and which I have very fond memories of.
It's a very special title because it was designed with much love and confidence and shows so in a variety of ways. If I had to name a game that not only looked like a charm but worked and felt just the same it would be Dust: An Elysian Tail. It was backed up by Microsoft as an original XBox Live Arcade game and took almost four years to make but was created mostly by just one guy.
Dust: AET is a Metroidvania action platformer (meaning you discover new powers along the way and do some backtracking with them) with a clean interface, gorgeous art, fantastic music, nice story, adorable characters, great voice acting, solid combat, rudimentary leveling/gear/crafting/shopping mechanics and platforming of mild/average difficulty.
Despite what some other reviewers/players/press people say: I love the voice acting. It's warm and colorful and fits the equally colorful style of the game (which does not mean it's an immature game; although some young deers running past me gave me some Disney vibes and some overarching topics include classic "teenage"-ishy things like the protagonist and his sidekick growing with their responsibilty along the journey there sure are some darker moods and themes too like war and genocide). Some people don't like the VA or certain characters but I think they are being unfair or misunderstand something. I think the VA is nailing it down and just like it was meant to be. it's cute and sweet and just nice, with much heart and soul that could be credited to a set of relatively new/inexperienced but maybe even more so passionate VAs. This is one of the few games where I had urges to look up contact data of the voice actors only so I could thank them for their efforts. I think I know bad voice acting when I see it and Dust: AET has none of that.
The music is fantastic. Again, in this game specifically, I noticed a behavior I don't see too often, least not that I would've been aware of it in other games as much: Some levels I loved to roam a couple of more times, or stay in them for a bit longer than I really had to, so I could keep listening to the powerful tracks running along some more. The always very beautiful art even in the somewhat "gloomy" levels added to it and made the game, with all the other things it has to offer, a constantly enjoyable and remarkably well-rounded experience from start to end.
The story is kinda interesting and ends fairly conclusive. Some questions remain unanswered though. Apparently there was more planned to it, what turned out to be game was originally meant to be an animated film called "Elysian Tail" and you can tell by some lore ideas that are sometimes brought up but not elaborated too much. Like what exactly the talking sword you're wielding is (there were meant to be seven of those, it seems, but the game never brings that up) or how your funny and adorable sidekick "Fidget" came to be a "Guardian" of that sword in the first place.
So, I'd love to see a sequel sometime in the future when the creator feels for it (well, all who appreciate this game as the gem it is seem to do). And maybe a Fidget plushie.

I highly recommend getting this game in its current state. Even with all the problems, its that good.
Its a paradox game, but it doesn't feel like a pradox game, because its not buggy on release and actually works. The tutorial is super, races are interesting, basically what was a DLC for other games is included in this one already (making your own custom race), and the music and atmosphere/graphics are all solid. Customizing the ships is cool, and the space battles can be fun to watch. The pops are complex and managing them can be interesting.
Problems:
1. AI is terrible. The enemies really don't understand how to win a war. In a game where all the AI countries start with pretty much the same resources (like in Civ), this leads to a situation where you as the player have a massive empire and everyone else has just divided up the galaxy evenly between them.
2. Fallen empires can be conquered, and all of their production facilities used by your pops. This is on top of the fact that defeating a fallen empire nets you their amazing super tech which puts your fleets light years ahead of your enemies in tech. Now, defeating them is no easy task, especially in the early/mid game, but its doable. They can't rebuild their fleets despite sitting on insane production, which makes conquering them too easy.
4. As far as I can tell, there is no benefit to having a balanced fleet with screens and cruisers protecting your BBs. In fact, they will die quickly as they go ahead of your BBs and get slaughtered waiting for them to catch up. There is no penalty for having an all BB fleet, and so you just end up building as many ships with the biggest guns you can get.
5. Leaders dying and science vessels having to research wreckage of your enemies gets annoying. More tasks need to be automated.
6. Putting fighter/bomber units on your ships doesn't work because the ships stay in the back and don't do anything.
7. The  "zerg" invasion is broken. It started off with a bang and fizzed quickly.
8. Designing the ships is cimbersome because there's no way to sort through the weapons and armor efficiently.
Knowing paradox, I'm confident they will patch these problems in the next 5 or 10 years, so I'm sure it won't be a problem by the time you buy it.

Like many of Paradox's grand strategy games (CK2, EU4), the DLC is going to make or break Stellaris. Is the base game playable? Definitely. Is the base game replayable? Maybe a couple of times.
Is the effort that went into Stellaris worth $40? Yes, but the DLCs are going to have to be epic or cheap!
I like lists, so here you go...
Pros:
-First and foremost, very unique pacing/tech "tree" for a space 4x. I feel this is the core of the game. If you don't like CK2 or EU4 pacing, you will hate Stellaris' pacing. I love it. More realistic!
-Simple yet interesting custom species.
-Simple galaxy creation; decent variety.
-Optional sagnant advance-technolgy AI starts.
-Quirky variety of FTL travel.
-No spearate scout ship class! (Yes, this is a pro! Just send a corvette!)
-Empire AND planetary AND researchable Edicts!
-Advanced government types (although could use fleshing out).
-Robots, Droids, and Sentients! Oh my!
-Simple spaceport customization (but could use more module options).
-Simple, interesting ship designer, with Auto-Best!
-Quick load times. Not overly demanding on system resources.
Neutral:
-Graphics. Paradox always does enough to make graphics interesting but never fantastic.
-Species can only colinize one type of planet at start. IRL, atmospheric chemistry is more important than biome, and arguably, for example, humanoids could colonize all of the biomes at start, especially assuming habitats would be available in 2200. Planet colonization limitations needs be fleshed out. I understand why they did it this way (simplicity), but it's still dull.
-Bombardment is awkwardly done, but whatever (see also: "armies/transports are lame" below).
-Government, Budget, and Demographics tabs are interesting but currently mostly useless.
-The species tab gets lost in the mix, but it can be especially important after Gene Tailoring. The tab gets cumbersome with high populations/planets.
-Fleet upgrading takes a long time, but just split the fleet and use different space stations, I guess. Maybe add a refueler/repair/upgrade base or more impactful modules.
-Dull vassalization system. Also, shouldn't uplifted species be integrated immediately?
-Needs many more non-science event chains. (See also: "factions are lame" below.)
-Fedarations are dull. I smell a DLC there.
Cons/Bugs:
-Semi-useless tutorial. Clicking-through does as much. Complex UI, so multiple click-throughs needed to get scope of tabs. Easy to forget "things I can do."
-Species traits need more impact on gameplay.
-Can feel slow;  not enough to do, especially early. "Fastest" isn't very fast.
-Conversely, there is no auto-scout option.
-Most Alerts are pointless. Only Hostile Empire Fleet, Survey, and Research Alerts are meaningful.
-Situation log needs ability to "track all."
-Other Empires are ridiculously adverse to trading you anything, even when you can crush them without thought, at which point negotiation is pointless.
-When maxing out on resource storage, improving storage, using them, or distributing them (to sectors) is annoying.
-Army management UI is awful. Transports are lame.
-Policies tab is confusing to navigate and a policy's detailed effects are difficult to predict.
-Too slavery-focused, and not enough pros to slavery.
-Needs more ethics divergence and faction interference/rebellion.
-Scientist deaths are particularly annoying; needs option to auto-hire and auto-assign to best job.
-Control over Sectors needs to be slightly greater (observation posts, option to take energy but not minerals, etc).
-I can uplift pre-sentients and advance post-neolithics, but can't do anything to those in between? WTF.
-The AI is moderately dumb. AI will not put up multiple fronts. They go straight for your homeworld almost always. They capitulate on relatively even-footing relatively quickly. When weak, they pull ships from defensible positions to attack. Etc, etc, etc.
-Inability to re-negotiate peace conditions.
-Stagnant Empires need to be less stagnant. They need SOME initiative, such as peace keeping or science regression or desire for transience or religious fanatacism or....
-Needs more achievements (these are sure to come).
-Needs more victory conditions (coming soon surely; ought to be part of free DLC).
Note: I have not played multiplayer.
TL;DR: Despite the length of my Cons/Bugs, Paradox does more good than evil; if you like 4x's, buy this game.

More accessible than any other Paradox strategy game. Stellaris has a lot going for it (cool techs, extensive customization and creation of player species, visually tasty ship combat) and it has a very nice learning curve.
The game also has some replayability. Species traits and ethics alter your options in various situations: A xenophobe militarist species may solve revolts on a conquered planet by killing the less obedient people on the planet. Xenophile species may resettle people or sent some of their own to conquered planets. Or if you are a more peaceful species you may have won that planet as an ally or protectorate in the first place. A variety of quests and events also bring variation to each playthrough.
[Scroll to the bottom for the summary]
[Update]
I've updated my review with the current outlook:
What has changed for the better:
- Game breaking bugs like immortal/indestructible enemy planets have been fixed!
- Balancing: They're not quite there yet, but ship fight balancing has improved substantially. Bigger Starports are actually worth it for the stronger ships now, too.
- More endgame events: Endgame hase been further approved by adding more things to it (like space monsters)
Remaining negative aspects:
- The galaxy still looks boring and repetitive. Systems and planets use the same textures and everything looks similar rather fast. Even small changeable things like the background of a star system map still look boring (they added some more colour variations in compared to the release game but they didn't put enough effort in it.)
- Not enough events. You can trigger special events when discovering a new planet or just discovering space (so called "anomalies"). From derelict vessels to the remains of ancient civilizations, a lot of things can happen. Anomalies add a lot of spice to the early-game. It's just unfortunate that they repeat very fast. Even a long time after release, you can be assured that your second playthrough will already have a fad taste because you will encounter the same "special events" over again. Adding more events would greatly enhance the game, but it's not done. This hurts replayability.
- Developer threats and player treatment: The devs explicitly say on their forums to players, that they will stop developing the game unless we, the players, buy their overpriced DLC. It's their business model to sell overpriced DLCs and they use that as a threat against players who complain about how little you get in their DLCs considering their high price tag. Buy it or we stop making patches. That is their strategy.
Many players even made good suggestions how to increase the worth of dlcs (like adding more anomalies! that would be huge without much work). Yet they ignore those suggestions and instead resort to making threats to their fanbase. Look at it on the forums, these things pop up there regularly.
- Core systems are still missing. Espionage, Traderoutes, Diplomacy - CORE systems of a grand strategy game are still either completely missing (espionage) or very basic and lacking in depth (trading, diplomacy,...). This is especially embarassing because people who knew games like EU IV know that the devs can do these systems much, much better. In Stellaris, the mentioned core systems lack so much depth that they're too easy to see through. Each of these systems is so basic that it's just sad. There is much room for improvement. The basic systems are good if you have no experience with strategy or grand strategy and it's nice for beginners - however, the core mechanics will be boring and pose little challenge faster than you think.
- Custom races: The Custom races turn out to be bland in the end. They can't be distinguished from each other except for their little pic and stats, they lack "character". To give you an example: Imagine you have a race that looks like the klingons in stellaris. only that due to randomization, the klingons are peaceful spiritualists looking for nirvana in your first playthrough, religious fanatics in your second playthrough and militaristic xenophobes who create superroboters in your third playthrough. In the end those "klingon" looking things are just nothing at all. They have no character.  The Problem doesn't get better when you create non-randomized races - you can add races to your playthrough with fixed characteristics (IE militaristic klingons!).
While those klingons will then be true to what you'd expect them to be, they still like any racial history or culture. All races are "faceless" and practically free of context and culture because of the race generator. It was a great idea on paper to have a race-generator for this kind of game, but in the end you'll have 20 empires in your game of which none have history or culture.
[Summary]:
Well after release, the devs polished some things that were problematic at release (gamebreaking bugs and balancing.) However, the devs also failed to patch the game in the places where work is seriously needed. Suggestions from the playerbase have been answered with threats to discontinue support of the game and the game's concept for replayability does not work out as good as most people believed at start. Unless the devs apologize to the players and start taking player suggestions seriously, I wouldn't recommend the game. The devs don't work on it enough to bring it to a level where it would be engaging and replayable enough. There are alternatives coming up this year that shape up better on every account.

Pay to win? More like Play to win!
Personally I think Dragons and Titans is a lovely little MOBA. I agree that it can't really compare to games like Dota and League of Legends, but the potential is certainly there.
The most common complaints I've seen in reviews are that the game would be Pay to Win and that the controls are clunky. One review even stated you can't attack and fly at the same time.
I find these arguments unfounded. All dragons are quite balanced so buying more with money hardly gives you an advantage. The tutorial gives you the crystals(the in game currency) to buy a dragon pack and a weapons pack, both containing 3 random dragons and 3 random weapons respectively. Through playing PVP or the single player campaign you can earn more crystals. I've had pvp games in which I earned about 300 crystals and you need 2500 for a weapons pack and 5000 for a dragons pack.
Further more there are a bunch of free to play dragons and weapons to choose from in PVP battles. These dragons and weapons rotate every other week between all the dragons and weapons available.
As for the keybinding, I will admit that its hard to get used to at first, but it's hardly clunky. Once you get the feel for it you'll be twisting and turning and breathing whatever your dragons breathing down on your foes. Flying and attacking at the same time is easy to do, some dragons even have homing attacks that will find your target no matter which direction you're facing.
There's 3 pvp maps with different game modes and the levels are well designed. Overall the PVP element is the best part of the game as it should be, but the single player campaign is a nice add on.
The single player campaign allows you to unlock dragons. Now I've seen a complaint about that in one of the reviews that you would need to clear 150 levels before unlocking the dragon. In truth you only need to play through every level once to unlock the dragon. But I agree that the difficulty is really high even when played in recruit mode. You'll die a lot, get frustrated a lot and if you're anything like me you'll just give up on it and go '♥♥♥♥ it I'm sticking to pvp'
But the thing I really like about this game is that you can endlessly combine weapons and dragons. Meaning that you could face off against a dragon with a weapon that shoots arrows one time and then be faced with that same dragon with the ability to drop mines and teleport the next time you face it. It also means that you can choose your own style of play.
Further more, the more you play a dragon or weapon, the more experience is awarded to them, allowing them to advance ranks and become faster and more powerfull. So really, the more you play the more powerful your dragons and weapons get and the more likely you are to win!
And if that isn't reason enough to give it a try. There's one argument that is sure to at least get me playing

Heroine's Quest: The Herald Of Ragnarok is a independent roleplaying game developed by Crystal Shard and published by Screen 7. The title is set in a fantasy realm and tasks your character, a burgeoning young adventurer, with saving the world from an ancient evil bent on bringing about Ragnarok and thus ending the world as we know it. As with most classic R.P.G.'s you choose your character class, there are three to pick from in this title, and as your character levels up you gain experience points for whichever abilities you use frequently like the old saying "the more you do something the better you get at it".
The story in this game is quite entertaining and chock full of viking lore and mythology. The gameplay and combat while simple are both quite fun and highly addictive. You'll die time and time again and scream to the heavens that you'll never play this @#$%& game again only to boot it up two hours later. There are many types of unique adversaries to battle and puzzling puzzles to solve. The dialog and voice acting is top notch. You'll converse with people and creatures which could terrify you or make you laugh your pants off with the strange and sometimes hilarious things that they say or do. The title has a great immersive feel to as it applies a timescale of morning, afternoon and evening to the questing. Your character also must feed herself, can suffer from exposure due to the harsh climate and needs sleep or rest to remain healthy just like in real life. The sound and music in this title are terrific and definitely capture the feel of the game perfectly.
If you're perceptive enough you will also get a kick out of the many pop-culture references and game developement jokes humorously sprinkled about the title...some of which will make you laugh out loud. The developers certainly aren't afraid to laugh at themselves or anyone else. This game is just fantastic and I am having so much fun playing it and one really great thing is that it is free which is shocking because I would have gladly paid for this amount of entertainment. If you're a fan of old-school roleplaying games, retro-games or just crave a great adventure title then you will not be dissapointed with this wonderful independent gem. One more thing to add, many people say that this title plays like the old "Quest For Glory" series of games which I myself am not familiar with but I think this game plays like Skyrim...if Skyrim had come out in 1991.

This is basically a tweaked version of Dungeon Defenders with a new infrastructure for online play called Playverse. So what’s good about it?
The Good:
There are some cool new features like Dash, Extra Spells from Items, Armor Asthetics, etc. All of these features are very much welcomed and are pretty fun. I do enjoy dropping down a lightning storm on a large group of minions that are knocking at the walls from an amulet I picked up. You can check out the features on the DD Eternity Website.
Playverse seems to add more tools for online play. Also it’s probably the main reason for Eternity as it’s what Trendy plans to use for cross platform play, which seems pretty cool.
At the time of this review I have only played to level 15, so I can’t speak too much for balance and security, but according to Trendy the items and are more balanced and the game has more protection from hacking (Most likely since it’s ran through Playverse).
The Bad:

Tooltips, Tooltips, Tooltips. How something so simple and prevalent in modern software seems to have eluded Trendy. There are tooltips but a lot of the new UI and the Playverse are missing these for a number of things.
This leads me to documentation. There’s no help or anything explaining all the new things like Crafting, Dyes, Why do I start with 4 characters I did not create with numbers in their names, etc.
You can't hide armor, or at least I can't find the option. There are some pretty cool costumes and it kind of sucks that you can't hide some ugly helmet with good stats that covers up a cool visor from your costume.
When an inventory screen(like merchant or forge) and your mouse is over an item to read the description, if somebody walks past your mouse the description goes away and you have to move the mouse back and forth to get it back. Maybe a minor gripe, but something they should fix since taverns can be a bit chaotic.
Notes:
There are Micro-Transactions, though they are for aesthetic items only. Currently there are some problems with joining games, though Trendy is aware of it and working on it. Only happened once to me, I just retried once and it worked. The tavern is not private, which doesn't bother me, but may bother some. It's probably like that to make the game more social. This is basically treated as a new game, so you will be starting from scratch with a new hero. Previous dungeon defender one heroes will not be available.
Conclusion:
If you want to play Dungeon Defenders online, with more balance, security, some interesting new features and the above listed limitations (
) then I’d pick this up on a good sale. Otherwise wait for Dungeon Defenders 2 and play the previous one.

Choplifter HD is a spiritual successor of the original Choplift on Apple II. The mechanics are simiar, but updated. The chopper is in 2D space: it can go left, right, up and down. It can turn left, right, or face the player (out), and this is important as enemies do come from 3 directions (left, right, and out). And you can't hit the enemy if you're facing the wrong way. The game is presented in 3D with parallax and real scrolling to give the impression of 3D but the actual movesments are 2D.
Different helicopters have different handling, such as firepower, speed, carrying capacity, fuel capacity, and so on. Armed helis have missiles and/or chain gun, and all helis need to rescue people (civilians or soldiers or even the occasional news crew).  As you play you will unlock better helos by achieving "stars" on the missions.
Enemies have AAA gun sites, soldiers with AK, soldiers with RPG, SAM sites, technical (gun trucks), APCs, tanks, enemy heli, enemy jets, and just general terrain obstructions.
Your objective is basically to rescue as many people that needs to be rescued as possible by flying there, kill enemies in your way, land next to the people (not ON them!) so they get on, then fly back to your base, drop them off, and repeat until either time runs out, or you rescued them all and/or other missions. It can get frantic, when you have enemies on all sides, missile lock on you, and so on.
In many ways this is a twin joystick shooter, as the left stick controls the chopper while the right stick controls the aim (laser sight pointing the chain gun).
Fuel is limited, and any use of "turbo" (speed boost) eats up fuel like crazy. And your helo won't fly without fuel. Rockets are limited in qty and reloaded only at base. Chaingun is infinite but there's a heat limit to prevent it from firing too much. Carrying capacity is limited  and the larger choppers don't fly as fast or move as nimbly as the smaller ones. On the other hand, they can often do everything in one trip rather than taking multiple trips.
There are various "campaigns" containing various missions, and each mission usually has a bonus objective as well as news crew to rescue (2 extra people!)
DLC packs adds extra helos to play with (some are very powerful) and more missions.
All in all, it's a fun little game, worth successor to the name.

Despite my love for Final Fantasy, the PC releases for the series were never that great. While Final Fantasy VII was salvaged by having a fairly simple implementation on the Playstation One, Final Fantasy VIII has a significant problem when compared to it's alternate platform.
Let's put it simply, the PC version of Final Fantasy VIII was terrible. It looks terrible, it sounds terrible. Music shipped with this release is an unexcusably terrible cacophany of MIDI instruments that lack in detail that made the Playstation One release as great as it was. Despite the potential for better hardware, the game looks fairly terrible when on the field and in certain 3D environments. Texture tiling is rampant in the overworld, whereas the Playstation One version managed to avoid that alltogether.
I love being able to play VIII on the PC, but it comes with the sheer bitter taste of knowing that what I'm seeing is nowhere near as good as it was on the first platform I played the game on. Even with it being as old as it is, it's a damned shame that the PC version of this game had it's artwork stripped bare of what made it look and sound so good.
That's not even getting into the playability part. With everything in the game being referenced as "Button 1" through whatever, it's maddening to try and map them. While you can fumble your way through the launcher's configuration, do NOT try to mess with the configuration inside the game, else you will get your controls all sorts of messed up and you won't be able to restore it. This is where even giving me the Playstation's references would have been helpful, but in this case it just failed hard, which resulted in me having to restart my game in order to get the controls back in order.
It can be done better, it has done better. For those with access to Amazon, or Playstation Network, consider finding a Playstation copy instead.

FFVII was the first FF game I've ever played and one of the first video games I've played, and until now, I still think that its the best in the entire FF series and one of the best games ever made in history (if not the best). I first played it on the PS, and now the PC. Overall I have played through the entire game for 7-8 times already, and I still couldn't get bored of it. The story was just epic, the characters lovable, memorable and engaging, and the gameplay fun and straight-forward. FFVII basically defined the JRPG genre to the rest of the world at the time it was first released. To say that this game was phenomenal would seem to be an understatement.
What is there to hate in this game? If you ask me, nothing. What is there to hate in this PC port? Plenty.
Basically the guys at SE had done nothing to make this PC port better in any way compared to the original PS version. The graphics and music became worse than it was before. It seems that playing this on the PS would be a better and wiser choice if you ask me.
So should you play FFVII? If you're a true gamer, you NEED to play this at least once in your lifetime. Not playing FFVII would be a disgrace to your fellow peers. If you've played it before, then you don't need me to tell you how awesome it is.
Should you buy this PC port on Steam? I don't recommend it. Its way better and wiser to experience what this legendary masterpiece has to offer by playing it on an emulator or if possible the original Playstation. If you still choose to buy it, wait for a sale.

I can understand how some people wouldn't enjoy this game, but I did. It feels like the game version of The Blue Planet documentary. You swim around and let the game guide you through a beautiful underwater world.
You can piece together the story yourself as it unfolds, or ignore it entirely. Although the game is linear, there are a few sections where you can explore around you and unlock new types of fish and collectibles. You can ride and control most of the fishes in the game (except the little ones, obviously) by holding the shift key; this is a cool feature, especially when you find a scary looking Basking Shark deep underwater with its mouth wide-open! You can't die in this game, I didn't know that at the time though and it was kind of scary swimming into the unknown dark depths seeing it slowly swimming towards me.
It's also fun to dive out of the water, the right mouse button allows you to swim faster, which you can click up to 3 times (each click makes you swim faster) and if you time it just right while swimming upwards you can basically imitate a dolphin, and every time you do it a whole bunch of fish dive out of the water with you.
I found it really relaxing to play, if you enjoyed Journey on the PS4, I'm sure you will enjoy this too.

An appropriate title, considering how thick the suspense is at times. Speaking of visual deception, somehow the graphical fidelity in this game is even more impressive than on day one, with the clean yet seemingly anachronistic technical limitations of 2005 serving as beauty marks on the ahead-of-its-time Jupiter EX engine.  Monolith created a truly Legendary FPS with this one.

Oh my god, this game... This game is as amazing as it may be hard.
First of all, you CANNOT play this game if you aren't able to passively tap the beat of a song while thinking about something else at the same time, this is NECESSARY to the gameplay. It makes this game a turn based dungeon crawler where every turn lets you think for less than a second. If you miss a beat, you skip a turn.
So there's what this is about : you play as Cadence, your everyday dungeon hero in a rogelike game where when you die, you'll have to restart BUT, at first the game introduces you to everything it has, starting by each zone in the game one after another, and then unlocking different characters with different gameplay mechanics, in order to keep the experience fresh.
In the first like 20 hours, you'll learn how to beat the game in every zone with every character. And then you will start trying to complete the full dungeon in a row with any character you'd have chosen.
Now, not only does this require a lot of time to reach (like, a LOT), but it also is kinda hard.
For I love hardcore games as much as I love RPGs, the positive point was it could keep me busy for a large amount of time, but this aspect can also scare casual gamers.
If you want to look for yourself, you'll see that beating the full game even with the easiest character has been done by 2% of the players, so the challenge is real, but it makes every achievement you get a real pride.
Buy it.

As a final note Stellaris has the potential to be a great game, but it needs a lot of fleshing out. now im not one for game development and i know Paradox tests the games extensively but surely someone should have noticed the lack of, well anything different to do late game besides wait for the next doomsday weapon, (or god forbid your death fleet of 1000 fleet capacity upgrading)

Too similar to other slow-paced mobas, this game only removes the floor from the levels and adds clunkiness to controls which doesn't make you feel like you're flying at all. Once I finished the entirely-too-patronizing handholder of a tutorial, and the main event tutorials, and saw my random selection of dragons and weapons, I knew the limitted vision of the creators wasn't going to keep me interested in this game. Bear in mind these are five-dollar dragons each. I got a dragon...made of wood. Then one...made of swords. The wood one, it blew THORNS like a reed pipe *toot toot toot* which brings me to the shallow sound design. Granted, it's a moba and isometric, but it'd be nice if the attacks, (since you only ever have four,) ought to be somewhat impacting or 'effective' sounding. The fire breathing sounds like a 10th-of-a-second loop of generic fireplace rumble. People say the screenshots don't reflect the game accurately, but I disagree, it's the angle of perspective from which they're taken that makes the game appear far more immersive than it actually is. The screenies look like they were shot from a TPS or at least quarter-down perspective, but in the main game this view isn't often available...the usual top-down affair is the mainstay. Click the screenies to view them in their full resolution and know, that's the BEST this game can look, from its most complimenting angle. All in all, have to recommend against this title, with so many more open and less expensive to enjoy mobas proliferating Steam these days. Just because this has dragons...doesn't make it worth playing. That's -all- it has. They aren't terribly attractive/compelling dragons anyways.

A quick review of this game:
What I first thought to become a mindless burn everything game, it quickly became clear to me that Little Inferno provides more than just burning things, although the burning plays the biggest part  of the game. Little inferno has a great atmosphere. You live in a house with your little cosy Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace while the world around you is freezing. The graphics add up to this atmosphere. They are very unique and have a lot of character. The music is beautiful as well! The item descriptions add a comical element to the game.
Gameplay-wise, the game offers little variaty, but is still fun to play. It took me 3h34 minutes to complete the game fully (including getting all combos, although I used the wikia for a few of them). At first you burn stuff to get to the next catalog, which gives you new items to burn. Then, you learn about the combo system and try to complete all combos. The difficulty is that you don't know which items you have to burn together to complete a certain combo (and there are 99 combos). The combo names give you some vague idea (e.g. Polar Bear Combo = Bear doll + South Pole). One great thing is that you can't 'screw up' the game, meaning by doing something wrong, you get a setback. If you burn an item, it'll always give you more money than you spend on it, so making mistakes in this game is lucrative.
You'll recieve letters from three different persons, the Weather man, your neighbour and a granny (who's name I forgot). These letters create the story and the background of the game. Some of them are funny, other are more informative, but none are too long that reading them becomes a hassle.
All in all a good game. I would recommend putting this game on your wish list if you like original games. Buy when on sale or when you have too much money.

This game is a brilliant throwback to classic adventure/rpgs such as Sierra's Quest for Glory series. It has a strong female protagonist, good gameplay, and a good story line filled with Norse mythology.
You choose between  3 classes, warrior/fighter (easiest to start with), mage or thief which will influence certain aspects of the game (for example how some puzzles are solved)
Voice acting is mostly well done too as is the musical score. There are optional side quests and mini games, and many puzzles have more than one solution. I also like the realism, not only do you need to make sure your character eats and sleeps sufficiently and doesn't freeze to death, but characters will react differently depending on who else is in the room.  For example if you talk to Lithrasir about Hervor  while Hervor  is in the room, what she says will be different than if he isn't, if they are present the character being talked about may react to what is being said as well
All in all this is a really fun adventure/rpg game that is well worth checking out, and it's free!!

Despite my love for Final Fantasy, the PC releases for the series were never that great. While Final Fantasy VII was salvaged by having a fairly simple implementation on the Playstation One, Final Fantasy VIII has a significant problem when compared to it's alternate platform.
Let's put it simply, the PC version of Final Fantasy VIII was terrible. It looks terrible, it sounds terrible. Music shipped with this release is an unexcusably terrible cacophany of MIDI instruments that lack in detail that made the Playstation One release as great as it was. Despite the potential for better hardware, the game looks fairly terrible when on the field and in certain 3D environments. Texture tiling is rampant in the overworld, whereas the Playstation One version managed to avoid that alltogether.
I love being able to play VIII on the PC, but it comes with the sheer bitter taste of knowing that what I'm seeing is nowhere near as good as it was on the first platform I played the game on. Even with it being as old as it is, it's a damned shame that the PC version of this game had it's artwork stripped bare of what made it look and sound so good.
That's not even getting into the playability part. With everything in the game being referenced as "Button 1" through whatever, it's maddening to try and map them. While you can fumble your way through the launcher's configuration, do NOT try to mess with the configuration inside the game, else you will get your controls all sorts of messed up and you won't be able to restore it. This is where even giving me the Playstation's references would have been helpful, but in this case it just failed hard, which resulted in me having to restart my game in order to get the controls back in order.
It can be done better, it has done better. For those with access to Amazon, or Playstation Network, consider finding a Playstation copy instead.

First thing I want to say about this game is extremely broken due to the animation system. To understand why it's broken, you first must know that there are two different attack types (light and heavy) and there are aerial combos that can be done regardless of if you hit  an enemy or not. You must also know that this game has unlockable skills which encourage you to backtrack to unlock chests,gear (modify stats that effect combat), and probably other stuff I don't know about because I have only put a little over 3 hours into the game at this point. Anyway, I will detail an animation glitch I found extremely early on in the game while fighting monsters that will shed some light on why this game is broken.
Hitting the light button twice while in the air will pushes the character up slightly in the air due to the second air slash. If you hit heavy and push the opposite direction, it will cancel the animation, putting you in a flying spin, which pushes you horizonal. This isn't really a problem until you realize that pushing the opposite direction again and hitting the light button,will cancel the flying spin animation. Hit the light button again, and you do the second air slash that pushes you up. To sum it up, the input should look like this (face left, jump, light slash, light slash, right + heavy slash, left+light slash, light slash, right+heavy slash, repeat till your heart's content)
Incase you can't visualize what this results in when you repeat the combo, let me put it bluntly: It allows you to fly , and the game wasn't designed with that in mind. Furthermore, if you do the technique I mentioned above near a vine wall, the flying spin will cancel when it hits the wall, allowing you to suedo wall jump climb it without the required skill. This allows you to get high level gear very early on in the game. Put it this way, before stumbling on a high level chest very early in the game by using the animation exploit I mentioned, my armor defense was 4, and it seemed like the best armor I could get. The chest I found had an armor rating of 180!!! That's 45x higher than gear for my level. Enemies now hit me and do no damage. I don't even have to fight enemies anymore, I can just fly around half the time and avoid large chunks of areas.
Now you are probably wondering why I still gave this game a thumbs up....well, the answer is simple.. The game is fun! If you enjoy fighting games or Metroidvania games (or both), this game is a must play. It will reward you regardless of if you exploit the animation with frame cancels (the one I mentioned above is just one example,I have found more animation glitches/cancel in and out of combat). The action is fluid, the platforming is solid, and the story is okay.
If I had to say one thing negative about the game it would be this: Furries....Furries everywhere! I don't even wanna know what kind of fan art is lurking around the internet.

FFVII was the first FF game I've ever played and one of the first video games I've played, and until now, I still think that its the best in the entire FF series and one of the best games ever made in history (if not the best). I first played it on the PS, and now the PC. Overall I have played through the entire game for 7-8 times already, and I still couldn't get bored of it. The story was just epic, the characters lovable, memorable and engaging, and the gameplay fun and straight-forward. FFVII basically defined the JRPG genre to the rest of the world at the time it was first released. To say that this game was phenomenal would seem to be an understatement.
What is there to hate in this game? If you ask me, nothing. What is there to hate in this PC port? Plenty.
Basically the guys at SE had done nothing to make this PC port better in any way compared to the original PS version. The graphics and music became worse than it was before. It seems that playing this on the PS would be a better and wiser choice if you ask me.
So should you play FFVII? If you're a true gamer, you NEED to play this at least once in your lifetime. Not playing FFVII would be a disgrace to your fellow peers. If you've played it before, then you don't need me to tell you how awesome it is.
Should you buy this PC port on Steam? I don't recommend it. Its way better and wiser to experience what this legendary masterpiece has to offer by playing it on an emulator or if possible the original Playstation. If you still choose to buy it, wait for a sale.

I'm here to write a review of a very pretty interactive screensaver, Abzu.
Let's go back a bit. I returned Abzu last year because I found it unplayable with keyboard and mouse. Now I have an Xbox controller so I bought it again. Exciting!
Abzu does not recognize Xbox controllers. Bummer. Isn't Xbox controller like um, very common? Popular? Judging by various forum posts it does not recognize many other controllers as well.
OK, I bought a $20 Logitech controller. It works.
So back to the review. I have to keep it short because my finger hurts from having to constantly keep the trigger pressed to move forward. Bad controls. No customization of controlls whatsoever. Why can't I just control the movement with a stick?
As an interactive screensaver this is pretty good actually. Calming, relaxing, nice music, pretty colors. $20 is way too much though. I paid $15 for KSP and got over 500 hours out of it. I'm done with Abzu after 1 hour. For $5 this would be a nice distraction.
But there is no way you can call this a game. Even some reviewers do not know what the point of Abzu is. I was hoping for an open world exploration game but you're always in a small area,  limted by walls an have to find a door to move to the next area, which is exactly the same as the previous area. Repetitive. Boring after 10-15 minutes.
The pretty-ness and novely wears off quickly.
And here I am again running into trouble with Steam game rating. I wish I could leave a neutral review or a star rating. Simply "Yes" or "No" are inappropriate fr this gam... um title.
As a relaxing interactive simulation this is rerally nice, but I can't really recommend this anyone because Koi Pond is cheaper and has way pretteir fish. It's not as interactive though.
I opened a ticket with 505 Games regarding the Xbox controller issue. This is a problem since the release of Abzu and they have not addressed it. If there is no solution I will ask Steam for a refund. Again.
And thanks for the fish.
PS. Steam says that I've spent over two hours playing the game. That's because I Alt-Tabbed it to the background and went googling to figure out what the heck the point of Abzu is and to open a ticket with 505 Games.

is a stunningly beautiful game with superb visual and audio design that tells a tale of caution.
The game takes place in the ocean, and love and care is put into every bit of its design. The setting is detailed, with numerous real life animals and plants and all the interactions between. Fish school, sharks hunt, you're able to be right in the middle of it. Even after the story line is complete the game works wonderfully as just a source of relaxation. Combined with the soundtrack it's easy to get lost just in watching all the small interactions between the various animals, and of course it's always possible to make your own fun by grabbing a shark or whale and breaching right alongside it.
has a full orchestra behind it that's well utilized, with songs ranging from the calm to the frantic, but always keeping a central theme.
story requires that one to pay careful attention to the environment. It's primarily conveyed through murals, not too unlike the ancient cave paintings that fill the history books. These murals tell the story of a civilization that took power from the world recklessly, and now are no longer to be found. There are signs of collapse everywhere, but across the course of the game you are able to fix and repair, restoring what once was. Ultimately the game is hopeful - massive damage has been done to the world but with some sacrifice things can be made whole again.

The game starts very strong, exploration and the initial vying for position is well done. You are tasked with expanding as quickly as possible in order to avoid being crushed to death by the other emerging empires. Anomoly hunting is fun and the side missions are solid (Some are broken and cannot be completed though). Finding small pre-space fairing civilizations is fun as well and you have a few (though really not many) options with how to deal with them. The ship design system is good as well. You can build your ships to any specification you want, though there doesnt seem to be any coherent explanation of what each module does and you can easily find yourself losing a fight where you outnumber the enemy 2 - 1 if you outfit your ships badly.
5-6 hours in and you will hit a wall. There is nowhere left to expand and the diplomacy system is really not very well fleshed out. There doesnt seem to be any good way to increase relations and you can be left without an ally for the entire game. Instead, you are forced to spend an hour building up a fleet and then invading the next empire over. Your fleet then will be in ruins and you will have to spend another hour rebuilding it. Rinse and repeat 20 + times. Military focused empires seem to be relatively unplayable right now because of this. I tried to play a kind of space Nazi but you get so many disadvantages that it become esentially impossible to progress. Another problem I had had is the lack of personally governable planets. There seems to be a hard cap of 5 (out of several hundred terraformable planets) and the rest must be delegated to a maximum of 3 or 4 governors. As you can probably guess, this means that your governors tend to outfight you after even a small amount of conquest and rebellions become constant (somehow even more common  than early patches Eu4).  To survey planets you have to individually press each star in turn. If you are playing a large map (1000 stars) or even a medium one (600 stars) this becomes very tedious, very fast and it can be incredibly difficult to tell which planets have already been surveryed which means you end up pressing on each of them 4-5 times throughout the course of a game.  Another problem I have is with the research. There doesnt seem to be any logical progression and if you want a specific research you may have to complete 10 or more completely unrelated projects.
The game feels incomplete, as if there were plans to have the late game more developed but there just wasn't time to finish it before release. The game as a whole is pretty good but there are some significant problems that come along with it. I would recomend picking it up in half a year, after there has been time to flesh out the late game and maybe a dlc or two has been released.

This review is written from the perspective of the game being a Space 4x game and will be based off of a comparison to other space 4x games.
Space 4x has been mostly a ‘niche genre’ for many years now. For years we (Space 4x fans) have had to endure a lot of indy titles with mixed results. Don’t get me wrong, I appreciate the efforts of these single unsung heroes pushing the genre forward and putting countless hours into a labor of love with no real guarantee of fair compensation for their efforts. But I’ve always felt the genre deserved more attention than it has received.
I was hopeful that this game being produced by Paradox would be something special. After putting approximately 46 hours into the game I can honestly say that I do indeed feel as though they have accomplished something very special in this game.
I’m still on my first play thru of the game after 46 hours (I selected a larger galaxy) and I am now approaching end game in this play through. I tend to “role play” my empire as it marches thru the ides of time to Galactic domination. This play thru I created a tall thin-race of peaceful & intelligent reptiles who are pacifists and weak for ground combat. I am finding that I still get drawn into a lot of armed conflicts although I did not want to “role play” this game that way. I’m not sure if it is just my nature of “me smash u face and take u planet” or if the mechanics of the game just lend to that. I think a little bit of both tbh.
I have seen many different interesting stories play out on multiple planets over the course of my play through. I won’t reveal the details here but they’ve been quite engaging and every time I think a story is “finished” about an hour later I get a new pop up with a new development. This has been a complete joy for me. All of these stories playing out across my empire. Everything from trying to ‘up lift’ less advanced species to saving your own colony from a subterranean species (and eventually getting embroiled in their own politics) who have lived under my people’s feet the whole time. --- I’ve read other people say that the galaxy seemed empty or lacked life. I don’t know what game these people were playing. Did their session bug out? Something doesn’t jive because my play through so far has been just chalk full of side stories that have on-going dialogue and ramifications.
The Graphics of the game are beautiful. I will zoom around my solar systems and just pan the camera around zooming in on my ships while placing a planet in a back ground or the star of the system to frame it and take screen shots. I love exploring the visual beauty of the game. I know that might sound silly to some of you but I personally appreciate the extra effort here. The only complaints I would have about the graphics are some of the ship sets (the Reptile set for example) look blocky and almost like they belong in a Lego game more than in a game where the rest of the graphics are so gorgeous. I also would have expected little details like the space station to change / grow in size as you add modules to it. It looks too small; especially when it is cranking out Battleship sized ships.
The mechanics of diplomacy are good. However, I would hope to see some changes in the future. Some of the things I like are that once an empire really likes you, they actually seem to really like you instead of just waiting for you to get weak so they can back stab you. I also like that IF conditions are correct they don’t expect the moon and the stars for little things. (Like wanting “1 million dollars” for a star map) You can also have empires request to be your vassals which I think is pretty neat. ---Some of the things I don’t like are that once you are in a federation you can’t take any action (like declare war) unless it is your turn to be president which can be LONG stretches of time if you are in a larger federation. It would be nice if you could request an act of war from the federation even when you are not the president, and just when you are president have a strong political power to try and force the federation into war. At least give us the ability to ASK if the others are willing to go to war.
The UI appears simple at first glance. There however is a LOT going on here and it’s the little buttons and sorta buried things that I am sure are probably keeping a lot of people from doing all the things they want to do (they probably assume you just can’t, when they just don’t see HOW) All in all, the UI is GOOD, clean, nice and uncluttered. However, they could have done a better job of making some stuff obvious. Maybe more popups on mouse over, better explanations. The ability to see what all strategic resource is used for. How to merge fleets easily (and keep your primary fleet names). How to equip your ground troops with advanced weapons, etc.  There are a plethora of things that I’ve kind of either stumbled upon or just kept pawing at the ui until I figured out the best way to do things.  There is a lot to keep track of, especially early game, and your first play through will probably leave you feeling a bit over whelmed at first.  I suggest a lot of pausing and exploring the UI buttons to see what they are for.
Some people decry the combat…and I sort of agree to some extent. All in all it’s not horrid, but it could have been done better. First though let me say when you have large fleets with varying laser types that it does looks pretty.  What I wish is that you could have established formations and differing roles for ships. You can sort of try to do that via choosing which combat computer to put in your ship but it doesn’t seem to work 100% correctly.  I personally would also have the ships be a much smaller scale in comparison the astrological bodies around them and have it where you can use asteroid field strategically (games of cat and mouse with the fleets etc) .  Pretty much once your fleet is engaged the opposing fleets will just smoosh into each other blowing each other to hell until someone wins. I have pulled off some nice “flanking” maneuvers by bringing in second fleets. I don’t think they get any inherent bonuses for flanking except that they are not getting shot at while unloading their ordinance upon the enemy. At the end of the day the combat is pretty and functional but you get no deep tactical control and that will be a minus for some (if not a lot) of people .
I am finding the end game to have turned into a sort of Arms race between me and my neighbors with a conflict erupting here and there. You do need to be careful who you declare war on as it can quickly domino into a massive scaled conflict. My most recent battle had something like 15 or so total empires involved because of the politics of who was allied to whom. At this point I’m trying to get my tech high enough so that I can poke a stick at a proverbial bear in the form of an ancient empire that doesn’t grow but has advanced tech and fleet sizes.
TLDR:
Graphics 8.5  / 10  Beautiful game over all (Only reason not higher was because the ship / station graphics could use some detailing)
Music 9.5 / 10  (The music is top notch)
UI 8 / 10  (UI itself is very good, but they need to include in game UI scaling and also better how to do things explanations)
Gameplay 9 / 10
Diplomacy 9 / 10 (One of the best in a space 4x I’ve seen, but still could use some refinement on the federation interfaces etc)
Added flair 10 / 10 No other 4x game has given so much towards little side stories. This is the icing for me.
All in all there are some things I would have done differently, but for me, to date this is the best Space 4x game ever released. It WILL set a new bar for others to strive for. I am elated to see a game of my favorite genre be done so well and I hope its success will draw the attention of more developers and the 4x community gets some love :P

This is my personal favorite of the series, you can't go wrong with this game.

It's short - about 10 hours for the first playthrough while talking to everyone and doing all the sidequests (but for a $15 price tag, if you intend to play it multiple times or 100% it, completely worth it). It's pretty trivial to get a particular equipment/stat/move combination that breaks all combat. Combat itself is generally pretty easy sprinkled with an occasional enemy that will take off a huge chunk of your lifebar and environmental hazards that do the same. There's a save point practically every other room so there's almost no punishment for failure. You never really do find out what the antagonist's motivations are. Crafting is heavily under-utilized, as by the time you're able to craft most of the blueprints you find, you've already got better equipment...
...and yet despite all these faults, it's still a fun game. It's incredibly charming, the voice acting is varied and incredibly well-done, the music is good and the controls are very tight. It's a rather linear metroidvania style game, and it doesn't lean too far in either direction between "Grimdark" or "Sugarcoated". It has a very good time split between story, travel, combat and bosses. You level at just the right pace that there is absolutely no grinding necessary. You don't have to be super good at the game to make progress, but it helps. The platforming puzzles are fairly easy to figure out and mostly rely on your execution to complete them. And (though this one is a little more personal) it's nice to finally see a fantasy game with lizard-like characters cast in a positive role and not delegated to being early-game barbarous savages.
Definitely worth picking up if metrodvanias are your thing.

I vividly remember the hype over Call of Duty: Black Ops. Black Ops was going to be the next best thing. It was going to be great, and fix all the problems in the previous Call of Duty games. I wasn’t a COD player at that time, and had a bit of a more balanced view of the release. I knew that Black Ops wasn’t going to be the impeccable masterpiece the COD community was hyping it to be. I believed that, like the games that had come before it, Black Ops was going to have its own fair share of problems too.
I vividly remember the community backlash when the game came out and players finally realized this. Most of the prominent members of the COD community grumblingly played Black Ops because it was the popular thing to do--until they eventually abandoned it and looked back to previous games, waiting anxiously for Modern Warfare 3 to come a savior. The golden age of Call of Duty seemed to be over.
Fortunately (or unfortunately to some) this is not where the story ends; for me, it was the beginning.
I started to play Black Ops in its prime, a few months after it came out. It was my first real Call of Duty game (my only previous experience with the series was Call of Duty 2) and I was excited to play the game most people were playing. I discovered that the communities’ extreme reaction to Black Ops was a bit uncalled for.
I originally braced myself for a pretty awful single player experience, but was pleasantly surprised at the story, plot, and characters. The single player is nothing revolutionary, but the characters are memorable (especially Woods) and the plot was compelling enough to make me sincerely want to see how it ended. I also found the missions, specifically the Vietnam missions, quite fun. Vorkuta is also highly memorable. In short, is a single player experience I could definitely see myself playing yet again.
Co-op is almost equally as fun. Taking out endless waves of the zombified Nazis and other undead, aided by Perk-a-Colas, random mystery box guns, and Pack-a-Punched power weapons is a blast every time. Play with a group of dedicated friends, and let the good times swarm! I don’t like all the maps, but if you have people willing to play with you, then the expansion packs could be worth your money; with that many maps to choose from, I believe it would be difficult not to find at least one map that you all will enjoy playing together. Just a personal thought of mine though-- I wish that there were some kind of progress system in zombies--not just a "lets see how many waves we can get through in one game" approach. The amount of points earned in each match could be used as experience points to level up--more like the multiplayer experience. Just an idea, but this could have created a deeper gameplay experience.
Of course, any Call of Duty player knows that the multiplayer is what makes or breaks an installment, no matter how good or bad the single player and/or co-op experiences are. For everything that Black Ops multiplayer does well, there are an equal number of points that flag for improvement. I think my favorite parts of the multiplayer are the emblems/playercards. Players have the ability to craft almost anything they want as a symbol for their playercard, and creative/ artistic players have the shapes to create some beautiful pieces of artwork!
The contract system is a fun way to gamble for extra CODpoints to spend on your custom classes. They are completely optional, and you can choose ones that conform to your personal skill level, but the greatest rewards come with the highest challenge. Daring players may also gamble with their hard-earned CODpoints in wager matches, but hardly anyone plays these modes anymore. CODpoints are new to the franchise, and I found it nice to spend cash-like money on equipment that I wanted.
While weapons still unlock at certain levels, perks, grenades, and other equipment are all yours to buy as soon as custom classes are unlocked at level 4. I find all of the weapons unique, easily recognizable, and fun to experiment with--almost characters in their own right. I don’t like to use all of them, and players could definitely debate whether some of them are balanced. Certain weapons seem to be the go-to choices, but I don’t personally don’t feel any of them are “over-powered”. All of them have their own checks and balances: The M60 can tear through players, but is quite inaccurate; the Skorpion is devastating at point blank range but damage falloff is incredibly sharp; and the Commando is the king of assualt rifles, but doesn't unlock until level 44. The list can go on, but I believe with all these safety measures put in place, every player should be able to find at least one weapon he can enjoy using.
The maps are one of the biggest areas that need improvement. While I actually enjoy them all, Treyarch could do well to experiment with a different color pallet. When white, green, and brown are all the maps come in (the exception being Nuketown), these colors get old very quickly. The expansion pack maps are much more aesthetically exciting, but don’t expect to find too many servers that have them in the map rotation. If you really want to play them, gather some friends and start a custom game.
A few other more minor things could use some tweaking. Hit markers were terrible when the game first came out, but have since been patched to the point where there are few issues with them, although I believe hitboxes tend to trail a tad too far behind the player. There are a couple of things that were never patched, however. Napalm strikes often have an invisible fire effect. Depending on the terrain over which the strike was laid down, there may be patches of earth left physically untouched by the fire, but players will still be killed if they run over these areas. Napalm and mortar strikes also have the bad habit of killing players in sturdy buildings when the strikes are directed on the roofs.
I also wish that players weren’t allowed to make an “invisible” class. I don’t usually complain about weapons or equipment in this game (except Second Chance, which I hate with a passion) because I believe they all have the right to be used since the developers put them in the game, but it seems far too unbalanced to be allowed to run Ghost (Pro), Ninja (Pro), and a suppressor on both primary and secondary weapons. I do have to admit, though, I have only encountered a handful of players who use this setup.
Overall, I find Black Ops a unique, but lukewarm experience. The weapons are striking and lively; the maps are not as exciting, but fun to play nonetheless. Contracts and CODpoints are interesting additions to the series, although some killstreaks can be frustrating to deal with. And both player emblems and custom classes can be beautiful or ugly, depending on the taste of the creator. All of the things done right mix with almost an equal blend of mistakes, creating an experience that is neither great nor bad. Ultimately though, I believe that COD players who approach Black Ops with an open mind, as the new branch of Call of Duty as it is, will find a lot of fun here. New players to the COD series may also enjoy Black Ops, although they should be prepared for a steep learning curve--this is still Call of Duty, and the gameplay is as fast and furious as it is deadly.
Was Black Ops the next great thing to happen to Call of Duty? That would depend largely upon who you ask, but my answer is no. Does it deserve to go down in history as the game that ended COD’s golden age? Again, my answer is no. It may not continue the legacy of the games before it, but Black Ops is not an ending; rather it is the beginning of a new age of Call of Duty. And in my eyes, from what I have seen through my time with Black Ops, that age is looking surprisingly bright.

It seems to be a rare occurance these days that I don't regret buying a game. This would be one of those rare occurance.
Story -
I feel a bit conflicted by this one. I want to say the story was engaging, fun and well told. The only thing stopping me from doing so is the fact I grew up and now understand the complexities of life, and in that regard the story left a few holes that would have been nice to fill. These should not detract from the experiance for most people. As spoilers are not my intent I will not cover those. I will say the story will probably be good for most people and great for kids.
Game play -
Simple and fun. Makes me think of Sonic 2 at times with how you fly all over the damn place, and Odin Sphere with the general look and feel. The difficulty curve does fall off quite a bit late game due to some of the items making your magic attacks ungodly over powered. Normal value ~700, with items ~8000. This will make cheesing the end of the game stupid simple. Besides that I have to say it was enjoyable.
Controls -
The controls are very responsive and quite simple - yet effective. I really think it shines in this aspect. There are no excessive actions, and everything is covered with the press of a single button.
Sound -
Great musical score. Covers the whole range from epic to touching and never really feels out of place. The voice acting is well done - the lines feel natural enough and are delivered well. It was one of the things I was actually paying attention to in this game as the creators drew my attention to it with some of their advertizing blurb - I was not disappointed. The fidget interactions are quite amusing, and she really does tend to steal the show. I love the way you delivered those lines Kimlinh - absolutly adorable.
Graphics -
Really does remind me of Odin Sphere. Which is to say beautiful sprite work. And I will have to admit I did not check to see if this was actually sprite based or 3D meant to appear sprite base. Etherway the effect is very well done. That is not to say some times the magic effect's don't♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the screen making everything hidden behind a cloud of firey death, but no points lost for that; as the solution is simply not to throw 6 million fire pillars down all over the map.
All of that being said - I liked it. I do however feel about 22.7% more "furry" now.

I picked this up on a whim when it was on sale for a couple bucks. I don't generally do side-scrollers, but the reviews got me wondering. Well, I officially LOVE this game. There are bits and pieces of various themes in literature and gaming throughout, many done so well, you might not catch them at first. Even the main character, Dust, has elements of the main character in the story Total Recall. Trust me, that's not giving anything away you won't guess in the first 20 min of the game... and it's nowhere near the whole story.
The writing, controls, action, and level designs are well thought-out and implemented. Some of the "twists" really aren't and some are quite well done. In terms of gameplay, I've always liked the more intricate-but-not-overwhelming type of combat system used here. There aren't many combos, but with what there is, there's enough strategy between enemies that simply button-mashing won't get you through the entire game and it doesn't really get old... just comfortable. While made with a controller in mind, I finished the game just fine with a keyboard and mouse.
While you can get most of the achievements with the first play-through, the achievement system within the game rewards you for geting them again on each play-through. There's only one that has a proper choice (two achievements, but you can only get one of the two on any given play-through) and the obligatory "beat the game on (higher difficulty)". I also though the additional challenge areas were a nice touch. I've only managed to get 4 stars on ONE of them so far.
The animation is a bit clunky during the full-animation cut-scenes (of which there are only about 3 in the whole game), but the voice acting is spot-on and every character, no matter how small their part, has a distinct personality and not just some generic NPC plant with random sayings.
I don't know if they plan to do another (I haven't looked that up yet), but I'd be on-board for a sequel, or at least a follow-up in the same universe. There's a lot they can still do with it, I think. But then, it's like finishing a good book; you really don't want it to be over. That was me after playing Bastion, after all...
TL;DR version:
Great game. If you have ANY enjoyment of story-driven action-adventure games, then: GET IT. PLAY IT. LOVE IT.

If you are this is definitely worth $10, and if not it's easily worth $5 to try it for awhile.
My 2 complaints: Some of the mid to late missions need knife-edged precision to beat which can be frustrating old-school style, and it's made worse by the fact that the DLC choppers (which effectively enable a God-mode ability) can only be used once you beat the mission in standard mode.  Secondly the narrative humor is usually groan-worthy at best and HORRIBLY IRRITATING at worst.

With the upcoming remake of Final Fantasy VII there will definitely be mixed reviews about which is better. the remake or the original? The least any newcomer to the Final Fantasy franchise can do is to play the original first before any potential shortcomings the remake may have to offer.
For most the 1997 release was their first Final Fantasy and is therefore special to them. Upon replaying FFVII on Steam I had such an overwealming nostalgia which quite honestly surprised me. I could remember everything so clearly even after almost 20 years since first playing it. Everything was the same as I had imagined it even back then, though I will say that this updated version has a few things which had been changed. Certain dialogue and so on, though I don't think this is such a major issue to many.
The Materia system is still top notch, though now I am certainly more cautious with what I use instead of throwing everything on a character just because I had it, as I would have done on my first playthrough. Plenty of mini games to keep one entertained when sick of grinding or just want to take a break from the story. The battle system was exciting for its time, especially with the added Limit Breaks which were a huge improvement on VI's Desperation Attacks. which were quite frankly rubbish. The fact you could save the special attack for a better time as well as evolve them into better ones by using them was a reason to try out every character, just to see what they did. With the new release, the old battle system will certainly be dead and buried so we can probably say goodbye to many of the epic moves and abilities we once encountered.
The soundtrack? 11/10. Nuff said.
If anything, this is one of my least favourite Final Fantasies in the franchise, though it was my first. Even though I prefer most of the others, this truly is a special game that will not only challenge you, but become a part of you in the process. It can be a bit of an eyesore to look at in this day and age, but if you love a story rich game then there's nothing really stopping you from buying this game.

Ten dollars. Only a few hours of gameplay. 16-bit graphics compared to the flashy 1080p stuff in standard games.
But... wow Half-Life 2: Lost Coast blew me away. It doesn't need flashy graphics or even fanservice to falsify its enjoyment. It just does things right, and boy that was one immensely enjoyable experience.
I think most of the magic of this game comes from knowing absolutely nothing about it. I got this game from a friend and just decided to play it since it looked very interesting and it was getting good responses. So I went in completely blind, knowing nothing but the game's name. And I'm glad I did, because everything the game presented to me was unexpected, notably dark in places, and very emotional, which would have been lost entirely if i watched someone else play it. So, if you happened to have been flooded by everything Half-Life 2: Lost Coast on tumblr (god help us) and the entire story's already laid out for you, the magic has been lost and the game won't be as incredible of an experience. I'm sorry.
Half-Life 2: Lost Coast's ability to completely turn the tables of its story depending on your actions is massive. Upon your game's startup, every little thing you do will be set in stone in the game's story pathing. If you're the type who immerses yourself into the game's charming music, laughs at the childish but hiliarious anctics, and is willing to hork down healing items just to prevent yourself from killing a monster just because a fight is difficult, the game rewards you. It opens up a very character-developing and world-unfolding story, along with some of the most emotionally invested boss battles I have ever experienced. You know a game is good when it breaks the fourth wall so well that you're shaking in your seat in true fear and can't stop the shivers, all while having to fight a hopelessly overpowered god of a boss. The amazing writing only starts once you beat the final few bosses, and the story doesn't stop being good from there onwards.
On the other hand, what makes this game different is that it keeps its dark side from you, and its entirely your choice to experience it. If you scoff at the game's sparing choice since you're too cool or grown up to possibly be nice to people, you can go around and intentionally sink your weapon into a monster who just wants to be a friend. And unlike many other games, this isn't just a simple "Oops, I killed another unnamed enemy, let's reset the game and nothing changes" moment... the weight of a dark choice is huge. It forever changes your playthrough. Reset the game, and the characters know. Events change. And with each curious kill, you, in turn, turn from the only human in a land of monsters into the biggest monster in a land of innocents. In the end, ignoring what Half-Life 2: Lost Coast sets out to do, which is to let you experience childlike innocence and fun, only makes it delibrately change the game into a quieter, more grim story. Very little character development, and the world isn't explained to you, nothing. There's very little reward for going through this route. Yet it is a choice you can do. Granted, you get two of the hardest boss battles by becoming the murderer and will be forced into Game Overs repeatedly from them, but even that is a message from the game... It's trying to stop you from getting to the end of this route. Before its too late.
It's as if you're doing deeds in an actual living, breathing world. And that's what makes it even more terrifying when you decide to become a murderer instead of a savior, because only you know that you're willingly going forward to obliterate every weakling in front of you. It's a test of your willpower, and it's your choice. The worst thing? The damage cannot be repaired. Go clean, or go home tainted. The game even gives you the choice to completely delete everyone's happiness after the most satisfying happy ending. The happiness you worked so hard to earn. And you can even become the murderer after saving the world, which will only permanently taint your game and never let you have a satisfying ending again. That's absolutely brutal, and yet that's still a choice. Amazing.
Yes, this game might not be for everyone. The humour may become dry after a while for some people, and tons of gamers nowadays like to bash at popular games instead of trying it out, just because they feel accomplished by doing it. But, if like me, you are willing to experience why everyone's been talking about this game, give it a shot. This game does the morality concept so well that other games can only dream of doing the same, and it is one not to be forgotten.
It is a sin to call Half-Life 2: Lost Coast a game. Doing that would categorize Half-Life 2: Lost Coast into the bland and consequence-free "kill-em-all" genres that a lot of games are falling into now.
Half-Life 2: Lost Coast a story-driven, emotional experience.
