If you scroll down the (serious) positive reviews for this game, you no doubt see many people expressing their nostalgic love for this legendary piece of their childhood. I stand among these people. For many of us who were kids in the 90s,
was and always will be the first truly
game we ever played. So I’ll admit that I am definitely biased to love it, as it was my personal favorite game during a number of years of my childhood. But that isn’t why I’m going to recommend that you consider trying it. You should consider it because
is a classic piece of video-game history that revolutionized the genre and because it’s a kickass game.
At the time it first released, there were a handful of other large RPGs with huge worlds and a lot of gameplay (relative to the era), but they were uncommon and unpopular in the Western world.
reached a pinnacle of awesomeness for RPGs that was unprecedented and subsequently elevated the genre into the mainstream gaming market outside of Japan. Not only did it have sound RPG fundamentals, but the sheer amount of variety of gameplay it offered was quite revolutionary for the genre. Chocobo racing and breeding, the motorbike scene, the snowboard scene, the Golden Saucer, the Don Corneo segment, and more all contributed to shattering the status quo for the genre. A lot of young gamers went from not knowing about RPGs to one of them being their favorite game ever. Not only that, but it became one of the cornerstones which provided a foundation for the genre to grow towards what it has become today. If there was a Video Game Hall of Fame,
would no doubt be in it.
Obviously, with more recent RPG blockbusters from franchises like
,
, and
, it is hard to continue to consider
to be an “epic” game by today’s standards. Somehow it still feels that way to me. Or at the very least: since I enjoy the genre, I still find it quite fun to play.
So I will admit that it definitely has been a long time since
was one of the best games in existence. That said, even after the erosion of the sands of time, the game still feels exciting, intriguing, and massive to me. Even on my 8th playthrough I pick up on new subtleties in the story or discover new secrets and items.
The story is interesting, if not a bit convoluted. (Some of the story was cut away to make it “less confusing for the Western market” or some such silliness. This wound up making it more confusing.) The Materia system is fun and, combined with the traditional XP leveling, continuously offers the satisfaction of progress as you play through the campaign. The world is intriguing and still semi-large(ish) even by modern standards. The characters are perfect clichés of the very clichés that they themselves introduced. And one of the best parts of the game will always be the intimidating boss battles with the signature music. It is doubtful there will ever be another kid who says
is his favorite game ever, but most modern fans of the genre will enjoy this game despite its age.
So there are a few reasons you may want to consider trying this game if you never have.
If you consider yourself a true aficionado of the gaming industry, you will probably want to play
at least once in your life. Even though there is a “remake” on the way (or out by the time you read this), I would argue you should play this version at least once to really experience a legendary piece of video game history in this semi-unadulterated state.
Or: if you don’t care about any of the historical mumbo-jumbo, and just are looking for a fun, turn-based JRPG, then you can comfortably look to
for that as well.

is a stunningly beautiful game with superb visual and audio design that tells a tale of caution.
The game takes place in the ocean, and love and care is put into every bit of its design. The setting is detailed, with numerous real life animals and plants and all the interactions between. Fish school, sharks hunt, you're able to be right in the middle of it. Even after the story line is complete the game works wonderfully as just a source of relaxation. Combined with the soundtrack it's easy to get lost just in watching all the small interactions between the various animals, and of course it's always possible to make your own fun by grabbing a shark or whale and breaching right alongside it.
has a full orchestra behind it that's well utilized, with songs ranging from the calm to the frantic, but always keeping a central theme.
story requires that one to pay careful attention to the environment. It's primarily conveyed through murals, not too unlike the ancient cave paintings that fill the history books. These murals tell the story of a civilization that took power from the world recklessly, and now are no longer to be found. There are signs of collapse everywhere, but across the course of the game you are able to fix and repair, restoring what once was. Ultimately the game is hopeful - massive damage has been done to the world but with some sacrifice things can be made whole again.

TL;DR: the game lacks depth in its current state and has some glaring AI and UI issues. Wait for patches and/or DLC.
The early stages of the game are a lot of fun. Scripted events are constantly popping up as you're exploring the galaxy and colonizing new planets. It feels fresh and exciting.
However, as the available space fills up, the game grinds to a halt and you begin to notice some glaring issues:
- The AI is too passive. After the initial expansion into the empty space, the AI empires basically go into hibernation. They never interact with you aside from asking for your star charts once a century. They never declare war on you and very rarely declare it on other AIs. The alliances and ideological differences they have with each other are largely meaningless since everyone just sits there and does nothing.
- The battle AI isn't much better. The only scenario in which it poses a challenge is when it happens to have a much bigger "stack of doom" than you, otherwise it's just going to sit in a corner and cry as you destroy its empire, not even trying to defend itself. As for your allies, their AI seems to be non-existent: they just stick to your biggest fleet and follow it around until the war is over.
- Even if we forget about the AI for a moment, there just aren't enough interesting systems to interact with other empires. Diplomacy is extremely basic and so is trade. A lot of systems you would expect in a game of this genre, like espionage, are just missing.
- The UI turns managing a large empire into a nightmare. Too many small annoyances to describe - let's just say you'll be doing a lot of unnecessary clicking and digging through submenus for information that should be available at a glance. I should mention that there is a system in place to minimize micromanagement of planets by assigning them to sectors, after which they will be developed and upgraded automatically. Sadly, the AI for sectors seems to be insane, building all the wrong stuff in all the wrong places.
- The performance in late stages is problematic. Large-scale battles result in massive FPS drops. Plus, as I already mentioned, not much happens after the initial expansion of empires, so you're forced to play at the performance-intensive "fast" and "fastest" speeds to alleviate boredom, which in my case means spending the majority of time at stuttery ~20 FPS (I have an i5-2400 so your mileage may vary).
There is potential here, and knowing Paradox they'll be supporting the game for years, but in its current state I cannot recommend it.
If you've ever been nostalgic for Quest for Glory or just like a little bit of rpg in your adventure games, this is far better than any freeware ought to be.

This is a great game with a rocky beginning - I highly suggest you get through the tutorial and play at least 2 or 3 of the 5v5 PVP battles before passing judgment.  In addition to the cool lore and novelty of a moba in which you fly on a dragon's back, there are several key features that I think are innovative and make this game different from the rest of the pack:
* Pressing spacebar lets you move backwards but still face forward, which makes for some interesting mechanics in outmanuevering your opponents.  Breathing fire on your opponent while backpedaling is also just fun!
* The typical 4 abilities of most MOBAs are split - you get 2 from your dragon and 2 from your weapon.  This means you can create a huge number of combinations of abilities, flexibility which is really cool especially once you unlock a lot of dragons and weapons.  In other words, the same dragon can be played in vastly different ways depending on weapon choice.
* The matches are typically fast, like 10-20 minutes, which is nice - I don't have to dedicate as much time to drop in and play a game here and there.
* There are no in-match items to buy.  I love this becuase I don't have to memorize a huge inventory to play the game (or spend time sitting there agonizing over my item choice).  I can just concentrate on the game itself.
* There is much less focus on killing minions, and much more focus on fighting the other players dragons.
The art is beautiful but a bit rough around the edges, and the interface is serviceable but could be a bit more intuitive.
At its core, Dragons and Titans is a great game that does key things differently from the MOBA crowd.  It fits great for me as a game I can drop in and play here and there without having to read tomes to catch up on what I missed or be screamed at for being a newb every moment when I play again and forget item builds...
It may not draw you in with its tutorial, but give it a chance to shine and it does not disappoint.

F.E.A.R. - First Encounter Assault Recon:
Intro:
An absolutely amazing FPS experience full of glorious bloody goodness! If you are a true FPS or horror game admirer, do not miss out on playing this game.
Nothing beats a mad fearguy shooting through a horde of replica soldiers, on his mission to reach Paxton Fettel.
The story is simple and so is your goal, but it doesn’t have to be anything complex, it works and I may go as far to say that it adds a bit to the atmosphere.
Graphic, controls, performance, & sound:
The combat/controls are very decent and so is the graphics of a 2005 game. Exploding bodies with a single shot from shooty is one of the things that always made me giggle in a rather cruel way. I especially like the graphical details of; weapon skins, bullet detail, explosives and fire in general.
Never had performance issues with this game, but again it’s from 2005; a nowadays low-end pc with a medium-end graphic card shouldn’t have too much trouble running this game.
There is a good amount of sound detail in this game that helps to trick and mislead you in situations of scares. The weapon sound is quality and the combat background music fits in nicely.
Artificial Intelligence:
The AI technology in this game is absolutely amazing; those replica soldiers will run, hide and kite you, like their life were at stake, eh I guess it is against a mad fearguy on the loose!
Overall:
My only dislike was the very similar level stages, but compared to the overall experience and long playtime value, it didn’t really matter to me.
I played this on the PS3. I plan to play it on the PC sometime in the future again on a harder mode. I personally prefer FPS on the PC and would recommend it over playing it on the PS3 - if you’re used to play FPS on the PC.
F.E.A.R. Extraction Point:
I didn’t expect much from this expansion first time I tried it, but color me surprised! It’s more spot on compared to the first one regarding scares, which I found to my liking.
If you enjoyed the first F.E.A.R. and felt like you didn’t get quite enough scares, this one may satisfy your desire on that point.
Alma also takes a larger role in this game as well and may aid you if the situation counts for it.
The weapon armory is very similar compared to F.E.A.R., which I didn’t mind at all, since I like most of the weapons.
The levels were great! A lot of fun and strange stages- Alma playing tricks on you and all that sort of stuff. The playtime value is also decent 6-8 hours depends on how long you spend on looking for goodies.

This game has started off on a pretty good foot, but it's exactly that....a start. There is a lot of things that are missing or I wish were included. Starting off with the victory conditions.
The first victory condition is colonizing 40% of all habitable planets. This does not seem military like and a lot of people will debate me on my next claim. You need military for this if you are playing with 29 other empires on a huge galaxy. As of now I have found no way to out colonize other empires to 40% before each star has already been snagged. If you play with less empires it's possible, but not with 29. This makes you have to build a huge military to the point you scare or impress other empires to become your vassal [then diplo-annex them later] or straight out take them over.

The second victory condition is eliminating every other empire. It's your straight foward domination victory. I have not achieved this goal, but I have witnessed other people do it and it is definately the harder to complete if playing with a lot of empires.

I am militaristic, I love military, but these victory conditions suck. It turns the game into a routine. How well can you prepare for one of the two victories. It reminds me of the Civ series, how precise is your strategy to ensure [in that game 5] victory?
One of the reasons I loved Paradox games is the leaders are usually weighed by multiple factors. Take my favorite game Victoria 2. The lead is determined by industry, prestige, and military. At the same time though there isn't really
victory. In most paradox games, I pick a country, try to defy history and shoot for the crazy random achievements. It's a game of "how far can I get this little country" or "can I make USA not suck?" instead of what Stellaris has become.
That my friends is the biggest issue. The victory conditions lose what made paradox games so cool and unique. There is other factors to be honest.
Diplomacy in CK2, EU4 and Vic2 are leaps ahead of Stellaris. Stellaris has a Civ V like diplomacy system. Because this game only has three resources there is no import export economy. In Vic2 if I needed quick supplies for my recruitments I would trade for the resources. But since there is NO industry in Stellaris there is no trade partners or reliance on trade. It ruins the feel of running a nation. What are my people doing? just working at energy, food and mineral factories?
While there are more issues with diplomacy Steam has a character limit on reviews so I am going to move on to my biggest gripe with this game.
Oh boy where to begin. So some back story for those who are unaware. In Victoria 2 you have a tab dedicated to your people. You can see their idealogies, the voters' idealogies, how many people want a certain policy, political parties represented in your upper house, reform clamour, who is getting what needs, taxes on each social class, the list goes on and on and on.

In Stellaris, all your people demographic does is show factions [like seperatists and loyalists] and the break down of species.
. This becomes a problem when changing policies. When it comes to letting my people migrate in my Military Dictatorship, do my people want it? will it make them happy? do they even care? WHO KNOWS!!!!!
There is also no change in government with elected leaders. For example, in Victoria 2 again, the country of Texas became Communist due to the immense support from voters. There is nothing like that here. It doesn't feel like a true empire. What's the culture of my people? What God do they worship? What is their political views? I KNOW NOTHING!!!
Half the fun of Vic2 was either doing what my people wanted, or see how long I could oppress them with such force. Both of those things are lost and it's not for the better.
So much work needs to be done to consider this game a Paradox game. For now though, it's a good start. Feels like an Early Access game but a good one.
I guess now before I introduce the TL;DR I will talk about the things that make this game worth the money if you can look past the few flaws I pointed out.
This seems to be a love hate relationship right now. Some people hate it, others like me love it. The best part about this game is the ship designer. Once you researched some tech you can swap out weapons, reactors, hull armor, thrusters, hyperdrive the whole 9 yards. This allows you to make the combatant you want. There is of course some things to consider, like making an all energy weapon ship might go against you if you go against an empire with defenses made for such attacks. So it's good to mix it up a little bit.
Along with combat is the ability to see the fights go down...well in space anyway. You can watch massive space battles and dang is it gorgeous. Sending troops planetside to annex a planet is of course unseen but can be followed through a stat screen.
Combat for me is great, there could be some tweaks like an espionage system to spot what empire has what kind of military, but for now I am good for where it's at.
The first hour of each playthrough is probably me creating the empire. It's unique to paradox, creating exactly how you want to start. I usually create a backstory, write it out in word, and have a narrative going into the game. Setting the victory conditions aside and just playing allows me to act like it's the good ol' days of paradox.
I hope they add more options or traits in the future but for now this is one of the best parts of this game. When you are done with an empire you made, you can make it appear in your later games. For example, If you made 2 empires. You could set one to always appear in a game and play with the other. My whole back story narrative thing makes this amazing.
I have been dying for a grand strategy that takes place in space. While this is a GS 4X hybrid, it quenches that thirst. From Black Holes to Floating Ceramics in orbit of a star there is tons of things to discover, research and observe. There is also some cool situations that will happen involving space such has


The workshop is already integrated, leaving me to hope there will be some Star Wars, Star Trek, Battlestar Galatica etc... mods.

Heroine's Quest: The Herald of Ragnarok is a classic graphical adventure game themed on Norse mythology with extensive combat and RPG mechanics in the vein of Quest for Glory. It is effectively an affectionate parody of classics such as King's Quest.
Please keep in mind that although the game designers are clearly FAMILIAR with Norse mythology, this game does not simply faithfully copy it - the mythical Norse characters are noticeably different in story and/or basic design from their namesakes, which to be honest is entirely consistent with classic adventure games. For instance, it is the Heroine who goes after Fafnir at Regin's request, as opposed to Sigurd who just sits around cooking great food all day. That said, savvy players may still pick up on details ahead of time, such as with Hervor.
As the dialogue in the game is fully voice-acted, you play as the nameless Heroine who must be female and who is never referred to by name. You may select one of three classes: Warrior, Mage, or Thief. Of these three, Warrior is considered easy, Mage is medium, and Thief is hard; the game will adjust the solutions to its puzzles according to which of these classes were selected. Warrior basically just muscles and fights her way through everything, you see, and is suitable for a first play until you're familiar with the general flow of the game.
After picking a class, you are given points to boost your starting stats or add new skills - after this point, you are more or less unable to learn skills you don't already have, such as the ability to cast magic or gather herbs. I strongly advise that your first run through the game be with a vanilla Warrior with all points dumped into Agility (in my experience the slowest stat to raise).
The game is divided into several chapters, each of which makes clear a basic story goal for the Heroine to complete such as "save the guy you just saw fall down half-dead in the snow". As a fair bit of warning, you may permanently miss out on sidequests if you proceed to the next chapter without doing them, so be sure that you've done all that you can do before moving on - the game has no time limit beyond keeping the Heroine from dying to starvation / sleeplessness / freezing, so you're free to grind your skills and farm silver from the various enemies.
Heroine's Quest features a rudimentary real time combat system - the reason I said to spam Agility is because you will go faster and the other guy will go slower. If an enemy catches up to you, then you have to fight it. The Heroine may not only attack from several directions, but she can also change her weapon outside of combat (presuming she has more than one) - some enemies are much easier to fight with specific weapons. She can also block (Warrior) and dodge in three directions (everyone), and may learn additional special attacks over the course of the game. Mage can use some of her spells in combat, as well.
The game's most frustrating feature by far has to be the hidden point values. Your Score itself will announce when you've accumulated a point, but your hero score and morality don't; the only indicator of those values to my knowledge is in an optional (but extremely useful!) bonus in the Warrior's endgame. Fortunately, the other two classes don't have access to that content anyway and therefore don't have to worry about their hidden values, but it's very frustrating for those of you who want a "perfect" run, especially since the game frequently updates to change what affects your hidden values.
All in all, Heroine's Quest is a wonderful game, especially considering that it is entirely payment-optional. Consider chucking a few bucks their way to help ensure they produce another game of this quality!

Definitely one of the most brilliant metroidvania games for its different approach to story and combat. Heavily recommended.
Pros:
+Fluid and responsive controls and combat (except for the Parry mechanic, see below)
+Beautiful graphics and level design
+Decent story and voice acting
+Fidget breaks the 4th wall a lot without it getting old
Cons:
-Crafting system inhibits your equipment progression a lot. You'll have to rely on level-ups and random drops for most of the game.
-The parry system makes sense (it's like tech in Kingdom Hearts), but the lack of a dedicated guard button makes some enemies a pain to take out. Parry also has very unintuitive timing and actually ends up stunning YOU sometimes.
-The enemies at the end of the game have very poor mechanical design, though I would owe this more to the broken Parry System than anything else.
The problems with parry and crafting are really just minor issues in a truly amazing game. They only warrant criticism because the rest of the game is so good.

As the Steam Store page mentions, LC is a tech demo that was originally planned as a section of the Highway 17 chapter in HL2. It is a free download and is automatically added to your Steam Library when you purchase a copy of HL2.
The demo is very short and you can probably rush through it in under 30 minutes. You have access to all of the weapons from the original game to fight your way up a cliff side and retake an ancient church which the Combine have garrisoned into an artillery platform.
The main purpose of the demo was to showcase Valve’s new HDR (High Dynamic Range) lighting and demonstrate how it integrates with the Source engine. Despite being released in 2005, the results still look relatively impressive today. Highlights include how light reflects on water and wet terrain, and how it refracts through glass. There is also an interesting section where HDR tries to imitate the iris of a human eye by using light blooms when the player is suddenly exposed to daylight after being in shadow.
Additionally, LC introduces a commentary mode to the HL series. In this mode, audio nodes can be found which play a track recorded by various members of the development staff. These nodes provide some insightful commentary if you are at all interested in the development process, or if you simply want to get a little more replay value.
There are some rough edges in the demo; I encountered some graphical flickering and occasions where the enemy AI would not respond as cleanly as in the original game. Despite this, LC is a beautifully presented and swift diversion that can easily be included in your play through of the HL2 series.

Red Alert 3 is a game that signals the end of a series. Not because it's a bad game, it's a fairly mediocre one, but because everything that defined Red Alert and made it different from the rest has gotten completely away from the designers.
The graphics has gone full on cartoon which might work for some people but for me it just makes me cringe. The science is silly as always but the units, particularly the animal units will make your sense of logic die a little. The national stereotypes are just bordering on full blown racism and the cleavage is in your face and everywhere.
The biggest feature of this game is the ability to play through all the campaigns in coop-mode and while is this a great feature it is also one that dies pretty fast. You can't just buy it and boot it up and expect there to be coop partners available.
All in all, it's not a terrible game, it's just not a very good one either. All the things that made Red Alert a special game has been completely ruined.

I didn't quite give this game a fair shakedown the last time I reviewed it, and I recently got the urge to replay and actually beat the game this time.
First, a sidenote - my previous time through the game, I ended up one conversation away from the final events in the game, without even knowing it. Awesome. During my second playthrough, I got to where I saved, and I figured "why not, lets do this quest!" and then I was suddenly fighting the last boss and I felt like a total fool. That aside, I never really gave the game the attention it deserved. I was playing it in fragmented bits, and eventually I just forgot the entire story and gave up, only to return a few years later and finish this recent playthrough.
The Witcher 2 is a fantastic game that oozes atmosphere and deserves high praise. A very "PC" feeling game, with a control scheme that makes Dark Souls combat work well on a keyboard and mouse, a robust crafting system that rewards careful thought, and an incredibly deep story that reminds me of Game of Thrones.
Geralt of Rivia is a great main character, and the writing style allows you to carve out exactly who your version of Geralt is. There isn't a black and white morality system with a bar to fill up, which is very refreshing considering how morality is generally approached in games. This means you don't need to feel bad about shaking down a peasant for a little bit of extra pay, and you can also be the hero of the town but not approach it in a manner that makes you gag. Without spoiling the story, Witchers operate on their own code and own morals and it means you don't really need to worry about pleasing anyone other than yourself. There are lots of decisions to be made, and many of these decisions echo throughout the game, with a few major decisions even altering the course of the entire game.
The middle chapter of the game is entirely different based on a few options made in act one. There are 16 possible endings, with multiple variations on each ending. There isn't a distinctly "good" ending to chase, either, which means you don't really need to worry about making correct decisions for a satisfying conclusion. The world of The Witcher isn't really a high-fantasy cliché, either. Ultimately, this means you can approach all the major decisions how you wish without much worry, and the weight of your decisions actually mean something.
This is not an easy game, either. You have to be constantly using all the tools at your disposal, and alchemy plays a key role in your survival. There are multiple viable ways to approach combat in the game, and the fact that it isn't just plain hack-and-slash is a breath of fresh air. It is entirely possible that you'll die a lot in the first bit of the game, until you learn how to approach each battle, and learn to continously buff yourself with potions, oils on your swords, and knowing how to approach enemies.
All of these factors come together to make a relatively dense game. It isn't very easy to casually play the game, and you can get lost with relative ease. The Witcher demands that you spend time getting to know the world, which has positives and negatives. You're kind of expected to have a bit of knowledge about how the first game played out, but you can figure it out by reading the journal and spending time in the game. It's actually kind of nice to have a game that doesn't go through a lengthy "And this is what happened last time!" segment that feels forced. The story isn't shoved down your throat and you have to really get into it.
The Witcher 2 goes on sale quite often, and if you have a PC that can handle the game, it would be criminal to not pick it up and give it a playthrough. You are definitely guaranteed an excellent time.

I grew up on the Quest for Glory series, playing the ever living heck out of them. Heroine's Quest is like a brand new Quest for Glory game, with the same style of writing, humor, the same kind of dialogue interactions and quest dynamics, the same kind of RPG mechanics worked in and overall it has the same kind of feel, yet has improvements made thanks to the advances of time. Having it be a Heroine just adds substantially to my enjoyment of this game. It's not often I get to actually play as my gender in a game that acknowledges it freely in its dialogue.
The voice acting is ridiculously good. Quest for Glory IV, back in 1994, had some of the very best voice acting you will ever hear in a video game, and this game is right up there with it. Compared to the wooden, monotone voice acting you get in so many other video games, it's such a treat.
This is a blast from my past and yet brand new to me, and it's all I ever wanted in a game. I only wish two things of it: that you could have romanced a female character (because yay girl love!) and that there was a sequel available I could play too.

This is one classy game. I played Quest for Glory back in the day and this is very much an homage to the form, with modern production values--it's got voiced dialogue, for one thing. Gameplay is a mix of adventure, RPG, there's a few survival elements (you have to eat occasionally and stay too long in the frozen woods and you'll freeze to death), and combat is fairly action-game--you have to dodge the right way to avoid certain enemy attacks, and recognize their tells to hit them when it's safe. The setting's extremely Norse, and while it doesn't deal -directly- with a lot of mythology, people who know their Norse will spot all sorts of little clues and call-outs.
This is the best free game on Steam, only on Steam to get a wider audience. There's no pay-to-win, no currency, it's just a game made because a group felt it should be made. It costs nothing but the space it takes to fill it, and it's rewarding to play and rewarding to beat. Sometimes I'll fire it up just to wander around and check it out once more.

Witcher 2 is an action- rpg and like it's predecessor, it's based on novels and short stories by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski. It's developed by Polish company CD Projekt Red.
Witcher games are about monster hunter called Geralt of Rivia, also known as Butcher of Blaviken. Geralt has two objectives during the game, to regain his lost memory and find the Witcher who slayed the king, while being accused of killing the king himself.
The main story is intriguing and full of surprises. It highly varies based on your decision in the end of first chapter. Second and third chapters have different locations, characters and story focus depenging on your path. This gives Witcher 2 great replayability since different plot points will be revealed. Just like the main questline, side quests offer the same thoughtful and witty writing. There's morally ambigious choices throughout the game and you never know when the consequences come back at you. But very often they will.
The negatives in the game would be the horrible Inventory system, it's a pain to navigate.No overwriting saves, so every save will be a new one and save folder can grow to even 5 gb. Too many saves also slows the launch menu and has been reported to sometimes even cause crashes. So I deleted my saves manually on occasion. I also wasn't a big fan of the combat changes. While the combat in first one was bit more tactical and rhythm based, now it feels a bit too button mashy. More tools to fight have been added though, like traps and throwing knives. I was also bothered that after killing an enemy, if there's another present, Geralt will automatically leap on the next one if you just keep on mashing the attack. Sometimes quite ridicilous distances.
Voice acting is stellar and the music makes Geralt's journey feel even more epic. The game was gorgeous when it first came out. Still looks good even today, which makes it harder to run well on older machines. Personally I enjoyed the first game a bit more, because of the story and even the combat. Though most people will prefer the more action oriented combat of this sequel. Witcher 2 is one of the best modern RPG:s and highly recommended to anyone looking for a great mature fantasy world.

To me this game is vast, requires a steep learning curve, and needs dedication before its beauty is seen. While I would consider my progress in this game in its infancy, I certainly like the playstyle. I haven't bought any of the DLC as I feel like I would get lost with all the extras when I don't know how to handle the current ones I own.
As far as gameplay goes, my laptop is starting to struggle with my 5 team, huge clustered, slow progress map on turn 500. I haven't seen any crashes or instability except for when zooming in and out of my map to look around.
One frustrating thing I have with the game is that the when you highlight a ship for movement and then move your cursor around the map, the ship is no longer highlighted for orders and it becomes an idle ship. Then when you tab to access that ship again, it refocuses on the same ship removing you from your position which creates the same scenario. The fact that the ship cannot stay highlighted infuriates me especially when I'm trying to get away from the Drengins.
On a positive note, the complex mechanics of the game keep the mind intrigued. Just when you think you had the fastest ships in the galaxy there will be a slow down causing you to rethink your long term attack strategy. This is exactly what I was asking for in a space management game such as this. While you do not control the performance of your units directly, knowing your chances and the risks associated with attacking the enemy fleet can keep the game exciting enough for the tacticians of the world.
I do find it lacking that special something, however. Maybe it's because I've only played 20ish hours of it (although it feels like I've spent more), but I haven't gotten hooked like I did with Star Wars Empire at War. Where is my giant class battleship that counts as 30 logistic points? Maybe that's something that I have to create in order to find.
The ship designer is cool, but I don't feel like many players, including I, know how to use it. It's just... there. If I had better instructions on how to use the tool that would be nice.
Otherwise I enjoy the game, and it's been fun to see how it has grown from Beta to the current release I'm playing now.
On a scale of golf cart to Lamborghini I give it a Mustang, one of those games that look sweet and sound sick, but just don't have enough juice to get you oogling over.

This game is simply incredible, one of very few games I've enjoyed from beginning to end. I've wanted to try it ever since I first heard about it after its release, and it went beyond my expectations. The art is beautiful and the soundtrack equally so. The fighting controls are easy to pick up for inexperienced or beginner players, and include attack combos for more skilful combat if you find them too plain. And the story only seems to deepen throughout the game before coming to an emotional conclusion. (Also you can't fall into holes and die instantly. Definitely a big plus in my opinion.)
A few technical issues did come up that I feel I should make note of. The first was a rather nasty glitch where pressing W or D on the map screen caused the game to crash, close, and prevent me with a crash log which needed to be force quit to get rid of it. The second was less major but still rather strange; two of the cinematics played completely without voices - one with music, one entirely silent - before freezing on the last frame. Nothing else happened until I paused and resumed, at which point the audio played by itself and the game resumed normally. It only occurred at the top of the mountains and when confronting the final boss, which leaves me confused as to why no other cutscenes were affected if it was a hardware issue.
Those problems aside, I absolutely loved this game and would highly recommend it. I bought it on sale but it's definitely worth full price.

Since this came on steam in 2013, I think it's appropriate to review it in the context of it being 2013.
This game doesn't hold up. It was amazing at the time, but everything is has has been done better by other games since. The world is under-developed by modern standards. The theme park, snowboarding and 'sex-club' sections are jarringly out of place, the tone and pacing is basically non-existant. The characters aren't fleashed out enough when you hold them up to modern standards, and don't cut them the slack that players were giving them back in 1996. Large parts of the game are tedious, from grinding missions, busy work, to not being able to skip the summon's intro cinematics.
Having said that, when playing, you can catch a glimpse of what people saw back around 20 years prior, it's worth having a look at because of it's status as a 'legacy' game. A game that's defined a large part of gaming's history.

Oh my ok let's do this;
THE GOOD
-Ships/Textures design is good

THE BAD

Hidden under the cover of the joys of burning dozens of items hides an important message in this game. In a world where everything is freezing, all you have is your Little Inferno playset, where you burn everything you buy and buy everything to burn to stay warm. The game is fairly simple, buy, burn, buy, combine, burn, get a new catalouge, repeat. The motonony of the game is interupted at times by messages by your neighbor, the Weather Man, or the owner of the Little Inferno's company. The game actually does has something to say under all of this, it works to show how consumerism consumes our lives where instead of us buying to buy, you just buy to burn the items immediately. Then you have no idea of the outside world, of your cold little town showing that your only true concern is the destruction of all the things you buy. There's many more subliminal messages lying under the main message that you can figure out throughout the whole game play. I love this game. While it's the same over and over each time, there's always more you will notice.

A great beginning -- but it needs a lot of work.
I've really enjoyed 4X games -- all the Civilizations, going back to Civ1, Alpha Centauri, Galactic Civilizations II.
Another game I've really enjoyed is Sins of a Solar empire.
This game feels like Civilization mixed with Sins. Sounds great at first! Actually, there is a lot to love in this game:
Good stuff:
* Great customization on your race. You can pick a variety of traits and also choose from some traits for your government that make the gameplay really varied. For instance, you can make a government which makes slavery more or less acceptable, or make a science based government that gives you science boosts.
* Cool tech tree. It feels very non-linear and different play throughs feel very different.
* You can choose from 3 different ways to travel: warp, hyperlanes and wormholes. This really changes up strategies!
* Graphics are really sexy, soundtrack is pretty cool too.
* Fun to explore and find habitable planets around you.
* A number of NPC civilizations which you can conquer or ignore.
* Rock-solid stable. I haven't had any crashes.
Bad stuff:
* Game feels unfinished. Early game is really fun, mid and late game are samey and don't have much depth.
* Diplomacy is REALLY basic. You can bribe other civs but it doesn't really do much for you. No nuance at all, no spying, diplomats, etc.
* A number of broken galactic events (invaders that can't be defeated, etc.)
* Allied fleet AI is really poor. Other civilizations will spawn fleets that follow around your largest fleet. This leaves other fronts and their home planet undefended.
* You can only directly command 5 planets at once. (you can get a few more with bonuses). After you reach your limit, you can put a "Sector AI" in charge of a semi-autonomous region. While this sounds great in theory, the sector AI is pretty dumb and makes lousy development decisions. I understand this was a design choice to avoid too much micromanagement, but the AI does an awful job on your behalf.
* You can't give detailed combat orders to your fleet. All your vessels tend to form a giant blob and just charge at each other. Most wars consist of you globbing together one big fleet and charging for your opponent's very large fleet.
* Lack of auto-explore or auto-improve for your scouts and workers. It's nice to point a worker or a scout at a system manually when you need to, but with 1000 star systems, you're going to spend a lot of time either clicking "Build Station" or "Explore System".
Conclusion:
The word on the street is that Paradox games typically are underwhelming at launch and then later patches/DLC fix and improve them. This game is a great foundation, but it really needs more development to shine. I'd give it a 6 / 10. My recommendation is DON'T buy this game right now. Wait for Paradox to fix it up. I really hope a lot of the weak areas are addressed in free patches as opposed to paid DLC. It would really irritate me to have to pay more when the game is in such an unfinished state right now.

Recently replayed, after reading a discussion on whether FEAR was better than HL2.  I personally think HL2 is better overall, but they're both great games and FEAR excels in areas where HL2 falls short in comparison.
PROS:
Excellent enemy AI
Great pacing
Great enemy encounters
Great lighting
Weapons*
Bullet time mechanic is fun to use (I'M SHOOTING ROCKETS OUT OF THE AIR HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥
Spooky at times (if you're into that)
CONS:
Very linear gameplay
Map design is not great**
Spooky at times (if you're not into that)
The shading has not aged well
* I love the weapons in this game, particularly some of the more unorthodox guns you come across later on.  They all feel appropriately powerful, and bullet impacts kick up dust and blow giant chunks into walls like you would not believe (it is incredibly satisfying).  That being said, I would be remiss if I didn't mention that the weapon sounds do not hold up by comparison, especially when compared to the audio from HL2.
** The maps are very labyrinthian; there's only one path from the start of a level to its end, and the path you take between encounters with enemies doesn't make very much sense in a narrative sense.  I frequently forgot where I was supposed to be heading, and relied on the presence of enemies to guage my progress through the level.  Occasionally the path taken will fork, and the player can find extra supplies or upgrades if both routes are explored, but the slow walking speed makes this tedious (routinely, I would walk halfway down one path, and then halfway down the other, until I figured out which one was the critical path).  I can't complain too much, since this is standard for this kind of shooter, but it is still a negative aspect.
Overall its a great game, and if you can overlook the somewhat poor level design you will find a shooter which has aged magnificently.

First off, if you have played, watched, or even HEARD of this game's masterpeice of a sequel and are a) a W3 fan wanting to get some insight into the world before, or b) an original Witcher player gearing up for its action-packed sequel (not likely), I advise you to abandon all your preconceptions before playing The Witcher 2. Do it. Leave them at the door and don't turn back. This is easily my least favorite of the trilogy, and one of the most rage-inducing games I have EVER played, but I must explain why I still consider it among my favorites.
At that, allow me to list the numerous gripes I have with it, for the sake of contrast with The Witcher 3:
-Potions cannot be downed on the spot. The first and formost problem with this game is this, I think. This idea is only passable in the context that you've already endured dozens of hours of hapless slaughter in your first playthrough because you had no idea something dangerous would be around a corner and gave no thought to taking some Swallow beforehand. A painful betrayal for Witcher 1 and 3 fans alike.
-Combat itself is clunky and aggravating. I can't even begin to describe how I felt about the combat. I appreciate that it captures the chaos of swordfighting aesthetically, but some parts are just atrocious, like the block mechanics and awkward quick access menu. You will often find yourself wandering into an easy-looking scuffle only to die four times before deciding to just stay away from that area. I've no shame in admitting that I spammed Igni and Quen in the first half of the game.
-Levelling and total game time disagree with each other. The original Witcher can be up to 10 hours LONGER than its sequel, itself averaging about 30 hours. It's forgivable at first, but one can only accomplish so much in 30 hours with the levelling system, which seems tailored to people who would rather commit to a single skill tree than flesh out their options, like I did (and barely scratched the late-game perks as a result.) It also adds insult to injury that Geralt doesn't really get better as he gets new skills, but just becomes less bad.
-The atmosphere of The Witcher 2 is far too fantastical in comparison to its flanking brothers, and to a newcomer I fear it may sell a misconception about the game's roots. The Temerian swamps in W1/3 (and the absence of dragons) feel more grounded in reality, but the sprawling locales of W2 don't fit. Geralt also seems to treat witchering as more of a part-time career in this game than what it actually is: a social caste and lifelong stigma.
In the end, all problems aside (but not out of view; some are plain inexcusable) The Witcher 2's story is an amazing spectacle and a necessary prelude to the events of its sequel. It's worth climbing the mountain just to see how drastically characters change and events unfold when guided by your choices (which are definitely more drastic here than either of the other entries). It's an intimidating mountain though. My best advice is to treat it like the long-awaited successor to the original and forget the improvements its 2015 installment exacted upon.

NOTE MY ACTUAL PLAYTIME WAS ABOUT 7 HOURS; Left the game running overnight which added about 14 hours to my playtime.
General impressions:
This is a very good "Metroid-lite" game, really targeted towards kids in the 10-12 year old range. Even on harder difficulty settings, combat offers little to no challenge unless you avoid purchasing weapon upgrades, etc. Certain AOE attacks can be pretty easily spammed, and the only difficulty comes with some light platforming and simple puzzles.
Additionally, the voice acting, while well done, has a real "wholesome children's TV" feel, with a few really irritating voice actors with high pitched cartoon-animal voices. Again, really professional actors, but feels geared towards kids.
The story is kind of a holocaust allegory, nothing too special that hasn't been done before, but it stays pretty much on target.
Controls were good and I was never frustrated by any difficulties contrlling the game.
Lots of collectables (in the form of hidden characters from other indie games), and it would take a while to 100% the game. Doing so requires backtracking a lot - double jumping, sliding, etc are all skills learned later in the game that are used to lock away a few items/zones in the earlier stages. All of these are pretty much totally optional. Unfortunately, there's no way to continue playing after beating the final boss, so going back to 100% the game requires reloading a save just before the final battle and  then backtracking - a bit irritating, and I felt like after my 7 hours of play I didn't really feel like I needed to play any more to get to 100% (I ended around 85% completion).
Graphics are very nice and on par with a game like Dragon's Lair in achieving an early-80s cartoon feel, though sometimes they're inconsistent, as though a few character models were either outsourced or problematic for the lead designer somehow.
All in all, I'd recommend this game for younger players, as well as anyone who wants a relatively stress-free adventure platformer that you can beat in 3-4 relaxed sessions.

* Lack of control in space battles e.g. no ship formations
* Art style a bit too sterile

New to the game? You'll love it. It never truly shines, but there is something delightful in equipping a flamethrower and baking crispy dino-treats. Or zooming around in Halo-esque vehicles causing general mayhem while you're being chased. This could be a very, very, very good game and at how cheap it is and it IS a good game. . . for a time.
Then there are the game modes that don't completely work. Game settings that never stick (I'm always having to change the visual settings even though I've saved them EVERY TIME.) A healing gun that sometimes won't heal (because the game doesn't properly show health bars.) Less than stellar UI. Boring and repetitive dinosaur mobs.
Maybe the reason why I  recommend this game is because I can see what this game COULD be. At the core, it's a incredibly fun multiplayer game that is easy to pick up. Sadly, though, the game doesn't feel complete. Most people will put this down after a few hours and never pick it back up. . . which is a shame! Add some more customization, make more maps, fix the other game modes! There is really not a game quite like this out there - similar, yes, but not quite.
TL;DR: Buy this game. It's cheap and good for a few hours with friends. But don't keep it out of mind and let's see what the future can bring.

First off, if you have played, watched, or even HEARD of this game's masterpeice of a sequel and are a) a W3 fan wanting to get some insight into the world before, or b) an original Witcher player gearing up for its action-packed sequel (not likely), I advise you to abandon all your preconceptions before playing The Witcher 2. Do it. Leave them at the door and don't turn back. This is easily my least favorite of the trilogy, and one of the most rage-inducing games I have EVER played, but I must explain why I still consider it among my favorites.
At that, allow me to list the numerous gripes I have with it, for the sake of contrast with The Witcher 3:
-Potions cannot be downed on the spot. The first and formost problem with this game is this, I think. This idea is only passable in the context that you've already endured dozens of hours of hapless slaughter in your first playthrough because you had no idea something dangerous would be around a corner and gave no thought to taking some Swallow beforehand. A painful betrayal for Witcher 1 and 3 fans alike.
-Combat itself is clunky and aggravating. I can't even begin to describe how I felt about the combat. I appreciate that it captures the chaos of swordfighting aesthetically, but some parts are just atrocious, like the block mechanics and awkward quick access menu. You will often find yourself wandering into an easy-looking scuffle only to die four times before deciding to just stay away from that area. I've no shame in admitting that I spammed Igni and Quen in the first half of the game.
-Levelling and total game time disagree with each other. The original Witcher can be up to 10 hours LONGER than its sequel, itself averaging about 30 hours. It's forgivable at first, but one can only accomplish so much in 30 hours with the levelling system, which seems tailored to people who would rather commit to a single skill tree than flesh out their options, like I did (and barely scratched the late-game perks as a result.) It also adds insult to injury that Geralt doesn't really get better as he gets new skills, but just becomes less bad.
-The atmosphere of The Witcher 2 is far too fantastical in comparison to its flanking brothers, and to a newcomer I fear it may sell a misconception about the game's roots. The Temerian swamps in W1/3 (and the absence of dragons) feel more grounded in reality, but the sprawling locales of W2 don't fit. Geralt also seems to treat witchering as more of a part-time career in this game than what it actually is: a social caste and lifelong stigma.
In the end, all problems aside (but not out of view; some are plain inexcusable) The Witcher 2's story is an amazing spectacle and a necessary prelude to the events of its sequel. It's worth climbing the mountain just to see how drastically characters change and events unfold when guided by your choices (which are definitely more drastic here than either of the other entries). It's an intimidating mountain though. My best advice is to treat it like the long-awaited successor to the original and forget the improvements its 2015 installment exacted upon.
I'm so glad I got this off my chest.

A point&click adventure with multiple possible playstyles and puzzle solutions, some combat and RPG elements and tons of optional things to do.
Upsides:
-A lot of content: it took me roughly 30 hours to beat the game on my first try (though I took my time to try and deal with every optional thing I came across). Even with so much content in a free2play game (kickstarted), the overall quality of the content is quite high. The layout is mostly non-linear so you can literally go on adventures and explore new stuff as you like. There are not only multiple ways to solve a situation/quest, but the results can vary quite a bit too.
-RPG elements: using a skill (any skill, not just combat-related) has a high chance to increase every time you use it. Even walking around aimlessly in the snow will boost your endurance and strength over time. There is also a hidden 'honour' value that is revealed at the end of the game.
-Three playable classes which can be customized even further by picking up to 2 additional starting skills. Since it's an adventure, there are obviously big similarities on what you do overall, but how you do it can be completely different. Some optional content is also genuinely reserved for certain classes / skills.
-All character dialogue is supported by voice acting.
-The music in this game is great.
-The setting (nordic mythology: odin, thor, loki, brunhild, fenrir, valkyries etc.) seems to have been taken quite seriously without diminishing the gameplay for the sake of it. The further you get into the game, the more fantasy elements you will come across.
-Day & Night cycle without any global time limit (as far as I know) so you can explore the game at your own pace. Still, the daytime can have a significant role in certain situations.
Depending on your taste:
-Trivia to other games and minor pop-culture humor (as is tradition with similar games back then I guess). However, this does not really influence the feel of the game overall (e.g. there are no 'joke' characters that belong to the actualy story etc.). Think of it as having tons of little not very meaningful eastereggs. In my oppinion, the humor is not as good as in some of the great classics, but it's nice to see how much effort they put into so many little details as well.
-Female protagonist who is not objectified (as in: the gender doesn't really influence the story, it just so happens that your character is a woman). I consider this a positive thing (I don't need huge boobies on my screen 24/7 as is the case with some other games) but you have no option to play a different (e.g. male) character, even when chosing a different class. Considering the vast amount of necessary art and voice-acting, this is quite understandable though.
-The game is quite challenging, especially at the very beginning. There are many ways to die or otherwise screw things up (even permanently!). Thankfully you can easily save and load in 50 different slots and there is also a difficulty slider. Personally, I like starting out in a creepy, hostile world and then growing more powerful in knowledge, skill and equipment. It feels like genuine accomplishments that have to be earned. Reaching a maximum score is also very difficult (there is sooo much optional content, you will not find it all on your first playthrough) so that's another motivation to try the game over with a different class.
Overall: 9/10

Attempting to do a perfect game run as I'm writing this review during my holiday. As far as how I'd rate this port, I'd give it a 7/10. You do need to log into a square enix account the first time you load up the game. After that however, you dont need to be connected online to play this game. Just disable cloud saves if you want to play offline. Still a bit annoying you have to do that, but once you do, you should be fine with playing the game.
My main issue with this port is that in the PS1 version, battle menus ran 60fps, which made slot limit breaks smooth. In this version, menus match the fps of battles, which mean they'll also be 15fps. You can feel it's a little slow compared to the ps1 version when one of your characters reaches a limit break and your bar, while moving up fast, feels more choppy compared to the ps1 version. Some of the mini games are also cut to 30 fps instead of the ps1 60 fps counterpart, such as the speed square and the snowboard mini game. Now I hear that there are fixes for this, but in return, your steam achievements for FF7 will not work, so in the end you have to decide whether it's worth it to sacrifice your achievements or put up with the slowdowns in this game.
Other than that though, this is still an outstanding classic for you to play, and even with those issues I mentioned, I ended up getting used to them after awhile. I really do like the achievements in this game too. All in all, I really do recommend this game if you're thinking about playing it, but if you want to have the best version of ff7, I would suggest playing it on PS1.

Heroine's Quest is at first glance an homage to the old RPG/adventure games of the late 80s, early 90's. But as soon as you spend some time with it you discover that it is so much more. It is an early 90s RPG if it were made today. And from that you get all the great things from those sort of games: great story that is also funny at times, complex and interesting quests that have different ways to approach and solve them, amazing atmosphere and great dialogue. All of this in exchange for some pixel graphics, which I am not a fan of, but it is evident they spent a lot of time creating the environments and characters in the game and then even animating all of them, which is not easy to do with pixel art.
The weak side of the game is the combat which is quite simplistic and basically just pushing one button most of the time, at least at the lower difficulties. It is interesting the way combat is done in this game and it is much more involved than I expected before starting to play the game, however as I said it is lacking in complexity and would've been more fun with more combat skills. This is most evident in the first half of the game or so when you only have one combat spell (as a sorceress) and dodging left, right or back. And that is pretty much all you can do in combat for the first 5-6 hours.
Some of the puzzles/quests are also annoying to accomplish because the goals that are presented are much too vague and you need to do a lot experimentation to finish them. It doesn't help that for much of the game you will have no fast travel option, so you will have to walk through the whole forrest every time you will get an idea for how to solve a certain quest, which leads to a lot of time wasted just walking back and forth.

There are two things in particular that make this game: the humour, and the co-op. Truth be told, I haven't played through either of the previous Red Alert games, so I wouldn't know how this is as a sequel. However, on it's own, this game is very fun, especially if you play through it with a friend. Not a lot of RTS games offer co-op throughout their campaign, and it was very welcome as co-op is guaranteed to improve any game. The comedy of the game was also great. I'm not saying it's particularly hilarious, it's just that it's an RTS that doesn't take itself seriously, which again, not a lot of RTS games do. It does have it's moments though that are genuinely funny, especially from the live-action performances of Tim Curry, George Takei, and JK Simmons. The story is also appropriately absurd and great if you don't want to take yourself seriously.
Gameplay wise, there are much deeper RTS games to play besides this one. Again, don't dismiss it because of that, it's still fun, but if you are looking for a very strategic RTS, this isn't the one. Not to say the strategic element is completely lacking, the three factions all have their own play styles which can translate into having to alter your strategy depending on who you are playing as and who you are fighting. All three factions can also build on land, air, and water which also have their own strengths and weaknesses. Water is also prominently built into each map, so navies are actually quite useful, another thing that not a lot of other RTS games do. Like I said before though, the gameplay is good, just not great.
Great game if you like RTS games and want a loony experience with one of your friends.

Update: As predicted previously this game only gets better as more mechanics are fleshed out throughout the game.
While I do have to admit that I have not played the late game as I keep restarting games to optimize my early and mid-game starts. I would like to share my thoughts on Stellaris so far.
It is easily apparent that Paradox have put a lot of work to create a framework that consists of different modules and mechanics, from a development perspective this should allow Paradox to easily add more to the game when it comes to complexity and tuning(not that there are any major issues at the moment).
A lot of people are complaining about mid-game being stale, I do not find this to be the case. Once the mid-game comes along I find myself trying to maximize naval capacity and have a fleet that is nearing that cap, being Militarist I put it to use. Wars are fast and furious, while it is not just about your naval fleet but also paying attention to your defensive and offensive armies. While I do admit that the AI is horrible some folks are already trying to optimize it via the LUA files and with some work from Paradox it is easily fixable more intelligence is added via IF-THEN statements.
In the current state the game plays fantastic, early game is fantastic and you will find yourself addicted to surveying systems to find high resource stations and decent planets and you will shout in glee once you find that 20+ Gaia planet. At normal speed there is plenty of tasks and micromanagement to keep your hands full at every second (day in the game) of every moment. Up the speed to Fast and you will have your hands full.
From a multiplayer aspect there are folks whining about corvette rushes, while this is an issue it is easily fixable by boosting the military power of stations and spaceports so that early corvette rushes get thwarted. I am sure there are others with even better solutions. Other than that MP is fantastic, I have been playing in the Stellaris MP steam group(shameless shoutout) and matches with 12+ players are running smoothly. Having this many players in a game along with 15AI to add some action to the early game gives the galaxy a feeling that it is very alive. The salt,politics and drama in voice chat are satisfying while everybody starts to fight over optimal planets/resources and federations begin to form.
While upkeep costs exist they do not hinder your science output if you keep your energy credits above 0, you can still sim city while being aggressive in the galaxy. Small things like research alternatives give an addictive randomness to the game and you will find yourself swearing at RNGJesus when you don't get that specific tech you needed.
This game is extremely satisfying and provides the excitement and adrenaline that so many other games in the sea of 4x/Grand Strategy do not provide. In the coming months and years I can see this game molding into one of the staples of the genre.
Issues that need to be fixed:
- MP balance issues (corvettes evasion is overpowered, worm hole is superior in relation to other initial FTL tech , Energy weapons generally outclass missles and kinetic weaponry)
- Spaceport , mining bases and early game defense is weak causing early rushes to be a problem
- Peace mechanics can be abused to stop players from joining a federation
- Number of planets does not scale well with science output (2% increase for every planet) , and there is no way to remediate this causing issues for Wide empires.

It's sweet and simple racing game meant to try and recreate what made Hang On the arcade classic it was. It does take out the epic crashes and wicked turns that made Hang On so difficult, so the only real challenge in the game is handling relatively easy turns while dodging other bikes, making Super Night Riders much less difficult than its spiritual ancestor. I might be biased or "hard-boiled", considering how much I played and eventually beat Hang On and Outrun, but I blew through the six main courses in a couple of sittings. I have nothing against easy games or easy modes, but you'd think a game meant to appeal to arcade fans might at least have a more challenging mode.
All that negativity aside, I still found the experience rather pleasant, especially for the low price point. There are two visual styles, one that is meant to look like early 3D and one that is meant to look like VERY early 3D. Neither of them look offensive to the eye, the environments in "Super" mode look downright pretty while keeping the look and feel of the classic Hang On environments. The race models themselves however look a tad bit cheap in Super mode- like a simplistic doll that was painted entirely red. In some ways I prefer the polygonal look of Classic mode for the racer models, but they don't do any favors for the environments. There are a few animations in it which give the racers a bit more natural feel, but not many. Overall it can be soothing as well nostalgic to watch the environments go by at such a speed.
The controls are quite good, which was a surprise, and are also quite simple. Accelaration, brake, and side-to-side is all you need. The music is pretty legit and has a nice 80s vibe, but can get a little repetitive over time, luckily you can switch tracks on the fly. Overall, quite fun for the price if you want a game you can just pick up and play for a little while when you don't know what else to do, as well as those who are annoyed that Hang On still hasn't come to Steam.

This game has its moments, and because it's cheap I'll give it a recommend.
Story 7/10 --- Voice Acting 2/10
There is a fairly decent story line and plot, however the voice acting is... well it's not really good at all. The voices don't match what the characters facial animations portray at all. Dust will be sad, but his voice actor (sorry but his was the worst for me) will sound angry and pretty childish. If you can't grab a few decent voice actors, it's 100x better to just leave the voices out completely.
Combat: 4/10
The problem for me was that this game became very tedious very quickly. You are only given a handful of moves and the combos get old fast, you aren't given very much freedom when it comes to combat, what with only the 3 or 4 real combos. And you will regularly find yourself flying to the edges of the map because your spin move aims at any enemy within a screen or two of your character, making it somewhat annoying during larger battles.
Graphics 7/10
I like the graphics, and the throwback menus are familiar and fun. The enemies and the world are varied and have a simple beauty. The dropoff here is for the cutscenes that go to a pretty horrible hand drawn world rather than the sharpness of the game itself. Granted, I can't draw that well so I shouldn't judge too harshly.
Difficulty 6/10
I played on 'Hardcore' so the 13 hour game time might be overstated for someone playing on normal or an easier difficulty. My game was completed in 10 hours, but I had 3 hours of consistent dying, which tells you something of the difficulty on hardcore.  I found it to be challenging, but because of the lack of combat versatility, I found myself really trying to stay interested in this game until the end. The majority of bosses can be easily defeated using the air combo. The biggest difficulty for me was from the environmental traps, traversing those on hardcore was very difficult.
Progression and Crafting 9/10
I very much enjoyed the character leveling up system and the crafting system. They were both simple to use and made the merchants actually necessary to build better gear. In hardcore it was necessary for me to keep on the lookout for better blueprints and I was encouraged to clear each screen before going to the next for gold and drops to use in crafting.
Overall I didn't hate this game, but when I was about 65% of the way through I was just trying to get through it. So again, I do recommend it for the price tag, but if you want to enjoy it more than I did, just read the text and don't listen to it, and play it on an easier setting. This game wasn't meant to be a long play, and hardcore just increases the time spent without adding much extra in terms of personal reward.

Good news is at the time of writing this its still supported game but the downside is that the DLCs are expenssive for what you get back from it. A bundle on sale maybe is a good solution.
Pros
+The ship builder is decent and lets you create a lot of different ships in all shape and sizes.
+You can add as many races as you like and play in a huge galaxies. (played on the largest map with 43 AI and it works well).
+Tech tree lets you choose different traits in specialization
Cons
-Ships change name seemingly randomly when they are upgraded.
-When your ships are in a fleet and you want more info on it you have to take it out of the fleet to be able to view it.
-No good way to manage starbases besides micromanaging which takes most of your time.
If you use the ingame method it will basicly spam down your shipyards as it will build many constructors.
-Roles of the ships are defined with the design and can not be modified prior to combat, if you have armed support ships or if you would like to engage with your normal guardians this really sets you up for failure, as they will wait to engage until the ones up front are shot up first.
-After the AI turns you will not know if your ships saw any hostile ships inside their sensor range UNLESS you were looking at that spot of the map as the turn went and you didnt blink.
This is a huge drawback and has forced me to build huge sensor platforms to actually know whats going on.
Personal preferences
I personally would like to see the ships having different modifiers for weapons/defenses vs size,
This to better reflect the differences between them.
Also adding different docks inside the shipyard to create more ships at the same time.
The docks would be different sizes so when you can build a larger class of ships you would need to build a larger dock.
Smaller ships should be cheaper(as with their stats being lower).
I would like to see the option to build custom tiny fighters to be carried in carrier modules and that could operate to a certain area outside the carrier fleet as well. the modules should have increased capacity but unable to regenerage fighters.
Also when upgrading I feel that the way it works now is slightly ridiculous, I think that either there should be a rule that 75% of base parts have to be the same or preferably all modifications inside a shipyard.

I haven't even finished this game yet and i can already tell that this is a hidden masterpiece of the 21st century. I don't even know where to start. The characters? They are very well crafted and their writing is comparable to some modern AAA titles, like The Witcher 3.
- First of all you have Teddy Floppy Ear. He is a war veteran and his ear is broken (or "floppy" as the people in-universe call it playfully, trying to not trigger Teddy's PTSD.) because he suffered a major concussion after saving his allies from a grenade. Luckily, the medics managed to patch every part of him up except the ear (which is why he has all those patches around his body).
- Then you have such characters as Igor "The Captain" Hamlovich. He is an old friend of Teddy, having worked in the navy, he knows him purely of the similiar carreer choice. He has his fair share of traumatic experiences, but i won't elaborate on that as it's a spoiler.
- Then there's also the gameplay of the game... oh BOY where do i begin. Forever Entertainment SA hired some of the world's best programmers to make the engine of this game. Industry stars such as Paul Walker, Edmund McMillen, Todd "Buy My Game" Howard and even Gabe Newell himself! This resulted in some of the best controls i have ever seen in any video game. The handling is butter smooth, the controls are very advanced and yet simple at the same time, making me feel like i'm actually there, steering that Fiat Maluch.
- The graphics of this game are some of the most top of the line graphics i have ever seen! The "Very high" setting is so gorgeous and so lifelike that i couldn't run it on my PC and i had to set it to "low" (which still looked comparable to some of the newer AAA games). The foliage feels very realistic, they modelled every single leaf on every single tree individually, the bushes move along to the wind which is also lifelike and forces you to change the way you move across the track if it's not blowing in your favor. The cars look very detailed and when i walked outside to compare the Polonez my neighbor has to the one on the screen i couldn't find a single difference (besides the various upgrades i had on my Polonez in-game, of course).
- I don't want to elaborate too much on the story, because it's very spoiler-heavy.
