Let me just get this out of the way, this game is fantastic. In fact I rate it higher than that other Final Fantasy that seems to get more attention. Maybe you agree with me or maybe you disagree but let me at least give you a couple of reasons that you shouldn't shy away from this gem. This game is unique and it is that same uniqueness that makes this game shine. Forget all the bad stuff people say about this game. Lets instead focus on the good that this game does.
Final Fantasy 8 did some wonderful things that no other FF title did. One of the most basic of JRPG principles, grinding battles. Well in short you don't need to really fight anything. I mean you can level up your charactors but there really isn't any real incentive to do it. For starters you are a student and you take a test early in the game. This test determines you pay or salary. Plus if you don't do so hot on the test you don't get a high salary. You can retake the test to do better and get paid more as well. So no need to really grind mobs for money as you get paid at regular intervals just like a job. I believe this is a plus as it allows for me to explore the world and without the need to stop and fight over and over. Also note, that bosses do not give out EXP at all. So theoretically, you could go thru the game at the starting level if you really wanted to.
So lets talk about the leveling system in the game, another plus to FF8's formula. The game uses a scaling system, which means the higher level you are the mobs scale to always give a challange of sorts. Which in every other game is a bad. I truely despise level scaling. It defeats the purpose of leveling to get stronger but this game bring a happy medium to play. FF8 intruduces the "Junction System". This entails a few things. One you "draw" magic from a couple of places. You can also "draw" from special points that refresh every so often to aquire more. You can "draw" from mobs as well. Now you can use these spells in battle which is fine, but let me say this game isn't really about magic as the other Final Fantasys. If there was a "grind" in the game its from drawing magic to aquire enough of it. So what is the point of magic if you don't really want to use them against mobs? Well as I was saying earlier, FF8 uses a "Junction System". This allows you to "Junction" magic to your main attributes. Your Hp, Mp, Att, etc. Doing this augments your abilites and makes you pretty damn strong. This is also how you overcome the level scaling to make your character stronger. You can level up but remember, mobs scale with you so this allows you to overcome this "handicap". If there is a "grind" in FF8, this is it. Which if you ask me, its far better "drawing" for magic than spending more time to grind for EXP for hours on end. I also told you that you could beat the game at the starting level. Which sounds bad but honestly beating the game at a lower level is way easier than a high level. Using the Final Battle as a reference, without spoiling, beating it at a low level was hard but certianly not difficult. But i will say beating it at max level was one of the most challenging battles I have ever done in a game before. It took me close to 2 hours to beat that battle. With the active battle and max level I was on the edge of my seat the whole time. Note that it took me many of times to even succeed in doing this. It was simply a rewarding feat to acomplish. I can also atest to this being the hardest boss I have fought from any of the other Final Fantasy titles.
Some tweaks have been done to the actual battle system. The main charactor uses a weapon called a gunblade. In battle you can attack like you normally would with no problems. But it has another feature that allows for it to do more damage. If you press a certain button at the precise time, you will pull the trigger and shoot as you attack. This effectively adds more damage to your normal attack. It uses a turn base battle system that is active, which means you have to think fast on your feet. No planning your attack like chess for the best move, you have to be quick and do something or just keep getting attacked over and over. Some might see that as a turn off which I can understand just be aware its there. Summons are back in this game as well. They will be mighty helpful. They also learn abilites as well. Most noteworthy is the "boost" ablity. This allows you to push a button repeatedly to amplifiy the damage done. Its a nice to be able to do that but after the bazillionth time it will get old. Still to this day I would have like to have a final ablitiy to just do max damage without that button mashing marathon. Also the animations for the summons are top notch for its time. Truely amazing but some are really long and overdone, would have been nice to be able to skip them. Annoying yes, dealbreaker no.
Probaly the most agreeable positive about FF8 is its included "card game". Triple Traid is its name and it is crazy fun that I am suprised was never given its own game. It sorta starts out slow but as you collect more cards you really start being sucked into it grasp. I personally have logged into FF8 just to play the card game and nothing else. So simple, but yet so much depth and strategy. Traveling to new areas brings about new rules to the game. Some of these rules are good and some downright brutal. Also there are "rare" cards to win from certain people. Some you might only have one chance to aquire so maybe using a guide isn't a bad idea in this area.
To talk about the story would ruin alot of it. I won't mention it but I'll hit on a few high points. I kinda throws you right into the middle of everything and you'll feel like you understand what's going on. Then you'll go from knowing what going on to not having the slighest clue. That formula happens multiple times in this game. But each time it happens the story gets deeper and more seems to be happening. It gets dangerously close to being to long. When I first played this on the Playstation 1, I was  wondering what was on disk 4 for the longest time. Even when I was at the end of disk 3 I felt like I had done so much I couldn't believe there was still a whole other disk to run though. Although in hindsight, disk 4 felt almost out of place and to this day I still believe it was only that way because the amount of data on a cd-rom wasn't enough to do it the way it should have been. I works but only like hitting a foul ball 1 foot away from being a home run.

Other worthy mentions are the locations. The cities are big and give a feeling of being alive. The music sets a nice tone to the atmosphere. Still some of my favorite music in the series, not that any really stand out but they fit the games vibe. They are rendered backgrounds but still beautiful to look at. Throughout the world you can use roads to navigate around. You also gain access to cars to drive around the overworld. These greatly help speed up travel times. There are a few other ways of travel but I don't want to spoil any crazy details. Although I will say the "airship" in this game is the freaking best of all the FF games.
What else is there in FF8? Quite a bit more if you ask me. For one it feels more like a world than past Final Fantasy titles. Or maybe I should say a little more grown up. This game as a whole seems more mature. But its overall experiance that makes it shine. The story goes up and down. There are high points and low points. But you are doing yourself a disservice if you pass on this up. Final Fantasy 8 knows its not like the rest of the series and its proud of that fact. If you give it a chance, you might be pleastantly surprised that you wished played it sooner.

One of the best RPGs ever made and one of my favorite games of all time.
In FF7 . you are trying to stop Sephiroth from absorbing the necessary energy he needs in order to destroy the plane. You control a group named Avalanche and you try to prevent that. The game is full of things to do : explore well hidden towns in the suprisingly enormous map (especially for the time it was released) , grind your way up the levels , find new equipment , fight bosses , enjoy the soundtrack and immerse yourself in an amazing storyline about the battle of good and evil.
The gameplay is incredibly enjoyable. The battles never get boring! Combat is turn-based , meaning your party will attack one member at a time , then it's the enemy's turn. You can use potions to buff your characters or simply to restore HP , make a basic attack or wait a few rounds until your Ultra-Supa-Dupa-Power attack becomes available in order to smash your enemies. Throughout the game you will meet different characters that can join your party - each one has his one specialties and disadvantages. Make sure you are properly geared up and loot everything you can and save FREQUENTLY!  Exploring the open world in order to find new towns or landmarks is very interesting , however it can sometimes get very frustating because of the random encounters you are forced to deal with once a while. You can run away from them , but this can make you lose money or even let your enemies steal precious gear while trying to. Boss Battles can take a while to finish , especially if you are not properly prepared. Levels are important in this game , so you should take your time to level up and grind a bit - don't just rush the story. Now , note that there are no big green arrows pointing to your next objective (like modern games). Therefore , you will need to listen to the characters' dialogues and use a bit of common sense in order to identify where you will need to go next. At some point of the game you will also be given vehicles you can use to travel the world faster (and safer ,s ince you won't get into random battles). Overall , the main gameplay aspects of the game (combat and exploration) are well done and long-term RPG players will feel familiar with the Mechanics of the game (such as Potion system , vehicles to travel the world , characters to join your party , equipment all around the world). Additionally , there are some nice mini-games that can earn you some money or other stuff (such as Chocobbo Racing) , however I found most of them not very appealing to me , so I didn't pay much attention.Keep in mind there are many ''special'' bosses you will have a chance to fight in order to get some incredibly rare and powerful gear - they are incredibly hard to defeat though and you might not really stand a chance unless you have really put many many hours into the game and Maxed Out most of your stats. Oh , and you can't explore or do anything after you are done with the main story , so make sure you are satisfied with your achievements throughout the game BEFORE you enter the final area of the game.
In the game , you play (mainly) as Cloud Strife -  a young man that still is unsure about his true identity and will try to find out who he really is. Apart from that , you are also part of the AVALANCHE group which was secretly formed to wage a rebellion against Shinra , an organisation which is absorbing Mako energy, destroying the natural world as we know it , in order to fullfilltheir own , dirty plans and take over the world. One of the most interesting and engaging villains of all time , Sephiroth , doesn't want you alive and you will also have to deal with him as he is going mad and loses control of his actions. There are many other side quests you can do as well and you will get to know more about the world around you - and obviously , there are many other stories that developer throughout the game , such as romantic relationships between the characters or conflicts! You get to decide what you will say in many of the dialogues and the cutscenes are really well done and drive-away some of the monotony constant gameplay can cause.
Unfortunately , FF7 is a game that hasn't aged very well (granted , it's 18 years old and was originally released on PlayStation 1 , so it's understandable). It still doesn't look that horrible , however and inspired many modern RPGs. The PC port is also not particularly good either , but most PCs will be able to easily handle it today , so it should no matter what run smoothly. There are many mods you can use to enhance your experience , however I prefer to play games they were meant to be so I didn't try any of them out. Perhaps the visuals aren't great , but the soundtracks of the game are still INCREDIBLE and make me feel incredibly excited.. It's a very weird feeling but the sound it makes when you enter a battle or when a cutscene is playing , it's just so refreshing! I am not an audiophile and I usually don't pay much attention to that sort of stuff , but this game stood out for me. Back to the visuals , the colors are decent and despite the aging graphics , the atmosphere in the dungeons or the snowed mountains for example is still top notch and will certainly not distract you from enjoying the game.
The characters development through out the game is special and some of the things that happen to them can be gamechanging. You will get emotionally attached to some of them , others you may not like them. And that is a very hard to come up with and something Square Enix put a lot of effort in order to develop. It's hard to find games that put so much emphasis that onto the character development . The characters this time make the story  , but the story also makes the characters. What I mean by that is , that what happens in the world affects the characters but what happens to the characters can also affect the world.
Final Fantasy 7 is a game for everyone . It is one of the games that felt nearly perfect and even though it might not have aged out as well as many would have wanted , it's still one of the best games of all time and for many the best RPG ever. All the critics and reviewers of the game in general can't just be dellusional - if you haven't played this game yet , you are missing out big time!

Legend is a “Golden Axe” inspired beat ‘em up, set in a standard medieval fantasy setting where a tyrant ruled over everyone and brought mayhem in his wake. Brave knights opposed him and managed to destroyed the evil tyrant, and imprison his dark soul. But you are not playing as one of these heroes; instead you are playing as one of the two clean-up crew members who are trying to stop another lesser evil from using the tyrant’s soul for his own nefarious purposes. A bit underwhelming regarding that you are playing the B-squad but how’s the rest of the Legend?
For a game that was made in 1994 by a small French studio with two people that were passionate about making games, Legend looks quite captivating on modern monitors, with detailed 2D sprites and hand-written animations. There are six fairly long levels in the game, and each one looks suitably different, with the first level starting at the peaceful castle outskirts that slowly transit into a menacing fog-ridden swamp. Music and sound effects are decent, with a couple of catchy musical tunes that unfortunately tend to repeat all the time. Your hero has decent fighting moves: sword and shield to attack and protect him, magical arrows that can be a powerful ranged tool against bosses but also take away a chunk of your health, thus making you weaker at the start of the next level. You can also collect vials of concentrated magic that you can use to unleash ultimate attacks that take away a sizeable chunk of health to all enemies on the screen, without being too powerful and outright killing them. Every new level introduces two new enemies into the fray, each one with a different set of attacks and moves. All of these are the strong points of Legend.
Minuses are the boss encounters that like to use impossible-to-block attacks, which makes these battles a bit cheap. They can be beaten, but you have to posses a millisecond-fast reaction time to defend yourself from their vicious attacks. Some of the later enemies also tend to use dash attacks that are very hard to block or avoid. The game is short, and the experienced players will take about 90 minutes to complete Legend, which is a bummer.
But these aren’t overwhelmingly negative experiences that will ruin you enjoyment of the game, and if you get it on a sale, you’ll have fun with a fairly difficult blast from the past. Legend gets a cautious recommendation from me.
Fun fact 1: Developers of this game later on founded Toka studio that were first to use motion capture technology in games.
Fun fact 2: There is also a full 3D reboot of this game on the PlayStation 1 from 1999 that according to the publisher might arrive on Steam soon as well.

Legend is a clunky mess of a beat-em-up that isn't very much fun to play. It isn't that it's an old game that doesn't hold up to today's standards. It's that it's a mediocre game that couldn't stand up to contemporary titles like Final Fight, Streets of Rage, Captain Commando, or even Golden Axe. This mediocrity hasn't exactly helped the game to age well.
Legend draws clear inspiration from the Capcom Dungeons & Dragons arcade game, and delivers a modicum of that title's visual charm by deliberately copying its setting and aesthetic. Gameplay is incredibly slow, which throws off the pace of the entire game and makes the controls unweildly. This can get frustrating in a hurry, because even peon enemies can take a serious beating on even the lowest difficulty setting, and they're programmed to swarm you from both sides. The entire game is a laborious trudge through mostly palette-swapped levels, packaged and sold as a ROM run in a bare bones SNES emulator. If Legend piques your interest, seriously, just download it for free.
A very creative and fun take on the roguelike genre, and a great game for those who have busy lives and just need some chillout time for 30 minutes to an hour.

Update: As predicted previously this game only gets better as more mechanics are fleshed out throughout the game.
While I do have to admit that I have not played the late game as I keep restarting games to optimize my early and mid-game starts. I would like to share my thoughts on Stellaris so far.
It is easily apparent that Paradox have put a lot of work to create a framework that consists of different modules and mechanics, from a development perspective this should allow Paradox to easily add more to the game when it comes to complexity and tuning(not that there are any major issues at the moment).
A lot of people are complaining about mid-game being stale, I do not find this to be the case. Once the mid-game comes along I find myself trying to maximize naval capacity and have a fleet that is nearing that cap, being Militarist I put it to use. Wars are fast and furious, while it is not just about your naval fleet but also paying attention to your defensive and offensive armies. While I do admit that the AI is horrible some folks are already trying to optimize it via the LUA files and with some work from Paradox it is easily fixable more intelligence is added via IF-THEN statements.
In the current state the game plays fantastic, early game is fantastic and you will find yourself addicted to surveying systems to find high resource stations and decent planets and you will shout in glee once you find that 20+ Gaia planet. At normal speed there is plenty of tasks and micromanagement to keep your hands full at every second (day in the game) of every moment. Up the speed to Fast and you will have your hands full.
From a multiplayer aspect there are folks whining about corvette rushes, while this is an issue it is easily fixable by boosting the military power of stations and spaceports so that early corvette rushes get thwarted. I am sure there are others with even better solutions. Other than that MP is fantastic, I have been playing in the Stellaris MP steam group(shameless shoutout) and matches with 12+ players are running smoothly. Having this many players in a game along with 15AI to add some action to the early game gives the galaxy a feeling that it is very alive. The salt,politics and drama in voice chat are satisfying while everybody starts to fight over optimal planets/resources and federations begin to form.
While upkeep costs exist they do not hinder your science output if you keep your energy credits above 0, you can still sim city while being aggressive in the galaxy. Small things like research alternatives give an addictive randomness to the game and you will find yourself swearing at RNGJesus when you don't get that specific tech you needed.
This game is extremely satisfying and provides the excitement and adrenaline that so many other games in the sea of 4x/Grand Strategy do not provide. In the coming months and years I can see this game molding into one of the staples of the genre.
Issues that need to be fixed:
- MP balance issues (corvettes evasion is overpowered, worm hole is superior in relation to other initial FTL tech , Energy weapons generally outclass missles and kinetic weaponry)
- Spaceport , mining bases and early game defense is weak causing early rushes to be a problem
- Peace mechanics can be abused to stop players from joining a federation
- Number of planets does not scale well with science output (2% increase for every planet) , and there is no way to remediate this causing issues for Wide empires.

It looks quite simple and superficial at first with the old fashioned catchy jingle and the sing-a-long lyrics...

I get to play with fire! and you spend your time methodically setting the acheivement list alight one combo at a time, sending things to Sugar Plumps and listening to the weather reports.
Until you start to think... I'm burning my toys. Why?
Why is it so cold? Why is there no sun?
And the game takes a depressing sort of turn as something happens to your neighbour and then all of a sudden you too find yourself cast out and upon seeing the world outside you realise things about yourself and the state of your own reality that will honestly make you cry. This game is a briliant sneaking satirical look at casting off the things of our childhood and that which distracts us and makes us realise that there is more to life than what we've been doing all this time. Dreams can come true when we stop getting distracted and try that little bit harder.
I'd recomend playing this game simply because of the feels it invokes as you play and I would congratulate the devs on such a thoughtful couple of hours that honestly could change a life.

9/10  Highly reccomended.
For a free game, there is a great deal of content available; more than I honestly expected.
To begin; this game is truly a labor of love to Sierra point and clicks of the day, especially that of "Quest for Glory". You'll find a whole slew of references littering the game world; see if you can find them all.
This game doesn't let itself be carried by the references though; wasting no time to introduce you to wonderful characters, all unique in their own ways. Each one helps carry the story all the way to it's end as you unravel the story behind the land of Midgard. (Except for that Wizard; hate him.) One of my favorite aspects of this story has to be the fact the main character's gender in relationship to her role is never questioned. It allows the plot to not be weighed down by pointless social baggage, and just focus on being a great story.
And the gameplay is nothing to ignore either. Taking a page from the combat of Quest for Glory you are given a chance to be interactive in with your character as they come face to face with the dangers of the land. Unlike a traditional battle system; you and your foe do not take turns slapping each other but instead must outmaneuver one another with dodging and countering. Because of this, you can't just tank your way through most fights by grinding and using the occasional potion to keep you alive, but must rely on your wits as well as your stats to defeat your foes.
My one complaint about this game is that it may be a bit brutal in the beginning for those who don't want to remove overworld status effects, and that some of the puzzles may be a little obtuse.
Still, I would recommend this to everyone looking to have a good time of try a point and click for the first time. For free; you can't go wrong.

People who have been rating this down because of the music don't care about the game. As a matter of fact, if they're letting some sub-standard music get in the way of the game, they probably don't even like the game to begin with and should be disregarded entirely.
First of all: the music isn't that bad. It's not bad at all, in fact, and certainly not enough to make people NOT reccomend the game. It has a retro feel to it, which, for any other game, people would be ♥♥♥♥♥♥ing over because #RETROISAWESOMELOL.
Second of all: yes, there is a second layer of DRM. Squeenix's login thing. I haven't had issues with my internet in long enough to accurately remember whether or not you actually NEED a constant stable connection, but I seem to recall that with FF7, you could play offline just fine as long as you had an account, which isn't difficult to create (and fake, if you so desire).
The game itself remains one of Final Fantasy's most underrated titles. People ♥♥♥♥♥ed about the need to "grind" magic for the "unintuitive" junction system, but how is it any worse than grinding hundreds of millions of XP in any other title? The characters are deep and relatable, to an extent (I mean, how well can you actually relate to a bunch of teenagers who were riased to be elite mercenaries during their childhood). The love interest plot developes naturally, though it gets somewhat rushed at one point late in the game when Female Love Interest (tm) goes into a coma and Male Love Interest (tm) who had previously been pushing her away constantly suddenly and abruptly realizes how much he needs her. This is essentially a SNES ROM image packaged in a cut-down version of the SNES9x emulator - no more, no less. You can ALT+Enter out of the game and use the menu to tweak a few image filtering settings and modify the controls (they map fine to an Xbox 360 pad, settings are saved when you quit the game). Controls are mapped, as expected, to the equivalent buttons on a SNES controller.
If you didn't grow up with SNES gaming, chances are you won't enjoy this. If you did grow up with such games, you know what to expect: the kind of sluggish, poorly animated, side-scrolling beat-em-up with copious Mode 7 effects that the SNES was numerously blessed with. For its era it's competently done, but it hasn't aged well. Should you get this in a bundle, you can have a few hours' fun with it, but it's not worth the normal €5 asking price.
If you're looking for a decent side-scrolling beater, you're better served on Steam by Streets of Rage, Double Dragon Trilogy or Double Dragon Neon.

Legend is a 2D Beat Em Up set in a fantasy world in where an evil King has recently been defeated and you are tasked with stopping the King's son Clovis from seizing his father's power as his own. To accomplish this you must stab, block and kick your way right into the heart of the castle over the course of 6 stages. We play as some random nameless dude that holds either a sword or an axe if you are playing local coop. They play exactly the same and the only differences are cosmetic. One of the things you must first do if you are planning to play with a joypad is to change the game into windowed mode via alt+enter and bind your buttons from the “Game” tab. There is no way to stretch the screen to fit your monitor annoyingly enough. Once in the level it takes only a few steps before you are swarmed by goons holding spears and must kill them all. It is at this point that you notice your character swings the sword with so little force you'd think he was fighting with an inflatable sword.

Our character controls really sluggishly and takes his sweet time to do anything. He walks like an old lady that is seriously tripping on some meds and he holds his shield up with the agility of a jaded tourist raising his hand up to shield his eyes from the sun. That is the most accurate description I could come up with to describe the gameplay. Being able to block is a cool idea but in this game your character moves and reacts so slow that you are just begging to be surrounded if you try to block. The range of your sword is very short making you have to be within kissing distance and the most common grunts holds a spear so you can imagine how that would turn out. You also have a long range attack that causes your character to throw dirt at your enemies and does quite a bit of damage, though doing this costs you a chunk out of your health bar. Enemies will often times drop potions which lets you perform a flashy magic attack that costs 2-3 potions a pop.

Magic attacks, while cool to look at, do very little damage and is near useless against bosses. So we have a character who seems as capable of taking down a world threatening dictator as your friendly neighborhood mailman. Luckily our character's long and hard years of training as a ballet dancer has paid off and he is a force to be reckoned with while in the air. He can gracefully move through the air after jumping and has an extremely powerful kick that will destroy any enemies in a few hits aside from bosses. Jumping does get around the issue of our character's slow movement speed though very few enemies can damage you while in the air making the game a breeze.  It is a choice between a nigh unplayable combat system or jumping around like a crackhead who thinks the floor is lava. Cranking up the difficulty in the options menu does nothing but increase the amount of life a boss starts with. On Easy they have half of their health bar, on Normal 75% and on Hard they have their entire health bar.

Bosses are the only real challenge in the game and are pretty fun to fight. On the first level alone you will fight a pole wielding martial artist and a demonic living tree. No matter how annoying it is to have to be consistently jumping throughout the whole game it is nothing short of awesome to kick a flying dragon boss into submission. Or fighting a werewolf like beast while freefalling through the air on a small platform. The boss fights are easily the high point of the game and what kept me pushing forward. Funnily enough the most dangerous enemy beside bosses are actually crows. They are one of the few enemies that can attack you in the air and they will drop health items upon defeating them by kicking them in their smug feathery faces. The health items in this game are either bread or roasted chicken legs and restore a small amount of your health bar. Other items that enemies infrequently drop are keys and gold. Keys are used after certain levels to open as many chests as you can on a small time limit and gold is simply your score with no use other than bragging rights.

If you are extremely lucky you may find a 1-up and may have up to 9 lives at any one given time. Graphics feature really good 16 bit pixel art with ton of detail in the environment and big character sprites. They look much better than many of the recent 16 bit indie games that are simply appealing to nostalgia while lacking any of the true artistic talent of those that made their vision true with what they had “back in the day”. I would still like the option to destroy that art by stretching the game to fit the screen however. After missions you are shown your next destination via a map that flies toward the screen using the Super Nintendo's Mode 7. I had no idea this was a SNES game until that moment and while it would have been a cool thing to see in the early 90's it looks terrible in this day and age. One thing this game really messed up on is how often they put something on the foreground that blocks your vision of the battlefield. It is very annoying how frequently something like a tree pops up to obscure enemies, items etc.

The music is a nice blend of upbeat music and your classic old timey fantasy tracks. A rather odd setting hidden in the options menu is to change the movement type from Normal to Turbo. What it tries to do is make it seem like you are moving faster but in reality the game is running about 25% faster which is like fixing a tire by peeling out of your garage in hopes that you get a boost like in Mario Kart and hope that it all works itself out. Good luck fighting the bosses that now move like Bruce Lee. The only glitch I experienced during my time with this game is that clicking 'new game' results in it booting up to the ending cutscene after I had finished the game until I shut Legend down and booted it back up. With all said and done the only real issue with Legend is its gameplay. In a genre all about the gameplay that is a fatal flaw and drags the game down. It is a real shame too, having great graphics, music and environments to fight in means nothing if the fighting feels terrible. This could have been a great game but ends up feeling like the poor man's Golden Axe. If you have no nostalgia towards Legend you can safely avoid this title.

The developers of Legend understood and got one basic thing about releasing an old Low Res Pixel game.
Integer scaling on a fixed scale.
It works great in windowed mode.
But for whatever reason in Full Screen mode it's fixed on it's own to some other scale. At 768p it seems fixed to 2x scale. When clearly it could handle 3x scale with room to spare.
It's not entirely perfect however as it does this at the internal 8:7 ratio of the SNES rather than the 4:3 output of it. Meaning the base resolution is 256x224. In full screen mode it seems to scale this within a 4:3 viewport though.
Whether it's correctly 4:3 (by having a non square Pixel Aspect Ratio) or not. It still looks very nice.
Keys are fully rebindable for controllers and keyboard as well.

A quite unique rhythm based retro random generated dungeon crawler. Seems like a quite peculiar mash up of genres.
In a way you would not expect those particular genres to work with each other but somehow this game pulls it off. It's a very unique compilation. On the outside its a dungeon crawler. You progress through a randomly generated dungeon gathering loot. Once you're dead the only thing you are left off is gold with which you can purchase unlocks, additional crates and items to be found in the dungeon. Any unspent gold goes away and you start from the start. And you start all over on each death with just a bigger chance of getting better things along the way.
The combat hover distinguishes it from the normal rouge like games. As its essentially a rhythm puzzle to be solved. In short - each enemy has a movement pattern in which he moves taking a move in the beat. Its easy to learn and tackle a single enemy but when different ones come at you at the same time fending all of them is quite the challenge. It makes for a very unique and satisfying combat when you pull all the moves in the right way.
The audio layer of this game is just amazing. Even more so as it's integral part of the game. It's worth getting the game for the soundtrack alone. I have no words to better describe it - just amazing. Well worth a listen to.
Graphicly it's nothing special, but nothing bad as well. The pixel aesthetic might not be the best pixel art I've seen but it does the job.
Sadly this will not be one of my favourite games ever. Simply because I'm bad at it. Not a big fan of a rhythm based part of it. Moving only on the beat seams a bit limiting and while the combat is quite enjoyable I was more often failing at it than not. In the end didn't feel interested enough to persevere longer than the first layer of dungeon.
I do however suggest checking it out. This game does perfectly what it sets out to do and its unique enough to surprise you. It will not be a game for everybody.

Definitely an experience those who like indie rogue-likes can't miss. Your fingers will dance to the beat and test your ability to think quickly but act at a constant rate. Only the arrow keys are required to play the game, but you are able to set ability keys to make life easier if you like.
Multiple characters to play as and each has a special quirk that you need to work with. The monk will instantaneously die if he breaks his vow of poverty - by picking up even a single coin. The miner has no weapons, but an infinite supply of bombs that he can set and kick at enemies - but his own bombs can still kill him. 'Bolt' has to move twice for every beat, essentially doubling the speed of the game - you now have to think and act even faster. Nine characters with nine different quirks, and a tenth character that has /all/ of the quirks together. Talk about difficult!
Mod support is great; the devs happily allow you to upload your own music to play the game with (which, yes, can both make the game much easier, or way harder) from within the game. Also within the game is a level editor. I strongly suggest using the soundtrack from Hotline Miami. Otherwise, you can both make and download new characters with different quirks, reskins of current characters and mod new items/themes into the game. All of which has steam workshop support, making it so you never really run out of new things to try - provided you enjoyed the base game enough.

Stellaris reminds me of games like Distant Worlds or Sins of a Solar Empire, if you like those games then you'll probably enjoy this as well. Though keep in mind, the end game is doubtlessly lacking in multiple respects.
+The scale of the two largest map sizes is impressive.
+Good empire customization, though some combinations could use a bit of balancing.
+Avaliable tech is semi-random (with specific limitations), meaning there isn't always the same optimal path for every stage of the game.
+A single playthrough will take a significant amount of time, a supurb time sink. (could also be a negative for some)
+Crusading Space Mushrooms!
However the game isn't without it's issues.
-Late game performance with 800 stars could be better.
-The AI could use some work with sensible building choices, I'm referring to sector AI in particular. If CPU usage is a concern maybe one solution could be to limit resource allocation once you reach a certain number of planets/sectors, as it's honestly more of a relevant problem in the early/mid game as opposed to later on.
-The victory conditions leave something to be desired. I honestly can't decide whether the problem is a lack of variety in the victories, or the idea that they exist at all. Regardless, I really feel like it should be more fleshed out overall, in one direction or another.
-The diplomacy could use some work, during my last game the only way I could aquire allies was by creating vassals. Nothing like forced friends!
Stellaris is quite a good game, if a bit short on content. I enjoy the game, and I'd also recommend it. If you're concerned then wait for some patches and the inevitable dlc, see how the game develops.

My first reaction to this game was: this game can only be valuable for nostalgia/historical factor, and I can't honestly recommend it to anyone else. But then I played it a little more, and it got me thinking.
This game faithfully recreates the gameplay of 80s arcade racers with all the important details, but with more modern visuals. The visuals are not mind blowing, but they look pleasant and are not dull.
The gameplay doesn't have a lot of variety, unfortunately, even compared to the 80s racers. There's only one vehicle you can choose, one type of "enemies", no unexpected nasties like an oil spill and such, and the track variety is pretty much limited to the visual theme. The tracks are handcrafted though and are nicely tuned in terms of the difficulty curve and the challenge.
So the gameplay is pretty bare bones and is intentionally archaic, and the natural question arises: can the 80s racer gameplay be engaging/compelling in %the_current_year? I've never played these games at the arcades, but I have played this kind on an NES, and I did enjoy it. Granted, those were among my first ever games. Even the mere fact of me controlling pictures on the screen was exciting.
I did enjoy playing this game, and a big part of it is nostalgia factor, but I have my reasons to believe that there's more than that. The design sensibilities of that era were defined by 2 factors: technology and the business model of the arcades. By the latter I mean those games were designed to get quarters out of people with the ruthlessness of a crack dealer. Those games were hard, because they didn't want you to get too much for your coin. That kind of difficulty is characterized today as "punishing difficulty" or "NES-level difficulty". But you also could always get better and beat the challenges you couldn't before. Those games wanted you to get back for more, after all. They were also bright, snappy, simple to understand, hard to master and as addictive as an experience served in small chunks can get. Sinister, evil games they were. Not like todays games relying on DLCs, microtransactions and hype. I am being sarcastic of course.
These sensibilities are mostly forgotten nowadays, and it is one reason why you may be interested in this game, to see how they games were "back in the day" without having to deal with 80s graphics. But they also made games fun and enjoyable. That's the only way games could get money at the time.
While I cannot recommend this game wholeheartedly, the gameplay is archaic and doesn't have a lot of variety, I do believe that the game at least deserves a try.

is one of my very favorite games of all time.  I thought it was only fair to begin with that, and now I'll explain why I feel that way!  First, this game is a story-driven 2-D action platformer.  This means there is a fair amount of jumping and timing involved, and a lot of fighting.  A great deal of care and art went into the crafting of this extraordinary title, and I will now proceed to list what sets it apart from the norm.
// Art - Music - Visual Concept //
As the title says, this section will discuss the creative concepts of the game, the art.  The art is breathtaking!  The characters sprites are well-animated, the portraits they use to talk are well-rendered and offer a variety of expressions ranging through their various emotional states.  The backgrounds in the stages are beautiful and often surreal with their fluffy and warm imagery, while others are morbid and quite spooky.  The enemies are surprisingly well done, and evoke an emotional response of mild disgust (e.g. They look barbed and rocky and slimy and the like).  The music is a sublime score that never fails to meet the occasion by offering immersion and creating the mood for a particular fight, or a jaunt through a spooky haunted house, or warm soothing tones for having reached a safe place and met new people!
The visual concept disturbs some people and takes a little while to get used to, if one hasn't seen many anthropomorphized animals before.  Every character in the game, as far as I am aware, is an animal in human form.  Dust himself is some type of white fox, I believe.  His companion, Fidget, is a flying red fox.  This adds a certain fantasy flare and otherworldliness to the entire game's setting.  Others may criticize the motif, but I find it refreshingly child-like and innocent.
// Voice Acting and Story //
Every line of dialogue in this game is fully voice acted, and it is all superb!  Some may express a deep resentment and critique for the voice of Fidget, which is quite childlike with a heavy lean towards sillyness, but I find it entirely appropriate and amusing for the character!  Dust is a compassionate hero with a dark past, and his voice matches accordingly.   Ahrah, your talking sword, is a deep and wise sagely type, who tells you all of what he knows while being ever prescient about future events.  The villagers are appropriately frightened, grateful, and emotional when the situation calls for it.  Scenes are quite emotionally touching.  Add to this the well-designed portraits, which have basic animations, nothing fancy, and you get the qualitative effect of a good book or radio program.   Very moving, if you let your imagination run even a little free.
As to the story at large, I don't want to give anything detailed away.  At the very beginning, Dust awakens with amnesia.  This sets the tone for the rest of game.  Who is he? What was he like? Where can he find the answers he seeks? Who are his friends, and who are his enemies? Will he ever know the truth about his past? This allows the player a greater deal of immersion into feeling as though they are the hero, Dust.  Dust has no strong past at first to define him, so the character can place their own persona in his.  As his story develops, one finds that his past is quite complicated.  It leads to emotional revelations and has a deep and meaningful affect on the player, in my opinion.  A good game knows not only how to provide a story, but how to immerse the player within that story.  That you feel you are there, that is important.
// Graphics //
2-D isn't exactly new, I know.  But Dust: An Elysian Tail does it with style!  The sprites are animated, the edges are smooth, the effects of spells are spectacularly specular, with good lighting effects!  The weather and lightning add immersion, there appears to be a very low PC requirement overall, and this game runs smooth as sherbert on my very antiquated computer.
// Gameplay //
This one is the most important to many.  How does it play?  Like you wield an arcane blade of martial knowledge that imbues you with the power of a hundred champions before you!  The combos are rather simple and easy to pick up.  There are two main attacks for Dust, and one for Fidget.  The primary attack has a simple combo, and the secondary attack can be added to mix it up.  X, X, X, X is simple and effective, with a knock-back at the end that clears the enemies in front of you, giving you breathing room.  X, X, Y, Y is a straight-forward smash and grab, you beat them a bit, then run forward, and suplex an enemy, effectively attacking and knocking back any that are behind you.  X, Y launches the attacked enemy into that air, where follow up combos are endless.  Holding Y causes your blade to spin, which is an infinite combo in itself, save that it will cause you to heat up and eventually hurt yourself if you use it for very long periods.  One can also jump and use the blade spin, causing them to essentially fly in an arc, or towards the nearest enemy.  This allows them to stay in the air indefinitely, and literally shoot upwards into the sky if there are enemies nearby.  Aerial combat in this game is probably the best I've seen in
action platformer.  It's easy to mess up and fall, but with the right training, it's much easier to stay in the air and endlessly attack all of your enemies.  Ground targets jumped into your path? Press X, Y and you'll attack, then grab, and body slam them into the ground, knocking back, and shooting upwards, other enemies.  Allowing you to essentially always be in the air attacking, avoiding the ground completely if you wish.
This brings us to Fidget.  Fidget's attacks are magical, she learns several spells as the game unfolds.  When she casts a spell, it is a joke, a lackluster affair, and it has no range at all.  However, if you use your blade spin while she casts an attack, it multiples the number of projectiles, and their strength, and becomes an AoE slugfest of doom for all of your enemies.  I play this game on Hardcore, and Fidget is the path to victory.  Her attacks deplete your 'Energy' meter, but this refills quite easily in a matter of mere seconds by slashing a few enemies inbetween spells.
What this effectively works out to is this, you can fly through the air spitting pillars of fire, and endlessly launching enemies and decimating them to refill your meter.  The game's enemies are smart enough that they will attempt to jump behind your current facing direction, and will attempt to time attacks for when you land and when you are most vulnerable, at the cooldown on your combos.
Add to this that there is a right and left dash that completely evade attacks, while using a modest amount of energy, and a parry system that allows you to daze and counterattack almost any opponent (this is actually almost essential for the stronger opponents) and you arrive at a game that puts many others to shame with the sheer fun of its combat!
The game also incorporates an inventory and equipment system.  You find items that aid in your base attributes, and offer some limited special abilities, like light radius around Dust for those dank, dark caverns!
// Mood - Immersion //
One of the most important elements in any game, to me; this game succeeds in all categories.   From the art, to the music, to the voice acting, to the combat, to the scenery.   You will travel from high-reaching statues of a bygone age of greatness standing like monoliths over grassy knolls and mountainsides, to dark and forboding swamps that seem quite full of danger, to haunted houses in sorrowful, barren, spooky and dark environs.   From snow to rain and back again.  Also, my personal favorite, caverns!  You will spend a considerable amount of the game in the underworld!  These caverns, in my humble opinion, are simply beautiful!
In conclusion. Buy this!

This is a very mixed bag.   First of all I recommend purchasing this release purely for the fact it is available legally, and will run without any major issues,  no hacks/mods/patches etc needed.
However,  I feel like the quality of this release is sub-par, compared even to the FF7 release.   FF8 was made for the PC -after- the technical failure that was the Final Fantasy VII PC version.  One of its features was higher resolution Full Motion Videos, and it did indeed deliver on this.   But I don't ever remember them looking as bad as they do in this release.   Whereas the  FF7 videos scaled up to 720p surprisingly well for their age.    Also some videos have very clearly show deinterlacing artifacts, which is puzzling  for something that should have been progressive from the start.      Not only did they do some kind of deinterlacing on some (or all?) parts of some videos,  but they did a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job, using cheap blend deinterlacing which can clearly be seen in some scenes.
I was secondly unimpressed with the background art.   Now we know in FF7,  they were rendered in low-res and the artwork was lost or unavailable to render again at that that point in time;   did they truly make the same mistake again with FF8?    I don't have the original PC version to compare with, so I don't know.   But  some of the background art arguably looks worse than even FF7 did in some areas.   At best it looks about the same;  a pixelated mess.
The most offensive act however, is one again, the MUSIC.   Square got blasted for the crappy MIDI renders they released with FF7 both originally,  and then again just recently.   They had the audacity to include the audio in OGG format;  audio of  rendered MIDI.   The finally got a clue and just recently patched the REAL  Playstation Soundtrack back into the game.
So why the hell did they not do the same for FF8?   OK it clearly appears to use a slightly more non-standard  format for its MIDI music (and that's what it is.... General MIDI) but could they seriously  NOT  patch in the  OGG support like they did for FF7?   Could they not have applied fan-made  PSF hacks and included the original Playstation Music Files  and instrument samples?
That is just a glaring slap in the face.   But I suppose we should be grateful that they released it on Steam from the start this time,  instead of lying to customers  that it would only ever be in the Square-Enix store, like they did with FF7.....
One other minor annoyances is they appears to have changed the Overture.   The sequence of images is not only ugly and grainy (like the original PC release) but they appear to have changed the sequence and omitted one or two images, throwing off the timing,  so you are sitting at the white FF8 Logo/Title  while the Overture actually finishes.

I know that this is an older game of the most beloved or hated game of the franchise of all time, this is probably this is the only  Call of Duty game I can review since most of the Call of Duty games I have are on console. While Black Ops is not the series' best entry (although for some reason people call it the best game ever for some reason), it's still an enjoyable experience with Treyarch's attempt at improving the single player campaign and the world famous multiplayer.
Single player campaign has you put in the shoes of Alex Mason, a soldier who is being interrogated for  a plot that he himself isn't familiar with, and throughout the game you recap Mason's past assignments leading up to the conclusion. Typical Call of Duty gameplay is to be expected in the campaign: Find two guns that work for you, go from point A to B, gun down enemies, occasional QTE's and the Michael Bay   flare that you would expect from a Call of Duty single player campaign. In all honesty, I believe that Treyarch does a better job at presenting their narrative than Infinity Ward does with the recent entries in the Call of  Duty franchise (...modern warfare 3). There are characters that you will care about in this game, admitting that most of these characters are stereotypes at least you care for them in some way. Replay Value isn't much, unless you're an achievement hunter who needs those acheivements.
Now Call of Duty isn't all about the singleplayer campaign, it's all about the multiplayer. This is your standard Call of Duty multiplayer that you would expect: simple to pick up, twitch trigger fingers, killstreaks, progression and customization options are all here. While the multiplayer is all fun; if it is your first time experiencing the madness of Call of Duty, to all of you regulars out there, nothing much has changed. While gameplay remains the same there is one system in Black Ops specifically that players will either love or hate: COD points. Basically instead of leveling up with experience in order in earn weapons in the game, you now have to purchase them with COD points as you level up. The change really bothered me as I found the annoyance of having to grind points in order to get the customized options or perks that I need to play online, so the shift I didn't enjoy all that well.
Is Call of Duty: Black Ops a bad game? As much as I despise the Call of Duty franchise, it's not a bad game, it is actually pretty okay. However does that justify the lack of improvements made to the game each year? No it doesn't! I feel that Call of Duty has now become part of the EA sports franchises' dilemma: slightly improved textures, a slightly improved gameplay mechanic, a slighty improved online features and all that released annually (altough Call of Duty improves more than any other EA sports franchise out there). I will recommend Call of Duty: Black Ops to anyone new to the franchise, while series loyalists may be disappointed with the outcome of the game, it is still one of the better Call of Duty games out there.
Final Score: 7/10 (Good)

I picked up this game quite eagerly after missing out on FF8 on the PS1. Sadly I was incredibly dissapointed in the poor job Square Enix had done in porting the game to Steam.
First problem, I had to navigate a menu that after refusing my Facebook account, forced me to sign up to Square Enix's website. A pain, but a minor one I would have forgotten.
Second problem, which damns the game and makes it unplayable, the sound. This appears petty, but the lack of the PS1 soundtrack, one of the games defining features, is lost with the MIDI versions which seriously takes away from the games atmosphere. This is especially damning when you consider how dated the games graphics are, which whilst not a problem on its own, the poor sound artifically ages the game and damages the experience. FF7 received a number of Mods and even an offical patch to fix the sound problem alone, I'd say its worth holding out for one of these until you buy.
It is a shame really, as the core gameplay is fantastic, the depth of the RPG mechanics still intact and there is a lot to pick apart in the story, though the lack of a good soundtrack (Which hopefully will be improved in the coming weeks) really does lessen the quality of the package. Hold off buying this until Square Enix or some modder updates the soundtrack, at which point I would actually recommend picking this up.

Wow!  There is not a better value on Steam.  If you grew up on the old Sierra adventure games like Quest for Glory, King's Quest, Police Quest, Conquests of the Longbow, or Space Quest, then you can easily spend 30+ hours playing this game.  I've not even completed the game once, yet, and I'm having a blast.  This is truly a spiritual successor to the Quest for Glory series, unlike Quest for Glory V.  Think of this game as the Quest for Glory V that should have been.  I'll give an explanation as to what I mean.
If you played QFG3 and QFG4 (or the VGA remakes of QFG1 and QFG2), then you're familiar with the QFG format.  It's a point and click adventure game with an RPG style of character development.  You get a character sheet in the beginning and spend some "free points" in different skills and attributes.  Then, you're dropped in the world to quest.  As you use skills, they level up.  All of the QFG games followed this format, but QFG5 changed the interface in a major way.  It was the first "3D" QFG game.  The character could be controlled with a turret-style control scheme, and combat wasn't compartmentalized the way it had been before.  So, the game felt very clumsy overall and didn't have the same feeling as the previous four titles.  This game brings everything about the QFG style of game right back where it belongs.
The game starts by having you select one of three classes, just like QFG.  The classes are essentially the same as the Fighter, Magic User, and Thief from QFG.  There isn't a Paladin class in this series, but there is an honor mechanic which could possibly imply a Paladin class in a sequel (PRETTY PLEASE LET THERE BE A SEQUEL!!!).  You then are able to distribute 50 points across your character sheet.  Your character will solve in-game problems in different ways based on your skills.  A Warrior might ram a door down.  A Rogue may pick the lock.  A Wizard may blast it or cast an Open spell.  And, these might not be the only options depending on the exact situation.  Maybe you just knock and trick the guy on the other side to open it so you can club him on the head.  There are skills for all of these actions, so you need to pay attention to your skill set when you make your character.
Once the game starts, you find yourself in a harsh, winter environment.  You're broke.  You have 15 coins, and a decent meal at another nearby town costs 8 coins.  You can't stay outside too long without freezing to death, and the weather is constantly sapping your stamina.  Along the way, you'll find ways to secure food and battle the cold, but life is hard at first.  You also don't have your equipment.  You have your weapon and some basic items, but you will be missing your gear pack due to the opening events of the game.  You'll meet the townsfolk, find ways to feed yourself, pick up quests, and get some leads on where to find your gear.  From there, it's up to you, really.  You could choose to immediately start doing quests to get some income and items.  You could opt to hunt monsters and train up your skills for a few days.  You could try and explore the map first.  The game world is yours.
Part of the beauty of the this game, just like the QFG games, is the humor embedded in every environment.  Something as simple as looking at a tree reveals a pun or some quirky quip.  Character dialogues are laced with references to your favorite Sierra games, phrases like "So, you want to be a Hero?"  Too many jokes to count exist in this game, and part of the replay value is finding them all.  I'm not even to the second map, yet, and I'm still uncovering things to chuckle at just around the two towns.  Occasionally, I smack my forehead, like when I found the gravestone that said, "Here lies Cedric Diggery.  Entered a graveyard alive.  Left dead."
This is truly a gem.  You are doing yourself a disservice if you don't have it in your library.  Download it and play it.  If you're new to the genre, be patient with it for an hour or so.  Not many games follow the same sort of RPG development as these games did, and most aren't as unforgiving.  When games like this one tell you you're tired, you'd better find someplace safe to sleep!  Fail to do so and you'll collapse and die where you're standing and be devoured by the creatures of the night.  Climb a tree without a sufficient enough climb skill and you may just fall out and break your neck.  Take some time to figure it out, and you'll be in for one the most treasured types of gaming experiences in gaming history.  There's a green button up there.  Press it.

This game has such a large following for a reason, it was the game that seemed to break much of the mainstream players into RPGs back in the late 90's. Of course there were earlier Final Fantasy games (and other RPGs like Chrono Trigger) that were amazing, but this one happened to come about when gaming was beginning to become much more widespread, and with the advent of 3-dimensional gaming, this was THE RPG to have on your Playstation. If you've ever wanted to see what all the fuss was about, I say give it a play at least once. Playing this is akin to going back and reading a Classic book just so that you can say that you have had the experience, except that you will probably have a lot more fun with this.
- The story is amazing and has depth to it that you may not expect. Yes it follows that trope of "hero has to save the world" but you may find your characters aren't as all-powerful as you might expect, and the story has an organic feel where your characters actually progress in personality as the story unfolds
- Characters in this game are memorable and all have their own personalities and reasons for joing up. Each character has character progression and you learn more about them as the game goes on. As the game's story unfolds you'll learn more about each character as they come to the forefront.
- The vastness of the world, and the multitude of sights there are to see will make it where you never feel like you're in the same place twice. Each area of the game has its own map layout, its own scenery, and its own vibe. The only time you ever feel like you've been there before is when you get to the snow area.
-The music is some of the most memorable and iconic music of the franchise as well as RPGs in general. There's a reason that this game's OST has been performed by grand orchestras in the past. You'll find yourself humming the tunes to the fights, parades, and Shinra as you go about your day
- The materia system for magic is actually interesting and allows you to combine and play with how the spells behave. Want to make your fire hit every enemy, leech HP, AND cause another effect? Then you can do it. Late game you can pull off some crazy combos by using Mime to mimic the last magics that your previous character cast.
- The graphics did not age too well if this is your first step back into 90's RPGs. It doesn't have the pop and vibrance of sprite-art like from the SNES years, and it doesn't have the polish and wow-factor of recent games. You will see harsh polygons on your character and the backgrounds, however gorgeous, will have some fuzz to them because of poly-count. In battle though the models look a little more polished and rounded off. But for running around, you have block hands and no nose.
- Turn-based battles can become a little tiresome if you're not a fan or not used to having to wait for your character's turn to hit. If this is your 1st step back in RPG time, you may find it bothersome if you're used to real-time combat.
- Late game if you have all the best materia and know how to cheese the materia combos, then every fight becomes a joke. If you can combo the strongest summon spell with the materia that causes it to cast more than once, and then your next character Mimes that cast, then you can cast the strongest spells in the game, over and over and over on each character. Emerald and Ruby WEAPON (hardest optional bosses in the game) as well as the Final boss become trivial if you have this combo set up. On the plus side, you have to put a lot of hours and complete some challenges to get the materia for this combo

This game was tough for me to review. I have a personal reason for liking it , which makes my review biased. Thinking as a general Steam customer I would not recommend it for the full price and the way the game is right now. However , I am recommending this game for the following reasons:
- *Personal Reason* : I played the original Outrun and Super Hang on. If you are a fan of these , than you should definitively get this game. You will probably feel like me: " its good , but it could be great with a few improvements" .
- The content is short for the price, but what is there is good.
- Devs have updated it after release. I tend to support every single game where the devs look hardworking and serious. I hope they keep improving this to the point anyone will be able to recommend!   ( I know, this should be only their obligation , but take a look around Steam and you will realize that unfortunately devs that update games have quickly become a huge plus ). Besides the updates up so far , to me there is a another solid evidence that this game is not intended to be a rip off or quick cash source that is soon abandoned after launch ( which is most of what you get in Steam lately unfortunately ) : the lack of trading cards.
What can be improved:

- Easier gameplay: a couple of bumps and you will run out of time. Since there are leaderboards for those who care to clear the courses with perfect performance, the time limit could be longer to make the game appealing and pleasant to a bigger amount of players.

Update: As predicted previously this game only gets better as more mechanics are fleshed out throughout the game.
While I do have to admit that I have not played the late game as I keep restarting games to optimize my early and mid-game starts. I would like to share my thoughts on Stellaris so far.
It is easily apparent that Paradox have put a lot of work to create a framework that consists of different modules and mechanics, from a development perspective this should allow Paradox to easily add more to the game when it comes to complexity and tuning(not that there are any major issues at the moment).
A lot of people are complaining about mid-game being stale, I do not find this to be the case. Once the mid-game comes along I find myself trying to maximize naval capacity and have a fleet that is nearing that cap, being Militarist I put it to use. Wars are fast and furious, while it is not just about your naval fleet but also paying attention to your defensive and offensive armies. While I do admit that the AI is horrible some folks are already trying to optimize it via the LUA files and with some work from Paradox it is easily fixable more intelligence is added via IF-THEN statements.
In the current state the game plays fantastic, early game is fantastic and you will find yourself addicted to surveying systems to find high resource stations and decent planets and you will shout in glee once you find that 20+ Gaia planet. At normal speed there is plenty of tasks and micromanagement to keep your hands full at every second (day in the game) of every moment. Up the speed to Fast and you will have your hands full.
From a multiplayer aspect there are folks whining about corvette rushes, while this is an issue it is easily fixable by boosting the military power of stations and spaceports so that early corvette rushes get thwarted. I am sure there are others with even better solutions. Other than that MP is fantastic, I have been playing in the Stellaris MP steam group(shameless shoutout) and matches with 12+ players are running smoothly. Having this many players in a game along with 15AI to add some action to the early game gives the galaxy a feeling that it is very alive. The salt,politics and drama in voice chat are satisfying while everybody starts to fight over optimal planets/resources and federations begin to form.
While upkeep costs exist they do not hinder your science output if you keep your energy credits above 0, you can still sim city while being aggressive in the galaxy. Small things like research alternatives give an addictive randomness to the game and you will find yourself swearing at RNGJesus when you don't get that specific tech you needed.
This game is extremely satisfying and provides the excitement and adrenaline that so many other games in the sea of 4x/Grand Strategy do not provide. In the coming months and years I can see this game molding into one of the staples of the genre.
Issues that need to be fixed:
- MP balance issues (corvettes evasion is overpowered, worm hole is superior in relation to other initial FTL tech , Energy weapons generally outclass missles and kinetic weaponry)
- Spaceport , mining bases and early game defense is weak causing early rushes to be a problem
- Peace mechanics can be abused to stop players from joining a federation
- Number of planets does not scale well with science output (2% increase for every planet) , and there is no way to remediate this causing issues for Wide empires.

This game has such a large following for a reason, it was the game that seemed to break much of the mainstream players into RPGs back in the late 90's. Of course there were earlier Final Fantasy games (and other RPGs like Chrono Trigger) that were amazing, but this one happened to come about when gaming was beginning to become much more widespread, and with the advent of 3-dimensional gaming, this was THE RPG to have on your Playstation. If you've ever wanted to see what all the fuss was about, I say give it a play at least once. Playing this is akin to going back and reading a Classic book just so that you can say that you have had the experience, except that you will probably have a lot more fun with this.
- The story is amazing and has depth to it that you may not expect. Yes it follows that trope of "hero has to save the world" but you may find your characters aren't as all-powerful as you might expect, and the story has an organic feel where your characters actually progress in personality as the story unfolds
- Characters in this game are memorable and all have their own personalities and reasons for joing up. Each character has character progression and you learn more about them as the game goes on. As the game's story unfolds you'll learn more about each character as they come to the forefront.
- The vastness of the world, and the multitude of sights there are to see will make it where you never feel like you're in the same place twice. Each area of the game has its own map layout, its own scenery, and its own vibe. The only time you ever feel like you've been there before is when you get to the snow area.
-The music is some of the most memorable and iconic music of the franchise as well as RPGs in general. There's a reason that this game's OST has been performed by grand orchestras in the past. You'll find yourself humming the tunes to the fights, parades, and Shinra as you go about your day
- The materia system for magic is actually interesting and allows you to combine and play with how the spells behave. Want to make your fire hit every enemy, leech HP, AND cause another effect? Then you can do it. Late game you can pull off some crazy combos by using Mime to mimic the last magics that your previous character cast.
- The graphics did not age too well if this is your first step back into 90's RPGs. It doesn't have the pop and vibrance of sprite-art like from the SNES years, and it doesn't have the polish and wow-factor of recent games. You will see harsh polygons on your character and the backgrounds, however gorgeous, will have some fuzz to them because of poly-count. In battle though the models look a little more polished and rounded off. But for running around, you have block hands and no nose.
- Turn-based battles can become a little tiresome if you're not a fan or not used to having to wait for your character's turn to hit. If this is your 1st step back in RPG time, you may find it bothersome if you're used to real-time combat.
- Late game if you have all the best materia and know how to cheese the materia combos, then every fight becomes a joke. If you can combo the strongest summon spell with the materia that causes it to cast more than once, and then your next character Mimes that cast, then you can cast the strongest spells in the game, over and over and over on each character. Emerald and Ruby WEAPON (hardest optional bosses in the game) as well as the Final boss become trivial if you have this combo set up. On the plus side, you have to put a lot of hours and complete some challenges to get the materia for this combo

While there are features of Black Ops that are interesting, all I will ever remember about the game was how horrible it played when it was first released.
My system, at the time, could handle some games I consider more impressive than Black Ops. When I loaded this game, I could not get it to stop lagging and stuttering even with my settings dropped as low as they could go. It did not change the problems even a little bit. These PC issues were widely reported, and for a while the official response was basically, "Your system sucks." This was, of course, refuted by people with monster rigs full of daisy-chained top-end graphics cards, but it still took weeks for patches to make the game playable.
Once I finally did get this running, I encountered what became the hallmark of later Call Of Duty games: Loosely tied together mission where a lot of big set pieces involving you running, fleeing, or watching things collapse dramatically in pre-planned fashion. There's not a great sense of cohesion, and I never cared about the characters. This game broke me of my COD habit thoroughly, because I had a moment where I just asked myself, "Why am I squinting down the barrel at these tiny people trying furiously to kill enough of them?" And the plot indicated that game makers just may be running out of viable threats towards white empires unless they invoke Nazis or Communists.
Here's a crazy idea: How about a non-white conflict? There are non-whites who've been fighting with guns for most of the last century. Sometimes with reasonably fancy guns. Maybe there's a story there somewhere.

This is a mix of the Sierra games of old (Space Quest, King's Quest) with the fighting mechanics of Sid Meier's Pirates & the rpg-level-system of Elder Scrolls (the more you use a specific trait/skill, the more that skill advances).
A typical issue with most of these adventure games is the resorting to trial-&-error need to be clicking-on-everything to progress the story. This is never an issue with the game except for only a couple of situations. This is pretty darned amazing considering the size of the game.
Writing, voice-acting, dialogues & humour are all 1st class. There is clearly a lot of research behind the study of norse folkfore to bolster the story's setting & it really shows. Characters fall into the usual tropes yet the story & story-telling is rich & vibrant with just the right amount of comical references
The puzzles & combat are rewarding & the music feels just right. The game gives you just the right amount of hints without removing the challenge. For the most part the thoughtful game design goes a long way toward making specific problems more easily resolved whilst still offering the possibility for multiple solutions (usually via the class specific's unique skill sets)
The pixel graphics are a nice touch with each sprite, backdrop & portrait boasting talent in abundance. There was never an instance where a small item or set piece had me confused as to what it represented, I only mention this because this used to be an issue with these types of games but I can gladly state that every piece is self-evident & well representative of what it portrays itself to be.
All in all I have played a lot of point n'click adventure games but this one manages to take the best aspects from the genre to make a more open experience that is sure to give the SCUMMy retro fans a fresh experience. I can easily recommend this game to fans of the genre but other gamers may get alienated by the referential humour & frustrated by the graphical throwback nature

Relaxing environmental games seem to be molding it's own little category.  The first experience that did this extremely well was
on the PS3.  In these types of games there isn't really a bad end in the traditional sense of gaming.  You can't die, you can't fail, the puzzles are simple.  It's meant to relax.
With Abzu, I can see someone who doesn't usually pick up a controller really enjoying it if they want something relaxing.  It's a great game to introduce people into gaming as well.  That being said, the story is extremely...muddled.  Any story there is ends up being very unsatisfying.  The controls are tight and well crafted.  Swimming is very fluid and there weren't any bugs that broke the game during the playthrough.
The music deserves a special mention in particular.  The score is very relaxing and at moments hits particularly good notes.  Moving from area to area has special musical symphonies in which the player can often be swept away or brought to a soft calm.  Bravo on the score.
The graphics have a stylized feel to them that really work.  In fact, combined with the music the graphics can really transport you to this underwater world.  The numbers of fish swimming, the swaying seaweed, the crafted artwork of the past peoples....all very well done to bring a singular vision to life.
Regardless, there isn't much depth to the experience.  The atmosphere will carry you or leave you craving a bit more put into the experience.
